He later returned to Afghanistan to teach at Kabul University and met the communist Nur Muhammad Taraki. In 1969 he was the only Khalqist elected to parliament, and from 1973 until the unification of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan in 1977 he was second only to Taraki in its Khalq faction.

On 18 April 1978 the Parchamite ideologue Mir Akbar Khyber was killed, and his funeral became a large demonstration. President Mohammad Daoud Khan arrested party members, and Amin, the main organiser, was one of the last Central Committee members taken, and was held under house arrest. When Taraki's arrest, the agreed signal, became known, Amin ordered the revolution to begin at 9 am on 27 April. With the overwhelming support of the military, the Saur Revolution succeeded, and Daoud, his family and high-ranking loyalists were killed.

Taraki headed the new government, with Amin as foreign minister and a deputy prime minister, and Amin soon became its strongman. Land reforms and other socialist measures provoked armed resistance, and by early 1979 25 of Afghanistan's 28 provinces were unsafe. The Herat uprising began on 29 March 1979. Amin's rivalry with Taraki grew, and on 16 September 1979 he took the posts of head of government, head of state and general secretary of the party. Taraki was later killed.

Amin's government failed to end the revolt, and army desertions continued. He tried to reassure Afghans that the regime was not anti-Islamic by rebuilding mosques and promising freedom of religion, but many Afghans, especially in rural areas, held him responsible for the regime's harshest measures, including thousands of executions. Thousands disappeared. The Soviet Union under Leonid Brezhnev mistrusted him after purges of the Parcham and feared he might turn towards the United States.

On 25 December 1979 Soviet forces crossed the frontier, and on 27 December Soviet operatives killed Amin at the Tajbeg Palace in Operation Storm-333. Babrak Karmal was installed as leader, and the Soviet intervention lasted nine years. The men of Amin's family were executed, and the women, including his daughter, were held in Pul-e-Charkhi prison until released in 1992.
hafsid-dynasty: The Hafsids were a Sunni Muslim dynasty of Berber descent, who also claimed Arab ancestry from the caliph Omar to legitimise their rule. Their name comes from Abu Hafs Umar ibn Yahya al-Hintati, a Berber of the Hintata confederation, a member of the Almohad Council of Ten and a close companion of Ibn Tumart, the founder of the Almohad movement. His son Abu Muhammad Abd al-Wahid governed Ifriqiya from Tunis from 1207 to 1221 for the Almohad caliph, with a considerable degree of autonomy.

As Almohad authority weakened, another Hafsid, Abu Zakariya Yahya, was placed in charge of Ifriqiya in 1228. A year later the caliph al-Ma'mun renounced Almohad doctrine, and Abu Zakariya used this as a pretext to declare his independence. He took the caliphal title Amir al-Mu'minin in 1236 or 1237, annexed Constantine and Béjaïa in 1230, took Algiers in 1235 and welcomed refugees from al-Andalus, some of whom he made officials and soldiers.

Under Abu Zakariya and his successor al-Mustansir, who reigned from 1249 to 1277, the Hafsids prospered from trade with Europe and the Sudan region. Louis IX of France died of dysentery at Carthage in 1270 during the Eighth Crusade. After 1277 internal conflict, aggravated by Aragon, divided the dynasty into an eastern branch at Tunis and a western branch at Béjaïa and Constantine. Abu Yahya Abu Bakr II reunited them from 1318. After his death in 1346 the Marinid ruler Abu al-Hasan conquered Tunis in 1347, and the plague epidemics of the mid-14th century reduced the population further.

Abu al-Abbas Ahmad II took Tunis in 1370 and centralised power, which began the dynasty's height under Abu Faris Abd al-Aziz II, who reigned from 1394 to 1434, and Abu 'Amr 'Uthman, who reigned from 1435 to 1488 and for a time made the whole Maghreb accept Hafsid suzerainty. In the 16th century the Hafsids were caught between Spain and the Ottomans. The Ottomans took Tunis in 1534, Charles V restored the Hafsid ruler as his tributary a year later, and the Ottoman reconquest of Tunis in 1574 ended the dynasty; its last caliph, Muhammad VI, was taken to Constantinople and executed.

The Hafsids encouraged learning and were the first to introduce madrasas to the Maghreb, beginning with the Madrasa al-Shamma῾iyya in Tunis in 1238 or 1249. The Great Mosque of al-Zaytuna became the country's leading centre of learning, and the historian Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in this period. By the mid-14th century Tunis had about 100,000 people. Nearly all of Ifriqiya became fully Arabized. Jews, whose communities had nearly disappeared under the Almohads, recovered under Hafsid tolerance, and Christian merchants and Catalonian mercenaries lived under treaties with European states.
hagakure: Hagakure, also called Hagakure Kikigaki, The Book of the Samurai or the Analects of Nabeshima, is a practical and spiritual guide for a warrior. It is drawn from the commentaries of the clerk Yamamoto Tsunetomo, a former retainer of Nabeshima Mitsushige, the third lord of Saga Domain. Tashiro Tsuramoto compiled the text from his conversations with Tsunetomo between 1709 and 1716, but it was not published until many years afterwards.

The book belongs to a time of peace. After the Tokugawa shogunate suppressed the Shimabara Rebellion in 1638, Japan saw no warfare for about two centuries, and private feuding and dueling between samurai were also suppressed. Tsunetomo was born in 1659, had no combat experience and worked as a scribe. The book reflects the problem samurai faced of keeping a warrior class in the absence of war, and the nostalgia of an old man for a vanished world.

The book records Tsunetomo's views on bushido, the warrior code of the samurai. It is sometimes said to hold that bushido is really the Way of Dying, or living as though one were already dead, so that a samurai must be ready to die at any moment in order to be true to his lord. Some readers take this to mean that bushido is a code of death, but others hold that its true meaning is that by keeping death constantly in mind a person can reach a state of freedom in which it is possible to fulfil perfectly one's calling as a warrior.

Hagakure was largely forgotten for two centuries. The first modern edition appeared in 1900 and drew little attention in the early decades of the century. It came to be seen as a definitive book of the samurai for the armed forces of the Empire of Japan only during the Pacific War. Mark Ravina has written that it serves less as an account of samurai tradition than as an example of what the Japanese army thought soldiers should believe about samurai practice. After the war the nationalist author Yukio Mishima, inspired by the work, wrote a book in praise of it.
haghartsin: Haghartsin is thought to have been founded in the 10th century, although the exact date is unknown; popular etymology derives its name from the Armenian words for moved around and for eagle. The Seljuks almost entirely destroyed the monastery in the 11th century, and from 1184 the Zakarid princes Zakare and Ivane renovated it, adding a žamatun on the western side of the Church of St. Gregory.

After his brother's death in 1213, Ivane left a dedicatory inscription recording that he had built the žamatun and given an orchard in Erewan so that mass would be said perpetually for Zakare. The two brothers chose Haghartsin as their family's burial ground. The 13th-century historian Kirakos Gandzaketsi credits the abbot Khachatur of Taron, a musician, with rebuilding and enlarging the monastery.

The complex has three churches, a gavit and a refectory. St. Astvatsatsin (St. Mary's), of 1281, is the largest building, with a sixteen-faced dome whose arcading makes its drum seem weightless. A relief on its eastern facade shows two men in monks' attire pointing at a model of the church and a dove between them, probably the founders, the Father Superior and his assistant; outside the south door stands a khachkar carved by Poghos. The small St. Stephen's dates from 1244.

The oldest large structure, St. Gregory's, probably of the 10th century, is entered through a 12th-century gavit whose corner sections carry figures of monks with crosses, staffs and birds. Legend holds that a hollow half-column there once opened to hide the monastery's riches in war. Beside it stands a royal sepulchre whose surviving gravestones, one reading King Smbat, are thought to mark kings of the Kiurikian dynasty, or by another view the Bagratuni kings Smbat II and Gagik I.

An important school of church music was located in St. Gregory's Church. The refectory, built by the architect Minas in 1248, is divided by pillars into two square parts roofed with intersecting arches and lined with stone benches, and it is still used for receptions after marriages and baptisms at the monastery. Armenia Fund carried out a major renovation in 2011, and in 2017 the monastery was incorporated into the Transcaucasian Trail.
haghpat-monastery: Haghpat Monastery, also called Haghpatavank, was built between the 10th and 13th centuries. It stands on a fertile promontory in the Javakheti Range, partway up a hillside overlooking the Debed River in the Lori region. The site was chosen to give protection and concealment while remaining inconspicuous, and the monastery is surrounded by many hamlets. Sanahin Monastery nearby was built around the same time.

The largest church, the Cathedral of Surb Nshan, was probably begun in 967-976 by Queen Khosrovanuysh and was completed in 991 by King Smbat II. It is a typical example of tenth-century Armenian architecture: its central dome rests on four large pillars of the lateral walls, and the outer walls are dotted with triangular recesses.

A fresco in the apse shows Christ Pantocrator. Its donor, the Armenian Prince Khutulukhaga, is depicted in the south transept, and the founder's sons, Princes Smbat and Kurike, appear with Queen Khosravanuysh in a bas-relief on the east gable.

Further buildings followed over the centuries. The small domed Church of Sourb Grigor dates from 1005. Two side chapels were added to the original church, the larger at the beginning of the 13th century and the smaller, known as the Hamazasp House, in 1257. A three-storey free-standing belltower was built in 1245. Other additions of the 13th century include the chapel of Sourb Astvatsatsin, a library and scriptorium, later converted into a storeroom, and a large refectory outside the monastery limits. Khachkars, or cross-stones, of the 11th to 13th centuries stand in the grounds; the best known is the Amenaprkich, or All-Savior, khachkar, which has stood since 1273.

In 1260 Prosh Khaghbakian led Georgian and Armenian forces with his Zakarid suzerains Avag and Shahnshah to support the smaller Mongol force of Hulegu at the siege of Mayyafariqin. When the city was captured after a siege of two years, the Muslims were massacred and the Christians spared. Christian relics were brought back to Armenia, many to Haghpat, which received the hand of the Apostle Bartholomew.

The monastery has been damaged many times. An earthquake around 1130 destroyed parts of it, and it was not restored for fifty years. It was attacked by armed forces over the centuries and damaged by another earthquake in 1988, yet much of the complex stands without substantial alteration. In 1996 UNESCO placed Haghpat and Sanahin on the World Heritage List, describing them as a masterpiece of religious architecture and a major centre of learning in the Middle Ages, the highest flowering of Armenian religious architecture, which blended Byzantine ecclesiastical and Caucasian vernacular styles.
hagia-sophia: Justinian's building was the third church on the site. The first, known as the Magna Ecclesia, or Great Church, because of its size, was consecrated on 15 February 360 under the emperor Constantius II. A second church, ordered by Theodosius II, was inaugurated on 10 October 415. It was destroyed, and on 23 February 532, only a few weeks later, Justinian began a third and entirely different basilica, larger and more majestic than its predecessors. He appointed two architects to design it, the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the geometer and engineer Isidore of Miletus.

The dome is carried on four spherical triangular pendentives, making the building one of the first large-scale uses of that element. It was the largest pendentive dome in the world until St Peter's Basilica, and its height is much lower than that of any other dome of such a diameter. After the vault first collapsed, the dome was rebuilt in 558. The church stayed the largest in the world for more than five hundred years, until the abbey church at Cluny was completed in the 12th century. The horseshoe-shaped upper gallery was reserved for the empress and her court. The Imperial Gate was originally used only by the emperor.

Under Justinian the interior had abstract designs on marble slabs and mosaics on the vaults, with a few figurative decorations. Figurative mosaics added later were destroyed during the iconoclastic controversy of 726–843, and the surviving mosaics are post-iconoclastic. The minarets are Ottoman additions, and the two western ones, by Selim II and designed by Mimar Sinan, are 60 metres high. Sinan also directed the building of buttresses, and 24 were added in all.

For nearly a thousand years Hagia Sophia was the religious centre of the Eastern Orthodox Church. In 1054 the envoy of Pope Leo IX, Humbert of Silva Candida, delivered the excommunication of Patriarch Michael I Cerularius there, an act considered the start of the East–West Schism. In 1204, during the Fourth Crusade, it became a Catholic cathedral under the Latin Empire, and it was restored to the Orthodox Church in 1261. Enrico Dandolo, the doge of Venice who led the Crusade, was buried in the church.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire on 29 May 1453, Mehmed II performed the Friday prayer there and ordered its conversion to a mosque. It was the principal mosque of Istanbul until the Sultan Ahmed Mosque was built in 1616. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk made it a museum in 1935, and in 2020 it was reclassified as a mosque. Its style became the model for Eastern Orthodox church architecture and was emulated by Ottoman mosques, including the Şehzade Mosque and the Süleymaniye Mosque.
haifa: Haifa lies on the Israeli Mediterranean coastal plain, at the mouth of the Kishon River and on the northern slopes of Mount Carmel around Haifa Bay. The city is split over three tiers: the lowest holds commerce, industry and the port, the middle level the older residential districts, and the upper level modern neighbourhoods. It is about 90 km north of Tel Aviv. The origin of its name is unclear; proposals include the high priest Caiaphas, a Hebrew root meaning to cover or shield, and the Hebrew words for 'beautiful shore'.

The earliest known settlement nearby was Tell Abu Hawam, a port and fishing village founded in the Late Bronze Age, in the fourteenth century BCE. Haifa is first mentioned in Talmudic literature about the third century CE, as a Jewish fishing village whose fishermen caught murex snails for purple dye. After the Arab conquest of the Levant it was overshadowed by the port of Akka.

Shortly after the First Crusade the crusaders took Haifa after a fierce battle with its Jewish inhabitants and Fatimid garrison, and it became a small fortified stronghold in the Principality of Galilee. Saladin's army captured it in July 1187 after the Battle of Hattin, and the crusaders under Richard the Lionheart retook it in 1191. In the 1760s the old settlement was moved 2.5 km east as a fortified town, today the Old City.

British forces captured Haifa in September 1918. Its population was 98 percent Arab in 1872, and Jewish immigration from 1881 changed the balance, so that by 1945 it was 55 percent Jewish and 45 percent Arab. During and after the Battle of Haifa in the 1948 war most of the Arab population fled or was expelled, and the Old City was later demolished.

Haifa is the third-largest city in Israel, with 297,082 inhabitants in 2024. The Baháʼí World Centre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a destination for Baháʼí pilgrimage, stands there. The city has a major seaport, the Technion and the University of Haifa, and the Carmelit underground railway. About ten percent of the population is Arab.
haigerloch: Haigerloch lies in the north-western part of the Swabian Alb, at between 430 and 550 metres above sea level, in the valley of the Eyach. The river forms two loops in a steep limestone valley, and the town is therefore also called the Felsenstädtchen, the rocky small town. It has nine districts, among them Bad Imnau, Gruol, Owingen and Weildorf. Around 1700 the physician Samuel Caspar discovered several small pools of mineral water in the valley, and in 1733 the Prince's Spring was uncovered and named after Prince Josef Friedrich of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen.

Haigerloch is first documented in 1095, on the occasion of a gift of the local castle, probably in the area of the Upper Town. By 1200 the Counts of Hohenberg appeared as local lords and built a new castle on the Schlossberg, and the lower town developed into a market town. Rudolf I awarded it a town charter before 1231. A battle between Zollern and Hohenberg was fought just outside the town in 1268, and Count Eberhard I of Württemberg besieged it in 1291 and again in 1347.

From 1356 the upper and lower towns were administered separately, until the lordship of Haigerloch was sold to Austria in 1381; the Habsburgs pawned it on several occasions. Under the Hohenzollern it later became the independent territory of Hohenzollern-Haigerloch within the Holy Roman Empire. The present castle was built on the Schlossberg as the residence of its counts, replacing the high-medieval structure. Haigerloch was the residence of the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen line between 1737 and 1769.

In the last months of the Second World War the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute of Physics, part of the German nuclear programme, was at Haigerloch. Its research reactor was built in a beer cellar beneath the palace church. The pastor's negotiations spared the facility from demolition by an American command on 24 April 1945.

The cellar is now the Atomkeller-Museum, which holds a replica of the reactor. Other sights include the Roman tower of the castle and the former synagogue. Salt has been extracted from the rock salt mine in the Stetten district since 1854.
haiku: Haiku grew out of the opening verse of renga, a long collaborative form of linked poetry, and of its later derivative renku. That opening verse was called hokku, and its position made it the most important, since it set the tone for the whole composition. By the time of Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) the hokku had begun to appear as an independent poem, and it was also used in haibun, a combination of prose and hokku, and in haiga, a combination of painting with hokku. Bashō raised haikai from a playful game of wit to serious poetry. Yosa Buson (1716–1784) was also a master of haiga, and Kobayashi Issa (1763–1827) made the genre accessible to wider audiences. Masaoka Shiki (1867–1902) gave the form its present name.

A traditional Japanese haiku has three phrases of five, seven and five on, the sound units called morae. A word such as haibun counts as four on in Japanese though two syllables in English, so a poem of 17 on may hold only 15 syllables. A kireji, or cutting word, usually ends one of the phrases and acts like a caesura or a sonnet's volta. A kigo, a word implying the season, is drawn from a list called a saijiki. These rules were not absolute: Bashō himself wrote a haiku of 18 on in a 6-7-5 pattern, and some verses lack a kireji. Free-form haiku, advocated by Ogiwara Seisensui and his disciples, give up the 17-on pattern.

Several women learned haiku from Bashō or his disciples in the early 18th century, among them Chiyo-ni. Hendrik Doeff, a Dutch commissioner at Dejima, wrote haiku in the early 19th century, and Paul-Louis Couchoud introduced haiku in France around 1906. They influenced the Imagists, notably Ezra Pound's poem of 1913, In a Station of the Metro. R. H. Blyth's four volumes of 1949–52 introduced haiku to the English-speaking world after the war. The carving of haiku on stone, as monuments called kuhi, has been a custom for many centuries.
haile-selassie: Haile Selassie was born Tafari Makonnen on 23 July 1892 in the village of Ejersa Goro in the province of Hararghe. His father was Ras Makonnen Wolde Mikael, and his mother, Yeshimebet Ali Abba Jifar, was of Oromo and Silte descent. His royal line descended through his paternal grandmother from the Shewan king Sahle Selassie. He became titular governor of Selale in 1906 and was appointed governor of part of Sidamo in 1907. On 3 August 1911 he married Menen Asfaw, and the marriage lasted fifty years.

He rose to power as regent of Empress Zewditu from 1916, after Lij Iyasu, the designated but uncrowned emperor, was deposed on 27 September 1916. In 1924 he toured Europe and the Middle East, chiefly hoping to win Ethiopia access to the sea, which the French Foreign Ministry told him would not be granted.

Tafari became Negus in 1928 and emperor in 1930, taking the name Haile Selassie, which he had received at baptism. He introduced a constitution in 1931 and abolished slavery in 1942. Fascist Italy invaded in 1935, partly to avenge its defeat at Adwa, and the League of Nations failed to protect Ethiopia. He went into exile in the United Kingdom, later travelled to Sudan, and returned after British forces, including Colonel Orde Wingate's Gideon Force, and Ethiopian resistance liberated the country.

After the war Ethiopia became a charter member of the United Nations. On 2 December 1950 the General Assembly's Resolution 390 (V) ceded Eritrea to Ethiopia, and the emperor later dissolved the federation and annexed it as a province. In November 1955 he introduced a revised constitution that made the lower house of parliament elected while he kept effective power. In 1963 he presided over the formation of the Organisation of African Unity and was its first chairman. Critics, among them Human Rights Watch, called his administration autocratic, and some sources say the Oromo language was in practice kept out of education and administration.

In February 1974 riots against inflation in Addis Ababa left five dead, the army mutinied, and strikes and protests followed. The Derg, a military junta, deposed him in 1974. It was revealed in 1994 that the Derg had killed him at the Jubilee Palace on 27 August 1975. His bones were found in 1992 under a concrete slab on the palace grounds, and he was buried on 5 November 2000 at the Holy Trinity Cathedral in Addis Ababa. He belonged to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Among followers of Rastafari, a movement that arose in Jamaica in the 1930s, he is viewed as a messiah, which he did not affirm.
hailu-tekle-haymanot: Hailu was a son of Negus Tekle Haymanot Tessemma of Gojjam, long a vassal kingdom within the Ethiopian Empire. When his father died on 10 January 1901, three of the sons fought over the succession, and Emperor Menelik II instead divided the province into three parts under governors of his own. In 1908 his daughter Sabla Wangel Hailu married Menelik's grandson and heir, Lij Iyasu, and in 1909 he married Assalafetch Wolde Hanna, a cousin of Taytu Betul, the empress.

As ruler of Gojjam, according to the historian Gebru Tareke, Hailu introduced new taxes, auctioned political and church offices, nearly monopolised the province's export trade and enlarged his estates in disregard of customary land allocation, which earned him the nickname birru, or dollars, Hailu. In 1924 he accompanied Ras Tafari Makonnen on his European tour, was given an honorary British knighthood, the KBE, and afterwards remodelled his father's palace at Debre Marqos on European lines.

When Tafari became Emperor Haile Selassie I in 1930, Hailu held on to the customs and tax revenues that other great lords gave up, and the historian Harold Marcus records that he sought favours from the American and British legations, hinting that he could block their access to Lake Tana and the Blue Nile. He was fined heavily and lost half his property in 1932, and after the escape of Lij Iyasu a tribunal convicted him of mendacity, corruption, tax evasion and treason. Ras Imru Haile Selassie replaced him in Gojjam.

On 2 May 1936, leaving for exile, Haile Selassie had Hailu taken from prison on his train, but released him at Dire Dawa; Hailu returned to Addis Ababa and submitted to the Italians, who gave him the Star of Italy and the Order of Saints Maurice and Lazarus. After a failed Ethiopian attack on Addis Ababa in July 1936 he assured two of its commanders, Aberra Kassa and Asfawossen Kassa, that they would not be harmed; they surrendered at Fiche on 21 December, and the Italians executed them.

The Italians returned him to power in Gojjam only at the very end of their occupation. In 1941 he handed Gojjam over to the returning emperor, lived confined to the capital with the dignities of a senior prince, and was given a state funeral on his death in 1950. In the view of Gebru Tareke, his death finished off the provincial ruling elite, which had been grudgingly yielding ground to the centralists since the closing decade of the nineteenth century.
hainan: Hainan consists of Hainan Island and more than 200 smaller islands in the South China Sea. Its name literally means South of the Sea, after its position south of the Qiongzhou Strait, a channel 20 kilometres wide that separates it from the Leizhou Peninsula of Guangdong. The province has a land area of 33,920 square kilometres, almost all of it the island, which is slightly smaller than Taiwan. Wuzhi Mountain, at 1,840 metres, is the highest peak. The climate is mostly tropical, and the island holds over 1,500 square kilometres of tropical forest. Earlier names for the island include Zhuya, Qiongya and Qiongzhou.

Hainan Island was recorded by Chinese officials in 110 BCE, when the Western Han dynasty established a military garrison there after the arrival of General Lu Bode. Over many centuries imperial authorities exiled people condemned as criminals or political dissidents to Hainan and northern Vietnam, where banished people were put to harsh labour in the tropical climate. The Hlai, a Kra-Dai-speaking people, are native to the island.

After 1912 Hainan was organised as the Qiongya Circuit within Guangdong, and in 1920 Sun Yat-sen proposed a Qiongya Special District. The Hainan Special Administrative District was formally established in 1949. On 1 May 1950, under the People's Republic of China, it became an Administrative Region Office, a branch of the Guangdong provincial government. On 13 April 1988 the National People's Congress decided to establish Hainan Province, and Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up programme made it a special economic zone.

The capital is Haikou on the northern coast, and Sanya on the southern coast is a well-known tourist destination. Han Chinese make up 82% of the population and the Hlai 15%. Most people speak Hainanese, a variety of Min Chinese, and most practise Chinese folk religion and Chinese Buddhism.
haiphong: Haiphong lies at the mouth of the Cấm River in the north-eastern coastal area of Vietnam. Its territory covers 3,194.72 square kilometres and includes the islands of Bạch Long Vĩ and Cát Bà and the Long Châu islands in the Gulf of Tonkin. The climate is humid subtropical, with hot, humid summers and warm, dry winters, with most rain between April and October.

Haiphong was the home of Lê Chân, one of the women generals who served the Trưng Sisters in their rising against Chinese rule in 40 CE. The rising lasted until 43 CE. Lê Chân is said to have established the Hải tần Phòng thủ, the Defense of the Coast, in the war against the Han general Ma Yuan.

Under French rule Haiphong ranked as a first-level city equal to Saigon and Hanoi, and in the last years of the nineteenth century the French proposed to make it the economic capital of Indochina. After the defeat of Japan in World War II, Vietnamese nationalists pressed for independence against the French return. French forces landed at Haiphong and met resistance in which three French soldiers died. In retaliation French ships, among them the cruiser Suffren, shelled the city and set it ablaze, an event that precipitated the First Indochina War. French infantry under Jean-Étienne Valluy then entered, fighting house to house with armour and aircraft in support.

In the Vietnam War the city was bombed by United States Navy and Air Force aircraft. Admiral Thomas H. Moorer ordered the mining of the harbour on 8 May 1972, effectively sealing the port. The mining caused no casualties, and the city's buildings were largely unaffected, as the United States had set a prohibited zone around the city. After the war Haiphong recovered its role as an industrial centre.

Haiphong is a major port, the Port of Haiphong standing on the Cấm River, and a centre of shipbuilding, steel and plastic pipes, textiles, cement and food processing. It is the first city in Vietnam and in mainland Southeast Asia to have been electrified. Route 5 leads west to Hanoi and Route 10 south towards Nam Định. A railway built by the French links the city with Hanoi and with Lao Cai on the Chinese border.
hairun: Hairun Jamilu, born about 1522, was a son of Sultan Bayan Sirrullah by a Javanese woman who practised pre-Islamic rites and lived away from the court. The Portuguese had built a fort on Ternate in 1522-1523 with the sultan's approval, and their captains soon dominated the court. In 1535, after Ternatans attacked a village of Christian converts on Halmahera in defiance of them, the Portuguese deposed the young Sultan Tabariji and raised his twelve-year-old half-brother Hairun in his place. His mother resisted the soldiers who came for him, seeing that he would be their puppet, and died in the tumult in a fall from a window.

At first Hairun lived inside the Portuguese fort, and the grandees wanted Tabariji back. Once allowed among his people he built up networks in Ternate, Makian and Moti and took a daughter of Sultan Mir of Tidore as consort. The Portuguese decided in 1544 to exile him and restore Tabariji, who had become a Christian in Goa, but Tabariji died at Melaka on the way; in Goa Hairun was received with honour, reinstated, and returned in 1546. He met the Jesuit Francis Xavier on cordial terms, but grew steadily more Islamic and resentful of Christianity.

He still fought beside the Portuguese against outside enemies. In 1550-1551 their joint forces took the royal seat of Jailolo after a three-month siege, and in 1560 they defeated Tidore at Tolo on Halmahera. After the Portuguese seized the clove harvest of Makian and imprisoned him in 1557, Ternatan chiefs allied with Tidore against them, until he was released on terms; the letter of vassalage he and his son Baab signed is the oldest preserved sealed letter in Indonesia. In the 1560s his fleets aided the Muslims of Hitu on Ambon against the Catholic missions, and attacks he encouraged on Christian settlements cost many lives.

Contemporary Portuguese letters denounced Hairun as a debauched and tyrannical oath-breaker. A reconciliation with the captain Diogo Lopes de Mesquita was arranged in 1570, and on 28 February Mesquita summoned him to the castle, admitted him without his bodyguards, and as he left Mesquita's nephew Martim Afonso Pimentel stabbed him near the gate. His son Babullah led the uprising that followed, and the garrison capitulated in 1575, opening a golden age of Ternate's power. A later account praised Hairun as a wise ruler, a brave warrior and a strong defender of Islam.
haiti: Haiti forms the western three-eighths of Hispaniola, the second-largest island of the Greater Antilles, and shares a border of 360 km with the Dominican Republic. It is the most mountainous country in the Caribbean, with plains covering only 22% of its territory, and the highest point is Pic la Selle at 2,680 m. The name comes from the Taino language and means land of high mountains. It was the native name for the whole island, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines restored it as the official name of independent Saint-Domingue, in tribute to the Amerindian predecessors.

Indigenous peoples have lived on Hispaniola for about 6,000 years. Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taino arrived during the 1st millennium BCE, and at the time of European contact the island was divided among five caciquedoms led by chiefs. Christopher Columbus landed on 6 December 1492 and claimed the island for the Crown of Castile. The 39 men he left behind founded La Navidad but were later killed by the Taino.

European diseases caused epidemics among the native people, the first recorded smallpox epidemic in the Americas breaking out on Hispaniola in 1507, and the encomienda system, which forced natives to work in gold mines and plantations, reduced their numbers further. Spain held the island until 1697, when the western part was ceded to France as Saint-Domingue, a plantation colony worked by enslaved Africans.

The Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804 made Haiti the first sovereign state in the Caribbean and the first country in the Americas to abolish slavery officially. The independent state began as an empire, later split into two and reunited in 1820, and a second empire under Faustin Soulouque ended with the return of the republic in 1859. The 19th century brought instability, international isolation and a crippling debt to France. United States forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, and the Duvalier family ruled as dictators from 1957 to 1986.

Haiti is a republic with Port-au-Prince as its capital and largest city, and about 11 million people, the most in the Caribbean. Its culture blends French and African customs with Spanish and Indigenous influences. The Citadelle Laferrière, built between 1805 and 1820, and the Sans-Souci Palace were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
haitian-creole: Haitian Creole took shape in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, where French colonists lived beside enslaved Africans who spoke various Niger-Congo languages. Its vocabulary comes largely from the French of the eighteenth century, but its grammar follows West African patterns, particularly those of Fongbe and Igbo. Words from Wolof, Fon, Kongo, Spanish, Taino and others also entered it. Often the French definite article stayed attached to the noun: la lune, the moon, became lalin.

In Saint-Domingue people of all classes spoke a Creole French, with lower and higher registers according to education and class, and it served as a lingua franca through the West Indies. The first written text in the French-lexicon creole is said to be a poem, Lisette quitté la plaine, composed in 1757 by Duvivier de la Mahautière, a white Creole planter.

Haitian Creole is not mutually intelligible with standard French. Its grammar is analytical: verbs are not conjugated, tense, mood and aspect are shown by markers placed before the verb, and there is no grammatical gender.  The definite article follows the noun. Many words that look like French have shifted in sense: frekan, from fréquent, means insolent or rude.

Spelling is phonemic and highly regular. The official system, set out by the Institut Pédagogique National, uses 32 symbols and keeps only the grave accent, on è and ò. It built on an orthography devised in 1940 by the Irish Methodist missionaries H. Ormonde McConnell and Primrose McConnell and revised with Frank Laubach. The three main dialects are the Northern, Central and Southern, centred on Cap-Haïtien, Port-au-Prince and Les Cayes.

Its place in schools and public life has been contested since at least the nineteenth century. Some Haitians see French as bound up with colonialism, while Francophones have dismissed Creole as the French of the uneducated. Until the late twentieth century Haitian presidents addressed their fellow citizens only in standard French, and until the twenty-first century elementary teaching was in French, a second language for most pupils. Even so, literary works in Creole existed by the end of the nineteenth century, among them Oswald Durand's Choucoune and Georges Sylvain's Cric? Crac!

The 1987 constitution named Creole and French the official languages and recognised Creole as the only language all Haitians share. It is spoken by more than 13 million people, including large communities in the United States, Canada, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and the Bahamas, and it is the most widely spoken creole language in the world.
haitian-revolution: In 1789 Saint-Domingue produced 60 percent of the world's coffee and 40 percent of the sugar imported by France and Britain, and its largest sugar plantations and concentrations of enslaved people lay in the north. Enslaved people were kept in check by whipping and worse punishments. The Code Noir of 1685, issued to regulate the treatment of the enslaved, was openly and consistently broken. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 26 August 1789 was ambiguous about slaves and colonial citizens. After the revolt of Vincent Ogé in 1790, France granted citizenship to free people of colour in May 1791. White planters refused to comply, fighting between the groups broke out, and on 21 August 1791 the enslaved rose.

When France declared war on Britain in 1793, the grands blancs asked British help, and Britain invaded Saint-Domingue, as did Spain. The French commissioners Sonthonax and Étienne Polverel offered freedom to enslaved people who would fight for them and in 1793 proclaimed abolition in the colony's provinces. On 6 May 1794 Toussaint Louverture turned from the Spanish to the French. The British sent about 30,000 men in 1795 but suffered heavily from disease, and at least three of every five British troops sent between 1791 and 1797 died of it. The British left Port-au-Prince on 18 May 1798, and Toussaint defeated the forces of Rigaud in the War of the South, taking Jacmel on 11 March 1800.

A French expedition arrived at Le Cap on 2 February 1802. Dessalines held the fort of Crête-à-Pierrot for about twenty days before slipping out on 24 March. Toussaint agreed to terms on 6 May 1802, was later seized and shipped to France, and died in prison at Fort-de-Joux. French plans to restore slavery brought a new revolt in the summer of 1802, while yellow fever killed about 10,000 French by mid-July and the commander Leclerc in November. After war between France and Britain resumed on 18 May 1803, the Royal Navy blockaded the colony. On 30 November 1803, 8,000 French soldiers boarded British ships under terms agreed with Dessalines.

On 1 January 1804 Dessalines declared Haiti a free republic. From February until 22 April 1804, on his order, the remaining white colonists were massacred. France recognised independence in 1825 only on condition that Haiti pay an indemnity of 150 million francs to former slaveholders. Estimates of the dead vary: Robert Scheina gave 350,000 Haitians and 50,000 European troops, and the Encyclopedia of African American Politics nearly 200,000 Black people and as many as 100,000 French and British soldiers, with yellow fever the largest cause. Historians such as David Geggus judge the effect on slavery limited, while W. E. B. Du Bois held that it made British abolition easier.
haitian-vodou: Vodou took shape amid the Atlantic slave trade of the 16th to 19th centuries, when the religions of enslaved Kongo, Fon and Yoruba people brought to Hispaniola mixed with the Roman Catholicism and Freemasonry of the French who held the colony of Saint-Domingue; it had taken the form of Vodou by around the mid-18th century. Haitian folklore holds that a Vodou ritual at Bois-Caïman sparked the Haitian Revolution in 1791, though historians debate such claims. After the Revolution the Catholic Church left Haiti for several decades, allowing Vodou to become the country's dominant religion.

The United States occupation of 1915 to 1934 drew outside interest, and Haiti's middle-class indigenist movement came to view Vodou more favourably. In 1941 the government launched Operation Nettoyage, a Church-backed campaign that destroyed many ounfòs, while President François Duvalier later hailed Vodou as "the supreme factor of Haitian unity". Emigration in the 20th century carried the religion abroad.

Vodou teaches the existence of a transcendent creator, Bondye, from the French Bon Dieu, who is remote from human affairs. Below Bondye are the lwa, spirits who usually take their names from West and Central African deities, are equated with Catholic saints and fall into nanchon, or nations, chief among them the Rada and the Petwo. Practitioners, who call themselves sèvitè, those who serve the lwa, seek the aid of the spirits and of the dead with offerings of food, liquor and sacrificed animals.

There is no central authority. Communal worship centres on the ounfò, or temple, run by an oungan or a manbo, a priest or priestess, and initiation typically has four levels. In the nocturnal ceremonies known as the dans, drumming, song and dance invite a lwa to possess a worshipper and speak through them. Drawings called vèvè, traced on the floor in cornmeal or ash, summon the lwa, and divination and herbal healing also play a large part.

Most Haitians practise both Vodou and Catholicism without seeing a contradiction, and several scholars see Haitian religion as a continuum between the two. In 1992 Desmangles put the number of Haitian practitioners at six million. Various scholars describe Vodou as one of the world's most maligned and misunderstood religions: Christians in Haiti have often presented it as Satanic, and films such as White Zombie (1932) have sensationalised it.
hajar-mountains: The Hajar Mountains, also called the Oman Mountains, separate the low coastal plain of Oman from the high desert plateau and lie 50 to 100 km inland from the Gulf of Oman. They run for 700 kilometres and are about 100 km wide, on the north-eastern corner of the Arabian Plate, from the Musandam Peninsula to the east coast of Oman.

Jabal Shams, at 3,009 metres, is the highest peak, in the central section, which is the highest and wildest terrain in Oman. East of the Samail Valley the Eastern Hajar run to the port of Sur. The Western Hajar include the mountains of Musandam, known as Ru'us al-Jibal, Heads of the Mountains, and those of the United Arab Emirates.

The range is the product of several phases of mountain building. In the late Cretaceous the Semail Ophiolite, a slab of oceanic crust, was thrust over the continental rocks of the Arabian margin. A second phase of deformation began in the Eocene, about 45 to 40 million years ago, and the present topography formed after the late Eocene; geologists dispute exactly when, and whether the collision of the Zagros Mountains drove it.

The Semail ophiolite is regarded as the most complete on Earth, with pillow basalt and exposures of the boundary between crust and mantle, and the Wadi Mayh sheath fold is one of the best exposed ever found. Eclogite at As Sifah records rocks carried about 80 km into the mantle and brought back to the surface.

The mountains are rich in plant life compared with most of Arabia and have a number of endemic species. Shrubland at lower elevations gives way to woodland, with wild olive and fig trees, and junipers higher still; pomegranates and apricots are grown in the cooler valleys. Mountain gazelles, the Arabian tahr and several species of gecko and lizard live there.

Domestic goats, camels and donkeys graze extensively, and clearing for towns and mining has damaged vegetation and water supplies. Oman has created the Wadi Sareen Reserve and an area of Jebel Qahwan to protect the Arabian tahr and the mountain gazelle.
hajj: The word ḥajj is similar to the Hebrew ḥag, 'festival', from the same Semitic root; the Hebrew term referred to the three pilgrimage festivals Israelites made to the Temple in Jerusalem each year. The present pattern of Hajj was established by Muhammad, but according to the Quran, elements of it trace back to Abraham. In Islamic tradition Abraham left his wife Hajar and his son Ishmael in the desert of ancient Mecca. Hajar ran seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah looking for water, and a spring then rose beneath Ishmael's foot. Abraham was later commanded to build the Kaaba with Ishmael's help and to invite people to make pilgrimage there. The Quran refers to these events in verses 2:124–127 and 22:27–30.

Hajj is an annual pilgrimage to Mecca and one of the Five Pillars of Islam. It is a once-in-a-lifetime duty for every Muslim who is physically and financially able to make the journey and to support their family during their absence. Its rites are carried out over five to six days, from the 8th to the 12th or 13th of Dhu'l-Hijja, the last month of the Islamic calendar. Because that calendar is lunar, the Gregorian date moves each year, and the season falls twice in one Gregorian year about every 33 years.

The pilgrim enters the sacred state of ihram, wearing unstitched white clothing, and walks seven times counterclockwise around the Kaaba, an act called tawaf, then walks seven times between Safa and Marwah. On 9 Dhu'l-Hijja, the Day of Arafah, pilgrims stand in vigil on the plain of Arafat, about 20 km east of Mecca, from noon until sunset; a pilgrim's Hajj is considered invalid without this. They spend a night at Muzdalifah, and on 10 Dhu'l-Hijja at Mina they throw seven stones at the largest of three pillars representing Satan.

After the sacrifice of an animal, pilgrims shave or trim their hair, and the festival of Eid al-Adha follows. The shorter pilgrimage to Mecca, Umrah, can be made at other times of the year but does not replace the Hajj.
hajo: Hajo stands on the banks of the Brahmaputra River, 25 km north-west of Guwahati, among hills that each carry places of pilgrimage. The name is derived from the Boro word hajw, meaning hill, and the town is also said to be named after Koch Hajo, a Koch tribal chief of the early 16th century. Its inscriptions, temples and monuments span about 1200 years, which makes it one of the important historical and archaeological sites of north-east India.

The oldest relic may be the Hajo pillar, a broken monolith without inscription in the precinct of the Hayagriva Madhava Temple, which locals call the Ashoka pillar. In 1959 Talukder conjectured that it was a Buddhist pillar of about 400 BCE, but the historian D. D. Kosambi noted that he offered no evidence for this, and no stupa or vihara is known at Hajo.

The Hayagriva Madhava Temple on Manikuta hill, dedicated to Vishnu in his part-man, part-horse form, was built in its present form by King Raghudeva Narayan in 1583. Local tradition holds that the first temple was built under the Pala dynasty in the 10th century, and the rows of elephants carved on its plinth are probably that old. The Kedareswara and Kamaleswara temples to Shiva on Madanachal hill date from the Ahom period.

On Garurachal hill stand the tomb of Giyasuddin Aulia and the Poa Mecca mosque, whose Persian inscription records that it was built in 1657 by an Iranian, Lutfullah Shirazi, names the Mughal prince Muhammad Shujauddin, a son of Shah Jahan, and calls the place Shuja'abad. When Spooner visited it in 1912 the brick mosque lay in ruins.

Hajo is a place of pilgrimage for Hindus, Buddhists and Muslims. Many Bhutias from Bhutan came as devotees, holding that the image of Hayagriva Madhava had once been in a monastery in Lhasa. The Doul, Bihu and Janmastami festivals are held at the temple each year, and the town keeps rare tortoises, which Hindus believe to be a form of the Kurma avatar of Vishnu.
hakata: Hakata lies on the eastern side of Fukuoka, on low plains beside the Mikasa River, with Hakata Bay to the north-west. It faces the Genkai-Nada, the channel that divides Japan from Korea, which made it a natural base for the sea trade with the continent. The Naka River separates the old merchant town from the opposite shore, where the castle town of Fukuoka grew. In the early Edo period old Hakata covered no more than a square kilometre, bounded by defensive lines along the Naka River, the Boshu Canal and the Ishido or Mikasa River.

Hakata is one of the oldest cities in Japan. In the Middle Ages it was a base for merchants trading with China and Korea and held Japan's first Chinatown, and Taira no Kiyomori is said to have built the artificial harbour of Sode-no-minato to increase its commerce. The town was burned in many wars, including the Mongol invasions. When Kuroda Nagamasa became lord of Chikuzen Province, most of his samurai lived across the Naka River at Fukusaki, which he renamed Fukuoka after his hometown; he built Fukuoka Castle with stones from the dismantled Tachibana and Najima castles.

Hakata and Fukuoka were merged in 1876, and in 1878 the prefecture named the joint settlement Fukuoka-ku, although Hakata had 25,677 people to Fukuoka's 20,410. In 1889 a vote split evenly between the two names; the city became Fukuoka, but the new railway station was called Hakata Station. An imperial decree of July 1899 opened the port to trade with the United States and the United Kingdom, and in 1972 the ward covering old Hakata was named Hakata-ku.

Hakata-ku holds the Fukuoka Prefectural Office, Hakata Station and Fukuoka Airport. The old Hakata area is still the centre of Hakata ningyō doll making, the town gives its name to Hakata-ori textile, and its festivals include the Hakata Gion Yamakasa in July.
hakka-people: The Hakka are a Han Chinese sub-ethnic group whose settlements are widely dispersed across southern China, and whose language is closely related to Gan, spoken in Jiangxi. Their name, written 客家, means guest families. They are distinguished from other southern Han by their dispersal and their tendency to occupy marginal, hilly land. They are commonly held to have come from the Central Plain in the north and to have arrived in the south much later than other southern Han. Earlier settlers had taken the fertile lowlands, assimilated local peoples and driven others, such as the Tanka, to the coasts and rivers, so the Hakka had to settle poorer territory.

The Hakka identify as Han, and a 2009 genetic study found them principally of Han descent, with a slight skew towards northern Han compared with other southern groups, despite recorded intermarriage with the Yao and the She. The word Hakka is sometimes also used for other southern Han groups on their southward migration, which complicates the historical record.

People of Hakka ancestry formed the mainstay of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, which began at the Hakka village of Jintian in Guiping, Guangxi, under Hong Xiuquan, whose first followers were Hakka peasants. The Cantonese regarded the Hakka as opportunists intruding on their territory, and friction between the groups sometimes turned violent. The Red Turban rebels, mostly of Cantonese ancestry, carried out a genocidal campaign against the Hakka during their revolt of 1854–1856, killing 13 village chiefs and 7,630 others on the way to Heshan and another 1,320 after taking it. The Xiang Army under Zeng Guofan massacred tens of thousands of Hakka in Guanghai, a region of Taishan.

Hakka went overseas in large numbers, chiefly to Malaysia, Taiwan, Singapore, Indonesia and Vietnam, and also to the Americas, the Caribbean, Mauritius and India. The first Hakka reached Australia in the 1880s and Tahiti in 1865. In Taiwan they are the second-largest ethnic group, descended largely from migrants from Guangdong and western Fujian who were the island's first agriculturalists.

Poor hill land shaped Hakka culture, and many men turned to military or public careers. Hakka women did not bind their feet and are known for taking on hard work that other groups reserved for men, perhaps from necessity. The Hakka hold Confucian values such as respect for family, ancestor veneration and learning. They built tulou, fortified earth buildings, in Fujian, Jiangxi and Guangdong, and a representative sample of ten Fujian tulou was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008. Their cuisine uses preserved meats and tofu and stewed and braised dishes, and their hill songs carry across valleys.
hakodate: Hakodate stands at the centre of the Kameda Peninsula in southern Hokkaido and is overlooked by Mount Hakodate. The region was originally populated by the Ainu, and the name Hakodate may derive from an Ainu word, hak-casi, meaning shallow fort.

Hakodate was founded in 1454, when Kono Kaganokami Masamichi built a large manor house in the fishing village of Usukeshi. His son Kono Suemichi was driven out into Kameda during an Ainu rebellion in 1512. In 1741 the Matsumae clan moved its Kameda magistracy to Masamichi's house in Hakodate. The Tokugawa shogunate took direct control of the town in 1779, which brought rapid development under the merchant Takadaya Kahei, honoured as the founder of its port. The Matsumae clan was restored to full power in 1821.

Under the Convention of Kanagawa, negotiated by Commodore Matthew C. Perry, Hakodate became in 1854 the first Japanese port opened to foreign trade, and it was fully opened on 2 June 1859 as one of five open ports of the 1858 Treaty of Amity and Commerce signed with the United States. From the Russian consulate Nicholas of Japan is credited with introducing Eastern Orthodox Christianity to Japan in 1861.

Hakodate was central to the Boshin War. The shogunate rebel Enomoto Takeaki fled there in the winter of 1868 with the remnants of his navy and a handful of French advisers, and they proclaimed the Republic of Ezo on 25 December. It failed to win international recognition. The rebels held the European-style Goryōkaku fort, and the naval Battle of Hakodate, fought from 4 to 10 May 1869, was a decisive victory for the Imperial Japanese Navy. Government forces defeated the secessionists and the fort and city were surrendered.

Hakodate is a port city in Oshima Subprefecture, Hokkaido, and the third largest in the island. It was the biggest city in Hokkaido until a fire on 21 March 1934 destroyed about two thirds of its buildings. The former Goryōkaku fort is now a public park, popular for cherry blossom viewing, and the foreign settlement, Orthodox church and other missionary churches are legacies of the port's opening.
hakon-grjotgardsson: Håkon Grjotgardsson, in Old Norse Hákon Grjótgarðsson, was the son and heir of Grjotgard Herlaugsson Lade, whom he succeeded as ruler of the petty kingdom of Trøndelag. He was known by the nicknames Håkon the Rich and Håkon the Old. His residence was at Ørlandet, at the mouth of the Trondheimsfjord, although the exact extent of his control over the area is not confirmed. He sought to extend his kingdom southwards.

Harald Fairhair advanced across the mountains of Eastern Norway to subjugate Trøndelag. After some fighting, Håkon and Harald entered a union of joint forces, and Håkon took up residence in the area of Lade gaard in Trondheim. His daughter Åsa married Harald and became the mother of Guttorm Haraldsson and Halfdan Haraldsson.

After Harald conquered Møre and Fjordane, he gave the governance of Møre to Rognvald Eysteinsson and that of Fjordane to Håkon, while Atle Mjove continued to govern Sogn. Håkon and Atle Mjove soon came into conflict over Sogn, and the dispute was settled by force of arms.

The quarrel over Sogn led to the Battle of Fjaler, in which Håkon was killed. Atle Mjove was severely wounded in the same battle and was taken to Atløy, where he also died. Håkon's son Sigurd Håkonsson was the father of Haakon Sigurdsson, and his daughter's marriage tied his family to the royal house.

Almost everything known of Håkon comes from a single source, Harald Haarfagres saga, composed by Snorre Sturlasson, so his career is known only as the saga tells it. Modern accounts of him appear in general histories of Norway and of the Viking world, such as Viking Empires by Angelo Forte, Richard Oram and Frederik Pedersen.
hakon-sigurdsson: Haakon Sigurdsson was the son of Sigurd Haakonsson, Jarl of Lade and ruler of Trøndelag and Hålogaland, and of Bergljot Toresdatter, daughter of Thorir Rögnvaldarson, Jarl of Møre. Adam of Bremen wrote that he was of the stock of Ivar and descended from a race of giants, while in the sagas Haakon claimed descent from Sæming, a son of Odin. He became jarl after his father was killed in 961 by the men of King Harald Greycloak. Haakon warred with Harald for some time, until he was forced to flee to Denmark, where he conspired with Harald Bluetooth against Harald Greycloak.

Harald Bluetooth and Haakon arranged the death of Harald Greycloak around 971, after which Harald Bluetooth invited his foster-son to be invested with new Danish fiefs. A civil war followed between Haakon and the surviving brothers of Harald Greycloak, and Haakon won it. He recognised the overlordship of Harald Bluetooth and around 973 to 974 went to Denmark to help him defend against the Holy Roman Emperor Otto II. Otto's forces successfully opposed Harald's attempt to throw off German rule, and after that Haakon paid no taxes to Denmark.

Haakon was a strong believer in the old Norse gods, even after Harald Bluetooth forced him to accept baptism around 975 and gave him clergymen to take to Norway. When a favourable wind came, Haakon ordered the clergymen back ashore and broke his allegiance to Denmark. In 977 Vladimir of Novgorod fled to him and gathered Viking warriors, and on his return the next year marched against Yaropolk I of Kiev. In 986 a Danish invasion fleet led by the Jomsvikings was defeated at the Battle of Hjörungavágr.

In 995 a quarrel broke out between Haakon and the Trønders just as Olaf Tryggvason, a descendant of Harald Fairhair, arrived. Haakon quickly lost all support and was killed by his slave and friend Tormod Kark while hiding in a pigsty at the farm Rimul in Melhus. His sons Eirik and Sveinn fled to the Swedish king Olof Skötkonung. The Skáldatal names poets at his court, among them Eyvindr Finnsson and Einarr skálaglamm. Snorri Sturluson tells his story in Heimskringla, and Adam Oehlenschläger's tragedy Hakon Jarl of 1805, on the conflict between paganism and Christianity, later inspired Smetana's symphonic poem of the same name.
hakor: Hakor, also called Hagar and known in Greek as Achoris or Hakoris, was a pharaoh of the 29th Dynasty. His accession and his relationship with his predecessor Nepherites I were long debated. After Nepherites died a dynastic struggle seems to have followed, in which Hakor, Psammuthes and possibly a figure called Muthis, mentioned only in Eusebius' epitome of Manetho, claimed the throne. In 1986 John D. Ray suggested that Hakor was Nepherites' heir, deposed in his second year by Psammuthes and restored a year later, and that he dated his reign from his first coronation as though the gap had never occurred. Alan B. Lloyd and Toby Wilkinson accept this view.

Once re-established, Hakor made considerable efforts to affirm his legitimacy, stressing his real or fictional descent from Nepherites. His building was extensive and he restored many monuments of earlier kings. At Karnak he finished the chapel for the sacred barque of Amun-Ra near the first pylon, begun by Psammuthes or possibly Nepherites I, and he possibly began a temple complex in northern Saqqara that was later developed under Nectanebo II. His building is attested at Luxor, Medinet Habu, El-Kab, El-Tod, Medamud and Elephantine, in the Temple of Hibis in Kharga Oasis and in Middle Egypt.

Hakor continued Nepherites' foreign policy and was allied with Evagoras I of Cyprus against the Achaemenids. After the peace of Antalcidas in 387 BCE, Egypt and Cyprus remained the only opponents of Artaxerxes II. It seems the Persians first attacked Egypt in 385 BCE and, after three years of war, the Egyptians defeated them. In 381 BCE Hakor sent Evagoras aid, money and 50 triremes, but when Evagoras came to Egypt in 380 BCE to beg for more he was sent back with only some money. Hakor then joined a short-lived alliance with Sparta and with Glos, and took the Athenian general Chabrias into his service.

Hakor was succeeded by his son Nepherites II, who kept the throne for only four months before an army general from Sebennytos, Nectanebo I, overthrew him. Nectanebo I called Hakor an usurper shortly after his death, though it has been suggested that the two were relatives, possibly both related to Nepherites I but rivals. Hakor's tomb has not been found. Only one funerary object can be linked to him, an ushabti inscribed with his name found at Mendes, which may indicate that his tomb was looted in antiquity, though this is unproven.
halabja-massacre: Northern Iraq was unsettled during the early stage of the Iran–Iraq War, and the militias of the Kurdistan Democratic Party and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan joined forces with Iranian support in 1982 and 1983. From 1985 the Ba'athist government under Saddam Hussein decided to eradicate pockets of Kurdish insurgents and to strike down the peshmerga by all means possible, including large-scale punishment of civilians and the use of chemical weapons. The attack on Halabja took place during the Anfal campaign, led by the Iraqi officer Ali Hassan al-Majid. Two days earlier Iran had captured the town as part of Operation Zafar 7.

The attack began on 16 March 1988 and lasted five hours. After a series of indiscriminate conventional attacks with rockets and napalm, Iraqi MiG and Mirage aircraft dropped chemical bombs on Halabja's residential areas. According to regional Kurdish commanders, aircraft coordinated by helicopters made up to 14 bombings in sorties of seven to eight planes each.

Eyewitnesses described clouds of white, black and then yellow smoke rising in a column. The United Nations later concluded that mustard gas and unidentified nerve agents had been used, and the BBC reported a mixture of mustard, tabun, sarin and VX. The attack killed between 3,200 and 5,000 people and injured 7,000 to 10,000 more.

The first pictures were taken by Iranian journalists, among them the photographer Kaveh Golestan, and a British ITN crew was airlifted in by the Iranians. Iraq did not comment publicly on the use of chemical weapons at Halabja until 23 March, and it ultimately denied responsibility and blamed Iran. The US Defense Intelligence Agency initially blamed Iran, but the majority of later evidence showed that Iraq had used the weapons.

Survivors, helped by peshmerga and Iranians, hastily buried most of the dead in makeshift mass graves. After Iraqi forces retook the town, troops in protective suits came to study the effects of their weapons, and the town was then razed with bulldozers and explosives. Surveys in the years afterwards found raised rates of cancer, miscarriage and birth defects. The Security Council condemned Iraq's use of chemical weapons against Iran in Resolutions 612 and 620 but did not mention their use against its own citizens.

Al-Majid was found guilty of ordering the attack and sentenced to death in June 2007, and he was hanged in January 2010. That year the Supreme Iraqi Criminal Tribunal defined the attack as a genocidal massacre against the Kurdish people, and the Parliament of Canada formally condemned it as a crime against humanity. Foreign firms had supplied precursor chemicals for Iraq's chemical weapons.
halberstadt: Halberstadt received market rights from King Otto III in 989 and became the administrative centre of the Saxon Harzgau. Its bishops had the Church of Our Lady built from about 1005. In 1179 the forces of Henry the Lion devastated the town in his conflict with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, and after Henry's fall the diocese became a prince-bishopric about 1180. The cathedral was rebuilt from 1236 and consecrated in 1491. Halberstadt joined a league of towns with Quedlinburg and Aschersleben in 1326, and from 1387 it was a member of the Hanse.

The citizens turned Protestant around 1540, and in 1566 the cathedral chapter elected the first Lutheran bishop, Prince Henry Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Wallenstein's troops occupied the town in 1629. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised the prince-bishopric into the Principality of Halberstadt, held by Brandenburg-Prussia, and the town became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701. From 1747 the official and poet Johann Wilhelm Ludwig Gleim made his house an intellectual centre of the German Enlightenment. It is now the Gleimhaus museum.

Halberstadt's Jewish community is recorded from the 13th century. Berend Lehmann founded a beth midrash, the Klaus, in 1703 and financed a Baroque synagogue completed in 1712, and the town had one of the largest Jewish communities in central Europe. The synagogue was burned in the pogrom of 9 November 1938. After local Nazi leaders refused to surrender, 218 American bombers dropped 595 tons of bombs on the centre on 8 April 1945. About 2,500 people were killed and most of the old town was reduced to rubble.

Halberstadt is now a town in Saxony-Anhalt and the capital of Harz district. Its cathedral is notable among those of northern Europe for keeping its medieval treasury almost complete, including the oldest surviving tapestries in Europe, from the 12th century. About 450 timber-framed houses stand in the centre, and the Klaus houses the Moses Mendelssohn Academy. A performance of John Cage's organ piece As Slow As Possible began in the Burchardikirche in 2001 and is scheduled to last 639 years.
haldimand-proclamation: In November 1775, on the eve of the American Revolution, the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant and Guy Johnson travelled to London to obtain a promise that if the Iroquois fought on the British side they would receive a grant of land in Canada. During and after the war American colonists confiscated the land and property of Loyalists. By early 1783 Brant had chosen the valley of the Grand River for settlement, and in 1784 Haldimand agreed.

The land first had to be bought from the Mississaugas of the Credit. On 22 May 1784 Colonel John Butler was sent to negotiate the purchase of about 3,000,000 acres between Lakes Huron, Ontario and Erie for £1180, a sale also known as the Between the Lakes Treaty. The proclamation followed three days after the Treaty of Fort Stanwix was signed between others of the Six Nations and the American government.

Issued at the Castle of St Lewis at Quebec, the proclamation recalled the early attachment of the Mohawk Indians to the King's cause and the loss of their settlement, and offered a safe retreat for them and others of the Five Nations who had lost their lands in the American states. It allowed them to settle on the banks of the Grand River, running into Lake Erie, six miles deep on each side from the lake to the head of the river, for them and their posterity to enjoy for ever.

Officials first read the grant as forbidding the Indians to lease or sell land to anyone but the government, while Brant held that Haldimand had promised freehold tenure like that of the Loyalist settlers. In 1793 Lieutenant Governor John Graves Simcoe declared that they could not lease their land, since British subjects could lease only from British subjects; Brant saw the right to lease or sell as a test of Indian sovereignty.

The Crown held that the grant was for all the Six Nations, while Brant said it was for those who lived on the land. The Crown also contended that the grant was limited to land it had already bought, though the head of the river lay some thirty miles beyond that purchase. A map from the survey of 1791 was later believed lost or destroyed, and the Crown relied on Thomas Ridout's survey of 1821, which drew the northern boundary near present-day Elora. In 1819 John Brant, son of Joseph Brant, protested that the Six Nations held writings proving otherwise.
haleakala: Haleakalā, also called the East Maui Volcano, is an active shield volcano that forms more than 75 per cent of Maui. The western quarter of the island is formed by another volcano, Mauna Kahalawai, also called the West Maui Mountains. Its tallest peak is Puʻu ʻUlaʻula, or Red Hill, at 3,055 metres. From the summit one looks down into a depression about 18 km across, 5 km wide and nearly 800 metres deep, with steep walls and a scattering of volcanic cones. Early Hawaiians used the name Haleakalā, house of the sun, for the whole mountain.

In Hawaiian folklore the depression at the summit was home to the grandmother of the demigod Māui, who helped him capture the sun and force it to slow its journey across the sky so that the day would be longer. Geologically Haleakalā began forming about 2 million years ago, building a shield along three rift zones. It has produced numerous eruptions in the last 30,000 years, including ten in the past 1,000 years, and is the only active volcano on Maui.

The summit basin is not a volcanic crater. Water and wind erosion, and possibly glaciers, carved two large valleys out of the rim, and their headwalls merged at the summit to form the depression, with the gaps of Koʻolau on the north and Kaupō on the south. The last eruption was long thought to have been about 1790, from a comparison of maps by La Perouse and Vancouver, but radiocarbon dating published in 1999 placed it between 1480 and 1600. The lava deposits of the Ahihi Kina'u and La Perouse Bay area belong to this last flow.

The crater and its surroundings lie within Haleakalā National Park, of 30,183 acres, which includes the summit depression, Kipahulu Valley and ʻOheʻo Gulch, with two main trails into the crater, Sliding Sands and Halemauʻu. Visitors come to watch the sunrise. Haleakalā Highway, completed in 1935, climbs to the summit. Because of the clarity and dryness of the air the summit is a site for ground-based telescopes, in an astrophysical complex known as Science City. The park shelters the endemic Haleakalā silversword and the nēnē.
halfdan-ragnarsson: Halfdan Ragnarsson, in Old English Halfdene or Healfdene and in Old Irish Albann, was one of six sons of Ragnar Lodbrok named in the Norse sagas. His brothers and half-brothers included Björn Ironside, Ivar the Boneless, Sigurd Snake-in-the-Eye, Ubba and Hvitserk. Because Halfdan appears in no source that mentions Hvitserk, some scholars suggest they were one man, Hvitserk, 'white shirt', being a nickname that set him apart from other men called Halfdan. Asser and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle name Halfdan and Ivar as brothers.

Halfdan led the Great Heathen Army that landed in East Anglia in the autumn of 865. According to the sagas, the sons of Ragnar organised it to avenge him on Ælla of Northumbria, who had supposedly had him thrown into a snake pit. The army invaded Northumbria, then in civil war between Ælla and Osberht, and conquered York late in 866. Ælla and Osberht both fell in a failed attempt to retake it, and the Danes installed a puppet king, Ecgberht.

The army then took Nottingham in Mercia and withdrew to York under a truce. After the conquest of East Anglia, where Ivar and Ubba are named as commanders, Halfdan became the main commander and led an invasion of Wessex in 870. The Danes fought the West Saxons nine times, including at Ashdown on 8 January 871, and Halfdan accepted a truce from Alfred. Coins minted in London in the following winter bear his name.

The army conquered Mercia in 874, deposing King Burghred and installing the puppet regent Ceolwulf. It then split, Guthrum going south against Wessex and Halfdan north against the Picts and the Britons of Strathclyde. He is generally agreed to be the Albann who, according to the Annals of Ulster, killed Eystein Olafsson, King of Dublin, in 875. Halfdan then sailed up the River Tyne, sacked the monasteries at Tynemouth and Jarrow, and camped at Gateshead. His men settled an area largely coextensive with the old Kingdom of Deira, and sources sometimes title him King of Jórvík.

Halfdan was deposed in Dublin while away in York. In 877 he returned to Ireland to recapture the city but met an army of Fair Heathens, usually taken to be the Viking population longest in Ireland, and was killed at the Battle of Strangford Lough. His surviving men returned to Northumbria through Scotland, fighting a battle in which Constantine I, King of the Picts, was killed. The Vikings of Northumbria had no king until Guthred was made king in 883.
halfdan-the-black: Íslendingabók, Heimskringla and Fagrskinna make Halfdan a member of the House of Yngling, and Heimskringla names his half-brother Olaf Geirstad-Alf. When his father was killed, his mother Åsa took the one-year-old Halfdan back to Agder, where he was raised, and at 18 or 19 he became king there. Some scholars suggest that his descent from the earlier Yngling kings of Vestfold was a later invention, made to link a conquering Halfdan and his son with the family praised in the Ynglingatal, whom he had displaced.

Halfdan is said to have divided Vestfold with his brother Olaf and forced King Gandalf of Vingulmark to cede half his kingdom. In Raumarike he killed the ruler Sigtryg Eysteinsson in battle and then defeated Sigtryg's brother Eystein, gaining half of Hedmark as well; these details appear only in Heimskringla. His first wife Ragnhild was a daughter of King Harald Gulskeg of Sogn, and when their young son, who had been named his grandfather's heir, died, Halfdan claimed Sogn without resistance.

Heimskringla adds that the sons of Gandalf tried to ambush him at night; he escaped into the forest, returned with an army, killed Hysing and Helsing and became king of all Vingulmark. The same saga says his second wife, also named Ragnhild, had been carried off by a berserker named Hake before Halfdan had her taken from him. Both sagas agree that she bore him a son named Harald.

Heimskringla, Fagrskinna, Ágrip and Historia Norwegiæ all relate that he drowned at the inlet of Røykenvik in the lake Randsfjorden on his way home from Hadeland, where ice had been weakened by cattle dung near a watering hole. He was buried in a mound at Stein in Ringerike. Heimskringla adds that each district of his kingdom wanted his grave, so his body was divided into four, giving four sites called Halvdanshaugen; by this account only his head lies in Ringerike.
haliacmon: The Haliacmon, in Greek Aliákmonas, flows entirely on Greek soil in the region of Macedonia and is 297 km long, with a drainage basin of 8,813 square kilometres. Three Greek rivers are longer overall, but each reaches Greece from another country. It rises in the Gramos mountains of Western Macedonia, near the border with Albania, flows east and then south-east near Kastoria, curves round the Vourinos mountains and turns north-east. Past Veria it enters the central Macedonian plains, an area of great importance to agriculture, and reaches the Thermaic Gulf west of the delta of the Axios.

The Latin name comes from the Ancient Greek, a compound of words for salt or sea and for anvil. In mythology Haliacmon was a river god, a son of Oceanus and Tethys. Pliny the Elder recorded a tradition that sheep which drank from the river turned white, while those that drank from the Axios turned black. The Ottoman Turks called it Ince-Karasu.

In antiquity the river marked a boundary. According to Julius Caesar it formed the dividing line between Macedon and Thessaly. In its upper course it watered Elimiotis, and further downstream it separated Pieria from Eordaea and Imathia. In the time of Herodotus it was apparently joined by the Loudias, the outflow of the lake of Pella, which has since changed course and flows directly into the Aegean.

Before a diversion dam was built near Aghia Varvara in the mid-1950s, the lowland river had no permanent bed and often flooded, forming extensive marshes. The dam at Polyfyto created a large artificial lake. The river passes Veria and Alexandreia, and at its mouth it has built an extended delta, part of the Axios-Loudias-Haliacmon Delta National Park, where about 90 per cent of Greece's mussels are produced and 215 kinds of birds have been observed.
halifax-nova-scotia: The area was called Chebucto until Halifax was established in 1749 by Governor Edward Cornwallis, who named it in honour of George Montagu-Dunk, 2nd Earl of Halifax. The Mi'kmaq name for the harbour is K'jipuktuk or Chebookt, meaning Chief Harbour or Great Harbour. They called the Halifax Peninsula, with the downtown area and Point Pleasant Park, Amntu'kati, and the hillside where the town was established was known, according to Thomas Raddall, as Goo-ow-ak-a-de, place of many pines.

Before 1749 the Colony of Nova Scotia had been administered from Annapolis Royal, near the western opening of the Bay of Fundy. In 1749 King George II ordered Cornwallis to establish Halifax as a new capital. Equipped with 13 transports and a sloop of war, Cornwallis founded the Town of Halifax on what is now the Halifax Peninsula on 21 June 1749. The original grid plan devised at the founding included a central military parade square, the Grand Parade, which has City Hall at one end and hosts the annual Remembrance Day ceremony at its cenotaph. The fortress of Citadel Hill overlooks the downtown.

Halifax is the capital and most populous municipality of Nova Scotia, and the most populous in Atlantic Canada. The Halifax Regional Municipality consists of four former municipalities amalgamated in 1996: Halifax, Dartmouth, Bedford and Halifax County. In the 2021 census 348,634 people lived in its urban area, which surrounds Halifax Harbour. The Port of Halifax and Dalhousie University are among its major employers, and the Royal Canadian Navy has major installations along the harbour. The Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21, an immigrant entry point prominent through the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s, opened as a National Historic Site in 1999.
halifax-resolves: By the spring of 1776 a strong movement in the colonies wanted separation from Great Britain. Its supporters, the American Whigs, later called Patriots, sought public backing for a general declaration of independence. The chief obstacle was that no delegate to the Second Continental Congress had been authorised by his home government to take any step leading to such a declaration. Advocates of independence therefore worked to revise the instructions of each colony's delegation and remove the restrictions on them.

The Fourth Provincial Congress of North Carolina was meeting in the town of Halifax when it adopted the resolution, and the name Halifax Resolves was given to it later. All 83 delegates present voted for it. It empowered the colony's three delegates to the Second Continental Congress, Joseph Hewes, William Hooper and John Penn, to join with the delegates of the other colonies in declaring independence, and it encouraged the delegates of every colony to push for it.

The resolves stopped short of telling North Carolina's delegates to propose independence themselves. That step was taken by Virginia in June with the Lee Resolution, and the Second Continental Congress issued the Declaration of Independence in July, less than three months after the vote at Halifax.
