Every year on 12 April the Halifax Historic District, a historic site run by the North Carolina Department of Cultural Resources, holds Halifax Day, with guided tours of historic buildings by interpreters in period dress, demonstrations of colonial crafts and, at times, re-enactors showing the soldiers and weapons of the Revolution. Two copies of the document survive, one in the State Archives of North Carolina and one held by the National Archives and Records Administration. For the 250th anniversary of independence in 2026 the National Archives copy returned to North Carolina and was shown at the Halifax Historic Site until 6 October 2026.
hall-heroult-process: Aluminium is the most abundant metallic element in the Earth's crust but is rarely found in its elemental state. Before the process, the metal was made by heating ore with elemental sodium or potassium in a vacuum, a complicated method that consumed expensive materials. Bars of aluminium were exhibited alongside the French crown jewels at the Exposition Universelle of 1855, and Napoleon III was said to have reserved his few aluminium dinner sets for his most honoured guests. When aluminium was chosen for the cap and lightning rod of the Washington Monument, completed in 1884, it still cost more than silver.

Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult devised the process independently and almost simultaneously in 1886. Some authors claim that Hall was assisted by his sister Julia Brainerd Hall, though the extent of her involvement has been disputed. In 1888 Hall opened the first large-scale aluminium plant in Pittsburgh, which became the Alcoa corporation.

Aluminium cannot be made by electrolysis of an aqueous salt, because hydronium ions readily oxidise the metal, and alumina melts at 2072 °C, which makes electrolysing it directly impractical. In the process alumina is dissolved in molten synthetic cryolite, which lowers the melting point. Cryolite also dissolves alumina well, conducts electricity and is less dense than liquid aluminium. Aluminium fluoride is usually added.

A direct current of under 5 V and 100 to 300 kA passes through the mixture. Liquid aluminium collects at the cathode, while oxygen from the alumina combines with carbon from the anode to form mostly carbon dioxide. The molten metal sinks to the bottom of the cell and is siphoned off every one to three days, and the cells run around the clock so that their contents never solidify. The theoretical minimum energy requirement is 6.23 kWh per kilogram of aluminium, but 15.37 kWh is commonly needed.

With cheaper electric power the process helped turn aluminium from a precious metal into an inexpensive commodity, which made it possible for Hugo Junkers to build metal aircraft by the thousands. Because smelting needs large amounts of cheap electricity, plants have often been sited where it is available, as at Kitimat in British Columbia, built by Alcan and powered by the Kenney Dam. In 1997 the American Chemical Society designated the process a National Historic Chemical Landmark.
hall-of-mirrors: The Hall of Mirrors was built between 1678 and 1684, in the third building stage of the Palace of Versailles under Louis XIV. It replaced a large terrace and several smaller salons facing the gardens. The terrace had been judged a misplaced element, exposed to the weather, and was demolished. The architect Jules Hardouin-Mansart designed and built the gallery, and Charles Le Brun created its interior decoration.

The hall is flanked by the Salon of War at the north end and the Salon of Peace at the south, which were joined to the king's and the queen's apartments. It is 73 m long, 10.50 m deep and 12.30 m high. No fireplaces were planned, since the room was too large to heat.

Seventeen windows open towards the park, and on the opposite wall are seventeen mirrors of the same size, each made up of many separate pieces of glass, more than 350 in all. The mirrors reflected the garden and the candlelight in the evening. Mirror glass was an expensive product, and the order was the first major one for the Manufacture royale de glaces de miroirs, a glass factory founded by Jean-Baptiste Colbert, which broke the Venetian monopoly on mirror making in Europe.

The ceiling paintings, directed by Le Brun, glorify Louis XIV as the Sun King and the successes of the first two decades of his personal rule. The central scene is titled The King rules by Himself. Most of the larger panels concern the Franco-Dutch War of 1672 to 1678, and others show episodes of the War of Devolution of 1667 to 1668. The original silver furniture was soon lost: the silver tables were melted down and coined on Louis XIV's order in 1689 to pay for the War of the League of Augsburg.

In the 17th century the hall served as a covered promenade for the king's visit to the chapel, and courtiers gathered there to meet him. It also housed court weddings, audiences for foreign embassies and balls, among them the Yew Tree Ball of 25 February 1745, at which Louis XV met the future Madame de Pompadour. Over 3,000 candles lit it in its prime.

On 18 January 1871, after the siege of Paris in the Franco-Prussian War, the German princes proclaimed William I emperor in the hall, in a ceremony led by Otto von Bismarck. Versailles was the headquarters of the German armies, and the hall was chosen because its ceiling paintings glorified French conquests of German territory. Georges Clemenceau chose the same room for the signing of the Treaty of Versailles on 28 June 1919. It remains reserved for official ceremonies of the French Republic.
hall-of-worthies: An institute of this name had existed in law long before the Joseon dynasty, but it became significant only when King Sejong the Great reformed it fundamentally in the 3rd month of 1420 and staffed it with talented scholars. At first a royal advisory body, it was restructured to include academic research and came to hold discussions of national policy, as well as overseeing the education of the king and crown prince; modern historians have likened it to a think tank. From 1426, under the practice of saga toksŏ, its scholars could research independently of government work, which has been likened to modern research grants. They worked in the Gwollaegaksa, government offices in Gyeongbok Palace.

Sejong created Hangul himself and revealed it in 1443. After writing the preface to the Hunminjeongeum, he set the Hall to write its detailed examples and explanations, a task led by its head, Chŏng Inji, and the work was promulgated in 1446 to raise the literacy of the people. In Sejong's 14th year the scholars compiled examples of filial piety, loyalty to the state and wifely devotion from Korean and Chinese history as the Samgang Haengshildo, written in Chinese characters and translated into Hangul some 30 years later.

When Ming envoys led by Ni Qian came in 1450 to announce the accession of Emperor Jingdi, they exchanged poems several times with the Hall's scholars Chŏng Inji, Sŏng Sammun and Sin Sukchu, a tradition now called Hwanghwajip. The Hall also took part in many of the scholarly and scientific publications that gave Sejong's reign its reputation as the golden age of Korean culture.

King Sejo disbanded the Hall in the 6th month of 1456 after many of its members, among them Sŏng Sammun, Pak P'aengnyŏn, Ha Wiji, Yi Kae and Yu Sŏngwŏn of the six martyred ministers, plotted to assassinate him following his usurpation of the throne from King Danjong. He also ended saga toksŏ, which King Seongjong (r. 1469–1495) revived. The Hongmun'gwan, or Office of Special Advisors, carried on much of the Hall's work without its prestige or output, and an attempt to make the Yemun'gwan its successor fell short of its predecessor in the judgement of the historian Peterson. Of the Gwollaegaksa, only Sujeongjeon Hall survives in good condition.
halland: Halland is one of the traditional provinces of Sweden, on the western coast of Götaland, bordering Västergötland, Småland, Scania and the Kattegat. Its name means Land of Rocky Slabs, from the Swedish hällar, referring to the coastal cliffs of the northern part. The rivers Viskan, Ätran, Nissan and Lagan flow through it to the Kattegat, and it is well known for its fertile soil and as an agricultural district. The Swedish provinces serve no administrative function; that is done by the counties, and Halland County is almost coextensive with the province.

The Bronze Age was probably a period of relative prosperity in Halland, with over 1,100 tumuli and grave mounds found. Around 200 CE villages began to form larger communities and small kingdoms, and during the 5th and 6th centuries large free-standing farms were created, as at Slöinge. The account of Ohthere of Hålogaland, who travelled to Hedeby in the 870s, shows Halland to have been Danish then, and it stayed so for most of recorded history. As part of the Scanian lands it came under the Scanian Law and took part in the Scanian Thing, one of the three Things that elected the Danish king.

From the 13th century Halland was the scene of considerable military action as Sweden, Denmark and to some degree Norway fought for supremacy in Scandinavia, and the wars made the province poor. It was invaded by Haakon IV of Norway in 1256, by Magnus III of Sweden in 1277 and by Eric VI of Denmark in 1294. It was split in two along the river Ätran for the next century. The Count's Feud, the Northern Seven Years' War and the Kalmar War all affected it, and one of the major battles of the Northern Seven Years' War was fought at Axtorna.

Under the Second Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645 Halland was transferred to Sweden for a period of thirty years, and the transfer was made permanent by the cession in the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658. The last battle in Halland was fought at Fyllebro on 17 August 1676, during the Scanian War. Under Danish rule the province had no coat of arms; when Charles X Gustav died in 1660, one with a lion had to be created for the newly acquired province, since each province was to be represented by its arms at the royal funeral. Calmer conditions after the wars let the province develop, and farming became one of the more efficient in Sweden by the end of the 19th century.
hallaton-treasure: The first find was made by Ken Wallace of the Hallaton Fieldwork Group, who turned up about 130 coins with a metal detector on 19 November 2000. Volunteers from the group and local community archaeologists then excavated the site with the University of Leicester Archaeological Services (ULAS), in what became one of the most important Iron Age excavations and community archaeology projects in Britain. The work showed that the hoard lay at an internationally important ritual site on a hilltop in the Welland valley.

The hoard is the largest of British Iron Age coins. Of the coins from the site, 4,835 can be attributed to the Corieltauvi, a find that more than doubled the number of Corieltauvian coins already recorded. One silver Roman coin has been dated by local museums to 211 BCE, making it the oldest Roman coin found in Britain; some archaeologists suggest it reached Britain before the conquest of 43 CE through trade or diplomacy. The hoard also includes jewellery and other objects. The site was probably enclosed by a ditch and palisade, and archaeologists believe it was an open-air shrine, the first of its kind discovered in the UK.

David Mattingly, an archaeologist at the University of Leicester, said the hoard had changed views of how significant the East Midlands were in this period, and that the Roman coin pointed to contact between the region and the Roman Empire despite its distance from the places where the Romans arrived, such as Colchester and Chichester.

The Roman Hallaton Helmet underwent nine years of conservation at the British Museum before going on display at Harborough Museum in 2012. In January 2011 it was announced that the museum would also show the skeleton of a dog, believed to have been sacrificed to guard the treasure. In 2012 a silver ring inscribed TOT was found in the same area. The inscription is believed to refer to the Celtic god Toutatis, who corresponds to the Roman Mars, and Adam Daubney, a specialist in such rings, suggests that he may have been worshipped at Hallaton. Leicestershire County Council acquired the ring for display at the museum.
halle-saale: Halle lies in the south of Saxony-Anhalt, in the Leipzig Bay, the southernmost part of the North German Plain, on the River Saale, a tributary of the Elbe. Leipzig is 35 kilometres away, and the two cities form the centres of the Central German Metropolitan Region.

Halle's early history is bound up with salt. The name of the river contains the Germanic root for salt, and salt has been harvested there since at least the Bronze Age. The salters, who wore a uniform with eighteen silver buttons, were known as Halloren, and the name was later given to chocolates shaped like those buttons.

The earliest documented mention of the town dates from 806. It became part of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg in the 10th century and remained so until 1680, when the Margraviate of Brandenburg annexed it together with Magdeburg. It was a member of the Hanseatic League at least as early as 1281, and an important location for Martin Luther's Reformation. The Moritzburg, built between 1484 and 1503 as the archbishops' residence, was destroyed in the Thirty Years' War. In 1840 Ludwig Wucherer opened the Magdeburg-Halle-Leipzig railway line, making Halle a rail hub. After the Second World War Halle was the capital of Saxony-Anhalt until 1952, and then of the district of Halle. When Saxony-Anhalt was re-established in 1990, Magdeburg became the capital.

Halle is the second largest city of Saxony-Anhalt, with around 226,000 inhabitants. Giebichenstein Castle, first mentioned in 961, stands above the Saale. Georg Friedrich Händel, later George Frideric Handel, was born in Halle in 1685 and spent his first 17 years there; his house is a museum, and the city has held a Handel Festival since 1922. The Francke Foundations are home to the Stadtsingechor zu Halle, one of the oldest boys' choirs in the world. The Nebra sky disc is exhibited in the State Museum of Prehistory.
hallein: Hallein is the capital of Hallein district in the Tennengau region. The town stretches along the Salzach river in the shadow of the Untersberg massif, close to the German border on the west. The municipal area includes the cadastral communities of Adnet II, Au, Burgfried, Dürrnberg, Gamp, Gries, Hallein proper, Oberalm II and Taxach. It is linked to the city of Salzburg by the suburban S-Bahn railway and by the A 10 Tauern Autobahn.

The area is known for the Hallein Salt Mine on the Dürrnberg plateau, and settlement has been traced back 4,000 years. A Celtic community lived there from 600 BCE until the Romans took over its Noricum kingdom in 15 BCE. In the middle of the 8th century Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria granted the estates to the Salzburg diocese, and from 987 they were held by St Peter's Abbey. Salt became crucial to the wealth of the Archbishopric of Salzburg, competing with the production of Reichenhall in Bavaria. Salt mining is first mentioned in a deed of 1198, and the name Hallein is documented from the early 13th century.

Beer brewing became common from the 15th century, and in 1489 Prince-Archbishop Leonhard von Keutschach acquired a large brewery whose Hofbräu Kaltenhausen beers became another main source of revenue. At the end of the 17th century Prince-Archbishop Kuenburg had the Protestant miners expelled, and several hundred of them emigrated to Walcheren and Zeelandic Flanders. Hallein became part of the Austrian Empire by 1816. In World War II the town had a work camp annex to the Dachau concentration camp, and afterwards a camp for displaced persons, Beth Israel, which closed in 1954.

Hallein is a historic town with about 21,150 inhabitants and the second largest in the state of Salzburg. The Keltenmuseum shows the Hallstatt and La Tène Celtic cultures and the development of salt mining through the Middle Ages and Renaissance. The Silent Night Museum documents the life of the composer Franz Xaver Gruber, who lived locally, and holds the guitar used by the lyricist Joseph Mohr.
hallel: Full Hallel (Hallel shalem) consists of all six psalms in their entirety, with a blessing at the beginning and the end. Partial Hallel (chatzi Hallel) omits the first 11 verses of both Psalms 115 and 116, and in Yemenite Jewish custom also Psalm 117 and Psalm 118:1–4. Ashkenazi Jews recite a blessing over Partial Hallel; some Sephardic Jews do not, and the Sephardic communities that do say a different form of it from the one used for Full Hallel.

The name Great Hallel is given to Psalm 136, or by other opinions in the Talmud to Psalms 135–136 or 134–136. Each verse of Psalm 136 ends with the refrain for his mercy endures forever, and it names twenty-six acts of divine kindness. It is recited at the Passover Seder after the standard Hallel.

Full Hallel is said on the first two nights and days of Pesach (one in Israel), on Shavuot, all seven days of Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah, and the eight days of Hanukkah, as part of the morning Shacharit service after the Amidah. Partial Hallel, a later custom, is said on the last six days of Passover and on Rosh Chodesh. The Talmud records a dispute between the Houses of Hillel and Shammai over how much of it to read before the Seder meal; the halacha follows Hillel.

No Hallel is said on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, days of judgement, nor on Purim, for which the Talmud gives three reasons, among them that the Jews remained subjects of the Achaemenid Empire. Many communities that identify with religious Zionism recite it on Israeli Independence Day, as the Chief Rabbinate of Israel instructs.

The New Testament accounts of the Last Supper say that Jesus and his disciples sang a psalm or hymn after the meal before going to the Mount of Olives, which may have been the Hallel. Its psalms have been set to music many times: Psalm 114 by Josquin des Prez and Mendelssohn, verses of Psalm 115 by Johann Sebastian Bach in his cantata BWV 196, Psalm 117 by Antonio Vivaldi and Mozart, and Psalm 118 by Léonin and Pérotin. The American composer Michael Isaacson's An American Hallel was first performed in 2009.
hallstatt-culture: The Hallstatt culture developed out of the Urnfield culture and was followed in much of its area by the La Tène culture. Paul Reinecke's scheme of 1902, based on finds from the south of Germany, divided the end of the Bronze Age and the Early Iron Age into four periods, Hallstatt A to D. Hallstatt A and B are regarded as Late Bronze Age, while Hallstatt C and D, dated roughly 800 to 620 BCE and 620 to 450 BCE, make up the Early Iron Age phase. Radiocarbon dating is hard to use here because of the so-called Hallstatt Plateau, so dating rests mainly on dendrochronology and on the changing fashions of brooches.

The community at Hallstatt itself was untypical of the wider, mainly agricultural, culture, since its economy exploited rich salt mines. These were extensively mined, with a peak from the 8th to the 5th centuries BCE, and the salt preserved textiles, wood, leather, shoes and miners' backpacks. Some 1,300 burials are known from the cemetery.

The culture fell into two zones. The western zone covered parts of north-eastern France, northern Switzerland, southern Germany, Bohemia and western Austria, and its elite were buried with a sword or dagger and sometimes a chariot. In the eastern zone, which included eastern Austria, Moravia, Slovenia and parts of Hungary and Serbia, warriors were buried with an axe, helmet and breastplate, and art more often told stories.

After about 600 BCE the founding of Marseille and the arrival of Greek and Etruscan goods led to long-range trade up the Rhône valley. Powerful local chiefdoms emerged that controlled the redistribution of luxury goods, among them the Greek Vix krater and the Greek cauldron from Hochdorf. At the end of the period many major centres were abandoned, and towns did not re-emerge across temperate Europe until the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE.

Farming was the base of the economy, but metalworking was advanced and iron became more common after about 800 BCE. Settlements were mostly small, though the largest, known as princely seats, were fortified hilltop sites with workshops, elite residences and rich burials. Heuneburg on the upper Danube and Mont Lassois in eastern France are typical, and some have been called the first cities north of the Alps.

Rulers lay under large tumuli in timber-lined chambers with wagons and bronze vessels. Ancient DNA has been taken to show matrilineal elites linked by marriage over distances of more than 100 km, and the archaeologist Dirk Krausse has suggested that some rulers may have been sacral kings. Later Hallstatt art in the west is generally agreed to be the early period of Celtic art, and the culture is commonly associated with speakers of Proto-Celtic.
halmahera: Halmahera, formerly known as Jilolo, Gilolo or Jailolo, has a land area of 17,780 square kilometres and is the seventh largest island of Indonesia. It is a volcanic island on an island arc that includes the Raja Ampat Islands, all uplifted by the northward movement of Australia and the subduction of the Pacific Plate. Dukono is an active volcano at the northern end of the island and Mount Ibu another on its northwest coast. Ultramafic rocks and ophiolites form the bedrock over large areas of the eastern peninsula. The flightless invisible rail and the palm Jailoloa halmaherensis are found only on the island.

Sparsely populated Halmahera has long had its fortunes tied to those of the smaller islands of Ternate and Tidore off its west coast. It was the site of the Sultanate of Jailolo, one of the four kingdoms of Maluku, the Maloko Kië Raha, with Ternate, Tidore and Bacan, in the era before the Dutch East India Company colonized the whole archipelago. The north of the island was the base of the Loloda Kingdom, one of the earlier Moluccan kingdoms of the 13th century, though it was not counted among the four prominent ones.

The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace visited Halmahera, as he described in his book The Malay Archipelago (1869). In February 1858, on Ternate or perhaps on Halmahera itself, between bouts of fever, he arrived at the idea of natural selection, wrote it down over the next couple of days and sent the letter to Darwin.

During World War II the island was the site of a Japanese naval base at Kao Bay. In 1999 and 2000 a dispute between the mainly Christian district of Kao and the wholly Muslim district of Malifut grew into religious fighting that spread through much of the North Moluccas, and thousands of people on Halmahera were killed.

Sofifi, the capital of North Maluku province, stands on the west coast of Halmahera, opposite Tidore; the provincial government moved there from Ternate in 2010. In that year the island itself had a population of 449,938, and about half of its inhabitants are Muslim and half Christian. Tobelo is the largest town. The coast is inhabited by the Tobelo people, while the Togutil, a small semi-nomadic related people of the interior, are estimated at 1,500 to 3,000 people.
halvad: Halvad lies at the southern edge of the Little Rann of Kutch, at an average elevation of 46 metres, on the banks of the Samatsar lake. The yellow earth of this semi-arid country and the town's buildings of local yellow sandstone give it a golden colour at sunrise. The Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary of the Little Rann lies close by, home to the Asiatic wild ass as well as nilgai, chinkara, houbara bustards and Indian coursers.

Halvad is an old fortified town and was a capital of the Jhala Rajputs before the seat of their state moved to Dhrangadhra. Its palace on the shore of the Samatsar lake has the parts of a Rajput palace: a zenana, a hall of public audience, a temple of the family goddess, a pleasure garden and offices. A carved gate leads to a square courtyard framed by two-storeyed wings with carved wooden columns, brackets and jalis, and at its centre rises a seven-storeyed octagonal tower known as Jhalawad Darshan or the Ek-Dandia Mahal, from which the surrounding villages can be seen.

Cenotaphs, hero-stones and paliyas, memorial stones of sandstone at the edge of the town, recall battles fought at its gates, men who died defending it and women who committed sati. Chatris of the 15th century, with carved columns, high plinths and pyramidal roofs, stand in the surrounding country. The Bhavani Temple and the Bhuteshwar Mahadev at the cremation ground are at least 500 years old and are protected monuments.

Halvad is a municipality of Morbi district in Gujarat, with 32,024 inhabitants at the 2011 census. Temples of Shiva stand on every side of the town, which is called the Chota Kashi, or small Kashi, and it keeps four old step-wells. The dargah of Maula Qazi on the west bank of the Samatsar lake is a place of pilgrimage for the Dawoodi Bohra community. The surrounding land grows cotton, groundnut, castor and other crops, and the town has some salt works.
ham-nghi: Hàm Nghi was born Nguyễn Phúc Ưng Lịch in Huế, the fifth son of Prince Nguyễn Phúc Hồng Cai and brother of Emperor Kiến Phúc. After Emperor Tự Đức died in July 1883, the regents Nguyễn Văn Tường and Tôn Thất Thuyết held power over the choice of emperors. Three emperors had already been removed or had died. The regents wanted a young ruler who shared their anti-French stance, and they chose Ưng Lịch, who had lived in poverty and simplicity with his mother rather than being educated in the palace. He was enthroned in the Thái Hòa Hall on 2 August 1884 with the reign title Hàm Nghi.

The Resident Superior, Pierre Paul Rheinart, sent troops into Huế to force the court to ask France's permission after the fact. The court's request, written in chữ Nôm, was refused until it was rewritten in Chinese characters. At the investiture on 17 August 1884 Tôn Thất Thuyết allowed only three French envoys through the Noon Gate, which was traditionally reserved for the emperor.

On 4 July 1885 an insurrection against the French broke out in the emperor's name, and after the French stormed the palace Tôn Thất Thuyết took Hàm Nghi into hiding. The French replaced him with his brother Đồng Khánh. Hàm Nghi withdrew into the hills around Laos with Tôn Thất Thuyết's force, and the Cần Vương edict called scholars and patriots to resist French rule.

In 1888 Hàm Nghi was betrayed by Trương Quang Ngọc, the head of his Muong guards, and captured while hiding near the Nai river. He was exiled to French Algeria, arriving on 13 January 1889, and was deposed and titled Duke Ưng Lịch. In Algiers he studied under the painter Marius Reynaud, and his painting moved from Orientalism towards Impressionism and Post-Impressionism. He signed his works Tử Xuân. The art historian Amandine Dabat, his descendant, argues that he was the first modern Vietnamese painter. He died on 14 January 1944 and lies in a simple grave at Thonac in the Dordogne. Under French pressure the Nguyễn dynasty gave him no temple name. Vietnamese history counts him among three patriotic emperors of the colonial period.
hama: The ancient settlement of Hamath was occupied from the early Neolithic to the Iron Age. After the fall of the Hittite Empire it was the capital of a Syro-Hittite kingdom known from the Hebrew Bible, which traded with Israel and Judah. In 853 BCE its king Irhuleni and Hadadezer of Aram-Damascus led a coalition against the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III at the Battle of Qarqar, a battle that seems to have been closer to a draw. Around 720 BCE Sargon II razed the city after a failed revolt, resettled it with 6,300 Assyrians and had its king flayed alive in Assyria.

Under the Seleucids the city was renamed Epiphaneia after Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and the Romans annexed Syria in 64 BCE. Five hundred Hamian archers were stationed on Hadrian's Wall from 120 CE. Muslim forces under Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah took the city in 638 or 639, and it regained its old name. The Crusader Tancred took it in 1108, but the Seljuks recovered it in 1114. Two earthquakes in 1157 shattered it, and Nur al-Din rebuilt its walls and, in 1172, its Great Mosque.

Saladin took Hama in 1175 and gave it four years later to his nephew al-Muzaffar Umar, beginning Ayyubid rule that lasted almost continuously until 1342. The Mongols sacked it in 1260. The historian and geographer Abu al-Fida governed the city from 1310 to 1332. Ibn Battuta visited in 1335. The Ottomans conquered it in 1516. It became part of the French Mandate of Syria after 1918, and a rising took place in the city in 1925 during the Great Syrian Revolt.

Hama lies on the Orontes 213 kilometres north of Damascus and is the capital of the Hama Governorate. Its seventeen norias, water wheels up to 20 metres across, were used for irrigation and now serve as a symbol of the city. In February 1982 government forces under the president's brother Rifaat al-Assad put down an Islamist revolt in the city, shelling quarters held by the insurgents and razing part of the old city. Government forces are alleged to have executed thousands of prisoners and civilians afterwards.
hamad-bin-abdullah-al-sharqi: Hamad bin Abdullah was headman of Fujairah town in 1879. The Al Qasimi of Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah and the Sultan of Muscat had long contested the coast of the Gulf of Oman, known as the Shamaliyah, and Sheikh Saqr bin Khalid Al Qasimi of Sharjah, who claimed it, had placed a slave named Sarur in charge of Fujairah. In the spring of 1879 Hamad led a rising that removed Sarur, but the delegation he sent to Saqr was imprisoned, a force retook Fujairah Fort with Baluchi mercenaries, and Hamad went into exile in Muscat.

Sultan Turki bin Said of Muscat, advised by the British to stay out, gave him no help. Late in 1879 or early in 1880 Hamad returned and took Fujairah Fort, eight of its defenders being killed. Under a peace arbitrated by the Ruler of Ras Al Khaimah he signed a document in 1881 confirming him as a dependent of Sharjah, but he went on playing Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah against each other. In 1884 he took Ghurfa and Al Bithnah Fort, which guarded the Wadi Ham, the main route inland from the coast.

When he again rejected Sharjah's suzerainty he used Bithnah to deny aid to the headman of Kalba, a relative of Saqr, and sought the protection of Humaid bin Abdullah of Ras Al Khaimah. In April 1902 Saqr gathered 250 mounted Bedouin against Fujairah; the British warned Muscat and Dubai not to join in, and the Political Agent in Bahrain, Gaskin, held two days of talks at Fujairah before giving up. His independence was accepted by all concerned except the British, who in 1903 again treated Fujairah as a dependency of Sharjah.

In 1925 Hamad bought a Baluchi girl from Muscat in breach of the embargo on the slave trade. In April the Political Resident, Francis Bellville Prideaux, anchored off Fujairah in the RIMS Lawrence and summoned him aboard; when Hamad refused, Prideaux bombarded the fort, destroying three of its towers and killing Hamad's daughter-in-law. Blaming the Wali of Kalba, Saeed bin Hamad Al Qasimi, whose daughter he had married, Hamad went to war with Kalba and Khor Fakkan in May 1926, and fighting went on for years. He died in the mid-1930s and was succeeded by his son, Saif bin Hamad Al Sharqi.
hamadan: Hamadan lies in the foothills of Alvand Mountain in midwestern Iran, at about 1,850 metres above sea level and some 360 kilometres south-west of Tehran. It is the capital of Hamadan province and is believed to be among the oldest Iranian cities. Classical sources call it Ecbatana, from Old Persian Hamgmatāna. The Ganj Nameh inscription and the monuments to Avicenna and Baba Taher are its main sights.

The city may conceivably, though improbably, be mentioned in cuneiform texts of about 1100 BCE from the time of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I, according to Clifford Edmund Bosworth. It is certainly mentioned by Herodotus, who says that the king of Media, Diokes, built Ecbatana in the 7th century BCE. It later became one of several capitals of the Achaemenid dynasty. The book of Ezra says that at Ecbatana a scroll was found that gave the Jews permission from King Darius to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.

Under the Parthians, whose capital was Ctesiphon, Hamadan was the summer capital, and the Sasanians built summer palaces there. After the Battle of Nahavand in 642 it fell to the Arabs. In 931 Mardavij, founder of the Al-Ziyar dynasty, plundered it after its people killed his nephew. The Seljuks took the last Kakuyid fortress in 1047 and later moved their capital from Baghdad to Hamadan. The Mongols destroyed it in 1220, and the Timurid invasions destroyed it again, but it thrived in the Safavid era. Benjamin of Tudela reported 30,000 Jews there in 1170.

In the 18th century the city was surrendered to the Ottomans and returned to Iran through the work of Nader Shah. During the First World War Russian, Ottoman and British forces fought over it and occupied it in turn. Avicenna entered the city when it was the capital of the Buyid dynasty, taught at its great school and completed many of his writings there.
hamaj: The Hamaj descended from people of the upper Blue Nile between Sennar and Ethiopia, known as the Shankalla, who lived there before the Arabs arrived and whose language belongs to the Koman branch. They were often targets of Funj slave raids, and hamaj, meaning riffraff, was a contemptuous name the Funj gave them. Funj society was strictly divided by skin colour: the Funj called themselves blue and the Hamaj red. Incorporated into the Funj Sultanate of Sennar in the 17th century, the Hamaj prospered, and according to the Funj Chronicle the family of a slave called Hamaj grew until it held power and prestige in the kingdom.

Sultan Badi IV angered the old Funj families by giving their lands to new non-Funj followers and by relying on slave armies. He made the Hamaj general Muhammad Abu Likaylik governor of Kordofan in 1747. The Funj armies there agreed to depose the sultan under Abu Likaylik's leadership, crossed the White Nile, were joined by Badi's son Nasir and surrounded Sennar. Badi was allowed to leave under an amnesty, and Abu Likaylik installed Nasir as sultan, beginning the regency.

Its sixty years were marked by constant strife between regents and sultans and within Abu Likaylik's family. Eight years after his accession Nasir was deposed, and he was executed when found conspiring to return. Regent followed regent, often by murder and revenge. The Funj nearly overthrew the Hamaj in 1785, when Sultan Adlan II seized Sennar and the regent Rajab was killed in November at the Battle of Taras, but the Hamaj later defeated Adlan and restored their regency. Kordofan was lost to the Keira Sultanate of Darfur in 1787, and by 1821 sultans and regents controlled little beyond the city of Sennar.

As the Egyptian army of Ismail Pasha advanced in 1821, the regent Muhammad wad Adlan was overthrown and killed by his cousin Hasan wad Rajab. Hasan fled towards the Ethiopian border, and the last Funj sultan, Badi VII, submitted in person, probably on 12 June. The Egyptians entered Sennar unopposed the next day and found the royal palace derelict. The Hamaj chieftain Idris Muhammad Adlan held out in the Funj mountains until 1826 and served there as shaykh until 1851. After that the Hamaj clans had little influence in Sudanese public life.
hamamatsu: Hamamatsu lies in western Shizuoka Prefecture, 260 kilometres south-west of Tokyo, between Lake Hamana to the west, the Tenryū River to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the south. It has a flat plain and the Mikatahara Plateau in the south and mountains in the north. The area has been settled since prehistoric times, and the Shijimizuka shell mound and the Akamonue Kofun tomb survive from the Jōmon and Kofun periods.

In the Nara period it became the capital of Tōtōmi Province. In the Sengoku period Hamamatsu Castle was the home of the future shōgun Tokugawa Ieyasu. The city flourished in the Edo period under a succession of daimyō as a castle town and a post town on the Tōkaidō highway between Edo and Kyoto. The Hamamatsu Kite Festival, held each May, is said to have begun about 430 years ago, when the lord of the castle marked the birth of his first son by flying kites.

After the Meiji Restoration Hamamatsu was a prefecture from 1871 to 1876 before it was united with Shizuoka Prefecture. The station opened on the Tōkaidō Main Line in 1889, the same year it became a town, and it became a city on 1 July 1911. An Army air base opened in 1926 and a flight school in 1933. The Tonankai earthquake of 7 December 1944 caused much damage, and US air raids largely destroyed the city in June 1945.

Hamamatsu is the largest city in Shizuoka Prefecture, with an estimated 780,128 inhabitants in 2023,. It is known as an industrial city, above all for musical instruments and motorcycles. Honda was founded there, and Yamaha, Suzuki, Kawai and Roland have headquarters in the city. A 1990 change in Japanese immigration law drew a large Brazilian Nikkei population to work in its factories. The Hamamatsu International Piano Competition has been held every three years since 1991, and the Museum of Musical Instruments opened in 1995.
hamani-diori: Hamani Diori was born on 6 June 1916 at Soudouré, near Niamey, the son of a public health officer in the French colonial administration. He attended the William Ponty Teachers' Training College in Dakar and worked as a teacher in Niger from 1936 to 1938, then became a Hausa and Djerma instructor at the Institute of Study Abroad in Paris.

In 1946, as headmaster of a school in Niamey, he helped to found the Nigerien Progressive Party (PPN), a regional branch of the African Democratic Rally. That year he was elected to the French National Assembly. He lost his seat in 1951 to his cousin and rival Djibo Bakary, regained it in 1956 and became its deputy-speaker.

After a referendum in 1958 granted Niger self-government, Diori became president of the provisional government, and in 1959 prime minister. Niger became independent on 3 August 1960, and the National Assembly elected him president in November. A coalition of Hausa, Fula and, most prominently, Djerma leaders, including chiefs and traditionalists, had supported him and gained him French favour.

Soon after independence he made the PPN the only legal party. His government favoured traditional social structures and close economic ties with France. He ruled through a small group of pre-independence figures on the PPN Politburo and often bypassed the cabinet, leading several ministries himself. Boubou Hama, President of the National Assembly, was among his most powerful advisers. As sole candidate he was re-elected unopposed in 1965 and 1970.

Diori was respected abroad as a spokesman for African affairs and an arbitrator in conflicts, but at home his administration was accused of corruption and could not relieve the famine of the Sahelian drought of the early 1970s. He put down a coup in December 1963 and narrowly escaped assassination in 1965, using French advisers and troops against his opponents; students and unions protested against what they called French neocolonialism. In 1972 his government voiced dissatisfaction with investment in uranium production during Georges Pompidou's visit.

Disorder followed allegations that ministers were misappropriating food aid, and critics said he was consolidating power by limiting cabinet posts to fellow Djerma, relatives and friends. On 15 April 1974 Lieutenant Colonel Seyni Kountché led a military coup that ended his rule. Diori was imprisoned for six years, and after his release in 1980 he remained under house arrest until 1987. He then moved to Morocco and died there on 23 April 1989, aged 72.
hamar: Hamar lies in the traditional region of Hedmarken on the shore of Mjøsa, Norway's largest lake, in the south-western part of Hamar Municipality; its built-up area reaches into the neighbouring municipalities of Ringsaker and Stange. The name comes from the old Hamar farm, Old Norse Hamarr, a word meaning rocky hill, on whose land the medieval market was first built. Its coat of arms, a black grouse on a pine tree, was granted on 2 June 1896, but an older version was already described in the Hamar Chronicle of 1553.

Between 500 and 1000 the nearby Åker farm was one of the main centres of power in Norway. Presumably after 1030, the centre moved to the peninsula now called Domkirkeodden, perhaps on the initiative of Harald Hardråde, who held property there. The town is said to have been at its height in the early 14th century, dominated by the cathedral, the bishop's manor and a fortress, and known for its apple orchards as well as its merchants, craftsmen and fishermen.

By 1587 merchants of Christiania had drawn all of Hamar's market trade to their own town, and Hamar lost its status as a kjøpstad; by the 17th century it had ceased to exist as a town and its site was farmed as Storhamar. Frederick III gave the estate to Hannibal Sehested in 1649. Plans for a new trading town on Mjøsa date from 1755, and the modern town was laid out on a grid by the army engineer Røyem. Johannes Bay arrived in October 1849 to organise its first elections, and Christian Borchgrevink became its first mayor. In 1860 the lake flooded the front streets, the worst flood recorded since 1789.

The Hedmark museum on Domkirkeodden shows the remains of the medieval cathedral under a protective glass housing, with the bishop's fortress and old farmhouses. Hamar is a railway junction between two lines from Oslo to Trondheim and home of the Norwegian Railway Museum, and it hosted figure skating, short track and speed skating at the 1994 Winter Olympics.
hambach-festival: The Palatinate on the west bank of the Rhine had been occupied by French Revolutionary troops in 1794 and incorporated into the French First Republic in 1801, and after Napoleon's defeat it passed to the Kingdom of Bavaria, whose people suffered high taxes and growing censorship. Student fraternities, the Burschenschaften, had carried the black, red and gold colours of the Lützow Free Corps since 1815, and though suppressed by the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819, the democratic movement revived after the French July Revolution of 1830 and the November Uprising in Poland, whose emigrants were warmly received in Bavaria.

In January 1832 journalists founded an association for freedom of the press and speech, which the state government banned almost at once. Because demonstrations were forbidden, its founders called a fair at Hambach Castle instead. Workmen, women, students and members of parliament came, with guests from France and a delegation of 17 to 20 Polish emigrants. Speakers including Philipp Jakob Siebenpfeiffer and Johann G. A. Wirth blamed Germany's weakness on its division into thirty-eight states, and Henry Brueggemann led the crowd in swearing the oath of the Swiss cantons as Schiller gives it in his Tell.

The meeting demanded liberty, civil and political rights, national unity and popular sovereignty against the Holy Alliance, but it reached no agreement on action: members of the Burschenschaften called for open revolt and a provisional government, which the journalists rejected. The song Fürsten zum Land Hinaus! originated at the festival and later became the unofficial anthem of the 1848 revolution.

Three of the four organisers fled the country, and Wirth, who stayed, was sentenced to two years in prison. On 28 June 1832 the Federal Convention tightened the Carlsbad Decrees again, and in 1833 Bavarian troops dispersed attempts to hold the festival on its anniversary, the year about 50 insurgents also failed to start a revolution by storming the Frankfurt guard house. Heinrich Heine called the festival a missed opportunity, yet it is counted a milestone as the first mark made by a republican movement in Germany. Its colours were adopted by the Weimar Republic and are used on the modern German flag.
hamburg: Hamburg lies at a sheltered natural harbour on the southern fanning-out of the Jutland Peninsula, between continental Europe to the south and Scandinavia to the north, with the North Sea to the west and the Baltic Sea to the northeast. It stands on the River Elbe at its confluence with the Alster and Bille, where the 110 km Elbe estuary begins. The city centre is around the Binnenalster and Außenalster, both lakes formed by damming the Alster. The Altes Land, part of the city, is the largest contiguous fruit-producing region in Central Europe.

Claudius Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE, reported the first name for the vicinity as Treva. The name Hamburg comes from the first permanent building on the site, a castle which Charlemagne ordered built in 808. It rose on rocky terrain in a marsh between the Alster and the Elbe as a defence against Slavic incursion and acquired the name Hammaburg, burg meaning castle or fort.

In 834 Hamburg became the seat of a bishopric, whose first bishop, Ansgar, later known as the Apostle of the North, founded the city's early Christian institutions. Two years later it was linked with Bremen to form the Bishopric of Hamburg-Bremen. The town was destroyed repeatedly in its early centuries. In 845 a fleet of 600 Viking ships sailed up the Elbe and destroyed it, when it had about 500 inhabitants. King Mieszko II Lambert of Poland burned it in 1030, and Valdemar II of Denmark raided and occupied it in 1201 and 1214. The Black Death reached Hamburg in 1350 and killed at least 60 per cent of its population, and the city suffered several major fires in the medieval period.

Hamburg was a member of the Hanseatic League and a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. Before the unification of Germany in 1871 it was a fully sovereign city state, and before 1919 it was a civic republic headed constitutionally by a class of hereditary Grand Burghers, or Hanseaten. Later disasters included the Great Fire of 1842, the Allied fire-bombing of 1943 and the North Sea flood of 1962.

Officially the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg, it is the second-largest city in Germany after Berlin and one of the country's three city-states, with Berlin and Bremen. Its population is over 1.9 million. The Port of Hamburg is Germany's largest. The Speicherstadt and Kontorhausviertel were declared World Heritage Sites by UNESCO in 2015.
hamburg-america-line: The Hamburg-Amerikanische Packetfahrt-Actien-Gesellschaft was set up in Hamburg in 1847 with the involvement of leading citizens of the city, among them Adolph Godeffroy, Ferdinand Laeisz, Carl Woermann and August Bolten, and with Berenberg Bank and H. J. Merck & Co. as its main financial backers. It served the market created by German emigration to the United States. In its early years it linked European ports only with North American ones such as Hoboken and New Orleans, and in time it opened lines to every continent.

The line carried many of the roughly two to three million Jews who left Eastern Europe for North America between 1880 and 1924 after the pogroms in the Russian Empire. In 1900 it built a large ocean liner terminal at Cuxhaven, linked to Hamburg by its own railway, which remained the main departure point for emigrants to North America until 1969. Its liner Austria sank in 1858 with the loss of 449 lives. The Mediterranean voyage of the Augusta Victoria from 22 January to 22 March 1891, with 241 passengers including Albert Ballin and his wife, is often called the first passenger cruise.

The liner Deutschland won the Blue Riband in 1900, 1901 and 1903, and in 1912 the Amerika was the first ship to warn the Titanic of icebergs. Ballin held that safety, size and comfort would always beat speed and planned the three largest liners yet built, the Imperator, Vaterland and Bismarck. The Vaterland was interned at Hoboken in 1914 and served the United States as the troopship Leviathan; after the war the other two went to Britain as reparations and became Cunard's Berengaria and White Star's Majestic. In 1939 the company's liner St. Louis could find no port in Cuba, the United States or Canada to accept the more than 950 Jewish refugees aboard and had to return to Europe.

The company lost almost its entire fleet in each world war. In the post-war years it rebuilt and turned to container cargo, and on 1 September 1970, after 123 years of independence, it merged with its old rival from Bremen to form Hapag-Lloyd. In 2008 the City of Hamburg and a group of private investors, the Albert Ballin Consortium, acquired Hapag-Lloyd. The Cuxhaven terminal is now a museum and cruise ship terminal.
hamburg-dramaturgy: Lessing wrote the essays while he worked as dramaturg for Abel Seyler's Hamburg National Theatre. The idea of a journal in which Lessing would comment as a critic on the theatre's work came from its founder, Johann Friedrich Löwen, and from Seyler, who agreed at first reluctantly but was won over by its success. German theatre was then in a new phase of self-reflection, with actors trying to show the inner and outer lives of their characters at once. The plays of the new bourgeois theatre had grown more detailed and complicated, and audiences often felt confused or left out; the series was in part a response to this.

The work is not a unified, systematic book but a series of 101 short essays written as commentary on the theatre's productions. They take up Aristotle's theory of tragedy, the theory of acting, the place of theatre in society, the means by which theatre moves its audience, criticism of actors and plays, problems of translation and an early theory of the psychology of the emotions. On the critic's task Lessing wrote that his discernment lies in distinguishing, whenever he feels pleasure or displeasure, how far that feeling should be credited to the writer and how far to the actor. He treated the judging of actors as harder than the judging of texts, since a performance depends on its circumstances.

Many of the Hamburg actors were angered by what they took as Lessing's disregard of their talents. The essays defined the new field of dramaturgy and introduced the term, and they influenced later German theatre artists, Bertolt Brecht among them. Helen Zimmern's English translation of 1890, reissued by Dover in 1962, leaves out nearly 30 per cent of the text; a complete annotated translation by Wendy Arons and Sara Figal, edited by Natalya Baldyga, was being published online at MediaCommons Press, to be followed by a print edition from Routledge.
hamburger-bank: The Hamburg City Council decided to found the bank in February 1619, after long negotiations with the city's civic bodies, to restore monetary stability during the Kipper und Wipper crisis of debased German coinage and to make trade between merchants simpler. The English merchant adventurers, Portuguese Sephardi Jews and Dutch religious refugees then living in Hamburg brought capital and knowledge to it. On 20 November 1619 a lending department, the Lehnbanco, was set up to make loans against collateral to merchants and to the city itself.

The bank was run without pay by two senators, two city elders, two treasury citizens and five bank citizens who held accounts there, and it had its premises in Hamburg City Hall. An account needed an opening deposit of at least 400 Lübeck marks, and bills of exchange above that sum had to pass through the bank. Its unit of account was the reichsthaler banco, worth 3 marks banco or 48 schillings banco; silver deposited was credited in these units, and account holders could pay one another without moving coin.

Contemporaries praised its integrity. The economist Paul Jacob Marperger wrote in 1717 that no bank in the world was better for the purity of its money, and the Savary brothers noted in 1750 that its exactness had won it a great reputation across Europe. Merchants kept their books in marks banco, and its daily rate for gold against silver was the most important of the rates it published.

Unsecured loans troubled the bank, and it was reformed in 1770, when its silver standard was also adjusted. Under Napoleonic rule it was looted and struck by economic crisis, but it survived. After the unification of Germany it became a branch of the Reichsbank at the end of 1875. The new national currency was named the mark partly to soften Hamburg's regret at losing its bank, and the mark banco was exchanged at 1.5 German marks.
hamdanid-dynasty: The Hamdanids ruled Upper Mesopotamia and Syria. They were a Shia Muslim Arab dynasty descended from Adi ibn Usama al-Taghlibi and the ancient Banu Taghlib tribe of Mesopotamia and Arabia, and historical sources sometimes call them Adawis or Taghlibis. The dynasty was founded by Hamdan ibn Hamdun. By 892 to 893 he held Mardin, after fighting the Kharijites of the Jazira. In 895 Caliph al-Mutadid invaded and Hamdan fled; he later surrendered and was imprisoned.

Hamdan's sons held office under the caliphs. Abdallah became governor of Mosul in 905 to 906, campaigned against the Kurds and was dismissed and reinstated. His brother Husayn was made governor of Diyar Rabi'a, revolted in 916 after a disagreement with the vizier Ali ibn Isa, and was captured and executed in 918. During their rule the Hamdanids intermarried with Kurdish dignitaries. Nasir al-Dawla, governor of Mosul and Diyar Bakr from 929, ruled so harshly that his own family deposed him. His lineage still ruled in Mosul, despite a heavy defeat by the Buyids in 979, until 990, after which northern Iraq was divided between the Uqaylids and the Marwanids.

Ali Sayf al-Dawla, the Sword of the Dynasty, ruled northern Syria from Aleppo between 945 and 967 and became the most important opponent of the re-expansion of the Christian Byzantine Empire. His court was a centre of culture and fostered Arabic literature, but it lost that standing after the Byzantine sacking of Aleppo. To stop the Byzantine advance Aleppo was put under the suzerainty of the Fatimids of Egypt, and in 1003 the Fatimids deposed the Hamdanids.

The Aleppo line was ruled in turn by Sayf al-Dawla, Sa'd al-Dawla from 967 to 991 and Sa'id al-Dawla from 991 to 1002, who was deposed by the ghulam Lu'lu' al-Kabir. In the Jazira the rulers after Nasir al-Dawla were Abu Taghlib from 967 to 978, then direct administration as part of the Buyid-controlled Abbasid Caliphate from 979 to 981, and two sons of Nasir al-Dawla in 989 to 990, who were deposed by the Uqaylid chieftain Muhammad ibn al-Musayyab.
hamdullahi: The ruins of Hamdullahi, also spelled Hamdallahi or Hamdallaye, lie 21 km south-east of Mopti in the Mopti Region of Mali, on a site east of the Bani River and west of the Bandiagara plateau. The name comes from the Arabic for "Praise to God". Walls of sun-dried mudbrick enclosed the town, which covered an area of 244 hectares, and the line of the walls and part of the street plan can still be seen in satellite images.

At the centre of the town the mosque and Seku Amadu's palace stood side by side, so that the seat of the ruler and the main place of prayer shared one site. Both were built of sun-dried brick, except for the enclosing walls of the palace, which were of stone. The mosque was rebuilt and reopened in 2004, and a town of the same name in the Mopti Region carries on the old capital's name.

Bintou Sanankoua rejects estimates that put the population of the capital in the hundreds of thousands. Working from the number of people who prayed at the mosque, she arrives at a figure of about 11,200. Most of the inhabitants were Fula, and they had come to the capital from every part of the Massina Empire.

The town fell to El Hadj Umar Tall, the Toucouleur conqueror, on 16 March 1862, after three major battles that cost more than 70,000 lives. Its capture marked the effective end of the Massina Empire, and the walled town that had served as the empire's capital for some four decades was afterwards abandoned and left in ruins.
hame-castle: The castle stands in Hämeenlinna, in Kanta-Häme, the city between Helsinki and Tampere. It was built on an island, but now sits on the shore of lake Vanajavesi. It consists of a central keep surrounded by curtain walls and enclosed by a moat. The keep once had five turrets, of which two can still be seen, and the curtain wall has a gatehouse, battlements, an octagonal brick corner turret and a round gun turret. The lower courses of both are of dressed granite and the upper ones of red brick.

The castle's age is disputed. Tradition ties its building to Birger Jarl's Second Swedish Crusade. A fortification of the early 1300s at Hakoinen, some 20 kilometres away, complicates the dating: a royal document of 1308 lists only one castle in Häme, Tauestahus, and the Novgorod First Chronicle mentions only one during the Russian raid on Häme in 1311, in terms that match the castle at Hakoinen.

Besides being a military fortress, the castle was a residence of Swedish nobility. It was partly restored in the early 1600s, and in 1639 the settlement beside it received town rights as Hämeenlinna. Through the 17th and 18th centuries Swedish rule neglected it, as its military interests turned to the southern Baltic, and during the Great Northern War it was briefly in the hands of the Russian army. After the Finnish War, when Finland became a grand duchy under Russian rule, the castle was turned into a prison.

The castle served as a prison until 1953, when large-scale restoration began. Since 1979 it has been a public museum run by the Finnish National Board of Antiquities, and its rooms are also hired out for events, among them Renaissance fairs.
hamengkubuwono-i: Hamengkubuwono I was born Raden Mas Sujana at Kartasura on 16 August 1717. His senior queen consort, Gusti Kanjeng Ratu Kencana, was his first cousin, a granddaughter of Pakubuwana I through his son Bendara Pangeran Harya Dipanegara of Madiun. His second queen consort, Gusti Kanjeng Ratu Kadipaten, was a daughter of Kyai Ageng Drepayuda. He also had several concubines, among them Bendara Raden Ayu Dayaasmara, a daughter of Ngabehi Kramaleksana.

He reigned as the first sultan of Yogyakarta from 1755 to 1792. Ratu Kencana's son Raden Mas Entho had been installed as crown prince before the Treaty of Giyanti, but he fell ill and died soon after a visit to Borobudur. The Kronik Suksesi Keraton Jawa 1755-1989 places the visit in late August 1758 and reports that the prince had a relationship with a Chinese woman, which was thought highly improper for a crown prince and angered his father.

The prince was believed to have died of food poisoning at the age of 19, though it is uncertain who ordered it: some accounts blame his father and others C. Donkel, the first VOC Resident of Yogyakarta. In 1758 Raden Mas Sundoro, the son of Ratu Kadipaten, born in 1750, was circumcised and appointed the new crown prince.

Hamengkubuwono I died at Yogyakarta on 24 March 1792 and was succeeded by Sundoro as Hamengkubuwana II, who lived until 1828. Another son, born to a concubine, Bendara Pangeran Harya Natakusuma, later became Paku Alam I, and his daughter by Ratu Kencana, styled Gusti Kanjeng Ratu Bendara, married Mangkunegara I. In 2006 he was made a National Hero of Indonesia for his fight against the Dutch and his establishment of Yogyakarta.
hamengkubuwono-ix: Hamengkubuwono IX was born on 12 April 1912 in Yogyakarta as Gusti Raden Mas Dorodjatun, the ninth son of Prince Gusti Pangeran Puruboyo, later Hamengkubuwono VIII. At the age of four he was sent to live with the Mulder family, who were Dutch and called him Henkie. He attended Dutch schools in Yogyakarta, Semarang and Bandung, and in 1930 went to the Netherlands, where he finished the Lyceum Haarlem in 1934 and then studied Indology at Leiden. He returned to the Indies in October 1939 without finishing, because of the start of the Second World War. His father died on 22 October 1939, and his relatives agreed that he should succeed.

He was crowned on 18 March 1940, after four months of negotiation with the Dutch governor, Lucien Adam, over the terms of the political contract. In his coronation speech he said that although he had tasted Western education, he was and would always be a Javanese. Under the Japanese occupation, which began in 1942, he kept autonomy in his area, and he is credited with sparing many of his people forced labour by manipulating agricultural statistics and with proposing the irrigation canal between the Progo and Opak rivers.

After the declaration of independence on 17 August 1945, he and Paku Alam VIII decided to support the Republic of Indonesia, which made him governor of Yogyakarta, now a Special Region. In early 1946 the capital was quietly moved to Yogyakarta, and he gave the new government funds. When Dutch troops occupied the city on 21 December 1948 and arrested Sukarno and Hatta, he stayed and refused to cooperate with Dutch plans to make him head of a federal state.

He conceived the General Offensive of 1 March 1949, in which Lieutenant Colonel Suharto's troops held Yogyakarta for six hours, with his palace used as a hideout; Suharto later claimed credit for the idea in his 1989 autobiography. The Dutch handed authority over Yogyakarta to him on 30 June 1949. He then served as minister of defence and in other posts, and as minister of economics, finance and industry from 1966 to 1973. In March 1978, after troops took over the Bandung Technological Institute when its students published a book against Suharto's re-election, he declined renomination as vice-president, citing his health.

He led the national Scout movement from 1968 and received the Bronze Wolf of the World Organization of the Scout Movement in 1973. He died on 2 October 1988 in Washington, D.C., after sudden internal bleeding, and was buried in the royal mausoleum of the Mataram monarchs at Imogiri. A museum in the palace at Yogyakarta is dedicated to him. He was named a National Hero of Indonesia, and his son succeeded him as Hamengkubuwono X.
hami: Hami, in Uyghur Kumul, lies in eastern Xinjiang on the border with Gansu. The city stands in a fault depression about 759 metres above sea level, under mountain ranges that rise to about 4,900 metres. Its climate is a dry continental desert one. The Tang pilgrim Xuanzang described it as the first of a string of oases supplied by the Tian Shan, whose water had been kept in underground wells and channels since time immemorial.

Its oldest known native name is Cumuḍa, given by the people Han sources call the Xiao Yuezhi in the 1st millennium BCE. In Chinese it was Yiwu under the Han and Yizhou under the Tang, and the Mongols called it Qamil. Marco Polo wrote of Camul, and from the Ming dynasty Chinese sources used the name Hami.

The Han set up military agricultural colonies at the oasis and struggled with the Xiongnu for control of it. It was noted for melons, raisins and wine. The Northern Wei occupied the region in 456 and raided the Rouran Khaganate from it, and the First Turkic Khaganate took control after the 6th century. The Tang asserted control in the 7th century, and the Tibetan Empire and the Tang vied for the region until the Chinese were repelled in 851. After the collapse of the Uyghur Khaganate a group of Uyghurs settled in the Hami region and brought linguistic and cultural change.

The Mongols conquered it under the Yuan dynasty. Gunashiri, a descendant of Chagatai Khan, founded the small state of Qara Del there, which accepted Ming supremacy, and the Ming established Kumul Hami in 1404. Oirat Mongols later controlled it, and it was conquered and converted to Islam in 1513. From the 18th century Kumul was the centre of the Kumul Khanate, a semi-autonomous vassal state within the Qing Empire and then the Republic of China as part of Xinjiang. Its last ruler was Maqsud Shah.

Hami is a prefecture-level city, formed in 2016 when the former county-level city merged with Hami Prefecture and became Yizhou District. It is still known for its sweet melons, and the Lanzhou–Xinjiang Railway and China National Highway 312 pass through it.
hamid-idris-awate: Awate was born in Gerset, between Tessenei and Golluj in south-western Italian Eritrea, and was of Beni-Amer descent. Accounts of his early life differ. According to many sources he served as an Eritrean ascari in the Italian conquest of Ethiopia and the East African Campaign before deserting after the Battle of Gondar; others say he was a non-commissioned officer in the Sudan Defence Force during the Second World War, or a farmer in the Ghinda area before becoming a shifta, an outlaw, in 1941.

In the early 1940s he settled in western Eritrea, gathered a band of 50 men and raided the Kunama and Nara from 1942 to 1948. The British authorities offered a large reward for his capture, and in 1951 he and his men surrendered after the British agreed not to prosecute him. After 1956 he took up arms again, in response to attacks by Christian highland shifta and in protest at the land policy of the Ethiopian officials who had taken control of Eritrea.

In July 1960 Eritrean students and intellectuals in Cairo founded the Eritrean Liberation Front, and Awate was persuaded, possibly by his fellow Beni-Amer Idris Mohammed Adam, to continue his fight under its banner; he asked for money and weapons and received a few old rifles. Warned by a Muslim in the police of a plan to arrest him in August 1961, he fled to Mount Adal, west of Agordat. On 1 September 1961 eleven fighters under his command attacked police posts in western Eritrea, and a fight of 30 minutes ended in stalemate.

On 27 May 1962 Awate told his unit that he felt unwell, and he died the next morning; by one account he first gave his gun to Kiboob Hajaj, urging the continuation of the revolution. His companions buried him in secret and kept his death hidden for four years. The Government of Eritrea raised a statue at his grave on 1 September 1994, and on 16 October 2011 the Italian town of Cologno Monzese dedicated a tree to him in its Garden of the Just of the World.
hamidullah-khan: Hamidullah Khan was born on 9 September 1894. He studied at the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, now Aligarh Muslim University, and at Allahabad University, where he graduated with a BA in law in 1915. On 5 September 1925 at Peshawar he married Maimoona Sultan Shah Banu Begum, a great-great-granddaughter of Shuja Shah Durrani of Afghanistan, and they had three daughters: Abida Sultan, Sajida Sultan and Rabia Sultan. He came to the throne of Bhopal in 1926, when his mother abdicated in his favour.

He was Chancellor of Aligarh Muslim University from September 1930 to April 1935 and a delegate to the Round Table Conference in London. Knighted with the GCIE in 1929 and the GCSI in 1932, he also held military rank, rising to Air Commodore in 1943, Air Vice-Marshal in 1945 and Major-General in 1946. During the Second World War he was present at the Battle of Keren and the Battle of El Alamein.

His term as Chancellor of the Chamber of Princes ran from 1944 to 1947, when India became independent as the Dominion of India. He was very close to Muhammad Ali Jinnah and on good terms with Louis Mountbatten, the Viceroy and Governor General. Despite pressure from Jinnah, he reluctantly agreed to have Bhopal join the Union of India, and his rule ended in 1949.

In 1947 he married a second wife, Aftab Jahan Begum, from a Bhopali Muslim family, and their daughter Farzana was born in 1948. He kept the title of Nawab until his death on 4 February 1960, and was succeeded in it by his second daughter, Sajida Sultan, Begum of Bhopal. His long list of honours ran from the Delhi Durbar medals of 1903 and 1911 to the Indian Independence Medal of 1947 and the Queen Elizabeth II Coronation Medal of 1953.
hamilcar-barca: Little is known of the Barca family before the Punic Wars. One suggestion is that it came from Cyrene; another is that it belonged to the landed aristocracy of Carthage. The epithet Barca, in Punic brq, means thunderbolt or shining. Hamilcar was the father of Hannibal, Hasdrubal and Mago and the father-in-law of Hasdrubal the Fair. He was 28 when he received the command in Sicily in 247 BCE, and he already had three daughters.

Hamilcar commanded the Carthaginian land forces in Sicily from 247 to 241 BCE with a small mercenary army and little money. Carthage invested few men in the island, and his aim was probably to keep a stalemate. He fought a guerrilla war against the Romans, moved his army by night to the slopes of Mount Eryx in 244 BCE and held it for about three years, supplied by road from Drepana. When the Romans in 241 BCE demanded that he surrender his army's arms and Roman deserters, he refused, and the army left Sicily under arms.

The army then rebelled over unpaid wages in the Mercenary War. After Hanno the Great failed to defeat the rebels, Carthage gave Hamilcar command of 10,000 men and 70 elephants. He won at the Bagradas, and when the rebels led by Spendius trapped him in a valley he was saved by the defection of the Numidian chieftain Naravas with 2,000 horsemen, who later married his third daughter. He then crushed the rebel army and crucified Spendius and other hostages outside Tunis. Hamilcar allied with Hasdrubal the Fair against Hanno's aristocratic party and avoided trial for having caused the war with unrealistic promises to his soldiers.

In 237 BCE Hamilcar led an expedition to Iberia, with Hasdrubal the Fair and the nine-year-old Hannibal. Before he left Hannibal is said to have sworn never to be a friend of Rome; some modern historians read this as lifelong enmity, others call that a distortion.

Hamilcar secured the gold and silver mines of the Sierra Morena, defeated the Turdetani and a 50,000-strong army under Indortes, whom he crucified, and in four years of campaigns subdued the country between Gades and Cape Nao. He probably founded Akra Leuke, now Alicante, in 235 BCE, and built a professional army of Iberians, Africans and Numidians that Hasdrubal inherited and Hannibal later led. When a Roman embassy came in 231 BCE he answered that he was gathering booty to pay Carthage's war indemnity.

He died in 228 BCE while besieging a town. Appian says he was thrown from his horse and drowned in a river; Polybius says he fell in battle against an unnamed tribe. A third version has the Oretani chieftain Orissus attack him as he retreated across the Júcar.
hamilcar-i-of-carthage: Hamilcar belonged to the Magonid house and is counted as king of Carthage from 510 to 480 BCE. By the end of the 6th century BCE Carthage had conquered most of the old Phoenician colonies of North Africa, among them Hadrumetum, Utica and Kerkouane, subjugated some of the Libyan tribes and taken control of parts of the coast from modern Morocco to the borders of Cyrenaica. A treaty with Rome signed in 509 BCE divided influence and trade between the two cities and is the first known source suggesting that Carthage controlled parts of Sicily and Sardinia.

In Sicily Carthage held Motya, Panormus and Soluntum by 500 BCE, and by 490 BCE it had concluded treaties with the Greek cities of Selinus, Himera and Zankle. From 485 BCE Gelo, tyrant of Syracuse, tried to unite the island under his rule. When his father-in-law Theron of Akragas deposed the tyrant of Himera in 483 BCE, Carthage decided to intervene, urged on by the tyrant of Rhegion, the deposed ruler's father-in-law.

Hamilcar spent three years preparing the largest Carthaginian overseas expedition to that date. Its sailing coincided with the expedition of Xerxes against mainland Greece in 480 BCE, which has led to speculation about an alliance between Carthage and Persia against the Greeks, although no firm evidence of one exists. Storms battered the fleet on the way, and the army was then destroyed at Himera by the combined forces of Himera, Akragas and Syracuse under Gelo.

Hamilcar died in that defeat. Carthage made peace with the Greeks and paid an indemnity of 2,000 silver talents, but it lost no territory in Sicily. At home the old government of entrenched nobility gave way to the Carthaginian Republic: kings were still elected, but the senate and the Tribunal of 104 gained the upper hand and the office of Suffet grew in influence.

Mainland Greeks cut off Carthage's sea-borne trade with the Middle East and the cities of Magna Graecia boycotted its traders, so Carthage developed trade with the West and caravan trade with the East. Hamilcar's son Gisco was exiled. For seventy years Carthage made no recorded moves against the Greeks, which has been taken as a sign that the defeat left it militarily crippled for a time.
hammer-deroburt: Hammer DeRoburt was born on Nauru on 25 September 1922. His maternal grandfather Daimon was head chief of the island from 1920 to 1930. After school on Nauru he attended the Gordon Institute of Technology in Geelong, Australia, and worked as a teacher. During the Second World War the Japanese deported him to Truk with most of the Nauruan population, and he returned in 1946 to work in the Department of Education. In 1953 he led the Nauru Workers' Organisation in a four-month strike that won higher wages and more training from the Australian administration. He was elected to the Local Government Council in 1955 and became Head Chief of Nauru in 1956.

As head chief he lobbied the United Nations Trusteeship Council directly. In 1957 he protested the British Phosphate Commission's continued exploitation of the island's phosphate. In 1962 he and two colleagues called for independence. When the Australian government offered resettlement on Curtis Island in Queensland, he insisted on full sovereignty over it, which was refused, so the council rejected resettlement altogether. He signed the Nauru Island Phosphate Industry Agreement in June 1967, which provided for Nauruan ownership of the phosphate reserves, and the Nauru Independence Act 1967 gave independence from 31 January 1968.

DeRoburt was elected the first president on 17 May 1968, when the constitution was adopted, and held the external affairs, internal affairs and island development portfolios. His government created the Nauru Phosphate Corporation, Air Nauru and Nauru Pacific Shipping Lines. In December 1976 Bernard Dowiyogo defeated him by nine votes to seven, and he returned to the presidency in 1978. His terms ran 1968 to 1976, 1978 to 1986, 1986 and 1986 to 1989, with a short interval under Kennan Adeang. In his last term Nauru brought a case against Australia in the International Court of Justice over the rehabilitation of mined land. He died in Melbourne on 15 July 1992.
hammir-singh: Hammir was the only child of Ari Singh, eldest of the nine sons of Lakshman Singh, Thakur of the village of Sisoda near Nathdwara, and of Urmila, a Chauhan Rajput from Unnava near Kelwara. When Alauddin Khilji besieged Chittorgarh, Lakshman Singh and seven of his sons died fighting to the death in saka, while their women committed jauhar. A wounded son, Ajay Singh, was smuggled out to Kelwara and sent for Hammir, who impressed him by killing Munja Balecha, a Bhil chief of Godwar, and was chosen as successor.

The Khaljis had given Chittorgarh to Sonagara Maldev, ruler of Jalore. Hammir's first attacks on it failed, his resources dwindled and many followers left, and he set out on a pilgrimage to Dwarka. At Khod in Gujarat the Charan mystic Aai Birwadi, held to be an incarnation of Hinglaj, urged him to return, and her son Baruji, a horse dealer, joined him at Kherwara with 500 horses. Maldev married his daughter Songari to Hammir, and with his Charan allies Hammir took Chittorgarh after Muhammad bin Tughluq came to the throne.

Rajput bardic chronicles such as the 17th-century Nainsi ri Khyat claim that Hammir defeated the sultan himself at Singoli, held him for six months and released him for Ajmer, Ranthambor, Nagaur, 5 million rupees and 100 elephants. These claims lack corroboration, and the Delhi army was led by another general. A Jain temple inscription of 1438 attests that Hammir's forces defeated a Muslim army, and Mewar may afterwards have been practically independent of the sultanate.

After regaining Chittor, Hammir built the Annapoorna Mata temple in Chittor Fort, dedicated to Aai Birwadi, and the old temple of Roopnarayan Ji in Sewantri. The Mahavir Prasad Prashasti calls him the vanquisher of the Turushkas, and the historian John Darwin counts Mewar among the few Hindu states that withstood the Turkic invasions. Baburao Painter made a silent film about him, Rana Hamir, in 1925.
hammira-mahakavya: Nayachandra Suri was not a contemporary of his hero. His grandfather and teacher, the poet Jayasimha Suri, knew six languages. Nayachandra was possibly a court poet of the Tomara ruler Virama: he states that he wrote the poem in answer to a challenge at Virama's court that no living poet could compose a kavya to equal those of Kalidasa, Bilhana and the other ancient poets, and that Hammira appeared to him in a dream urging him to write it.

Scholars differ on the date and place: Cynthia Talbot suggests it was composed to please a Chauhan ruler, Phyllis Granoff that it was written at the Tomara court around 1420. His disciple Nayahamsa copied the manuscript in 1496, and N. J. Kirtane based the first edition on that copy.

The poem has 1,500 verses in 14 cantos. It opens with an invocation using words of double meaning that can refer to either a Hindu deity or a Jain tirthankara. Cantos 1 to 4 treat Hammira's ancestors, beginning with Chahamana, a hero said to have sprung from the sun to protect Brahma's sacrifice at Pushkar; cantos 5 to 7 describe his sports and festivities; the next cantos tell of his conquests, from Malwa to Abu and Shakambhari.

The last third tells of his war with Ala-ud-Din Khalji, provoked when Hammira gave refuge to rebel Mongol nobles, among them Mahima Sahi. After defeats of Ullu Khan's armies and the death of Nusrat Khan, the fort falls through betrayal: the general Ratipala, promised the governorship of Ranthambore, persuades another general, Ranamalla, to desert, and the granary proves empty. The queens and daughters burn themselves, and Hammira, wounded in a final sortie, cuts his own throat.

N. J. Kirtane, who translated the poem into English in 1899, dismissed its account of the early kings as filled with fanciful conceptions but judged it fairly historic from Prithviraja III to Hammira. Asoke Kumar Majumdar called parts of it very unreliable, and R. B. Singh rated it below the Prithviraja Vijaya, composed two centuries earlier. Kalika Ranjan Kanungo called it pseudo-historical; Muni Jinavijaya presented it in 1968 as a national poem of an Indian hero against a foreign ruler.
hammuda-pasha-bey: Hammuda was the son of Murad I Bey and an odalisque named Yasmine, both from Corsica. His father married him to Princess Aziza Othmana, a granddaughter of Othman Dey. Her inheritance and the property Hammuda gave her formed the largest habous, or religious endowment, in the country, believed to total almost 90,000 hectares, whose revenues supported the needy and religious buildings in Tunis, Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem until it was dissolved in 1957. His later marriages mostly sealed political alliances.

Hammuda led many expeditions against dissident tribes in the north-west and south of the country.
