In 1637 he arranged the election of Usta Murad, an old corsair and friend of his father, as dey, and from the next dey, Ahmed Khodja Dey, he obtained a bodyguard of almost 600 foot soldiers drawn from the sipahis. Djerba, held by the pasha of Tripoli, was annexed for good in his reign, largely through the diplomacy of Yusuf Dey. By 1647 he appointed all officials and controlled the janissaries of Tunis, and in 1659 Sultan Mehmed IV named him pasha.

When a French squadron came to curb Tunisian piracy, he signed a treaty on 25 December 1665 giving the French consul precedence and the right to trade throughout the country. He built many souks of the Medina of Tunis, palaces including the Dar Hammouda Pacha, a hospital, and in 1655 the Hammouda Pacha Mosque in the Turkish style with an octagonal minaret. In 1643 he bought the old Hafsid palace at Le Bardo and enlarged it with orchards, a hammam and a funduq.

From 1663, tired by age, he handed power step by step to his three sons: Murad II Bey received the beylik, Mohamed el-Hafsi Bey the south, and Hussein Bey the districts on the border with Algeria. Hammuda died on 13 April 1666 at Dar El Bey and was buried in the mausoleum beneath his mosque. The chronicler Bin Abi Dinar al-Kairaouani wrote that in his reign merchants could travel everywhere without arms.
hammudid-dynasty: The Hammudids traced their descent from Idris ibn Abdallah, founder of the Idrisid dynasty and a great-grandson of Hasan ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad. In the Andalusian civil war, after the caliph Sulayman took Córdoba from Hisham II in 1013, he rewarded the Berber chiefs who had backed him with lands in southern al-Andalus, and two Hammudid brothers, Ali ibn Hammud and al-Qasim ibn Hammud, received the governorship of Algeciras, Ceuta and Tangier. As Sulayman's power collapsed, they set out to take power themselves, trusting their lineage to set them apart from other local lords.

Claiming to act for Hisham II, Ali marched on Córdoba in 1016, defeated Sulayman and had him executed for the former caliph's murder, and took power on 3 July 1016 as caliph al-Nasir. Many of his supporters, disappointed when Hisham was declared dead, proclaimed the Umayyad Abd al-Rahman IV, and Ali was assassinated on 22 March 1018. His brother al-Qasim became caliph al-Ma'mun, but Ali's son Yahya took Córdoba in August 1021 as caliph al-Mu'tali. Recalled on 9 November 1025, Yahya found an empty treasury and no working government, left his vizier in charge and returned to Málaga.

From Málaga Yahya kept the caliphal title and, after taking Algeciras with help from the Zirids of Granada, ruled an independent taifa. Idris I al-Muta'ayyad, who succeeded him in 1036, fought the Abbadid taifa of Seville and won the Battle of Écija in 1039. After Idris the realm was divided, Málaga going to his son Yahya II al-Qa'im and Algeciras to Muhammad ibn al-Qasim. The saqaliba general Naya al-Siqlabi overthrew Hasan al-Mustansir, but Naya was assassinated the same year and the family regained the throne.

For the next decade members of the family fought one another. Idris II al-Ali ruled Málaga twice, alternating with kinsmen such as Muhammad I al-Mahdi and Idris III al-Muwaffaq, while in Algeciras Muhammad was followed in 1048 by his son al-Qasim al-Wathiq. In the end the Zirids, once their allies, took Málaga, and Algeciras fell to the rival Abbadids in 1058.
hammurabi: Hammurabi was the sixth Amorite king of Babylon and the son of Sin-muballit. His reign came after the fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur in 2004 BCE, when Mesopotamia was divided among several kingdoms ruled by Amorite dynasties, of which Isin and then Larsa were the strongest in the south. Babylon had been a secondary city until an Amorite dynasty took root there around 1880 BCE with Sumu-la-El. Babylonian sources give Hammurabi a reign of 43 years. The first two decades are poorly documented, and the names of the years of that time refer chiefly to public works and offerings to the gods.

Elam, whose heartland lay in the south-west of present-day Iran, expanded into the Mesopotamian plain and subjugated Eshnunna. This led to war with a coalition of kingdoms that included Babylon and Mari, and the Elamites were eventually repelled with great difficulty with the help of troops from Mari and other northern kingdoms. Strengthened by this success, Hammurabi went on to conquer the kingdoms of Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari. Almost all of Mesopotamia came under Babylonian rule, so that it is possible to speak of an empire. His conquests seem to have come mainly from opportunities as they arose, not from a prepared imperial plan.

Hammurabi is best known for his law code, which is said to have been inspired by Shamash, the Babylonian god of justice. It was written towards the end of his reign and is known mainly from a large stele, which shows the king facing Shamash. It has a prologue, a set of provisions and an epilogue. It is not the only Mesopotamian legislative collection, nor the oldest, but it is the longest known. Its status is debated, and in its prologue and epilogue it presents itself as a commemorative inscription that celebrates his sense of justice. The prologue names the gods who bestow sovereignty, Enlil, Marduk and Ishtar, and his descent from the founder of his dynasty.

Hammurabi also carried out public works. The 33rd year of his reign commemorates a canal named in his honour, which gave perennial water to Nippur, Eridu, Ur, Larsa, Uruk and Isin. He rebuilt sanctuaries, including the ziggurat of Zababa at Kish. Letters found at Mari and at Larsa, more than 200 of the latter addressed to his subordinates, make his the best documented of the Mesopotamian reigns. His son Samsu-iluna failed to maintain the empire. Hammurabi was later revered as a great conqueror, then chiefly as the ideal lawgiver, and archaeologists rediscovered him in the late 19th century. He is seen as an important figure in the history of law.
hampshire: Hampshire is bordered by Berkshire to the north, Surrey and West Sussex to the east, the Solent to the south, Dorset to the west and Wiltshire to the north-west. Undulating hills characterise much of it, with a belt of chalk running from the Hampshire Downs in the north-west to the South Downs in the south-east. The Loddon and Wey drain north into the Thames, while the Itchen and Test flow south into Southampton Water. The south-west holds the New Forest, one of the largest expanses of ancient woodland remaining in England. The county historically contained Bournemouth, Christchurch and the Isle of Wight.

The region is believed to have been continuously occupied since the end of the last Ice Age, its first inhabitants being Mesolithic hunter-gatherers concentrated around the river valleys. Hampshire was incorporated into the Roman province of Britannia soon after the invasion of 43 CE, and its political leaders are generally believed to have accepted this peacefully. Its chief town, Venta Belgarum, now Winchester, became capital of the Belgae. A fortification near Southampton, Clausentum, belonged to the Saxon Shore forts, and a New Forest pottery industry exported widely across southern Britain. The West Saxons moved south in the late seventh century and incorporated Hampshire into their kingdom. The name is attested as Hamtunscir in 755, from the Saxon settlement of Hamtun, now Southampton.

After the Norman Conquest London became the capital, but Winchester remained important, and the New Forest was a prized royal hunting forest, where King William Rufus was killed while hunting in 1100. The Domesday Book of 1086 records 44 hundreds. From the 12th century the ports grew with trade, wool and cloth, fishing and shipbuilding, and by 1523 at the latest Southampton had outstripped Winchester in population. In the two world wars the county played a crucial military role through the Royal Navy base at Portsmouth, the army camp at Aldershot and Netley Hospital. Supermarine, designer of the Spitfire, was based in Southampton, which led to severe bombing of the city in the Second World War.

Hampshire is a ceremonial county in South East England with an area of 3,769 square kilometres and Southampton as its largest settlement. Portsmouth lies in the south-east, Winchester in the centre, and Basingstoke and Andover in the north. Hampshire County Council sits at Castle Hill in Winchester. Its county day is 15 July, St Swithun's Day. The Hambledon Club, formed about 1750, created many of cricket's early laws, and the Battle of Cheriton was fought near Winchester in 1644.
hamu-kanzibe: Hamu was the eldest son of King Mpande, but his father did not favour him, and Zulu succession turned on whose mother Mpande would finally name his Great Wife. Mpande favoured first Umtonga, then Mbuyazi, and at last decided on Cetshwayo. The rivalry led in 1856 to the Battle of Ndondakusuka, in which Mbuyazi and several other sons of Mpande died, and from then on, if not earlier, Cetshwayo was the de facto king while Mpande kept the ceremonial duties.

In 1861, after Cetshwayo ordered the deaths of his half-brothers by Nomantshali, Mpande's favourite wife, Umtonga fled to the Boers of the Utrecht district; the strip of land Cetshwayo offered them for his return became the Disputed Land that led in part to the Anglo-Zulu War. Mpande lived until 1872. To forestall his rivals, chief among them his half-brothers Umtonga and Hamu, Cetshwayo invited the British, in the person of Theophilus Shepstone, to his coronation in September 1873.

Under the Zulu law of succession known as ukuvuza, Hamu was inKosi, or chief, of the Ngenetsheni people of north-western Zululand, whose lands had included part of the Disputed Land. As eldest he had inherited the chiefdom from his uncle Nzibe, the senior son of Senzangakhona, and he kept his stronghold at kwaMfemfe.

Hamu fought on Cetshwayo's side in the Second Zulu Civil War and sat on the Zulu royal council, the iBandla, until 1879. In late 1878 he opened negotiations with the British in the hope of their support for his taking the Zulu throne, and in March 1879 he joined the forces of Evelyn Wood at Kambula. In retribution Cetshwayo sent an army unit to destroy the Ngenetsheni villages and cattle, an act that set the stage for the Third Zulu Civil War of 1883 to 1884.
hamza-ibn-ali: The chief sources on Hamza, the Christian chronicler Yahya of Antioch, the Muslim historian Ibn Zafir and Hamza's own epistles, often contradict one another. According to Ibn Zafir he was originally a felt-maker who emigrated to Fatimid Egypt. He does not appear to have been active before 1017 or 1018, though he may have been in Cairo by 1013. His teaching followed that of al-Hasan ibn Haydara al-Farghani al-Akhram, who had preached that God was manifest in al-Hakim until he was murdered while riding with the caliph.

Hamza took the title leader of the adepts, and his earliest dated epistle comes from July 1017. In an earlier, undated epistle his followers, called for the first time the People of Monotheism, swore obedience to al-Hakim. Unrest forced the caliph to suspend the mission in 1018/19, a year the Druze calendar does not count. The faith took its name from al-Darazi, a like-minded preacher and rival whose relation to Hamza is unclear. On 19 June 1019, the Day of al-Kāʾina in Druze tradition, Hamza's followers proclaimed their beliefs in the Mosque of Amr at Fustat and were lynched by the crowd.

Turkish soldiers then stormed al-Darazi's house and attacked the Raydan Mosque, which Hamza wrote that he held for a whole day with twelve followers until a miraculous appearance of al-Hakim drove the attackers off. With al-Darazi dead, by 1019 Hamza was the almost undisputed leader of the movement, and he organised it like the official Isma'ili daʿwa, with missionaries and a hierarchy of ranks. According to al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, after al-Hakim's disappearance Hamza fled to Mecca, where the Sharif of Mecca had him beheaded before a gate of the Kaaba.

Thirty of the 113 Epistles of Wisdom, numbers 6 to 35, are attributed to Hamza. His teaching drew on Iranian Isma'ili thought, especially Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani, and on neoplatonic ideas of the universal intellect and the world soul. He held that in each cycle of history God takes human form, that the Fatimid caliphs from al-Qa'im onward were such incarnations, and that the proclamation of al-Hakim's divinity closed the cycle of Muhammad and abrogated the Quran and the Sharia. In their place he preached a spiritual law of seven moral principles, and he cast himself as the incarnation of the Universal Intellect.
hamzah-fansuri: Most of what is known of Hamzah Fansuri's life comes from the takhallus bait, the pen-name stanza that ends each of his poems, from the work of his disciple Hasan Fansuri and from commentaries on his poems, and many details are uncertain. His name suggests that he came from Barus, which the Arabs called Fansur, or spent much of his life there. A link to Ayutthaya in Siam has also been proposed, though he may have travelled there rather than been born there.

He joined a Sufi order and is thought to have worked at the court of the Aceh Sultanate. He travelled widely, visiting the Malay Peninsula, Mughal India, Mecca, Medina and Baghdad, and was one of the earliest Southeast Asians known to have made the hajj.

His thought drew on medieval Islamic scholars, above all Ibn Arabi's doctrine of Waḥdat al-Wujūd, the unity of being, then popular in Persia and Mughal India, which taught that all reality is one and that everything that exists is part of the divine. Hamzah saw God as immanent in all things, including the individual, and sought union with the indwelling spirit of God. He used the doctrine of seven stages of emanation, the martabat, through which God manifests himself in the world, ending in the Perfect Man.

Thirty-two of his poems survive, usually of 13 to 15 stanzas and some of up to 21, each naming him in its last stanza. Scholars have noted his technical skill in rhyme, his blending of Arabic words into Malay verse and his fondness for puns. Three prose works survive: Sharab al-'ashiqin, The Lovers' Beverage; Asrar al-'arifin, The Secrets of the Gnostics; and Kitab al-Muntahi, The Adept, a collection of Arabic and Persian quotations discussed in Malay.

His death is generally placed around 1590 or earlier, though a later date in the reign of Sultan Iskandar Muda has also been proposed. His teachings were promoted by the Aceh theologian Shamsuddin al-Sumatrani. After Nuruddin ar-Raniri judged them heretical, holding that they did not conform to the belief that God remains unchanged by his creation, Sultana Taj ul-Alam, under his influence, tried to erase Hamzah's works and name, and his writings were burnt.
hamzat-bek: Hamzat Bek was born in 1789 in the village of Hutsal, or Gotsatl, in the Avar Khanate, to a noble father and a commoner mother, which made him a member of the janka class. His father was close to the Avar khan Ali Sultan Ahmad, and Hamzat spent part of his youth at the khan's residence in Khunzakh, where the khan's widow Pakhu Bike arranged his education in Shafi'i law and Arabic. He gave up drink on meeting the reformer Ghazi Muhammad and joined his movement to impose sharia in place of customary law, though he never joined the Naqshbandiyya-Khalidiyya Sufi order.

He became one of Ghazi Muhammad's main commanders in the holy war against Russia, raiding Georgian settlements in the Alazani valley of Kakheti in the autumn of 1830. In June 1831 he went to negotiate with the Russians, was taken prisoner and sent to Tiflis, and gave his son as a hostage for his release; he rejoined the struggle when the boy died in captivity. Arriving too late to help at Gimry, he was proclaimed imam by the Dagestani ulama and notables at the initiative of the Naqshbandi sheikh Muhammad al-Yaraghi.

At first his rule reached only a few villages, and he used force to bring communities back under the imamate while also proposing peace with Russia if it would not interfere with sharia. In October 1833 he forced Gergebil to accept his rule, defeating the shamkhal, the khan of Mehtuli and the Aqusha confederation. Pakhu Bike, pressed by the Russians, secretly tried to have him murdered in March 1834. After a fight during negotiations killed her sons Nusal and Umma, he stormed Khunzakh and ordered the killing of Pakhu Bike and the women of the royal family.

He was assassinated at Khunzakh in revenge for the destruction of the Avar ruling family, and Shamil succeeded him. The massacre tarnished his reputation, though the eyewitness Hajji Ali called him learned and wise. The historian Moshe Gammer argues that his swift succession preserved the movement, that destroying the khanate let the imamate spread over central Dagestan, and that his regular appointment of deputies (na'ibs) began the imamate's state structures. Michael Kemper describes his reign as a brief aristocratic interlude between Ghazi Muhammad and Shamil.
han-chinese: Han Chinese trace their ancestry and culture to the Huaxia, a confederation of agricultural tribes of the late Neolithic and early Bronze Age that lived along the Guanzhong and Yellow River basins in northern China. Early Chinese history is largely mythical: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian records successive overlords, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, for whom little reliable archaeological evidence exists. The name Han people first appeared during the Northern and Southern period and was inspired by the Han dynasty, and the Chinese language and script came to be called the Han language and Han characters.

Qin and Han rule sent settlers south. Qin Shi Huang is said to have sent several hundred thousand men and fifteen thousand women to settle Lingnan under a general named Zhao Tuo, and the Han emperor Wu later ordered a further two hundred thousand men to build ships to attack and colonize the region. Successive migrations southward fused the newcomers with the peoples south of the Yangtze, while the centres of Han wealth and culture moved from the Yellow River basin to Jiangnan. By the Tang and Song dynasties the Han were the main inhabitants of the fertile lowlands and cities of the south.

Han Chinese have often held the dominant positions of governance, but dynastic rule was in notable periods held by others, among them the Liao (916–1125), the Jin (1115–1234), the Yuan (1271–1368) and the Qing (1644–1912). Sun Yat-sen made the restoration of Han rule a tenet of the 1911 Revolution, which overthrew the Manchu-led Qing and established the Han-dominated Republic of China.

Scholars such as Kevin Carrico and Dru Gladney argue that a single Han identity, set against Manchu rulers, is a modern development promoted by nationalists near the end of the Qing. Liang Qichao coined the term Zhonghua minzu between 1902 and 1905 to refer to the Han; it later became a wider concept for all the peoples of China. Han Chinese make up about 91 percent of the population of China. Their literary heritage includes the Analects, the Tao Te Ching and the Four Great Classical Novels.
han-dynasty: The Han dynasty was established by Liu Bang after the short-lived Qin dynasty collapsed within four years of the death of Qin Shi Huang. Two former rebel leaders, Xiang Yu of Chu and Liu Bang of Han, fought for hegemony, and Liu Bang defeated Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia in 202 BCE. He took the title of emperor and is known after death as Emperor Gaozu. Chang'an, modern Xi'an, became the capital. The dynasty took its name from Hanzhong, the small fief on the Han River that Xiang Yu had given Liu Bang. The Western Han lasted until 9 CE, and the Eastern Han formally began on 5 August 25 CE, when Liu Xiu became Emperor Guangwu.

The Xiongnu defeated the Han in 200 BCE, and the court responded with marriage alliances and payments of tribute. Emperor Wu changed this policy in 133 BCE with a series of campaigns that took the Hexi Corridor and the Tarim Basin from the Xiongnu, helping to establish the Silk Road. He also annexed Nanyue in 111 BCE and Dian in 109 BCE, and in 108 BCE Han forces conquered Gojoseon and set up the Xuantu and Lelang commanderies in Korea. From his reign onward the court sponsored Confucianism, and in 124 BCE he established the Imperial University. To finance his campaigns he nationalised the salt and iron industries in 117 BCE, monopolies repealed under the Eastern Han.

Wang Mang, regent after the death of Emperor Ai, interrupted the dynasty with his Xin dynasty from 9 to 23 CE. After 92 CE palace eunuchs became involved in violent power struggles with the consort clans of the empresses. The Yellow Turban and Five Pecks of Rice rebellions, led by Taoist religious societies, challenged imperial authority in 184. After the death of Emperor Ling in 189 the eunuchs were massacred by military officers, and governors became warlords who divided the empire. The dynasty ended in 220 when Cao Pi, king of Wei, usurped the throne from Emperor Xian.

The emperor stood at the apex of society and was in theory unlimited in power, but ministers pressed him through institutions such as the court conference, and emperors were often minors ruled over by a regent. Below him came the kings of the Liu clan, and the empire was divided into provinces, commanderies and counties, plus semi-autonomous kingdoms that lost autonomy after the Rebellion of the Seven States. Taxes were paid in coin, and the poll tax stimulated a money economy. Han technology included papermaking, which the Han tradition credits to Cai Lun in 105, rudders, raised-relief maps and seismometers. Today the majority ethnic group of China calls itself the Han people.
han-fei: Han Fei was born into the ruling family of the State of Han in the last phase of the Warring States period, which made him unlike most philosophers of his age, who came from outside the aristocracy. Scholars place his birth at about 280 BCE, though the exact year is unknown. Some have read his writings as addressed to his cousin, the King of Han. The Records of the Grand Historian, compiled by Sima Qian, say that he studied alongside the future Qin chancellor Li Si under the Confucian philosopher Xun Kuang, and that a stutter kept him from presenting his ideas in court, though he wrote with great skill.

The Han Feizi is a later anthology traditionally attributed to him. Sima Qian lists among its essays Solitary Indignation, Five Vermin, Inner and Outer Congeries of Sayings, Collected Persuasions and Difficulties in the Way of Persuasion, which he puts at about one hundred thousand words. Modern scholars differ over how much of the book is his; the sinologist Goldin has held that the outline of his life is probably not far from the truth, while Masayuki Sato doubted that all of Sima Qian's details are accurate.

Han Fei drew together the methods of earlier thinkers: Shang Yang's emphasis on laws, Shen Buhai's on administrative technique and Shen Dao's on authority. A ruler who mastered position or power (shi), technique (shu) and law (fa) could, in his view, hold firm control of the state. He stressed holding actual outcomes accountable to speech, joined to a system of two handles, punishment and reward. Like his teacher Xun Kuang he took human nature to be without virtue, but he proposed to steer people through their own self-interest rather than through moral education.

According to Sima Qian, King Ying Zheng of Qin read Han Fei's works and said that if he could meet their author he might die without regrets. Han Fei came to the Qin court and presented an essay asking the king not to attack Han. Yao Gu and Li Si used it to have him imprisoned on grounds of probable loyalty to his homeland, and Li Si then forced him to drink poison. The Qin king afterwards regretted his death. A different account, in the Stratagems of the Warring States, has the king order his execution after he slandered the Qin diplomat Yao Jia.

After the early fall of the Qin dynasty, the succeeding Han dynasty officially vilified the Legalist school. Even so, its ideas continued to influence later dynasties, and Han Fei's thought is sometimes compared with that of Niccolò Machiavelli.
han-liner: Han Lin'er's father, Han Shantong, came from a family of hereditary sect leaders and declared himself the King of Light, the saviour awaited by a millenarian belief that combined elements of Manichaeism and Buddhism. He claimed to be a seventh-generation descendant of Emperor Huizong of Song. The authorities arrested him, and his supporters rose at Yingzhou on 28 May 1351. Under Liu Futong the rebels called themselves the Red Turban Army and vowed to restore the Song. Han Lin'er went into hiding after his father's arrest, and the Yuan government finally executed Han Shantong in January 1355.

In March 1355 Han Lin'er arrived in Bozhou and, with Liu Futong's support, was crowned emperor of the Great Song, with the era name Longfeng (Dragon and Phoenix) and the religious title Lesser King of Light. Real power lay with his ministers: Liu soon had the first prime minister, Du Zundao, assassinated and took his place. Rebels at Hezhou submitted to the Song, and Zhu Yuanzhang, confirmed as their third in command, led them to take Nanjing in 1356. Song armies raided as far as Shaanxi, the Yuan summer capital of Shangdu and Pyongyang in Korea, and the regime set up five provinces between 1356 and 1359.

Song power peaked in 1357–1358. In June 1358 Liu took Kaifeng, the old Song capital, and Mao Gui attacked the Yuan capital, Dadu. But the commanders acted independently and fought one another, and in September 1359 the Yuan general Chaghan Temur drove Han from Kaifeng. With only a few hundred soldiers left, the court survived at Bozhou and then Anfeng.

In February 1363 troops of Zhang Shicheng, together with Mongol forces, attacked Anfeng and killed Liu. Zhu Yuanzhang rescued Han, against the advice of the Confucian official Liu Ji, and moved his court to Chuzhou, across the Yangtze from Nanjing. Han lived there under Zhu's control and drowned in the Yangtze on a journey to Nanjing. Zhu afterwards removed mention of the Song and the Red Turbans from official documents, suppressed the White Lotus faith and made Neo-Confucianism the state ideology.
han-shantong: Han Shantong was born in Luancheng, Hebei, and claimed descent from Emperor Huizong of Song (1082–1135), the penultimate emperor of the Northern Song dynasty. His following grew out of the hardship after the Yellow River flood of 1344, which caused heavy casualties, displacement, hunger and epidemics and brought crisis to Dadu, the Yuan capital. Popular discontent with the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty came to a head with the great construction project of rerouting the Yellow River in 1351.

During the works Han claimed to have found a stone image with only one eye and a prophecy of revolt inscribed on its back, an account recorded in the Caomuzi that probably reflects beliefs already widespread in Henan. He proclaimed the rebirth of Maitreya Buddha and the near coming of the King of Light, and apparently took the title himself: no record says so, but after his death his son was known as the King of Light the Young. Liu Futong became his staunch supporter. When their plot was discovered, Han was executed.

His son Han Lin'er became the symbol of the rebellion that followed, with Liu Futong as its leading general, and Zhu Yuanzhang, the future founder of the Ming dynasty, was still Han Lin'er's subordinate as late as 1363. Although the military power of Han and Liu declined after 1359, Lin'er was probably seen as a legitimate future emperor until he drowned in a pond in 1366 or 1367. It has been suspected that the drowning was staged by Zhu Yuanzhang's agents, who was by then close to victory.

Historical sources on the years before the founding of the Ming were destroyed or heavily censored to hide the founding emperor's humble origins and his ties to the rebels, so information on Han Shantong and other rebel leaders is very scarce.
han-shizhong: Han Shizhong was born to a poor farming family in a village of Shanxi in 1089. In 1105, when Western Xia attacked the Song, he enlisted in the army of Yan'an Prefecture and became known for his archery and courage. During a stalemate at Yinzhou he broke into the city himself and killed one of its defending generals, which spurred the Song army to take it. When his superiors reported his deeds and asked for his promotion, Tong Guan, then in charge of border affairs, doubted the report and agreed only to make him a lieutenant.

In 1125 he helped suppress bandits and rebels in Damingfu and Shandong. In 1127 he was given a thousand men to escort Zhao Gou, Prince of Kang, to safety in the south, where the prince took the throne as Emperor Gaozong and founded the Southern Song. Han urged the emperor to recover the lost northern lands, but his advice was not taken. In 1129 he argued against withdrawing to Hunan, holding that the Huaihe and Zhejiang regions were rich and essential, and in 1131 he put down the peasant rising of Fan Ruwei, taking Jianzhou after a siege of six days.

In 1134, stationed at Zhenjiang as envoy of Jiankang, Zhenjiang and Huaidong, he set ambushes in the swamps near Dayi Town and lured a Jin cavalry force into them, capturing over 200 Jin officers, among them the general Ta Boye. The Battle of Dayi Town was counted among the Southern Song's Thirteen Military Achievements. After further victories in 1140, at Jikou near Huaiyang, he was made Grand Tutor and Duke of Ying.

When Yue Fei was imprisoned, Han asked the chancellor on what charges; the reply, that no evidence was needed, became a Chinese proverb for a trumped-up charge. The execution showed Han how far corruption had spread at court, and he retired from military service. He died on 16 September 1151. The History of Song praised him as a warrior equal to 10,000 men, and Yang Wanli named him with Yue Fei among the generals the Jin feared. He was credited with military inventions, among them modified bows and armour, a jumping course for training cavalry and an archery range. His wife, Liang Hongyu, was also known for her military ability.
han-xin: Han Xin was born in Huaiyin, in the old state of Chu, in 231 BCE. He was very poor, could not obtain a government post or become a merchant, and often relied on others for his meals.

In 209 BCE he joined Xiang Liang's rebel army against the Qin dynasty and afterwards served Xiang Yu, Xiang Liang's nephew. He held only the post of langzhong, and Xiang Yu ignored the strategies he proposed. In 206 BCE he deserted and went to Liu Bang.

At first he received no important role, and he was nearly executed for breaking military law before Xiahou Ying spared him and recommended him to Liu Bang. In late 206 BCE Han Xin had soldiers pretend to repair the gallery roads while another army secretly passed through Chencang and surprised Zhang Han. This stratagem later became one of the Thirty-Six Stratagems.

In 205 BCE Han Xin and others captured Wei Bao, King of Wei. In 204 BCE he asked Liu Bang for 30,000 troops to attack Yan and Zhao in the north and Qi in the east. In Qi he defeated the combined armies of Tian Guang and the Chu general Long Ju, who was killed. In 203 BCE he asked to be made Acting King of Qi. Liu Bang was angry, but Zhang Liang and Chen Ping urged him to agree, and he appointed Han Xin King of Qi in full.

After Xiang Yu died in 202 BCE, Han Xin sheltered the Chu general Zhongli Mo and refused Liu Bang's order to arrest him. Liu Bang, now Emperor Gaozu, feared his influence and demoted him to Marquis of Huaiyin in late 202 BCE. Around 197 BCE Han Xin is said to have promised Chen Xi help from inside the capital if he rose in revolt. When Chen Xi rebelled, Han Xin stayed behind, claiming illness. In early 196 BCE he was accused of taking part in the rebellion and executed in the Hall of Zhong, Changle Palace, on Empress Lü's orders, and his three clans were exterminated.

Sima Qian judged that Han Xin would have rivalled the Duke of Zhou had he been more modest. Several Chinese idioms come from his life, including the shame of crawling between someone's legs and the saying that with Han Xin the more soldiers the better.
han-xiongnu-war: Chinese states had clashed with the steppe peoples who later became the Xiongnu since the Warring States period, and northern states built long walls against their raids. In 215 BCE the Qin general Meng Tian drove the Xiongnu out of the Ordos region, but in the civil war after the fall of the Qin the Xiongnu, now united in a large nomadic empire under Modu Chanyu, returned. Emperor Gaozu of Han was trapped in an ambush at the Battle of Baideng, and decades of formal peace followed, kept by marriage alliances while the Xiongnu still raided the borderlands.

Emperor Wu, the seventh Han sovereign, abandoned this policy for an effort to remove the northern threat for good. In 133 BCE a Han plan to lure Junchen Chanyu into an ambush at Mayi with wealth and promises of defections failed, and raids on both sides grew.

In late 129 BCE a Han force of 40,000 cavalrymen made a surprise attack on the Xiongnu at the frontier markets. Between 127 and 119 BCE the generals Wei Qing and Huo Qubing led a series of large campaigns: Wei Qing took the Ordos in 127 BCE, where about 100,000 people were resettled in the new commanderies of Wuyuan and Shuofang, and Huo Qubing drove the Xiongnu from the Qilian Mountains in 121 BCE. A decisive campaign in 119 BCE pushed them north beyond the Gobi Desert.

With the Hexi Corridor in Han hands, commanderies were set up at Jiuquan and Wuwei by 115 BCE and the walls were extended west of Dunhuang. Loulan, Jushi, Luntai, Dayuan and Kangju were brought into tributary submission between 108 and 101 BCE, and a protectorate was established in 60 BCE. A Xiongnu civil war broke out in 57 BCE; Huhanye Chanyu submitted to the Han in 53 BCE, and in 36 BCE Chen Tang and Gan Yanshou killed his rival Zhizhi Chanyu at his capital.

After 46 CE a succession dispute split the confederation into the Northern Xiongnu and Southern Xiongnu, and the southern ruler Bi submitted to the Han in 50 CE. In 89 CE General Dou Xian led 40,000 troops against the Northern Xiongnu, chased the Northern Chanyu into the Altai Mountains and accepted the surrender of 200,000 Xiongnu from 81 tribes, destroying the Xiongnu state. His victory inscription on Mount Yanran was rediscovered in the Khangai Mountains of central Mongolia in 2017 by a joint Sino-Mongolian expedition.
han-zhao: The founders of Han-Zhao came from the Southern Xiongnu, who had been resettled across the northern frontier in 50 CE and served the Han dynasty as a buffer against nomadic enemies. After their government dissolved in 188, the warlord Cao Cao reorganised the remaining Xiongnu in 216 into the Five Divisions, confined to the Fen River valley in modern Shanxi, where they served as cavalry. Their elites adopted the surname Liu, since Xiongnu rulers had made marriage alliances with the ruling Liu clan of the Han. Liu Yuan, son of the commander Liu Bao, was sent as a hostage to Luoyang and brought up in Confucian scholarly culture. Traditional history makes him a descendant of Modu Chanyu, but modern scholars have questioned this.

In 304, during the War of the Eight Princes, the Five Divisions offered Liu Yuan leadership. He was hailed as Grand Chanyu and then became King of Han, declaring that he would restore the fallen Han dynasty. Famine forced him to move his capital several times, and after 308 it was settled at Pingyang. He died in 310. His eldest son, Liu He, was killed within a week by his half-brother Liu Cong, who took the throne.

Under Liu Cong the Han army, with Shi Le, destroyed the Jin imperial army and sacked Luoyang in 311, capturing Emperor Huai of Jin in the Disaster of Yongjia. Liu Yao, a cousin, crushed the Jin court at Chang'an five years later. Both captured emperors were made to serve as cupbearers before being executed. The state was nonetheless weak, since generals outside Shanxi, above all Shi Le, acted as independent warlords. After Liu Cong died in 318, the consort kinsman Jin Zhun killed his successor in a coup.

Liu Yao and Shi Le put down the coup, and Liu Yao moved the capital to Chang'an. When he had Shi Le's envoy executed, Shi Le declared independence and founded the Later Zhao. In 319 Liu Yao renamed his state Zhao and honoured Modu Chanyu in the ancestral temple. War between the two Zhao states began in 324. In 328 Liu Yao was captured at the Battle of Luoyang and executed, and in 329 his son Liu Xi was driven from Chang'an and killed.

The regime used Chinese offices such as chancellor and grand marshal beside a Xiongnu structure of military and aristocratic government. The Chanyu Platform, headed by the Grand Chanyu, held military power and managed the affairs of minority tribes, but ranked below the emperor. This dual administration reinforced the separation between Hu and Han peoples, and many Sixteen Kingdoms states later adopted it. Liu Yao also opened an Imperial University at Chang'an taught by Confucian scholars.
hanacpachap-cussicuinin: The hymn first appears in the Ritual, formulario e institución de curas, a manual for priests in Quechua and Spanish that Juan Pérez Bocanegra, a third order Franciscan, published at Lima with Geronymo de Contreras in 1631. The hymn itself is in Quechua only, without translation. Its score, for four voices, is printed on pages 708 and 709 with the first verse beneath it, and the remaining verses follow on pages 710 to 712. It is the earliest work of vocal polyphony printed in the New World.

On page 707 Bocanegra states that he wrote the prayer in Sapphic verse in honour of the Immaculate Virgin, for cantors to sing in processions, on entering the church and on Our Lady's days and feasts. Some have questioned his authorship, citing what they see as a basic slip in the music, but since his name runs through the whole book it seems highly unlikely that anyone else wrote it.

Each of the twenty verses has five eight-syllable lines and a closing four-syllable phrase, printed in italics, often an epithet that sometimes leads into the next verse; what Bocanegra meant by Sapphic verse is unclear. The setting is strophic, for treble, alto, tenor and bass, homorhythmic and syllabic, with the harmony of Renaissance sacred music and a rhythm dividing into 3+3+4+3+3+4. Its character is close to the cachua, a native dance, and it is considered the musical counterpart of the paintings of the Cuzco school.

The text is an ode to Mary full of images of love and nature drawn from Quechua culture, and its epithets can be read both in an orthodox Catholic way and as a continuation of older religious practice. Two terms for the Pleiades, qullqa and qatachillay, are prominent, while a third, unquy, is absent, perhaps to keep the song apart from the Taki Unquy movement.

The hymn has been recorded widely since the early 1990s, by Ensemble Elyma under Gabriel Garrido, the Boston Camerata under Joel Cohen, Jordi Savall's La Capella Reial de Catalunya and many others. Most performances use only a few verses; Ex Cathedra under Jeffrey Skidmore issued the first full version in 2007.
hanafi-school: The Hanafi school emerged from the legal tradition of Kufa in Iraq, where Abu Hanifa lived and where jurists were known for independent reasoning, or ra'y. Abu Hanifa attended the study circle of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman for about twenty years and inherited it at Hammad's death. He and his students systematised ra'y and the method of analogical reasoning, qiyās. Where qiyās gave an unsuitable result, early Hanafis used juristic discretion, istiḥsān. There is no record of treatises by Abu Hanifa himself. His teachings were passed on by his disciples Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani. Traditionists accused the Hanafis of preferring ra'y to hadith, and al-Shafi'i criticised istiḥsān as subjective.

The school won the support of the Abbasid state, which wished to unify the legal system and preferred Hanafi judges. Abu Yusuf served as a judge in Baghdad, and Harun al-Rashid later appointed him chief judge. In the 9th century the school changed from a personal school around individual jurists into a legal community with a doctrine handed down from teachers to students. It became the prevailing school in Transoxiana, especially under the Samanids, and this region was a centre of classical Hanafi scholarship from the 10th to the 12th centuries. It gave rise to the Maturidi school of theology.

The Seljuk rulers favoured the eastern Hanafis and appointed them to official posts, and in the 11th and 12th centuries the Hanafi and Maturidi schools spread west into Syria, Anatolia and western Persia. The Ottoman Empire adopted the school as its official school of law, and by the 16th century the Şeyḫülislâm was chief religious and judicial authority. Between 1869 and 1877 the Ottomans issued the Mecelle, a codification of Hanafi jurisprudence.

In India the Mughal emperor Awrangzib ordered the compilation of Hanafi fatwas, completed between 1664 and 1672 as the al-Fatawa l-ʿAlamgiriyya. The East India Company later based Anglo-Muhammadan law partly on a translation of the Hidaya. The Hanafi school is the largest of the four main Sunni schools. It is estimated at around 800 million followers, about 45 per cent of Muslims, and predominates in the Balkans, Central Asia, the Caucasus, Turkey, the Levant and South Asia.
hanamkonda: Hanamkonda, officially Hanumakonda and also called Anmakonda, lies a short distance north of Warangal, about 7 kilometres from it and about 150 kilometres from Hyderabad, and forms a tri-city with Warangal and Kazipet. Its Sanskrit name is said to have been Hanumadachala, the hill of Hanuman, the follower of Rama in the Ramayana. It lies in the semi-arid region of Telangana, with a hot, dry climate: summer runs from March to mid-June, the monsoon from June to September and winter from mid-October to early February.

The surrounding district was known as Sabbi sayira, or Sabbi one thousand, and formed part of the empire of Kalyani, and the land of Hanamkonda was called Anmakonda Vishaya. It was the older capital of the Kakatiya kings, who moved their seat to Warangal during the reign of Ganapati Deva; the reasons are unknown, though the hill fort may have been strategically better placed. Warangal's Sanskrit name was Ekasaila, one rock, rendered in Telugu as Orumgallu.

Rudra I raised Warangal's standing, his nephew and successor Ganapati gave it a stone wall, and Ganapati's daughter and successor Rudramma Devi completed its fortifications. From the beginning of the 14th century the city faced repeated wars with the Tugluq dynasty, and Mohammed bin Tugluq took it in 1323 and renamed it Sultanpur.

Hanamkonda is the headquarters of Hanamkonda district. Its monuments include the Thousand Pillar Temple, a temple of the type called Trikutalayam, dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu and Surya and later damaged by Muslim invaders; the Padmakshi Temple, believed to date from the first quarter of the 12th century; the hilltop Bhadrakali Temple; and the Jain site of Aggalayya Gutta, whose rock-cut images include a figure of Shantinatha about 9.1 metres high and one of Parshvanatha about 4.0 metres high. Kakatiya University and the National Institute of Technology are among its institutions.
hand-cannon: The hand cannon, also called the gonne or handgonne, is regarded as the first true firearm and the successor of the fire lance. It is the simplest metal-barrelled firearm, and unlike the matchlock it has no firing mechanism and is ignited by hand through a touch hole. In 1259 a fire-emitting lance made of a large bamboo tube appeared, which, according to the History of Song, spewed out a pellet wad with a sound heard five hundred or more paces away. Fire lances then changed from bamboo, wood or paper barrels to metal ones.

A rock sculpture at the Dazu Rock Carvings, dated to 1128, may show a hand cannon, but scholars dispute this. Hand cannons saw widespread use in China during the 13th century. The History of Yuan reports that in 1287 troops under Li Ting used them against the Mongol prince Nayan, causing great confusion among the enemy. The oldest extant dated hand cannon is the Xanadu Gun, whose era date corresponds to 1298.

The earliest reliable evidence of cannons in Europe is a register of the municipality of Florence from 1326, and by 1338 hand cannons were in wide use in France. The Loshult gun, a Swedish example of about 10 kg from the mid-14th century, is among the oldest survivors. In the Islamic world the textual evidence is debated: metal-barrel cannon are securely described from 1365.

Cannon are attested in India from 1366. Goryeo in Korea learned of gunpowder from China by 1372 and produced hand cannons by 1377, and Đại Việt soldiers used them by 1390 to kill the Champa king Che Bong Nga. Japan was aware of gunpowder warfare from the Mongol invasions, but firearms were not produced there until the Portuguese introduced matchlocks in 1543.

A hand cannon consists of a barrel, a handle and sometimes a socket for a wooden stock. It could be held in two hands, with a second person igniting it with smouldering wood, coal, red-hot iron rods or slow matches, or rested and fired by one gunner. Early projectiles were rocks, pebbles and arrows, then stone balls, which were replaced by iron balls from the late 14th to the 15th century. Later versions gained a flash pan, and then a hinged metal lid to keep the priming dry. In 15th-century Europe, corned powder, shot ammunition and the flash pan led to the matchlock arquebus, the first firearm with a trigger.
handan: Handan lies in the south-west of Hebei province, at the southern end of the province, where it borders Xingtai to the north and the provinces of Shanxi, Henan and Shandong to the west, south and east. It is one of the oldest cities in China, first settled around 6500 BCE by the Cishan culture. Its name has stayed unchanged for over 3,000 years and first appears in the Bamboo Annals. A Tang dictionary explained it as the city at the end of Mount Han, but jade writings found at Houma in 1965 spell the second syllable as the word for red, which suggests that the mountain was named for its reddish-purple colour.

In the early Western Zhou the area belonged to the state of Bei, and later to Wey. The Di people conquered it in 661 BCE and held it for over 40 years; Jin defeated them in 588 BCE and absorbed it. In 386 BCE Marquess Jing of Zhao moved the capital to Handan, the state's second capital after Zhongmu, and began large-scale construction. It remained the capital for 158 years until the Qin conquered Zhao. King Wuling of Zhao made his state one of the most stalwart foes of Qin and pioneered the use of walls to secure new frontiers. Handan fell with the virtual annexation of Zhao by Qin in 228 BCE.

Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian says that the future Qin Shi Huang was born in Handan while his father lived there as a Qin hostage. By the late Western Han it was remembered as one of the era's great metropolitan centres, with developed commerce, handicrafts and iron working. After Liu Xiu captured it in his conflict with Wang Lang, it was reduced from a regional capital to a county seat. After the Han, Ye, in present-day Linzhang, overshadowed it as a capital of several dynasties until 580. The Xiangtangshan Caves nearby are a Buddhist cave-temple complex of the sixth century.

The opening of the Jinghan railway and Handan station in 1906 gave the county town a new place on a national north-south route, and after Japan's surrender in 1945 Handan was established as a city for the first time.

The prefecture-level city has about 9 million inhabitants, and its municipal government sits in Congtai District. It grew after 1949 through rail links and the coal and iron of nearby Fengfeng, with iron and steel, textiles and other industries. Handan is called the capital of Chinese idioms, with more than 1,500 attributed to it, among them learning to walk in Handan, for imitating others badly. Guangfu Ancient City in Yongnian is associated with Yang Luchan and Yang-style tai chi.
handover-of-hong-kong: Britain took Hong Kong Island in 1841 during the First Opium War, a conflict that grew out of the smuggling into China of opium grown in India. Three treaties with Qing China defined the territory: the Treaty of Nanking of 1842 ceded the island in perpetuity, the Convention of Peking of 1860 added the Kowloon Peninsula and Stonecutters Island, and the Convention for the Extension of Hong Kong Territory of 1898 leased the New Territories for 99 years, until 1997. Apart from the Japanese occupation of 1941 to 1945, Hong Kong remained a British colony throughout.

In March 1979 Governor Murray MacLehose raised the question of Hong Kong with Deng Xiaoping, and in September 1982 Margaret Thatcher visited Beijing. Deng refused any compromise on sovereignty: China regarded the treaties as unequal and would recover the whole territory. Britain proposed to give up sovereignty but keep the administration; China held the two inseparable, and at the sixth round of talks, in November, Britain formally abandoned the idea. The Sino-British Joint Declaration, signed by Zhao Ziyang and Thatcher in Beijing on 19 December 1984, set the transfer for 1 July 1997 under the principle of one country, two systems, with Hong Kong's capitalist system to remain unchanged for 50 years.

The Basic Law, the region's future constitution, was promulgated on 4 April 1990. After the Tiananmen Square protests and massacre of 1989, a wave of emigration peaked in 1992, when 66,000 people left. The last governor, Chris Patten, a career politician, introduced electoral reforms that enlarged the electorate and strained relations with Beijing.

The ceremony took place on the night of 30 June 1997 at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, attended by Prince Charles, Tony Blair and Patten for Britain and Jiang Zemin, Li Peng and the first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, for China. With about 6.5 million people, Hong Kong had held 97 percent of the population of the British Dependent Territories. It became China's first special administrative region, followed by Macau in 1999. After the 2019-2020 protests, the national security law of 2020 and the electoral changes of 2021 led the British government to declare China in a state of ongoing non-compliance with the Joint Declaration.
handsome-lake: Handsome Lake was born Hadawaʼko (Shaking Snow) around 1735 in the Seneca village of Canawaugus, on the Genesee River near present-day Avon, New York, into his mother's Wolf clan. His mother, Gahonnoneh, later had a son, Cornplanter, by a Dutch fur trader and gunsmith; Governor Blacksnake, Red Jacket and Half-Town were also relatives. Handsome Lake is a traditional Hoyaneh name among the Seneca, conferred by the clan mothers when the previous holder dies or is removed.

He saw Seneca society decline from the prosperity of the fur trade. In 1779 the Continental Army's Sullivan-Clinton Campaign burned whole villages, and in his despair he is said to have seen the Three Sisters, the spirits of corn, beans and squash. After the Treaty of Canandaigua of 1794 the Haudenosaunee lost most of their land in New York and Pennsylvania, and many moved to the Haldimand Tract in Upper Canada. Alcohol, which Handsome Lake himself drank to excess, deepened the damage to family life.

In 1799, ill after many years of drinking, he had visions of four spiritual messengers who gave him ideals to enforce among his people, among them learning English and keeping their land. He stopped drinking, and when he recovered he began to preach. He condemned drunkenness, marital abuse, abortion, the abandonment of spouses and children, the sale of land, overconsumption and witchcraft. His code joined the traditional Haudenosaunee way of life with Quaker values, though how much contact he had with Christianity before his visions is unclear. Opponents held that he was giving up the old ways. In 1802 he visited Washington with Cornplanter, and President Thomas Jefferson endorsed his code.

Handsome Lake died on 10 August 1815. With the help of his relatives his visions were written down and published in 1850 as the Code of Handsome Lake, and from the 1820s it became the custom to recite it every September at Tonawanda. Arthur C. Parker recorded his story of how America was discovered, in which the devil, posing as the Lord, sends a young minister to the new land with cards, money, a fiddle, whiskey and blood corruption, and the minister finds Christopher Columbus to take him there.
hanging-gardens-of-babylon: The gardens were described as an ascending series of tiered gardens holding a wide variety of trees, shrubs and vines, resembling a large green mountain built of mud bricks. The Greek word behind the name, kremastos, means overhanging and refers to trees planted on a raised structure such as a terrace. They were said to stand in the city of Babylon, near present-day Hillah in Iraq's Babil province.

According to one legend, they were built beside a palace called the Marvel of Mankind for the Median wife of Nebuchadnezzar II, Queen Amytis, who missed the green hills and valleys of her homeland. The Babylonian priest Berossus, writing about 290 BCE, gave this account, and Josephus later quoted it. The gardens have also been attributed to the queen Semiramis, a figure of legend.

Five classical writers describe them in some form. Berossus is the earliest known mention and the only source to credit Nebuchadnezzar II. Diodorus Siculus, probably drawing on Cleitarchus and Ctesias of Cnidus, speaks of a Syrian king and gives a square garden with sides of about four plethra and an uppermost gallery 50 cubits high, watered from the Euphrates. Quintus Curtius Rufus places the gardens on a citadel and also names a Syrian king. Strabo says the water was raised by a screw, as does Philo of Byzantium, who praises the engineering of so much deep soil raised above the surrounding land.

No surviving Babylonian text mentions the gardens, and Nebuchadnezzar's long inscriptions do not mention any garden, nor his wife Amytis. No archaeological evidence has been found at Babylon. It is possible that traces lie beneath the Euphrates, which flowed east of its present course in his time, and little is known about the western part of the city. Herodotus describes Babylon without mentioning them. Three explanations have been offered: that they were a poetic ideal of an eastern garden, that they existed and were destroyed around the first century CE, or that the tradition refers to another place.

The Oxford scholar Stephanie Dalley proposes that they were the gardens Sennacherib (reigned c. 705/704 to c. 681 BCE) built at his palace in Nineveh. Sennacherib's inscriptions call the palace and garden a wonder for all peoples and describe water screws. An aqueduct at Jerwan, built of over two million dressed stones, carried water to Nineveh, and a wall panel of his grandson Assurbanipal shows the garden in maturity. Dalley suggests that the two cities became confused over the centuries; the garden's position at Nineveh has not been confirmed.
hangul: Before Hangul, Korea had used Hanja, Chinese characters, since antiquity. The script was difficult, which limited its use mostly to the upper class and left commoners largely illiterate, and it was poorly suited to a language not closely related to Chinese: Korean pronunciation and ideas could be represented only indirectly. The Joseon king Sejong the Great, who reigned from 1418 to 1450, was responsible for Hangul's creation, and most scholars believe he was personally and significantly involved.

Because records are lacking, it is unknown when work began or what the process was. The script was first introduced, probably in a mostly complete form, to Sejong's court in the 12th month of 1443 of the Korean calendar, roughly 30 December 1443 to 28 January 1444. It was officially published in 1446 in the text Hunminjeongeum and its companion commentary, the Haerye. Part of the effort that followed produced the Yongbiŏch'ŏn'ga, the first work of Hangul literature.

The original name, Hunminjeongeum, means 'Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People'. Modern Korean orthographies use 24 basic letters, called jamo: 14 consonants and 10 vowels. Combinations bring the total to 51. The letters are arranged in syllable blocks made of an initial consonant, a vowel and an optional final consonant. Linguists classify the script as a phonographic alphabet, and some have called it a featural script, one in which letter shapes encode features of speech.

The letters were designed to be graphically simple, traditionally of only straight lines, dots and circles. The shapes of five basic consonants are based on those of the human speech organs, and most of the other basic consonants are derived from them by adding lines to show progressively harsher sounds.

Sejong tried to spread Hangul through government and society with limited success. In the 15th century it was rarely used, mainly in Seoul among people close to the court, and it began to spread beyond Seoul in the 16th century. Women and Buddhists were significant early adopters, and women often taught it at home, though it was rarely taught in Confucian curricula. The elite looked down on it for centuries.

After Korea ended its isolation in the 1870s the script came to be seen as a symbol of national identity, and reform movements, together called the Hangul Movement, arose. Under Japanese colonial rule from 1910 its use was repressed to varying degrees, and it expanded after the 1919 March First Movement. After 1945 usage diverged in the two Koreas; North Korea's Compendium of Korean Language Norms appeared in 1966 and South Korea's Hangeul Orthography in 1989. Hangul is now the predominant script for Korean.
hangzhou: Hangzhou lies in northwestern Zhejiang province, at the southern end of the Grand Canal, which runs to Beijing, in the south-central part of the Yangtze River Delta. The city centre is built around the eastern and northern sides of West Lake, just north of the Qiantang River, the largest river in Zhejiang. Each year a tidal bore races up the Qiantang through Hangzhou, reaching up to 12 m in height. The climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot, humid summers and chilly, drier winters.

The Hemudu culture inhabited Yuyao, 100 km south-east of Hangzhou, as far back as seven thousand years ago, when rice was first cultivated in southeast China. The jade-carving Liangzhu culture, named for its type site just northwest of the city, lived in the surrounding area around five thousand years ago. Hangzhou was established as a county seat in 221 BCE and later served as the capital of the Wuyue Kingdom (923 to 997).

Under the Tang dynasty the poet Bai Juyi, as governor, had a stronger and taller dyke built to hold the water of West Lake, which the surrounding farmland depended on, and had willows planted along it. In 1089 another poet-governor, Su Shi, used 200,000 workers to build a 2.8 km causeway across the lake from mud dredged from its bottom.

Hangzhou became the capital of the Southern Song dynasty after the Jurchens conquered most of northern China and captured Kaifeng in the Jingkang Incident of 1127. The surviving imperial family had retreated south, and Emperor Gaozong moved from Nanjing to Shangqiu to Yangzhou before settling at Hangzhou. The city was besieged and captured by the Mongol armies of Kublai Khan in 1276. The historian Patricia Buckley Ebrey noted that the Mongols spared Hangzhou and the Zhao royal family of the Southern Song, while they had killed the Jurchen Wanyan royal family by the hundreds at the Siege of Kaifeng in 1232. The new Yuan capital was Dadu (Beijing), but Hangzhou remained an important commercial and administrative centre for the south.

The port remained important until the middle of the Ming dynasty, when its harbour slowly silted up. Under the Qing it held an imperial army garrison. The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom occupied the city in 1856 and 1860, and it was heavily damaged in its conquest, occupation and reconquest by the Qing army.

Hangzhou is the capital and most populous city of Zhejiang province and a sub-provincial city. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in or near it: the West Lake Cultural Landscape, the Grand Canal and the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City. Its native residents speak the Hangzhou dialect, a Wu dialect, and its cuisine is regarded as representative of Zhejiang cooking.
hanish-islands: The Hanish Islands form an archipelago in the Red Sea consisting of three major islands at the centre of an array of smaller islets and rocks. The northern island is Zuqar, the southern is Great Anish, and the significantly smaller Little Anish lies between them. The name may derive from a local word hanash meaning snake or serpent.

The Ottoman Empire claimed the archipelago until its dissolution after the First World War, after which the Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 left the sovereignty and political status of the islands indeterminate. Italy exercised loose control over the fishermen who frequented the islands, through its proximity to Italian Eritrea. In 1938 Italy and the United Kingdom signed an agreement that left the issue unresolved, each agreeing not to exercise sovereignty outside the stationing of agreed officials. In 1962 the United Kingdom signed a treaty affirming that it would keep up the lighthouses on the archipelago, and responsibility for them passed to Yemen in 1989.

Eritrean independence groups used the archipelago, particularly Zuqar Island, as a base for attacks on Ethiopian military interests, which led Ethiopia to want control of it. Eritrea became independent in 1991 and tried to negotiate and exercise sovereignty, particularly over Great Anish. In 1995 the breakdown of negotiations with Yemen led to the Hanish Islands conflict. In 1998 both countries agreed to accept arbitration, and the Permanent Court of Arbitration determined that the archipelago belonged to Yemen, granting several small islands and islets to Eritrea. The conflict claimed the lives of 4 to 15 Yemenis and 12 Eritreans.

The archipelago became the scene of intense fighting during the Yemeni civil war, when forces loyal to the former president Ali Abdullah Saleh and Houthi insurgents fought forces loyal to the acting president Abd Rabbuh Mansur Hadi, backed by a Gulf Arab coalition. The islands, previously under the pro-government Yemeni National Resistance, were captured by the Houthis in September 2026.
hanlin-academy: Membership of the Hanlin Academy was confined to an elite group of scholars, who performed secretarial and literary tasks for the court. One of their primary duties was to decide on an interpretation of the Chinese classics, which formed the basis of the imperial examinations that aspiring bureaucrats had to pass to reach higher government posts. Painters working for the court were also attached to the academy.

Its academicians included the poets Li Bai (701 to 762), Bai Juyi (772 to 846) and Su Shi (1037 to 1101), the historian Ouyang Xiu (1007 to 1072), the chancellor Shen Kuo (1031 to 1095) and the painter Zhang Zeduan (1085 to 1145). Zhao Mengfu served as rector from 1314 to 1320. Later members included Ji Xiaolan, editor in chief of the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, the military official Zeng Guofan, the diplomat Chen Lanbin and the educator Cai Yuanpei.

The Ming dynasty founded a Bureau of Translators under the academy in 1407, after the first expedition of Zheng He to the Indian Ocean. It dealt with the memorials delivered by foreign ambassadors and trained specialists in foreign languages. It had departments for Jurchen, Mongol, Korean, Ryukyuan, Japanese, Tibetan, Persian, Vietnamese and Burmese, for Shan groups on the south-western borders, for the Old Uyghur language of Turfan and for Sanskrit. Departments for Lao and Thai were added in 1511 and 1579. Word lists were compiled for Malay, as spoken in the Malacca Sultanate, and for Cham, the language of Champa.

The Qing dynasty revived the bureau and changed the second character of its name from yi meaning barbarian to a character for the Yi people, a change made because the Manchus were sensitive to references to barbarians. The later Tongwen Guan, set up by the Qing to translate Western languages, came under the Zongli Yamen rather than the Hanlin.

The Beijing buildings and library of the academy were badly damaged by fire during the Siege of the International Legations in 1900. The Kansu Braves, fighting the Eight-Nation Alliance, set fires near the British Legation as an intimidation tactic, and on 22 and 23 June the flames spread to the academy. An eyewitness, Lancelot Giles, wrote that the old buildings burned like tinder. An attempt to save the Yung Lo Ta Tien was given up because heaps of volumes were already destroyed, and the fire consumed many ancient texts. The academy nevertheless operated continuously until it was closed during the Xinhai Revolution of 1911.
hann-munden: The place is first mentioned in 802, in a deed of donation of Gimundi to the abbey of Fulda. The name means confluence in old German, since the Fulda and Werra join there to form the Weser. The prefix Hannoversch, meaning Hanoverian, was added in the 19th century to tell the town apart from the similarly named Prussian town of Minden. City rights may have been granted in the latter half of the 12th century.

The French inventor Denis Papin built a steam-pump-powered paddlewheel boat in 1704 and in 1707 used it to travel down the Fulda from Kassel to Münden as a demonstration. The town was also the site of the Royal Prussian Academy of Forestry, whose botanical gardens were laid out for it, and which later merged into the University of Göttingen and moved to its main campus in 1970.

About 700 well-preserved half-timbered houses draw visitors, and some are more than 600 years old. The Gothic Lutheran church of St Blasius, from the 14th and 15th centuries, holds the sarcophagus of Duke Eric I of Brunswick-Calenberg, who died in 1540. The town hall was built in the 14th century, and only its central Gothic hall remains, with a facade renewed between 1603 and 1618. The old bridge over the Werra is one of the oldest stone bridges in the country.

Remains of the 12th-century city walls, renewed in the 15th century, survive. The Tillyschanze, a lookout tower of 1881 to 1885, commemorates the siege of the town by Count Tilly in 1626. The Welfenschloss was built in Gothic style by Duke Eric I in 1501 and rebuilt in Weser Renaissance style after a fire in 1560.
hannah-arendt: Hannah Arendt was born Johanna Arendt in 1906 in Linden, Prussia, into a secular, educated and well-established Jewish family of merchants from Königsberg. Her father died when she was seven. Her mother, an ardent Social Democrat, raised her on strict Goethean lines, with the reading of Goethe's complete works. After secondary school in Berlin she studied at the University of Marburg under Martin Heidegger. She obtained her doctorate in philosophy at Heidelberg in 1929 under Karl Jaspers, with a dissertation on love in Augustine. In 1929 she also married Günther Stern, in Potsdam.

In 1933 the Gestapo briefly imprisoned Arendt for illegal research into antisemitism. She fled Germany with her mother, crossing the Ore Mountains by night into Czechoslovakia, and in Geneva she committed herself to the Jewish cause. She settled in Paris, where she worked for Youth Aliyah, helping young Jews emigrate to the British Mandate of Palestine. When Germany invaded France she was detained as an alien by the French government. She escaped and reached New York on 22 May 1941. There she became a writer and editor, worked for Jewish Cultural Reconstruction and became an American citizen in 1950. She taught at many American universities but declined tenure-track appointments.

The Origins of Totalitarianism of 1951, her first major book, examined the roots of Stalinism and Nazism in three essays: Antisemitism, Imperialism and Totalitarianism. The Human Condition of 1958 distinguishes political from social concepts, and labour from work, and develops a theory of political action in a public realm. Of human actions she singles out forgiving past wrong and promising future benefit. Between Past and Future collects eight essays written between 1954 and 1968, and her biography of Rahel Varnhagen, finished in 1938, was published in 1957.

Arendt never developed a systematic political theory and kept apart from schools of thought. The tradition most closely identified with her is civic republicanism, from Aristotle to Tocqueville, centred on active citizenship and collective deliberation. She is also remembered for the controversy over the trial of Adolf Eichmann and for the phrase the banality of evil. Her husband Heinrich Blücher died on 31 October 1970. She had a near-fatal heart attack while lecturing in Scotland in May 1974, and died of another in her New York apartment on 4 December 1975. Her ashes were buried beside Blücher's at Bard College, and her last work, The Life of the Mind, was left unfinished.
hannibal: Hannibal was one of the sons of the Carthaginian general and statesman Hamilcar Barca and an unknown mother, and was most likely born in Carthage. His name combines the name Hanno with the god Baal Hammon, and its exact vocalisation is debated. He had two brothers, Hasdrubal and Mago. His brothers-in-law, Hasdrubal the Fair and the Numidian king Naravas, were close associates of his father in the Mercenary War and the Punic conquest of the Iberian Peninsula. Rome's defeat of Carthage in the First Punic War had left deep tension, and Hannibal pledged to his father never to be a friend of Rome.

In 218 BCE Hannibal attacked Saguntum, an ally of Rome in Hispania, which sparked the Second Punic War. He invaded Italy by way of the Alps with North African war elephants, and about 10,000 Celtic tribesmen joined his army in the Po Valley. He won victories at Ticinus, Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae. At Cannae in 216 BCE he seized the supply depot on the Apulian plain; the Roman army there is estimated by some at 100,000 but more likely 50,000 to 80,000.

The war then settled into a stalemate. Following the strategy of Fabius Maximus, called Cunctator, the Romans refused open battle and wore down Hannibal's army with smaller forces. Carthaginian defeats in Hispania prevented his reinforcement, and he held most of southern Italy for about 15 years without a decisive victory.

In 203 BCE a Roman invasion of North Africa under Scipio Africanus led to his recall to Carthage. At the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE the Romans had the superior cavalry, after King Masinissa of Numidia changed sides, while the Carthaginians had more infantry and 80 elephants. Hannibal was defeated, ending the war.

After the peace left Carthage with an indemnity of ten thousand talents, Hannibal was elected suffete, or chief magistrate. He reorganised the state's finances to end corruption and recover embezzled funds so that the indemnity could be paid without raising taxes. The reforms were unpopular with members of the Carthaginian aristocracy and in Rome, and he went into voluntary exile.

He served as a military adviser to Antiochus III the Great at the Seleucid court in his war with Rome. After Antiochus lost at the Battle of Magnesia, Hannibal fled again, stopping in Armenia and reaching the court of Bithynia. There he was betrayed to the Romans and died by suicide, poisoning himself.
hannibals-crossing-of-the-alps: After its defeat in the First Punic War Carthage had lost Sicily and Sardinia and paid tribute to Rome. Hamilcar Barca, a leader of the Barcine party, set out in 238 BCE to conquer Iberia, whose resources would replace those of Sicily and give the Barcas a base for a war of revenge; in nine years he conquered the south-east of the peninsula. Hannibal, well informed on Roman politics, sent embassies from 220 BCE to the Padane Gauls of the Po valley, who offered money, food and guides.

After the Siege of Saguntum Hannibal wintered at Cartagena. He left his brother Hasdrubal in charge of Carthaginian Iberia, swapped the native troops of Iberia and of Africa between the two to minimise desertion, and subdued Catalonia in a swift campaign in three columns so that the Romans would have no bridgehead behind him.

The march from the Pyrenees to the Rhône was mostly uneventful, though Massalia urged the tribes east of the river to side with Rome. The consul Publius Scipio, delayed by an uprising of the Boii and Insubres in the Po region, sent his army up the Rhône too late to catch the Carthaginians. Hannibal pressed on to beat the onset of winter. In Theodore Ayrault Dodge's reconstruction, he found the passes held by the Allobroges and seized them at night, after lighting many camp-fires to suggest he was settling down.

The descent on the steeper Italian side, over snow that thawed by day and refroze at night, cost many men their footing and their lives. A landslide had broken about 300 yards of the path, and a detour through deep snow proved impossible and cost many pack animals. The army, sick and healthy alike, rebuilt the mule path in relays, and the next day the cavalry and pack animals could cross and go down to the pastures below.

The two main sources, Polybius and Livy, were born about 20 and 160 years after the crossing, and no archaeological evidence is available, so the route is disputed. Dodge argued for the Little St Bernard Pass, John Francis Lazenby for the Col de Clapier and W. C. Mahaney for the Col de la Traversette, where peat bogs show ground heavily disturbed by animals and humans. In his 2022 book Hannibal in the Alps, Jona Lendering concluded that the sources cannot settle the question.
hanno-the-navigator: The name Hanno was given to many Carthaginians, and ancient texts do not identify the navigator clearly. Some authors call him a king; others use the Latin dux or imperator. The Greek version of his account calls him a basileus, a word also used for other high Carthaginian officials. Scholarly consensus places him in the fifth century BCE and identifies him as a member of the aristocratic Magonid family; R. C. C. Law takes him to be a son of Hamilcar I.

The gold trade had been a vital foundation of Carthaginian power from the fifth century BCE, and the wish to secure the gold route to West Africa may have been the original reason for exploring the coast.

Carthage sent Hanno with a fleet of 60 ships to explore and colonise the north-west coast of Africa. He sailed through the Strait of Gibraltar and founded or resettled seven colonies on the coast of present-day Morocco, then continued some distance south, meeting various peoples. The account gives 30,000 men for the expedition, a number some scholars question, suggesting about 5,000.

How far he went is disputed. Harden reports a consensus that he reached at least Senegal, with estimates of the distance ranging from under 1,100 to at least 4,800 kilometres, and others propose Sierra Leone, Cameroon or Gabon. Raymond Mauny argued that ancient navigators could not have sailed much beyond Cape Bojador, because winds and currents would hinder the return. The account ends with an island of hairy people called Gorillai by Hanno's interpreters; their skins were brought to Carthage, and Pliny the Elder says they survived until Carthage was destroyed.

Hanno's Periplus is one of the few surviving ancient accounts of exploration written by the explorer himself. The original, probably in Punic, is lost, and the surviving Greek abridgement of 101 lines exists in two manuscripts of the 9th and 14th centuries. Conrad Gessner printed the first Latin translation at Zurich in 1559. Most attempts to locate the places it names from its sailing distances have failed, and some scholars suspect the Carthaginians altered it to protect their trade.

Pliny the Elder and Arrian both knew the text. Pliny claimed that Hanno sailed from Gades to Arabia, which modern scholarship considers unrealistic. A lunar crater is named after Hanno. Interest in the voyage grew in the 16th century, when European exploration was flourishing.
hanns-eisler: Johannes Eisler was born in Leipzig on 6 July 1898, the third child of Rudolf Eisler, a professor of philosophy of Jewish descent, and Marie Ida Fischer, a Lutheran. The family moved to Vienna in 1901. His brother Gerhart became a communist journalist and his sister Elfriede a leader of the Communist Party of Germany. Too poor for lessons or a piano, he taught himself music. Drafted into the Austro-Hungarian Army in 1917, he was injured several times at the front. He studied under Arnold Schoenberg from 1919 to 1923.

In 1925 Eisler moved to Berlin, where he supported the Communist Party, and his music turned towards political themes and, to Schoenberg's dismay, a more popular style with influences from jazz and cabaret. He grew close to Bertolt Brecht, and the collaboration lasted for the rest of Brecht's life. He wrote music for The Decision in 1930 and The Mother in 1932, and their Solidarity Song became a militant anthem sung throughout Europe. Their Ballad of Paragraph 218 was the first song to protest laws against abortion.

The Nazi Party banned his music in 1933, and he worked in several cities before emigrating to the United States in 1938. He taught at The New School for Social Research and from 1942 lived in Los Angeles, where he wrote eight Hollywood film scores. Two of them, Hangmen Also Die! and None but the Lonely Heart, were nominated for Oscars in 1944 and 1945. With Theodor W. Adorno he wrote Composing for the Films, published in 1947.

The Cold War ended his American career. He was among the first on the Hollywood blacklist, and the House Committee on Un-American Activities accused him of being the Karl Marx of music. Charlie Chaplin, Igor Stravinsky, Aaron Copland and Leonard Bernstein organised benefit concerts for his defence, and he left for Prague on 26 March 1948. In East Germany he composed the national anthem of the German Democratic Republic. He died of a heart attack in East Berlin on 6 September 1962 and is buried near Brecht in the Dorotheenstadt cemetery. The Hochschule für Musik Hanns Eisler Berlin is named after him.
hanoi: Hanoi lies on the Red River, whose curved course around the city was symbolised as a dragon. Several of the city's older names contain the Chinese word for dragon: it was first called Long Biên, then Tống Bình and Long Đỗ, and after its recapture in 866 by the Tang general Gao Pian it was renamed Đại La. Medieval Muslim sources between the 9th and 12th century called it Luqin, a term derived from Longbian.

Stone tools of the Sơn Vi culture, 10,000 to 20,000 years old, have been found at Ba Vì and Đông Anh. From about 10,000 to 4,000 years ago the area was under water as the sea rose, and the region is believed to have been inhabited continuously for the last 4,000 years.

Around the third century BCE a fortified citadel, later named Cổ Loa, was built in the area; it was the first political centre of the Vietnamese civilisation before Chinese influence, with an outer embankment covering 600 hectares. In 179 BCE Nanyue annexed the region, and Zhao Tuo left the indigenous chiefs in control of the population. For the first time the area formed part of a polity headed by a Chinese ruler.
