In 1010, under the Lý dynasty, Emperor Lý Thái Tổ established the capital of Đại Việt in what later became central Hanoi and named it Thăng Long, meaning ascending dragon. In 1428 King Lê Lợi renamed it Đông Kinh, eastern capital, a name used until 1789. In 1802 the Nguyễn dynasty moved the national capital to Huế, and the city was renamed Hanoi in 1831. The French took control in 1888 and shaped the city's architecture to their tastes. Hanoi was the capital of the French protectorate of Tonkin from 1883 to 1949 and of French Indochina from 1902 to 1945. Ernest Hebrard drew up a development plan in 1924, which was partly carried out.

After the August Revolution and the fall of the Nguyễn dynasty, the Democratic Republic of Vietnam made Hanoi its capital. The city was part of the State of Vietnam from 1949 to 1954 and again of the Democratic Republic from 1954 to 1976. In 1976 it became the capital of the unified Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

Hanoi is the capital and second most populous centrally governed city of Vietnam, with about 8.7 million people. Its Old Quarter, near Hoàn Kiếm Lake, keeps most of its original street layout, descended from the 36 streets where merchants specialised in trades such as silk, jewellery or bamboo. The city also holds the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum and the French colonial Hanoi Opera House and St. Joseph's Cathedral. UNESCO gave Hanoi the title City for Peace on 16 July 1999.
hanover: Hanover lies at the confluence of the River Leine and its tributary the Ihme, in the south of the North German Plain and northwest of the Harz mountains. Its position at a natural crossroads and on the upper navigable reaches of the Leine shaped its growth. The river linked it to the Hanseatic League city of Bremen, and east-west traffic skirting the Harz between the Low Countries and Saxony or Thuringia passed through it.

Hanover was founded in medieval times on the east bank of the Leine. Its original name, Honovere, may mean high river bank, though this is debated. A small village of ferrymen and fishermen, it became a comparatively large town in the 13th century and received town privileges in 1241. It was the capital of the Principality of Calenberg from 1636 to 1692 and of the Electorate of Hanover from 1692 to 1814. From 1714 to 1837 it was by personal union the family seat of the Hanoverian kings of Great Britain and Ireland.

In July 1803 Napoleon imposed the Convention of Artlenburg, and about 35,000 French soldiers occupied the country. George III did not recognise the convention, and many Hanoverian soldiers emigrated to Britain, where the King's German Legion was formed; it later played a part in the Peninsular War and at Waterloo in 1815. The electorate became the Kingdom of Hanover in 1814. After 1866 Hanover was the capital of a province of Prussia, and the city passed 100,000 inhabitants in 1875. It lay in the British zone of occupation after the Second World War and became part of the new state of Lower Saxony in 1946.

Hanover is the capital and largest city of Lower Saxony, with a population of 535,932 in 2021. It is a major crossing of railway lines and motorways and one of the world's leading exhibition cities; its fairground, extended especially for Expo 2000, is the largest in the world, and the Hanover Fair has been held since 1947. The Great Garden of the Royal Gardens of Herrenhausen is an important European Baroque garden. The palace there was largely destroyed by Allied bombing and reopened after reconstruction in 2013.
hans-adam-dorten: Dorten was born in Endenich and went to school in nearby Bonn; his father owned a porcelain manufacturing company. He studied law at Heidelberg University, the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München and the University of Bonn, took a doctorate in law at Leipzig University in 1907, and worked at the district prosecutor's office in Düsseldorf before becoming a junior judge at Waldbröl in 1912. Conscripted on 3 August 1914, he served in the 54th Corps, rose to Hauptmann and received the Iron Cross. In 1918 he was put under military arrest for violent criticism of the Kaiser, and the end of the war spared him a court-martial.

Early in 1919 he moved to Wiesbaden and turned to politics with an anti-Socialist, pro-Rhineland programme, paid for from his own wealth and that of his rich wife. He met Konrad Adenauer and other Rhineland politicians but never won the leadership of the separatist movement, partly because he refused any accommodation with the Social Democratic Party and partly because he called for closer economic ties with France. During 1919 he held talks at his Wiesbaden home with officers of the French army of occupation, among them General Mangin.

The Rhenish Republic proclaimed on 1 June 1919, with Dorten as its president, failed within a week in the face of popular protest and the opposition of the municipal councils, while the French kept a strict neutrality. The Supreme Court at Leipzig issued a warrant for his arrest for treason, which could not be served in the occupied Rhineland. In October 1923 he and Josef Matthes set up a provisional government of the Rhenish Republic in Koblenz, and the next month he proclaimed a government for the southern Rhineland at Bad Ems; this too failed.

Many historians read his aim as a Rhineland separated from Prussia, which was widely blamed for the war, within a more federal Germany, rather than full independence. He opposed the passive resistance to the occupation as ruinous for Rhinelanders, a view that ran against the popular mood. On the night of 31 December 1923 he left for Nice, where he returned to the law in 1927 and took French citizenship in 1928. He finished his memoirs, La Tragédie Rhénane, in 1937; they were published in 1945, and in German translation in 1979.
hans-christian-andersen: Hans Christian Andersen was born in Odense on 2 April 1805. His father, also named Hans, had an elementary school education and introduced his son to literature by reading him the Arabian Nights; his mother, Anne Marie Andersdatter, was an illiterate washerwoman. After his father's death in 1816 the boy attended a local school for poor children and had to support himself, working as an apprentice to a weaver and later to a tailor.

At 14 he moved to Copenhagen to seek work as an actor and was accepted into the Royal Danish Theatre for his soprano voice, which soon broke. A colleague told him he considered him a poet, and Andersen turned to writing. Jonas Collin, the theatre's director, persuaded King Frederick VI to pay part of his schooling at Slagelse and later Elsinore, which lasted until 1827.

His first story, "The Ghost at Palnatoke's Grave", appeared in 1822. In 1829 he had considerable success with the short story "A Journey on Foot from Holmen's Canal to the East Point of Amager", followed by a play and a short volume of poems. A small travel grant from the king in 1833 let him begin the first of many journeys through Europe, and he reached Rome in October 1834. His travels in Italy shaped his first novel, The Improvisatore, a fictionalized autobiography published in 1835 to instant acclaim.

Andersen's first fairy tales were issued in three booklets by C. A. Reitzel in Copenhagen between May 1835 and April 1837. The first, of 8 May 1835, held "The Tinderbox", "Little Claus and Big Claus", "The Princess and the Pea" and "Little Ida's Flowers"; the first three were based on folktales he had heard in childhood. In June 1847 he visited England and met Charles Dickens. In 1857 he stayed five weeks at Dickens's home, Gads Hill Place, after which Dickens stopped writing to him, which Andersen never understood.

In early 1872 Andersen fell out of his bed and was severely hurt, and soon afterwards he showed signs of liver cancer. He died on 4 August 1875 at Rolighed, a country house near Copenhagen belonging to his friends Moritz G. Melchior and his wife. By then he was internationally revered, and the Danish government paid him an annual stipend as a national treasure. His 156 fairy tales in nine volumes have been translated into more than 125 languages and have inspired ballets, plays and films.
hans-egede: Hans Poulsen Egede was born on 31 January 1686 at Harstad in Norway, far north of the Arctic Circle. His mother was Kirsten Jensdatter Hind, a local merchant's daughter, and his father Povel Hansen Egede was a civil servant. An uncle, a clergyman, schooled him, and in 1704 he went to the University of Copenhagen, where he earned a bachelor's degree in theology. He was ordained on 15 April 1707 and given a parish in Lofoten. There he heard stories of the old Norse settlements in Greenland, with which contact had been lost centuries before. From 1711 he asked Frederick IV of Denmark-Norway for permission to search for the colony and found a mission.

Egede founded the Bergen Greenland Company with capital from Bergen merchants. The ship Haabet and two smaller ones left Bergen on 2 May 1721 with Egede, his wife Gertrud, four children and forty other colonists, and on 3 July they founded Hope Colony at Nuup Kangerlua. Searching for months for Norse descendants, he found only the Kalaallit and began learning their language. Many colonists suffered scurvy and most went home. His 1723 expedition found the churches and ruins of the Eastern Settlement, though he took them for the Western one.

In 1724 he baptised his first child converts. In 1728 a royal expedition under Major Claus Paarss moved the colony to the mainland and built the fort Godt-Haab, the future Godthåb. His book The Old Greenland's New Perlustration appeared in 1729.

A smallpox epidemic raged among the Inuit from 1734, and in 1735 it took Gertrud. Egede carried her body back to Denmark, leaving his son Poul to continue the work. In Copenhagen he became superintendent of the Greenland Mission Seminary and in 1741 Lutheran Bishop of Greenland. He died on 5 November 1758 at Stubbekøbing on Falster. He is remembered as the Apostle of Greenland, credited with reviving Danish-Norwegian interest in the island, and the Royal Danish Geographical Society founded the Egede Medal in his honour in 1916. His son Poul published the four Gospels in Greenlandic in 1744.
hans-holbein-the-younger: Holbein was born in the free imperial city of Augsburg, a son of the painter Hans Holbein the Elder, whose trade he and his older brother Ambrosius followed. By 1515 the brothers had moved to Basel, a centre of learning and the printing trade, where they were apprenticed to Hans Herbster and found work designing woodcuts and metalcuts for printers. That year they added pen drawings to the margins of a copy of Erasmus's The Praise of Folly, early evidence of Holbein's wit and humanist leaning.

Holbein travelled to England in 1526 with a recommendation from Erasmus and was welcomed into the circle of Sir Thomas More, who called him a wonderful artist. He painted the Portrait of Sir Thomas More and a group portrait of More's family, now known only from a sketch and copies. In Basel, where Luther's major works were first published, his Dance of Death of 1523 to 1526 refashioned the medieval danse macabre as a reformist satire in woodcuts.

Back in England in 1532, he found favour with the Boleyn family and Thomas Cromwell rather than with More's circle, and he portrayed Lutheran merchants of the Hanseatic League at the Steelyard. By 1535 he was King's Painter to Henry VIII, producing portraits, festive decorations and designs for jewellery, plate and other objects. Cromwell's execution in 1540 damaged his career. He kept his post, turned again to private commissions and painted some of his finest miniatures.

Holbein held that everything began with a drawing. He always made preparatory studies of his sitters, in black and coloured chalks on unprimed paper in his first English period and on pink-primed paper with pen and brush from 1532. His portraits were prized for their likeness, yet he embedded layers of symbolism and allusion in them. He added Italian elements, notably single-point perspective and antique motifs, to a style rooted in the late Gothic. About twelve certain miniatures survive, and many designs on Greenwich armour were based on his patterns.

Holbein died between 7 October and 29 November 1543. He founded no school, and his images of Henry VIII, Erasmus, More and Cromwell have fixed their appearance for posterity, leading John North to call him the cameraman of Tudor history. His friend Amerbach and Amerbach's son Basilius collected his work, forming the core of the Holbein collection at the Kunstmuseum Basel.
hans-kelsen: Hans Kelsen was born on 11 October 1881 in Prague into a middle-class, German-speaking Jewish family. His father, Adolf Kelsen, came from Galicia and his mother, Auguste Löwy, from Bohemia. The family moved to Vienna in 1884. After the Akademisches Gymnasium he studied law at the University of Vienna, taking his doctorate on 18 May 1906 and his habilitation on 9 March 1911. His first book, on Dante's theory of the state, examined the two swords doctrine of Pope Gelasius I. A research scholarship in 1908 took him to Heidelberg for three semesters, where he studied with the jurist Georg Jellinek.

Kelsen was the principal architect of the Austrian constitution of 1920, which with amendments remains in force. In drafting the constitutions of Austria and Czechoslovakia he limited the domain of judicial review to a narrower focus than John Marshall's American model. He received a lifetime appointment to Austria's constitutional court and served on it for almost a decade in the 1920s. In 1931 he answered Schmitt in the essay Who Should Be the Guardian of the Constitution?, defending judicial review against the executive authority Schmitt favoured.

The rise of totalitarianism forced him out of Austria, then Germany, then Switzerland. In 1940 he fled Europe on the last voyage of the SS Washington, sailing from Lisbon on 1 June. He gave the Oliver Wendell Holmes Lectures at Harvard Law School in 1942. Roscoe Pound supported him for a Harvard post, but Lon Fuller opposed it, and Kelsen never held a permanent position in an American law school. He worked in the political science department at Berkeley until his retirement in 1952.

Kelsen called his theory the pure theory of law, Reine Rechtslehre, a value-independent description of law. It treats law as a hierarchy of norms (Stufenbau), an idea he took from his colleague Adolf Merkl, in which each norm derives from a higher one until a basic norm, the Grundnorm, is reached. He held that legal science uses normative, not causal, reasoning, and he excluded natural law and justice from the study of positive law. He rewrote his short book of 1934 as a much enlarged edition in 1960, translated into English in 1967.

He also wrote on international law, sovereignty and democracy, and a long treatise on the United Nations that served as a standard textbook in the 1950s and 1960s. Roscoe Pound called him in 1934 the leading jurist of the time. His influence is strongest in Europe and Latin America and weaker in common-law countries, where the pure theory was rarely understood in the United States. The Austrian government founded the Hans Kelsen-Institut in 1971 to document and continue his theory.
hans-kudlich: Johann Kudlich, known as Hans, was born on 23 October 1823 into a peasant family at Úvalno, then called Lobenstein, near Opava in Upper Silesia, a part of the Austrian Empire that now lies in the Czech Republic. Since the 1700s the empire had enforced a decree known as the Robot Patent, under which farmers had to serve a yearly quota of unpaid labour for the noble landowners.

Kudlich became a leader of the movement to end these feudal obligations in the Austrian Empire under Ferdinand I of Austria. Elected to the Austrian Reichstag early in 1848, at the age of 25, he introduced a bill to abolish forced servitude, and the legislature approved it. He was popularly called the Bauernbefreier, the liberator of the peasants. Until the end he worked to rally support for the revolution, but the parliament was dissolved by force on 7 March 1849, after the rising that had briefly taken control of Vienna was crushed.

Kudlich fled first to Germany and then to Switzerland, where he took a medical degree in Bern and Zurich. In 1853 he left Switzerland for the United States and settled in Hoboken, New Jersey, where he was known as John and worked as a physician. In 1861 he co-founded the Hoboken Academy, a German-American school that later merged with the Stevens Preparatory School, afterwards Stevens Academy, which closed in 1974. He also wrote his memoirs, Rückblicke und Erinnerungen, published in three volumes in Vienna, Leipzig and Budapest in 1873, and Die Revolution des Jahres 1848, printed at Litoměřice in 1913.

Kudlich died in Hoboken in November 1917. In 1925 his ashes and those of his wife, Louisa Kudlich, born Vogt, were placed in the mausoleum at the foot of the Hans Kudlich Observation Tower, which stands in his birthplace of Úvalno. The tower thus brought the man the peasants had called their liberator back to the village where he had been born.
hans-sachs: Hans Sachs was born on 5 November 1494 in the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg, the son of a tailor. As a child he attended a singing school held in a Nuremberg church, which awakened in him a taste for poetry and music, and he also attended the Latin school. At fourteen he began an apprenticeship as a shoemaker. At seventeen he set out as a wandering journeyman on his Wanderjahre, working at his craft in many towns, including Regensburg, Passau, Salzburg, Munich, Osnabrück, Lübeck and Leipzig. In 1513 he reached the small town of Wels, where Emperor Maximilian I passed through with his court and had the young poet placed in the palace at Innsbruck.

Sachs later left the court and went to Munich, where he took up a kind of apprenticeship as a mastersinger under the linen weaver Lienhard Nunnenbeck. In 1516 he settled in Nuremberg for the rest of his life. He married Kunigunde Creutzer in 1519, and all seven of their children died before him. After her death he married the young widow Barbara Harscher in 1561.

The Reformation was the great event of his intellectual life. In 1523 he wrote the poem about the nightingale of Wittenberg in honour of Luther, and four prose dialogues in which his sympathy with the reformer was tempered by counsels of moderation. The Nuremberg town council reproved him and forbade him to publish more pamphlets or rhymes, but it soon threw in its own lot with the Reformation.

Sachs wrote over 6,000 pieces, though counts vary widely because it is not always clear whether a piece stands alone or belongs to a larger work. About 4,200 are mastersongs proper. The others include poems, carnival plays, tragedies, comedies, prose dialogues, fables and religious tracts. He kept working as a shoemaker throughout his life, and as far as is known the Mastersingers did not as a common practice write or sing for money.

His mastersongs were not published, being intended for the Nuremberg Meistersinger school, of which he was the leading spirit. His fame rests mainly on his spoken poems, which include his plays. He succeeded best in the short Shrovetide play, the Fastnachtsspiel, where characterisation and humorous situation matter more than dramatic form. Some of his farces have been played on the modern stage. Albert Lortzing made him the subject of an opera in 1840, and he is a leading character in Richard Wagner's Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg (1868).
hans-von-bulow: Hans von Bülow was born in Dresden into the old and prominent House of Bülow, the son of the novelist Karl Eduard von Bülow. From the age of nine he studied with Friedrich Wieck, the father of Clara Schumann, but his parents insisted that he read law and sent him to Leipzig. There he met Franz Liszt, and the premiere of Wagner's Lohengrin in 1850 decided him on a career in music. He obtained his first conducting post, in Zürich, on Wagner's recommendation.

His sharp tongue alienated many musicians, and he was dismissed from the Zürich post for this reason, though he was beginning to win renown for conducting new and complex works without a score. In 1851 he became a student of Liszt, and in 1857 he married Liszt's daughter Cosima.

In 1864 Bülow became Hofkapellmeister in Munich, where he won his principal renown. In 1867 he also became director of the reopened Königliche Musikschule there, teaching piano in Liszt's manner until 1869. Meanwhile Cosima had begun an affair with Wagner and in 1865 bore him a daughter, Isolde. Bülow refused a divorce until she bore a third child, Siegfried; it was finalized in 1870, and Cosima then married Wagner. Bülow never spoke to Wagner again, though he went on conducting his works.

He was the soloist in the world premiere of Tchaikovsky's Piano Concerto No. 1 in Boston in 1875, and he championed Brahms. From 1878 to 1880 he was Hofkapellmeister in Hanover, which he left after quarrelling with a tenor in Lohengrin. At Meiningen he insisted that the musicians play all their parts from memory. He later served in Berlin as principal conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic from 1887.

Bülow was the first to perform the complete cycle of Beethoven's piano sonatas from memory, and with Sigmund Lebert he produced an edition of them. He gave titles to all of Chopin's Opus 28 Preludes, of which only the Prelude No. 15 in D flat major, the Raindrop, is still widely known by his name. He used his influence to give the young Richard Strauss his first regular post as a conductor. He introduced the five-string double bass and the pedal timpani into the orchestra; the latter are now standard.

Chronic headaches, caused by a tumour of the cervical radicular nerves, afflicted him, and after about 1890 his health failed. He sought a warmer, drier climate and died in a hotel in Cairo in 1894, ten months after his final concert.
hanseatic-league: The Hansa grew from Lübeck and a few other North German towns in the late 12th century and expanded between the 13th and 15th centuries until it encompassed nearly 200 settlements across eight modern countries, from Estonia and Russia in the north-east to the Netherlands in the west. The Scandinavians had led Baltic trade before it, and the sailors of Gotland sailed up rivers as far as Novgorod. Well before the term Hanse appeared in a document in 1267, guilds, or hansas, formed in different cities to trade overseas, especially with the less developed eastern Baltic, which supplied timber, wax, amber, resins and furs. The dominant language of trade was Middle Low German.

The league established Kontors, trading posts with considerable legal autonomy, in Bruges, Bergen and London beside the Peterhof in Novgorod. The one in London, the Steelyard, grew into a walled community with warehouses, a weigh house, a church, offices and homes. The weakening of imperial power under the late Hohenstaufen dynasty pushed the towns to form a looser network of cities. The Hansa dominated maritime trade in the North and Baltic Seas, and its economic power enabled it to impose blockades and even wage war against kingdoms and principalities.

The league declined as transatlantic trade developed after the discovery of the Americas, and short-term contracts made its model of privileged guaranteed trade obsolete. Local feudal lords asserted control over towns, and Kiel was expelled in 1518 for harbouring pirates. By the mid-16th century its weak connections left it vulnerable, and it disintegrated in 1669.

Even at its peak the Hansa was a loosely aligned confederation with no permanent administrative body, treasury or standing military force, and it never became a legal person. Its one central institution was the Hansetag, an irregular diet that met in Lübeck; many towns did not attend, and decisions did not bind a city whose delegates were absent. The Grand Master of the Teutonic Order, the only autonomous landed state that was a member, was often seen as its head. Only a few members were free imperial cities, though many temporarily escaped domination by local nobility. Its most emblematic ship was the cog.
hansetag: The diet was the supreme governing body of the Hanseatic League, with no higher authority above it, so that it formed a direct line of communication with the member towns and the League had few levels of leadership. It managed trade privileges, ratified contracts, conducted foreign and military affairs, ordered blockades and admitted or excluded members, while regional conferences dealt with regional matters.

All the Drittels, the thirds of the League, attended the first meeting at Lübeck on 2 February 1356. They had existed as informal alliances of towns before they were formally established: the Wendish-Saxon, the Westphalian-Prussian and the Gotlandian-Livonian-Swedish. Besides the members, guests such as prince-electors and the Emperor sometimes attended.

Attendance was poor. Usually only 10 to 12 towns sent envoys, since most did not want to pay the cost of the journey, and fines for repeated absence did not cure the problem. The best-attended diet, that of 1447, drew 39, only about half.

At the end of each meeting the minutes were written up, and the decisions agreed were compiled in a Hanserezess, or recess, which served as a legislative record. These recesses are a valuable source for historians, although only those up to 1537 have been published. Long after the last diet of 1669, the Hanseatic Days of New Time were begun in 1980 to renew ties between the former towns of the League.
hanukkah: After the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE, Judea became part of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. In 200 BCE King Antiochus III the Great of Syria defeated Ptolemy V Epiphanes at the Battle of Panium, and Judea passed to the Seleucid Empire. Antiochus III guaranteed the Jews their ancestral customs and the practice of their religion in the Temple. His son Antiochus IV Epiphanes reversed this policy, apparently after a dispute over the leadership of the Temple and the office of High Priest.

Some modern scholars, following the Second Book of Maccabees, see the king as intervening in a civil war between traditionalist Jews and a Hellenizing faction. These groups contested the office of High Priest, with figures bearing Hebrew or Aramaic names such as Onias set against Hellenizing priests with Greek names such as Jason and Menelaus.

In the traditional account, the Second Temple was looted and its services stopped, and Judaism was outlawed. In 167 BCE Antiochus IV ordered an altar to Zeus set up in the Temple, banned circumcision and had pigs sacrificed on the altar. The priest Mattathias and his five sons launched a revolt. After Mattathias died, his son Judah, known as Judas Maccabeus, took command and won campaigns against Seleucid forces.

In 164 BCE the rebels recovered Jerusalem and the Second Temple, which was cleansed and rededicated. The Jewish historian Josephus, in his Jewish Antiquities, says that Judas ordered yearly eight-day festivities, which Josephus calls the festival of Lights. The story is told in the First and Second Books of Maccabees, held canonical by the Roman Catholic and Orthodox Churches but not part of the Masoretic Text.

Hanukkah begins on 25 Kislev and lasts eight nights. Each night a light is added to the nine-branched menorah, the extra light, the shamash, being used to kindle the others. Customs include the hymn Ma'oz Tzur, the game of dreidel, gifts of money called gelt, and fried foods such as latkes and jam-filled doughnuts, recalling the tradition of a small flask of oil that kept the Temple's menorah alight for eight days.

The festival is of rabbinic origin and, in religious terms, relatively minor. It grew in cultural weight under Zionism, which stressed the Hasmonean victory, and in North America, where from the nineteenth century Reform leaders such as Isaac Mayer Wise made it a children's celebration. Because it often falls near Christmas, it also took on a role as a Jewish counterpart to the season's festivities.
hanuman-chalisa: The word chālīsā comes from chālīs, forty in Hindi, for the forty chaupais, or quatrains, of the hymn, not counting the couplets at the beginning and end. It was written by Tulsidas, a poet-saint, reformer and philosopher of the 16th century, known for his devotion to Rama. Tulsidas was acclaimed in his lifetime as a reincarnation of Valmiki and lived in Varanasi until his death. He founded the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple there, believed to stand where he saw Hanuman, and started the Ramlila plays, a folk-theatre adaptation of the Ramayana.

The work has forty-three verses: two introductory dohas, forty chaupais and a doha at the end. The first doha begins with shrī guru, referring to Shiva, who is considered Hanuman's guru. The first ten chaupais describe Hanuman's form, knowledge, virtues, powers and bravery. Chaupais eleven to twenty describe his service to Rama, with the eleventh to fifteenth telling his part in reviving Lakshmana. The twenty-first speaks of the need for his divine grace. At the end Tulsidas asks Hanuman to reside in his heart and in the hearts of devotees, and the last doha asks him to dwell there with Rama, Lakshmana and Sita.

Hanuman is a general among the vanaras who fought for Rama against the rakshasa king Ravana, and in the Shaiva tradition he is also an incarnation of Shiva. The text presents him as a deity in his own right as well as a devotee, stresses bhakti throughout and says that whoever recites it will be granted protection, spiritual merit and even liberation.

Millions of Hindus recite the hymn every day, many know it by heart, and it is traditionally recited on Tuesday and Saturdays, the days devoted to Hanuman. Before the 1980s no commentary had been composed on it, which Rambhadracharya attributes to its absence from printed editions of Tulsidas's collected works. Indubhushan Ramayani wrote the first brief commentary, and Rambhadracharya's Mahaviri commentary in Hindi of 1983 was called the best by Rama Chandra Prasad.

It is one of the best-selling Hindu religious books. Hari Om Sharan's rendition, released in 1974 by the Gramophone Company of India and re-released in 1995, is regularly played in temples and homes across Northern India, and others who have sung it include Hariharan, Pandit Jasraj, M. S. Subbulakshmi and Lata Mangeshkar.
hanuman-dhoka: The palace stands in the Durbar Square of central Kathmandu; dhoka means door or gate in Nepali. The Hanuman Gate is on the west side of the square. The statue of Hanuman beside it is draped in red cloth under an umbrella, its face smeared with red paste, and on the left a stone Narasimha of 1673 devours the demon Hiranyakashipu. The buildings are grouped around courtyards called chok.

The eastern wing, with ten courtyards, is the oldest part, dated to the mid 16th century; King Pratap Malla enlarged the palace in the 17th century with many temples. Mohan Chok, built in 1649, was the residential courtyard of the Malla kings, and a Malla heir had to be born there; its golden waterspout, the Sun Dhara, served the kings' daily ablutions. Mul Chok is dedicated to Taleju Bhawani, the tutelary goddess of the Malla family, whose image is brought to its temple during the Dashain festival.

In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah added four lookout towers in the south-east, among them the nine-storey Basantapur Tower, whose struts carry erotic carvings. The buildings around Nasal Chok, named after an image of the dancing Shiva, were built by the Rana rulers, and the Maha Vishnu Temple there fell in the 1934 Nepal-Bihar earthquake. The royal family lived in the palace until 1886 and then moved to Narayanhiti Palace, but Birendra was crowned king in Nasal Chok in 1975.

The palace houses the Hanuman Dhoka Palace Museum, run by the Nepalese government, with sections on the Shah dynasty, which ruled until 2006, the Tribhuwan Museum and the King Mahendra Memorial Museum. Outside stands a stone drinking fountain inscribed in fifteen languages.
hanwant-singh: Hanwant Singh was born on 16 June 1923 into the Rathore dynasty of Marwar, whose kingdom was the third largest of the Indian princely states. In 1943 he married Princess Krishna Kumari of Dhrangadhra. They had three children: a son, Gaj Singh Rathore, who succeeded him, and two daughters, Sailesh Kumari, who married into Banswara, and Chandresh Kumari Katoch of Kangra.

He succeeded his father as Maharaja of Jodhpur on 9 June 1947 and held the title until his death. In 1948 he met Sandra McBryde, a 19-year-old Scottish nurse, with whom he had a brief affair. He later married the Muslim actress Zubeida, who converted to Hinduism and took the name Vidya Rani; they had a son, Hukum Singh Rathore, known as Tutu Bana. The marriage drew a rebuke from the royal family, and he went to live in Mehrangarh.

After independence and the formation of Rajasthan as a state of India, he founded a new political party, the Akhil Bhartiya Ramrajya Parishad, in 1952. He campaigned for his party's candidates in both the Indian general election and the state Assembly elections, which were scheduled for February 1952.

On 26 January 1952, after only four hours of sleep, he took off in a small aircraft with Zubeida. The plane crashed near Sumerpur, killing them both; he was 28. Their son Tutu was brought up by Rajmata Krishna Kumari and studied at Mayo College in Ajmer. He married Rao Rani Rajeshwari Kumari Rathore, a daughter of Rao Raja Daljit Singh of Alwar, and was found beheaded on the streets of Jodhpur on 17 April 1981.

In 2011 the wreckage of the aircraft, a Beechcraft Bonanza, a light six-seater, was discovered inside Jodhpur Central Jail. In 2012 the Mehrangarh Fort Museum, which Maharaja Gaj Singh had founded in 1972, formally asked the jail to transfer the wreckage to the museum.
hanyu-pinyin: Matteo Ricci, a Jesuit missionary, wrote the first book to use the Latin alphabet for Chinese, published in Beijing in 1605, and Nicolas Trigault published another in Hangzhou twenty years later. Neither influenced the Chinese literati, and both were useful chiefly to Westerners. Thomas Wade produced the Wade–Giles system in 1859, and Herbert Giles improved it in his Chinese–English Dictionary of 1892; English-language publications outside China used it until 1979.

Hanyu means the Han language, that is, Chinese, and pinyin means spelled sounds. Each syllable of Standard Chinese is spelled as an optional initial and a final, each written with one or more letters, and diacritics mark the four tones, though they are often left out when Chinese names are spelled in non-Chinese texts.

A group of mostly Chinese linguists developed it in the 1950s, including Wang Li, Lu Zhiwei, Li Jinxi, Luo Changpei and Zhou Youguang, who has been called the father of pinyin. Zhou was an economist by profession, and Premier Zhou Enlai gave him the task after the Committee for the Reform of the Chinese Written Language was created in 1955. The group drew on Gwoyeu Romatzyh of 1928, Latinxua Sin Wenz of 1931 and the diacritics of bopomofo; Zhou later said he was the son of pinyin, the result of a long tradition from the late Qing dynasty. A first draft was written in January 1956.

The first edition was approved and adopted at the Fifth Session of the 1st National People's Congress on 11 February 1958. It was introduced in primary schools to teach pronunciation and used to raise adult literacy, but it did not become widely used until after the Cultural Revolution; by the 1980s students learned it from an early age. During the Cold War, using pinyin rather than Wade–Giles outside China was seen as a political statement. After the United States and China established diplomatic relations in 1979, Western publications on mainland China began in the early 1980s to use it.

The International Organization for Standardization published it as ISO 7098 in 1982, and the United Nations began using it in 1986. China's National Common Language Law of 2001 gave it a legal basis, and Taiwan adopted it as its official romanization in 2009. Computer input methods use it, and some Chinese dictionaries arrange their entries by it.
hanzhong: Hanzhong is a prefecture-level city in the south-west of Shaanxi province, bordering Sichuan to the south and Gansu to the west. Its name means middle of the Han River. It lies in the centre of the Hanzhong Basin on the banks of the Han River, the largest tributary of the Yangtze, with the Daba Mountains to the south and the Qin Mountains to the north, which form the northern limit of southern China. The Qin Mountains shield the city from cold winter winds, so its winters are warmer than those at similar latitudes to the east.

References to Hanzhong before the Qin unification of China are few. The Book of Documents speaks of an area called Liangzhou, and Sima Qian of a Bao state, both believed to refer to it. The area has been called Nanzheng since about 900 BCE; one account says that people of the Western Zhou state of Zheng fled south after Duke Huan of Zheng was slain by the Quanrong, though the veracity of the story is controversial. Under the Qin it was the Hanzhong Commandery.

When the Qin dynasty collapsed, Liu Bang, later the founding emperor of the Han, was made lord of Hanzhong and spent several years there before raising an army against his rival Xiang Yu in the Chu-Han contention. He named his dynasty after the region rather than his birthplace, Pei County, so that Hanzhong gave its name to the Han dynasty. In the later Eastern Han, Zhang Lu led an independent theocratic government there backed by the Way of the Celestial Masters, until he surrendered Hanzhong to Cao Cao after the Battle of Yangping.

The region lay on the route from the Central Plain to the Sichuan Basin, which made it strategically important in the Three Kingdoms period. Cao Cao lost it to Liu Bei, who took the title of King of Hanzhong, and the tomb of the Shu Han chancellor Zhuge Liang remains there. In 784 Emperor Dezong of Tang fled to Hanzhong when Chang'an was captured, and under the Northern Song its tax revenue was just behind that of regional capitals such as Kaifeng and Chengdu.

Under the Ming dynasty the Wanli Emperor installed his fifth son, Zhu Changhao, as king of Hanzhong, and he built a large palace; it was looted when he fled to Sichuan in 1643 before Li Zicheng's rebel army. The People's Liberation Army took Hanzhong in December 1949. The city is centred on the Hantai District and has a museum, the ancient Hutou Bridge and the Zhangqian Memorial Museum among its sights.
haojing: Haojing and Fengjing stood on opposite banks of the Feng River, Feng on the west bank and Hao on the east, and together the two settlements were known as Fenghao, the capital of the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1046 – c. 771 BCE). Archaeological discoveries indicate that the ruins of Haojing lie next to the Feng River, around the north end of Doumen Subdistrict in present-day Xi'an, Shaanxi Province.

The two halves had different roles. Fengjing became the site of the Zhou ancestral shrine and gardens, while Haojing contained the royal residence and the seat of government. The name Zongzhou marked its role as the capital of the vassal states, most of them ruled by clans claiming collateral descent from the royal Ji family.

Ji Chang, posthumously honoured as King Wen, moved the predynastic Zhou capital about 100 kilometres east from Qiyi to Fengjing in the mid-11th century BCE. Traditional accounts place the move five years before the Battle of Muye, which present scholarship dates to c. 1046 BCE. After his son Fa, King Wu, defeated the Shang and founded the Zhou dynasty, he moved his court across the river to the shore of Lake Hao.

During the reign of King Cheng (1042–1021 BCE) the Duke of Zhou built a second settlement at Luoyi, also known as Chengzhou, to reinforce control of the eastern part of the kingdom. Although King Cheng was permanently stationed there, Haojing remained the main centre of operations until the time of King Zhao (r. 996–977 BCE), when Chengzhou took over that role.

In the reign of King You (r. 781–771 BCE) the Marquess of Shen overran Haojing with the support of Quanrong nomads from the west, ending the Western Zhou. All the royal buildings of Haojing were razed to the ground, although it is not known whether those of Fengjing were destroyed as well. The newly enthroned King Ping (r. 770–720 BCE) then formally moved the capital east to Chengzhou. For some time afterwards there were still people who called themselves Western Zhou and gave the name Zongzhou to Chengzhou.
happy-birthday-to-you: The melody comes from the song Good Morning to All, traditionally attributed to the American sisters Patty and Mildred J. Hill, although the claim that the sisters composed the tune is disputed. Patty Hill was a kindergarten principal in Louisville, Kentucky, and her sister Mildred was a pianist and composer. They introduced the song to Patty's kindergarten class as one that young children would find easy to sing, and published it in their 1893 songbook Song Stories for the Kindergarten with the Chicago publisher Clayton F. Summy.

Kembrew McLeod stated that the sisters likely copied the tune and the idea from earlier songs such as Happy Greetings to All of 1858, but the law professor Robert Brauneis disputes this, noting that those songs had quite different melodies. The birthday words themselves first appeared in print as the last four lines of Edith Goodyear Alger's poem Roy's Birthday, published in 1901 with no reference to singing. Early printings of the song carried no credits or copyright notices.

The song has four short lines. The person being honoured is named in the third line, and because names differ in length the measure that holds the name is traditionally marked with a fermata. Among English speakers it is sung by guests at a party, often as a cake is brought in, and wishes such as and many more are sometimes added.

In the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and most of the Commonwealth, a guest then leads three cheers of hip hip hooray. In parts of the United States and Canada, especially at young children's parties, singers sometimes continue with How old are you now and count up to the person's age.

The song's copyright was long contested. The Summy Company registered a copyright in 1935, crediting Preston Ware Orem and Mrs. R. R. Forman, and Warner/Chappell Music bought the company that held it in 1988 for US$25 million. Warner claimed the copyright would run to 2030 and collected licensing fees, about US$2 million a year before the lawsuit. In the European Union the copyright expired on 1 January 2017.

In 2013 the filmmaker Jennifer Nelson sued Warner/Chappell, relying on Brauneis's research. A federal judge, George H. King, ruled that the 1935 copyright covered only a specific piano arrangement, not the lyrics or melody. Warner/Chappell later agreed to pay US$14 million to those who had paid licensing fees, and the court declared the song to be in the public domain. One well-known performance was Marilyn Monroe's rendition to President John F. Kennedy in May 1962.
haqnazar-khan: Haqnazar, also known as Haqq-Nazar, Khaknazar Khan or Ak Nazar Khan, was the son of Kasym Khan and Khanik Sultan Khanim and the younger brother of Muhammed Khan. For much of his early life he went by his middle name, Haider, given in honour of his father's Shaybanid uncle Sheikh Haidar; he took the name Haqnazar, from the Arabic for truth and the Turko-Persian for vision, only on becoming ruler of the Kazakhs. During the reigns of Taiyr Khan and Buidash Khan he lived under one of the Nogai princes, and he assisted Taiyr Khan and Tugim Khan in the First Kazakh Civil War.

After the deaths of Taiyr Khan and of Tugim in 1538, Haqnazar took the title of khan and seized the territories of Ahmed Khan in the west and of Buydash Khan in the east. The khanate then faced rivals on every side: the Nogai Horde in the west, the Khanate of Sibir in the north, Moghulistan in the east and the Khanate of Bukhara in the south. He brought the northern regions of Saryarka back into the khanate, retook Saray-Juk and the lands around it from the Nogai Horde, and in war with the Khivan Khanate the Kazakhs won the Mangyshlak Peninsula.

His campaign to bring Jetisu into the khanate ended in defeat when the Oirats joined the war on the side of Moghulistan. In the north he defeated Kuchum Khan of Sibir, reunited the Kazakh tribes and became the sole ruler of the khanate, the first since Taiyr Khan, receiving the Persian title Shah-i-Turan, King of Turan. In 1570 he defeated the Nogai Horde at the Battle of Emba and reached Astrakhan, where Russian forces drove the Kazakhs back. His rule of more than 40 years brought the khanate back towards the power it had held under Kasym Khan.
haqqi-al-azm: Haqqi al-Azm was born in Damascus, then part of Ottoman Syria, in 1864. He was educated at the Lazarist missionary school in Damascus and then at the military academy in Istanbul. He began as a government clerk and rose to inspector-general at the Ministry of Awqaf, the religious endowments, but lost the post in 1911 when the Committee of Union and Progress, the Turkish nationalist party, took control of the ministry.

After failing to win a seat in the Ottoman parliamentary election of 1912, he moved to Cairo and helped found the opposition Ottoman Party for Administrative Decentralization. The Committee of Union and Progress read the party's correspondence with French and British agents as proof that it sought to detach the Arabic-speaking provinces from the empire, and in 1913 al-Azm and other leaders were sentenced to death in absentia. He lived in exile in Cairo, where he also headed the local bureau of the Central Syrian Committee, a French-backed body that promoted the separation of Syria from the Ottoman Empire.

After the First World War he opposed any role for the Hijaz in Syria and called the Arab Revolt the Hijazi revolt. He sided with the French mandate authorities, and as governor of the State of Damascus he reportedly won friends in the administration by handing out jobs. He narrowly escaped an assassination attempt while visiting Quneitra with the French High Commissioner, Henri Gouraud.

In 1932, after the election of Muhammad Ali Bey al-Abid as president, al-Azm was invited to form a cabinet. The nationalist leaders boycotted parliament, and his government met strong opposition from the National Bloc throughout its two years. He died in Cairo in 1955 at the age of 91.
harald-bluetooth: Harald, son of Gorm the Old and Thyra Dannebod, consolidated his rule over most of Jutland and Zealand. He undertook large building projects: roads, bridges, the expansion of the Danevirke and a network of ring fortresses. The five surviving fortresses, at Aggersborg, Fyrkat, Nonnebakken, Trelleborg and Borgring, were built between about 970 and 980 to a uniform geometric design with circular ramparts and four gateways near the cardinal directions. Archaeologists read them as evidence of his ability to mobilise manpower and control strategic routes. The Ravning Bridge near Jelling, built about 979-980, was some 760 metres long and used about 1,200 oak posts. He also introduced the first nationwide coinage in Denmark.

Around 965 he raised the larger Jelling stone in memory of his parents, which credits him with winning the whole of Denmark and Norway and turning the Danes to Christianity. How he was converted is contested. Widukind of Corvey, a contemporary, names a cleric Poppa who carried a heated weight of iron unburned, while Adam of Bremen, writing about a century later, says Otto I forced the conversion after a defeat, a claim that may have served the archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen in their claim to jurisdiction over Denmark. After his conversion Harald had his father's body reburied in a church beside the old burial mound.

His rule in Norway, after the killing of Harald Greycloak, probably lasted no more than a few years in the 970s. In 973 he attacked Saxony after the death of Otto I, and in 974 Otto II counter-attacked and took Haithabu and the Danevirke. After 983 Harald regained some of the lost territory, with troops of his own and Obodrite allies driving the Germans out.

Soon after, his son Swein Forkbeard rebelled and deposed him. Harald died shortly afterwards, probably in 986, though some accounts give 985. According to Adam of Bremen he died of his wounds at Jumne, and his body was taken to the Trinity Church at Roskilde. His nickname Bluetooth first appears in a chronicle written about 1140. The traditional explanation is a conspicuous dark tooth. The Bluetooth wireless specification was named after him in 1997, on the analogy that it unites devices as he united the tribes of Denmark.
harald-fairhair: Almost nothing of Harald's biography is certain. A few fragments of praise poems by his court poet Þorbjörn Hornklofi survive, but the accounts of his life come from sagas written down about three centuries after his lifetime, none of them older than the twelfth century. The sagas differ on many points. Heimskringla, written around 1230, is the most elaborate but not the oldest or most reliable.

Heimskringla says he succeeded his father, Halfdan the Black, who drowned in Randsfjorden, to several small kingdoms in Vestfold, with his mother's brother Duke Guthorm as protector. He is described as a descendant of the Yngling dynasty. The sagas also differ on his mother's ancestry and on his age at accession, which is given as ten in some accounts and sixteen in the Flateyjarbók.

According to Fagrskinna and Egil's Saga, Harald vowed not to cut his hair until he had become overlord of Norway. He is said to have fought many battles, the decisive one at Hafrsfjord against Kjotve the Rich and Haklang, after which all of Norway paid him tribute. Ragnvald jarl then cut his hair and gave him the name Fairhair, where before he had been called lúfa, apparently meaning matted or shock hair. Old Norse fagr means beautiful rather than blond.

Egil's Saga says the people of Norway were then heavily taxed. Anyone suspected of rebellion could flee, become a tenant, or lose hands and feet, and the saga says most chose to flee. Íslendingabók, the earliest narrative source, differs from later tradition in not presenting Harald as the cause of settlement in Iceland. Historia Norwegiæ, about 1220, says he was the first to rule the whole coastal region rather than all of Norway.

In old age, the sagas say, he shared power with his favourite son Eirik Bloodaxe. The sagas give him from 11 to 20 sons, twelve of them named as kings, and their quarrels continued into the next reign.

Since the nineteenth century, when Norway was in a personal union with Sweden, Harald has been a national icon and a symbol of independence, and in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries he was regarded as having unified Norway into one kingdom. His standing as a historical figure has been questioned. Peter Sawyer began to cast doubt on the sagas in 1976, and around 2000 a few historians argued that Harald did not exist, or not in the way the sagas describe him.

Even the voyage to the west that Heimskringla and the Orkneyinga saga describe, to clear the islands of Viking refugees, is no longer accepted without question; Thomson wrote in 2008 that it comes as a shock to realise it might not be true.
harald-hardrada: Harald was born in Ringerike in Norway, in 1015 or possibly 1016, to Åsta Gudbrandsdatter and her second husband Sigurd Syr, a petty king of Ringerike and one of the strongest and wealthiest chieftains of the Uplands. Through his mother he was the youngest of three half-brothers of King Olaf Haraldsson, later Saint Olaf. In 1030, aged fifteen, he fought beside Olaf at the Battle of Stiklestad, where they were defeated by forces loyal to Cnut. Harald escaped to a remote farm, crossed into Sweden and reached Kievan Rus' about a year after the battle.

Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise welcomed him and made him a captain of his forces. Around 1033 or 1034 Harald and about 500 men went on to Constantinople and joined the Varangian Guard. He was found fighting on nearly every frontier of the empire, against Arab pirates in the Mediterranean, in Asia Minor and probably against the Pechenegs, and Snorri Sturluson calls him leader over all the Varangians. He grew extremely rich and sent his wealth to Yaroslav for safekeeping.

Harald left Novgorod in early 1045 and reached Sigtuna in Sweden at the end of 1045 or early in 1046. In 1046 he joined Sweyn of Denmark in raids on the Danish coast, and Magnus the Good, unwilling to fight his uncle, agreed to share the kingship, which Harald held alone from the following year. He married Tora Torbergsdatter of a powerful Norwegian family to secure domestic support. Harald developed a Norwegian currency and a coin economy, started trade with Kievan Rus', the Byzantine Empire, Scotland and Ireland, and according to later sagas founded Oslo.

From 1048 until 1064 he raided Denmark almost every year in a war against Sweyn. In 1049 he pillaged and burned Hedeby, the most important Danish trade centre, which never recovered as a civil town. Although he won most engagements, he never occupied Denmark. His epithet harðráði has been translated as hard in counsel, tyrannical, ruthless, severe or resolute, and it is not clear it was used in his lifetime.

Tostig Godwinson invited Harald to claim the English throne, and in September 1066 Harald invaded northern England with 10,000 troops and 300 longships. He beat the forces of Northumbria and Mercia at the Battle of Fulford on 20 September, and York surrendered on 24 September. On 25 September Harold Godwinson's army surprised the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge, where Harald had brought only light armour, and Harald was killed early in the battle, struck in the throat by an arrow. His army was wiped out. His body was moved to Nidaros the next year. Historians often consider his death the end of the Viking Age.
harappa: Harappa lies in Punjab, about 24 kilometres west of Sahiwal, and takes its name from a modern village near the former course of the Ravi River. The river now runs eight kilometres to the north. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were the two major cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation. Harappa is regarded as the type site of the civilisation, which is why it is sometimes called the Harappan civilisation, a term the Archaeological Survey of India has used more commonly since 1947.

The excavators divide the occupation into phases. The Ravi phase began around 3300 BCE, and the Kot Diji phase, c. 2800 to 2600 BCE, saw the settlement enclosed with massive mud-brick walls and platforms, with broad north-south streets and separate areas for housing and craft work. Trade was older than the city itself. Unfinished shell bangles show that raw shell was carried inland from the coast, and copper tools and beads of lapis lazuli, carnelian, agate and amazonite show links with sources in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Baluchistan and Afghanistan. In the Harappan phase, c. 2600 to 1900 BCE, the site covered at least 150 hectares.

From about 1900 BCE the civilisation slowly declined, and the Late Harappan phase lasted until about 1300 BCE. Seals, weights and writing went out of use, though faience making and some pottery techniques continued. Mortimer Wheeler once suggested that invaders had destroyed the cities, but later excavations at Harappa found no evidence of an invasion or destruction. The evidence points rather to natural causes, such as a gradual drying of the climate. Harappa itself may never have been completely abandoned.

Charles Masson was the first European to report on the ruins, in 1826. The mounds were still in good condition when Alexander Cunningham visited in 1853 and 1856, but they were then quarried for brick when the railway through Punjab was built. Cunningham estimated that they had supplied ballast for about 100 miles of the Lahore to Multan line.

Daya Ram Sahni began the first large-scale excavation in January 1921, and Wheeler dug in 1946. The Harappa Project of the University of California, Berkeley worked with Pakistan's Department of Archaeology from 1986, and fieldwork continued until 2010. In 2004 the site was added to the tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and the modern town is a small crossroads town of about 15,000 people.
harar: Harar stands on a hilltop in the eastern part of Ethiopia, about 500 kilometres from Addis Ababa and 1,885 metres above sea level. Its people called it Harar-Gey, or simply Gey, meaning the city. For centuries it was a major commercial centre linked by trade routes with the rest of Ethiopia, the Horn of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and Asia. The old walled city, Harar Jugol, covers about 60 hectares and is divided into five quarters. It has five ancient gates: Assum Bari, Argobba Bari, Suqutat Bari, Badro Bari and Asmadin Bari.

It is unclear when Harar was founded, and proposed dates run from a Qurayshi settlement in the late 7th century to a local creation in the 10th century. Islam had gained a foothold on the plateau by the 10th and 11th centuries through trade with Zeila, and by the 13th century it was the predominant religion. A history of the city records that the saint Abadir Umar ar-Rida and other religious leaders settled on the plateau about 1216.

In 1520 Harar became the capital of the Adal Sultanate under Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad. Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, called Gragn, killed the sultan in 1525 and made Harar the centre of campaigns that ravaged most of Christian Ethiopia. After his defeat in 1543, his widow Bati del Wambara renewed the war, and in 1551 Nur ibn Mujahid married her and became ruler.

In the 17th century Ali ibn Da'ud founded the Emirate of Harar, a dynasty that ruled for the next two centuries. His successor Abdullah improved relations with the Oromo by marrying five of his sons to Oromo women, and the emirate extended its economic influence from Shewa to Zeila and began to mint its own coins. In 1887 the army of Menelik II conquered Harar and appointed his nephew Ras Makonnen as governor. Makonnen had the main mosque torn down and replaced it with an Orthodox church.

Harar is the capital of the Harari Region, and Harar Jugol was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006. UNESCO describes it as considered the fourth holiest city of Islam, with 82 mosques, three of which date from the 10th century, and 102 shrines. Harari houses, called gey gar, form a distinct type whose layout dates back to 1754. They stand in walled compounds arranged around a courtyard. The French poet Arthur Rimbaud settled in Harar as a merchant between 1880 and 1891, and his house is one of its landmarks.
harare: Harare lies in north-eastern Zimbabwe, in the Mashonaland region, on one of the higher parts of the Highveld plateau at an elevation of 1,483 metres. Its climate is subtropical highland, cooler and drier than a tropical or subtropical climate because of the altitude and a cool south-easterly airflow. The original landscape could be described as parkland, and Harare Kopje, at 1,540 metres, is the highest point in the city. The name comes from the village near Harare Kopje of the Shona chief Neharawa, whose nickname was he who does not sleep.

The Pioneer Column, a military volunteer force of settlers organised by Cecil Rhodes for the British South Africa Company, founded the city as a fort on 12 September 1890. It was named Fort Salisbury after the British prime minister, the 3rd Marquess of Salisbury, and became known simply as Salisbury. Company administrators demarcated the city and ran it until Southern Rhodesia achieved responsible government in 1923. Salisbury was declared a municipality in 1897 and became a city in 1935.

After the Second World War the city expanded rapidly with its designation as capital of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1953 to 1963, with significant immigration from Great Britain, Southern Africa and, to a lesser extent, Southern Europe. Suburbs such as Alexandra Park and Mount Pleasant sprawled outwards as motor vehicle ownership grew, while mostly black suburbs like Highfield suffered from overcrowding. The Federation was dissolved in 1963. Ian Smith's Rhodesian Front government declared Rhodesia independent of the United Kingdom on 11 November 1965 and kept Salisbury as the capital, and the country was internationally recognised as independent under the name Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980.

The city was renamed Harare on 18 April 1982, the second anniversary of independence. Before the change the black residential area now called Mbare was known as Harari. Investment in education and healthcare produced a growing middle class, and the Eastgate Centre and the New Reserve Bank Tower became landmarks of the period.

Harare is the capital and largest city of Zimbabwe, with 1,849,600 inhabitants in the 2022 census and an estimated 2,487,209 in its metropolitan province, which also includes Chitungwiza, Epworth and Ruwa. It is the country's financial, commercial and communications centre and a trading centre for tobacco, maize, cotton and citrus fruits. About 90 percent of its people are Shona-speaking. The University of Zimbabwe, founded in 1952, is in the city, and the National Gallery, the National Archives and the Harare Gardens stand in its central district. The city hosted the 1995 All-Africa Games and the 2003 Cricket World Cup.
harbin: Harbin lies in southern Heilongjiang on the south bank of the middle Songhua River, at the south-eastern edge of the Songnen Plain. The terrain is generally flat and low. It is the northernmost of China's major cities and has long, dry and freezing winters, which have earned it the nickname Ice City. The city government says the name means 'swan' in Jurchen, while other sources derive it from a Manchu word meaning 'a place for drying fishing nets'.

Human settlement in the area dates from at least 2200 BCE. Wanyan Aguda, founder of the Jin dynasty, who reigned from 1115 to 1123, came from the Jurchen Wanyan tribes living near the Ashi River. In 1115 he established the Jin capital, Shangjing Huiningfu, in what is now Acheng District of Harbin. Wanyan Liang moved the capital to Yanjing, now Beijing, in 1153, and Wanyan Yong restored the city as a secondary capital in 1173.

The modern city dates from 1898, when the Russian Empire built the Chinese Eastern Railway. The Polish engineer Adam Szydłowski drew plans for the city, and the Russians made it the base of their administration of the railway. The settlement grew into a city within five years, with settlers from across the Russian Empire, including Ukrainians, Poles, Jews, Georgians and Tatars. In the 1920s it was considered China's fashion capital.

Japan invaded Manchuria after the Mukden Incident of September 1931, and Japanese forces occupied Harbin within hours. From 1932 until 1945 it was the largest city of the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Soviet Army took the city on 20 August 1945 and handed it to the People's Liberation Army in April 1946. Most of the European community left in the early 1950s, so that by 1964 the Russian population was reduced to 450.

Harbin is the capital and largest city of Heilongjiang, with a metropolitan population of 10,009,854 at the 2020 census. Its Russian and European legacy survives in Central Street and in Saint Sophia Cathedral. UNESCO named Harbin a City of Music in 2010, and the city is known for its winter ice sculpture festival.
harda-district: Harda district is a district of Madhya Pradesh in central India, with its headquarters at the town of Harda, which is also known as Hridaynagari. It was organised in 1998 and is part of the Narmadapuram Division. It covers 2,644 square kilometres. The district lies in the valley of the Narmada River, which forms its northern boundary, and the land rises toward the Satpura Range to the south. Its neighbours are the districts of Sehore to the north, Narmadapuram to the northeast and Betul to the southeast. It is divided into three Janpad Panchayat areas, Harda, Timarni and Khirkiya, and six tehsils: Harda, Timarni, Khirkiya, Sirali, Rahatgaon and Handia.

The 2011 census counted 570,465 people, an increase of 20.25 per cent over 2001, with a density of 171 inhabitants per square kilometre. Hindus made up 92.46 per cent of the population and Muslims 6.77 per cent. At the census 89.88 per cent spoke Hindi as a first language, 6.52 per cent Korku and 1.76 per cent Gondi. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes made up 16.28 and 27.99 per cent. About 20.92 per cent of the population lived in towns. The district has four municipalities, Harda, Timarni, Khirkiya and Sirali, and two seats in the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly.

Joga Fort stands on an island in the middle of the Narmada at Joga village, 45 kilometres from Harda. Handia has the Riddheshwar Mandir and a ghat on the Narmada, and Makrai has a historic fort. The district was also the setting for the film Ammaa Ki Boli, Matrubhoomi, shot at Ranhai Kala, which deals with the consequences of female infanticide.
harem-conspiracy: Ramesses III, son of the pharaoh Setnakhte and Queen Tiy-Merenese, ruled Egypt for 31 years and had gone to Thebes to celebrate the Heb-Sed, the festival of renewal held after thirty years of a reign. He had never set a clear order of succession among his sons. After the death of his first heir, Amun-her-khepeshef, he chose Ramesses IV, who was probably younger than another son, Khaemwaset. This may have led a secondary wife, Tiye, to believe that her own son Pentawer could also pass over his elder brothers and take the throne.

The attack came on day 15 of the second month of Shemu, when the king was probably in the royal harem in the Western Tower of Medinet Habu; the date fell during the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, whose bustle the plotters used. Tiye won over officials and servants to carry messages out of the harem. The pantry chief Pebekkamen spread word to the women's relatives, urging them to stir up the people to rebellion, helped by the butler Mastesuria, the overseer of cattle Panhayboni and officials of the harem. Panhayboni obtained a pass from Pairy, overseer of the king's treasury, to reach the closely guarded king.

His mummy shows no outward wounds, and it was long thought he survived the attack for a time. CT scans have since shown that his throat was cut to the bone, a rapidly fatal wound, so the trials recorded in his name were in fact held by Ramesses IV.

Ramesses IV named twelve magistrates to try the case in five trials, recorded in the Judicial Papyrus of Turin, where the accused appear under names of infamy that turn their meaning into curses. Twenty-eight people were executed, among them Pebekkamen, Mastesuria, Panhayboni and Pairy; some, Pentawer among them, were allowed to take their own lives, and four, including two judges and the captain of the police, had their ears and noses cut off for consorting with the accused women. Tiye's punishment is not recorded. The mummy known as Unknown Man E, wrapped unembalmed in a ritually impure goatskin, shares half his DNA with Ramesses III and appears to be Pentawer.
hargeisa: Hargeisa lies in a valley in the Galgodon, or Ogo, highlands at an elevation of 1,334 metres. The Laas Geel complex on its outskirts holds Neolithic cave paintings in an excellent state of preservation, in ten rock alcoves. They show human figures with raised hands facing long-horned, humpless cattle, and a French team found them in 2002, though local people had known of them for centuries. The climate is hot and semi-arid but tempered by the altitude, with most of the roughly 400 millimetres of annual rain falling between April and September.

Oral poetic accounts say Hargeisa began as a watering and trading stop for nomads and caravans, and the modern settlement grew from the Big Commune founded around 1860 by Sheikh Madar Shirwa, a Qadiriyya scholar born in Berbera who had studied at Harar. He and his companions founded a religious commune, introducing farming on large sorghum plantations in place of pastoral wandering, caring for the sick and elderly and promoting a common religious identity above tribe. One account derives the name from Harar as-sagir, little Harar, another from a Somali phrase for a place to sell hides and skins.

In 1888 the British established a protectorate in British Somaliland with Berbera as its capital. The capital was later moved to Hargeisa, which was granted capital status in 1941. The protectorate became independent on 26 June 1960 and united days later with the former Italian Somaliland to form the Somali Republic. On 31 May 1988 the Somali National Movement attacked Hargeisa, and the government of Siad Barre answered with shelling and aerial bombardment of the city. Up to 90 percent of it was destroyed in what is described as the Isaaq genocide. After the collapse of the central government and the declaration of independence of the Republic of Somaliland, reconstruction began, financed largely by local entrepreneurs and by remittances from relatives abroad.

Hargeisa is the capital and largest city of Somaliland, a partially recognised state that is still considered internationally part of Somalia. It hosts the parliament, the presidential palace and the government ministries. Its population was estimated at about 30,000 in 1958. It is a commercial centre for retail, trading, construction and stone-cutting, and the University of Hargeisa is one of several colleges and universities there.
hari-singh: Hari Singh was born in September 1895 at the Amar Mahal Palace in Jammu, into the Dogra Rajput royal family. He was the only surviving son of Raja Amar Singh, brother of Maharaja Pratap Singh, who had no child, so that Hari Singh was heir presumptive. At the age of 13 he was sent to Mayo College in Ajmer, and when his father died in 1909 the British appointed Major H. K. Barr as his guardian. Pratap Singh appointed him commander-in-chief of the State Forces in 1915, and in 1918 he was made a Knight Commander of the Order of the British Empire. In 1919 he sailed from Bombay for Britain, and spent a year studying government, transport, industry, education and sanitation.

After Pratap Singh died on 23 September 1925, the British overruled his choice of an adopted heir, Raja Jagat Dev Singh of Poonch, and Hari Singh's coronation took place from 22 to 28 February 1926. On the recommendation of the Glancy Commission, a Praja Sabha was set up in April 1932, with 75 members: 12 officials, 16 state councillors, 14 nominated and 33 elected. A written constitution for the state followed on 7 September 1939. He made primary education compulsory, prohibited child marriage and opened places of worship to low-caste subjects. He also faced an agitation in Kashmir in 1931.

In 1947 Jammu and Kashmir could join India or Pakistan or remain independent. Hari Singh wished to stay independent for the time being, since both dominions were in the grip of partition violence and the state had a Muslim-majority population. He signed a standstill agreement with Pakistan on 14 August 1947. An uprising began in Poonch on 6 October, and a Pakistan-backed Pashtun tribal invasion reached Muzaffarabad on 22 October. He appealed to India for help, Lord Mountbatten advised accession first, and Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947. Indian troops repelled the invaders in what became the first Indo-Pakistan War.

Under pressure from Jawaharlal Nehru and Vallabhbhai Patel, Hari Singh made his son Karan Singh Prince Regent in June 1949 and left for Bombay, where he lived for the rest of his life. He remained titular Maharaja until the monarchy was abolished in 1952. He died on 26 April 1961, and his ashes were scattered over Jammu and Kashmir and immersed in the Tawi River at Jammu. Singh remained a controversial ruler. The Amar Mahal Museum in Jammu, inaugurated in 1975, displays the gold throne on which he sat.
hari-singh-nalwa: Hari Singh was born on 29 April 1791 in Gujranwala, in the Majha region of Punjab, to Dharam Kaur and Gurdial Singh of the Uppal Khatri community. His father died in 1798, and at ten he was initiated as a Khalsa. In 1804 his mother sent him to the court of Ranjit Singh over a property dispute; impressed by his family's service to the maharaja's ancestors and by his skill as a horseman and musketeer, Ranjit Singh decided in his favour and made him a personal attendant. That year, by tradition, he killed a tiger with a dagger, earning the name Baghmar, Tiger-killer.

Commissioned a sardar in 1804, he fought at Kasur in 1807 aged sixteen and won his first independent command at Sialkot. He was badly wounded by a fire-pot while climbing the walls of Multan in 1810, fought at Attock in 1813, and was chiefly instrumental in taking the citadel of Multan in 1818, a siege in which 1,900 Sikhs were killed. In the Kashmir expedition of 1819 he routed the army of Raja Agarullah Khan of Rajouri, and at Mangal in 1821 his 7,000 men defeated a tribal force reported at 25,000 to 30,000.

His administration covered a third of the empire: he was governor of Kashmir in 1820–21, of Greater Hazara from 1822 to 1837 and twice of Peshawar, and he set up a mint for revenue collection. In 1831 he led a diplomatic mission to Lord William Bentinck, Governor-General of British India, and voiced strong reservations about having Kharak Singh acknowledged as heir. At least 56 buildings are attributed to him, among them the planned fortified town of Haripur, built in 1822.

In 1837, while troops were away for the wedding of Nau Nihal Singh, Afghan forces of Dost Mohammad Khan surrounded his lieutenant Mahan Singh and 600 men at Jamrud. Riding to their rescue, Hari Singh was mortally wounded; by Hari Ram Gupta's account he was struck by two bullets, while the Afghan chronicle Siraj al-Tawarikh says he fell in a duel with Wazir Akbar Khan. He asked that his death be kept secret until reinforcements came, and he was cremated in the fort. Martial ballads, a 1967 film song and a postage stamp of 2013 recall him.
harichavank: Excavations in 1966 showed that Harich existed in the 2nd century BCE and was a fortress town. The monastery's founding date is unknown, but it was probably in being by the 7th century, when its oldest building, the domed Church of St. Gregory the Enlightener, was raised in the style named after the church of St. Hovhannes at Mastara. The Kipchak Turks occupied and altered the monastery from 1120 to 1191, and the Zakarids restored its traditional decoration after they regained power.

The Cathedral of the Holy Mother of God dominates the complex. It was ordered by Zakare Zakarian, commander-in-chief, who with his brother Ivane ruled Eastern Armenia, after he bought Harich from a family of the Pahlavuni dynasty. It is a cruciform church with two-storey sacristies in each arm and a tall twenty-sided drum, a design later repeated at Gandzasar. A relief on the eastern facade shows the two brothers holding a model of the church; it was covered in 1895 by a marble plaque of the Madonna and came to light again when the plaque was removed.

A vassal of the Zakarids, Vahram, added the narthex before 1219. The larger gavit, built of stones up to 3.5 metres long, rests on four pillars under a stalactite ceiling. South of the monastery stands the Hermitage Chapel on a cliff, and the cemetery holds the ruins of a 5th-century basilica.

The princes' privileges made Harichavank a large centre of learning, known for its school and scriptorium. In 1850 it became the summer residence of the Katholikos of Echmiadzin, and the grounds were extended northwards within walls and towers, with offices, a refectory, a school, a hostel, an inn and stores. Ornamented tombstones of the 5th and 6th centuries from its cemetery are now in Armenia's State History Museum in Yerevan.
harihara: Harihara is the dual representation of the Hindu deities Vishnu (Hari) and Shiva (Hara), and is also known as Shankaranarayana. The name is sometimes used as a philosophical term for the unity of Vishnu and Shiva as different aspects of the same Ultimate Reality, Brahman. This idea is discussed in texts of Advaita Vedanta and in some schools of Shaivism, such as Virashaiva. Hinduism includes large traditions focused on Vishnu, with his avatars such as Rama and Krishna, and on Shiva. The Puranas and various traditions treat both as aspects of the one Brahman, and Harihara is a symbolic representation of that view.

Some of the earliest sculptures of Harihara are found in the surviving cave temples of India, such as caves 1 and 3 of the 6th-century Badami cave temples. The earliest mention of the being is probably in the Vishnu Parva of the Harivamsha, where Markandeya discusses it. In one legend, Vishnu appeared as the enchantress Mohini, and Shiva, besotted, tried to embrace her; she reverted to Vishnu's true form, and the two deities fused into Harihara. According to the Skanda Purana, the devotees of Shiva and Vishnu disputed which god was supreme, and to end the quarrel the two merged into one being.

In art Harihara is split down the middle, one half Shiva and the other Vishnu. The Shiva half has the matted locks of a yogic master piled high on the head and sometimes wears a tiger skin, reserved for the most revered ascetics. The Vishnu half wears a tall crown and other jewellery, representing his responsibility for maintaining world order, and his black skin represents holiness. These distinctions broadly express the duality of humble religious influence in the ascetic and authoritative secular power in the king or householder. Harihara has been part of temple iconography throughout South Asia and Southeast Asia.
harihara-i: Harihara, also called Hakka and Vira Harihara I, was the eldest son of Bhavana Sangama, chieftain of a cowherd pastoralist community that claimed Yadava descent. Little is known of his early life, and most accounts rest on speculative theories. According to one, he and his brother Bukka were commanders of the Kakatiya king of Warangal; after that king was defeated by Muhammad bin Tughlaq, they were taken to Delhi as prisoners and converted to Islam, then escaped and returned to Hinduism under the influence of the sage Vidyaranya. Ballappa Dandanayaka, a nephew of the Hoysala king Veera Ballala III, married a daughter of Harihara, which links him to the Hoysala court.

Harihara began his rule on 18 April 1336. He built a fort at Barkuru on the west coast, and inscriptions show him governing the northern parts of present-day Karnataka from Gooty in 1339. His early campaigns secured the valley of the Tungabhadra River, and he extended his control into parts of the Konkan and the Malabar Coast. When Veera Ballala III died fighting the Sultan of Madurai in 1343, Harihara took over the whole of the Hoysala lands. An inscription of 1346 recording a grant to the Sringeri matha calls him ruler of the whole country between the eastern and western seas, with Vidya Nagara as his capital.

His brothers shared the work of government: Kampana held the Nellur region and the fort of Udayagiri, Muddppa the Mulabagalu region, Marappa Chandragutti, and Bukka was his second in command and later his successor. Harihara strengthened the old fort of Badami against the Delhi rulers and fortified Gooty against the Hoysala kings.
