Udayin, or Udayabhadra, is named in Buddhist and Jain texts as Ajatashatru's successor, while the Puranas place him fourth after Darshaka. The later succession differs from text to text: the Puranas name Nandivardhana and Mahanandin, Buddhist tradition Anuruddha, Munda and Nagadarshaka. The historians K. T. S. Sarao and Keay suggest that court intrigues and murders made the throne change hands often, perhaps with rival claimants ruling at the same time. According to the Mahavamsa, the minister Shishunaga overthrew the dynasty, while Jain texts say Udayin was killed by an assassin of a rival kingdom.

Ancient texts describe gramakas, village headmen who led village assemblies, and mahamatras, high-ranking officials with executive, judicial and military functions. The period coincided with the Achaemenid conquest of the Indus Valley under Darius I, from about 517/516 BCE.
harz: The Harz, also called the Harz Mountains, is a highland in northern Germany that extends across parts of Lower Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. It is 110 kilometres long, from Seesen in the north-west to Eisleben in the east, and 35 kilometres wide, with an area of 2,226 square kilometres. It is divided into the Upper Harz in the north-west, up to 800 metres high apart from the Brocken massif, and the Lower Harz in the east, up to around 400 metres, whose plateaus can support arable farming. The Brocken, at 1,141.1 metres, is its highest summit. The name comes from the Middle High German Hardt or Hart, meaning hill forest.

Homo erectus hunted in and around the Harz some 700,000 to 350,000 years ago, and Neanderthals later left tools in caves such as the Einhorn Cave. In ancient times dense forests made the region almost inaccessible. The Harz was first mentioned as Hartingowe in an 814 deed of the Carolingian king Louis the Pious. Settlement names ending in -rode, meaning cleared woodland, appear from the mid-ninth century.

Mining in the Harz has its origins about 3,000 years ago, in the Bronze Age. The seven Upper Harz mining towns, among them Clausthal and Zellerfeld, and some thirty other villages owed their boom to mining and smelting, and the imperial town of Goslar mined silver-bearing lead ore from the Rammelsberg for centuries. Miners built the Upper Harz Water Regale, a system of ditches and ponds whose hydropower made silver mining possible; about 70 kilometres of ditch and 68 ponds are still used. In 1588 the Nordhausen doctor Johannes Thal published Silva hercynia, the first book on regional flora in the world, describing the flowers of the Harz.

During the Nazi era the Harz was an important site of the armaments industry, and in the last stage of the war its factories were increasingly staffed with slave labour. Several hundred forced labour and concentration camps stood there. The camp of Dora near Nordhausen, a subcamp of Buchenwald, supplied prisoners for the tunnels of the Mittelwerk, where the V-2 and V-1 weapons were produced, and more than 20,000 prisoners died there. Until 1990 the Inner German border ran through the western third of the Harz, and the Brocken and other peaks near the border lay in a military restricted area. Today the Harz National Park and the Brocken draw many visitors, and Goethe, Heinrich Heine and Hans Christian Andersen walked in these mountains.
harzburg: The castle, also called the Große Harzburg, stood on the Großer Burgberg, 482.80 metres high, above the Radau valley. It is named Hartesburg in a deed of 1071, from the Harz, Hart in Middle Low German. During Henry IV's minority the Saxon nobles had grown stronger, and the castle was raised between 1065 and 1068 in a programme of castle building across the Duchy of Saxony, sited by the king's architect, Bishop Benno II of Osnabrück, to protect the imperial palace of Goslar and the Rammelsberg mines. It held a large three-roomed great hall and a collegiate church, where Henry buried his brother, Duke Conrad II of Bavaria, and his son Henry.

According to the chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld, the Saxon Rebellion broke out on 29 June 1073, when nobles marched on the king at Goslar and he fled with the Imperial Regalia to the Harzburg. Besieged by forces under Otto of Nordheim and Bishop Burchard II of Halberstadt, he escaped to Franconia on the night of 10 August. Under the Treaty of Gerstungen of 1074 he agreed to slight his castles but pulled down only the walls and towers, and that spring peasants plundered the Harzburg and destroyed it. The outrage helped Henry defeat the rebels at the Battle of Langensalza on 9 June 1075.

Rebuilt under Emperor Frederick I during his conflict with Henry the Lion, the castle was completed by Emperor Otto IV, who died there on 19 May 1218. It was pledged to the Counts of Wernigerode in 1269, occupied about 1370 by Duke Otto of Brunswick-Göttingen, and in the early 15th century became a robber baron's castle under the sons of Hans von Schwicheldt. It changed hands several times in the Thirty Years' War, and demolition of what remained began in 1650.

Only fragments of the foundation walls, the towers and the well survive; one of the two bergfrieds has been partly rebuilt, and a modern bridge crosses the rock-cut moat. The 19-metre Canossa Column, raised in 1877 in honour of Otto von Bismarck, stands on the plateau, which is reached by the Burgberg Cable Car.
harzgerode: Harzgerode lies in the lower eastern part of the Harz mountain range on the Selke River, south of Quedlinburg, and is linked to Gernrode and Quedlinburg by the narrow gauge Selke Valley Railway. The surrounding mountains were for centuries a significant mining area, mainly for fluorite and silver, as at the preserved Glasebach Pit near Straßberg. The Lower Harz Pond and Ditch System is a historic example of mining water management.

The settlement was first mentioned in connection with the Benedictine abbey of Hagenenrod in the Selke valley, founded in 975. King Otto III granted the abbey market, minting and customs rights in 993. Around 1000 the counts of Ballenstedt, forebears of the House of Ascania, served as its protectors. It lost its minting rights in 1035, when Emperor Conrad II had the mint moved to Nienburg. After the German Peasants' War of 1525 the abbey's local possessions fell to the Ascanian princes of Anhalt and its buildings decayed.

After a division of the Principality of Anhalt in 1252, Harzgerode became part of Anhalt-Bernburg, and its town privileges were renewed in 1338. Its sheltered position spared it many military conflicts, but fire repeatedly destroyed it: every building but seven was razed on Midsummer's Day 1635, 42 houses burned on 30 June 1722 and 52 on 23 October 1817. The Anhalt princes took the rule back from the Counts of Stolberg in 1535, and in 1635 Prince Frederick made Harzgerode Castle the residence of his principality of Anhalt-Harzgerode.

Harzgerode is a town in the district of Harz in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. In 2009 the towns of Güntersberge and Harzgerode and several neighbouring municipalities joined to form the present town, and Neudorf was added in 2010. Nearby stand the ruins of Anhalt Castle, which gave its name to the whole state of Anhalt.
hasan-al-utrush: Hasan was born in Medina around 844, the son of a descendant of Husayn ibn Ali through Ali ibn Husayn Zayn al-Abidin and of an unnamed slave woman from Khurasan. He joined Hasan ibn Zayd when the latter established his rule over Tabaristan in the 860s, but fell out with his brother and successor Muhammad ibn Zayd. Seeking a realm further east, he allied himself with Muhammad ibn Abdallah al-Khujistani, ruler of Khurasan, who imprisoned and scourged him; the beating cost him his hearing and gave him the name al-Utrush, the Deaf.

Back in the service of Muhammad ibn Zayd, he fought in the disastrous battle at Gurgan in 900, after which Tabaristan lay open to Samanid occupation. Attempts with the Justanid king of Daylam to recover the province in 902 and 903 failed. He then preached in person among the unconverted Gilites and Daylamites north of the Alburz mountains and founded mosques; they recognised him as imam with the name al-Nāṣir liʾl-Ḥaqq, Defender of the True Faith, and he compelled the Justanid Justan ibn Vahsudan to swear allegiance to him.

In December 913 he crushed a far larger Samanid army under Muhammad ibn Sa'luk at Burdidah on the river Burrud, west of Chalus; his son-in-law Abu Muhammad al-Hasan ibn al-Qasim massacred a detachment that surrendered at Chalus. The capital Amul opened its gates, and after the murder of the Samanid ruler Ahmad ibn Isma'il he extended his rule over Tabaristan and Gurgan, beat back a Samanid counter-attack after 40 days, and received the submission of the Bavandid Sharwin II.

Disputes over the succession troubled his last years: his own sons were thought unfit, and Abu Muhammad, after a quarrel in which he briefly took the old imam captive, was named heir. Hasan died in Amul in January or February 917. The Sunni historian al-Tabari wrote that "the people had not seen anything like the justice of al-Utrush". His tomb in Amul became a major site of pilgrimage for the Daylamite and Gilite Shi'ites, his branch of Zaydi Islam was named the Nasiriyya after him, and the Zaydis of Yemen still recognise him as an imam.
hasan-buzurg: Hasan Buzurg was the son of Amir Husain Jalayir and Öljetei Khatun, a daughter of Arghun Khan, and his sister Soyurghatmish Khatun was married to Öljaitü Khan. In 1323 he married Baghdad Khatun, daughter of Amir Chupan, the most influential man at the court of the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id Bahadur. Abu Sa'id became enamoured of her, and she was forced to divorce Hasan and marry the Ilkhan.

In 1331 the Grand Vizier Ghiyas al-Din ibn Rashid al-Din accused Hasan of plotting against Abu Sa'id. His mother persuaded the Ilkhan to spare his life, and he was imprisoned in the castle of Kemah, but in 1332 his name was cleared and he was sent as governor to Rûm.

After 1335 Hasan raised a child of the royal line, Pir Husayn, who was crowned in Anatolia on 20 July 1336 as Muhammad Khan. On 24 July he defeated the rival claimant Musa at the Battle of Qara Darra, where Ali Padshah, the governor of Baghdad, was killed, and he married Abu Sa'id's widow Dilshad Khatun. In 1337 he defeated Togha Temür and Musa, but on 16 July 1338 the Chobanids under Hassan Kuchak beat him at Naushahr, and Muhammad was killed.

By the peace of late 1338 he lost Azerbaijan and Anatolia but kept Diyar Bakr, Iraq, Khuzestan and Baghdad. He raised Jahan Temür as Ilkhan, was defeated with him on the Jaghatu on 26 June 1340 and deposed him, and sought help from the Mamluk Sultanate. After he stopped recognising Togha Temür in 1344 he ruled with the title ulus beg, as a governor, leaving the throne empty. In 1347 his forces drove back an army sent by Malek Ashraf against Baghdad.

Hasan Buzurg died in July 1356 and was buried in Najaf, and his son Shaikh Awais Jalayir succeeded him. His lifelong use of the title ulus beg and his raising of several Ilkhans suggest that he meant to restore the unity of the Ilkhanate. In that he failed, and in some ways he hastened its break-up, but he built a state that ruled Iraq and parts of Persia for over half a century. He is also remembered for his friendship with Safi-ad-din Ardabili, whose descendants founded the Safavid dynasty.
hasan-i-sabbah: Very little is known of Hasan's early life. The main source is Sargozasht-i Seyyednā, possibly his autobiography, according to which he was born in Qom in Persia to a Twelver Shia family. The family soon moved to Rayy, where he studied languages, philosophy, astronomy and mathematics, especially geometry. Rayy was also a home of Ismaili missionaries, whose mission was directed from the Fatimid caliphate in Cairo.

At the age of 17 he converted to Ismailism and swore allegiance to the Fatimid caliph. The chief missionary of the region, 'Abdu l-Malik ibn Attash, made him a deputy missionary and advised him to study in Cairo. Hasan left Rayy in 1076 and reached Egypt on 30 August 1078 after a roundabout journey. He stayed about three years and supported Nizar, the caliph's elder son, as the next imam. After he displeased the army chief Badr al-Jamali, he was briefly imprisoned and deported, and he reached Isfahan in 1081.

Hasan then toured Persia on behalf of the mission. When the vizier Nizam al-Mulk sent soldiers to capture him, he withdrew into the Alborz Mountains. In 1088 he found the castle of Alamut in the Rudbar area, which guarded a valley about fifty kilometres long and five wide. His followers took it, according to the account without significant bloodshed, by first winning over the villages of the valley and then infiltrating the fort, in 1090.

Alamut became the headquarters of the Nizari mission. Hasan lived there austerely, studying, writing and directing the mission, and he declared Persian the language of Nizari holy literature, so that Nizari writing from Persia, Syria, Afghanistan and Central Asia was set down in Persian for centuries. Legend says he never left his quarters except twice to climb to the roof, but this is considered highly doubtful, given his work in organising the movement.

Hasan died on 12 June 1124. His Nizari followers called him Sayyidna, Our Master, and visited his mausoleum in Rudbar until the Mongols demolished it. Although the movement came to be associated with assassination, Hasan did not introduce it as a religious duty, since other sects had used it, and it is not clear that he advocated it himself. A Nizari assassin is called a fida'i, a devotee. Western tradition, through Marco Polo, called the leaders of the movement the Old Man of the Mountain. The Mongols captured and destroyed Alamut in the 13th century.
hasan-ibn-ali: Hasan ibn Ali was born in Medina in about 625, the firstborn of Muhammad's daughter Fatima and Muhammad's cousin Ali. Hasan was raised in Muhammad's household until the prophet's death, when he was about seven, and early sources widely report Muhammad's love for him and his brother Husayn. He is part of the ahl al-bayt, Muhammad's family, and of the ahl al-kisa, which comprises Muhammad, Ali, Fatima and their two sons.

Hasan did not play a major role under the first three caliphs, Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman. After Ali became caliph he were sent to Kufa, where they raised an army of some 6,000 men, and Hasan fought in the Battle of the Camel in 656 against Aisha, Talha and Zubayr.

After Ali was assassinated by the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam in January 661, Hasan was acknowledged caliph in Kufa. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the governor of Syria, did not recognise him and marched an army of sixty thousand men to Maskin, north of present-day Baghdad, while urging Hasan in letters to give up his claim.

Hasan sent a vanguard under Ubayd Allah ibn al-Abbas, but he was severely wounded in an attempted assassination by a Kharijite, which demoralised his army and led to widespread desertion. Ubayd Allah and most of his troops also defected after Mu'awiya bribed him. In August 661 Hasan signed a peace treaty with Mu'awiya on the condition that Mu'awiya should rule in accordance with the Quran and the Sunnah, that a council should name his successor and that Hasan's supporters should receive an amnesty. He ruled as caliph from January until August 661, then withdrew to Medina and did not engage in politics.

Hasan most likely died on 2 April 670. The early sources are nearly unanimous that he was poisoned, and Mu'awiya is usually identified as the instigator. His death removed an obstacle to the succession of Mu'awiya's son Yazid I.

Critics have called the treaty with Mu'awiya a sign of weakness. His supporters hold that abdication was inevitable after his soldiers mutinied and that he sought unity and peace among Muslims, which a Sunni hadith says Muhammad had foretold. In Shia Islam Hasan is the second Imam, who succeeded Ali and was followed by his brother Husayn, and the imamate and the caliphate are viewed as separate institutions.
hasan-ibn-zayd: Hasan was descended from Hasan ibn Zayd ibn Hasan, a great-grandson of Ali, the son-in-law of Muhammad and fourth caliph. In 864 he was living in Ray in northern Iran. Neighbouring Tabaristan, a mountainous region on the southern shore of the Caspian Sea, had remained largely untouched by the Muslim conquests of the 7th century and was ruled by the native Dabuyid dynasty until the Abbasid Caliphate conquered it in 759/60. Its Islamization began only after 840 under the Tahirids, the Abbasids' viceroys for the East. Most of its people became Sunni, but pro-Alid Shi'ite missionaries also found followers there.

In the 860s the Tahirid Muhammad ibn Abdallah ibn Tahir governed western Iran, with his brother Sulayman ibn Abdallah ibn Tahir as his deputy in Tabaristan and Gurgan. Resentment of their fiscal agents led in 864 to a rising in Ruyan, Kalar and Chalus under two sons of Rustam, who called on Hasan to lead them. He was recognised as emir by part of the population and won the allegiance of the Justanid king of Daylam, Vahsudan ibn Marzuban.

His rule was repeatedly broken by invasions. Sulayman drove him out in 865, though he recovered the province within the year; the Abbasid general Muflih forced him into Daylam in 869; and in 874 Ya'qub al-Saffar, angered that Hasan sheltered his enemy Abdallah al-Sijzi, defeated the Zaydid forces at Sari. Torrential rain and disease soon forced Ya'qub's army to withdraw. From 867 Hasan usually held Gurgan, and at times Rayy, Qazvin (865–868) and Qumis (873–879). In Khurasan he backed Abu Talha Mansur ibn Sharkab against Ahmad ibn Abdallah al-Khujistani and shared his defeat in 878/879.

Hasan died at Amul on 6 January 884 and was succeeded by his brother Muhammad ibn Zayd; the Zaydids ruled Tabaristan until 928. Historians praised him as a just and equitable ruler, but outside Ruyan and Kalar enthusiasm for his rule seems to have waned quickly, owing to his enforcement of Shi'ism, his repression of the Sunni majority and his reliance on Daylamite soldiers.

Relations with the local Iranian rulers varied. The Qarinids of western Tabaristan supported him, the Bavandids in the east were usually hostile, and when the Justanid Khurshid turned against him Hasan had him replaced by his brother Justan. The Orientalist Frants Buhl wrote that Hasan possessed rare energy and a capacity for stubborn resistance, and was sincerely religious, well educated and a patron of letters.
hasan-kuchak: Hasan Kuchak was born about 1319 to Timurtash and Daulat Khatun while his father was viceroy in Anatolia. After the Mamelukes executed Timurtash in 1328, Hasan had to hide from his father's rivals for a time. In 1336 the Jalayirids under Hasan Buzurg, masters of western Persia, put the puppet Muhammad Khan on the Ilkhanid throne. To unite the Chupanid family, Hasan Kuchak claimed his father was still alive and had a slave, Qara Jari, possibly an offspring of Chupan, impersonate him; Timurtash's widows were even married to the impostor. The Mameluk Sultan Al-Nasr Muhammad tried to expose the fraud with little success, and Chobanids such as Hasan's cousin Pir Hosayn, governor of Tabriz, deserted Hasan Buzurg.

On 16 July 1338 Hasan Kuchak and his brothers defeated Hasan Buzurg at Alataq near Van, executed Muhammad Khan and occupied the region of Tabriz, making Hasan, at 19, de facto leader of the Ilkhanate's realm. After Qara Jari's failed bid for power, he raised Sati Beg, sister of Abu Sa'id and widow of Chupan, to the throne. When Togha Temur invaded from Khurasan at Hasan Buzurg's behest, Hasan offered him Sati's hand, forwarded the letters of assurance he obtained to the Jalayirids, and so halted their advance. He then forced Sati to marry a new puppet, Suleiman Khan, and on 26 June 1340 defeated the Jalayirids in the Zarrinarüd valley near Maraga.

Not all the Chobanids stayed loyal. His uncle Surgan went over to Hasan Buzurg and plotted with Togha Temur, but their forces were beaten by Hasan's brother Malek Asraf in 1341, and Surgan was imprisoned at Karahisar. A quarrel over Fars set Malek Asraf, Pir Hosayn and their uncle Yagi Basti at odds, and Pir Hosayn was poisoned in Tabriz in 1342.

Near the end of 1343 Hasan Kuchak was murdered by his wife Izzat Malik, a daughter of Hajji Jabash, reportedly because she feared her infidelity would be discovered. He was buried in Tabriz. As he left no successor, Malek Asraf, Yagi Basti and Surgan divided the Chupanid lands, until Malek Asraf became sole ruler. His name survives on an inscription in the Ostād-Šāgerd mosque in Tabriz, built during the reign of Suleiman Khan.
hasankeyf: Hasankeyf is a town on the Tigris in the Hasankeyf District of Batman Province, Turkey. It has been an ancient settlement under many names: possibly Ilanṣurā in the Mari Tablets of 1800-1750 BCE, Cephe, Cepha or Ciphas in Roman times from a Syriac word for rock, and, after the Arab conquest of 640, Hiṣn Kayfa, meaning rock fortress. The surrounding cliffs hold thousands of caves, many of them multi-storied and with their own water supply, and churches and mosques were also carved into the rock.

In the Bronze Age the area was probably part of the Hurrian kingdoms and by the 14th century BCE of Mitanni; between the 9th and 7th centuries BCE it belonged to the Neo-Assyrian Empire. In Roman times Hasankeyf was a legionary base on the frontier with the Sasanian Empire and for a time capital of the province of Arzanene. Muslim forces most likely took it in 640.

The Seljuk sultan Barkiyāruq granted it to the Artuqids in 1101 or 1102, and in 1104 Joscelin I of Edessa was held prisoner there after the Battle of Harran. Control of the Diyarbakır to Mosul road along the Tigris brought the Artuqids prosperity, and the Artuqids and their successors the Ayyubids built the Small Palace and the Great Palace and a bridge across the Tigris. The period made the town a staging post on the Silk Road. Ayyubid rule began in 1232 and was insecure from the start.

Ayyubid emirs still governed in the 15th century under the Aq Qoyunlu, whose ruler Uzun Hassan took the town in 1462 after a six-month siege. The Safavids held it briefly from 1504, and the Ottoman Empire took it in 1514 or 1517.

Until the 1980s Armenian, Aramean and Arab Christian families lived in cave houses by the river, and Arabic is still spoken in the town. Turkey declared it a natural conservation area in 1981. The Ilısu Dam project flooded the town despite local and international objections, and by 1 April 2020 the water had reached an elevation of 498.2 metres, covering it. Only some monuments were moved. The town had a population of 4,329 in 2021.
hasanlu-lovers: Hasanlu lies in the Qadar River valley on the southern shore of Lake Urmia and was occupied from the sixth millennium BCE until its destruction by fire. Excavation revealed burnt mudbrick walls, thick layers of ash and about 246 skeletons of people of many ages left where they were killed in the streets and buildings; some lay in groups with head wounds and severed limbs, which suggests mass executions. The attackers are unknown: most scholars name the Urartians, though the Assyrian Empire was also active in the region. The city had no writing, and its original name is unknown.

The pair lay in a plaster-lined brick bin, facing each other, the left skeleton reaching towards the other with its right hand, with nothing else but a stone slab under one head. Neither shows a fatal wound; the archaeologist Oscar White Muscarella thought a hole in the right skull was made by a workman's pickaxe. One view is that they crawled into the bin, probably covered then, to hide, and the probable cause of death is asphyxiation when burning debris sealed them in.

The right skeleton, SK 335, was a young adult of about 19 to 22, identified as male mainly from the pelvis. The left, SK 336, was about 30 to 35 and was first identified as female, but its cranium is male and its pelvis mixed, and the anthropologists Page Selinsky and Janet Monge, comparing ancient DNA with the skeletal evidence, concluded that both were male. Oxygen isotopes show that both were born and raised near Hasanlu. The pair were shown at the Penn Museum from 1974 until the mid-1980s.

The name Hasanlu Lovers comes from their intimate pose, and before the DNA tests they were taken for a man and a woman; Muscarella, a co-director of the excavations in the 1960s, said, "I knew at first sight who was the female". Some researchers criticise the sensationalism around the find. Killgrove and Geller argue that modern culture primes viewers to expect a heterosexual couple, and Geller warns against projecting present ideas of sex and gender onto the past: the true relationship between the two remains unknown.
hasdai-ibn-shaprut: Hasdai ibn Shaprut, also known as Abu Yusuf ben Yitzhak ben Ezra, was born around 915 in Jaén. His father, Isaac ben Ezra, was a wealthy and learned Jew. In his youth Hasdai acquired a thorough knowledge of Hebrew, Arabic and Latin, the last of which was then known in Spain only to the higher clergy, and he also studied medicine. His family came from either Byzantium or Armenia, and there is no record of his having a wife.

Appointed physician to Caliph Abd al-Rahman III of Córdoba, Hasdai gained the caliph's confidence and became his confidant and counsellor. Without the title of vizier he was in effect minister of foreign affairs, and he also controlled the customs and ship dues in the port of Córdoba. He arranged the caliph's alliances with foreign powers and received the envoys sent to Córdoba. In 956 he handled an embassy headed by John of Gorze, sent by Otto I, persuading the envoys to ask for another letter that would contain nothing offensive to Islam. John of Gorze said he had never seen a man of such subtle intellect.
In 958 Hasdai persuaded Queen Toda of Pamplona to come to Córdoba with her son and her grandson Sancho I of León to ask the caliph for aid, and he is known for treating Sancho's obesity.

An embassy from Constantine VII in 949 brought a codex of Dioscorides' work on botany, and Hasdai, with a learned Greek monk named Nicholas, saw it translated into Arabic. He kept his position under the caliph's son and successor, al-Hakam II.

Hasdai was active on behalf of the Jews and of Jewish learning. He wrote in Hebrew to the king of the Khazars, a Jewish state in Central Asia, asking about its origins and organisation, although the historian Shaul Stampfer has questioned the authenticity of the reply attributed to the Khazar king. He wrote to Empress Helena of Byzantium pleading for religious liberty for the Jews of her empire, and sent gifts to the talmudic academies of Babylonia. He appointed Moses ben Hanoch, a scholar ransomed from pirates, to direct a school in Córdoba, which helped move Jewish learning in Spain away from dependence on Baghdad.

He bought Hebrew books from the East and supported scholars such as Menahem ben Saruq and Dunash ben Labrat, and his time marks the start of the flowering of Andalusi Jewish culture, with its poetry and the study of Hebrew grammar. He died in Córdoba.
hasdrubal-barca: Hasdrubal Barca was the son of Hamilcar Barca and brother of Hannibal and Mago Barca; little is known of his early life. He was present, with Hannibal, when their father died in battle against the Iberians. When Hannibal marched for Italy in 218 BCE he left Hasdrubal in Iberia with 13,000 infantry, 2,550 cavalry and 21 war elephants, with orders to follow to Italy in 217 BCE. Instead he spent six years against the brothers Gnaeus and Publius Cornelius Scipio, who had caught the Carthaginians by surprise and won the Battle of Cissa.

In 217 BCE the Roman fleet under Gnaeus Scipio crushed the Carthaginian fleet at the Battle of Ebro River, and the dismissal of poor Iberian crews led to a rebellion of the Turdetani, which occupied Hasdrubal through 216 BCE. In 215 BCE he offered battle at Ibera.

He used his cavalry superiority and tried to envelop the enemy, but the Romans broke through his thinned centre and defeated each wing separately. The Scipios' victory kept him from reinforcing Hannibal; the classicist Howard Scullard thought it may have prevented the Romans being expelled from Iberia. Mago and Hasdrubal Gisco then joined him, ending the Barcid family's undisputed command.

In late 212 BCE Hasdrubal, with Mago Barca and Hasdrubal Gisco, routed the Roman armies at the Battle of the Upper Baetis and killed both Scipios, giving the Carthaginians Iberia up to the Ebro. In 209 BCE Scipio Africanus captured Carthago Nova while the Carthaginian armies were dispersed, and defeated Hasdrubal at the Battle of Baecula, though Hasdrubal retreated with two thirds of his army. Summoned to join Hannibal in 208 BCE, he crossed the Pyrenees to avoid Scipio, wintered in Gaul and crossed the Alps in spring 207 BCE, helped by roads Hannibal had left and by Gallic recruits.

Hasdrubal's messengers to Hannibal were captured, and he was checked by two Roman armies and forced to give battle at the Metaurus, where he was decisively defeated. As his army broke up he charged into the fray and died, and his head was thrown into Hannibal's camp. Edward Shepherd Creasy included the battle in The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World, because it left Hannibal stranded in Italy.
hasdrubal-gisco: Hasdrubal Gisco, whose Punic name is given as ʿAzrubaʿal son of Gersakkun, was sent to Iberia with an army after Hasdrubal Barca's defeat at the Battle of Dertosa in the spring of 215 BCE, and arrived in 214 BCE. His coming ended the absolute command of the Barcid family there. In 212 BCE the two Roman commanders, Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, took the offensive. Hasdrubal, Mago Barca and Numidian cavalry under Masinissa defeated Publius Scipio near Castulo, where he was killed. Hasdrubal then joined Hasdrubal Barca, and together they trapped Gnaeus Scipio near Ilorca; he too was killed, less than a month after his brother.

After Hasdrubal Barca left for Italy, Hasdrubal Gisco retired to Lusitania to gather mercenaries. In 207 BCE he was near Gades with Mago, and in 206 BCE he raised his army to 70,000 infantry and 4,500 cavalry. Scipio Africanus, the son of Publius Scipio, attacked him and Mago and defeated them heavily at the Battle of Ilipa.

Hasdrubal then crossed to North Africa and persuaded Syphax, king of the Masaesyli of western Numidia, to ally with Carthage, by offering him his daughter Sophonisba in marriage. When Scipio landed in Africa in 204 BCE, he faced Hasdrubal and Syphax with 80,000 infantry and 13,000 cavalry. During negotiations Scipio and his new ally Masinissa approached the camp by stealth and set it on fire; Polybius says the Carthaginians and Numidians lost over 40,000 dead. Hasdrubal and Syphax, joined by about 4,000 Celtiberian mercenaries, offered battle again and were defeated at the Battle of Bagbrades.

Hasdrubal returned to Carthage, where he killed himself in 202 BCE to avoid being lynched by a mob. Livy calls him the best and most distinguished general of the war after the three sons of Hamilcar, yet quotes Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus describing him as a general who showed his speed chiefly in retreat. He had a great gift for diplomacy and three times raised large armies, in Iberia and Africa, after severe defeats. Polybius says he tried to extract money from Andobales, whom he calls the most faithful friend the Carthaginians had in Iberia, and when Andobales refused, falsely accused him and forced him to give his daughters as hostages.
hasdrubal-the-fair: Hasdrubal the Fair, in Punic ʿAzrobaʿl, was a Carthaginian military leader and politician. Livy's History of Rome records him as the son-in-law of Hamilcar Barca and the brother-in-law of Hannibal. He followed Hamilcar in his campaign against the governing aristocracy at Carthage at the close of the First Punic War, and in the career of conquest in Hispania that came after. In 237 BCE the two set out for the peninsula.

Around 231-230 BCE Hasdrubal allegedly acted in Hamilcar's name to make the Numidian tribes of northern Africa submit to the Barcid family, and Numidia soon fell within Carthage's sphere of influence. After Hamilcar died in 228 BCE, while fighting Iberian tribes, Hasdrubal succeeded him in command and followed orders from Carthage, because Hamilcar's sons were too young. Hannibal, the elder, was then 19.

Unlike his predecessor, Hasdrubal largely preferred diplomacy to military campaigns. In keeping with the customs of the time, he demanded hostages from the realms that submitted to Carthage, to deter them from breaking their treaties. He extended the territory by this diplomacy and consolidated it by founding the city and naval base of Qart Hadasht, which the Romans later called Carthago Nova, as the capital of the new province. Modern Cartagena descends from it.

He also made a treaty with the Roman Republic that fixed the River Ebro, the classical Iberus, as the boundary between the two powers. The treaty followed appeals to Rome from the Greek colony of Emporion and from Iberian Saguntum, both fearful of the growth of Punic power. Hasdrubal accepted it reluctantly, since Punic dominion in Iberia was not yet secure enough to risk a premature conflict.

Seven years after Hamilcar's death, Hasdrubal was assassinated in 221 BCE by a slave of the Celtic king Tagus, who thus avenged the death of his own master. His successor was his brother-in-law Hannibal Barca, the son of Hamilcar.
hasekura-tsunenaga: Hasekura Rokuemon Tsunenaga was born in 1571 in Okitama district, in what is now Yonezawa in Yamagata Prefecture. His father was Yamaguchi Tsuneshige, and the family claimed ancestral ties with Emperor Kanmu. A mid-level noble samurai of the Sendai Domain, he served the daimyō Date Masamune directly and received an annual stipend of 1200 koku. He was of roughly the same age as Masamune, who entrusted him with several important missions as his representative. In 1597 he served for six months as a samurai in the Japanese invasion of Korea under Toyotomi Hideyoshi.

The Franciscan friar Luis Sotelo persuaded Tokugawa Ieyasu and his son Tokugawa Hidetada to send a representative to New Spain, and a Japanese embassy was planned to accompany the explorer Sebastián Vizcaíno back there. A galleon, the San Juan Bautista, was built in 45 days, and Date Masamune, in charge of the project, named Hasekura to lead the mission. It left on 28 October 1613 with around 180 people, including samurai, merchants, sailors and some 40 Spaniards and Portuguese. It reached Acapulco on 25 January 1614 after three months at sea, and Mexico City in March. In July the embassy changed ships in Havana, and on 5 October 1614 it arrived at Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

Hasekura entered Seville on 23 October 1614 and met King Philip III in Madrid on 30 January 1615, delivering Masamune's letter and an offer of a treaty. Bad weather held the embassy at Saint-Tropez on the way to Italy. It reached Rome on 20 September 1615, and on 3 November Hasekura gave Pope Paul V two gilded letters, requesting a trade treaty between Japan and Mexico and missionaries for Japan. In April 1616 the king declined a trade agreement, since the embassy did not appear to be an official one from the ruler of Japan, who had ordered missionaries expelled in January 1614.

Hasekura left Seville in June 1616, crossed Mexico again in 1619, and sailed from Acapulco to Manila and then to Japan, reaching Nagasaki in August 1620. Japan had changed: persecution of Christians had begun in 1614, Ieyasu had died in 1616, and the country was moving towards isolation. Two days after his return to Sendai, an edict ordered Christians there to abandon their faith. What became of Hasekura is unknown; rumours said that he abandoned Christianity, was martyred, or practised in secret. His son Tsuneyori was beheaded in 1640 for failing to denounce Christians in his household.

His journey was forgotten in Japan until the Iwakura mission was shown documents in Venice in 1873. Statues of him stand in Acapulco, Havana, Coria del Río and several places in Japan. About 700 inhabitants of Coria del Río bear the surname Japón, identifying them as descendants of members of his delegation.
hashid: Hashid was already a well-known tribe in the 1st millennium BCE and appears often in Sabaic inscriptions. With the tribes Humlan and Yarsum it belonged to a confederation called the Sum'ay, which worshipped the god Ta'lab. The inscriptions name the Banu Hamdan as chiefs of Hashid; the Hamdan later gained control of part of Bakil and gave their clan name to a confederation that took in both. Medieval Yemeni genealogies make Hashid and Bakil the sons of Jashim bin Jubran, a descendant of Hamdan. In the late 3rd century the Hamdan tribes changed their allegiance to Himyar.

Muhammad first sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to call the Yemenis to Islam, and when the Hamdani tribes of the highlands responded coldly he sent Ali ibn Abi Talib, who converted them. After Muhammad's death the Hamdan stayed Muslim and kept out of the ridda movement. Late in the 9th century they invited the Imam al-Hadi Yahya bin al-Hussain to Sa'da, and from then on Zaidi teaching prevailed in the north. Writers have often called Hashid and Bakil the two wings of the Zaidi imamate, though many tribes refused the imams the temporal and legal role they claimed, and imams down to Imam Yahya and Imam Ahmad complained of the tribes' political power.

After the 1962 revolution Abdullah ibn Husayn al-Ahmar led the confederation for decades as its paramount shaykh. He allied with Ali Abdullah Saleh, who relied on this coalition to take power in 1978, and served as Speaker of Parliament until his death on 29 December 2007. His son Sadiq al-Ahmar succeeded him. In 2011 the new leadership sided with the protesters of the Arab Spring and launched a Hashid insurgency, which played a central part in the Battle of Sana'a and in the protests that forced Saleh to step down in February 2012.

The break between the al-Ahmar family and Saleh, who kept the loyalty of some Hashid tribes, divided the confederation. This division, together with the suspension of Saudi financial support over the alliance of the al-Ahmar family with the Muslim Brotherhood, contributed to the confederation's defeat in the conflict with the Houthis, and many of its tribes, among them the Bani Suraim, Usaimat and Uzer, made peace with the rebels or joined them.
hashim-al-atassi: Hashim al-Atassi was born in Homs in 1875 into the large, landowning and politically active Atassi family. He studied public administration in Istanbul and graduated in 1893. Up to 1918 he served as governor of Homs, Hama, Baalbek, Anatolia and Jaffa. In 1919 he was elected chairman of the Syrian National Congress.

On 8 March 1920 the Congress declared independence as a constitutional monarchy under King Faisal I, and Atassi became prime minister. He appointed Abd al-Rahman Shahbandar foreign minister to seek alliances in Europe in an attempt to prevent a French mandate. The French High Commissioner Henri Gouraud presented an ultimatum, and Atassi's cabinet was dissolved on 24 July 1920, when the French defeated the Syrian Army at the Battle of Maysalun.

In October 1927 Atassi met a group of notables and founded the National Bloc, a coalition that sought full independence by diplomatic rather than violent means. He was elected its permanent president. In 1928 he was elected president of the Constituent Assembly, charged with drafting Syria's first republican constitution. The French high commissioner dissolved the assembly in May 1930, and Atassi was imprisoned for several months on Arwad Island.

In 1934 President Mohammad Ali al-Abid negotiated a treaty with France that kept the Syrian Mountains under French control. Atassi criticised it, arguing that no independence was valid unless it covered all of Syria, and called a 60-day strike. On 22 March 1936 he headed a Bloc delegation to France, where over six months he negotiated a Franco-Syrian treaty promising independence over 25 years.

Atassi returned to Syria in triumph on 27 September 1936 and was elected president in November. By the end of 1938 France had shown no intention of ratifying the treaty, and the cession of the province of Alexandretta to Turkey angered Syrian nationalists. He resigned on 7 July 1939 and retired to Homs. In 1943 he endorsed Shukri al-Quwatli for the presidency instead of standing himself.

After the coup of Husni al-Za'im in March 1949 and his overthrow in August, Atassi formed a provisional cabinet that included the Baath Party's Michel Aflaq, and women voted for the first time on 15 and 16 November 1949. He was then nominated for a second term as president. His talks with Iraq about a union angered the military leader Adib Shishakli, and on 24 December 1951 he resigned in protest at Shishakli's second coup. When Shishakli fell on 24 February 1954 he resumed the presidency. He left office in 1955. Atassi died in Homs in December 1960, during the union with Egypt, and his state funeral was the largest in the city's history.
hasidism: In the late 17th century several trends came together among the Jews of the southern edge of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, especially in what is now Western Ukraine. The most prominent was the spread of Kabbalah, once an esoteric teaching practised by a few, through cheap printed pamphlets. The same current had fed the Sabbatean movement of Sabbatai Zevi, who declared himself Messiah in 1665. Israel ben Eliezer, about 1698 to 1760, called the Baal Shem Tov, is regarded as the founder. He was a folk healer who became wealthy and well known, and most of what is told of him comes from hagiographic accounts. His follower Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezhirichi, succeeded him and turned his ideas into a movement.

Hasidic thought draws heavily on Lurianic Kabbalah and to an extent popularises it. Its most basic theme is the immanence of God in the universe. Its defining doctrine is that of the tzadik, the Righteous One, also called the Rebbe, as an inspiration and the figure around whom followers are organised. Hasidim are organised in independent groups called courts or dynasties, each headed by a hereditary Rebbe, and these often keep the name of the Eastern European town where they began, as Satmar, Belz and Vizhnitz do.

Worship stresses devotion, and wordless melodies called nigunim are a means of reaching devekut, cleaving to God, in prayer and communal gatherings. Many Hasidim use Galician Yiddish among themselves. Hasidic tales, a genre of hagiographies and anecdotes, were often passed on orally, and the earliest collection dates from 1815.

Early in the 19th century the tzaddiqim became a leading power across most of Eastern Europe, even in Lithuania, a stronghold of the opposing Misnagdic camp. Less than three generations after the Baal Shem Tov's death the movement had hundreds of thousands of followers by 1830. In the early 20th century emigration to America, urbanisation, World War I and the Russian Civil War uprooted the shtetls that had been its base. In the Soviet Union repression of religion brought rapid secularisation, though a few Hasidim, especially of Chabad, practised in secret for decades. Today most Hasidim live in Israel and the United States.
haskalah: Haskalah, Hebrew for wisdom, erudition or education, arose as a defined outlook in the 1770s. Its first centre was Berlin, and the example of the Prussian Jew Moses Mendelssohn (1729-1786) shaped it, as did Aaron Halle-Wolfssohn and Joseph Perl. Mendelssohn's success as a philosopher and man of letters showed that Jews could be integrated and accepted among non-Jews. His German translation of the Torah gave ambitious young Jews a bridge into secular knowledge, and the Biur, a grammatical commentary prepared under his supervision, was meant to counter traditional rabbinical methods of exegesis.

The Maskilim shared a literary canon that began in Berlin. Their central enterprise was reviving Hebrew as a literary language for secular purposes; its restoration as a spoken tongue came much later. They standardised grammar, coined neologisms and wrote poetry, magazines and plays. The quarterly Ha-Meassef, begun at Koenigsberg in 1783 by students of Mendelssohn, already called its publishers Maskilim, and the name Haskalah became standard in 1860, when the Odessa newspaper Ha-Melitz took it as its motto.

What marked the movement was its challenge to the rabbinic elite's monopoly over Jewish intellectual life. The Maskilim pursued two agendas at once, urging Jews to acculturate to the modern state while remaining a distinct group, and the movement ranged from moderates to radicals. Haskalah was largely a single-generation experience, since the children of the Maskilim usually went further towards acculturation and assimilation.

The Haskalah spread through Europe. In Poland-Lithuania, the heartland of rabbinic Judaism, it worked with the Russian government of the Pale of Settlement on secular education, while its writers satirised Hasidic mysticism. Joseph Perl's Megalleh Temirim, published in Vienna in 1819, is said to be the first modern Hebrew novel. Its last stage ended at the close of the 19th century, after the 1881 pogroms in Imperial Russia turned many adherents towards proto-Zionist groups such as Hibbat Zion.

It led to a secular Jewish culture that stressed history and identity over religion, to political engagement in the struggle for emancipation and, later, to Zionism. It also fed the birth of the Reform movement and provoked responses within Orthodoxy, among them the Mussar movement in Lithuania and Torah im Derech Eretz in Germany. Its alliance with governments in plans for secular education brought it into sharp conflict with the Orthodox.
hasmonean-dynasty: After Alexander the Great conquered the Achaemenid Empire around 333 BCE, the region was contested between the Seleucid Empire to the north and the Ptolemaic Kingdom to the south, and Jerusalem changed hands seven times between 319 and 302 BCE. Hellenisation pitted Jews who embraced it against traditionalists. In 168 BCE Antiochus IV Epiphanes, forced by Rome to withdraw from Egypt, moved to assert strict control over Coele Syria and Phoenicia. According to 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees and Josephus, he sacked Jerusalem and its Temple, suppressed Jewish religious observance and imposed Hellenistic practices.

The Maccabean Revolt followed. The author of 1 Maccabees saw it as a rising of pious Jews against the king and against the Jews who supported him, while 2 Maccabees presented it as a struggle between Judaism and Hellenism, a view that modern scholarship tends to share. Judah Maccabee, using guerrilla warfare, won control of the country, and after his death in 160 BCE his brother Jonathan led the rebels.

Jonathan became High Priest in 152 BCE. His brother Simon assumed the leadership in 142 BCE as High Priest and Ethnarch, and an assembly in 141 BCE confirmed him as leader until a faithful prophet should arise. The Roman Senate recognised the dynasty around 139 BCE. Aristobulus I took the title of king in 104 BCE after jailing his brothers and his mother. The dynasty expanded into Perea, Samaria, Idumea, Galilee and Iturea, which Alexander Jannaeus conquered, forcibly converting its people to Judaism according to Josephus.

When Salome Alexandra, the only queen regnant, died in 67 BCE, her sons fought a civil war: Hyrcanus II, backed by the Pharisees, against Aristobulus II, backed by the Sadducees. It ended when Pompey captured Jerusalem in 63 BCE and made the kingdom a Roman client state. In 40 BCE a Parthian army conquered the Levant. The Roman Senate named Herod king, and he displaced the last reigning Hasmonean in 37 BCE.

The dynasty lasted 103 years before it yielded to the Herodian dynasty. Herod tried to bolster his legitimacy by marrying a Hasmonean princess, Mariamne I, but he had the last male heir, Aristobulus III, executed in 36 BCE. The books of 1 and 2 Maccabees are the main sources for the dynasty's origins. They cover the period from 175 to 134 BCE and present the salvation of the Jewish people as coming from God through the family of Mattathias. They are held as canonical scripture by the Catholic, Orthodox and most Oriental Orthodox churches and as apocryphal by Protestant denominations.
hassan-al-banna: Hassan al-Banna was born on 14 October 1906 in Mahmudiyya, a rural town of the Nile Delta. His father, Sheikh Ahmed Abd al-Rahman al-Banna al-Sa'ati, was a Hanbali imam, muezzin and mosque teacher who classified the traditions of Ahmad ibn Hanbal. At thirteen he took part in demonstrations during the Egyptian Revolution of 1919, published political pamphlets and founded youth reform societies.

The family moved to Cairo in 1924 after economic difficulties. He had gone there in 1923 to study at Dar al-Ulum, an institution that trained teachers in modern subjects, enrolling against his father's wishes. In Cairo he read the Salafi scholar Rashid Rida and attended his lectures. The abolition of the Ottoman caliphate in 1924 struck him as a calamity.

After finishing his studies in 1927 al-Banna became a primary school teacher in Ismailia, where foreign influence was stronger than elsewhere in Egypt. He preached in cafes as well as mosques. In March 1928 six workers of the Suez Canal Company, complaining of injustices under foreign control, appointed him their leader, and the Muslim Brothers were born. At first the Brotherhood was one of many small Islamic associations. After he moved its headquarters to Cairo in 1932 it grew quickly, with branches in every Egyptian province by the late 1930s and, a decade later, 500,000 active members and as many sympathisers.

He built a mass movement on mosques, welfare associations and neighbourhood groups, with businesses, clinics and schools attached and members organised in cells called usar, or families. The movement took part in the Arab revolt in Palestine in 1936 to 1939. Al-Banna called on Muslims to prepare for jihad against colonial powers, and the Brotherhood allowed a secret military wing.

Al-Banna presented Islam as a comprehensive system of life, with the Quran and Sunnah as the only acceptable constitution, and called for the Islamization of the state, economy and society. He criticised Western materialism, British imperialism and the traditionalism of Egypt's ulema. He appealed to Egyptian and pan-Arab patriotism but rejected Arab nationalism and regarded all Muslims as one community. He developed an Islamic fiscal theory in which zakat would be reserved for social expenditure to reduce inequality.

In December 1948, after the Brotherhood sent volunteers to the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, Prime Minister Nokrashy Pasha outlawed it, impounded its assets and jailed many members. When a student member of the Brotherhood then murdered Nokrashy Pasha, al-Banna issued a statement condemning the killing. On 12 February 1949 he and his brother-in-law Abdul Karim Mansur were shot as they waited for a taxi in Cairo, and he died of his wounds. King Farouk and his Iron Guard were accused of being behind the assassination. His son-in-law Said Ramadan emerged as a major leader of the Brotherhood in the 1950s.
hassan-gouled-aptidon: Hassan Gouled Aptidon was born on 15 October 1916 in the small village of Gerisa in the Lughaya district of British Somaliland, into the Mamassan subset of the Issa clan. He began his career in the 1930s as a nurse and was stationed at Dikhil in 1932, and was later an entrepreneur. In 1946 he founded the Somali and Dankali Youth Club with Mahamoud Harbi Farah. They were elected together to the colony's Representative Council in 1951, then separated, and Gouled was elected French senator against Harbi.

Gouled sat in the French Senate from 1952 to 1958 and campaigned against Harbi, who sought to join the territory to neighbouring Somalia. He was vice-president of the Government Council from 1958 to April 1959, and a member of the French National Assembly from 1959 to 1962, when he lost his seat. He led the Democratic Union Issa in the 1960s, was education minister under Ali Aref Bourhan from 1963 to 1967 and was briefly jailed in July 1967. Elected to the Territorial Assembly in 1968, he later became Minister of the Interior.

In 1974 he called a vote with the support of François Mitterrand. He became president of the African People's League for Independence, created in February 1975, and was President of the Governing Council on 18 May 1977. The Chamber of Deputies elected him President of the future Republic of Djibouti on 28 May 1977.

After an attack on the Zinc Palm in December 1977 he banned the main opposition party and set up a one-party system. In 1981 he declared his party, the People's Rally for Progress, the only legal one, and was elected without opposition on 12 June 1981 with 84.58 per cent of the vote. The Djiboutian Civil War began in 1991. A referendum in September 1992 allowed four parties, and in the December 1992 elections the People's Rally won all 65 seats. He was re-elected for a fourth term in May 1993 with 60.7 per cent.

On 4 February 1999 he announced his retirement. His nephew Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, who had increasingly handled affairs for him, was chosen as the party's candidate, won the April 1999 election and succeeded him on 8 May 1999. Gouled Aptidon died at his home on 21 November 2006, aged 90.
hassan-ibn-al-numan: Hassan ibn al-Nu'man al-Ghassani came from the Ghassanid tribe, which had led the Arab tribal confederates of the Byzantine Empire in Syria in the century before the Muslim conquest of the region in the 630s. Some of the tribe stayed in Syria and joined the Syrian army, the core of the Umayyad military. Caliph Abd al-Malik appointed him to reconquer Ifriqiya, lost to the Berbers under Kasila and the Byzantines at the Battle of Vescera in 682, and gave him 40,000 men, a force of unprecedented size for North Africa.

The chronology of his campaigns is uncertain, as the medieval sources give different dates. He first took Carthage, the Byzantines' fortified capital in the province, which its inhabitants seem to have deserted, and defeated the Byzantines and Berbers at Bizerte. After a fleet sent by Emperor Leontios retook Carthage in 697, he recaptured it in 698 and destroyed it, tearing down its walls, cutting off its water and making its harbours unusable.

He then marched against the Berber queen al-Kahina, who ruled the Aurès. She dealt him a heavy blow at the Battle of Meskiana, and he withdrew from Ifriqiya to Tripolitania, where he waited three to five years for reinforcements. With fresh troops and some 12,000 Berbers who had turned against her, he defeated her at Gabes and pursued her into the Aurès, where she was killed near the modern town of Tobna.

From Kairouan he set up a central diwan to register and pay the troops and to collect the kharaj from the Christian inhabitants, and he enrolled Berber converts in it with a stake in income-producing lands. He is credited with rebuilding the Great Mosque of Kairouan. In March 699 he founded the medina of Tunis, where 1,000 Coptic labourers from Egypt built warships for the caliph's fleet.

In 704 the governor of Egypt, Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan, had him dismissed in favour of Musa ibn Nusayr and confiscated his spoils as he passed through Egypt. The historian Hugh N. Kennedy called him "in many ways, the real founder of Muslim North Africa", and the Berbers he recruited proved crucial in the conquest of the Iberian Peninsula under al-Walid I.
hassan-ii-of-morocco: Hassan was born on 9 July 1929 at the Dar al-Makhzen in Rabat, during the French protectorate, the eldest son of Sultan Mohammed V and his second wife, Lalla Abla bint Tahar. He studied Islamic sciences in Fez and then at the Royal College in Rabat, and took a law degree in 1951 and a master's degree in public law in 1952 at the University of Bordeaux.

French authorities exiled the royal family on 20 August 1953, first to Corsica and then to Madagascar. Hassan advised his father during the exile, returned with him on 16 November 1955 and took part in the negotiations of February 1956 that led to independence. In April 1956 his father named him commander-in-chief of the new Royal Moroccan Armed Forces.

Hassan became king on 26 February 1961, after his father died following surgery, and also held the office of prime minister. In 1962 he and his aides wrote Morocco's first constitution. It defined a constitutional monarchy with several parties, made Islam the state religion and gave the king the title Amir al-Mu'minin, with a person described as inviolable and sacred.

The opposition parties, among them the UNFP and the Istiqlal, protested against it. Morocco fought the Sand War with Algeria in 1963, and student protests in Casablanca in March 1965 became riots whose repression left hundreds dead. In June he dissolved parliament and suspended the constitution, ruling directly for more than five years under a state of exception. In 1969 Morocco recovered Sidi Ifni from Spain.

He survived two coup attempts. On 10 July 1971, during his birthday party at Skhirat, army cadets stormed the palace; about 400 people were reportedly killed by the rebels and loyal troops killed more than 150. On 16 August 1972 air force jets fired on his aircraft over Tétouan, killing eight people. Later he organised the Green March of 1975 into the former Spanish Sahara, after which Morocco controlled much of the territory and the conflict with the Polisario Front began.

The decades from the 1960s to the late 1980s are called the Years of Lead, when thousands of dissidents were jailed, killed, exiled or forcibly disappeared. The opposition leader Mehdi Ben Barka disappeared in Paris in October 1965. In 1990 Hassan set up the Consultative Human Rights Council, and in 1991 he pardoned two thousand prisoners, including political prisoners held in secret prisons such as Tazmamart.

The first opposition-led government was elected in 1998. Hassan died in Rabat on 23 July 1999 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Mohammed VI, who in 2004 created the Equity and Reconciliation Commission to investigate abuses committed during his father's reign.
hassan-tower: The tower and its mosque were commissioned by Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur, the third caliph of the Almohad Caliphate, a Berber Muslim empire in the Maghreb and Iberia. He decided to build a new fortified imperial capital, called al-Mahdiyya or Ribat al-Fath, on the site of the present medina of Rabat, with new walls reaching far beyond the old Kasbah, and an enormous mosque of which the tower was to be the minaret. Construction began in 1191, although 1195 is sometimes cited because Mármol reported that Ribat al-Fath commemorated al-Mansur's victory at the Battle of Alarcos.

The minaret was modelled on that of the Koutoubia Mosque in Marrakesh, as the Giralda of Seville was, and drew on the Lighthouse of Alexandria for its height and its ramps. Why it is called the Hassan Tower is unknown, though the name is attested as early as the 13th century.

The mosque stands on the high south bank of the Bu Regreg river and measured 183 by 139 metres, which would have made it the largest in the western Islamic world, larger than the Great Mosque of Cordoba. Historians think it may have served the Almohad troops who gathered there before campaigns. Its hypostyle hall was divided into 21 aisles, and it had cylindrical stone columns built from drums of differing height, an innovation that slowed the work.

The tower is built of sandstone that has turned red ochre, with a square plan 16 metres on each side. It stands 44 metres high, but its intended height was at least 64 metres and possibly 80, which would have made it slightly taller than the original Giralda. Ramps rather than stairs would have let the muezzin ride a horse to the top.

Al-Mansur died in 1199 and the mosque was left unfinished, with only the beginnings of its walls and 348 columns, and his successors lacked the resources or the will to finish it. The capital stayed at Marrakesh. Nearly everything portable was stripped for reuse elsewhere, and the 1755 Lisbon earthquake did some damage. In the 20th century French and Moroccan archaeologists excavated and reconstructed what remained.

The Mausoleum of Mohammed V, designed by the Vietnamese architect Cong Vo Toan and completed in 1971, now stands at the southeastern corner of the site. The complex was placed on UNESCO's tentative list in 1995 and gained World Heritage status in 2012 as part of historic Rabat.
hassaniya-arabic: Hassaniya is a variety of Maghrebi Arabic. It was spoken by the Beni Ḥassān Bedouin tribes of Yemeni origin, who extended their authority over most of Mauritania and Western Sahara between the 15th and 17th centuries. In the pre-modern period it was the language of the region around Chinguetti. It completely replaced the Berber languages originally spoken in this region, although its location exposed it to influence from Zenaga Berber and Pulaar, and G. S. Colin found traces of South Arabian in the speech between Rio de Oro and Timbuktu.

Although clearly a western dialect, Hassaniya is relatively distant from other Maghrebi varieties. There are several dialects of it, which differ chiefly in pronunciation. Its phonology has both very innovative and very conservative features. All phonemes of Classical Arabic are represented apart from two that have merged, and the interdental consonants have been preserved. It has 31 consonant phonemes, or 43 counting marginal cases, and has gained an additional emphatic consonant from Zenaga Berber and a series of palatal consonants from Niger–Congo languages of the south. As in most Maghrebi dialects, short vowels are generally dropped in open syllables.

Hassaniya is normally written in the Arabic script. In Senegal the government adopted the Latin script for it by Decree 2005–980 of 21 October 2005. Many educated speakers switch between languages: in Western Sahara between Hassaniya, Modern Standard Arabic and Spanish, since Spain previously controlled the region, and elsewhere between Hassaniya and French. Hassaniya is spoken in Mauritania, Western Sahara, southern Morocco, Algeria, Mali, Senegal, Niger and Burkina Faso, and the number of speakers is about three million, most of them in Mauritania.
hasselt: Hasselt lies between the Campine region, north of the Demer, and the Hesbaye region to the south. The name derives from the Germanic word Hasaluth, which refers to the common hazel.

Hasselt was founded in about the 7th century on the Helbeek, a tributary of the Demer. In the Middle Ages it became one of the free cities of the county of Loon, whose borders were roughly those of the present province of Limburg. It is first named in a document in 1165. In 1232 Arnold IV, Count of Loon, gave the city the same freedoms as those enjoyed in Liège. From 1366 the county was ruled directly by the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, until annexation by France in 1794.

Under the First French Empire Maastricht was the capital of the Department of the Lower Meuse. After the defeat of Napoleon in 1815 the area became part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, and King William I renamed the department after the medieval Duchy of Limburg, a duchy that had never included Hasselt or Maastricht. Belgium split from the Netherlands in 1830, but the status of Limburg was settled only in 1839, when it was divided into Belgian and Dutch parts. Hasselt became the provisional capital of the Belgian province. In ecclesiastical terms Belgian Limburg became independent of the Diocese of Liège only in 1967, when Hasselt became the seat of a new diocese.

Hasselt is known for jenever, a gin. It escaped the ban on the production and sale of the drink imposed in 1601 by Albert VII, Archduke of Austria, and Isabella Clara Eugenia, because it belonged to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. Jenever production was the most important industry in Limburg in the 19th century, with most distilleries in Hasselt.

Hasselt is the capital and largest city of the province of Limburg in the Flemish Region of Belgium and the seat of the Catholic diocese of Hasselt. The Gothic St Quentin's Cathedral, begun in the 11th century, and the Refuge of Herkenrode Abbey, of 1542, the city's oldest civic building, stand there, and Hasselt University was established in 1971.
hassi-messaoud: Hassi Messaoud lies in Ouargla Province in eastern Algeria, 85 kilometres south-east of Ouargla. The name means the well of Messaoud in Arabic, after Messaoud Rouabeh, a well-digger in the region. A water well was dug in 1917, and before oil was found the place was not heavily populated. The oil field is a Cambrian sandstone reservoir 270 metres thick, in a dome 3,300 metres deep that covers 1,300 square kilometres of the Oued Mya structural basin. The climate is hot desert, with average highs above 40 degrees from June to September and about 44 millimetres of rain a year. Sandstorms are common between March and June.

A refraction seismic survey showed the structure, and the Md No. 1 well discovered oil in 1956. After the discovery the French built two petroleum bases. After oil and gas were nationalised the bases became the property of Sonatrach, the national company. In 1984, after a new administrative zoning, Hassi Messaoud became a municipality with a local assembly, and people began to settle there independently. Sonatrach brought in about 2,000 ready-built houses.

Hassi Messaoud had 45,147 inhabitants in 2008, against 40,360 in 1998, and more than 60,000 by a non-official count, not counting those living in the company bases. More than 800 wells lie within 25 kilometres of the town. It stands on the N3 highway between Touggourt and Biskra to the north and Illizi and Djanet to the south, and Oued Irara Airport serves it. The commune comprises seven localities, among them Haoud El Hamra, Gassi Touil and El Gassi.
hasta-siempre-comandante: The song was written in 1965 by the Cuban composer Carlos Puebla as a reply to the farewell letter Che Guevara left when he went to foster revolution in the Congo and later in Bolivia, where he was captured and killed. Its title comes from part of Guevara's well-known saying Hasta la victoria siempre, until victory, always. Its words recount key moments of the Cuban Revolution and describe Guevara and his role as a revolutionary commander.

Like many of Puebla's songs, and in line with Cuban and Caribbean tradition, it consists of a refrain and a series of five verses. Each verse is a quatrain rhyming ABBA, and each line is written in eight syllables. In the third verse, for example, the lines run from the breeze that burns with spring suns to planting the flag in the light of a smile.

The song became widely known after Guevara's death, and many artists on the left made their own versions. More than 200 versions exist. Among those who have recorded it are Compay Segundo, Soledad Bravo, Óscar Chávez, Robert Wyatt, Silvio Rodríguez, Ángel Parra, Wolf Biermann, Maria Farantouri, Jan Garbarek, George Dalaras and Enrique Bunbury. A recording by Los Calchakis is often wrongly credited to Buena Vista Social Club, and Carlos Puebla's own recording is often mistakenly credited to Víctor Jara, who never sang it.

The most commercially successful version was Nathalie Cardone's, produced by Laurent Boutonnat. It reached number 2 on the French Singles chart, topped the Wallonia charts and stayed 38 weeks on the French charts. At the same time the Argentine model Inés Rivero released a version titled Che Guevara (Hasta Siempre), which reached number 18 on the French Singles chart and spent 15 weeks on the French charts. The first eight lines of the song serve as the prologue to a song in the Malayalam film Left Right Left.
hastinapura: The name Hastinapura means the City of Elephants, from the Sanskrit hastina, elephant, and pura, city, and the city is said to have been named after King Hasti. In the Mahabharata it is the capital of the Kuru kingdom of the Kauravas, where the hundred Kaurava brothers were born to Queen Gandhari, wife of King Dhritarashtra. In Jain tradition it is the birthplace of three of the 24 Tirthankaras: Shantinatha, Kunthunatha and Aranatha.

Excavations in the early 1950s by B. B. Lal of the Archaeological Survey of India aimed mainly to place Painted Grey Ware among the ceramic industries of the early historical period. Lal also found correlations between the Mahabharata and his finds. In his account the first phase, before about 1200 BCE, left only scattered Ochre Coloured Pottery. The second, from about 1100 to about 800 BCE, is characterised by Painted Grey Ware. Its walls were of mud, mud brick or reeds, and charred rice grains are among the earliest evidence of rice cultivation in the subcontinent.

Lal found a major erosional scar in the mound, which he linked to a great flood in the Ganga perhaps around 800 BCE. The Mahabharata says that in the reign of the Kuru king Nichakshu a flood carried away much of Hastinapura, after which the capital moved to Kaushambi, and Lal suggested that this may have a historical basis. Later phases brought Northern Black Polished Ware, baked brick, the first iron objects and coins, and the period from about the 2nd century BCE to about the 6th century CE seems to have been its heyday.

Lal thought the site abandoned several times. An excavation of 2021–22 instead suggested continuous occupation from antiquity until the late medieval period, found Indo-Greek and Gupta coins and seals, and said nothing of a flood. Hastinapur appears in the Ain-i-Akbari as a pargana of Delhi sarkar, and Abu'l-Fazl calls it an ancient Hindu settlement.

Hastinapur is a small township in the Doab region of Uttar Pradesh, about 37 kilometres from Meerut and nearly 96 kilometres north-east of Delhi, re-established by Jawaharlal Nehru on 6 February 1949. It is considered one of the holiest places for Hindus and Jains. Among its temples are the Pandeshwar Temple, dedicated to Shiva, and the Karna Temple, and among the Jain sites the Digamber Jain Bada Mandir, built in 1801, and the Jambudweep and Kailash Parvat complexes.
hastings-banda: Hastings Kamuzu Banda was born Akim Kamnkhwala Mtunthama Banda near Kasungu, to Mphonongo Banda and Akupingamnyama Phiri. No birth was registered, so his date of birth is unknown. After attending village and mission schools he was baptised in 1910. He studied at the Wilberforce Institute in Ohio, graduating from its high school section in 1928, and later at the University of Edinburgh, which awarded him the Scottish Triple Qualification in 1941.

He became an elder of a parish in the Church of Scotland. In 1951 he moved to the Gold Coast, and Malawian Congress leaders, among them Henry Chipembere and Kanyama Chiume, later asked him to return and lead their cause.

Banda opposed the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, formed in 1953, because he feared it would cost Nyasaland's Africans further rights. He reached Nyasaland on 6 July 1958 after an absence of about 42 years and toured the country speaking against the federation. By February 1959 Rhodesian troops had been flown in and a state of emergency declared. On 3 March he was arrested in Operation Sunrise and held in Gwelo in Southern Rhodesia.

He was released in April 1960 and invited to London for talks on independence. After elections in August 1961 he became de facto prime minister, a title formally granted on 1 February 1963. In December 1962 the British Secretary of State R. A. Butler essentially agreed to end the federation.

A month after independence Banda dismissed four ministers who had proposed limits on his powers, and the dissidents fled the country. The constitution of 6 July 1966 made Malawi a republic and Banda its first president, the only candidate, and formally made the Malawi Congress Party the sole legal party. The party made him president for life in 1970, and the legislature did the same for the country in 1971. His title included the word Ngwazi, meaning saviour or conqueror in Chichewa.

In 1983 three ministers and a member of parliament who had favoured multiparty politics died in what was officially a traffic accident. Adult citizens had to carry party cards, the Malawi Young Pioneers acted as the party's paramilitary wing, and films and books were censored. Human rights groups estimate that at least 6,000 people were killed, tortured or jailed without trial. With the end of the Cold War, donors pressed for reform, and in 1993 Banda agreed to a referendum that ended the one-party system. He was defeated in the elections that followed and died in South Africa on 25 November 1997.
hatamoto: The word literally means the base of the flag, the men who guarded it on the battlefield. In the Sengoku period many lords had such direct retainers, but it is the Tokugawa system that the term now chiefly names. The earlier shogunates had called their official retainers gokenin; under the Tokugawa the hatamoto were the upper vassals and the gokenin the lower, and the Edo-era men were also called jikisan hatamoto, direct shogunal hatamoto, to set them apart from those who had served various lords.

The shogunate counted as hatamoto the families that had served the Tokugawa since their days in Mikawa, but the ranks also took in retainers of defeated houses such as the Takeda, Hōjō and Imagawa, cadet branches of lords' families, heirs of lords whose domains had been confiscated, such as Asano Daigaku, and descendants of the old provincial governors. Becoming a hatamoto was called bakushin toritate, promotion to the shogunate.

The kuramaitori drew their income straight from Tokugawa granaries, while the jikatatori held land scattered across Japan. The richest heads of families with provincial fiefs, the kōtai-yoriai, had duties of alternate attendance like the daimyō, and those with about 8,000 koku or more were called taishin hatamoto. The line between the upper hatamoto and the fudai daimyō lay at 10,000 koku, and a few, such as the Hayashi family of Kaibuchi, were promoted across it. A hatamoto of 500 koku kept seven non-samurai servants, two swordsmen, a lancer and an archer, and those living in Edo policed their own districts.

The popular phrase eighty thousand hatamoto far exceeded their real number; adding the gokenin brought the total to about 17,000. Hatamoto patronised the martial arts and ran dojo in and around Edo, and the family of Yagyū Munenori became hereditary sword instructors to the shogun. Well-known hatamoto included Ōoka Tadasuke, Katsu Kaishū, Enomoto Takeaki and the Westerners William Adams and Jan Joosten van Lodensteijn. Many fought on both sides in the Boshin War of 1868, and afterwards they remained retainers of the main Tokugawa line and followed it to its new domain of Shizuoka.
hatay-province: Hatay lies mostly outside Anatolia, along the eastern coast of the Levantine Sea, and borders Syria to the south and east. Its second-largest city is İskenderun, formerly Alexandretta. About 46 per cent of the land is mountain, 33 per cent plain and 20 per cent plateau and hillside. The Orontes River runs through it and reaches the Mediterranean at a delta in Samandağ.

The area has been settled since the early Bronze Age. It belonged in turn to the Akkadian Empire, the Amorite kingdom of Yamhad and the kingdom of Mitanni, and was then ruled by Hittites and Neo-Hittite peoples, from whom the modern name derives. It was the centre of the Seleucid Empire, home to the four Greek cities of the Syrian tetrapolis, and from 64 BCE Antioch was an important centre of the Roman Empire. The Rashidun Caliphate conquered the region in 638, and the Crusaders took it in 1098 and made it the centre of the Principality of Antioch. The Ottoman sultan Selim I took it from the Mameluks in 1516.

Under the Ottomans the area was the sanjak of Alexandretta. After the First World War it was placed under the French mandate for Syria. A French-Turkish treaty of 20 October 1921 made the sanjak autonomous, and it then had 220,000 inhabitants, 87,000 of them Turks, alongside Arabs, Jews, Assyrians, Kurds and Armenians. In 1936 Turkey complained to the League of Nations about the treatment of the Turkish community, and the sanjak was given autonomy in November 1937.

Hatay State, a transitional entity, existed from 7 September 1938 to 29 June 1939. France was willing to return the area to Turkey in exchange for a pact against possible European aggression. On 29 June 1939, after a referendum that has been called rigged, Hatay became a Turkish province. Syria disputed both the separation and the annexation, and about 50,000 people, among them 22,000 Armenians, are estimated to have left for Syria.

Hatay is Turkey's southernmost province, with its capital at Antakya, the ancient Antioch, and a population of 1,686,043 in 2022. Its people include Sunni Muslims and Alawites, with Syriac Orthodox, Maronite, Antiochian Greek and Armenian communities. Its sites include Alalakh, Tell Tayinat and the Hatay Archaeology Museum at Antakya, with a large collection of Roman mosaics. The province was heavily damaged by the earthquakes of 2023.
hathigumpha-inscription: The seventeen lines cover about 15 by 5.5 feet of rock. They begin on the overhanging brow of the cave, where the first eight are visible from the front, and continue on its sloping roof. Handwriting analysis suggests that three scribes worked on it. Lines 1 to 6 are well preserved, but the middle lines, 7 to 15, are worn by rain, dripping water, dust and hornets and can be read in many ways. Minor inscriptions on the walls below were added in the 10th and 11th centuries.

Richard Salomon describes its year-by-year account of Kharavela's deeds as close to pure panegyric, an early example of the prashasti style. It records public works, gifts to monks, Brahmins and the people, festivals and arts, and a war against the Satavahana king Satakarni. It also names a canal built by a Nanda king and extended by Kharavela to the Kalinga capital, and a Yavana king forced to retreat to Mathura. R. D. Banerji and K. P. Jayaswal read his name as Dimita and identified him with Demetrius I of Bactria, a reading Sircar and others reject on chronological grounds.

A. Sterling published the inscription in Asiatic Researches in 1825. James Prinsep printed an eye-copy by Kittoe in 1837, Alexander Cunningham a tracing in 1877, and Bhagwan Lal Indraji the first cast in 1884; Indraji first identified the king as Kharavela. Bühler judged the script no earlier than the 2nd century BCE and no later than the 1st, and Sircar placed it in the second half of the 1st century BCE or the first decades of the 1st century CE.

Because the text is badly weathered, readings vary widely, and Salomon holds that no single standard version can be established. Walter Spink argues that dating Satakarni by early readings put many Buddhist monuments of central India two or three centuries too early.
hathor: Cattle imagery is frequent in the art of Predynastic Egypt, as are images of women with upraised, curved arms like horns, and both may represent goddesses connected with cattle. The Gerzeh Palette, from the Naqada II period, shows a cow's head with inward-curving horns surrounded by stars, which suggests a link with the sky.

Hathor herself is not unambiguously mentioned or depicted until the Fourth Dynasty, c. 2613 to 2494 BCE, although some objects that refer to her may be earlier.
