When she does clearly appear, her horns curve outward. Her Egyptian name, ḥwt-ḥr, is usually translated as house of Horus, but it can also mean my house is the sky.

The Egyptologist Robyn Gillam calls Hathor a type of deity rather than a single entity, and suggests that the royal goddess promoted by the Old Kingdom court absorbed many local goddesses, who were then treated as her manifestations. Texts speak of Seven Hathors, and sometimes of as many as 362.

As a sky goddess she was mother or consort of Horus and Ra, and so the symbolic mother of the pharaohs. She was also one of the goddesses who acted as the Eye of Ra. Her other concerns were music, dance, love, sexuality and motherhood, and the sistrum, a rattle, was important in her worship. The Seven Hathors appear in New Kingdom tales at births, foretelling how the characters will die.

She was shown as a cow, as a woman with a cow's head, and most often as a woman wearing a headdress of cow horns and a sun disk. Hathor also helped the dead cross into the Duat, and the Theban necropolis was portrayed as a mountain with her cow emerging from it.

From the Fourth Dynasty Hathor was the goddess most closely linked with the king, and late Old Kingdom rulers promoted her cult in the provinces to bind those regions to the court. More temples were dedicated to her than to any other Egyptian goddess. At Dendera, her oldest temple in Upper Egypt, which dates to at least the Fourth Dynasty, kings made additions across Egyptian history, and the last version, from the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, is among the best preserved of that time.

Many festivals involved drinking and dancing, such as the Festival of Drunkenness on the twentieth day of the month of Thout. In households women prayed to her for children, and the only known surviving birth brick is decorated with an image of a woman holding her child between images of Hathor. Isis increasingly overshadowed her after the New Kingdom, but she continued to be venerated until the early centuries CE.
hathumod: Hathumod was born in 840 to Count Liudolf of Saxony and the Frankish noblewoman Oda, of the rich and powerful Liudolfing family. Their ancestors had only recently been converted to Christianity, which may explain her unusual Germanic name, meaning battle courage. Oda's mother, Aeda, may have been abbess of Herford Abbey, the oldest women's monastery in Saxony, which followed the Benedictine rule, and Hathumod was sent there to be educated as a child.

Liudolf and Oda decided to found a new religious community for women on their allodial lands at Gandersheim, with their daughter as its abbess. Pope Sergius II gave his consent in Rome and sent them home with relics of Pope Anastasius I and Pope Innocent I.

Hathumod was installed as abbess in 852, when she reached the canonical age of 12. She never left her convent, and as many as five of her sisters eventually joined her. Some time after 852 the monk and historian Rudolf of Fulda sent her a dedicated copy of his life of Saint Leoba, but no further contact is known; she seems to have preferred ties with the abbeys of Herford and Corvey.

In 874 an epidemic struck north-western Europe; by Rudolf of Fulda's account it killed nearly a third of the people of Gaul and Germany. Hathumod caught the illness while caring for the sick. Her first biographer says that she spoke prophecies and saw visions of heaven during her long struggle with it. She died in late November and was buried in the church at Brunshausen beside her father.

Her sister Gerberga succeeded her and in 881 moved the remains of Hathumod and their father to the abbey church at Gandersheim; another sister, Christina, followed Gerberga in 896. Nearly all that is known of Hathumod comes from the Vita Hathumodae, written soon after her death by Agius, a monk of Corvey, which the historian Julia M. H. Smith has called the high point of Carolingian hagiography about women. Scholars disagree whether Agius was her brother, her father's brother, a friend or a fellow monastic.

Agius describes her as pious, learned and ruling her nuns by the Benedictine rule, though Gandersheim remained a house of secular canonesses. In the 10th century her nephew Henry the Fowler became king of Germany. His wife, Matilda of Ringelheim, appears to have tried to suppress the memory of Hathumod, Oda, Gerberga and Christina, and the poet Hrotsvit, a canoness of Gandersheim, gave more room to Hathumod's mother and grandmother in her work on the abbey.
hatikvah: Imber emigrated to Ottoman-ruled Palestine in 1882 and read his poem to the pioneers of the early Jewish villages: Rishon LeZion, Rehovot, Gedera and Yesud Hama'ala. Shmuel Cohen, a very young resident of Rishon LeZion with a musical background, sang the poem to a melody he knew from Romania, after seeing the emotional response of the farmers who had heard it. His adaptation helped the poem spread quickly through the Zionist communities of Palestine, and it was adopted as an anthem by the Hovevei Zion and later by the Zionist Movement.

The melody is based on "La Mantovana", a 16th-century Italian song composed by Giuseppe Cenci (Giuseppino del Biado) around 1600. It circulated widely in Renaissance Europe under other titles, among them the Polish "Pod Krakowem" and the Romanian "Cucuruz cu frunza-n sus". Its best-known earlier use was by Bedřich Smetana in Vltava, from Má vlast. The tune follows a minor scale, which is uncommon in national anthems and often heard as mournful, although the title and words are optimistic. The first line of the refrain, "Our hope is not yet lost", has been compared with the openings of the Polish and Ukrainian anthems, and may allude to the vision of the dried bones in Ezekiel 37.

The Zionist Organization held anthem competitions in 1898 and 1900 and judged all the entries unsatisfactory. Imber's poem was popular nonetheless, and at the Sixth Zionist Congress in 1903 it was sung by those opposed to the proposal for a Jewish state in Uganda. Only at the Eighteenth Congress in Prague in 1933 did a motion formally adopt it as the movement's anthem. The British Mandate government briefly banned its public performance from 1919.

In 1948 the song was unofficially proclaimed the anthem of the State of Israel. It became official only in November 2004, when the Knesset sanctioned an abbreviated version, the first stanza and refrain. Some religious Jews have objected that it never mentions God or the Torah, and some non-Jewish citizens of Israel, particularly Arab citizens, find that its focus on Jewish aspirations makes it hard to identify with.
hats-party: The Hats took their name from the tricorne hat worn by officers and gentlemen. They rose in opposition to Count Arvid Horn, who had governed Sweden since 1719 and, after the defeat in the Great Northern War, had kept France at a distance, drawn closer to Great Britain and made no real effort to regain the lost Baltic empire. Opponents of his peaceful policy mocked his followers as Night-caps, and when the estates met in 1738 these names became party badges.

The Hats routed the government, and Horn was compelled to retire after 33 years in high office. In power, they aimed to restore Sweden as a great power and to renew the traditional alliance with France, which welcomed a Swedish government that would uphold French interests in northern Europe and financed the party generously for two generations.

The war with Russia ended in defeat, and an inquiry into its conduct was proposed in the Riksdag. The Hats avoided it by giving precedence to the succession, as King Frederick I had no legitimate children. Empress Elizabeth of Russia offered to restore most of Finland if Adolph Frederick of Holstein, her heir's uncle, were elected successor, and by the Treaty of Åbo of 7 May 1743 her terms were accepted. Russia kept only the land beyond the Kymi river, known as Old Finland.

At France's urging the Hats then entered the Seven Years' War in the Pomeranian theatre. French money was not enough for a long war, and after several years of unsuccessful fighting they made peace, the war having cost Sweden 40,000 men. At the Riksdag of 1760 an impeachment of their leaders seemed inevitable, but their parliamentary tactics kept the Hat government in office for four more years.

At the Riksdag of 1765 the leader of the Caps, Ture Rudbeck, was elected marshal of the Diet over the Hat candidate, Frederick Axel von Fersen, and the Hats won only ten of the hundred seats on the secret committee. They returned briefly to power in 1769 but were soon defeated again. After King Gustav III's coup d'état of 1772 moved Sweden towards absolute monarchy, both Hats and Caps disappeared as political forces.
hatshepsut: Hatshepsut was the eldest daughter of Thutmose I and his great royal wife Ahmose. After her father's death she was married to her half-brother Thutmose II, when she was fourteen or fifteen. The couple had at least one daughter, Princess Neferure. When Thutmose II died, his son Thutmose III inherited the throne as a child of two, and Hatshepsut ruled first as his regent.

By the seventh year of the reign of Thutmose III, around 1472 BCE, she had assumed the position of pharaoh beside him, taking the full royal titulary and sharing his regnal count, which backdated her accession to Year 1. Thutmose III became junior coregent. She is depicted in statues with the regalia of the office, including a false beard, and the images are seen as symbolic. Priests told a story of divine birth in which Amun conceived her through her mother, and the Oracle of Amun proclaimed her pharaoh.

She re-established trade networks disrupted during the Hyksos occupation and funded an expedition to the Land of Punt, around Year 9, which returned with 31 living myrrh trees and frankincense. She was one of the most prolific builders in Egypt. She erected twin obelisks at Karnak and built the Red Chapel and the Temple of Pakhet, which the Greeks called the Speos Artemidos. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, with its focal point Djeser-Djeseru, is considered a masterpiece of ancient architecture. Her last dated attestation is Year 20, and she no longer appears in Year 22.

Her death is presumed in Year 22 of Thutmose III. She was probably buried in KV20 in the Valley of the Kings with her father, though Thutmose I was later moved to another tomb. A mummy from tomb KV60 was proposed in 2007 as hers, partly because a molar found in a canopic box seemed to fit its jaw, but in 2011 the tooth was identified as a lower molar while the mummy lacked an upper one, casting doubt on the identification.

Late in the reign of Thutmose III and into that of his son Amenhotep II, her cartouches and images were chiselled from walls and her statues at Deir el-Bahari were torn down and buried in a pit. Why this was done is not clear; scholars have proposed political necessity, the securing of Amenhotep II's uncertain claim, and a ritual deactivation of statues. The erasure confused nineteenth-century Egyptologists such as Jean-Francois Champollion, who found feminine verbs beside a bearded king. James Henry Breasted called her the first great woman in history of whom we are informed.
hattians: The Hattians inhabited the land of Hatti in central Anatolia in the Bronze Age. They spoke the Hattian language, which was neither Semitic nor Indo-European. They are attested archaeologically from the Early Bronze Age and in later Hittite and other sources, and their main centre was the city of Hattush. Scholars use the names as a convention for the pre-Hittite population of central Anatolia, and it is not known whether related inhabitants of neighbouring city-states ever saw themselves as Hattians. The term Proto-Hittite is inaccurate, because Hittite is an Indo-European language.

Archaeological sites in central Anatolia from the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE are attributed to the Hattians. At Hattush the finds show a complex culture with social stratification. Most scholars believe the first Hattian states existed in the period of the Akkadian Empire, on the basis of later Hittite and Assyrian sources. A Hittite version of a story about Naram-Sin of Akkad, from about 1400 BCE, names Pamba of Hatti among 17 allied kings, although this is not attested in Akkadian versions or contemporary sources.

The Hattians were organised in monarchical city-states, ruled as theocratic kingdoms or principalities. Assyrian merchants set up trading colonies called karum throughout eastern and central Anatolia, and during the first centuries of the 2nd millennium BCE an Assyrian colony existed in Hattush. Faced with Hittite expansion from about 2000 BCE, the Hattians were gradually absorbed, by about 1700 BCE, into the new order. The Hittites kept the name of the land, Hatti, and made it the usual name of their own state.

About 150 short specimens of Hattian text have been found among Hittite cuneiform tablets, mostly religious or cultic in character, and Hattian appears to have remained alive until at least the end of the 14th century BCE. Some scholars relate it to the Northwest Caucasian languages. Hattian religion involved worship of the earth, personified as a mother goddess, to ensure good harvests. The pantheon included the storm-god Taru, represented by a bull, and the sun-goddess Furušemu, represented by a leopard. The Hittites took over much of it, and the legends of Telipinu and the dragon Illuyanka originate in Hattian civilisation.
hattic-language: Hattic, or Hattian, was an agglutinative language spoken by the Hattians in Asia Minor and is the oldest attested language of Anatolia from before the arrival of Hittite speakers. Scholars call it Hattic to distinguish it from Hittite, the Indo-European language of the Hittite Empire. The Hittites called it hattili. No attestation of its name exists in Hattic itself. The name is related to the Assyrian and Egyptian designation of an area west of the Euphrates as the Land of the Hatti.

Its heartland ranged from Hattusa, then called Hattus, northward to Nerik, and cities such as Tuhumiyara and Tissaruliya are also mentioned in it. Hittite speakers conquered Hattus from Kussara to its south in the 18th century BCE. They absorbed or replaced the Hattic-speaking ruling class but kept the name Hatti for the region. The name of the inhabitants is likewise identified with the biblical Heth, from which the English word Hittite derives.

No document has been found in which native speakers wrote their own language, so scholars rely on indirect sources and on mentions by the Hittites, their neighbours and successors. Hattic words appear in religious tablets of Hittite priests from the 14th and 13th centuries BCE, where a note between the lines of signs states that the priest is now speaking in Hattic. Roots of Hattic words also survive in the names of mountains, rivers, cities and gods, and in some mythological texts.

Published Hattic documents are catalogued in the Catalogue des textes hittites. Those from Hattusa span CTH 725 to 745, and five of them are Hattic and Hittite bilinguals. CTH 737 is a Hattic incantation for the festival at Nerik. One key, if fragmentary, bilingual is the story of the Moon God Who Fell from the Sky.

Hattic formed a collective plural with the prefix fa-, as in fa-shaf, gods. The genitive was marked with the suffix -(u)n, so fur, land, gives furun, of the land. Known words include katte, king, fel, house, hilamar, temple, pinu, child, and ashaf, god. Hattic gods include Furun-Katte, King of the Land, a war god, the sun goddess Furu-Semu and the moon god Kasku.
hattusa: The earliest traces of settlement on the site date from the 6th millennium BCE. Toward the end of the 3rd millennium BCE the Hattian people settled there and called the place Hattush. Assyrian merchants set up a trading post there in the 19th and 18th centuries BCE. A burned layer shows the city was destroyed around 1700 BCE; King Anitta of Kussara took credit and erected an inscribed curse on anyone who resettled it. The city was nevertheless rebuilt. Around 1650 BCE the Hittite king Labarna moved the capital from Neša to Hattusa and took the name Hattusili, the man from Hattusa.

The capital later moved north to Sapinuwa under Tudhaliya I after attacks by the Kaskians, and south to Tarhuntassa under Muwatalli II. In the mid-13th century BCE Mursili III returned the seat to Hattusa, where it remained until the end of the Hittite kingdom in the 12th century BCE.

At its peak the city covered 1.8 square kilometres, in an inner and an outer part surrounded by massive walls erected under Suppiluliuma I, c. 1344 to 1322 BCE. The inner city held a citadel with large administrative buildings and temples, and the royal residence stood on a high ridge called Büyükkale. The outer city to the south had elaborate gateways decorated with reliefs of warriors, lions and sphinxes, and four temples. Modern estimates put the population at around 10,000. Houses of timber and mud brick have vanished, leaving only the stone walls of temples and palaces.

The city was destroyed with the Hittite state around 1200 BCE, as part of the Late Bronze Age collapse. Excavations suggest it was abandoned gradually over several decades, and a regional drought has been suggested. The final burning probably came after the royal family, elites and state apparatus had left, and agricultural communities with a different material culture settled in the ruins as early as the 12th century BCE.

The French archaeologist Charles Texier brought attention to the ruins after his visit in 1834. In 1905 and 1906 Hugo Winckler of the German Oriental Society began excavating the royal fortress. Thousands of tablets were recovered, mostly in the then unreadable Hittite language, and a few Akkadian texts identified the site as Hattusa. Systematic German excavations continue, and the site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1986.

About 30,000 clay tablets from Hattusa form the main corpus of Hittite literature, among them official correspondence, contracts, legal codes, cult procedures and oracles. One tablet records the terms of a peace between the Hittites and Egypt under Ramesses II after the Battle of Kadesh, in 1259 or 1258 BCE.
hattusili-i: Hattusili I was possibly a nephew of the wife of his predecessor Labarna I, Tawananna, whose name was apparently a title used as a given name. Tawananna was a daughter of PU-Sarruma, and one brother is known, Papahdilmah, who fought with Labarna for the throne and lost. Papahdilmah could possibly have been Hattusili's father, but another brother of Tawananna could have been. His wife was named Kadduši, and his grandson Mursili I succeeded him.

At the beginning of his reign he used the title Labarna. It is uncertain whether he was a second king so named, or identical to Labarna I, whom Hittite chronologies treat as his predecessor. He is the earliest Hittite ruler for whom contemporary records have been found.

During his reign he moved the capital from Neša, near modern Kültepe, to Hattusa, near modern Boğazkale, taking the throne name Hattusili to mark the occasion. In addition to King of Hattusa he took the title Man of Kuššara, a reference to the prehistoric capital of the Hittite people. His reign is dated c. 1650–1620 BCE on the middle chronology, or c. 1640–1610 BCE on the low middle chronology.

The Annals of Hattusili I, a bilingual Hittite and Akkadian tablet found in 1957, give details of five years of campaigning, though Trevor Bryce considers it a copy written in the 13th century BCE. In it he claims to have extended the Hittite domain to the sea. He reached Sanahuitta and Zalpa in the first year and sacked Zalpa, claimed to have subdued Alalakh and other Syrian cities in the second, and raided Arzawa in the third. In the fourth he took Sanahuitta after a siege of five months. In the fifth he crossed the Euphrates, claiming that no one before him had done so except Sargon of Akkad.

His Succession Proclamation, written in the first person, tells of his return wounded from his last campaign. On his deathbed he is angered by his heir, who is conspiring with his mother and cousins, and he designates his grandson Mursili I as king instead, urging the army and officials to obey him. The Testament and the Annals survive only as late 13th-century BCE copies. Mursili did become king and continued the campaigns, conquering Aleppo and sacking Babylon.

Hattusili may also have reintroduced cuneiform to Anatolia. It had fallen out of use there when Assyrian influence waned at the end of the karum period, and the script used in his reign derived from Syrian cuneiform, so he may have brought Syrian scribes back from his Syrian campaigns.
hattusili-iii: Much of what is known of Hattusili's childhood comes from the Apology, a biographical account written on a stone tablet during his reign. He was the youngest of four children of the Hittite king Mursili II and Queen Gassulawiya. By his own account he was a sickly child who was not expected to reach adulthood, and he credited the goddess Ishtar with saving his life and remained her devoted patron. As the youngest son he did not inherit the throne, which passed to his older brother Muwattalli II.
Before becoming king he married Puduhepa, a priestess of Ishtar, who later became an important queen in her own right. They had three children, among them his successor Tudhaliya IV.

Under Muwattalli II he governed the northern lands of the empire, put down opposition by force and turned to conquering new territory around them. When the king moved the capital from Hattusa to Tarhuntassa, Hattusili was left to suppress the rebellions that followed. On Muwattalli's death his nephew Urhi-Teshub, the son of a concubine, became king as Mursili III. Hattusili at first supported him, since Muwattalli had wished it.

Mursili III soon moved the capital back to Hattusa, which reduced Hattusili's power, and stripped him of all his territories except Hapkis and Nerik. When Nerik was taken from him too, Hattusili set out to seize the throne.

After deposing Mursili III, Hattusili exiled him to Syria. He appointed Kurunta, another son of Muwattalli II whom he had raised himself, to govern Tarhuntassa. He kept up correspondence with many neighbouring kingdoms, and his letters with the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II led, roughly fifteen years after the Battle of Kadesh, to the first recorded peace treaty, the Eternal Treaty, also called the Treaty of Kadesh.

His reign is notable for the large body of letters and accounts found from it: more than two hundred letters were unearthed at the royal palace in Hattusa. They include the Apology, the Tawagalawa letter and the Arzawa letters, and are among the few primary sources for the Hittite empire of the time. His eldest son Nerikkaili was heir apparent, but Hattusili removed him from the succession in favour of the younger Tudhaliya.
hatuey: Hatuey was a cacique, or chief, of the Taíno cacicazgo of Guanaba on Hispaniola, in what is now La Gonave in Haiti, and lived from the late 15th into the early 16th century. Before Diego Velázquez set out from Hispaniola in 1511 to conquer the people of what is now Guantánamo Province in easternmost Cuba, Hatuey crossed to the island with a party of four hundred in canoes to warn its inhabitants of what to expect from the Spaniards.

Bartolomé de las Casas later attributed to Hatuey a speech to the Taíno of Caobana, in which he showed them a basket of gold and jewels and called it the God of the Christians, for whose sake, he said, the Spaniards conquered and killed them. He proposed that they dance areitos in its honour, in the hope that it would order the Christians to leave them unharmed.

The Taíno chiefs of Cuba did not respond to his message, and few joined him. He turned to guerrilla tactics and for a time kept the Spaniards confined, killing at least eight of their soldiers. The Spaniards hunted him with mastiffs and tortured Indigenous people for information until they captured him.

On 2 February 1512 he was tied to a stake and burned alive at Yara, near the present-day city of Bayamo. In Las Casas's account, a priest offered him heaven if he accepted Jesus; Hatuey asked whether Spaniards went there and, told that they did, said he would rather go to hell than be among such cruel people.

Hatuey is regarded as one of the first fighters against Spanish colonialism in the New World. The town of Hatuey, south of Sibanicú in Camagüey Province, bears his name, and so has a beer brewed in Santiago de Cuba since 1927, first by Compañia Ron Bacardi and after the nationalisations of 1960 by a state brewery. His image is the emblem of the Cohiba cigar brand. He appears in the opera Hatuey: Memory of Fire and in the work of artists such as Ric Garcia, and the 2010 film Even the Rain, shot in Bolivia, includes his execution in its film within a film.
hauran: The Hauran spans parts of southern Syria and northern Jordan. It is bounded in the north by the Ghouta oasis, to the west by the Golan Heights and to the east and south by desert steppe. Traditionally it has three subregions: the Nuqrah and Jaydur plains, the Jabal Hauran massif, also called Jabal al-Druze, and the Lajat volcanic field. The Nuqrah is a low plateau of fertile basalt soil. The plain receives an average 250 millimetres of rain a year, enough for grain, while the Jabal Hauran rises above 1,800 metres and receives more rain.

Settlements in the region, then generally called Bashan, appear in the Amarna letters and the Book of Deuteronomy. The Aramean kingdom of Damascus and the Kingdom of Israel contested it, and the Assyrian Empire held it from 732 to 610 BCE. The Seleucids took it from the Ptolemies after the Battle of Panium in 200 BCE, and the Nabatean kingdom expanded to Bosra and Salkhad. The Roman Empire extended its influence to all of Syria by 63 BCE and formally annexed the Hauran in the 2nd century CE.

The Hauran prospered under Roman rule and in the Byzantine era, when the Byzantines relied on Arab tribes, among them the Salihids and Ghassanids, to guard it. Muslim forces arrived in April 634 and took Bosra in May, and after the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 the whole region came under Muslim rule. It became part of the Ottoman Empire in 1516. Under the French Mandatory period, after the Great Syrian Revolt that began there, its plains formed a district of the State of Damascus and the Jabal Hauran the Jabal Druze State. The Hauran remained the main grain source of the Levant until northern Syria overtook it in the mid-20th century.

The population is largely Arab and religiously mixed: Sunni Muslim agrarian clans on the plains, a Druze majority in the Jabal Hauran and Greek Orthodox and Greek Catholic communities in its western foothills. The largest towns are Daraa, Ramtha and Suwayda. Because basalt was the common building stone, the Hauran has a distinct all-basalt architecture, and some 300 towns and villages contain ancient structures, among them Bosra, Qanawat, Shahba, Salkhad and Umm al-Jimal.
haut-rhin: Haut-Rhin, meaning Upper Rhine, is one of the original 83 departments of the French Revolution. It was created on 4 March 1790, by the law of 22 December 1789, from the southern half of the province of Alsace, known as Haute-Alsace. In 1798 it absorbed Mulhouse, formerly a free city and the last Swiss enclave in the south of Alsace, and in 1800 it took in the whole department of Mont-Terrible. In 1814 it lost the territories that had belonged to Mont-Terrible, which were returned to Switzerland except for the former County of Montbéliard, and in 1816 Montbéliard was transferred to Doubs.

In 1871 most of it was annexed by the German Empire under the Treaty of Frankfurt, and the remaining French part later formed the Territoire de Belfort, so named since 1922. The department returned to France in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles but remains administratively separate from Belfort. In 1940 it was annexed de facto by Nazi Germany, and France recovered it in 1944.

Haut-Rhin borders the Territoire de Belfort and the Vosges department and the Vosges Mountains to the west, Bas-Rhin to the north, Switzerland to the south and Germany to the east, where the frontier follows the Rhine. A fertile plain lies at its centre. The population was 770,738 in 2023. Mulhouse is the most populous commune and Colmar, the prefecture, the second.

Alsace and the neighbouring Moselle department keep a legal system slightly different from the rest of France. Its statutes date from the period 1871 to 1919, when the area belonged to the German Empire, and Paris accepted after 1919 that some local laws would remain. Notably, there is no formal separation of church and state there. On 1 January 2021 Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin were merged into the European Collectivity of Alsace.
haute-loire: Haute-Loire, which means Upper Loire, is a landlocked department surrounded by the departments of Loire, Ardèche, Lozère, Cantal and Puy-de-Dôme. The Loire rises in its southern part and flows north, creating a wide valley with ranges of the Massif Central on either side. The highest point is Mont Mézenc at 1,753 metres, and the average elevation is 719 metres. Part of the north lies in the Livradois-Forez Regional Natural Park, a protected area of farmland and woodland.

The first known inhabitants were hunter-gatherers, later followed by pastoralists. The Gaulish tribe of the Vellavi later controlled the region. Between 462 and 477 it was incorporated into the Visigothic Kingdom, ending Roman political control. After Clovis I won the Battle of Vouillé in 507, Velay came under Frankish rule. In about 928 the area became a fiefdom of the Count of Toulouse and later came under the Count of Poitiers.

Haute-Loire is one of the original 83 departments created during the French Revolution, on 4 March 1790. Two thirds of it, centred on Le Puy-en-Velay, is the old Velay, and its distance from Toulouse had allowed it a great deal of autonomy. During the Second World War French partisans, aided by Allied supply drops, liberated the department. Le Puy-en-Velay was besieged by mid-August 1944, and on 18 August Germans trying to escape in a convoy of fifty trucks were ambushed. The town fell the next day.

Le Puy-en-Velay is the prefecture and the largest town, and the department had 228,654 inhabitants in 2023. The cathedral of Le Puy is a gathering place for pilgrims before they set out for Santiago de Compostela, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998. Another pilgrimage site is a 12th-century chapel on a rocky pinnacle, reached by 268 steps. Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, was born in 1757 at the Château de Chavaniac.
haute-savoie: Haute-Savoie takes its name from the historical region of Savoy, as does the neighbouring department of Savoie to the south. To the north it borders the Swiss canton of Geneva and Lake Geneva, to the east the canton of Valais and Italy's Aosta Valley, and to the west the department of Ain. It has the largest range of elevations of any French department: its lowest point is 250 m in the Rhône Valley and its highest is Mont Blanc, at 4,810 m. Because the country is mountainous, passes matter to trade and economic life, among them the Col de la Forclaz and the Mont Blanc Tunnel, which links Chamonix to Courmayeur.

Savoy was governed by the House of Savoy from 1032 to 1860, and the Dukes of Savoy ruled the region from 1416 to 1720. After the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 the territory of modern Haute-Savoie and neighbouring Savoie became part of the Kingdom of Sardinia. France annexed the region by the Treaty of Turin, formalised on 24 March 1860.

From November 1942 to September 1943 Haute-Savoie was under military occupation by Fascist Italy. The Maquis des Glières, a band of Free French Resistance fighters, operated from the department. In the winter of 1943–1944 German troops burned down around 500 farms in response to Resistance activity. The first Winter Olympic Games were held at Chamonix in 1924.
hava-nagila: Hava Nagila, Hebrew for 'Let us rejoice', is a Jewish folk song. Its melody is based on a Hassidic niggun, a slow chant of the 19th century that has been attributed to the Sadigurer Chasidim of what is now Ukraine. Daniel Gil has recreated this version from a traditional song collected by Susman Kiselgof. Members of the community began to settle in Jerusalem in 1915, and Abraham Zevi Idelsohn wrote in 1932 that he had been inspired by that melody.

The song was composed in 1918 to celebrate the Balfour Declaration and the British victory over the Ottomans in 1917, and it was first performed in a mixed choir concert in Jerusalem. Idelsohn (1882–1938), a professor at Hebrew University, was cataloguing Jewish music and teaching musical composition. He gave his class, which included the cantorial student Moshe Nathanson, a slow 19th-century niggun and set them to add rhythm and words to make a modern Hebrew song. Both Idelsohn and Nathanson have been named as its composer, and the text was probably refined by Idelsohn.

The song is traditionally sung at celebrations such as weddings, bar and bat mitzvahs and other Jewish holidays, and it spread quickly through the Jewish diaspora. Idelsohn published his arrangement in 1922 in the Hebrew song book Sefer Hashirim, its first publication. In the same year he made the first commercial recording of it, for the Polyphon label, as part of a series of 39 Hebrew folk songs.

The Israeli folk duo Ran & Nama made what is likely the earliest recording of the version later widely known across the world, on an album of 1959. Harry Belafonte recorded it the same year for Belafonte at Carnegie Hall, and rarely gave a concert without singing it. He said that most Jews in America learned the song from him. Dick Dale and the Del Tones published a surf rock version in 1963, Bob Dylan performed it as a talking blues in the early 1960s, and George Lam released a Cantonese adaptation in 1987.

Supporters of the Dutch football club AFC Ajax commonly sing it in the stadium. At the 2012 Summer Olympics Aly Raisman won the floor exercise final to a performance set to its tune, becoming the first American woman to win gold in that event.
havana: Havana lies on the northern coast of Cuba along the Straits of Florida, south of the Florida Keys, where the Gulf of Mexico joins the Atlantic Ocean. The city extends mostly westward and southward from a bay, which is entered through a narrow inlet and divides into three main harbours. The Almendares River crosses the city from south to north.

The city stands mostly on low hills. A limestone ridge about 60 metres high slopes up from the east and culminates in the heights of La Cabaña and El Morro, where the Spanish built fortifications overlooking the eastern bay.

In the early 16th century Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded the town of San Cristóbal de la Habana on the southern coast of Cuba, at the mouth of the Mayabeque River, now the town of Batabanó. The low and swampy land caused the settlement to fail. In those years the Spanish established settlements on the northern coast, among them La Chorrera, at the mouth of the Almendares River. The town that became Havana grew up beside Puerto de Carenas, the Careening Port, in 1519, and the quality of the harbour led to the change of location.

Havana overtook Santiago in the mid-16th century because of the advantages of its harbour and became the capital of the island. It became a fundamental place for the Spanish colonial empire in the Americas and a stopping point for galleons returning to the Iberian Peninsula, and walls and forts were built to protect it from naval attacks. After the Cuban War of Independence a new constitution was adopted in 1901.

Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba and the seat of its government. It is the country's main port. The population in 2021 was 2,142,939. Its economy first developed on its location as one of the early great trade centres of the New World, and sugar and a slave trade first brought riches to the city.

Old Havana, Habana Vieja, contains the core of the original city and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Its landmarks include the Fortress San Carlos de la Cabaña, El Morro Castle, built because of the threat to the harbour from pirates, and the Fortress San Salvador de la Punta, built in the 16th century. The University of Havana was established in 1728.
havel: The Havel flows through four German states: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Brandenburg, Berlin and Saxony-Anhalt. It is a right tributary of the Elbe, which it joins at Havelberg. The direct distance from its source to its mouth is only 94 kilometres, far less than the river's own length. South of Spandau, where the Spree joins it, the river widens into a broad lake that extends, through some narrower reaches, to Potsdam. Among its features there are the Großer Wannsee, the island of Schwanenwerder and the island of Pfaueninsel, and the river passes Brandenburg an der Havel before reaching the Elbe.

Earlier Greek and Latin sources, such as the Germania of Tacitus, wrote the river's name as Habola, Habula or Havela. The name is related to German words such as Haff and Hafen, meaning a harbour or port. The Slavic people who later moved into the Havel area were called Heveller in German sources, and occasionally Havolane.

In the twentieth century the river became part of a political frontier. During the partition of Germany, the stretch where the Havel enters Berlin formed the border between East Germany and West Berlin, and border control points were set up for vessels on it. In the 1950s the Havel Canal was built, joining the river at Hennigsdorf and running to Paretz, so that East German vessels could avoid the stretch of river under the political control of West Berlin.

The Havel is navigable from the Mecklenburg Lake District to its confluence with the Elbe. Its upper reaches carry little other than leisure traffic, but further downstream it is an important link in the German commercial waterway network, carrying traffic from the Rhine and the North Sea to Berlin and Poland. Canals connect it to the Oder and to the Elbe, among them the Oder-Havel Canal and the Elbe-Havel Canal.

In its lower course the Havel passes through a series of locks, for example at Spandau, Rathenow and Havelberg. At Potsdam the navigation splits into two channels, and at Brandenburg an der Havel commercial shipping uses a separate canal north of the city centre, while leisure craft pass through the town itself.
havelberg: Havelberg is a town in the district of Stendal in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. It stands on the Havel, and part of the town is built on an island in the centre of the river. The two parts were incorporated as a town in 1875. It has a historical centre with many well-preserved wooden buildings, for example in Kirchstraße and Scabellstraße.

The Bishopric of Havelberg was founded by Otto I, then a prince and later Holy Roman Emperor, though the bishop tended to live in Plattenburg or Wittstock, a few miles to the north. Anselm of Havelberg was an early bishop. The Slavic revolt of 983 brought the town under the control of the pagan Wends, when it was known by its Slavonic name Hobolin. It was restored to Christian German rule only in 1147 with the Wendish Crusade. In 1359 Havelberg joined the Hanseatic League and developed into a trade centre with a booming economy, remaining a member until 1559.

Havelberg was part of Brandenburg for most of its history. It was a strong fortress, which imperial troops took from the Danish in 1627 during the Thirty Years' War, the Swedes recaptured in 1631, 1635 and 1636, and the Saxons retook in 1637. After the East German states were dissolved in 1952 it became part of the district of Magdeburg, and with the refounding of the states in 1990 it passed to Saxony-Anhalt.

St Mary's Cathedral stands on a hill above the old town. It was gradually transformed into a Gothic building between 1279 and 1330. The parish church of St Laurentius dates from around 1300, and the oldest house, the Beguinenhaus at the Salt Market, was built of sandstone in 1390. A former monastery houses the Prignitz Museum, established in 1904.
haveli: The word haveli comes from the Arabic hawali, meaning partition or private space, and was popularised under the Mughal Empire without any architectural meaning. Early havelis served the Muslim rulers of the subcontinent and became an important part of Mughal cities, blending local and Islamic traditions. Houses built round courtyards are far older in the region, with early examples from the Neolithic period. In the medieval period some Vaishnava sects of Gujarat and the Rajputana kingdoms also called their temples havelis, before the word came to mean the townhouses of the merchant class.

The heart of a haveli is the chowk or courtyard, around which family life revolved. It worked as a lightwell and ventilated the house in a hot, dry climate, while arcades or high walls kept the rooms cool. The courtyard could separate the quarters of men and women: in Shekhawati a typical haveli had an outer court for men and an inner one for women, and the largest had three or four courts on two or three storeys. Common materials were brick, sandstone, marble, wood, plaster and granite. The sacred tulsi plant was often kept in the courtyard, which also served for weddings and festivals.

For the Marwaris of Rajasthan havelis were status symbols and homes for extended families, closed on all sides with one large gate. Between 1830 and 1930 Marwari merchants built havelis in Shekhawati and Marwar and had them painted by artists working under Mughal influence. In Jaisalmer the merchants' houses were carved in yellow sandstone with jharokhas, or balconies. The first there, Patwon Ji ki Haveli, is a cluster of five houses begun in 1805 by Guman Chand Patwa, a trader in jewellery and brocades, one for each of his five sons. In Lahore the Haveli of Nau Nihal Singh, of the mid-19th century, is the only Sikh-era haveli that keeps its original ornament.
havelland: The River Havel flows round the Havelland in a U-shape between Oranienburg in the north-east and Rhinow in the north-west, while the River Rhin and the Rhin Canal form its northern edge. Besides the county that bears its name, the historic region takes in the south of Ruppin Land with the Rhinluch, the western part of Spandau, parts of Potsdam, the town of Brandenburg an der Havel and several villages of Potsdam-Mittelmark.

Wide glacial valleys, the urstromtal lowlands, shape the country. Above them rise plateaux like islands, mostly ground moraines of the Ice Age, with end moraines of the Saale and Weichsel glaciations; the largest is the Nauen Plateau, whose dry sandy soils carry fields and woods. North of it lie the former marshes of the Havelland Luch and the Rhinluch, and to the south small morainic hills between the lakes of the Havel.

The larger towns grew up at the crossings of the Havel: Spandau, Potsdam, Brandenburg and Rathenow, with Rhinow, Premnitz, Nauen and Friesack as other centres. From 1700 to the 1950s large areas, above all in the north, were drained by canals. The lakes and wetlands long hindered roads and railways, though the river itself became an important waterway, especially between Brandenburg and Oranienburg.

The writer Theodor Fontane gave the region a place in German literature. His ballad Herr von Ribbeck auf Ribbeck im Havelland made it widely known, his heroine Effi Briest grew up there, and it received a volume of its own in his accounts of walking through Brandenburg, the Wanderungen durch die Mark Brandenburg.

The Havelland is thinly populated and largely given over to arable and cattle farming, with fruit and vegetables grown especially around Werder. Its western part between Rhinow and Pritzerbe belongs to the West Havelland Nature Park, which holds the Lower Havel Lowlands, the largest inland wetlands of Western Europe. The region also serves as a recreation area for Berlin.
haw-phra-kaew: King Setthathirath ordered the temple after moving his capital from Luang Prabang to Vientiane, and it was raised on the grounds of the royal palace in 1565 and 1566. It served as the king's personal place of worship, so unlike other temples in Laos it had no resident monks. The Emerald Buddha stayed there for more than 200 years, until General Chao Phraya Chakri, who founded the Chakri Dynasty of Thailand, seized Vientiane in 1779, carried the image off to Thonburi and destroyed the temple. The image now stands in Wat Phra Kaew in Bangkok and is considered the palladium of Thailand.

King Anouvong rebuilt the temple in 1816 with a new image in place of the lost one, but when he rebelled against Siam to regain full independence, Siamese forces razed Vientiane in 1828. Louis Delaporte drew the ruins around 1867. The French rebuilt the temple between 1936 and 1942, under French Indochina, on the surviving structures and the old plan, though the result resembles a 19th-century Bangkok-style ordination hall. In the 1970s it became a museum, and it was restored again in 1993.

The former temple stands on Setthathirath Road, south-east of Wat Si Saket, in a landscaped garden. Stone Buddhas of the 6th to 9th centuries and bronze standing and seated Buddhas of later periods line its terrace, and more images fill the sim, the main ordination hall, whose carved wooden doors survive from the old temple. Inside are a wooden copy of the Phra Bang, the palladium of Laos, a gilded throne for the Emerald Buddha, Khmer stone steles, wood carvings, a bronze frog drum and Buddhist manuscripts on palm leaves. The garden holds a stone jar about 2,000 years old from the Plain of Jars on the Xieng Khouang Plateau.
haw-wars: The bands were known by their banners. Black Flag and Yellow Flag units crossed from China into Tonkin in 1865 and set up bases in the upper Red River Valley. The Black Flags under Liu Yongfu fought the French and won a certain legitimacy from the Vietnamese ruler Tự Đức, while the Yellow Flags were broken up by Vietnamese and Black Flag forces; after their leader Huang Chung-ying was captured and executed in 1875–1876, their remnants harassed the Tai federation of Sip Song Chau Tai and north-eastern Laos.

From about 1872 Red Flag and Striped Flag bands crossed into Laos, then a tributary state of Siam. The Red Flags sacked Điện Biên Phủ in 1873, and the Striped Flags seized Muang Phuan and the Plain of Jars the same year. In 1874 a joint army of Chao Oun Kham, king of Luang Prabang, and Tự Đức was routed and Chao Ung, prince of Phuan, was killed; the Haw then sacked Vientiane, demolishing its Buddhist temples in search of loot.

King Chulalongkorn sent Siamese forces across the Mekong at Nong Khai in 1875, but the Haw withdrew into the mountains of Phuan and Houaphanh and returned to plunder once the army left. A second expedition, of 1884–1885, made up largely of Isan and northern Thai levies, was recorded by the British surveyor James McCarthy, who described villages whose people had been slaughtered, mutilated or carried off. Malaria proved a worse enemy than the Haw, and an assault on a Haw stockade on 22 February 1885 failed after the commander-in-chief, Phraya Raj, was wounded.

McCarthy concluded that the Governor of Yunnan had sent the Haw to harass the French; this may have been true of the Black Flags in Tonkin, but there is no direct indication of official Chinese involvement in Laos. Siamese and finally French pressure forced the bands to retreat to China, and the wars were followed by the Franco-Siamese conflict of 1893, in which the French asserted control of the region. Memorials to the Thai and Lao dead stand in Nong Khai, near Wat Angkhan and the Garden of Sorrows, where widows came to grieve.
hawaii: Hawaii consists of 137 volcanic islands that make up almost the entire Hawaiian archipelago, spanning 1,500 miles in the Pacific Ocean about 2,000 miles southwest of the U.S. mainland. The eight main islands, from northwest to southeast, are Niʻihau, Kauaʻi, Oʻahu, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Kahoʻolawe, Maui and Hawaiʻi, after which the state is named. The archipelago is physiographically and ethnologically part of Polynesia. The name Hawaiʻi is very similar to Proto-Polynesian *Sawaiki, reconstructed as meaning homeland, and one explanation names it for Hawaiʻiloa, a figure of oral tradition said to have discovered the islands.

The date of human arrival is debated. Early archaeological studies suggested Polynesians from the Marquesas or Society Islands arrived as early as the 3rd century CE. Some archaeologists think a later wave from Tahiti around 1100 CE introduced a new line of high chiefs, the kapu system, human sacrifice and the building of heiau, as Hawaiian tradition tells of Paʻao. Others say no evidence supports a later influx and treat Paʻao as myth, and more recent studies place the first settlement at around 900 to 1200 CE. The islands were home to numerous independent chiefdoms.

In 1778 the British explorer James Cook was the first known non-Polynesian to arrive. European and American explorers, traders and whalers followed, and introduced diseases such as syphilis, tuberculosis, smallpox and measles. The indigenous population fell from an estimated 300,000 in the 1770s to 60,000 in the 1850s and 24,000 in 1920, though estimates of the pre-contact figure range from 150,000 to 1.5 million. Hawaii became a unified, internationally recognised kingdom in 1810.

Sugar plantations had a strong foothold by the 1840s and were tightly controlled by American missionary families and businessmen known as the Big Five. In 1893 resident American and European capitalists and landholders overthrew the monarchy. Hawaii was an independent republic from 1894 until 12 August 1898, when it became a U.S. territory. It was attacked by Japan on 7 December 1941 and admitted as a state on 21 August 1959. In 1993 the U.S. government formally apologised for its role in the overthrow.

Hawaii is the 50th state of the United States, with its capital and largest city, Honolulu, on Oʻahu, where two thirds of residents live. Hawaiian was added to the state constitution in 1978 as an official language alongside English. Kamehameha III chose Honolulu as capital for its natural harbour, the present-day Honolulu Harbor, and the previous capitals were Lahaina on Maui and Kailua-Kona on Hawaiʻi. The aboriginal culture is Polynesian, and lūʻau and hula have spread in modified form to the wider United States.
hawaii-admission-act: Hawaii had been an organised incorporated territory of the United States since 1900, when the Hawaiian Organic Act established it. In 1946 the United Nations listed it as a non-self-governing territory under United States administration, together with American Samoa, Guam, the Panama Canal Zone, Puerto Rico, the Territory of Alaska and the United States Virgin Islands. Bills to create a state had stalled in congressional hearings since the early 1900s, partly from fear of a state with an Asian American plurality and doubts about the loyalty of its residents.

After John A. Burns of the Hawaii Democratic Party was elected the territory's delegate to Congress, southern leaders called his election evidence that Hawaii was a haven for communism. Burns lobbied hard against these charges and the race-based objections, and later argued that the most effective opposition had always come from within Hawaii itself.

Some Native Hawaiians protested against statehood. On 17 January 1946, the 53rd anniversary of the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom, Territorial Senator Alice Kamokila Campbell testified against it before a joint congressional committee at Iolani Palace. In 1947 she opened the Anti-Statehood Clearing House, and on 29 March 1949 she won a suit that stopped the Hawaii Statehood Commission from spending public money on lobbying.

The act, formally An Act to Provide for the Admission of the State of Hawaii into the Union (Public Law 86-3), dissolved the territory and created the state. The new state comprised all the islands of the territory, with their reefs and territorial waters, except the atoll of Palmyra Island, and did not include the Midway Islands, Johnston Island, Sand Island or Kingman Reef.

In the plebiscite of 27 June 1959, out of a population of about 600,000 and 155,000 registered voters, some 140,000 votes were cast, the highest turnout Hawaii had seen. At least 93% of voters approved on every major island, and fewer than 8,000 votes rejected the act. Statehood took effect on 21 August 1959.
hawaiian-organic-act: After the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom in 1893, the government of the new Republic of Hawaii lobbied for annexation by the United States. Annexation was approved by President William McKinley, and Hawaii became part of the territory of the United States on 12 August 1898. The Organic Act, enacted on 30 April 1900, then organised the islands as the Territory of Hawaii and gave them a constitution and government.

The act made Honolulu, on Oahu, the territorial capital. Anyone who had been a citizen of the Republic of Hawaii on or before 12 August 1898 became a citizen of the United States. The offices of the republic, from its president and ministers of foreign affairs, the interior, finance and public instruction to its auditor-general, surveyor-general and marshal, were abolished, while its laws stayed in force and suits were brought in the name of the Territory of Hawaii. Office holders found guilty of taking bribes lost the right to vote and to hold office unless pardoned.

The act created a bicameral legislature, whose Senate had 15 members with four-year terms, elected from four districts: the island of Hawaii with four senators, Maui, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi and Kahoʻolawe with three, Oahu with six and Kauaʻi and Niʻihau with two. The House of Representatives had 30 members with two-year terms from six districts. Members were paid $1,000 for each general session, with travel money of 20 cents a mile. Senators had to be at least 30 years old, representatives 25, and both citizens of the United States with three years' residence in Hawaii; the original text required senators to be men, a rule that stood until 1922.

During the Second World War section 67 of the act, which derived from Article 31 of the Constitution of the Republic of Hawaii of 1895, came before the United States Supreme Court in the question of what martial law allowed and whether civilians could be tried by military courts. An amendment of 1956 enlarged the Senate to 25 members and the House to 51 from the elections of 1958. The act was replaced by the Hawaii Admission Act on 21 August 1959, when Hawaii became a state.
hawaiian-sovereignty-movement: The movement looks back to the Kingdom of Hawaii, which Kamehameha I formed by conquering the archipelago between 1795 and 1810. In the first century of contact with the West, disease and war reduced the Hawaiian population by 90 per cent, to 53,900 in 1876. On 17 January 1893 a coup organised mostly by Americans within the kingdom's legislature, supported by armed sailors landed from the USS Boston, began the overthrow of the monarchy, although the United States and other powers had formally recognised the kingdom.

The modern movement grew in the 1960s and 1970s alongside other indigenous activist movements. In 1976 Walter Ritte and the group Protect Kahoolawe Ohana sued in federal court to stop the Navy's bombardment training on Kahoʻolawe, and on 6 January 1976 activists set out to land on the island. Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi, formed in 1987 with Mililani Trask as its first leader, reported 21,000 members in 1997, and in 1993 it led 10,000 people to the Iolani Palace on the centenary of the overthrow.

The Nation of Hawaiʻi, whose head of state is Dennis Puʻuhonua Kanahele and which favours a republic rather than a restored monarchy, occupied Kaupo Beach near Makapuʻu in 1993 and gave it up in exchange for ceded lands at Waimānalo, where it set up a village and a place of refuge. Later campaigns opposed the Mauna Kea Observatories and the Thirty Meter Telescope on a mountain that groups such as Mauna Kea Anaina Hou hold sacred.

In 1993 the State of Hawaiʻi passed Act 359 to help Native Hawaiians be governed by a sovereign nation of their own choosing, and President Bill Clinton signed Public Law 103-150, the Apology Bill, which commits the United States to reconciliation. Bills for federal recognition, the Akaka Bill of 2000 and the Native Hawaiian Government Reorganization Act of 2009, divided opinion: sovereignty groups objected that they legitimised illegal land transfers, while other critics rejected ancestry-based sovereignty as racial exclusion.

In Rice v. Cayetano the Supreme Court ruled in 2000 that limiting a state election to Native Hawaiian voters was forbidden by the Fifteenth Amendment, and the elections were opened to all registered voters. On 29 September 2015 the Department of the Interior announced a procedure to recognise a Native Hawaiian government.
hawara: Hawara is an archaeological site of ancient Egypt, south of Crocodilopolis, also called Arsinoë and now Medinet el-Fayum, at the entrance to the depression of the Fayum oasis. It is the site of a pyramid built by King Amenemhat III of the 12th Dynasty, the last powerful ruler of that dynasty. The pyramid is believed to be later than his so-called Black Pyramid at Dahshur. About 2 km to the south stood the intact pyramid tomb of Neferuptah, a daughter of Amenemhat III.

Like the Middle Kingdom pyramids built after Amenemhat II, it was made of mud brick round a core of limestone passages and burial chambers and faced with limestone. Most of the facing was later pillaged for other buildings, and today the pyramid is an eroded mound of mud brick. The burial chamber was cut from a single quartzite monolith that Petrie estimated at 110 tons. The entrance passages held concealed trapdoors of about 20 tons and blind passages and shafts meant to waste the time of robbers, yet Petrie found that none of the trapdoors had been slid into place. Burnt bone, wood and charcoal in the chamber suggest that robbers burned the wooden coffins and the mummy.

The huge mortuary temple beside the pyramid is believed to be the basis of the building with galleries and courtyards that Herodotus called the Labyrinth, also mentioned by Strabo and Diodorus Siculus. Its demolition may date in part to the reign of Ptolemy II, when a large building programme at Arsinoë may have taken its limestone columns and blocks. Pharaoh Sobekneferu of the 12th Dynasty also built at the complex.

Karl Lepsius first located the Labyrinth in modern times, in 1843. Petrie excavated at Hawara in 1888. North of the pyramid he found a vast necropolis with 146 portraits on coffins from the Roman period, the Fayum mummy portraits, among the few surviving painted portraits from classical antiquity. He also found papyri of the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, including a scroll with parts of books 1 and 2 of the Iliad, the Hawara Homer, now in the Bodleian Library in Oxford.

Petrie's first season can be followed in four phases: the pyramid itself, a short survey of the Labyrinth site, the northern cemetery after a painted portrait turned up among the Scattered Tombs, and the Crocodile Tomb-Chapels to the north-east. The entrance to the pyramid is now flooded to a depth of 6 metres by water from the Abdul Wahbi canal.
hawiye: The Hawiye trace their lineage to Sheikh Ahmed bin Abdulrahman bin Uthman, known as Sheikh Hawiye. Oral tradition and Arabic hagiologies remember him as a saint called Hawi al-Ulum, conservator of knowledge, a name shortened in time to Hawiye, and carry his genealogy back to Aqeel bin Abu Talib. Some scholars regard such claims as historically untenable. The anthropologist Ioan Lewis held that traditions of descent from noble Arab families are most probably figurative expressions of the importance of Islam in Somali society. Tradition places his tomb at Qundhuro in the Haraghe region, where his eldest son Karanle is buried beside him.

The 12th-century writer Al-Idrisi placed the Hawiye on the coast between Ras Hafun and Merca and in the lower basin of the Shabelle river, the first documentary reference to a specific Somali group. Ibn Sa'id, who lived from 1214 to 1274, called Merca their capital.

In the 13th century the Hawiye, with the Rahanweyn, came under the Ajuran Empire, whose domain reached from Hobyo in the north to Qelafo in the west and Kismayo in the south. The Ajuran are themselves said to descend from the Jambelle branch of the Hawiye, and Lee Cassanelli describes Ajuran power as resting on spiritual pre-eminence and Hawiye kinship solidarity.

According to local oral tradition as Cassanelli reports it, the Hiraab Imamate was an alliance of closely related groups of the Gorgaarte division. Its founders rebelled because the Ajuran rulers had grown proud, neglected sharia law and imposed heavy taxes. With Mogadishu as its capital, the imamate ruled from the Shabelle valley and the Benadir to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. The explorer John Kirk, visiting in 1873, met Imam Mahmood at Mogadishu and saw about twenty large dhows there and at Merca loading grain, much of it for Zanzibar.

At independence in 1960 the first president, Aden Adde, the first prime minister, Abdullahi Issa, and the founder of the army, Daud Abdulle Hirsi, were all Hawiye. Hawiye leaders formed the United Somali Congress in opposition to President Siad Barre, whom General Mohamed Farrah Aidid, of the Habar Gidir, overthrew in 1991. From late 1991 Mogadishu was divided between the factions of Aidid and of President Ali Mahdi Muhammad, of the Abgaal. The stalemate lasted until 2006, when the Islamic Courts Union, a predominantly Hawiye organisation, ended the rule of the factional warlords, before an Ethiopian intervention overthrew it. The Hiraab hereditary leadership survives to this day.
hawwara: The Hawwara are held to be the heirs of the ancient western Bavares. In classical antiquity they were among the principal tribes of the Masaesyli state, and the district that Quodvultdeus of Carthage called Avaritana provincia became known in the Middle Ages as bilad Haouara, the country of the Hawwara of the Aurès. In the Byzantine period they were one of the two major ruling confederations of the tribal principality there. During the Arab Muslim conquest of the Maghreb they were subdued by Musa ibn Nusayr and Arabised. From the eighth to the twelfth century their lands reached east to Tawergha, Waddan and Zella, bordering the Mazata tribe.

In the 10th century part of the Hawwara served in the Fatimid army that conquered Egypt, Syria, Palestine and Jordan, received land grants from the Fatimid caliphs and became dominant in El Beheira. In al-Andalus in the eleventh century families of Hawwara origin founded small kingdoms, among them the Dhulnunid dynasty of the Taifa of Toledo, and the towns of Alhaurín el Grande and Alhaurín de la Torre take their names from them. In 1380/1381 the Mamluk sultan Barquq settled Hawwara groups in Upper Egypt and granted the iqta' of Girga to the Hawwari chief Isma'il ibn Mazin, who was succeeded by Umar, eponym of the Banu Umar clan.

According to Al-Maqrizi, Hawwara and Arabs of Upper Egypt attacked the governor of Aswan in April 1396, and in 1412 Hawwara tribesmen attacked the Banu Kanz there, killing many of the men, taking the women and children into slavery and leaving the city in ruins. After sacking al-Fayyum in 1485 the Hawwara became the true rulers of Upper Egypt. The traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt wrote that many Christian Copts there were bound to Hawwara sheikhs as servants, and that the sheikhs handed this possession on to their descendants.

The confederation is made up of numerous tribes and clans, among them the Gharyan, Misrata, Tarhuna, Warfalla, Maslata and Razin. The Hawwara live chiefly in Tripolitania and are among the most prominent tribes of Upper Egypt, with branches mainly in Qena; they are also found in Morocco and Algeria, and in Sudan, where they are called Hawwaweer.
hay-bunau-varilla-treaty: From 1882 Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had built the Suez Canal, worked on a canal across the Isthmus of Panama, then part of Colombia. Landslides, mud, failing equipment and disease defeated the effort, which ended in bankruptcy by 1889. Philippe-Jean Bunau-Varilla then became an important shareholder of the Compagnie Nouvelle du Canal de Panama, which still held the concession and valuable assets for building a canal.

Early in 1903 the United States negotiated the Hay–Herrán Treaty with Colombia, which would have given it control of the canal and bought the French-held land for $40 million. When the Congress of Colombia rejected it on 12 August 1903, the French investors faced losing everything. Confident that President Theodore Roosevelt would support him, Bunau-Varilla met Manuel Amador, leader of the Panamanian independence movement, at the Waldorf-Astoria hotel in New York and wrote him a cheque for $100,000 to fund a renewed revolt. In return he would represent Panama in Washington.

In November 1903 Panama, tacitly supported by the United States, proclaimed its independence, and on 13 November the United States recognised the new republic. Bunau-Varilla, who was not Panamanian and had not been in Panama for seventeen years, was appointed its ambassador. The treaty was negotiated in Washington, D.C., and New York City. Panama was to receive up to $10 million and an annual rent of $250,000, while the United States bought the shares and assets of the French company for $40 million, as the Hay–Herrán Treaty had stipulated. Panama never legally became an American colony: the United States governed only the Canal Zone.

The treaty was a source of conflict between the two countries from the start. The Canal Zone became a racially and socially segregated area, set apart from the rest of Panama. The conflict peaked on 9 January 1964, when a Panamanian flag was torn during a clash between Panamanian students and Canal Zone Police over the right to fly it beside the United States flag. United States Army units helped suppress the riots that followed, and after three days about 22 Panamanians and four American soldiers had been killed. Panama remembers the day as Martyrs' Day.

These events were a significant factor in the American decision to negotiate the Torrijos–Carter Treaties, which abolished the 1903 treaty and led to the handover of full control of the Panama Canal on 31 December 1999.
haya-people: Linguistic evidence places the arrival of the Haya in the Kagera Region in the time of the Bantu expansion, and they belonged to the iron-making Urewe pottery culture. The first strong evidence of Early Iron Age settlement along Lake Victoria in Buhaya dates from around 200 BCE. Between 800 and 1500 CE Bantu peoples from further north, whose descendants founded Bunyoro-Kitara and Buganda, are said to have brought new breeds of cattle and varieties of banana. The archaeologist Peter R. Schmidt, excavating under a sacred shrine tree at Kataruka at the elders' request, found an iron furnace carbon-dated to the 1st millennium BCE.

Oral history says that clans founded Haya kingdoms from around the 16th century, among them the Bankango of Kyamtwara and the Bakama of Kiziba. Kyamtwara broke up in revolts in the late 18th century into Kihanja, Bukara, Lesser Kyamtwara and Bugabo. By the mid-19th century the Haya were linked to Arab, Swahili, Nyamwezi and Sumbwa trade, in which the Arabs sought chiefly ivory and slaves. The Anglo-German Agreement of 1890 placed Buhaya under German rule, and Emin Pasha founded a post at Bukoba that November. Under Lieutenant Franz Richter hundreds of Haya from Bukara were killed in the Ngogo massacre.

In 1963 independent Tanzania abolished traditional kingship; five Haya kings took government posts and the others remained honorary kings with ritual duties. In 1978 Idi Amin's invasion of the Kagera Region in the Uganda-Tanzania War led to the fall of his government.

Haya kings, or bakama, ruled with absolute power through chief ministers, councils, county chiefs and village headmen, and assigned duties to clans: in Kiziba the Batunda were royal bodyguards and the Bashonde royal brewers. Boys of ten to twelve were trained at court under the omuteko age-set system. The Haya are patrilineal, organised in clans with animal totems, and each male head of a household keeps a shrine to his ancestors.

Farming centres on the banana grove (kibanja) around the homestead, with family plots and communal grasslands; the Kagera Region is said to produce nearly half of Tanzania's bananas. Coffee beans are sun-dried and chewed rather than brewed. The traditional house, the mushonge, is a round reed and grass building with a conical peak, though most Haya now live in square houses with iron roofs.
hayam-wuruk: Hayam Wuruk, also called Rajasanagara, was a Javanese Hindu ruler of the Rajasa dynasty and the fourth emperor of Majapahit. According to the Nagarakretagama, he was born in the Saka year 1256, corresponding to 1334, the year Mount Kelud erupted. Its author, Mpu Prapanca, argued that this was a divine sign that Shiva had manifested himself on earth in the king. His name can be translated as scholar rooster. He was the only son of Queen Tribhuwanotunggadewi and Prince Kertawardhana, and his mother was a daughter of Kertarajasa Jayawardhana, the founder of Majapahit. Both the Pararaton and the Nagarakretagama praise him as a gifted student of archery, fencing and music.

In 1350 Queen Dowager Gayatri died at a Buddhist monastery. Tribhuwana had ruled under her auspices and had to give up the throne, and Hayam Wuruk inherited it at the age of 16 under the regnal name Sri Rajasanagara Jayawishnuwardhana. The prime minister Gajah Mada was then at the height of his career, and under their rule Majapahit extended its power across the archipelago. In 1365 Mpu Prapanca wrote the Nagarakretagama in praise of the king, describing his royal tour of villages, shrines and vassal kingdoms in East Java. Hayam Wuruk sent ambassadors to China from 1370 to 1381. During his reign the Ramayana and the Mahabharata became ingrained in Javanese culture through wayang kulit puppets.

According to the Pararaton and the Kidung Sunda, he was expected in 1357 to marry Dyah Pitaloka Citraresmi, daughter of King Linggabuana of the Sunda Kingdom. In the Bubat incident the Sunda royal party and Majapahit troops fought, and the princess and the whole party died. Court officials blamed Gajah Mada, who had intended to demand Sunda's submission. Hayam Wuruk then married Paduka Sori.

Hayam Wuruk died in 1389. His daughter Kusumawardhani was married to her cousin Wikramawardhana, who succeeded him. The empire then fell into chaos and decline in a contest over the succession between Wikramawardhana and Wirabhumi, a son of the king by a concubine, which ended with Wirabhumi's defeat in the Regreg war. His reign furthered the Indianisation of Javanese culture through the spread of Hinduism.
hayashi-razan: Hayashi Razan, also known as Hayashi Dōshun, built his life's work on early studies with Fujiwara Seika (1561–1619), the first Japanese scholar known for a close study of Confucius and his commentators. Seika, a court noble who had become a Buddhist priest, turned from Buddhism to Confucianism and gathered scholars around him whose thought was shaped by the Song philosopher Zhu Xi. Their teaching treated the individual as a functionary in a society that settles naturally into a hierarchy of four classes: samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants.

In 1607 Razan was accepted as a political adviser to the second shōgun, Tokugawa Hidetada, and he went on to serve as tutor and adviser to the first four Tokugawa shōguns. He held the honorific title Daigaku-no-kami, which became hereditary in his family, as did the headship of the shogunate's Confucian academy, later known as the Yushima Seidō, which stood at the head of the country's system of education and training. Equating the samurai with the cultured governing class, he helped legitimise the military government in its first years and urged samurai to cultivate learning, summed up in his saying, no true learning without arms and no true arms without learning.

Razan blended Confucian and Shinto practice, arguing that Shinto was a provisional and local form of Confucian ideas, which allowed a Confucian reading of shrine rituals. In a private essay, Jimmu Tennō Ron, he argued that Emperor Jimmu and the imperial line descended from an offshoot of a Chinese royal house through Wu Taibo, a view considered too dangerous to publish widely. He is also credited with first listing the Three Views of Japan.

Razan died on 7 March 1657. His third son, Hayashi Gahō, succeeded him as the shogunate's chief scholar, finished works his father had begun and in 1670 published the 310 volumes of the Honchō-tsugan, a comprehensive history of Japan; Gahō and his brother Hayashi Dokkōsai edited Razan's collected writings. His ideas dominated the shogunate's ideology until the end of the 18th century, and some Japanese scholars have called him the founder of modern historical research in Japan for his comparatively dispassionate approach. He influenced Arai Hakuseki.
hayat-tahrir-al-sham: Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham was formed on 28 January 2017 as a merger of several armed groups: Jabhat Fatah al-Sham, the Ansar al-Din Front, Jaysh al-Sunna, Liwa al-Haqq and the Nour al-Din al-Zenki Movement. The unification was led by Abu Jaber Sheikh, a former second emir of Ahrar al-Sham, who became its first emir. He had seen the al-Nusra Front's earlier affiliation to al-Qaeda as harmful to the rebel cause and wanted the Islamist factions united. Its commanders came mainly from Jabhat Fatah al-Sham and from Ahrar al-Sham.

The group's later leader, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had begun his military career in 2003 in Iraq, where he joined al-Qaeda in Iraq. After his release in 2011 he was tasked with establishing the al-Nusra Front as al-Qaeda's branch in Syria, and he later led that group.

The merger came after fighting in Idlib in January 2017 between al-Nusra loyalists and rival Islamist groups, particularly Ahrar al-Sham. A series of assassinations of its leaders and clerics followed between September and November 2017. The group then moved against al-Qaeda loyalists, which strengthened its hold on Idlib, and al-Qaeda's leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri, denounced its turn away from Salafi-jihadist positions. In January 2019 it seized dozens of villages from rivals, and a deal gave it leadership of the civil administration across rebel-held Idlib. From 2017 to 2024 it gave allegiance to the Syrian Salvation Government, its civilian administration there.

HTS defended Idlib against government offensives in 2019 and 2020, with Turkish support. In November 2024 it launched an offensive in northwestern Aleppo and took the city of Aleppo four days into it. By 4 December it held most of Aleppo and Idlib governorates and was advancing on Hama. The Assad government fell on 8 December 2024, and on 29 January 2025 the group's dissolution was announced, with its forces to become part of state institutions.

HTS officially followed the Salafi school, although the High Council of Fatwa of the Syrian Salvation Government also included scholars of Ash'arite and Sufi traditions. It was estimated to have between 6,000 and 15,000 members in 2022. Some analysts describe its rule in Idlib as pragmatic, with low taxation, no compulsory veiling for women and a volunteer religious police dismantled within months of its creation in 2020. Others, including reports by the United Nations, the United States and human rights organisations, document arbitrary arrests, torture, restrictions on women and obstruction of aid in the areas it governed. The United States designated it a Foreign Terrorist Organization in May 2018.
hayreddin-barbarossa: Hayreddin was born on Lesbos, and was called Khizr or Hızır as a child. His father, Yakup Ağa, was a sipahi who had taken part in the Ottoman conquest of the island in 1462 and became an established potter. His mother, Katerina, was a Greek Orthodox woman from Lesbos. Of the four sons, Oruç, Ilyas and Khizr all became seamen. The brothers turned privateers against the Knights Hospitaller based on Rhodes. The Knights killed Ilyas in a fight, and Oruç rowed as a galley slave for the Order for four years until his father paid a ransom.

In 1503 Oruç made the island of Djerba his base, and Khizr joined him. The brothers were later allowed to use the port of La Goulette, near Tunis, on condition of giving one third of their spoils to its sultan. Between 1504 and 1510 Oruç carried Muslim Mudéjars from Spain to North Africa, and the title Baba Oruç, meaning Father Oruç, is said to have become Barbarossa in Spain, France and Italy.

In 1516 the brothers took Jijel and Algiers from the Spaniards. In 1517 Oruç offered Algiers to the Ottoman sultan Selim I, who accepted it as a province. Oruç and his brother Ishak were killed in combat near Tlemcen in 1518.

Khizr then offered his allegiance to Selim and in 1519 received the title of beylerbey, with janissaries, galleys and cannons. He defeated a Spanish and Italian army that tried to retake Algiers in 1519 and raided the coasts of Provence and Spain. In 1533 Sultan Suleiman appointed him Kapudan Pasha. In 1534 he sailed with 80 galleys, raided Calabria and the Gulf of Naples, and captured Tunis, forcing the Hafsid sultan Mulay Hassan to flee.

Barbarossa retired to Constantinople in 1545, leaving his son Hasan Pasha in charge in Algiers, and dictated his memoirs, five hand-written volumes known as the Gazavat-ı Hayreddin Paşa. He died in 1546 in his seaside palace at Büyükdere on the Bosphorus. He is buried in a mausoleum built in 1541 by the architect Mimar Sinan near the ferry port of Beşiktaş, at the site where his fleet used to assemble. The Ottoman supremacy in the Mediterranean that he established lasted until the Battle of Lepanto in 1571.
haytham-ibn-khalid: Haytham was the son of Khalid ibn Yazid al-Shaybani and the grandson of Yazid ibn Mazyad al-Shaybani, both governors of Arminiya for the Abbasid Caliphate, a province covering most of the Transcaucasus. According to al-Ya'qubi, Yazid ibn Mazyad settled so many Arabs of the Rabi'a there in 787–788 that they became a majority, and the historian Aram Ter-Ghevondyan placed these settlements chiefly in Shirvan. Yazid's son Muhammad, appointed in 802/3, fortified himself in Shamakhi and made eastern Albania his family's domain. Haytham's elder brother Muhammad ibn Khalid governed Arminiya from Ganja, while Haytham held Shirvan.

The Ta'rikh Bab al-abwab, preserved by the historian Münejjim Bashi, records that after the murder of the caliph al-Mutawakkil disturbances broke out and Haytham made himself independent in Shirvan, while his brother Yazid ibn Khalid did the same in Layzan and was styled Layzanshah. The Persian titles mark the start of the family's Persianization. Little else is known: the chronicle says he fought the infidels of Sarir, the Christian kingdom north of Shirvan, and that his castle stood near a gate called al-Khass. Its year of his death is left blank, and the historian Ashurbeyli concludes from the silence of the sources that his reign was short.

His son Muhammad succeeded him, followed by a grandson, Haytham, who led expeditions against the Christians and gave the grain of pious endowments to the needy.
