Under the next ruler, Ali ibn Haytham, the house collapsed: at the pass of Shandan he and the amir of al-Bab were captured with 10,000 Muslims, and in 917 he was overthrown and killed by Abu-Tahir Yazid ibn Muhammad, lord of Layzan and a descendant of Haytham's brother. The dynasty continued through that branch, and in 918 Abu-Tahir founded the town of Yazidiya, later Shamakhi.
hazael: Hazael was a king of Aram-Damascus who is mentioned in the Bible. His place of birth is unknown: he was probably born in the greater Damascus region, and historians favour both Bashan and the Beqaa Valley. He is first named in 1 Kings 19:15, where God tells the prophet Elijah to anoint him king of Syria.

In the biblical account, years later the Syrian king Ben-Hadad II, probably the Hadadezer of the Tel Dan stele, was ill and sent his court official Hazael with gifts to Elijah's successor Elisha. Elisha told Hazael to tell the king that he would recover, but revealed that the king would be assassinated and that Hazael would commit atrocities against the Israelites. Hazael denied that he was capable of such deeds. He returned to Damascus, told the king that he would recover, suffocated him and seized power.

Under Hazael, Aram-Damascus became an empire that ruled over large parts of contemporary Syria and historical Palestine. The Bible says that he led the Arameans against the allied forces of Jehoram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah and defeated them at Ramoth-Gilead. He repelled two Assyrian attacks, seized Israelite territory east of the Jordan River and took the Philistine city of Gath. He also tried to take Jerusalem, without success. His death is mentioned in 2 Kings 13:24.

Excavations at Tell es-Safi, the site of Gath, have revealed dramatic evidence of its siege and conquest by Hazael. An archaeomagnetic study has suggested that Hazael's campaign also destroyed Tell Zeitah, Tel Rehov and Horvat Tevet.

Most scholars see the monumental Aramaic inscription found at Tel Dan as erected by Hazael after he had defeated the kings of Israel and Judah. Decorated bronze plaques from chariot horse harness, identified by their inscriptions, have been found at two Greek sites, the Heraion of Samos and the temple of Apollo at Eretria on Euboea. The inscription reads that the object was given by Hadad to Hazael from Umq in the year that he crossed the river, which must be the Orontes. These heirlooms were probably part of the loot taken when Tiglath-Pileser III took Damascus in 733/2 BCE, and they passed into Greek, probably Euboean, hands.

French archaeologists found ivory bed decorations at Arslan Tash in northern Syria in 1928. One carries an Old Aramaic inscription with the name Hazael, and the bed seems to have belonged to him. Fragmentary ivories that mention Hazael were also found at Nimrud in Iraq.
hazarajat: Hazarajat, also called Hazaristan, is a mostly mountainous region of the central highlands of Afghanistan, among the Kuh-e Baba mountains at the western end of the Hindu Kush. Its boundaries have always been inexact and shifting, but it is roughly marked by the Bamiyan Basin to the north, the headwaters of the Helmand River to the south, Firuzkuh to the west and the Unai Pass to the east. The highest peaks reach between 4,600 and 5,200 m. The rivers of Kabul, Arghandab, Helmand, Hari, Murghab, Balkh and Kunduz rise there.
The north-east is the site of ancient Bamiyan, a centre of Buddhism and a key caravanserai on the Silk Road. In the north-west, Ghor was long known for its mountain fortresses.

The area was ruled successively by the Achaemenids, Seleucids, Mauryas, Kushans and Hephthalites before the Saffarids Islamized it. The Samanids, Ghaznavids and Ghurids followed, then the Delhi Sultanate. Genghis Khan and his Mongol army invaded in the 13th century, after which the Qarlughids created a local dynasty that gave a few decades of self-rule. Later the region belonged to the Mughal Empire and the Durrani Empire.

Until the late 19th century the Hazarajat remained somewhat independent, and only the authority of local chieftains was obeyed. Nomadic Kuchi herders camped there in summer and overran Hazara farmland and pastures. The authority of the Afghan state was extended into the region under Abdur Rahman Khan, whose government singled out the Hazaras as particularly troublesome, with disastrous consequences for them.

As the Afghan state weakened in 1979, uprisings freed the Hazarajat from state rule. During the war that followed, local mirs and a new group of young radical commanders ruled it. Most Hazara groups united in 1987 and 1989 to form the Hizb-e-Wahdat. Under the Taliban, a revolt broke out in 1997 at Mazar-e Sharif when Hazaras refused to be disarmed, and in 1998 six thousand Hazaras were killed in the north. In March 2001 the two giant Buddhas of Bamiyan were destroyed.

Hazarajat is the homeland of the Hazara people, who form the majority of its population, and denotes an ethnic and religious zone. It consists mainly of the provinces of Bamyan and Daikundi, with parts of Ghazni, Zabul, Ghor, Maidan Wardak, Sar-e-Pol, Balkh, Samangan, Uruzgan and Parwan, and it is not an official region. Its people speak Hazaragi, an eastern dialect of Persian with different accents in different districts, among them Behsudi, Jaghori and Daikundi.
he-chaozong: Few surviving figures can be given to He Chaozong with confidence. One that may be genuine carries a hidden inscription that shows only under ultraviolet light, and its carving is restrained, without the flowing robes of many other pieces attributed to him, which may be attractive only on the surface. The 1763 gazetteer entry shows that he had already won a considerable reputation in his own day.

His seals raise questions of their own. On one Guanyin figure attributed to him, every character of the He Chaozong seal appears in reverse. This suggests that at least some seals on Dehua porcelain figures worked like brands, perhaps made of metal, which could be pressed into the clay the wrong way round. On this seal and on another, the outer border was incised by hand after the characters had been impressed into the body of the figure.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries Dehua potters revived his manner. The best known of them, the ceramicist Su Xuejin (1869–1919), is said to have recreated it so closely that the originals cannot be told apart from his work. Many such pieces can be assumed to bear the old master's seal. One heavily potted statue of Manjusri with a single He Chaozong seal is clearly a revival piece, perhaps a close recreation of an original, and shows none of the mannered robes typical of much late Ming and early Qing Dehua statuary.

Other figures point to still later production. A thinly potted Guanyin with the usual Dehua gourd seal stamped above the square He Chaozong seal belongs to a later period than the master, though it seems to come from the same studio as the Manjusri, if not from the same hand.
heart-of-darkness: In 1890 Joseph Conrad was appointed by a Belgian trading company to serve on one of its steamers on the Congo River. The captain fell ill and Conrad took command, guiding the ship up the Lualaba River to the company's innermost station, Kindu, in the Congo Free State. He began to write eight years later. The tale appeared in three parts in Blackwood's Magazine in February, March and April 1899, the February number being the magazine's thousandth issue. It was collected in Youth, A Narrative; and Two Other Stories, published by William Blackwood on 13 November 1902. More than twenty models have been proposed for the ivory agent Kurtz.

The story opens on the Thames, where Charles Marlow tells his friends how he became captain of a river steamboat for an ivory company. In Africa he finds a station where dying labourers lie near a railway under construction, and he hears of Kurtz, a first-class agent in charge of a distant trading post. Marlow's own steamboat is wrecked, and months of repairs follow before the two-month journey upriver.

At the Inner Station a Russian wanderer tells him that Kurtz is worshipped by the local people and is gravely ill. Marlow sees severed heads on posts around the station. Kurtz is carried aboard but dies on the way downriver, whispering the words The horror! The horror! Back in Europe, Marlow visits Kurtz's fiancée and tells her that his last word was her name. The river is never named, but the setting is the Congo Free State, then the private colony of King Leopold II.

The book drew little comment from critics in 1902, and F. R. Leavis later called it a minor work. By the 1960s it was a standard text in many schools and colleges. In a lecture of 1975 the Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe called it an offensive and deplorable book that dehumanised Africans. His critics reply that he does not separate Marlow's view from Conrad's and that the novella condemns colonial rule; E. D. Morel, who led opposition to Leopold's rule, called it the most powerful thing written on the subject.

T. S. Eliot took an epigraph for The Hollow Men from it in 1925, and Achebe's Things Fall Apart of 1958 answers it. Francis Ford Coppola's film Apocalypse Now of 1979 moves the story to the Vietnam War.
heavy-cavalry: Heavy cavalry, also called shock cavalry, was meant to deliver a battlefield charge and to act as a tactical reserve. Its equipment differed greatly by region and period, but its riders generally sat on large, powerful warhorses, wore body armour and fought with lances, swords, maces, battle axes or war hammers, and their mounts might be protected by barding. They were distinct from light cavalry, whose tasks were raiding, reconnaissance, screening, skirmishing, patrolling and carrying messages.

Iranian tribes such as the Massagetae were believed to have originated the cataphract, a horseman with man and beast fully encased in armour, and the Persians already used such units by the time of Alexander's invasion. The Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus described Persian horsemen whose bodies were so covered in iron plates that arrows could lodge only at the openings for the eyes and nose. Among the Greeks, cavalry long played little part because of hoplite warfare and mountainous terrain, but the Theban commander Epaminondas used heavy horse to effect at Leuctra and Mantineia. Philip II of Macedon, who had spent his youth as a hostage in Epaminondas's house, built the Companion cavalry, the first force known to represent archetypal heavy cavalry.

The metal stirrup, invented in 4th-century China, reached Europe by the late 6th or early 7th century and was in widespread use by the 8th; it is thought to have helped create the early knightly classes, though the argument that it produced feudalism is not fully accepted. In the 10th century the army of the Byzantine emperor Nicephorus II relied on cataphracts as its nucleus. In China armoured lancers spread under the Western Han, and fully armoured horsemen were the main striking force of the Northern dynasties from the 4th to the 6th century.

From the late 15th century the cuirassier became the main form of European heavy cavalry, and a regiment of cuirassiers killed the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus at the Battle of Lützen in 1632. Napoleon raised the number of French cuirassier regiments to fourteen, though they declined as infantry firearms improved. The twelve French heavy cavalry regiments of 1914 still wore their cuirasses in the opening stages of World War I. Today such regiments are ceremonial, and armoured fighting vehicles such as the tank fill the niche.
hebat: Her worship had its roots in the north of modern Syria. Texts from Ebla of the third millennium BCE name her Ḫalabāytu, which Alfonso Archi reads as she of Ḫalab, that is Aleppo; another proposal derives the name from the root ḫbb, to love. She was a minor goddess at Ebla, always linked there with Aleppo, and was already paired with Adad, the weather god of that city. Later she was worshipped in the kingdom of Yamhad, at Alalakh and at Emar, where she was associated with sikkānu stones, and names such as Puduḫepa and Abdi-Heba, servant of Ḫepat, invoke her.

Epithets such as queen, lady of heaven and queen of heaven marked her high place, and a Hurrian ceremony for her concerned allašši, ladyship, as Teshub's concerned kingship. She could also be invoked in rites of midwifery. In Hurrian offering lists, the kaluti, she heads a circle of deities that includes her son Šarruma, her daughters Allanzu and Kunzišalli and her attendant Takitu. In the Song of Ullikummi, part of the Kumarbi Cycle, the monster blocks the entrance of her temple, cutting her off from the other gods, and she sends Takitu to learn the fate of her husband Teshub.

She held the first place among the goddesses in the Hurrian traditions of Aleppo and Kizzuwatna, displacing Šauška, who kept that place in eastern centres such as Nuzi. Hittite sources first mention her when Ḫattušili I carried her statue off from Ḫaššum, and she and Teshub later headed the dynastic pantheon. At Yazılıkaya she stands on a leopard with her children. Queen Puduḫepa's prayer equates her with the Sun goddess of Arinna, though scholars such as Piotr Taracha doubt the idea reached ordinary worship. In the first millennium BCE she was paired with the Luwian weather god Tarḫunz in Tabal, and the goddess Hipta, known from Lydia, may be a late form of her.
hebei: Hebei means north of the river, from its position north of the Yellow River on the North China Plain. In the Yu Gong the region is recorded as Jizhou, which gave it the abbreviation Ji, and its nickname Yanzhao comes from the states of Yan and Zhao that held it in antiquity. The west of the province rises into the Taihang Mountains and the Yan Mountains run through the north, beyond which lie the grasslands of Inner Mongolia. The Bohai Sea lies to the east, and the province entirely surrounds Beijing and Tianjin on land.

In the Warring States period Jin was partitioned and much of its territory in Hebei went to Zhao. Under the Han dynasty the area was ruled as You Prefecture in the north and Ji Province in the south. At the end of the Han, Yuan Shao overcame Gongsun Zan there but was defeated by Cao Cao at the Battle of Guandu in 200. The northern frontier position made Hebei change hands often in the age of the Sixteen Kingdoms. The Northern Qi had its capital at Ye, near modern Linzhang. During the Tang dynasty the area was officially called Hebei for the first time, and a Great Yan State existed there from 756 to 763 during the An Lushan Rebellion.

Emperor Gaozu of the Later Jin ceded much of northern Hebei to the Khitan Liao dynasty. These Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun, which lay within the Great Wall, became a weakness in Chinese defence for the next century. After the Jingkang Incident of 1127 the Southern Song gave up all of North China to the Jurchen Jin dynasty. Between 1048 and 1128 the Yellow River ran directly through the province. Under the Yuan the area was administered directly from the capital Dadu. In the Ming it became Beizhili, and the Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing in 1421. The Qing called it Zhili, meaning directly ruled, and the Republic of China created the province of Hebei in 1928, when the capital moved to Nanjing.

Hebei is a province of North China with Shijiazhuang as its capital and largest city; its population was 74.6 million at the 2020 census. After the founding of the People's Republic, the regions around Chengde and Zhangjiakou were merged into it. The Tangshan earthquake of 28 July 1976 killed about 242,000 people by the official count. Five UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie there, among them the Great Wall, the Chengde Mountain Resort and the Qing imperial tombs. The Zhaozhou Bridge, built during the Sui dynasty, is the oldest standing bridge in China.
hebrew: Hebrew is a Northwest Semitic language and belongs to the Canaanite languages. It was the spoken language of the Iron Age kingdoms of Israel and Judah from about 1200 to 586 BCE, and epigraphic evidence supports the view that the earlier layers of biblical literature reflect their language. The earliest examples of written Paleo-Hebrew date to the 10th century BCE. Two claims for older inscriptions are disputed: Amihai Mazar called a shard from Khirbet Qeiyafa, which its discoverer Yossi Garfinkel thought might be the earliest Hebrew writing, proto-Canaanite, and a claimed curse tablet from Mount Ebal is rejected by practically all professional epigraphers apart from its discoverer's team.

Nearly all the Hebrew Bible is written in Biblical Hebrew, much of it in a dialect that scholars believe flourished around the 6th century BCE. For this reason Jews have called it Lashon Hakodesh, 'the holy tongue', since ancient times. The Bible itself calls it Yehudit, 'Judean', and the name Ivrit appears in the Mishnah. Hebrew is written from right to left in an abjad of 22 letters. The ancient Paleo-Hebrew alphabet resembled the Canaanite and Phoenician ones, while the modern 'square' script, Ashurit, developed from the Aramaic script.

Scholars debate how far Hebrew remained a spoken vernacular after the Babylonian exile, when Old Aramaic was the predominant international language. It ceased to be a regular spoken language between 200 and 400 CE, as it declined after the unsuccessful Bar Kokhba revolt against the Roman Empire. It survived as the language of Jewish liturgy, rabbinic literature, commerce between Jews of different native languages and poetry. The first dated book printed in Hebrew was published by Abraham Garton in Reggio in 1475. With the rise of Zionism in the 19th century it was revived as a spoken language, led by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, and Modern Hebrew became the main language of the Yishuv in Palestine and then the official language of the State of Israel.
hebrew-bible: The Hebrew Bible, also called the Tanakh or Mikra, is the canonical collection of Hebrew scriptures. Its name Tanakh is an acronym from the initials of its three divisions: the Torah, the five books of Moses; the Nevi'im, the Prophets; and the Ketuvim, the Writings. Its authoritative form in Judaism is the Masoretic Text, compiled by Jewish scribes between the 7th and 10th centuries CE, which counts 24 books. It is mostly in Biblical Hebrew, with some passages in Biblical Aramaic, in Daniel and Ezra and at Jeremiah 10:11.

The books were composed and edited in stages over several hundred years. The scholar John J. Collins writes that all of it received its final shape in the postexilic, or Second Temple, period. Tradition ascribes the Torah to Moses, but the Torah itself credits him with writing only some sections, and scholars date it to the 1st millennium BCE, after Israel and Judah had developed as states, while allowing that older oral proverbs, stories and songs may be included. The Torah probably gained canonical status first, perhaps as early as the 5th century BCE. The Nevi'im were canonical by the 2nd century BCE, and Daniel, written about 164 BCE, was not grouped with them.

The Masoretes later gave the consonantal text its vowel system, chiefly Aaron ben Moses ben Asher in the school of Tiberias. Scholars also use the Septuagint, a Greek translation made by Greek-speaking Jews of Alexandria, the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Syriac Peshitta and the Dead Sea Scrolls, which sometimes differ from the Masoretic Text.

Scholars see the collection as a mix of folklore and history, with some narratives after the 9th century BCE partly supported by archaeology and many traditional accounts debated. Some stories may draw on older sources, and scholars have pointed to similarities between the Genesis flood and the Gilgamesh flood myth. Historians such as Fergus Millar and David Goodblatt hold that the Bible, as national history and source of law, helped form the national identity of ancient Jews.

The Septuagint was influential on early Christianity, and the books of the Hebrew Bible form the Christian Old Testament, arranged differently in Protestant editions and joined by further books in Catholic and Orthodox ones. In Islam the Tawrat is often identified with the Pentateuch and sometimes with the other books. Rashi's commentary is the major commentary on the Chumash.
hebrides: The Hebrides are the largest archipelago in Scotland and the British Isles, with a combined area of 7,285 square kilometres. The Inner Hebrides, closer to the mainland, include Islay, Jura, Skye, Mull, Raasay, Staffa and the Small Isles. The Outer Hebrides form a chain of more than 100 islands and skerries about 70 kilometres west of the mainland, among them Lewis and Harris, North Uist, Benbecula, South Uist and Barra. Their rocks range from Precambrian strata, among the oldest in Europe, to Paleogene igneous intrusions. Pliny the Elder, around 77 CE, wrote that there were 30 Hebudes.

The islands were settled in the Mesolithic era around 6500 BCE or earlier. The standing stones at Callanish date to the 3rd millennium BCE, and Cladh Hallan, a Bronze Age settlement on South Uist, is the only site in the UK where prehistoric mummies have been found. Scottish Gaelic arrived from Ireland with the growing influence of the kingdom of Dál Riata from the 6th century CE.

Viking raids began towards the end of the 8th century, and in the following decades the Hebrides came under Norse control and settlement, especially after Harald Fairhair's victory at Hafrsfjord in 872. The Norse called the islands Suðreyjar, the Southern Isles. In 1098 Edgar of Scotland formally signed the islands over to Magnus III of Norway, who had conquered Orkney, the Hebrides and the Isle of Man in a swift campaign. His skald Bjorn Cripplehand recorded that in the Uists the king dyed his sword red in blood.

As the Norse era closed, Norse-speaking princes gave way to Gaelic-speaking clan chiefs, including the MacLeods of Lewis and Harris and Clan Donald. By the early 14th century the MacDonald Lords of the Isles, based on Islay, were in theory their feudal superiors. James IV forfeited their lands in 1493. Many islesmen supported the Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745, and after Culloden the clan system was broken up and the islands became a series of landed estates.

The culture of the inhabitants has been successively influenced by Celtic-speaking, Norse-speaking and English-speaking peoples, and the names of the islands derive from the different languages spoken there. Much of Scottish Gaelic literature and music has historically originated in the Hebrides. The economy depends on crofting, fishing, tourism, the oil industry and renewable energy. The islands have less biodiversity than mainland Scotland, but a significant number of seals and seabirds.
hebron: Hebron lies in the Judaean Mountains at 930 metres above sea level, 30 kilometres south of Jerusalem and about 43 kilometres north-east of Beersheba. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the Levant. Excavations around Tel Rumeida reveal strong fortifications from the Early Bronze Age, and the city flourished in the 17th and 18th centuries BCE before a fire destroyed it. In Arabic the city is al-Khalil, from the epithet Khalil al-Rahman, Friend of the Merciful, given to Abraham.

Genesis says the city was formerly called Kiryath-arba. After the destruction of the First Temple most Jewish inhabitants were exiled, and Edomite presence is attested in the Persian and Hellenistic periods. The settlement at Tel Rumeida was destroyed, probably during John Hyrcanus's conquest of Idumaea around 112 or 107 BCE, and later layers show a population with Jewish characteristics, though the evidence cannot say whether this was settlers or converted Idumaeans. Herod the Great built the wall that still surrounds the Cave of the Patriarchs. During the First Jewish-Roman War the town was laid waste by Sextus Vettulenus Cerialis.

The Rashidun Caliphate took Hebron in 638 and turned the Byzantine church over Abraham's tomb into a mosque. The Crusader Godfrey de Bouillon captured the city in 1099 and renamed it Castellion Saint Abraham; the sanctuary became a church until Muslim rule returned. In 1260, after Baibars defeated the Mongol army, minarets were added, and six years later he barred Christians and Jews from the sanctuary. Sephardi Jews settled in Hebron after the expulsion from Spain. The British occupied the city on 8 December 1917. Jordan held it from 1948 and Israel from the Six-Day War of 1967; under the Hebron Agreement of 1997 Israel withdrew from 80 percent of the city, which passed to the Palestinian Authority.

Hebron is the capital of the Hebron Governorate, with 201,063 people inside the city limits. It is a commercial and industrial centre, known for limestone, grapes, ceramics, glass and metalworking. The Cave of the Patriarchs is said to hold the tombs of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and their wives; its Isaac Hall serves as the Ibrahimi Mosque and the Abraham and Jacob Hall as a synagogue. The Old City, with narrow winding streets and stone houses, is one of the best preserved sites of the Mamluk era and was inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2017.
hecataeus-of-miletus: Hecataeus was the son of Hegesander and came from a very wealthy family of Miletus, a city then under Persian rule in the satrapy of Lydia. He was active at the time of the Greco-Persian Wars. After travelling widely he settled in his native city, where he held a high position and devoted himself to writing geographical and historical works.

When Aristagoras, acting tyrant of Miletus, called a council of leading Ionians to organise a revolt against Persian rule, Hecataeus tried without success to dissuade his fellow citizens. In 494 BCE, when the defeated Ionians had to sue for terms, he was one of the ambassadors sent to the Persian satrap Artaphernes, whom he persuaded to restore the constitutions of the Ionian cities.

Two works are known, both surviving only in fragments. The Periodos ges, meaning Journey round the Earth or World Survey, was written in two books, the first on Europe and the second on Asia, which included Africa. It began at the Straits of Gibraltar and ran clockwise round the coasts of the Mediterranean and Black Sea, giving the peoples and places met on a coastal voyage. More than 300 fragments are preserved, mostly as citations for place names in the work of Stephanus of Byzantium.

His other work, the Genealogies, was a book on mythography in four books, of which fewer than forty fragments remain. It took a sceptical view of the traditions of families who claimed descent from gods. He is also credited with improving the map of Anaximander, which showed the world as a disc encircled by Oceanus.

Hecataeus is the first known Greek historian and was one of the first classical writers to mention the Celtic and Illyrian peoples. He was probably the first of the logographers to attempt a serious prose history and to use a critical method to separate myth from historical fact, although he accepted Homer and other poets as trustworthy authorities. Herodotus, though he contradicts Hecataeus at least once, owes him the concept of a prose history.
hecate: Hecate's earliest appearance in literature is in Hesiod's Theogony in the 8th century BCE, where she is described as a goddess of great honour with domains in sky, earth and sea. Evidence suggests she originated among the Carians of Anatolia, where most names invoking her, such as Hecataeus and Hecatomnus, are attested, and where her unrivalled cult site stood at Lagina. She may derive from local sun goddesses. The earliest evidence of her cult comes from Selinunte in Sicily, where she had a temple in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE.

Hecate was associated with borders, city walls, doorways and crossroads, and so with realms beyond the world of the living. Her cult titles reflect this role: Enodia, on the way; Propylaia, before the gate; Triodia, who frequents crossroads; and Klêidouchos, holding the keys. She was expected to avert harmful spirits from the house or city she guarded, and so could also refuse to avert them. As holder of the keys between realms she is recognized as a chthonic goddess. In the 3rd century BCE Theocritus describes her unlocking the gates of death, and she appears with Hermes guiding Persephone back from the underworld.

By the 1st century CE her chthonic and nocturnal character had made her a goddess heavily associated with witchcraft; in Lucan's Pharsalia the witch Erichtho invokes her. She was also tied to plant lore, medicines and poisons, and Apollonius of Rhodes says Medea was taught medicine by her. Dogs were among her most important attributes, and garlic was a favoured offering. Her lunar role rests on late evidence: no artwork before the Roman period connects her to the Moon.

Hecate's cult became established in Athens about 430 BCE, when the sculptor Alcamenes made the earliest known triple-formed statue for her new temple. Home shrines often took the form of a Hekataion, a carving of a triple Hecate facing three directions around a central pillar, and larger ones stood at public crossroads, such as on the road to the Acropolis.

Athenians honoured her at the Deipnon, a meal served to Hecate and the restless dead once a lunar month at the dark moon. It was set out at a small shrine by the front door, since the street and the doorway form a crossroads where she dwelled, and might include cake or bread, fish, eggs and honey. The Romans often knew her as Trivia, an epithet shared with Diana, and in the Roman era she was closely identified with Diana and Artemis.
hecatomnid-dynasty: The earliest known member of the family was Hyssaldomus, dynast of Mylasa, father of Hecatomnus and of a woman named Aba. Louis Robert suggested he was the first satrap of Caria, but there is no conclusive evidence. The Hecatomnids were one of many minor Carian dynasties, and the names Mausolus and Pixodarus, which Herodotus records among the dynasts of Cindye during the Ionian Revolt, suggest the family ruled that town before moving to Mylasa. Caria had been governed from Sardis as part of Lydia until Tissaphernes was executed in 395 BCE; Hecatomnus, its first Carian satrap, was in office by 392 BCE, when he made war on Evagoras of Salamis.

Hecatomnus' five children formed two married pairs, Mausolus with Artemisia and Idrieus with Ada, while the youngest, Pixodarus, married outside the family; since neither pair is known to have had children, their marriages are thought to have been symbolic. Only men were called satrap or struck coins, but Hecatomnid women issued laws and led military actions, and each widow ruled alone. Mausolus and Artemisia II succeeded in 377 BCE and took Lycia after the Revolt of the Satraps. After Mausolus died in 353/2 BCE, Artemisia suppressed a revolt of the Rhodians, leading a fleet to the island herself.

Idrieus and Ada I followed about 351/0 BCE, and Idrieus built more at the sanctuary of Labraunda, the centre of the cult of Zeus Labraundeus, than Mausolus had. Ada ruled alone from about 344/3 BCE until Pixodarus deposed her about 341/0 BCE and exiled her to Alinda. Pixodarus issued the Letoon trilingual in Greek, Lycian and Aramaic and was the only Hecatomnid to strike gold coins. On his death in 336/5 BCE the Persian Orontobates, husband of his daughter Ada II, became satrap.

When Alexander the Great reached Caria after the Battle of the Granicus in 334 BCE, Ada I, by tradition, came to him from Alinda and adopted him as her son. He ousted Orontobates during the Siege of Halicarnassus, in which Ada took a leading part, and left her to rule Caria from Halicarnassus. She then disappears from the record and may have died at any time between 334 and 323 BCE; after Alexander's death the Macedonian Asander became satrap. The dynasty's best-known monument is the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
hecatomnus: Hecatomnus was the son and successor of Hyssaldomus, a dynastic ruler of Mylasa. He had probably supported the Persian satrap Tissaphernes and may have served him as a hyparch, a subordinate official. Caria had until then belonged to other satrapies, usually that of Lydia. Its creation as a satrapy of its own was part of the reorganisation of Persian power in western Anatolia by Artaxerxes II after the revolt of Cyrus the Younger, and Hecatomnus was the first non-Persian raised to the rank of satrap. His power thus rested both on royal appointment and on his standing as a local dynast.

No later than 390 BCE the king appointed him to command naval forces for the war against Evagoras I of Cyprus. Diodorus and Isocrates report that Hecatomnus secretly paid Evagoras to hire mercenaries and was ready to rebel. The historian Stephen Ruzicka doubts this: Hecatomnus showed no disloyalty at any other time and, not being a Persian noble, could not hope to win over other officials. Ruzicka suggests the rumour came from Evagoras himself, either to discredit Hecatomnus before the king or to impress the Egyptian king Hakor, from whose court it may have reached Athens through the general Chabrias. Hecatomnus made Mylasa his capital, and his coins show Zeus Labrandenos carrying a labrys.

Isocrates says he was still ruling in 380 BCE, and Ruzicka places his death in 377 or 376 BCE. His daughters Artemisia and Ada married their brothers Mausolus and Idrieus. In 2010 police arrested looters digging in what was later believed to be his tomb, where a marble sarcophagus and frescoes were found, though many objects had already been sold. The tomb is on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites and is valued for the study of Carian art as a forerunner of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus. A golden crown stolen from it has been identified and is to be returned to Turkey.
hechingen: Hechingen lies in central Baden-Württemberg, about 60 kilometres south of Stuttgart and 90 kilometres north of Lake Constance. The town stands at the foot of the Swabian Alps below Hohenzollern Castle. Research suggests that the Battle of Solicinium, fought in 368 between the invading Alamanni and a Roman army led by Emperor Valentinian I, probably took place in what is now the north of Hechingen, and that the lost city of Solicinium stood where the town's Roman museum is today.

The Counts of Hohenzollern founded the town in 1255 as their new capital. It lay on an imperial highway running from the middle Neckar south by way of Rottweil to the upper Rhine and the Alpine passes. The counts grew steadily weaker through financial problems. After a siege in 1388, Eberhard II, Duke of Württemberg gained feudal rights over the territory, and a fire destroyed the town in 1401. Friedrich XII of Hohenzollern sold his whole fortune to Württemberg in 1415, and in 1423 the castle was taken and destroyed. His nephew Jos Niklaus later won imperial permission to rebuild it and cancelled the agreement with Württemberg, so Hechingen stayed Hohenzollern, though provincial and largely agricultural.

When the county was divided in three, Hechingen became the residence of the counts of Hohenzollern-Hechingen, whose territory of the town and 26 villages changed little until the 19th century. Count Eitel Friedrich IV made it a centre of art, music and Renaissance architecture, building the convent church of St Luzen and the Friedrichsburg palace. The town stayed Catholic through the Reformation but suffered in the 30 Years' War, with imperial, Swedish, Württemberg and Bavarian troops, plague in 1635 and a complete plundering in 1638 by the troops of Bernard of Saxe-Weimar. Bavarian troops stayed until 1650.

Constantine, the last reigning prince, married Eugénie de Beauharnais, and from 1826 the couple made Hechingen a cultural centre of southern Germany, receiving guests such as Hector Berlioz and Franz Liszt. After the Revolution of 1848 the county passed to Prussia in 1850. In the Second World War industries and parts of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, including its Institute for Physics, were moved to Hechingen from bombed cities, and in April 1945 American troops of the Alsos Mission entered the town in search of material for the German nuclear energy project.

Hechingen belongs to the Zollernalbkreis, which absorbed its district in 1973, and is twinned with Joué-lès-Tours in France and Hódmezővásárhely in Hungary. Textile and machine-making industries, many of them Jewish enterprises, had made it one of the region's important economic centres by 1871.
hector-berlioz: Hector Berlioz was born on 11 December 1803 at La Côte-Saint-André, in the département of Isère, the eldest child of Louis Berlioz, a physician. He moved to Paris in 1821, aged seventeen, and at his father's insistence enrolled in the School of Medicine, forcing himself to continue despite his revulsion at dissecting bodies. In 1824 he composed a Messe solennelle, which was performed twice and then suppressed; a copy was found in 1991. His first opera, Les Francs-juges, was never performed and survives in fragments, the best known being its overture.

Berlioz won the Prix de Rome in 1830 with the cantata La Mort de Sardanapale, having modified his natural style to please the judges after his Cléopâtre of the previous year had been thought to betray dangerous tendencies. In the same year he wrote the Symphonie fantastique, in which an idealised portrait of the Irish actress Harriet Smithson recurs as an idée fixe. After a concert on 9 December 1832 she finally met him, and they married; the marriage foundered, and she died in June 1862.

In the 1840s he struggled as a composer, completing the song cycle Les Nuits d'été to poems by Théophile Gautier and publishing articles on orchestration that became his Treatise on Instrumentation. After the failure of La Damnation de Faust he turned increasingly to conducting, appearing in London from 1851 and in Germany.

Berlioz called four large works symphonies, but his idea of the genre differed greatly from the classical German pattern, since he used the symphony to tell a story. His three completed operas were never written to commission. Benvenuto Cellini was an outright failure, and Les Troyens, a five-act, five-hour work, was too large for the Opéra: only its last three acts were staged in Paris, in November 1863, and were cut further during a run of 22 performances. The experience demoralised him, and he wrote almost no more music.

Opinion was divided for many years between those who thought him an original genius and those who found his music lacking in form. When Richard Strauss revised the Treatise on Instrumentation in 1905 he added new material but left Berlioz's text unchanged. Berlioz died in Paris on 8 March 1869, aged 65.
hedayat-allah-khan: Hedayat-Allah Khan, also spelled Hedayatollah Khan, was a Gilaki prince, the son of Agha Jamal Fumani, a tribal chieftain of Fuman descended from the Dubbaj clan, which had ruled Gilan in the late 15th and early 16th centuries and claimed descent from the Sasanian Empire and the prophet Isaac. In 1749, two years after the death of Nader Shah, Agha Jamal and a certain Agha Safi seized Gilan.

During the war between the Zand and the Qajars, the Qajar chieftain Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar made the province submit and in 1752 married Agha Jamal's daughter. On 6 November 1752 Agha Jamal was killed at Shaft by Agha Hady Shafti, who took control of the province. Four months later Mohammad Hasan Khan seized and executed Agha Hady and appointed Hedayat-Allah governor of Gilan.

When Karim Khan Zand conquered Iran in 1760, he replaced Hedayat-Allah with an associate of his own. Hedayat-Allah returned while Karim Khan was campaigning in Azerbaijan, but was soon seized and fined 12,000 tomans, and Karim Khan's cousin Nazar Ali Khan was made governor. In 1767 Karim Khan restored Hedayat-Allah as ruler under Zand suzerainty and married his own son Abol-Fath Khan Zand to Hedayat-Allah's sister.

Under his rule Gilan flourished. He drew Armenians, Russians, Jews and Indians to Rasht and kept an elegant court there, funded by the silk industry and the sea trade between Bandar-e Anzali and Astrakhan. The Cambridge History of Iran nonetheless judges him treacherous and bloodthirsty even by the standards of his age. In 1782 Agha Mohammad Khan invaded Gilan. Hedayat-Allah sent two envoys, Mirza Sadeq and Agha Sadeq Lahiji, to make peace and withdrew to Shirvan, but no terms were agreed and the Qajar ruler raided Rasht and seized its riches.

Hedayat-Allah later returned, allegedly with Russian help, and Agha Mohammad Khan, who saw the whole Caspian coast threatened, marched on Rasht again, joined by the local ruler Mehdi Beg Khalatbari. The Russian consul in Gilan supplied the Qajars with weapons. Hedayat-Allah tried once more to flee to Shirvan but was caught by men of a local ruler, by most accounts Agha Ali Shafti, who killed him to avenge the slaughter of his own family a few years earlier. His treasure fell to the conqueror, and Gilan came fully under Qajar rule.
hedeby: Hedeby lay between the Frankish Empire and the Danish Kingdom, at the head of the narrow, navigable Schlei inlet, which connects to the Baltic Sea. A portage of less than 15 km led to the Treene River, which flows into the Eider and so to the North Sea, so goods and ships could be pulled overland and the dangerous voyage round Jutland avoided. The Old Norse name Heiðabýr means heath-settlement. Around 965 the chronicler Ibrahim ibn Yaqub described it as a very large city at the very end of the world's ocean.

Hedeby is first mentioned in the chronicle of Einhard, which records that Charlemagne stayed there in the summer of 804. In 808 the Danish king Godfred destroyed a rival Slav trading centre, Reric, and resettled its merchants at Hedeby. The Danevirke, an earthen wall across the south of Jutland, joined the town's defences to form a barrier from the western marshes to the Schlei. Hedeby became the seat of a bishop in 948, minted its own coins from 825 and took part in the slave trade that sent captives east towards the Islamic world.

Excavation shows a busy local economy of textile, comb, leather, iron and gold working, with a glass furnace active between 850 and 900. Richly furnished graves suggest an aristocracy. The visitor al-Tartushi, from Cordoba, found the town poor. In 1050 King Harald Hardrada of Norway burned it with fire ships during a conflict with King Sweyn II of Denmark. West Slavs sacked and burned it in 1066, after which it was slowly abandoned and its tolls passed to Schleswig across the Schlei.

The site was rediscovered by Sophus Muller in 1897, and excavation began in 1900. Because nothing was built there afterwards and the waterlogged ground preserved wood, the finds are exceptional, including the wrecks of several Viking ships. Only about 5 per cent of the settlement and 1 per cent of the harbour have been investigated. The Hedeby Viking Museum opened beside the site in 1985, and Hedeby and the Danevirke were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018.
heden-ii: Heden, also written Hedan or Hetan, was called the Younger. One of the chief sources for his life is the Passio minor sancti Kiliani. It tells that his father Gozbert married Geilana, the widow of his own brother, and was reproved for it by Saint Kilian, who paid for his boldness with his life. After divine vengeance struck Gozbert, Heden was driven from the realm and his mother Geilana ruled as duchess in 689. He returned as an adult some time later and took over the duchy before 704.

The duchy of his family lay around the river Main, and only under Heden did the dukes take an extensive interest in the lands to the east, the region now called Thuringia. His claim there may have come through his wife Theodrada; Theotbald, who may have ruled Thuringia before him, was perhaps her brother.

The support of Heden and Theodrada was instrumental in establishing Christianity in Thuringia. In a donation made at Würzburg, his capital, on 1 May 704, with the consent of his wife, his son Thuring and the Frankish magnates Rocco and Doda, he granted the bishop Willibrord Arnstadt, Mühlberg and Großmonra. A document dated 18 April 716 or 717 enlarged that grant, giving hereditary estates on the Saale and at Hammelburg to the counts Cato and Sigeric, the tutor or regent Ado and the magnates Adogoto and Hereric.

Through his wife Heden had links to the Rodoin family and to the family of Gundoin, Duke of Alsace, and he had ties to the monastery of Weißenburg in Alsace. His daughter Immina entered the family's monastery of Marienberg. The 12th-century Vita Bilihildis, based on earlier sources, names the husband of Saint Bilihild as a duke called Hetan, who may have been Heden.
hedwig-jagiellon-duchess-of-bavaria: Hedwig was born in Kraków on 21 September 1457, the eldest daughter of King Casimir IV of Poland and Archduchess Elisabeth of Austria. In 1468 Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary, asked for her hand, hoping to win an ally against his rival for the Bohemian throne, George of Poděbrady, and he was backed by Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II. But Casimir had been allied with George since 1462, and the queen opposed the match outright. Matthias asked again in 1469, 1471 and 1473 before a final refusal.

To guard his south-western border with Bohemia, Casimir sought a closer alliance with Bavaria. After talks at Łęczyca and Radom, Hedwig agreed on 30 December 1474 to marry George, son and heir of Duke Louis IX of Bavaria-Landshut, with a dowry of 32,000 Hungarian złoty. Because the couple were closely related, Pope Sixtus IV granted a dispensation on 26 May 1475.

Hedwig left her family at Poznań on 10 October 1475 with a retinue of about 1,200 knights and reached Landshut on 14 November. The wedding was held that day at St. Martin's Church, conducted by Bernhard von Rohr, Archbishop of Salzburg, before Emperor Frederick III, his son Maximilian and many German princes, and 9,000 people attended the feast the next day.

She became duchess-consort in 1479 on the death of her father-in-law. The marriage was unhappy: her husband was known as a drinker and a womaniser, and in 1485 he sent her away from the court at Landshut to Burghausen Castle, where she lived with her own court and servants but, according to contemporary chroniclers, deprived of all the pleasures of the world. The couple had five children, among them Elisabeth, who married Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine, and Margaret, later abbess at Neuburg an der Donau.

Hedwig died unexpectedly at Burghausen on 18 February 1502 and was buried in the Cistercian monastery of Raitenhaslach; her tombstone was destroyed when the monastery was secularised in 1803. She kept little contact with her family, and on 31 January 1503 her brother, King Alexander of Poland, wrote to her husband that he had not known she had died eleven months before.
hedwig-of-silesia: Hedwig was born in 1174 at Andechs Castle in the Duchy of Bavaria, a daughter of Count Berthold IV of Andechs, margrave of Carniola and Istria, and his second wife Agnes of Wettin. Her sister Agnes married King Philip II of France, a marriage annulled in 1200, and her sister Gertrude, killed in 1213, married King Andrew II of Hungary, so that Hedwig was the aunt of Elizabeth of Hungary. Her youngest sister Matilda became abbess of the Benedictine Abbey of Kitzingen in Franconia, where Hedwig received her education. At the age of twelve she married Henry I the Bearded, heir of the Piast duke Boleslaus the Tall of Silesia.

Henry succeeded his father in 1201, and Hedwig became Duchess of Silesia. He struggled with his Piast relatives, first with his uncle Mieszko IV Tanglefoot, who seized the Upper Silesian Duchy of Opole. In 1229 Henry was captured at Płock Castle by Duke Konrad I of Masovia, and Hedwig went to Płock to plead for him and obtained his release. After the death of Władysław III Spindleshanks in 1231 Henry became Duke of Greater Poland, and the next year High Duke at Kraków, the first Silesian Piast to hold both Silesia and the Seniorate Province in accord with the 1138 testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth.

At Hedwig's request Henry established the Cistercian convent at Trzebnica in 1202. The couple supported the donation of an Augustinian provostry at Nowogród Bobrzański and a commandery of the Knights Templar at Oleśnica Mała, and Hedwig founded several hospitals for the sick and lepers and gave her fortune to the Church. According to legend she went barefoot even in winter, and when the Bishop of Wrocław urged her to wear shoes she carried them in her hands. After Henry died in 1238 and was buried at Trzebnica she moved into the convent, taking a lay sister's habit without vows, and invited German religious and settlers who founded towns and villages.

Hedwig saw her son Henry II the Pious killed at the Battle of Legnica in 1241, during the first Mongol invasion of Poland, after which Silesia fragmented into several Piast duchies. She died on 15 October 1243 and was buried at Trzebnica with her husband. Pope Clement IV canonised her in 1267, at the suggestion of her grandson Władysław, Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg. She is the patron saint of Silesia, and her feast day is 16 October. In 1773 Frederick the Great had St. Hedwig's built in Berlin for Catholic Upper Silesian immigrants, and it has been the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Berlin since 1930. In March 2020 her remains, missing for centuries, were reported found in a silver casket at Trzebnica.
hegra: Hegra lies in the Hejaz region of Medina Province, about 20 km north of the town of Al-'Ula, 400 km north-west of Medina and 500 km south-east of Petra. The site is on an inland plain at the foot of Jabal al-Uwayrid, among isolated sandstone outcrops whose fine grain suited rock carving. The climate is extremely arid, with under 50 mm of rain a year, but the site sits in a natural gully that collects runoff. The Nabataeans cut about 130 wells into the rock and grew date palms, wheat, barley, olives, pomegranates, figs, lentils, peas and alfalfa.

Inscriptions in Lihyanite script on nearby Mount Athleb date from the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE and show early settlement. The city's growth came in the 1st century CE under the Nabataean king Aretas IV (9 BCE – 40 CE), who made Hegra the kingdom's second capital after Petra. The Nabataeans held a monopoly on the trade in incense, myrrh and spices, and Hegra, linked to the Red Sea port of Egra Kome, was the main staging post on the north-south caravan route. In 106 CE the Romans under Trajan annexed the kingdom, and Hegra became part of the province of Arabia.

A Latin inscription of 175–177 CE calls it the civitas Hegrenorum, and soldiers of the Legio III Cyrenaica were stationed there until the late second or early third century. As the trade route shifted from the overland axis to the sea route through the Red Sea, the city lost its place, and many experts believe that it lost its urban functions by late antiquity, mainly through desertification. Later the site was a station on the Hajj road, and between 1744 and 1757 an Ottoman fort was built there. The English traveller Charles Montagu Doughty reached the ruins in 1876.

The monumental tombs are the best-preserved remains. Many carry Nabataean inscriptions above the entrance that work as legal documents, recording ownership, burial rights and dates by the reigns of Nabataean kings. The façades borrow motifs from Assyria, Phoenicia, Egypt and Hellenistic Alexandria, and the largest tomb, al-Farid, is over twenty metres high. Muslims know the place as Mada'in Salih, after the prophet Salih, whom the Quran sent to the Thamud, who were punished for their idolatry. UNESCO proclaimed it a World Heritage Site in 2008, the first in Saudi Arabia.
heian-kyo: Heian-kyō was built across the Kadono and Otagi districts of Yamashiro Province, in what is now central Kyoto. The planned city measured about 4.5 kilometres from east to west and 5.2 from north to south, less than a third of the area of Tang Chang'an. Unlike Chang'an it had no continuous city wall. The Daidairi, containing the imperial palace and principal government offices, occupied the northern centre, and the avenue Suzaku-ōji ran south from it to the Rajōmon, dividing the city into the Left Capital to the east and the Right Capital to the west.

The grid was divided into nine jō, numbered from First to Ninth, and each half into four north–south bō, each split into 16 chō. Buddhist temples were tightly restricted, and Tō-ji and Sai-ji, near the southern end, were the principal state temples allowed. In 823 Emperor Saga entrusted Tō-ji to Kūkai, who developed it as a centre of Shingon Buddhism.

In 784 Emperor Kanmu moved the capital from Heijō-kyō to Nagaoka-kyō, but within a decade plans were made for another move. Officials surveyed the Kadono area in 793. Kanmu entered the new capital on 18 November 794, and it was named Heian-kyō soon afterwards. Construction continued for more than a decade and largely ended in 805, but substantial areas of the grid were never developed.

The Right Capital, particularly its low-lying western areas near the Katsura River, declined, while settlement spread north and toward the Kamo River. The Rajōmon collapsed in a storm in 980 and was never rebuilt. Fires increasingly disrupted use of the Daidairi, emperors lived in aristocratic residences, and a fire in 1227 destroyed what remained of it. By around 1220 the name Kyoto had largely replaced Heian-kyō.

From the late 12th century political authority shifted to warrior governments such as the Kamakura shogunate, while Kyoto remained the home of the emperor and court. The Ōnin War of 1467–1477 caused extensive destruction, and in the late 16th century Toyotomi Hideyoshi rebuilt much of the city and in 1591 built the earthen ramparts called the Odoi. The central government was moved to Tokyo in 1869, and Japanese reference works treat that year as the end of Kyoto's formal status as capital.

Elements of the ancient plan remain in modern Kyoto, where the line of Senbon-dōri is identified with Suzaku-ōji. The present Kyoto Imperial Palace does not stand on the ancient palace site but developed from a later residence, and it was preserved at Emperor Meiji's direction.
heiau: Heiau varied with their purpose and setting. They might be rectangular, square or rounded, and stood on hills, cliffs, level ground, valleys and coastlines; some koʻa, or fishing shrines, were built underwater. Large heiau were built by prominent people and small ones by the humble. The missionary Hiram Bingham described one between Mauna Kea and Hualalai as a square of piled lava rock 100 feet across, with walls eight feet high and eight pyramids of lava rock around it.

An older form, closer to the marae found elsewhere in Polynesia, is preserved on Nīhoa and Necker Island: stone platforms, sometimes tiered, with stone uprights near their edges. In the rest of the island chain it was generally replaced by the forms visible today.

The heiau most often preserved are war temples of the later period, such as the Pu'ukohola Heiau National Historic Site: large stone platforms carrying houses for priests, sacred drums and the kiʻi, images of the temple's gods, with altars, ahu, for offerings of plants, animals and people. Only the kahuna and certain high chiefs could enter. Puʻu O Mahuka, the largest heiau on Oahu at almost two acres, also served to track fire signals from the Wailua complex on Kauai.

Agricultural heiau, called Hale-o-Lono after the god of fertility, include Kaneaki at Makaha, built in the 17th century. A heiau's purpose could change, since later generations added to sacred ground: Ulupo heiau in Kailua, said to have been built by the menehune, is thought to have served first for farming and later as a luakini.

Missionaries arrived in 1820, and most of the aliʻi, including Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani, converted to Christianity. Eleven years passed before Kaʻahumanu proclaimed laws against indigenous religious practices; the heiau were then officially abandoned, and many were broken up and ploughed under for fields of sugar cane. Some families responsible for heiau kept up their care. Kaneaki is now fully restored and Pahua in Hawaii Kai partly restored, and Puʻuhonua o Honaunau, a place of refuge in South Kona, includes a heiau complex.
heidelberg: Heidelberg lies on the eastern edge of the Upper Rhine Plain, where the Neckar leaves its narrow valley between the Odenwald and the Little Odenwald and begins its last stretch towards Mannheim, about 20 kilometres downstream, where it joins the Rhine. The old town lies in the valley on the south bank, dominated by the ruins of the castle, 80 metres above the river on the slopes of the Königstuhl. On the north bank rises the Heiligenberg, or Holy Mountain, along which runs the Philosophers' Walk.

Between 600,000 and 200,000 years ago, Heidelberg Man died at nearby Mauer; his jaw bone, found in 1907, is the earliest evidence of human life in Europe. In the 5th century BCE a Celtic refuge and place of worship was built on the Heiligenberg, and a fort followed around 40 CE. The first reference to Heidelberg itself is in a document of Schönau Abbey dated 1196, taken as the town's founding date. In 1156 the castle and its settlement passed to the house of Hohenstaufen, and in 1214 the Palatinate passed to Ludwig I, Duke of Bavaria. In 1356 the Golden Bull confirmed far-reaching rights for the counts palatine, who were also electors.

The university played a leading part in scholasticism, Renaissance humanism and the German Reformation, and in April 1518 Martin Luther was received there to defend his Ninety-five Theses. The library, founded in 1421, is the oldest existing public library in Germany. The castle on the higher slope was destroyed by a gunpowder explosion in 1537. Heidelberg fell to the Grand Duchy of Baden in 1803, and Grand Duke Charles Frederick re-founded the university, naming it Ruperto-Carola after its two founders. The university reopened in 1945 on the initiative of a small group of professors, among them Alfred Weber and Karl Jaspers.

Heidelberg is the fifth-largest city in Baden-Württemberg, with about 163,000 inhabitants, roughly a quarter of them students. It belongs to the Rhine-Neckar Metropolitan Region, centred on Mannheim. It is a scientific centre, home to the European Molecular Biology Laboratory and four Max Planck Institutes, and has been named a City of Literature by UNESCO's Creative Cities Network.
heidelberg-castle: In 1155 Frederick Barbarossa made his half-brother Conrad of Hohenstaufen Count Palatine, and the region became known as the Electoral Palatinate. The first mention of a castle at Heidelberg dates from 1214, when Louis I, Duke of Bavaria, of the House of Wittelsbach, received it from the Hohenstaufen emperor Frederick II. A document of 1303 names two castles: an upper one on the Kleiner Gaisberg, destroyed by lightning in 1537, and a lower one on the Jettenbühl, the present site, founded sometime between 1294 and 1303.

When Ruprecht became King of Germany in 1401 the castle was so small that on his return from his coronation he had to camp in the Augustinians' monastery. He wanted more space for his court and guests and more defences, to make it a fortress.

The ruin stands about 80 metres up the northern Königstuhl hillside and dominates the view of the old town. It counts among the most important Renaissance structures north of the Alps. The Friedrichsbau, built between 1601 and 1607 by the architect Johannes Schoch for Elector Friedrich IV, carries statues of the electors' ancestors by Sebastian Götz and holds the court chapel; it is the best preserved part of the castle.

Frederick V married Elizabeth Stuart, daughter of the English king, and brought the engineer Salomon de Caus to Heidelberg, where he began an enormous garden on the mountain slope. Contemporaries regarded the earthworks it required as the eighth wonder of the world.

After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 the Palatinate was left undefended. General Tilly took the town on 16 September 1622 and the castle a few days later. The Swedes captured Heidelberg in 1633, imperial troops retook the castle in 1635, and the new elector Charles Louis moved into the ruined building on 7 October 1649. French troops destroyed much of it in 1689 and again in 1693, and a lightning strike in 1764 destroyed rebuilt sections.

Afterwards the ruins served as a quarry, and townsfolk took stone, wood and iron from them. August von Kotzebue protested in 1803 against Baden's intention to pull them down. At the start of the 19th century the ruin became a symbol of the patriotic movement against Napoleon, and Romantic painters, J. M. W. Turner among them, painted it repeatedly. By 1880 Mark Twain mentioned it as a ruin.
heidelberg-catechism: Frederick III, who ruled the Electoral Palatinate from 1559 to 1576, was the first German prince to profess Reformed doctrine while officially Lutheran. The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 had granted toleration only to Lutherans under Lutheran princes, and Frederick sought to even out the religious situation of his largely Lutheran realm within the mainly Roman Catholic Holy Roman Empire. He commissioned a catechism meant to give a fixed form of Christian doctrine, to instruct the young in school and church and to equip pastors and teachers. It was also aimed against Roman Catholic teaching, the Anabaptists and strict Gnesio-Lutherans such as Tilemann Heshusius and Matthias Flacius, who resisted his Reformed leanings, above all on the Eucharist.

The introduction credits the whole theological faculty at Heidelberg and the superintendents of the church. Zacharias Ursinus is usually regarded as the principal author, and Frederick wrote the preface and closely oversaw the work. Scholars disagree on its theological roots, seeing it as Genevan, as Zurich Reformed in the spirit of Heinrich Bullinger, or as both Reformed and Lutheran, especially Melanchthonian.

The text has 129 questions grouped into 52 Lord's Days, one for each Sunday of the year. After two opening questions it has three parts: the misery of man, man's redemption, which expounds the Apostles' Creed and the sacraments, and thankfulness, which treats the Ten Commandments and the Lord's Prayer. The first question asks what is thine only comfort in life and in death, and answers that the believer belongs, body and soul, to Jesus Christ. Each statement rests on biblical texts. Lord's Day 30, in editions after the first, condemns the Catholic mass as accursed idolatry.

A synod at Heidelberg approved the catechism in 1563. Strict Lutherans kept attacking it, and in 1566 Frederick defended it at the Diet of Augsburg against charges brought by Maximilian II of violating the Peace of Augsburg, saying it rested on scripture. It then spread quickly. Dutch synods at Wesel, Emden, Dort and the Hague adopted it, and the great Synod of Dort made it one of the Three Forms of Unity with the Belgic Confession and the Canons of Dort. Ministers were to preach on a section each Sunday.

A 1719 Palatinate edition including Lord's Day 30 provoked so strong a Catholic reaction that Elector Charles III Philip banned it, until protests from Reformed countries reversed the ban. It influenced the Westminster Shorter Catechism, and many Reformed churches, especially of Dutch origin, still use it.
heidelberg-university: Heidelberg University was founded in 1386 on the instruction of Pope Urban VI and was the third university established in the Holy Roman Empire, after Prague (1347) and Vienna (1365). The Great Schism of 1378, which produced rival popes in Avignon and Rome, made it possible for Heidelberg, a relatively small city and capital of the Electorate of the Palatinate, to gain a university of its own. German rulers and churchmen supported the pope in Rome, and the German students and teachers in Paris lost their stipends and had to leave.

Between 1414 and 1418 professors of theology and law took part in the Council of Constance as counsellors to Louis III. It first taught the nominalism known as the via moderna. In 1412 realism and the teachings of John Wycliffe were forbidden, but around 1454 the university decided that realism would also be taught, so that two ways were taught in parallel.

Martin Luther's disputation at Heidelberg in April 1518 made a lasting impression, and his followers among the masters and scholars became leading Reformationists in south-west Germany. When the Electorate of the Palatinate turned to the Reformed faith, Otto Henry, Elector Palatine, made the university a Calvinist institution, and members of its divinity school took part in creating the Heidelberg Catechism in 1563. In 1803 Karl Friedrich of Baden, to whom the part of the Palatinate on the right bank of the Rhine had been allotted, reestablished it as a state institution. He divided it into five faculties, and it has borne his name together with that of Ruprecht I ever since.

After the Nazi seizure of power in 1933 the university supported the regime like other German universities. It dismissed many staff and students for political and racial reasons, and members of the faculty and students took part in book burnings on 17 May 1933. The inscription over the New University, The Living Spirit, was changed to The German Spirit.

Women have been admitted since 1899. Modern scientific psychiatry, psychopharmacology, experimental psychology, mathematical statistics and modern sociology were introduced as disciplines by Heidelberg students or faculty. Among its historical scientific achievements are the invention of spectroscopy and of the Bunsen burner and the discovery of the elements caesium and rubidium.
heijo-kyo: Heijō-kyō, also called Heizei-kyō and sometimes Nara no miyako, was the capital of Japan during most of the Nara period, from 710 to 740 and again from 745 to 784. Empress Genmei ordered the imperial capital moved from Fujiwara-kyō in 708, and the move was complete in 710. The city was modelled on Chang'an, the capital of Tang-dynasty China, though it lacked walls.

Merchants and traders from China, Korea and India introduced various foreign cultures to the city through the Silk Road, and it flourished as Japan's first international and political capital. Its population peaked at between 50,000 and 100,000. The city formed an irregular rectangle and covered more than 25 square kilometres.

The central street of the capital, the Suzaku-ōji, ran 3. 7 kilometres from north to south, from the Rajōmon Gate, the main entrance to the city in the south, to the Suzakumon Gate, the main gate on the south side of the palace complex. It was designed not only as a road but to receive foreign envoys, and its size and the streetscape around it were meant to be spectacular. Excavations since 1974 have traced its route.

They show a width of about 74 metres between the centres of the side gutters, and about 85 metres between the east and west embankments at Sanjō. Below the road of the Nara period lay the remains of an earlier road 23 metres wide. A 220-metre stretch was designated a National Historic Site in 1984, and in 2010 a part of the avenue, 70 metres wide and 210 metres long, was restored south of the Suzakumon Gate.

The site lies in the modern city of Nara. The imperial palace is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with other places in Nara, under the name Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara. In the area of the old capital stand ancient Buddhist temples, some of them also listed: Daian-ji, Gangō-ji, Kōfuku-ji, Saidai-ji, Tōdai-ji and Yakushi-ji. The Daigokuden and the Suzakumon have been reconstructed. The year 2010 marked 1,300 years since the establishment of the capital, and events with displays of national treasures and cultural properties were held in and around Nara Prefecture from 24 April to 7 November 2010.
heil-dir-im-siegerkranz: The song served as the imperial anthem of the German Empire from 1871 to 1918. Before the Empire was founded it had been the royal anthem of Prussia, and it remained the royal anthem after 1871. Its melody derived from the British anthem "God Save the King". The German Empire never had an official anthem of the kind later adopted by the Weimar Republic and the Federal Republic, so the song is often considered the official anthem of the Empire only by custom. Together with "Die Wacht am Rhein", it held the status of an unofficial national anthem.

After the proclamation of the German Empire the word König in the text was replaced by Kaiser. The Kaiser Wilhelm named in the verses was at first William I, who reigned until 1888. His son Frederick III reigned for only 99 days and was succeeded by Wilhelm II. Because Wilhelm II travelled so often, one joke of the time renamed the song "Heil Dir im Sonderzug", meaning "Hail to Thee in Thy Royal Train".

The song never became popular across the whole of Germany. Its borrowed British melody counted against it, and it failed to win the support of most German nationalists. It was never recognised by the southern German states, such as Bavaria or Württemberg. The Kingdom of Bavaria had an official hymn of its own, the "Bayerische Königshymne", which begins "Heil unserm König, Heil!" and was likewise sung to the melody of "God Save the King". "Die Wacht am Rhein", another patriotic hymn, was so popular that it was often regarded as an unofficial national anthem as well.

After the beginning of World War I in 1914, Hugo Kaun set the text of the anthem to new music, to remove the similarity to "God Save the King". Near the end of the war the German Empire was overthrown, and "Das Lied der Deutschen" was adopted as the national anthem of its successor, the Weimar Republic. The same melody still lives on elsewhere: Liechtenstein has "Oben am jungen Rhein" (1920) sung to it, and the Hawaiian anthem "Hawaiʻi Ponoʻī", composed by the Prussian Kapellmeister Henri Berger, is a variation of it.
heilbronn-league: Many German Protestants stayed neutral in the early years of the Thirty Years' War. This changed after Emperor Ferdinand issued the Edict of Restitution in 1629, which required property transferred since 1552 to be returned, in nearly every case from Protestants to the Catholic Church, and allowed his armies to plunder the lands they crossed. Saxony and Brandenburg-Prussia joined Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden after his invasion of the Empire in 1630, a campaign financed by France.

Gustavus was killed at Lützen in November 1632 and succeeded by his six-year-old daughter Christina, and the chancellor Axel Oxenstierna took over Swedish policy. He doubted his allies: Elector John George of Saxony regarded Sweden as great a threat as the Imperial armies and proposed a Protestant neutrality pact, and France suspended its subsidies. In March 1633 Oxenstierna invited the Upper Rhenish, Lower Rhenish-Westphalian, Swabian and Franconian Circles to Heilbronn; an attempt to recruit the Hansa cities failed.

France resumed its subsidies on 7 April 1633, paying them directly to Sweden, which secured Swedish control. Oxenstierna became Director with an absolute veto over military affairs, assisted by a council of ten, three of them Swedes. The members undertook to fund an army of 78,000 but provided less than a third of the money. The Germans agreed to fight until Sweden received just compensation, and Oxenstierna promised a return to the borders of 1618. Saxony and Brandenburg supported the League without joining it.

The League won a series of victories against the Catholic League, but its members' aims diverged. Sweden wanted to keep Swedish Pomerania and its hold on the Baltic, while the German allies sought the territorial position of 1618, which would undo the gains of France and Sweden. After the Imperial victory at Nördlingen, Ferdinand, mediated by Denmark-Norway and Hesse-Darmstadt, agreed a draft with John George known as the Pirnaer Noteln. It became the basis of the Peace of Prague, which dissolved both leagues, although fighting in Germany went on until 1648.
heiligenkreuz-abbey: Heiligenkreuz Abbey, whose name means Holy Cross, lies in the village of Heiligenkreuz in the southern part of the Vienna Woods, about 13 km north-west of Baden. Margrave Leopold III of Austria founded it in 1133 at the request of his son Otto, soon to be abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Morimond in Burgundy and later Bishop of Freising. Its first twelve monks came from Morimond with their abbot Gottschalk, and the date of consecration was 11 September 1133.

On 31 May 1188 Leopold V of Austria presented the abbey with a relic of the True Cross, which Baldwin IV of Jerusalem had given him in 1182. It is still kept there and has been displayed in the Chapel of the Holy Cross since 1983. The Babenberg family richly endowed the abbey, and it founded many daughter houses, among them Zwettl in 1138, Lilienfeld in 1206 and Neuberg in Styria in 1327.

The abbey church combines two styles. Its façade, naves and transept, dedicated in 1187, are Romanesque, and the choir of the 13th century is Gothic. The austere nave is a rare example of Romanesque architecture in Austria. As in most Cistercian churches the façade has three simple windows as a symbol of the Trinity, and a Baroque bell-tower was added on the north side. The inner court holds a Baroque Holy Trinity Column designed by Giovanni Giuliani and completed in 1739.

The chapter house contains the graves of thirteen members of the House of Babenberg, among them Duke Leopold V, Duke Frederick I and Duke Frederick II. The remains of Otto of Freising lie under the altar of the Blessed Sacrament. The abbey suffered in the Turkish wars of 1529 and 1683, and in the second Turkish soldiers burnt down much of the precinct, which was rebuilt on a larger scale in the Baroque style under Abbot Klemens Schäfer. It was spared dissolution under Emperor Joseph II.

The abbey has been an important Austrian centre of music for more than 800 years, and many manuscripts have been found there, notably those of Alberich Mazak. An institute for philosophical and theological studies was established in 1802 and became a Hochschule in 1976. In 2007 Pope Benedict XVI raised it to a Pontifical Athenaeum, and he visited the abbey in September 2007.

In April 2008 monks of the abbey recorded an album of Gregorian chant, released as Chant: Music for Paradise, which went triple platinum in Austria. The film director Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck wrote the screenplay of The Lives of Others in a cell of the abbey in 2002. HBO premiered the documentary Top Ten Monks about the community in December 2010.
heilongjiang: Heilongjiang is the northernmost and easternmost province of China, with the country's northernmost point at Mohe along the Amur and its easternmost at the confluence of the Amur and Ussuri rivers. It borders Jilin to the south, Inner Mongolia to the west and five regions of Russia to the north and east. Its name means black dragon river, the Chinese name of the Amur. Mountain ranges, among them the Greater and Lesser Khingan, cover much of the province, and the Greater Khingan holds China's largest remaining virgin forest. The east and southwest are flatter and drained by tributaries of the Amur, including the Songhua, Nen and Mudan rivers. Winters are long and bitter, and the far north is subarctic.

Ancient Chinese records name the Sushen, Buyeo, Mohe and Khitan among the peoples of the region, and Mongolic Donghu lived in its west. The eastern portion was ruled by the Bohai Kingdom, then by the Khitan Liao dynasty. The Jurchen Jin dynasty (1115 to 1234), which later ruled much of north China, arose within the borders of modern Heilongjiang.

Heilongjiang was created as an administrative unit in 1683, in the Kangxi era of the Qing dynasty, from the northwestern part of Jilin. It was supervised by the General of Heilongjiang, whose seat moved from Aigun to Nenjiang in 1690 and to Qiqihar in 1699, probably for reasons of supply. Manchuria was closed to Han Chinese migration. In 1858 and 1860 the Qing were forced to give up all land beyond the Amur and Ussuri rivers to the Russian Empire, which gave the province its present northern and eastern borders. Manchuria was then opened to Han settlement, and by the early twentieth century the Han had become the dominant group.

Japanese forces invaded in 1931 and completed their conquest in 1932, and the province became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo. After the Soviet Army defeated Japan in Manchuria in 1945, Heilongjiang became the first province, and Harbin the first major city, to be wholly controlled by the communists. Heilongjiang and Songjiang provinces were merged in 1954.

Heilongjiang's capital and largest city is Harbin. Most residents are Han Chinese, many descended from migrants during the Qing dynasty, from from Shandong and Hebei, and ten indigenous minorities are officially recognised, among them the Manchu, Daur, Oroqen and Hezhen. The Daqing oilfields are an important source of petroleum, and the province has China's largest plantations of rice, corn and soybeans, on fertile black soil.
heimskringla: Heimskringla was written in Old Norse in Iceland. No manuscript attributes it to an author, and some scholars assume it was written about 1230 by the Icelandic knight, poet and historian Snorri Sturluson (1178/79–1241). The first surviving works that credit him are 16th-century Danish translations by the Norwegians Peder Claussøn Friis and Laurents Hanssøn. The title was first used in the 17th century and comes from the opening words of one manuscript, kringla heimsins, "the circle of the world". Its sources include earlier kings' sagas such as Morkinskinna and Fagrskinna, 12th-century Norwegian histories and oral traditions, notably skaldic poems.

The work is a collection of sagas about Swedish and Norwegian kings. It opens with the Ynglinga saga, the mythological prehistory of the Ynglings, who trace their line to Freyr and the people who came with Odin from Asgard. The later sagas are devoted to single rulers, beginning with Halfdan the Black and Harald Fairhair, and fable and fact intermingle at first, the accounts becoming more reliable as the collection proceeds. The saga of Olaf II of Norway is the central part, his reign of fifteen years taking up about a third of the whole.

The saga of Harald Hardrada follows his expedition to the East, his time in Constantinople, Syria and Sicily, and his death at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066, a few days before Harold Godwinson fell at Hastings. The saga of Sigurd the Crusader tells of a Norwegian voyage as far as Palestine. The narrative runs to 1177.

Until the mid-19th century historians put great trust in the factual truth of the sagas. Early in the 20th century saga criticism, pioneered by the Swedish historians Lauritz and Curt Weibull, pointed out that the work was written several centuries after most of the events it describes. The Norwegian historian Edvard Bull said that all illusions had to be given up that it bore a deeper resemblance to what actually happened. It is still used as a source, with caution, and its content is judged more credible for recent times.

Later Icelandic writing about Scandinavian kings was based on it. The first complete translation, into Danish, was made around 1600 by Peder Claussøn Friis and printed in 1633, and Samuel Laing's English version appeared in 1844. In the 19th century, as Norway gained independence, it became an important national symbol, and in 1900 the Storting subsidised new translations into both written forms of Norwegian.
