heinkel: Ernst Heinkel had been chief designer for the Hansa-Brandenburg aviation firm in the First World War. He founded his own company at Warnemünde in 1922, after the restrictions on German aviation imposed by the Treaty of Versailles were relaxed. By 1929 its compressed-air catapults were launching short-range mail planes from the decks of the Norddeutscher Lloyd liners Bremen and Europa.

Its first major aircraft success after the war was the all-metal, single-engined He 70 Blitz, a high-speed mail plane and airliner built for Deutsche Luft Hansa in 1932, which broke a number of speed records for its class. The twin-engined He 111 Doppel-Blitz followed. Among the firm's chief designers were the twin brothers Siegfried and Walter Günter and Heinrich Hertel. Its headquarters, later called Heinkel-Nord, stood in Rostock, and after the Anschluss of 1938 a second works, Heinkel-Süd, was set up at Schwechat in Austria.

In the Second World War the He 70 and above all the He 111 were adapted as bombers for the Luftwaffe. Heinkel also built the He 177 Greif, the Luftwaffe's only heavy bomber to enter service, which was never deployed in large numbers and was troubled by engine fires. The firm was less successful with fighters: the He 112 lost to the Messerschmitt Bf 109, and the He 100 failed through political interference at the Reich Aviation Ministry. The He 219 night fighter was the first Luftwaffe front-line aircraft with retractable tricycle undercarriage and the first operational military aircraft to use ejection seats, but was built in limited numbers. From 1941 the company was merged with the engine maker Hirth as Heinkel-Hirth.

In 1939 the He 176 and He 178, flown by Erich Warsitz, became the first aircraft to fly under liquid-fuel rocket and turbojet power. Heinkel was the first to bring a jet fighter to prototype stage, the He 280, but the ministry favoured the rival Messerschmitt Me 262. In early 1942 RAF photographic interpreters at Medmenham saw the He 280 in reconnaissance photographs taken after a raid on the Rostock factory. Very late in the war the single-jet He 162 Spatz flew and barely entered service. Heinkel used between 6,000 and 8,000 prisoners from Sachsenhausen concentration camp to build the He 177.

After the war Heinkel was forbidden to build aircraft and made bicycles, motor scooters, the Perle moped and the Kabine microcar, introduced in 1956. It returned to aircraft in the mid-1950s, building Lockheed F-104 Starfighters under licence for the West German Luftwaffe. In 1965 it was absorbed by Vereinigte Flugtechnische Werke, which Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm took over in 1980; the line later became part of Airbus.
heinrich-barth: Heinrich Barth was born in Hamburg on 16 February 1821, the third child of Johann Christoph Heinrich Barth, who had built up a successful trading business, and his wife Charlotte Karoline. Both parents were orthodox Lutherans. He excelled at languages and taught himself some Arabic. In 1839 he enrolled at the University of Berlin, where he heard the geographer Karl Ritter and the historian Jakob Grimm, and in July 1844 he defended a doctoral thesis on the trade relations of ancient Corinth.

In January 1845 he set out on a grand tour that his father funded. After two months in London learning Arabic, he crossed France and Spain and reached Tangier in August. He travelled overland across North Africa, up the Nile to Wadi Halfa and on through Sinai, Palestine, Syria, Asia Minor and Greece, examining the remains of antiquity everywhere. He returned to Hamburg on 27 December 1847.

The Prussian ambassador Christian von Bunsen secured places for Barth and the astronomer Adolf Overweg on James Richardson's expedition, which the British government had chosen to open commercial relations with the states of the central and western Sudan. The party left Tripoli early in 1850 and crossed the Sahara with great difficulty. Barth reached Agadez in October 1850, and a memorial tablet there honours him as the first European to enter the city. Richardson died in March 1851 and Overweg in September 1852, leaving Barth to carry on alone.

He was the first European to visit Adamawa, in 1851, and reached Timbuktu in September 1853. When he returned to Tripoli in September 1855 his journey had covered upward of 12,000 miles (19,000 km), from Lake Chad and Bagirmi in the east to Timbuktu in the west. In Timbuktu his friendship with Ahmad al-Bakkai al-Kunti led to his staying in the man's house and receiving protection from an attempt to seize him.

Barth was interested in the history and culture of African peoples rather than in commercial exploitation. He was not the first European to notice local oral traditions, but he was the first to consider seriously their methodology and use for historical research, and he investigated the history of regions such as the Songhay Empire.

His account, published in English and German as Travels and Discoveries in North and Central Africa (1857–1858), runs to five volumes of about 3,500 pages and was cited by Darwin. It gave the first European evidence that the Sahara had once been a savanna. He died in Berlin on 25 November 1865, aged 44.
heinrich-bullinger: , and Anna Wiederkehr. The couple lived as husband and wife although not legally married, because the bishop of Constance waived the penalty for clerical concubinage in return for an annual fee. At eleven he was sent to the St. Martin's Latin school in Emmerich, where he studied Jerome, Horace and Virgil, and in 1519 he entered the University of Cologne. Reading Peter Lombard and the Decretum Gratiani led him to the church fathers, and then to the Bible and to Martin Luther. Believing that salvation came through God's grace rather than good works, he was converted to Protestantism and in 1522 took his Master of Arts degree.

In 1523 Bullinger became a teacher at the Cistercian monastery of Kappel Abbey, on condition that he take no vows and not attend mass. He began a systematic programme of Bible reading, and by 1525 the abbey had abolished mass. He met Huldrych Zwingli and Leo Jud in 1523, became Zwingli's friend and ally, and in 1528 was ordained a parish minister of the Reformed church of Zürich.

On 17 August 1529 he married Anna Adlischweiler, a former nun, and they had eleven children. After Zwingli was killed in the Second Kappel War, Bremgarten was re-catholicised and Bullinger and his family fled, losing almost all their possessions. Three days later he preached in the Grossmünster, and on 9 December 1531 Zürich asked him to be Zwingli's successor as antistes. He kept the office until his death.

Bullinger opposed war as a means of spreading the Reformation. He built the church's government on a synodal order that became a model for other Reformed churches in German-speaking areas, and served as school principal. He wrote against the Anabaptists yet allowed them freedom of worship, and no Anabaptist was executed in Zürich during his leadership. With John Calvin he drafted the Consensus Tigurinus of 1549 on the Eucharist.

In 1562 he wrote a personal statement of faith that became the Second Helvetic Confession of 1566, adopted by Reformed churches in Scotland, Hungary, France and Poland. He also wrote the Decades, fifty sermons on the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer and the sacraments.

Bullinger died at Zürich on 17 September 1575 and was succeeded as antistes by Zwingli's adopted son Rudolf Gwalther. About 12,000 letters to and from him survive, the most extended correspondence preserved from the Reformation, and his writings exceed Luther's and Calvin's combined. He opened Zürich to Protestant fugitives, many of them English, and in England between 1550 and 1560 there were 77 editions of the Latin Decades against two of Calvin's Institutes. His idea of the covenant influenced covenant theology.
heinrich-friedrich-karl-vom-stein: Heinrich Friedrich Karl vom und zum Stein was born on 25 October 1757 on the family estate near Nassau, the ninth child of Karl Philipp Freiherr vom Stein and Henriette Karoline Langwerth von Simmern, and came from an old Franconian family. Like many of his generation he admired Frederick the Great. In 1773 he went to the University of Göttingen to study jurisprudence, and he also studied English history and politics. He then went to Wetzlar, the legal centre of the Holy Roman Empire, and on to Regensburg to observe the Imperial Diet. He reached Berlin early in 1780 and took service in the Prussian monarchy, in the department of mines and manufactures.

In June 1785 Stein was sent as Prussian ambassador to Mainz, Zweibrücken and Darmstadt. In November 1787 he was appointed director of the chamber of war and domains for the king's possessions west of the Weser. From 1796 to 1803 he was supreme president of the Westphalian chambers at Minden, where he had the Ruhr canalised as an outlet for the region's coal. In 1804 he became minister of state for trade, abolishing restrictions on internal trade. In 1807 the king dismissed him as refractory and obstinate after he declined the foreign ministry, but after the Treaty of Tilsit Frederick William III called him back, on 8 October 1807, with very wide powers.

Stein was then for a time virtually dictator of a reduced, nearly bankrupt Prussia. The October Edict, issued at Memel on 9 October 1807, abolished serfdom throughout Prussia from 8 October 1810, swept away distinctions of land tenure between noble and peasant land and abolished class limits on occupations. On 19 November 1808 he issued a municipal ordinance giving local self-government to Prussian towns and to villages of more than 800 inhabitants. He also supported the military reforms associated with Gerhard von Scharnhorst, which made military service obligatory for all classes.

A letter of his hoping for a national rising like Spain's was seized by French agents, and in December 1808 Napoleon declared him an enemy of France and confiscated his property. He resigned on 24 November 1808, fled Berlin on 5 January 1809 and lived in the Austrian Empire until Tsar Alexander I summoned him to Saint Petersburg in 1812. In 1813 he administered East and West Prussia, where an assembly ordered a militia, and after Leipzig he supervised the liberated territories. He died at Schloss Cappenberg on 29 June 1831. Research has shown that his credit for the reforms of 1807 and 1808 must be shared with Theodor von Schön and others.
heinrich-heine: Heine was born on 13 December 1797 in Düsseldorf, then in the Duchy of Berg, the eldest of four children of the textile merchant Samson Heine and Peira, née van Geldern. He was called Harry in childhood. His uncle Salomon realised that he had no talent for trade, and it was decided that he should study law, so in 1819 he went to the University of Bonn. There he was a radical liberal, but he was more interested in history and literature, heard the critic August Wilhelm Schlegel lecture, and began to acquire a reputation as a poet. He also wrote two tragedies, Almansor and William Ratcliff, which had little success in the theatre.

It was extremely difficult to make a living as a writer in Germany, and Heine never had enough money. In Hamburg in January 1826 he met Julius Campe, who remained his chief publisher for the rest of his life. Books under 320 pages had to be submitted to censorship, so Campe printed dissident works in large type to run longer. Heine's travel writings, the Reisebilder, were a success. He left for France in 1831, drawn by the July Revolution, by freedom from German censorship and for a time by Saint-Simonianism. In Paris he became a celebrity, counting Victor Hugo, Frederic Chopin and Franz Liszt among his acquaintances, and wrote everything in German, translating it into French with a collaborator.

After the German Diet banned the Young Germany writers in November 1835, his name was added at Metternich's insistence, but he went on commenting on German politics from a distance. In the 1840s his verse became more political and satirical. The most popular of his political poems was The Silesian Weavers, based on the weavers' uprising of 1844.

In May 1848 Heine fell paralysed and did not leave what he called his mattress-grave until his death on 17 February 1856. A hair analysis in 1997 confirmed chronic lead poisoning. Many composers set his poems, among them Robert Schumann in the song cycle Dichterliebe and Friedrich Silcher in his setting of Die Lorelei. The Nazis removed or destroyed all monuments to him and, from 1940, banned his books. His line from Almansor, spoken after the burning of the Quran at Granada, was engraved at the site of the 1933 book burning on Berlin's Opernplatz.
heinrich-himmler: Heinrich Luitpold Himmler was born in Munich on 7 October 1900 into a conservative middle-class Catholic family. His father, Joseph Gebhard Himmler, was a teacher, and his godfather, Prince Heinrich of Bavaria, had been tutored by his father. He attended a grammar school in Landshut, did well in his schoolwork but struggled in athletics, and suffered lifelong stomach complaints. He served in a reserve battalion in the First World War without seeing combat and joined the Nazi Party on 1 August 1923. As a member of Ernst Röhm's paramilitary unit he took part in the Beer Hall Putsch, was questioned but not charged, and lost his job.

Himmler joined the SS in 1925. On the resignation of its commander Erhard Heiden in January 1929 he became Reichsführer-SS with Hitler's approval and over the next year grew the force from about 290 men to about 3,000. Early in 1934, as Hitler and other leaders feared a coup by Röhm, Hermann Göring handed control of the Prussian secret police, the Gestapo, to Himmler on 20 April, and Hitler appointed him chief of all German police outside Prussia. Reinhard Heydrich became head of the Gestapo two days later. From 1943 he was also chief of the Kriminalpolizei and Minister of the Interior, and he controlled the Waffen-SS.

In 1939 Himmler, Heydrich and Heinrich Müller carried out a false flag operation to give a pretext for the invasion of Poland, and the Einsatzgruppen, repurposed as death squads, murdered some 65,000 intellectuals and other civilians by the end of that year. At the Wannsee meeting of 20 January 1942 Heydrich told the attendees that Hitler had placed Himmler in charge of the plan for the final solution. In speeches at Poznań in October 1943 Himmler referred explicitly to the extermination of the Jewish people. As Reich Commissioner for the Consolidation of German Nationhood he was deeply involved in Generalplan Ost, whose aim was to enslave, expel or exterminate the native population of the east.

After the 20 July 1944 plot against Hitler, Himmler formed a commission that arrested over 5,000 suspected opponents, and Hitler's reprisals brought the execution of more than 4,900 people. In March 1945 he tried without Hitler's knowledge to open peace talks with the western Allies. Hitler learned of this on 28 April, dismissed him from all his posts and ordered his arrest. British forces captured him, and he committed suicide in British custody on 23 May 1945. He played a central role in the genocide of an estimated 5.5 to 6 million Jews and in the deaths of millions of other victims.
heinrich-parler: The family name comes from Parlier, meaning foreman. Heinrich Parler was probably born in Cologne, where his earliest known work was supervising construction at Cologne Cathedral, and he later lived and worked in Gmünd, an Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire. Around 1333 he was invited to become construction manager of the Holy Cross Minster there, where building had begun in 1315 to replace a Romanesque church with a Gothic basilica.

Parler amended the plan and completed the nave as a hall church, the first of its kind in southern Germany, with rounded pillars and leaf-wreath capitals, elongated tracery windows and complex coloured vaults. His style became more pronounced in the choir, whose foundation stone was laid in 1351 and on which his son Peter Parler (1333–1399) worked beside him. Designed as an ambulatory with chapels set flat between the buttresses, it needed fewer internal columns and let the aisles rise as tall as the nave. He also made sculptures more lifelike than earlier churches had. Neither father nor son lived to see the consecration in 1410.

As was customary, he oversaw other building sites too. Though it is undocumented, he most likely designed the Frauenkirche in Nuremberg with Peter, its design strikingly close to Holy Cross, and the same comparison applies to the choir of Augsburg Cathedral, begun in 1356. He may also have had a hand in the design of Ulm Minster, begun in 1366, though members of his family are more clearly documented there.

Many other masons took up and developed his architecture and sculpture, and the Parler style spread across central Europe, from St. Martin's Church in Landshut, St. Lorenz in Nuremberg, St. George's Minster in Dinkelsbühl and St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna to churches of the Hanseatic League from the Netherlands to Poland and St. Mary's in Helsingør, Denmark. His eldest son, Johann Parler the Elder, worked at Zwettl and at Basel Cathedral. A brother may have been the foreman Peter von Reutlingen, presumed builder of the Marienkirche and the Nikolaikirche in Reutlingen.
heinrich-rubenow: Rubenow was born in Greifswald into a prominent patrician family active in the city's civic administration. Details of his early life are sparse; he is believed to have received the formal education usual among the urban elite of the Baltic region, and he went on to study law, which became the basis of his later civic and academic career.

Back in Greifswald he served as Ratssyndikus, the council's legal adviser, and then for several terms as Bürgermeister, working to strengthen the city's legal and administrative structures in a period of significant regional change. He took the decisive part in founding the university: he won the support of Duke Wartislaw IX of Pomerania, obtained papal approval, and after its formal inauguration in 1456 became its first Rector, shaping its early structure, statutes and academic culture.

His reforms and the authority he gathered as Bürgermeister sharpened long-standing tensions between the patrician families, the guilds and rival factions within the council, and these came to a violent head at the end of 1462. On 31 December 1462 he was murdered in Greifswald by political opponents; contemporary and later chronicles describe the killing as the result of factional hostility rather than a personal dispute. It was one of the most turbulent episodes in the city's medieval history and had lasting repercussions for its government.

He is regarded as one of the most influential figures in the early history of Greifswald and of the wider region of Pomerania. The University of Greifswald acknowledges his role as its founder in its commemorative publications and institutional histories, and his work on the city's administration and legal structure left a durable imprint on its development.
heinrich-schliemann: Heinrich Schliemann was born on 6 January 1822 in Neubukow in Mecklenburg-Schwerin, the fifth of nine children of a poor Lutheran pastor. His mother died when he was nine. His father had schooled him in the tales of the Iliad and the Odyssey, but the family's poverty made university impossible, and at fourteen he became a grocer's apprentice. Later he said his passion for Homer began when he heard a drunken miller recite Homeric verses. In 1841 a ship on which he sailed as a cabin boy foundered in a gale, and he came ashore in the Netherlands and became a bookkeeper in Amsterdam.

In 1846 the firm B. H. Schröder & Co. sent him to St Petersburg as its general agent. He learned languages by a system of his own, and by the end of his life could converse in a dozen besides German. In 1851 he went to California, where his brother had grown rich in the gold fields, and bought and resold gold dust in Sacramento.

Several of the stories in his autobiography of 1881 about this time, including his meeting with President Millard Fillmore and the date of his American citizenship, are contradicted by other evidence. He returned to Russia in 1852, married Ekaterina Petrovna Lyschin and made a profit trading in indigo dye. By 1858 he was wealthy enough to retire.

In 1868 Schliemann visited sites in the Greek world and published Ithaka, der Peloponnesus und Troja, arguing that Hissarlik was Troy. The English amateur Frank Calvert had identified Hissarlik and persuaded him to dig on land his family owned, after Schliemann's soundings at Pınarbaşı disappointed him. By 1873 his trench had revealed nine buried cities.

On 15 June 1873 he found gold that he took to be Priam's Treasure, and later admitted that his story of his wife Sophia carrying it away in her shawl was untrue, since she was in Athens. He smuggled the treasure out of the Ottoman Empire and, after being sued, paid compensation. His collections reached Berlin in 1881 and were taken to Moscow by Soviet forces in 1945.

In 1876 he began digging at Mycenae, under the supervision of Panagiotis Stamatakis, and found the Shaft Graves with their skeletons and gold, among them the so-called Mask of Agamemnon. He later excavated at Orchomenus, at Tiryns with Wilhelm Dörpfeld and again at Troy. The layer he took for Homeric Troy is now dated to between 3,000 and 2,000 BCE, too early for the Trojan War. His excavation of nine layers has been criticised as destructive of significant remains, and he died on 26 December 1890.
heinrich-von-bruhl: Brühl was born on 13 August 1700 at Gangloffsömmern, the son of Johann Moritz von Brühl, Oberhofmarschall at the court of Saxe-Weissenfels, who was ruined and had to give up the family estate. After serving as a page to the dowager duchess of Saxe-Weissenfels, he entered the Saxon court at Dresden as a Silberpage on 16 April 1719 and won the favour of Elector Frederick Augustus I, King Augustus II of Poland, for whom he raised money. In 1731 he became Chief Receiver of Taxes and Minister of the Interior of Saxony.

When Augustus II died in 1733, Brühl gained the trust of his heir, Frederick Augustus II, by bringing him the late king's papers and jewels at once, and he raised money for the heir's election as King Augustus III of Poland. Made a Reichsgraf on 27 November 1737, he was in effect sole minister from 1738, and the title of Prime Minister was created for him in 1746. He controlled all access to the king, took large grants of land and drew the salaries of many offices at once.

Brühl played a part in the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756 that brought the Habsburgs and France together, but to meet the king's demands he ran up debts and greatly reduced the army. At the start of the Seven Years' War the Saxon army numbered only 17,000 men, and after a few weeks it surrendered at Pirna for want of supplies and was dissolved. Frederick II of Prussia mocked him as having more garments, watches, laces, boots and slippers than any man of the age.

Brühl died in Dresden on 28 October 1763, a few weeks after Augustus III. The new elector, Frederick Christian, ordered an inquiry into his administration, and his fortune, including palaces at Pförten, Oberlichtenau and Wachau-Seifersdorf, was sequestered but later restored to his family. His spending also served the arts: the Meissen Swan Service of over 2,200 pieces was made for him, the architect Johann Christoph Knöffel began his palace and terrace on the Elbe in 1736, and his picture gallery was bought by Empress Catherine II of Russia in 1768.
heinrich-von-gagern: Heinrich von Gagern was born at Bayreuth on 20 August 1799, the third son of Hans Christoph Ernst, Baron von Gagern, a liberal statesman from Nassau. Educated at the military academy in Munich, he fought at Waterloo as an officer of the Duke of Nassau. He then studied law at Heidelberg, Göttingen and Jena, where he joined the Urburschenschaft, and spent some time in Geneva in 1819 to complete his studies.

From 1821 he worked as a lawyer in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, and in 1832 he was elected to its second chamber. His open opposition to the government's unconstitutional course led to his dismissal from state service in 1833, and he lived for years on a farm his father rented at Monsheim, occasionally publishing criticism of public affairs, until the revolution of 1848 brought him back.

At the Heidelberg meeting and the Vorparlament in Frankfurt he impressed the delegates with the breadth and moderation of his views, and when the national parliament met on 18 May he became its first president. He did most to establish the principle of a united empire with a common parliament and to carry the election of Archduke John as regent.

On 11 December, after Schmerling and the Austrian members left the cabinet, he became head of the imperial ministry, and on 18 December he put forward his programme: Austria was to be excluded from the new federal state but bound to it by a treaty of union. It was accepted after a hard struggle, but on 20 May, seeing no hope of agreement with the radical democrats, he and his friends resigned.

He tried to steer the Prussian Northern Union towards a national policy and sat in the Erfurt parliament, but gave up on Prussia's wavering course and served as a major for Schleswig-Holstein in the First Schleswig War in 1850. In 1862 he declared for the Great German party, and from 1864 to 1872 he was Hessian envoy in Vienna. He died at Darmstadt on 22 May 1880.
heinrich-von-kleist: Bernd Heinrich Wilhelm von Kleist was born on 18 October 1777 in Frankfurt an der Oder, in the Margraviate of Brandenburg. After a scanty education he entered the Prussian Army in 1792, served in the Rhine campaign of 1796 and retired in 1799 as a lieutenant. He studied law, philosophy, natural sciences and Latin at the Viadrina University, and in 1800 took a post in the Ministry of Finance in Berlin. The next year he visited Paris and settled in Switzerland, where he read his first drama, the tragedy The Schroffenstein Family, to Heinrich Zschokke and Ludwig Wieland.

In 1807, on a journey to Dresden, Kleist was arrested by the French as a spy and held in the Fort de Joux. In 1808 he published the journal Phöbus with Adam Heinrich Müller, and in 1810 and 1811 he edited the Berliner Abendblätter. Penthesilea (1808) takes its Amazon queen from a Greek source and shows wild passion. The romantic play Käthchen of Heilbronn (1808) kept its popularity for many years, and the comedy The Broken Jug (1808) made his name in that genre. Die Hermannsschlacht (1809) is anti-Napoleonic propaganda, and The Prince of Homburg, one of his best works, was first published by Ludwig Tieck in 1821.

His Collected Stories of 1810 and 1811 include Michael Kohlhaas, about a Brandenburg horse dealer in Martin Luther's day, as well as The Earthquake in Chile and The Marquise of O. His essays on aesthetics and psychology touch on questions discussed by Kant, Fichte and Schelling.

Kleist met Henriette Vogel in 1809 through Adam Müller. According to the autopsy report she had cancer. On 21 November 1811 they travelled from Berlin to the Wannsee, left farewell letters, and Kleist shot her and then himself on the shore of the Kleiner Wannsee near Potsdam. They were buried in a common grave there. The Eleventh Edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica called him by far the most important North German dramatist of the Romantic movement. The Kleist Prize for German literature is named after him.
heinrich-von-plauen: Every male member of his family was baptised Heinrich, so he is called the Elder to distinguish him from his relative Heinrich von Plauen the Younger. Born in the Vogtland around 1370, he came to Prussia around 1390 as a guest of the Teutonic Order and later became a full member. He held no important post until 1402, when he became Komtur of Nessau, and in 1407 he was promoted to Komtur of Schwetz.

He did not fight at Grunwald on 15 July 1410. On hearing of the defeat he gathered 3,000 men and reached Marienburg, the Order's capital, before the Polish and Lithuanian armies, writing to Germany as if he were Grand Master for troops and money. The siege lasted from 26 July to 19 September, and King Jogaila, unprepared for a long one, had to withdraw; by the end of October von Plauen had retaken all but the border fortresses. In November he was chosen 27th Grand Master over officials of higher rank.

He signed the Peace of Thorn on 1 February 1411, which left the Order its core lands but required an indemnity of six million Prague groschen in four instalments. To pay it he imposed a levy on the Prussian cities, enforcing it on Thorn and on Danzig, which held out under blockade until 5 April 1411. He had Nicholas von Renys of the Lizard Union beheaded at Graudenz for helping the Poles. He made the last payment on time in January 1413, then rejected the border ruling of Emperor Sigismund's envoy and prepared a new war against Poland.

The attacks of late summer 1413 failed, stopped by disobedient knights, and on 9 October Michael Küchmeister von Sternberg, the grand marshal, who favoured peace talks, removed him. Küchmeister became Grand Master, and von Plauen was first given a minor fortress, then arrested when Jogaila demanded his return to office. He was released from jail in Danzig in 1418 and became procurator of Lochstädt near Königsberg, where he died in 1429.
heinrich-xxii-prince-reuss-of-greiz: Heinrich succeeded his father on 8 November 1859 at the age of thirteen, and his mother, Caroline of Hesse-Homburg, ruled as regent until he came of age at 21. The daughter of an Austrian general and the wife of an Austrian officer, she was vehemently anti-Prussian, and during the Austro-Prussian War Prussian troops occupied Reuss and stayed until a payment of 100,000 thalers was made.

Heinrich took the government into his own hands on 28 March 1867 and gave the principality its first constitution. He remained anti-Prussian all his life, rejecting Prussian measures such as the Kulturkampf and civil marriage, and like his subjects he refused fully to accept that the Hohenzollern emperors had precedence over other royal houses. Asked about his relationship with the Emperor, he would say only that they were allies for the common defence of the German Federation.

He refused to allow a memorial to Emperor Wilhelm I, though one was later forced upon him, would not tolerate mourning at the deaths of Wilhelm I and Frederick III, and forbade celebrations of the anniversaries of the German victories of 1870. Most of the territory he ruled was his private property, which made him very wealthy. At the end of his rule Reuss had fewer than 70,000 people and covered 122 square miles.

On 8 October 1872 Heinrich married Princess Ida of Schaumburg-Lippe, daughter of Adolf I, Prince of Schaumburg-Lippe. They had six children, among them his successor Henry XXIV and Princess Hermine, whose second husband, in 1922, was Wilhelm II. Heinrich died of heart trouble on 19 April 1902.

His only son was mentally and physically disabled and clearly unable to rule, so a regency was arranged. A younger branch of the family was next in line, and there was concern because Heinrich had disliked it. In the end his distant cousin Heinrich XXVII of Reuss zu Schleiz was chosen; his wife, Elise of Hohenlohe-Langenburg, was a cousin of both the Kaiser and Empress Augusta Viktoria, and he had served with Wilhelm in the Hussars of the Guard, which repaired relations between the houses of Hohenzollern and Reuss.
hejaz: The name comes from the Arabic verb meaning to separate, because the region divides the Najd in the east from the Tihamah in the west. It lies along the Red Sea Rift, bordered by the Red Sea on the west and Jordan and the Gulf of Aqaba on the north. Its volcanic landscape includes lava fields known as harrat, among the largest alkali basalt regions on earth. Its history has often centred on oasis cities such as Yathrib, later Medina, Fadak, Khaybar, Taymah and Al-Ula, which grew rich on trade, especially the incense trade that carried goods north from South Arabia.

In antiquity the Thamud, attested from the 8th century BCE to the 5th century CE, were based in the north-west around Hegra, and the Kingdom of Lihyan ruled from Dedan in the Al-Ula oasis. The Nabataeans occupied the north-west from the 1st century BCE until the Roman Empire annexed their kingdom in 106 CE. The Quraysh, a tribe of the Mudar confederation, ruled Mecca and cared for the Kaaba. In 622 Muhammad brokered a treaty between pagan Arab and Jewish tribes at Medina, the Constitution of Medina.

The Hejaz was at the centre of the first Islamic state and the Rashidun Caliphate, whose capital was Medina from 622 to 656. Mecca was the capital of the Zubayrid Caliphate from 683 to 692, after which Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan brought the region back under the Umayyads. From 967 to 1916 the local sharifs governed the semi-sovereign Sharifate of Mecca, acknowledging the suzerainty of various dynasties, among them the Ayyubid Sultanate, the Mamluk Sultanate and, from 1517, the Ottoman Empire. On 23 December 1925 Sharif Hussein surrendered to the Saudis, and in 1932 the kingdoms of Hejaz and Nejd were renamed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

The Hejaz forms the western region of Saudi Arabia and includes Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Tabuk, Yanbu, Taif and Al-Bahah. Jeddah is its largest city, and Hejazi Arabic is the most widely spoken dialect. Mecca and Medina are the first and second holiest sites in Islam. Al-Hijr, with rock-cut structures credited to the Thamud, was the first World Heritage Site in Saudi Arabia.
helen-of-troy: Helen is a figure of Greek mythology said to have been the most beautiful woman in the world. She was believed to be the daughter of Zeus by Leda or Nemesis, and the sister of Clytemnestra, Castor and Pollux. In her youth she was abducted by Theseus, who left her with his mother Aethra or an associate at Aphidnae or Athens, until her brothers Castor and Pollux invaded Athens and returned her to Sparta.

When she came to marry, kings and princes from around the world sought her hand. Her father Tyndareus feared giving offence to those he rejected, and Odysseus proposed that all the suitors swear to defend the chosen husband against anyone who quarrelled with him. This was the Oath of Tyndareus. Menelaus was chosen because he had offered the most gifts, and he and Helen ruled Sparta after Tyndareus and Leda abdicated. They had a daughter, Hermione.

Paris, a Trojan prince, came to Sparta on a supposed diplomatic mission. Aphrodite had promised him the most beautiful woman in the world as a reward for judging her the most beautiful of the goddesses. Most ancient sources, following Homer, hold that Helen fell in love with him and went to Troy willingly, though she is sometimes shown as abducted. Menelaus called on the other suitors to honour their oaths, and the Trojan War began.

Accounts of her time in Troy contradict one another. Homer shows her as ambivalent, regretful of her choice yet sly in restoring her reputation, while Virgil's Aeneid has her feign Bacchic rites and signal to the Greeks from a tower. Euripides, Stesichorus and Herodotus denied that she went to Troy at all and placed her in Egypt for the war.

In Homer's account Helen returned to Sparta with Menelaus. In another version, used by Euripides in Orestes, Apollo saved her and she was taken up to Mount Olympus, becoming a sea goddess who watched over sailors with Castor and Pollux. Her major cult centres were in Laconia, and at Therapne she shared a shrine with Menelaus. She was also worshipped in Attica and on Rhodes. Images of her appear from the 7th century BCE, and the elopement or abduction was a popular motif in Classical Greece.
helena-dragas: Helena was born into Serbian nobility around 1372. Her father Konstantin was a magnate who held Kyustendil during the fall of the Serbian Empire and was a grandson of the Serbian king Stefan III Dečanski. Her stepmother, Eudokia of Trebizond, was a daughter of Alexios III of Trebizond. Konstantin fell at the battle of Rovine in 1395, fighting as a vassal of the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I against Mircea I of Wallachia.

She married the Byzantine emperor Manuel II Palaiologos in February 1392, and was crowned as holy empress the next day. No record explains why the marriage was arranged, though dynastic marriages between the Byzantine and Serbian dynasties were not unprecedented. She was traditionally described as known for beauty, piety, wisdom and justice.

Little is known of her as empress. When Manuel was absent in 1393 he made his own mother regent rather than his wife. In 1425 Manuel abdicated and became a monk, and after his death on 21 July 1425 Helena became a nun at the Monastery of Kyra Martha. She helped to found a home for old people, The Hope of the Despaired, at the Monastery of St John in Petrion.

Her vows did not take her from the court, and she is better documented as empress dowager. She advised both John VIII and Constantine XI. In 1439, when John VIII was in Italy and learned that the patriarch of Constantinople had died, he refused to name a successor until he had consulted her. She led the anti-unionist party at court that opposed union of the Orthodox and Catholic churches, which her sons favoured, and her influence is credited with slowing it. In the end she gave her consent, or at least stopped actively opposing it, in line with John's wishes.

After John VIII died in 1448 the succession was disputed between Constantine and his younger brother Demetrios. Helena backed Constantine and served as regent until he arrived from Mistra. She persuaded Sultan Murad II to intervene in his favour. Constantine called himself Constantine XI Dragases Palaiologos after her, the only one of her sons to take her name.

Helena died in Constantinople on 23 March 1450. Constantine is recorded as saying that her death had deprived him of a valuable adviser. The Orthodox Church venerates her as Saint Hypomone, which means patience, and commemorates her on 29 May, the day of the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans and of Constantine's death.
helena-of-adiabene: Helena was queen mother of Adiabene, a vassal state of the Parthian Empire. Her husband Monobaz I was probably also her brother, and she was the mother of both Izates II and Monobaz II. According to Josephus she was the daughter of King Izates, while Moses of Chorene makes her the chief wife of Abgar V, king of Edessa. She became a convert to Judaism around the year 30 CE.

What is known of her rests on Josephus, Movses Khorenatsi, Kirakos Gandzaketsi and the Talmud. Josephus, though younger, was almost her contemporary: he lived in Jerusalem while she lived and was buried there, and wrote much of his work from first-hand knowledge.

During a famine at Jerusalem in 45–46 CE she sent to Alexandria for grain and to Cyprus for dried figs for the sufferers, although the Talmud, in Bava Batra 11a, credits this to Monobaz II instead. The Talmud also records her gifts to the Temple in Jerusalem: a golden candlestick over its door, whose reflected rays at sunrise told everyone that it was time to read the Shema, and a golden plate inscribed with the passage of the Torah read when a wife suspected of infidelity was brought before the kohanim.

The Talmud tells that she vowed to become a Nazirite for seven years if her son Izates came back safe from war. When she went to Judea at the end of that time, the School of Hillel told her to observe the vow anew, and after it she became ritually impure and had to repeat it, so that she was a Nazirite for twenty-one years; Judah bar Ilai, however, said fourteen.

Helena was buried in the pyramidal tomb she had built in her lifetime, three stadia north of Jerusalem, whose catacombs are known as the Tombs of the Kings. A sarcophagus found there bears an Aramaic inscription that scholars read as "Our mistress, the Queen". Louis Félicien de Saulcy discovered it in the nineteenth century but took the remains for a queen of the First Temple period; the anger of the Jewish community of Jerusalem halted his dig, and the finds went to the Louvre. Ruins believed to be her palace were excavated by Doron Ben-Ami in the City of David in 2007.
helena-of-bulgaria-empress-of-serbia: Helena descended from three prestigious medieval Balkan ruling families, the Komnenos, the Asenides and the Shishmanides. She was the daughter of the despot Sratsimir and Keratsa Petritsa, a granddaughter of Shishman I, ruler of Vidin, and a niece of Tsar Michael III Shishman Asen. Besides Tsar Ivan Alexander, her brothers included the despot John Komnenos Asen, ruler of Kanina and Valona. Through her grandmother she descended from Tsar Ivan Asen II and Irene Komnina. The frescoes of the Church of the Holy Virgin in Matejce show her and her son not as Nemanjić rulers but as descendants of the Asen and Komnenos houses.

Stefan Dušan was crowned King of Serbia at Svrčin on 8 September 1331, and the marriage, most likely held on 26 April 1332, was arranged as part of a peace between Bulgaria and Serbia. Their son was Stefan Uroš V. A daughter, Theodora, became a consort of the Ottoman Sultan Orhan at the age of twelve, and the historian John V. A. Fine identifies a possible second daughter with Irene, wife of Gregorios Preljub, the Serbian governor of Thessaly.

On Dušan's death in 1355 Helena was regent for her son for two years and received lands between the lower Vardar and the Mesta and the Chalcidic peninsula, holding court at Serres. Her principality there was neutral and autonomous: a note on a charter of 1360 to 1361 says that the holy tsaritsa rules alone in Serres.

Helena became a nun in 1359 under the name Jelisaveta, yet remained active in politics for some time. In her last years she oversaw the rebuilding and renovation of several monastic communities. A manuscript of the Hilandar Monastery gives the day of her death as 7 November 1374. She was canonised under the name Saint Elizabeth and her relics are venerated. According to the Bulgarian historian Plamen Pavlov, one of her hands is kept in a silver box at the Savina monastery near Herceg Novi on the Bay of Kotor in Montenegro; the relics came there in 1759 and before that may have been at the Tvrdoš Monastery near Trebinje.
helian-bobo: Liu Bobo was a younger son of Liu Weichen, chief of the Tiefu tribe, and a descendant of the southern chanyu Liu Qubei. In 391 Tuoba Gui of Northern Wei captured his father's capital Yueba, Liu Weichen was killed by his own men, and his clan was slaughtered. Bobo escaped to Moyigan of the Poduoluo tribe, a vassal of Later Qin, who married him to one of his daughters.

Emperor Yao Xing of Later Qin was struck by the tall, eloquent young man and, against his brother Yao Yong's warning that Bobo was cruel and treacherous, made him a general and the Duke of Wuyuan, with some thirty thousand tribesmen to defend Shuofang. When Yao Xing made peace with Northern Wei in 407, Bobo rebelled, killed his father-in-law Moyigan and claimed descent from Yu the Great.

For years he refused to settle in a city, relying on the mobility of his cavalry to raid Later Qin where it was weak. In 407 he ambushed Tufa Rutan of Southern Liang in a canyon, and in 409 Yao Xing himself barely escaped him at Ercheng. In 413 he had his general Chigan Ali build Tongwan; workmen were executed if an iron wedge could pierce the steamed earth of its walls. That year he took the surname Helian, which Chen Sanping derives from the Xiongnu word for sky.

When Liu Yu of Jin destroyed Later Qin in 417 and then left Chang'an to his young son Liu Yizhen, Bobo's sons isolated the city and crushed its retreating garrison, and Bobo stacked the skulls of the Jin dead into a mound. He then took the title of emperor, but kept his capital at Tongwan. Traditional historians describe him as growing ever more cruel, killing on a whim and mutilating officials who looked at him or contradicted him.

In 424 his plan to replace Crown Prince Helian Gui with Helian Lun set his sons fighting; Gui killed Lun and was killed in turn by Helian Chang, whom Bobo then made crown prince. Bobo died in the Yong'an Hall at Tongwan in late 425, aged forty-five. Helian Chang had twenty-five thousand labourers build the Jiaping Mausoleum, burned the halls built above it and offered several thousand horses as a sacrifice.
helian-chang: Neither Helian Chang's birth year nor his mother is known. He first appears in 414, when his father Helian Bobo made him Duke of Taiyuan, apparently as his third son. In 417 and 418 he took part in the campaign against Chang'an, cutting off Tong Gate so that the Jin forces could not escape, and he then besieged the Jin general Zhu Lingshi and his brother Zhu Chaoshi at Caogong Castle by cutting off its water, capturing and killing them.

In 424 Helian Bobo decided to replace Crown Prince Helian Gui with another son, Helian Lun. Helian Gui killed Helian Lun at Gaoping, but Helian Chang then attacked Helian Gui by surprise, killed him and brought his troops back to Tongwan, and his father made him crown prince.

A fierce soldier, Helian Chang tried to expand his state, and in 426 his generals Hulu Gu and Wei Fa dealt Western Qin a heavy blow. In late 426 Emperor Taiwu of Northern Wei crossed the frozen Yellow River and surprised Tongwan during a feast for the winter solstice; a Wei officer set the palace on fire, and a false report that the capital had fallen led the Xia to abandon Puban and Chang'an. In 427, misled into thinking the besieging Wei army had run out of food, Helian Chang left Tongwan to attack it, nearly captured the emperor but was defeated, and fled to Shanggui.

Tongwan fell, and the Wei captured its nobles and the imperial clan, among them the empresses of Helian Bobo and Helian Chang; Taiwu took three of his sisters as concubines. In early 428 Helian Chang counterattacked a Wei army weakened by disease and besieged it at Anding, but the Wei officers Anchi Jia and Yuchi Juan struck at him during an assault; he fell from his horse and was taken.

At the Wei capital Pingcheng, Taiwu gave him the western palace, supplies fit for an emperor, the title Duke of Kuaiji and his sister Princess Shiping in marriage, and took him hunting despite officials' fears. In 429 his presence helped the minister Cui Hao silence two former Xia astrologers who opposed a campaign against Rouran. Made Prince of Qin in 430, he was used to persuade the defender of Pingliang to surrender. In 434 he fled west from Pingcheng and was intercepted and killed west of the Yellow River, after which Northern Wei executed his surviving brothers. His era name was Chengguang, 425 to 428.
helian-ding: Neither Helian Ding's birth year nor his mother is known. He was a son of Helian Bobo, founder of Hu Xia, who thought little of him as a delinquent and frivolous youth and gave him little authority. His brother Helian Chang, who became emperor in 425, relied on him as one of his chief generals and in early 427 sent him from Tongwan to retake Chang'an, where he reached a stalemate with the Northern Wei general Daxi Jin. When Tongwan fell, he abandoned the campaign and joined his brother at Shanggui.

After Helian Chang was captured at Anding in 428, Helian Ding gathered the remaining troops at Pingliang and took the throne. Daxi Jin pursued him without enough food and water, and when a Wei deserter revealed this, Helian Ding attacked and captured Daxi. The Wei commanders of Anding and Chang'an fled, and Xia recovered Chang'an and the Guanzhong region. His request for peace was answered with an order to surrender, which he refused.

In 430 he allied with Emperor Wen of Liu Song, agreeing to divide Northern Wei's lands north of the Yellow River along the Taihang Mountains, but neither ally moved first, and late in 430 Emperor Taiwu attacked Pingliang. Lured into battle by the Wei general Tuxi Bi, Helian Ding was defeated and besieged on the Chungu Plains, broke out badly injured and fled to Shanggui. His brothers Helian Shegan and Helian Duluogu surrendered Pingliang, and his empress was given to the Wei general Doudai Tian as a concubine.

In 431 his uncle Helian Weifa took Nan'an, the last city of Western Qin, where the starving people had turned to cannibalism, and Helian Ding executed the Western Qin prince Qifu Mumo and his clan. He then crossed the Yellow River at Zhicheng to seize the lands of Northern Liang, but the Tuyuhun khan Murong Mugui had foreseen this, and his brothers Murong Muliyan and Murong Shiqian captured Helian Ding during the crossing, ending Xia. Late in 431 Murong Mugui offered him to Northern Wei and was made Prince of Xiqin, and early in 432 he handed him over to be executed.
heliand: The poem was probably written at the request of Emperor Louis the Pious, as an answer to Saxon ambivalence toward Christianity. The Saxons had been forced to convert in the late 8th and early 9th centuries, after 33 years of conflict between the Saxons under Widukind and the Franks under Charlemagne. Around the time of writing the Saxon stelinga, the lower social castes, rose in revolt. A Latin praefatio, first printed by Matthias Flacius in 1562 and generally deemed authentic, says the emperor commanded a Saxon poet to render the Old and New Testaments in verse in his own tongue.

The poet worked not from the New Testament directly but from the pseudo-Tatian Gospel harmony, and knew the commentaries of Alcuin, Bede and Rabanus Maurus. Scholars disagree whether he was unlearned, like Caedmon, or a Christian Saxon able to read Latin who followed the calling of a scop, or minstrel. Early scholars such as Wilhelm Braune held that he also wrote the Old Saxon Genesis, but consensus has moved away from that view.

The work is divided into fitts, or songs. Repeated words and phrases, and sentences that begin in the middle of a line for the sake of alliteration, read awkwardly on the page but suit a poem sung after dinner in a mead hall or monastery. Neumes written above the text in one manuscript suggest that it may have been sung. Scholars disagree whether its tone shows a Germanized Christianity, with its traditions of fighting and enmity, or a Christianized Germany, given its message that it is better to be meek than mighty.

Two nearly complete manuscripts survive. The Cotton manuscript in the British Library, probably written in the second half of the 10th century, breaks off in the journey to Emmaus; the Munich manuscript, formerly at Bamberg and now in the Bavarian State Library, begins at line 85. Fragments came to light at Prague in 1881, in the Vatican Library in 1894, at Straubing in 1979 and at Leipzig in 2006.

Franciscus Junius transcribed a fragment in 1587, George Hickes first printed the poem in 1705, and Johann Andreas Schmeller published the first modern edition in 1830, giving the work its name. Eduard Sievers's edition of 1877, printing the two main manuscripts side by side, became the standard. Many historians agree that Martin Luther owned a copy and cited it to encourage translating the Gospels into the vernacular.
helicopter: The fourth-century Daoist book Baopuzi by Ge Hong reportedly describes some of the ideas inherent to rotary-wing aircraft. Designs similar to the Chinese toy appeared in some Renaissance paintings, and in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries Western scientists developed flying machines based on it. The word helicopter is adapted from the French hélicoptère, coined by Gustave Ponton d'Amécourt in 1861 from the Ancient Greek helix, spiral, and pteron, wing.

Engines held back the early machines. Rubber bands and similar devices limited them to toys and small models, and steam engines lacked the power for manned flight. The internal combustion engine at the end of the nineteenth century made lifting humans possible. In the early 1920s the Argentine Raúl Pateras-Pescara de Castelluccio demonstrated one of the first successful applications of cyclic pitch.

A helicopter's rotor consists of a mast, hub and blades. The torque of a single main rotor must be countered, and the design Igor Sikorsky settled on for his VS-300 was a smaller tail rotor at the end of a tail boom. Between 1939 and 1943 the VS-300 went through four iterations and became the basis for modern helicopters. Twin-rotor designs carry more payload, and coaxial, tiltrotor and compound helicopters also fly. The pilot works the cyclic, the collective, the anti-torque pedals and the throttle, and hovering is the most demanding task. If the engine fails, the helicopter can enter autorotation.

Heinrich Focke designed the transverse twin-rotor Fw 61, which first flew in June 1936. Hanna Reitsch flew it inside the Deutschlandhalle in Berlin in February 1938, and it set records between 1937 and 1939. On 11 December 1951 Charles Kaman's K-225 became the first turbine-powered helicopter. Because it can take off and land vertically and hover, a helicopter does work that was impossible or slow for other aircraft, including transport, military roles, firefighting, search and rescue, medical transport and aerial observation.
heligoland-zanzibar-treaty: After the Berlin Conference of 1884, Germany had been losing out in the Scramble for Africa. The German East Africa Company under Carl Peters had acquired a strip of land on the Tanganyikan coast, which led to the Abushiri Revolt of 1888, but it never had any control over the islands of the sultanate of Zanzibar. Meanwhile the construction of the Kiel Canal, begun in 1887, made control of the German Bight essential to Emperor Wilhelm II's plans for the Imperial Navy. The islands of Heligoland, which had belonged to the dukes of Holstein-Gottorp and had been a British possession since 1814, lay across those approaches. The treaty served the aim of the German chancellor, Leo von Caprivi, of a settlement with the British.

Under the agreement of 1 July 1890, Germany gained Heligoland, the Caprivi Strip in present-day Namibia, which gave German South-West Africa access to the Zambezi, and a free hand on the coast around Dar es Salaam, the core of German East Africa. In exchange Germany handed over its protectorate over the small sultanate of Wituland on the Kenyan coast, with parts of East Africa that Britain needed for a railway to Lake Victoria, and pledged not to interfere with British actions towards the independent sultanate of Zanzibar, meaning the islands of Unguja and Pemba. The treaty also set the German sphere of interest in South-West Africa and settled the borders between Togoland and the Gold Coast and between Kamerun and Nigeria.

Britain gave up a naval base that covered the approaches to the main German bases in the North Sea. It soon declared a protectorate over Zanzibar and gained full control of the sultanate in the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896. Wilhelm II's naval policy later ended hopes of an accommodation with Britain and helped bring Britain and France together in the Entente cordiale of 1904.

The popular name was introduced by the former chancellor Otto von Bismarck, who wanted to attack his successor Caprivi over an agreement that Bismarck himself had arranged. It implied that Germany had swapped an African empire for a tiny island, trousers for a button, and imperialists took it up and complained of treason. Carl Peters and Alfred Hugenberg called for what became, in 1891, the Pan-German League. G. K. Chesterton described Heligoland as another fragment of the British robe that Lord Salisbury had cast away almost contemptuously in the North Sea.

The islanders had only a minor part in the talks, and the British press called for a vote on the island. The treaty kept the existing laws and promised the continuation of local practices: no taxes until 1918, exemption from duty until 1910, and conscription only for those born in 1890 or later.
heliocentrism: Heliocentrism was opposed to geocentrism, which placed the Earth at the centre. The sphericity of the Earth was widely recognised in Greek and Roman astronomy from at least the 4th century BCE, but its daily rotation and yearly orbit around the Sun were not universally accepted until the Copernican Revolution. The first non-geocentric model was proposed by the Pythagorean Philolaus, who taught that a central fire lay at the centre of the universe, with the Earth, Sun, Moon and planets revolving around it. Aristarchus of Samos developed a fully heliocentric model in the 3rd century BCE. It did not replace the view of a stationary Earth, and from the 2nd century CE the predominant model was the geocentric one of Ptolemy's Almagest.

Other traditions came close to it. Aryabhata, in the Aryabhatiya of 499, proposed that the Earth spins on its axis and gave the planets' periods with respect to the Sun, though most scholars hold that his system was not explicitly heliocentric. In India, Nilakantha Somayaji, in the Tantrasamgraha of 1501, revised a planetary system in which the planets orbit the Sun and the Sun orbits the Earth, similar to the one Tycho Brahe later proposed. Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium elaborated the heliocentric model in geometrical detail, derived its parameters from observations and provided tables for computing the positions of stars and planets. In reality his system did not predict the planets' positions any better than the Ptolemaic system.

In 1533 Johann Albrecht Widmannstetter lectured on the theory in Rome, and Pope Clement VII and several cardinals listened with interest. In 1539 Martin Luther remarked that someone wanted to turn the whole of astronomy upside down, and cited Joshua, who bade the sun and not the earth stand still. Giordano Bruno was the only known person to defend Copernicus during his own lifetime, and was condemned by the Roman Inquisition and burned in Rome in 1600. Galileo Galilei reported with his telescope that Jupiter has moons and that Venus shows a full range of phases.

The Galileo affair did little to slow the spread of heliocentrism, and by 1686 Fontenelle's Conversations on the Plurality of Worlds was introducing it to the general public. After the observations of William Herschel, Friedrich Bessel and others it was realised that the Sun, though near the barycenter of the Solar System, is not central in the universe, and modern astronomy distinguishes no universal centre.
heliodorus-pillar: The column stands about 17.7 feet above a square platform and, unlike the Ashokan pillars, is neither tapered nor polished. Its shaft passes from eight facets to sixteen and then thirty-two, and ends in a short round section below a bell capital; bands of half-rosettes and a festoon with birds mark the junctions. The Garuda that crowned it is lost, though a fragment in the Gujari Mahal Museum at Gwalior is thought to belong to it.

The main inscription, in the Brahmi script of the Sunga period and in Monumental Prakrit, names Heliodorus as the son of Dion and the envoy to King Kasiputra Bhagabhadra in that king's fourteenth regnal year. Early scholars took Bhagabhadra for the fifth Sunga ruler, but he was probably a local king. A second inscription quotes a verse of the Mahabharata on three steps to immortality: control, generosity and attention.

Alexander Cunningham found the pillar near Besnagar, where the Betwa and Halali rivers meet, so thickly crusted with red paste by local worshippers, who called it Khamba Baba, that he saw no inscription. A team led by H. H. Lake cleaned it in 1909–1910 and found the Brahmi texts, which John Marshall reported.

Excavations under D. R. Bhandarkar in 1913–1915 and under Khare in 1963–1965 showed that the pillar was one of eight on a north-south line before an elliptical temple to Vasudeva, with a brick foundation and probably a wooden superstructure, rebuilt after floods. Susan Mishra and Himanshu Ray count the site among perhaps the earliest Hindu temples archaeologists have found.

Dated closely to the reign of Antialkidas, the pillar is the first after the Pillars of Ashoka to be linked to a datable inscription, and its motifs help to date the reliefs of Stupa No. 2 at Sanchi to the last quarter of the 2nd century BCE.

Scholars disagree about what it says of Heliodorus. Thomas Hopkins held that he was presumably not the first Greek to take up Vaishnava devotion. Harry Falk sees the dedication as a normal Greek practice of honouring foreign gods to share their power, not a conversion. Allan Dahlquist proposed in 1962 that Vasudeva might mean Indra, a reading that later scholars such as Kuiper rejected.
heliopolis-ancient-egypt: Heliopolis was the capital of the Heliopolite or 13th nome of Lower Egypt. Its Egyptian name, Iunu, meant "the Pillars", and the Pyramid Texts of the Old Kingdom call it the "House of Ra". The Greeks called it Hēlioúpolis, "City of the Sun", because they identified Ra and Atum, whose principal cult stood there, with their own sun god Helios. It appears in the Hebrew Bible as On. The city was occupied from prehistoric times, when it was a settlement of Stone Age farmers, and it expanded greatly under the Old and Middle Kingdoms.

Heliopolis was the chief cult centre of Atum, who came to be identified with Ra and then with Horus as Ra-harakhty. Its main temple was the "Great House" or "House of Atum". Its priests held that Atum or Ra was the first being, rising self-created from the primeval waters. A decline in the importance of Ra's cult in the Fifth Dynasty led to the Ennead, a group of nine major deities that placed the others below Ra-Atum. Under Akhenaten in the Eighteenth Dynasty a temple of the Aten was built here, and the cult of the Mnevis bull, another embodiment of the Sun, kept its altar in the city.

Herodotus states that the priests of Heliopolis were the best informed of all the Egyptians in matters of history, and Ptolemy II had Manetho, the chief priest, draw his history of the ancient kings from its archives. Alexander the Great halted here on his march from Pelusium to Memphis. The Ptolemies favoured the cult of Serapis, and Alexandria eclipsed Heliopolis as a seat of learning. By the first century BCE Strabo found the temples deserted and the town almost uninhabited, though priests were still present.

Under Roman rule many of its obelisks were taken away. The taller Vatican obelisk was removed by Caligula, and Augustus took the Obelisk of Montecitorio to Rome. Two smaller ones, called Cleopatra's Needles, later went to London and New York. In the Middle Ages the growth of Cairo and Fustat created a demand for building stone, and builders stripped the ruins of the temples.

The ancient city lies 15 to 20 metres below the streets of Al-Matariyyah, Ain Shams and Tel Al-Hisn in northern Cairo. The obelisk of Senusret I of the Twelfth Dynasty still stands where it was raised, marking the site of the great Temple of Ra-Atum. It is 21 metres high and is believed to be the oldest surviving obelisk in the world. Some crude brick walls can be seen in fields, and a few granite blocks bear the name of Ramesses II. Tombs were excavated in 2004, and parts of a colossal statue of Psamtik I were found in 2017.
helios: Helios most likely has Proto-Indo-European origins. His name is the inherited Greek word for the Sun, cognate with Latin sol, Sanskrit surya and Old Norse sól. Walter Burkert wrote that Helios and the dawn goddess Eos are of impeccable Indo-European lineage in both etymology and status, and the imagery of a chariot-driving solar deity is likely Indo-European too. In Greek mythology Helios is the son of the Titans Hyperion and Theia and the brother of Eos and Selene. He was not among the regular and more prominent deities but a more shadowy member of the Olympian circle, though among the most ancient.

Helios was pictured driving a chariot from east to west each day, rising from the river Oceanus and setting under the earth in the west. At night he was said to travel east in a golden boat. Because the Sun sees everything, he was invoked as a witness to oaths, and he was among the three deities called on in the Iliad to witness the truce between Greeks and Trojans. The best-known story is that of his son Phaethon, who asked to drive the chariot for a day and failed with disastrous results.

In the Odyssey, Odysseus's men kill and eat the sacred cattle that Helios kept at Thrinacia, and at his request Zeus strikes their ship with a thunderbolt. According to Pindar, Helios received no land when the gods divided the earth, and he asked for an island he had seen rising from the sea. This was Rhodes, his major cult centre, where the Colossus of Rhodes, a gigantic statue of the god, stood at the port until an earthquake destroyed it.

Helios was a relatively minor deity in Classical Greece. In late antiquity his worship grew, as he took on elements of Apollo and the Roman sun god Sol and was equated with Mithras. On 25 December 274 the emperor Aurelian instituted a state cult of Sol Invictus, or Helios Megistos, and in the 4th century the emperor Julian made Helios the central divinity of a short-lived revival of traditional Roman religion.

The earliest humanoid images of Helios, from the late sixth and early fifth centuries BCE, show a bearded man on a chariot; later art shows him young and beardless with a radiant crown. The element helium takes its name from him.
hellanodikai: The Hellanodikai were a kind of agonothetes, the magistrates chosen in Greek states to establish and run public games; their method of selection depended on the government of the state, and some games had officials of their own name, such as the athlothetes of Athens. The origin of the Olympic officials is lost in prehistory. In Doric legend Hercules, the founder of the games, would have been the first. There may at first have been only one Hellanodikas, perhaps only in legend, but the number grew as high as twelve before settling at ten in 348 BCE.

The office was at first hereditary; later one Elean from each of the ruling families was elected, for a single Olympiad, with new elections for each games. For the ten months before the games the judges lived in Elis in a building of their own, the Hellanodikaion, close to the gymnasiums where the athletes trained, and were instructed in the rules by the nomophylakes, the guardians of the law.

They supervised the athletes' training, rejecting those not performing well enough and judging each on behaviour, character and morality as well as power and stamina; trainers had to be present but were punished if they intervened. Those approved were entered on a list called the leukoma. Two days before the games the judges led the eligible athletes in procession from Elis to Olympia. They acted as the organising committee, attended every ceremony and event, supervised individual contests under a senior Hellanodikas, policed the games and presented the crowns and palm branches to the winners.

The judges were known for their fairness and held in high regard, and the success of the games was credited to them. Although bribery and cheating among athletes were common, only one case of corruption among the judges is recorded, when a Hellanodikas won two equestrian events. After it the judges were no longer allowed to compete, and it remained the only blemish on their record, so far as the record survives.
hellenica-oxyrhynchia: The work survives in two major fragments. The London papyrus deals with battles of the late Peloponnesian War, above all the Battle of Notium. The Florentine papyrus, found in 1934, deals with events of the early 4th century BCE. The whole history seems to have continued Thucydides, covering the years from 411 to 394 BCE, much as Xenophon's Hellenica did; a fragment of Xenophon's work has also been found at Oxyrhynchus.

In the 19th century historians presumed that Xenophon, a contemporary of the events he described, was always to be preferred to Diodorus Siculus, who wrote much later. The first papyrus, found in 1906, agreed more with Diodorus than with Xenophon on several key issues. This led to a re-evaluation of the two, and modern historians now prefer the account of Diodorus at a number of points.

The author's name is not recorded in the surviving fragments, and scholars usually call him simply the Oxyrhynchus historian. His identity has been debated at length without consensus. Early suggestions included Ephorus and Theopompus, though most were strongly objected to on grounds of style, presentation or subject matter. The likeliest candidate seems to be Cratippus, an Athenian historian of the 4th century BCE whose work is known to have continued Thucydides, but objections have been raised, and the historian of ancient historiography Bruno Bleckmann has argued again for Theopompus.

The work is praised for its pragmatism and style, though it has detractors. The classicist H. D. Westlake judged its author a competent and most conscientious historian who drew on the best possible sources and tried to interpret them impartially, but who lacked distinction in thought and style: in his words, a second-rate Thucydides.
hellenistic-period: The Greek world was fragmented after the Peloponnesian War and the battles of Leuctra in 371 BCE and Mantinea in 362 BCE, which let the northern kingdom of Macedon rise to predominance under Philip II. When Alexander the Great died on 10 June 323 BCE he left a sprawling empire made up of largely autonomous satrapies and no chosen successor. His generals, the Diadochi, or Successors, disputed who should be king of Macedon, and the empire broke apart in the Wars of the Diadochi. Greek kingdoms arose across West Asia, northeast Africa and South Asia, including the Seleucid Empire, the Ptolemaic Kingdom, Pergamon, the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom and the Indo-Greek Kingdom.

The Hellenistic states of Asia and Egypt were run by an occupying elite of Greco-Macedonian administrators backed by a standing army of mercenaries. Monarchs ran their kingdoms as royal estates and were expected to lead their armies in the field and act as patrons of the people. Ptolemy, who had been appointed satrap of Egypt, declared himself king in 305 BCE and made Alexandria his capital. Seleucus I received Babylonia and built an empire that at its height held central Anatolia, the Levant, Mesopotamia and Persia, though Pergamon, Bactria and Parthia later broke away.

Greek colonists and the Greek language spread to these realms, which also adopted local practice, so Hellenistic culture was a fusion. A Greek dialect called Koine became the common language of the ancient world. The age saw the rise of New Comedy, the Septuagint translation of the Hebrew Bible and the philosophies of Stoicism, Epicureanism and Pyrrhonism, and the mathematician Euclid and the polymath Archimedes belong to it. Alexandria, with its Library and Mouseion, was the centre of the preservation of earlier Greek literature.

Rome took over the Hellenistic world piece by piece. Attalus III bequeathed Pergamon to the Roman Republic in 133 BCE, Rome conquered Greece in 146 BCE, and Pontus fell in 63 BCE. The Battle of Actium in 31 BCE and the conquest of Ptolemaic Egypt the following year eliminated the last major Hellenistic kingdom. Scholars have proposed other end dates, but most accept 31 or 30 BCE. Nineteenth-century scholars often held the period to be a decline from classical Greece, a comparison now regarded as unfair.
heller-coin: The Heller, also called the Haller or Häller, and in Latin sources denarius hallensis, takes its name from the city of Hall am Kocher, today Schwäbisch Hall. Silver coins stamped on both sides, the Häller Pfennige, were also called Händelheller because they often depicted a hand. A distinction was made between white, red and black hellers. The composition deteriorated over time as copper was mixed in, until the coins were no longer thought of as silver. There were 576 hellers in a Reichsthaler, and the word also named a silver unit of weight equal to one 512th of a Mark.

In Swabia the heller at first matched the pfennig, with 240 hellers to a Carolingian pound, but an imperial edict of 1385 halved its value, so that 8 hellers equalled 4 pfennigs or one Kreuzer. In Bohemian Upper Lusatia the cities of Bautzen and Görlitz coined in alternate years in the 15th century, and the silver content of the Görlitz heller fell steadily.

Because the coins were of low value and uneven quality, it was common in the High and Late Middle Ages to weigh large sums of hellers and to deal in the total weight, which produced amounts in pound hellers. In Electoral Saxony from 1668 the small coins called Näpfchenheller became a nuisance in the Ore Mountains, where people dropped them in the collection bag, and Annaberg introduced special church pfennigs in response.

The Coinage Act of 9 July 1873 replaced the old currencies with marks and pfennigs, and the heller disappeared, apart from the last Bavarian hellers, which remained valid for some time after 1878 as half-pfennig coins. The word lived on elsewhere. In Austria-Hungary it was one hundredth of the krone from 1892 until 1918, and in Czechoslovakia and its successor states the haléř or halier was one hundredth of a koruna. The Czech National Bank removed the coins from circulation in 2008. In Switzerland the haller was the lowest coin from the late Middle Ages and survived as a nominal unit until the end of the 18th century.

From the Middle Ages the heller was a symbol of low worth. German speech keeps the idiom keinen roten Heller wert, not worth a red heller, along with eine Schuld auf Heller und Pfennig begleichen, to settle a debt in full, and seinen letzten Heller verlieren, to lose one's last heller. Ein Heller und ein Batzen is a student and soldier's song with words by Albert von Schlippenbach and music by Franz Kugler.
hellweg: In the Middle Ages Hellweg was the official and common name for the main travelling routes of Germany. Their breadth was set as an unimpeded passage the width of a lance, about three metres, which the landholders along the way had to maintain. Used without an adjective, the name usually means the Westphalian Hellweg, running from the lower Rhine east to the Teutoburg Forest, with the slopes of the Sauerland to its south, and linking the imperial cities of Duisburg, where the Ruhr meets the Rhine, and Paderborn.

At Paderborn it very probably joined at least two other main imperial roads, one leading east to the Harz mountains and the middle Elbe, the other north to the lower Weser and lower Elbe. The name is usually derived from Low German helwech, the wide bright clearway through the forest. Others derive it from a salt road, or read it as a way of the dead, as Grimm's dictionary does with Helvegr, the road to Hel.

As a corridor of long-distance overland trade, the Westphalian Hellweg was used by Charlemagne in his Saxon wars and was later kept up under imperial supervision. In the 10th and 11th centuries it was the preferred route of the Ottonian and Salian kings and emperors, who travelled along it at least once a year between their main estates in Saxony and the imperial city of Aachen when they were not in Italy or on campaign; important imperial palaces stood at both Duisburg and Paderborn. With the rise of coal and steel, medieval towns founded along the route, such as Gelsenkirchen, Bochum, Essen and Dortmund, grew into industrial centres that absorbed most of the region's population growth.
helmand-river: The Helmand, historically also called the Etymandros, is the longest river in Afghanistan and the main watershed of the Sistan Basin, which has no outlet to the sea. It rises in the Sanglakh Range of the Hindu Kush, in the north-east of Maidan Wardak Province, about 40 kilometres west of Kabul, where the Unai Pass separates it from the watershed of the Kabul River. It flows south-westward for 1,150 kilometres through Daykundi and Uruzgan provinces and past the city of Lashkargah in Helmand Province.

Beyond Lashkargah it enters the desert of Dasht-e Margo and then reaches the Sistan marshes and the Hamun-i-Helmand lake region around Zabol, on the border between Afghanistan and Iran. Smaller rivers such as the Tarnak and the Arghandab flow into it. The Arghandab is its chief tributary and has a major dam north of Kandahar, and the Kajaki Dam stands on the Helmand itself.

The name comes from the Avestan Haētumant, meaning dammed or having a dam, which referred to the river and the irrigated areas around it. The word is related to the Sanskrit Setumatī. The Avesta mentions the Helmand valley by name as the Aryan land of Haetumant, one of the early centres of the Zoroastrian faith in what is now Afghanistan.

By the late first millennium BCE and the early first millennium CE, communities of Hindus and Buddhists were so numerous in the Helmand and Kabul valleys that the Parthians referred to the region as India. From 1758 to 1842 the Helmand formed the northern border of the Brahui Khanate of Kalat.

The river is managed by the Helmand and Arghandab Valley Authority and is used extensively for irrigation, although a build-up of mineral salts has reduced its usefulness for watering crops. For much of its length it is free of salt. Its waters are essential to farmers in Afghanistan, and they also matter to farmers in the south-east of Iran, in the province of Sistan and Baluchistan.
helmin-wiels: Helmin Magno Wiels was born on 9 December 1958 into a lower-middle-class family from Westpunt. He worked as a social worker and radio maker before joining Niun paso atras, Papiamento for No step backwards, and forming Aliansa Sivil, the Civil Alliance.

In 2005 he founded Pueblo Soberano, or Sovereign People, a leftist party that won the popular vote in the elections of October 2012. Associated Press reports described his outspoken style as charismatic but sometimes divisive. He campaigned for Curaçao's independence from the Kingdom of the Netherlands and for closer ties with its South American neighbours, and wanted to stop U.S. Air Force surveillance planes on counter-drug missions in the Caribbean from using Willemstad's airport as a base.

He argued that an independent Curaçao should make Papiamento, English and Spanish its official languages, because, in his words, "Dutch is a dead language, the same as Greek or Latin". He had recently denounced the sale of Robbie's Lottery numbers through UTS, a public telecommunications company with no licence to sell them.

Wiels had received written death threats, and according to the Minister of Justice, Nelson Navarro, the government had given him security staff. On 5 May 2013 he sent his bodyguard home and went to Marie Pompoen Beach on the eastern side of the island, where at about 5 pm two men shot him five times and fled in a gold-coloured car.

His successor as party leader, Donald Balentina, suggested a political vendetta, while Ronald Plasterk, the Dutch Minister of the Interior and Kingdom Relations, said it could also be because of the way he took on corruption, the drugs world or something else. Police arrested Elvis Kuwas, known as Monster, a gunman of the No Limit Soldiers drug gang of the Koraalspecht district, which had planned the killing and paid him €23,000. In late August 2014 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for three murders, including Wiels's, and the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the ruling in July 2016.
helmold-of-bosau: Helmold was born near Goslar and grew up in Holstein.
