He was taught in Brunswick by Gerold, the future bishop of Oldenburg, and later came under the direction of Vicelinus, the Apostle of the Wends, first in the Augustinian monastery of Faldera, afterwards known as Neumünster. He became a deacon about 1150 and in 1156 parish priest at Bosau on the Großer Plöner See. He was a friend of both bishops of Oldenburg, Vicelinus, who died in 1154, and Gerold, who died in 1163.

At Bishop Gerold's instigation Helmold wrote his Chronica Slavorum, a history of the conquest and conversion of the Polabian Slavs from the time of Charlemagne to 1171, meant to show how Christianity and German influence gained a footing among the Wends, above all in eastern Holstein. As an eyewitness he describes the missionary work of Vicelinus, the founding of the bishopric of Oldenburg and its move to Lübeck, the merciless subjugation of the Wends and the settlers, chiefly Westphalian and Dutch, brought to their lands. The first part ends with 1168, the second with 1171.

Helmold could be a critical writer: he called Henry the Lion out for money and said that among Henry's troops in the Wendish Crusade there was only talk of money, never of Christianity. For the earliest period he drew on the church history of Adam of Bremen and other records, which he summarised unreliably, but he is the most important source for his own time, relying on what Vicelinus and Gerold told him. His trustworthiness was questioned in the 19th century because of his hostility to the archbishops of Bremen, though he is not held to have falsified facts intentionally.

The chronicle was first printed by Siegmund Schorkel at Frankfurt am Main in 1556, and Abbot Arnold of Lübeck continued it down to 1209. Heinz Stoob published the modern edition of the Latin text with a German translation, first in 1963.
helmut-kohl: Helmut Kohl was born on 3 April 1930 in Ludwigshafen, the third child of Hans Kohl, a Bavarian army veteran and civil servant, and Cäcilie Kohl. He joined the Christian Democratic Union in 1946, at the age of 16. In 1958 he took a doctorate in history at Heidelberg University, and then worked for a foundry and for the Industrial Union for Chemistry.

He was elected the youngest member of the Rhineland-Palatinate parliament in 1959. On 19 May 1969 he became minister-president of that state. As a reformer he focused on schools and education: his government abolished school corporal punishment and the parochial school, and he founded the University of Trier-Kaiserslautern. In 1973 he was elected national chairman of the CDU.

Kohl led the opposition under Chancellor Helmut Schmidt. The Free Democratic Party broke with its coalition partner in 1982, and on 1 October 1982 a constructive vote of no confidence deposed Schmidt, the only time a chancellor has been removed in that way. Three days later the Bundestag elected Kohl chancellor of a CDU/CSU-FDP coalition. His government stationed NATO mid-range missiles despite strong opposition from the peace movement.

On 22 September 1984 Kohl met the French president François Mitterrand at Verdun, and their long handshake became a symbol of Franco-German reconciliation. After the revolutions of 1989 his government acted decisively, and reunification followed in 1990. With Mitterrand he was an architect of the Maastricht Treaty, which established the European Union and the euro. He moved the federal capital from Bonn back to Berlin, though government offices relocated only in 1999. He lost the 1998 election to Gerhard Schröder and resigned as party leader.

In 1999 it emerged that the CDU had received and kept illegal donations during Kohl's leadership; Der Spiegel reported that he had not benefited personally but had run the party's finances outside the legal boundaries. His reputation suffered in Germany, though abroad he was still regarded as a European statesman. In 1998 the European heads of state or government named him Honorary Citizen of Europe, an honour previously given only to Jean Monnet. Kohl died on 16 June 2017 in Ludwigshafen, aged 87, and was buried in Speyer after a European act of state in Strasbourg.
helmut-schmidt: Helmut Schmidt was born on 23 December 1918 in Barmbek, a working-class district of Hamburg. He graduated from the Lichtwark School in 1937 and volunteered for military service that year, joining an anti-aircraft battery of the Luftwaffe. After brief service on the Eastern Front in 1941, including the Siege of Leningrad, he worked from 1942 at the Ministry of Aviation. From December 1944 he served as an Oberleutnant in the Flak artillery on the Western Front, and he was captured by the British in April 1945. He joined the Social Democratic Party in 1946 and read economics at the University of Hamburg.

Schmidt entered the Bundestag in 1953, and his sharp speeches won him the nickname Schmidt-Schnauze, Schmidt the Lip. From 1961 to 1965 he was Hamburg's senator of the interior. During the flood of 1962, in which 300 people drowned, he used all means at his disposal, including federal police and army units, even where that overstepped his legal authority. He is credited with saving a further 1,000 lives and rehousing thousands of homeless people, which gave him a reputation as a Macher, someone who gets things done. In Willy Brandt's government he served as defence minister from 1969 to 1972 and finance minister from 1972 to 1974.

He became chancellor on 16 May 1974, after Brandt resigned in an espionage scandal. The worldwide recession was his main problem, and he held to a tough line on public spending. With the French president Valéry Giscard d'Estaing he helped begin the world economic summits in 1975, signed the Helsinki Accords that year and helped set up the European Monetary System in 1978. He was re-elected in 1976 and 1980, but his coalition fell apart in 1982 when its partner, the Free Democratic Party, changed sides.

After leaving the Bundestag in 1986 Schmidt remained a public voice, as co-publisher of the weekly Die Zeit from 1983 and as the author of memoirs such as Men and Powers. He was a gifted pianist and recorded Mozart and Bach concertos. He died at his Hamburg home on 10 November 2015, aged 96, and a state funeral was held on 23 November. The University of the Federal Armed Forces in Hamburg bears his name.
helmuth-von-moltke-the-elder: Helmuth Karl Bernhard von Moltke was born on 26 October 1800 in Parchim, Mecklenburg-Schwerin, the son of Generalleutnant Friedrich Philipp Victor von Moltke, a German in Danish service. In 1806 French troops burned his father's country house and plundered his townhouse in Lübeck, leaving the family impoverished. At twelve he entered the Royal Danish Military Academy at Copenhagen, and in 1818 he became a page to King Frederick VI of Denmark and a second lieutenant. At twenty-one he left Denmark for the Prussian army, despite the loss of seniority, and after the general war school he graduated in 1826.

As a young officer Moltke worked on the military survey in Silesia and Posen and in 1832 was seconded to the general staff at Berlin. He wrote a short romance, The Two Friends, in 1827, and studies of Holland and Belgium and of Poland. In 1835 he took leave to travel in south-eastern Europe, and Sultan Mahmud II asked him to help modernise the Ottoman army. He stayed two years at Constantinople, learned Turkish and surveyed the city, the Bosporus and the Dardanelles.

On 29 October 1857 the new king appointed him Chief of the Prussian General Staff, a post he held for thirty years. He changed armament and communications, introduced staff rides, revised mobilisation and began a formal study of European politics for campaign planning. In 1860 he added a Railway Section; a contemporary wrote that he never made an important decision without consulting the railway timetables. He also commanded in the Second Schleswig War and the Austro-Prussian War.

In the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 his plans for a railway deployment south of Mainz, revised every year, were adopted without dispute. Five days after the mobilisation order he was made Chief of Staff of the Army for the war, with the right to issue orders equivalent to royal commands. He was made a count in October 1870 after Sedan and a field marshal in June 1871.

Moltke sat in the Reichstag from 1871 to 1891 and oversaw the General Staff's official histories of the wars, the history of the Franco-Prussian War appearing between 1874 and 1881. After the war he was a national hero, and more than fifty monuments to him were raised in Germany. He married Marie Burt in 1842 and remained devoted to her after her death in 1868. He died on 24 April 1891. He was the earliest-born person whose recorded voice survives: two wax cylinders made on 21 October 1889 hold a line of Hamlet and a passage of Faust.
helots: Ancient authors gave several accounts of where the name came from. Hellanicus linked it to the village of Helos, in the south of Sparta, and Pausanias repeats that its inhabitants were the first slaves of the Spartan state. Modern linguists connect it with a root meaning to be captured. Antiochus of Syracuse wrote that Lacedaemonians who did not join the expedition were judged slaves and named helots, while Ephorus of Cyme made them the perioikoi of Helos, reduced to slavery after a failed revolt.

Conquest was clearly part of the story: Messenians, conquered in the Messenian Wars of the 8th century BCE, became in Herodotus a synonym for helots. Theopompus said the earliest helots descended from Achaeans whom the Dorians had conquered, though not all Achaeans were reduced to helotry; the city of Amyclae kept a special status.

Helots were assigned to citizens to do domestic work or to farm their klēroi, the plots into which Messenia was first divided. They handed over a fixed share of the harvest and kept the surplus. Plutarch gives the amount as 70 medimnoi of barley for a man and 12 for a woman, while the poet Tyrtaeus speaks of half the produce; scholars debate both. Laconia and Messenia were fertile, so helots could often live fairly well. They lived in families, and some owned property: in 425 BCE some had their own boats, and in 223 BCE 6,000 bought their freedom for 500 drachmas each.

Spartan treatment was harsh. Thucydides says that most Spartan institutions were designed for security against the helots. Aristotle reports that the ephors declared war on them each year, and Myron of Priene that they received beatings regardless of wrongdoing. Some modern scholars read these accounts as ideological scorn rather than daily cruelty. Helots also followed Spartans as servants and light troops at Plataea, and Herodotus counts seven for each Spartan.

Helots could be freed, especially for military service. Thucydides tells that freedom was promised to those who carried supplies to the besieged Spartans on Sphacteria, and Xenophon that more than 6,000 volunteered when the Thebans invaded Laconia. The 700 helots who served Brasidas in Chalcidice in 424 BCE were freed as the Brasidians, and freed helots were called neodamodeis.

The earthquake of 464 BCE brought a major revolt, in which helots and perioikoi of Thouria and Aithaia, mostly of Messenian ancestry, held Mount Ithome. Plutarch says the Crypteia and other ill-treatment began after it. The Athenians later settled helots at Naupactus and garrisoned Pylos with Messenians. The helots were largely liberated by the Theban commander Epaminondas after the Theban–Spartan War.
helsingborg: Helsingborg stands at the narrowest part of the Øresund, the strait between Sweden and Denmark, about 4 km from the Danish city of Helsingør on the opposite shore. It is one of the oldest cities of what is now Sweden and has been the site of permanent settlement officially since 21 May 1085. Its position was very important for Denmark, which at that time controlled both sides of the strait.

From 1429 Eric of Pomerania introduced the Sound Dues, a levy on trading vessels passing through the sound between Helsingør and Helsingborg. The dues were one of the main sources of income for the Danish Crown. They were first directed against the Hanseatic League, and crossing traffic such as fishermen did not pay them.

After the Dano-Swedish War of 1657 to 1658 and the Treaty of Roskilde, Denmark had to give up all its territory on the southern Scandinavian peninsula, and Helsingborg became Swedish. King Charles X Gustav of Sweden landed there on 5 March 1658 to take personal possession of the Scanian lands, and a delegation led by Peder Winstrup, bishop of Lund, met him. The town then had barely 1,000 people. Denmark recaptured Scania twice but could not hold it, and the last attempt came in 1710, when 14,000 men landed near Helsingborg. The Battle of Helsingborg was fought just outside the city on 10 March, and the town recovered slowly, with only 1,321 inhabitants in 1770.

From the middle of the 19th century industrialisation made Helsingborg one of the fastest-growing Swedish cities, rising from 4,000 people in 1850 to 20,000 in 1890 and 56,000 in 1930. A train ferry linked it with Helsingør from 1892. In October 1943 it was one of the main landing points for Danish Jews, over 7,200 of whom, with 680 non-Jews, were smuggled across the Øresund to Sweden in three nights.

Helsingborg is the seat of its municipality in Scania, the second-largest city of that province after Malmö, with a population of 151,404 in 2024. Its medieval fortress, Kärnan, about 600 years old, stands in the city centre among old stone churches. Ferries still cross to Helsingør around the clock, and IKEA has its international corporate headquarters in the city.
helsingor: Helsingør stands at the narrowest part of the Øresund strait. Together with Helsingborg in Sweden, about 4 km across the water, it forms the northern reaches of the Øresund Region, which is centred on Copenhagen and Malmö. The first part of the name is believed to come from the word hals, meaning neck or narrow strait, and the ending from the Old Norse aurr or eyrr, a gravel or sandy shore. The town is first mentioned as Hælsingør in the Liber Census Daniæ of King Valdemar the Victorious, dating from 1231.

Around 1200 the first church, Saint Olaf's Church, was built; its oldest parts date from the 13th century and show that the fishing village had grown into a town of importance. The town as it is known today was founded in the 1420s by King Eric of Pomerania, who established the Sound Dues in 1429.

Ships had to stop at Helsingør to have their cargo taxed, and the income paid for a castle called Krogen, which Frederik II rebuilt in the 1570s as Kronborg. From 1479 to 1581 the number of ships passing through the strait grew 6.5 times, and in 1672 Helsingør was the third-largest town in Denmark. The abolition of the dues in 1857, by the Copenhagen Convention, was a heavy loss, and population grew slowly in the following decades.

During the Second World War the town was one of the main transport points in the rescue of Denmark's Jews. After Georg Ferdinand Duckwitz, a German diplomatic attaché, passed on word on 28 September 1943 of an order to deport them, Danes hid Jews in houses, farm lofts and churches in north Zealand and carried them in fishing boats and ferries across the Øresund to Sweden. In three nights over 7,200 Jews and 680 non-Jews were taken to safety in Helsingborg and Malmö.

The Helsingør shipyard, founded in 1882, employed 3,600 people at its height in 1957 and closed in 1983. The Wiibroe brewery, founded in 1840, brewed its last beer there in 1998. The old dockyard now holds a cultural centre, opened in 2010, and the Danish Maritime Museum. Kronborg Castle is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Shakespeare's Hamlet, set mostly there under the English spelling Elsinore, has been performed in its courtyard every year since 1937. The ferry line to Helsingborg is the busiest car ferry route in the world.
helsinki-final-act: The Final Act was the document signed at the closing meeting of the third phase of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, held in Helsinki between 30 July and 1 August 1975, after two years of negotiations known as the Helsinki Process. All then-existing European countries except Andorra and Hoxhaist Albania signed it, together with the United States and Canada,to improve détente. It did not have treaty status and did not need ratification by parliaments, so it was not binding. Henry Kissinger told Gerald Ford in August 1974 that the United States had never wanted the conference but had gone along with the Europeans.

The Final Act was arranged in four groupings called baskets. The first, the Declaration on Principles Guiding Relations between Participating States, set out ten points, among them sovereign equality, refraining from the threat or use of force, inviolability of frontiers, territorial integrity, non-intervention in internal affairs, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, and equal rights and self-determination of peoples. The second basket promised economic, scientific and technological cooperation. The third dealt with family reunions, marriages and travel, the conditions of journalists and cultural exchanges. The fourth set out procedures to monitor implementation and to plan future meetings. The United States sought a ban on radio jamming but found no consensus because of Soviet opposition.

Many Americans of Eastern European descent feared that the agreement would accept Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and the forced incorporation of the Baltic States. Ford told a group of them in July 1975 that American policy on the Baltic States would not change, and that the Final Act denied annexation of territory in violation of international law. Ronald Reagan made the accords a centrepiece of his campaign against Ford in the 1976 Republican primaries, and Jimmy Carter attacked them as a legitimation of Soviet domination of Eastern Europe.

The document was seen both as a step toward reducing Cold War tensions and as a diplomatic boost for the Soviet Union, because of its clauses on frontiers. Its human rights provisions nevertheless became the basis for the work of the Helsinki Watch, which monitored compliance and evolved into the International Helsinki Federation and Human Rights Watch. The historian John Lewis Gaddis wrote that the accords gradually became a manifesto of the dissident and liberal movement. They also served as the groundwork for the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
helvetic-republic: The Helvetic Republic was a sister republic of France that existed during the French Revolutionary Wars. The Old Swiss Confederacy had consisted of self-governing cantons united by a loose military alliance, ruling over subject territories such as Vaud. French armies entered on the grounds of liberating the Swiss from a system deemed feudal, and some Swiss, including Frédéric-César de La Harpe, had called for intervention. The invasion proceeded largely peacefully, and on 5 March 1798 French troops overran the country and the old Confederacy collapsed. The name came from the Helvetii, the Gaulish inhabitants of the Swiss Plateau in antiquity.

The constitution, designed mainly by the Basel magistrate Peter Ochs, set up a Grand Council and a Senate and a five-member Directory. It also created a single Swiss citizenship in place of citizenship of a town or village, which led to conflict over common land that wealthier citizens did not want to share with the generally poor new citizens. Cantonal sovereignty and feudal rights were abolished, and the republic had more than six constitutions in four years.

Resistance was strongest in the Catholic centre, partly because of limits on freedom of worship. Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden raised about 10,000 men under Alois von Reding, but the French general Schauenburg's victory near Sattel led Schwyz to surrender on 4 May 1798. A further uprising in Nidwalden was crushed that year, with villages burnt by French troops. The treaty of alliance of 19 August 1798 broke the Confederacy's tradition of neutrality. Unitarians, who wanted a united republic, struggled with Federalists, who wanted cantonal sovereignty. In 1799 Switzerland became a battle zone between French, Austrian and Russian armies, and by 1802 the republic was 12 million francs in debt, with the Stecklikrieg civil war under way.

Napoleon Bonaparte, First Consul of France, summoned both sides to Paris and considered Switzerland federal by nature. The Act of Mediation of 19 February 1803 abolished the republic and restored the cantons. Its Directory resembles the Federal Council, and the period was a step toward the Federal Constitution of 1848. For the first time the population was defined as Swiss, not as inhabitants of a canton. Judgements still differ: Carl Hilty called it the first democratic experience on Swiss territory, conservatives see national weakness, and Vaud, Thurgau and Ticino count it as liberation from other cantons.
helvetii: According to Julius Caesar the Helvetii were divided into four subgroups, of which he names the Verbigeni and the Tigurini; Posidonius names the Tigurini and the Tougeni. They had no kings at the time of their clash with Rome but seem to have been governed by a class of noblemen. The earliest attestation of the name is a graffito of about 300 BCE from Mantua, in Etruscan letters. Ptolemy and Tacitus place the Helvetii originally in southern Germany, north of the Rhine, and their move to the Swiss Plateau is usually placed in the late 2nd century BCE.

The Tigurini joined the raids of the Cimbri and Teutones, and in 107 BCE they killed the consul L. Cassius Longinus at the Battle of Burdigala. In 58 BCE, after the nobleman Orgetorix, who had planned a new migration, died before he could be tried, the Helvetii burned their homes and set out with the Raurici, Latobrigi, Tulingi and a group of Boii, intending to settle among the Santones. Caesar closed the bridge at Geneva against them and attacked the part of their force still on the east bank of the Saône. He then caught them near Bibracte, where they retreated and later surrendered.

Caesar allowed the Helvetii to return and rebuild their homes, and Cicero later counted them among the allied tribes bound by treaty. Caesar reports a total of 368,000 people, of whom 263,000 were Helvetii, and a census of 110,000 survivors. Modern scholars think these figures far too high: only one of fifteen Celtic oppida in their territory shows destruction by fire, and Furger-Gunti estimates about 160,000 emigrants and 40,000 warriors.

The Helvetii were subjugated after 52 BCE. Under Augustus Celtic oppida such as Vindonissa and Basilea became Roman garrisons, and a Helvetian uprising was crushed in 68 CE by Aulus Caecina Alienus. The Swiss Plateau was incorporated into Gallia Belgica in 22 BCE and into Germania Superior in 83 CE, and the Helvetii were largely Romanised by the 2nd century. In the later 3rd century Roman control weakened and the Alemanni invaded. The Alemanni and Burgundians settled permanently in the 5th and 6th centuries, and the Helvetii were largely assimilated, contributing to the origin of the modern Swiss people.
helvis-of-ramla: Helvis was the daughter of Baldwin I of Ramla and his wife Stephanie of Flanders. Stephanie had earlier been married to Guy of Milly and had three sons by him, Guy, Henry and Philip of Milly, and with Baldwin she also had a son, Renier. Around 1137 or 1138 Helvis married Barisan, constable of the county of Jaffa.

When her father died in 1138, Helvis and Barisan inherited Ramla and the castle of Mirabel. In 1143 or 1144 her brother Renier claimed them, which suggests that he was younger and had then come of age. Meanwhile, probably around 1141, King Fulk of Jerusalem granted Barisan the newly built castle of Ibelin, perhaps as a reward for his support during the revolt of Count Hugh II of Jaffa in 1134, perhaps as compensation for the coming loss of Ramla and Mirabel. Renier died childless between 1146 and 1148, and the lordship returned to Helvis and Barisan.

They had five children: Hugh, Baldwin and Balian of Ibelin, Ermengarde, who married Elinand of Tiberias, and Stephanie. After Barisan's death in 1150 Ibelin passed to their eldest son, Hugh, and Helvis soon married Manasses of Hierges, constable of Jerusalem and a relative of Queen Melisende, who probably arranged the match. At about this time Melisende's son, Baldwin III of Jerusalem, came of age and claimed the kingdom. Manasses took the queen's side, and Baldwin III besieged and captured Mirabel and sent Manasses into exile. Helvis's sons supported Baldwin III, possibly because they resented their mother's marriage and the loss of Ramla and Mirabel that followed.

Helvis and Manasses seem to have remained married despite his exile, since she never married again. They had two daughters: Helvis, who married Anselm of Brie, and Isabella, who married Hugh of Mimars. After her death Ramla and Mirabel passed to her eldest son, Hugh of Ibelin, and through her the lordship of Ramla became part of the inheritance of the Ibelin family.
hemachandra: Hemachandra was born Caṅgadeva at Dhandhuka, in present-day Gujarat, on the full moon day of the month of Kartika. Sources differ on the year, but 1088 is generally accepted. His father, Cāciga, was a Moḍha Bania and his mother, Pāhini, was a Jain. The Jain monk Devacandra Sūri, who visited Dhandhuka, was impressed by the boy's intellect and took him to Khambhat, where he was placed in the care of the local governor Udayana. He was initiated as a monk and given the name Somacandra, trained in religious discourse, philosophy, logic and grammar, and at 21 was ordained an ācārya of the Śvetāmbara school at Nagaur in present-day Rajasthan, taking the name Hemacandra.

Gujarat was then ruled by the Chaulukya dynasty from Aṇahilavāḍa, now Patan, and Hemachandra lived there during the four monsoon months of each year, when Jain monks stay in one place, and wrote most of his works there. He was introduced to the king Jayasiṃha Siddharāja, who in 1135 conquered Malwa and brought back the manuscripts of Bhoja. Siddharāja admired a treatise on Sanskrit grammar among them and asked his scholars for one as lucid. Hemachandra studied eight treatises from Kashmir and wrote the Siddha-Hema-Śabdanuśāśana, named for himself and the king, which the king had paraded through the streets on an elephant.

He later became adviser to Kumārapāla, whom tradition says he had hidden from Siddharāja under a pile of manuscripts; scholars regard the story as a common folk motif. Kumārapāla was a Shaiva, but he became a devoted follower of Hemachandra and a champion of Jainism, and animal slaughter was banned in the state. Hemachandra himself is said to have bowed before the Shiva lingam at Somnath, saying that he bowed to whoever had destroyed the passions, whether Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva or Jina.

His grammar covers Sanskrit and several forms of Prakrit and gives the only known grammar of Apabhraṃśa, the precursor of Gujarati; the king had copies made and had scholars teach it, with a public examination every year. The Dvyāśraya Kāvya, a poem on the history of the Chaulukya dynasty, illustrates it. His Triṣaṣṭi-śalākā-puruṣa-caritam retells the lives of the 63 great figures of Jainism, and the Yogaśāstra sets out the Jain path. He also wrote lexicons, works on poetics and prosody, and, around 1150, described the Fibonacci sequence while analysing the rhythms of Sanskrit verse. He announced his death six months ahead and fasted in his last days, the Jain practice called sallekhana, before dying at Patan.
hemadri: Hemadri Pandita, popularly called Hemadpant, was born into a Deshastha Brahmin family of Paithan whose origins lay in Karnataka, and he was brought up in Maharashtra by his father, Kamadeo. A later biography describes him as a Rigvedi Brahmin of the Vatsa gotra, citing his own Chaturvarga Chintamani for the information.

Hemadri served as prime minister of the Seuna, or Yadava, kingdom, which ruled the western and southern part of India. He was at once a diplomat, an administrator, an architect, a poet, a theologian and a scholar. During his years in office the Yadava kingdom reached its height; soon afterwards Alauddin Khalji, the Turkic ruler of Delhi, and his successors brought Yadava rule to an end.

He is credited with several reforms of government and daily life. He introduced the Modi script, a cursive way of writing Marathi, into government correspondence, where it remained in use until the end of Peshwa rule, and he devised the Mestakas to standardise the procedures of state administration. He is also said to have introduced pearl millet, bajari, as a staple crop.

His chief work, the Chaturvarga Chintamani, is an encyclopedic treatment of dharma that describes, among much else, thousands of vratas, religious vows, with the way each is to be performed. He also wrote the Āyurveda Rasāyan, a commentary on the medical treatise Ashtānga Hṛdayam, with descriptions of diseases and their remedies, and a short historical work, the Hemadpanti Bakhar, or Hemadpant's Chronicle, is ascribed to him. He supported artists and writers such as Bopadev, studying their books and offering his own criticism. The Hemadpanti style of architecture, in which buildings and temples were raised without lime, is named after him.
hemis-monastery: The monastery stands in Hemis on the bank of the Indus River, and the village lies on the Leh-Manali Highway. In 1672 the Ladakhi king Sengge Namgyal re-established it. In its courtyard a gallery holds paintings of the Eighty-Four Mahasiddhas, the great tantric masters, made in the 17th century with ground mineral pigments. The festival is held in the rectangular courtyard before the main door, open but for two raised square platforms with a sacred pole at the centre.

In 1894 the Russian journalist Nicolas Notovitch claimed that Hemis was the source of an unknown gospel, the Life of Saint Issa, Best of the Sons of Men, which said that Jesus had travelled to India in his lost years. Notovitch said the monks showed it to him in the library while he recovered from a broken leg and that his guide translated it. Historians regard the evidence as his own fabrication, which he allegedly admitted, and the Bible scholar Bart D. Ehrman wrote that no recognised scholar doubts that the whole story was invented.

The Indian Pandit Swami Abhedananda later claimed to have read the same manuscript on a visit to Hemis in 1921, translated for him by a local lama, and published an account that largely matched Notovitch's. After Abhedananda's death one of his disciples asked about the documents at the monastery and was told that they had disappeared.

The Hemis festival, held in early June, honours Padmasambhava, Guru Rinpoche, whom believers hold to have been born on the 10th day of the fifth month of the Monkey year. It opens with an early morning ritual on the roof of the gompa, where a portrait is displayed to the sound of drums, cymbals and pipes. Its mask dances, known in Ladakh as chams, belong to the tantric Vajrayana tradition.
hemu: Contemporary accounts of Hemu's early life are incomplete because of his humble background, and the Mughal historians Bada'uni and Abu'l-Fazl, who served at Akbar's court, were often biased. It is generally accepted that he was born into a Hindu family of limited means and spent his childhood in Rewari, south-west of Delhi, and he worked young as a trader in saltpetre.

After Sher Shah Suri died in 1545, his son Islam Shah ruled the Sur Empire, and Hemu became superintendent of the market in Delhi. Islam Shah liked to place Hindus in command alongside Afghan officers so that they could spy on each other, and he gave Hemu the responsibilities of a high-ranking officer. Islam Shah died on 30 October 1553, and his 12-year-old son Firoz Shah was killed within three days by his uncle Adil Shah Suri. Hemu backed Adil Shah and rose to chief minister, and Abu'l-Fazl wrote that he undertook all appointments and dismissals and the distribution of justice.

Hemu is reputed to have won 22 battles for Adil Shah, many of them against Afghans who had rebelled. He defeated Taj Khan Karrani at Chibramau and again at Chunar, though Karrani escaped each time. After Humayun died on 26 January 1556, Hemu marched rapidly from Bengal and drove the Mughals out of Bayana, Etawah, Sambhal, Kalpi and Narnaul, and the governor of Agra fled without a fight.

Tardi Beg Khan, Akbar's governor in Delhi, met him at Tughlaqabad. According to Bada'uni, Hemu's army included 1,000 war elephants and 50,000 cavalry. The Mughal van and left wing drove back the enemy, but Hemu charged with a reserve of 300 elephants and picked horsemen, and the Mughal officers fled. He took Delhi on 7 October 1556 and assumed the title of Vikramaditya. Historians disagree about what this meant: Satish Chandra doubts that Hemu declared himself independent, while others, citing Ahmad Yadgar, say that he raised the royal canopy and had coin struck in his name.

On 5 November 1556 the Mughal army met Hemu at Panipat. He led his army on an elephant, and the battle was turning in his favour when a Mughal arrow wounded him in the eye and he collapsed unconscious. His army panicked and broke, and about 5,000 dead lay on the field. Bairam Khan asked the 13-year-old Akbar to behead the captive Hemu, and according to the contemporary Muhammad Arif Qandhari he did so and took the title of Ghazi. Hemu's head was sent to Kabul and his body was gibbeted on a gate of Delhi. Abu'l-Fazl praised his spirit, courage and enterprise. Supporters erected a memorial to him at Panipat, known as Hemu's Samadhi Sthal.
hen-wlad-fy-nhadau: When it was composed the song was known as Glan Rhondda, Banks of the Rhondda. It was first performed in the vestry of the original Capel Tabor in Maesteg, in January or February 1856, by Elizabeth John of Pontypridd, and it soon became popular in the locality. The composer James James was a harpist who played for dancing in the public house he ran. The tune was meant to be in six-eight time but was slowed to its present three-four tempo when large crowds began to sing it.

Its popularity grew after the Llangollen Eisteddfod of 1858, where Thomas Llewelyn of Aberdare won a competition for an unpublished collection of Welsh airs that included Glan Rhondda. The adjudicator, John Owen, known by the bardic name Owain Alaw, asked to include it in his Gems of Welsh melody (1860–1864). That volume gave it the title Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau and sold in large numbers, which spread the song across Wales.

At the Bangor Eisteddfod of 1874 the song was sung by the soloist Robert Rees, known as Eos Morlais. It was increasingly sung at patriotic gatherings and gradually became a national anthem. On 11 March 1899 Madge Breese sang it for the Gramophone Company in the first recording made in the Welsh language.

In 1905 the Welsh rugby team hosted the first touring team from New Zealand, which began every match with a haka. In reply the Wales player Teddy Morgan led the crowd in singing the anthem, which is said to have been the first national anthem sung at the start of a sporting event. Over the next four decades it became the more popular anthem in Wales, although the official anthem was then God Save the King. It was sung with other anthems before sporting events until 1975, when officials decided it should be sung alone.

Like the other anthems of the United Kingdom, it has no official status in law, but it is used at government ceremonies, including the opening of the Senedd, and at receptions of the British monarchy since the 1970s. Usually only the first stanza and chorus are sung, in Welsh. In 1978 Geraint Jarman a'r Cynganeddwyr recorded a version with electric guitars for an album of the same name, inspired by Jimi Hendrix's version of the Star-Spangled Banner.

The tune has been adapted for the anthems of Cornwall, Brittany and Y Wladfa, the Welsh settlement in Patagonia, where Lewis Evans wrote Gwlad Newydd y Cymry. The refrain's phrase Pleidiol wyf i'm gwlad, I am devoted to my country, was printed on the edge of pound coins minted in 1985, 1990, 1995 and 2000, and appears in the Royal Badge of Wales adopted in 2008.
henan: Henan means south of the river, the river being the Yellow River, though changes in its course and in administrative boundaries mean that about a quarter of the province now lies north of it. The province is also abbreviated Yu, after Yuzhou, the name of the region in the ancient system of nine provinces. Most of it forms part of the North China Plain, called the breadbasket of China, with floodplains in the east and mountains in the west. The Yellow River enters from the north-west, and its silt has raised the river bed and caused floods that shaped the region. Mount Song and its Shaolin Temple lie near Zhengzhou.

Prehistoric cultures such as the Yangshao and Longshan were active in what is now northern Henan. The later Erlitou culture has been controversially identified with the Xia dynasty. The Shang dynasty, from about 1600 to about 1046 BCE, had its capitals in the province, and the oracle bone inscriptions found at Yinxu in Anyang give insight into its writing, rituals and social structure. After the Zhou overthrew the Shang at the Battle of Muye, the political centre moved away from Henan for the first time. Under the Han, Luoyang became the political and cultural heart of the empire.

Henan passed repeatedly between rival regimes from 220 to 589, yet remained an agricultural base. Emperor Yang of Sui had the Grand Canal extended to Luoyang. In the Five Dynasties period Kaifeng became the capital of four dynasties, and under the Song, who reunified China in 982, Kaifeng overtook Luoyang and Chang'an as the largest city in China and in the world. In 1127 the Jurchens captured Kaifeng and took the Song emperor prisoner, and in 1194 the Yellow River changed course, displacing millions.

After the rebel Li Zicheng took Luoyang in 1641, his forces besieged Kaifeng three times. During the third, Ming troops breached the Yellow River dikes to flood the rebels. The water submerged the city, and of its 378,000 residents only 30,000 survived. A dike breach at Zhengzhou on 30 September 1887 killed over two million people by one account, with estimates from 930,000 to 7 million. In 1938 the government led by Chiang Kai-shek bombed the Huayuankou dam to halt the Japanese advance, causing floods that killed hundreds of thousands. A famine followed in 1942–43.

Henan is a province of central China with Zhengzhou as its capital. Four historical capitals of China, Luoyang, Anyang, Kaifeng and Zhengzhou, lie within it. It has a population of over 99 million, the third largest of any province and the largest among inland provinces. The capital moved from Kaifeng to Zhengzhou in 1954 because of the city's importance for rail transport.
henck-arron: Henck Alphonsus Eugène Arron was born in Paramaribo on 25 April 1936. After finishing high school in 1956 he went to the Netherlands to study banking and worked for several years at the Amsterdamsche Bank. Back in Suriname he joined the staff of the Vervuurts Bank and in late 1963 became deputy director of the Volkskredietbank. He had joined the National Party of Suriname, the main Creole party, in 1961, and became its chairman in 1970.

In 1973 Arron formed a coalition with the pro-independence Nationalist Republican Party that won that year's general election, and he became prime minister on 24 December 1973. He led the final negotiations for independence, finding an ally in the Dutch Labour Party, which wanted it as soon as possible. His announcement in February 1974 that Suriname would seek independence before the end of 1975 surprised many observers, since his own party had no majority in favour of it.

Independence came on 25 November 1975 amid social unrest, economic depression and rumours of corruption, and in the first years about a third of the population emigrated to the Netherlands. Arron won a further term in the 1977 elections, in which the country's leaders were accused of fraud. When non-commissioned officers of the new Suriname National Army tried to form a union over corruption and poor pay, he refused to recognise them and had their leaders arrested, with a trial set for 26 February 1980. On 25 February the military under Dési Bouterse overthrew and jailed him.

Released under house arrest in 1981, after corruption charges were dropped, Arron returned to banking and became managing director of the Surinamese People's Credit Bank. When the military government, under pressure from the United Nations, the Netherlands, France and the United States, allowed a return to democracy, he was elected vice-president, serving from 26 January 1988 under President Ramsewak Shankar until another coup by Bouterse in December 1990. He died of cardiac arrest at his brother's home in the Netherlands on 4 December 2000, having been invited to speak on 25 years of Surinamese independence. That year he received the Grand Cordon of the Honorary Order of the Yellow Star.
hendrick-theyanoguin: Theyanoguin was born in Westfield, Massachusetts, to a Mohawk noblewoman and a royaner, or sachem, and under the Mohawk matrilineal system belonged to his mother's Bear Clan. Known in childhood as Long Bow, he took the name Hendrick, possibly on becoming a Christian; the French later called him Tête Blanche for his white hair. In 1710 he inherited the royaner title Saquainquaragton. Until the late 20th century his life was confused with that of an earlier Wolf Clan royaner, Hendrick Tejonihokarawa, as both appeared in English sources as Hendrick Peters.

During King George's War he became a leading figure at Canajoharie, the Upper Village on the south bank of the Mohawk River, where he formed his bond with William Johnson. Johnson's accounts name him more than any other Indigenous American, recording boots, a laced coat, medicine, money and private presents. In June 1744 he led the Mohawk delegation that renewed the Covenant Chain at Albany with Governor George Clinton of New York, and in July 1745 he told the Pennsylvania diplomat Conrad Weiser that the Albany commissioners had cheated the Mohawks out of their land.

In 1746 he led 46 Mohawks to a conference in Montreal with the Marquis de Beauharnois, governor of New France, raiding Isle La Motte on the way back, and in the spring of 1747 he led a war party to the St. Lawrence River. In 1753 he voiced Mohawk anger at fraudulent land patents and the rum trade, and in January 1755 he went to Philadelphia at the invitation of Governor Robert Hunter Morris, returning in May with assurances that Pennsylvania would recognise Mohawk land claims.

When the French threatened Albany he led over 200 Mohawks down the Hudson Valley to join Johnson, though he feared having to fight Catholic Mohawks from Canada. At Lake George he warned of his men: "If they are to fight they are too few; if they are to be killed they are too many." Too old and corpulent to travel on foot, he rode one of Johnson's horses; it was shot from under him in the attempted surprise south of Lake George, and he was bayonetted. His son Sahonwadie, Young Hendrick, later settled at Canajoharie.
hendrik-carloff: By his own testimony Carloff was born in the Duchy of Finland, and he began his career as a cabin boy. In 1637 the Dutch West India Company employed him in Dutch Brazil, first as a soldier and then as a writer, and from 1645 to 1649 he served at Fort Elmina and Fort Nassau on the Gold Coast. Feigning illness, he returned to Europe hoping to find backers for a plan of his own.

After twelve years with the company he entered the service of Louis de Geer, who founded the Swedish Africa Company at Stade, as its commander and director. He occupied Butre in 1650, Anomabu in 1651 and Orsou in 1652. Sailing home in September 1652, his ship Christina, carrying about twenty bags of gold and 6,500 elephant teeth, was seized and taken to Plymouth. In Sweden he was knighted on 3 May 1654.

On 27 March 1657 he went over to King Frederick III of Denmark and became director-general of the Danish Africa Company. His ship Glückstadt, with 18 cannons and 48 crew, reached the coast on 25 January 1658 and took Fort Carolusborg two days later, when the gate was opened in the morning; the governor, Johann Philipp von Krusenstjerna, was arrested and about 185 kg of gold and several tons of ivory were seized. For Charles X Gustav of Sweden this was a reason to break off peace talks with Denmark.

From 1665 he advised the French West India Company under Jean-Baptiste Colbert and contracted to carry enslaved people from Africa to the French West Indies in return for sugar. In 1669 he sailed from Le Havre to Africa, where 1,000 slaves were embarked; over 750 were delivered in Martinique.

In 1676 he was appointed commissioner-general for a Dutch plan to resettle Tobago, abandoned after an English attack in 1672, and Jacob Binckes sailed with the expedition. Admiral Jean d'Estrées attacked the colony in 1677, and on 12 December a French cannonball set off the fortress's gunpowder store, killing about 250 men. Carloff's own part is unclear: he had been at odds with Binckes and seems to have been taken into custody. Little more is recorded of him, and he died in or after 1677.
hendrik-van-rheede: Van Rheede was born on 13 April 1636 into a noble family that played a leading part in the life of the province of Utrecht. His mother, Elisabeth van Utenhove, died in 1637, and his father, Ernst van Rheede, when he was four. The youngest of seven children, he left home at fourteen and in 1656 joined the Dutch East India Company (VOC) as a soldier, serving under Admiral Rijcklof van Goens against the Portuguese on the west coast of India.

During the siege of Cochin in 1663 he was ordered to arrest the old queen, Rani Gangadhara Lakshmi, which saved her from the massacre of the royal family, and he became the first councillor of the kingdom under the VOC's king, Vir Kerala Verma. He later served at Jaffna, Quilon and in Ceylon. His preference for negotiation over Van Goens's repressive measures brought a forced resignation in 1669, but he was soon given command of Dutch Malabar, where he fought the Zamorin of Calicut in 1671.

Back in Amsterdam from June 1678, he became Lord of Mijdrecht in 1680. In 1684 the Council of Seventeen sent him to inspect the Cape Colony, Ceylon and Dutch India against corruption. At the Cape he recommended measures for forestry and viniculture and ruled that slave children be taught to read and write, and the area of Groot Drakenstein was named after him. He died at sea off Bombay on 15 December 1691, some say poisoned, and was buried at Surat.

Work on the Hortus Malabaricus began in 1674. Its Latin volumes give plant names in Latin, Sanskrit, Arabic and Malayalam, covering the Malabar of his time, the stretch of the Western Ghats from Goa to Kanyakumari. Its medical knowledge was drawn from palm-leaf manuscripts by the Ezhava healer Itty Achuden, with the Konkani physicians Appu Bhatt, Ranga Bhatt and Vinayaka Pandit, and the botanists Jan Commelin and Johannes Munnicks edited it. Carl Linnaeus, in his Genera Plantarum of 1737, judged Rheede the most accurate of the three authors he trusted.
hendrik-verwoerd: Hendrik Frensch Verwoerd was born in Amsterdam on 8 September 1901 and remains the only foreign-born prime minister of South Africa. His father, a grocer and lay evangelist, moved the family to South Africa in 1903 out of sympathy for the Afrikaners after the Second Boer War. He took a doctorate in psychology at Stellenbosch University in 1925, studied in Germany from 1926 to 1927, and in 1928 became professor of applied psychology at Stellenbosch.

In 1937 he became the first editor of Die Transvaler, which supported Afrikaner nationalism. In 1943 he sued The Star for libel after it called him a Nazi propagandist, and Justice Mallin dismissed the case, finding that he had supported Nazi propaganda and made his paper a tool of the Nazis in South Africa.

After the National Party won the election of 26 May 1948, Verwoerd entered the Senate and in October 1950 became minister of native affairs. He drafted thirty-two bills between 1950 and 1953, more than in the previous two decades, and wrote the Bantu Education Act of 1953, which put black education under his ministry. He called his policy separate development, and justified apartheid abroad as good-neighbourliness.

He became prime minister on 2 September 1958. The Promotion of Bantu Self-government Act of 1959 provided for the resettlement of black South Africans in eight ethnic reservations, later ten, and abolished their parliamentary representation. Opposition was heavily repressed: tens of thousands were detained and the African National Congress and the Pan Africanist Congress were banned. David Pratt shot and wounded him on 9 April 1960. A referendum of white voters on 5 October 1960 approved a republic with 52 percent. In March 1961 he withdrew South Africa's application to remain in the Commonwealth after a resolution that racism was incompatible with membership, and the Republic of South Africa came into existence on 31 May 1961.

On 6 September 1966 Dimitri Tsafendas, a parliamentary messenger, stabbed Verwoerd in the House of Assembly in Cape Town. He was pronounced dead on arrival at Groote Schuur Hospital, and a state funeral in Pretoria was attended by a quarter of a million people. Tsafendas was found insane and held until his death in 1999, though a 2018 report concluded that he acted from a political motive.

Verwoerd is often called the architect of apartheid, though it began in 1948 under D. F. Malan. His actions prompted United Nations General Assembly Resolution 1761 of 1962 and South Africa's growing international isolation. Many places named after him have been renamed, among them the Verwoerd Dam, now the Gariep Dam, and the town of Verwoerdburg, now Centurion.
hengist-and-horsa: The Old English names Hengest and Horsa mean stallion and horse. Bede, writing in the 8th century, makes the brothers sons of Wictgils, son of Witta, son of Wecta, son of Woden, and the 9th-century History of the Britons attributed to Nennius gives a longer line reaching back to Geta, whom it calls the offspring of a heathen idol. Modern scholars regard the pair as mythical, pointing to their alliterative animal names, their seemingly constructed genealogy and the unknown nature of Bede's sources.

In the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Vortigern invites the brothers to fight the Picts; they land at Ebbsfleet, defeat the Picts and send home for more men. Under 455 it records that they fought Vortigern at Aylesford, where Horsa died, and that Hengist then ruled with his son Esc. Further victories follow at Crayford in 457, where four thousand Britons are said to have been killed, and in 465, and the last entry, for 473, has the Britons fleeing from the English like fire.

The History of the Britons tells a fuller story. Hengist wins Kent by giving his daughter to Vortigern in marriage, sends for his son Ochta and Ebissa, and is driven back to Thanet by Vortigern's son Vortimer. At a feast meant to seal a peace he has his men hide knives, gives the signal nima der sexa and massacres the British leaders, the episode known as the Treachery of the Long Knives. In the 12th century Geoffrey of Monmouth expanded the tale, naming the daughter Rowena.

In Geoffrey's version Hengist is captured by Eldol, Duke of Gloucester, after a battle near Kaerconan and beheaded. Tradition placed his burial at Hengistbury Head, but its mounds date to the Bronze Age. Rudolf Simek sees horse-head gables in Lower Saxony, still called Hengst und Hors around 1875, as a sign that the pair were first horse-shaped mythological beings, while J. R. R. Tolkien argued that the Hengest of Beowulf was a historical man. Thomas Jefferson proposed the brothers for the Great Seal of the United States in 1776, and two British gliders of the Second World War bore their names.
hengistbury-head: Hengistbury Head, formerly also called Christchurch Head, is a sandstone headland joined to Southbourne, a suburb of Bournemouth, and marks the eastern end of Poole Bay; its high ground is called Warren Hill. The Mudeford spit, a sand bar running from it, closes Christchurch Harbour from the south. Long part of Hampshire, it was placed in Dorset by the Local Government Act 1972. The name was recorded as Hedenesburia in an early 12th-century deed, and the antiquary Francis Grose wrongly linked it in 1779 with the Jutish leader Hengist.

An open-air camp of the Creswellian culture, dated to around 14,100 years ago, has yielded more than 13,000 stone artefacts and is probably the largest site of its period. Mesolithic hunter-gatherers used the headland once the sea had flooded the valley below. In the Bronze Age it was an important seaport, and its round barrows held axes, cremation urns and the high-status burial of a young woman with amber, copper alloy and gold.

Around 700 BCE a settlement was founded and the headland was cut off by the Double Dykes, two banks and ditches. Its people smelted iron and refined silver from silver-bearing copper, and thousands of bronze coins of the Durotriges suggest a mint. More North Italian wine amphorae have been found here than at all other sites of southern England together; most date from before 50 BCE, and the trade seems to have declined about the time of Caesar's campaigns in Gaul.

Iron-rich stones from the headland went into Christchurch Castle in the 11th century. Andrew Yarranton's harbour pier of 1693 failed, and from 1848 to 1872 the Hengistbury Mining Company quarried the ironstone boulders that hold the headland together, which with later erosion cost it up to a third of its area. In 1910 the first international aviation meeting in Britain was held there, during which Charles Rolls was killed, and in the Second World War the army occupied it with a radar station.

Bournemouth Borough Council bought the headland in 1930 to keep it as open space. It is a Scheduled Ancient Monument and a Local Nature Reserve, declared in 1990, and part of the Christchurch Harbour Site of Special Scientific Interest; a visitor centre displaying its archaeology opened in December 2013.
hengyang: Hengyang straddles the Xiang River about 160 kilometres south of the provincial capital Changsha. Mount Heng, one of the Five Sacred Mountains, lies 45 kilometres north of the city proper. Hengyang is also called the Wild Goose City, after the wild geese that used to rest here while flying south for the winter. Its humid subtropical climate has long, hot, humid summers and a brief winter.

The former name of the city was Hengzhou. It was the capital of a prefecture in the Tang dynasty, and officials out of favour at court were sent there as superintendents, among them Li Jingxuan, banished in 680. In the 750s the superintendent Chen Xi'ang used a private army to dominate his nominal superior, until a surprise attack killed him in 760. After falling to rebels under Yang Shiyuan, Hengzhou was recovered by Ma Yin, who made it part of his power base during the collapse of the Tang and later declared himself king of Ma Chu in the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

During the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, Wu Sangui declared himself Emperor of the Great Zhou and set up an imperial court at Hengzhou in 1678, then died of illness later that year. His grandson Wu Shifan retreated to Yunnan, and the Qing recovered Hengzhou the next year. The Battle of Hengyang was the longest defence of a single city in the Second Sino-Japanese War. After Changsha fell to the Imperial Japanese Army on 19 June 1944, Hengyang became the next target in the Ichi-Go offensive.

Hengyang is a transport hub where the Beijing–Guangzhou railway and the Hunan–Guangxi railway meet, and its industries include chemicals, mining equipment, textiles and paper. The city was badly damaged in the Second World War and few historical buildings survive, among them Shigu Academy, Dragon Tower, Laiyan Pagoda and Nantai Temple. It was the birthplace of the Ming scholar Wang Fuzhi and of the revolutionary Luo Ronghuan. The urban dialect belongs to the New Xiang group.
henri-alexis-brialmont: Brialmont was born in Venlo, in Limburg, on 25 May 1821. The whole of Limburg was then claimed by Belgium after the Belgian Revolution, until the Treaty of London of 1839 divided it. His father, Mathieu Brialmont, had been a captain in Napoleon's Grande Armée, served the Dutch and then the Belgian army, and became Minister of War in 1850. A poor pupil, Henri-Alexis still entered a military academy, and in 1859 he married the daughter of Louis de Potter, a leading figure of the Belgian Revolution.

He was commissioned in the engineers in 1843 and rose quickly: private secretary to the war minister, General Baron Félix Chazal, from 1847 to 1850, then the staff corps, colonel in 1868, major-general in 1874, when he took charge of Antwerp's fortifications, and lieutenant general in 1877. He ended as Inspector-General of the Army, retiring in 1892. During the Franco-Prussian War he was chief of staff of the Army of Antwerp, but he never served in a war.

He campaigned throughout his life for a larger army and navy, which brought him into conflict with Walthère Frère-Orban and the Liberals, and he argued for universal military service in place of the system of paid replacements. Leopold, Duke of Brabant, the future King Leopold II, shared his ideas, and Brialmont backed colonial expansion and helped to found the Congo Free State, though he declined to become the king's aide-de-camp. He founded the newspaper La Belgique Militaire in 1872 and wrote many books on fortification.

Brialmont held that forts had to stand several miles outside a city to keep long-range artillery away from it; his stood on average 4 kilometres out, in a ring of concrete works with retractable gun cupolas, and he urged wire entanglements against infantry as early as 1879. Twelve forts were built at Liège and nine at Namur between 1887 and 1892. In 1882 King Carol I of Romania commissioned him, as a private citizen, to design a ring of 18 forts around Bucharest, built from 1883 to 1900; the roads linking them became the basis of the city's ring road.

Brialmont died in Brussels on 21 July 1903. His forts were at the heart of the Belgian defence in 1914, at Liège, Namur and Antwerp, but gave way to German 420 mm and Austrian 305 mm howitzers. Some were upgraded and fought again in May 1940.
henri-christophe: Claims about Christophe's birthplace and early life have been contested since the early nineteenth century. He was born Christophe Henry on 6 October 1767, probably in Grenada but perhaps on Saint Kitts, the son of an enslaved mother and a free father, and was brought as a slave to the north of Saint-Domingue. He may have served in 1779 as a drummer boy in the Chasseurs-Volontaires de Saint-Domingue, a regiment of free people of colour that fought at the siege of Savannah. A popular story that he managed the hotel La Couronne in Cap-Français is not supported by the hotel's sales records. On 15 July 1793 he married Marie-Louise Coidavid, of the free black community of Cap-Français.

From the slave uprising of 1791 Christophe distinguished himself as a soldier and rose quickly to colonel. He fought for years beside Toussaint Louverture in the north, became commander-in-chief at Cap-Français, and by 1801 had been promoted to brigadier-general. After the French deported Louverture and sent more than 20,000 new troops under the Vicomte de Rochambeau, Jean-Jacques Dessalines led the fight that defeated them, and Christophe took charge of the north, where he supervised the first stages of building the Citadelle Laferrière.

In 1805, under Dessalines, he took part in the invasion of Santo Domingo, where he attacked the towns of Moca and Santiago. Dominican accounts, such as those of Gaspar de Arredondo y Pichardo and Alejandro Llenas, describe killings of prisoners and priests, the burning of towns, and the taking of captives to Haiti in the hundreds. A conspiracy of senior officers against Dessalines followed, which Christophe did not report; he was proclaimed head of a provisional government on 16 October 1806, and Dessalines was assassinated the next day.

After a power struggle with Alexandre Pétion, who became president of the Republic of Haiti in the south, Christophe withdrew to the Plaine-du-Nord and was elected president of the State of Haiti on 17 February 1807. In 1811 he made the north a kingdom and was crowned Henry I by the archbishop of Milot, renaming Cap-Français Cap-Henry. He created a nobility, which grew from 87 titles to 134, and named his son Jacques-Victor Henry as heir. He built the Citadelle Laferrière, the Sans-Souci Palace, a royal chapel at Milot and other palaces.

He kept plantation output up by corvée, forced labour in place of taxes, which the Haitian people resented, while Pétion divided land among peasants in the south. He reached an agreement with Britain, and in 1814 his ministers exposed French schemes to recover the colony. In 1820, unpopular, ill and fearing a coup, he shot himself. His son was assassinated ten days later, and General Jean-Pierre Boyer reunited the two parts of Haiti.
henri-coiffier-de-ruze-marquis-of-cinq-m: Cinq-Mars was the son of Marshal Antoine Coiffier de Ruzé, marquis d'Effiat, Superintendent of Finances and a close friend of Cardinal Richelieu, who took the boy under his protection when his father died in 1632. He was the second youngest of five children; his brothers were Martin de Ruzé, Marquis d'Effiat, and Jean Ruzé d'Effiat. Through his father's standing he came to court very early.

In the 1630s he commanded a company of the king's guards, and on 27 March 1638 he was granted the charter of Grand Master of the King's Wardrobe. In 1639 he became Grand Squire of France, which entitled him to be called Monsieur le Grand. After the exile of the royal favourite Marie de Hautefort he gained great influence over Louis XIII. Richelieu believed he could easily control him, but Cinq-Mars pressed the king for favours, urged him to remove or execute the cardinal and refused the posts outside Paris that Richelieu offered; their quarrel became public in 1639–1640.

In 1641 he took part in the failed rebellion of the Comte de Soissons. The next year he conspired with Gaston, Duke of Orleans, and with Spain, at war with France since 1635, to dismiss or assassinate Richelieu and sign a peace returning the strongholds France had conquered. The Spanish assembled 18,000 men in the Sedan region to support the conspirators. The meetings lacked discretion, and Richelieu's spies uncovered the plot in June 1642.

Cinq-Mars was imprisoned and tried on 6 September 1642, found guilty of high treason and beheaded on the Place des Terreaux in Lyon on 12 September with his accomplice, François Auguste de Thou. The writer Tallemant relates that the king showed no emotion and said he would like to see the grimace Cinq-Mars was making on the scaffold.

His story inspired Alfred de Vigny's novel Cinq-Mars, published in 1826, an opera of the same name by Charles Gounod, first performed on 5 April 1877, and a cantata by Barbara Strozzi on his execution. A painting by Paul Delaroche shows Richelieu in a barge ahead of the boat carrying Cinq-Mars and de Thou to their execution.
henri-de-la-tour-d-auvergne-viscount-of-: Turenne was the second son of Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon and sovereign Prince of Sedan, and of Elizabeth, daughter of William the Silent, Prince of Orange. He was born on 11 September 1611 into a Huguenot family. Physical weakness hampered him, and after his father died in 1623 he devoted himself to bodily exercise and largely overcame it. At fourteen he joined the camp of his uncle Maurice of Nassau as a private in his bodyguard in the Eighty Years' War. Frederick Henry of Nassau gave him a captaincy in 1626, and in 1630 he entered French service.

Turenne rose to prominence in the Thirty Years' War by capturing the fortress of Breisach in 1638, and became Marshal of France on 16 May 1643. In 1648 he defeated the Imperial army at Zusmarshausen. During the Fronde he first sided with the princes and was defeated at Rethel on 15 December 1650. He returned to royal service in May 1651, crushed the Prince of Condé's revolt at the Faubourg St Antoine on 2 July 1652 and re-occupied Paris. His victory at Arras in 1654 was a turning point against the Spanish, and Dunkirk in 1658 helped end that war. Louis XIV made him Marshal General of France two years later, and he converted to Catholicism only in 1668.

In the Dutch War of 1672 he accompanied the king's army to the gates of Amsterdam, where flooding checked him. In January 1673 he forced Brandenburg to make peace. With the allies in Alsace in the winter of 1674, he made a swift, secret march along the Vosges and defeated them at Turckheim on 5 January 1675. His troops looted the town in revenge for its resistance. Within weeks he had recovered Alsace.

Turenne was killed by an Imperial cannonball at the battle of Salzbach on 27 July 1675. He was buried at St Denis with the kings of France and, after the revolutionaries spared his remains in 1793, Napoleon had them moved in 1800 to the church of the Invalides in Paris. Napoleon advised soldiers to read and re-read his campaigns. Turenne avoided great battles, his maxim being few sieges and many combats.
henri-de-la-tour-dauvergne-duke-of-bouil: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne was born on 28 September 1555 at the castle of Joze-en-Auvergne, near Clermont-Ferrand. His parents were François de La Tour d'Auvergne, Viscount of Turenne, and Éléonore de Montmorency, eldest daughter of Anne, 1st Duc de Montmorency. After the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572 he took part in the siege of La Rochelle, but later returned to Protestantism. Compromised in the conspiracy of La Mole and Coconnat in 1574, he joined the Malcontents of François, Duke of Alençon, in 1575.

In 1576 he joined the Protestant party of Henry of Navarre, the future Henry IV, and negotiated the Peace of Nérac between Protestants and Catholics in 1579. Named lieutenant general of Upper Languedoc in 1580, he took part in the siege of Paris in 1590 and took Stenay from the Catholic League in 1591. After his first wife died in 1594, he married Elisabeth of Nassau, a daughter of William the Silent, in 1595. That year he was defeated at Doullens in Picardy by Fuentes, governor of the Spanish Low Countries, and in 1596 he was sent to England to renew the alliance with Queen Elizabeth I.

Compromised in the conspiracy of Biron in 1602, he fled to Geneva the following year and in 1606 had to accept a French protectorate over his duchy of Bouillon. On the death of Henry IV he entered the Council of Regency for the young Louis XIII and intrigued against the duc de Sully and Concini, the favourite of the regent Marie de' Medici. In April 1612 he went to London as her ambassador with a large following; according to the Venetian ambassador Antonio Foscarini, his instructions included an offer to marry Princess Christine of France to Prince Henry.

He died at Sedan on 25 March 1623. His only child by Charlotte de La Marck, a son, was born and died on 8 May 1594. By Elisabeth he had several children: Frédéric Maurice de La Tour d'Auvergne, who married Eleonora Catharina van den Bergh; daughters who married into the houses of La Trémoille, La Rochefoucauld and Durfort; and Henri, vicomte de Turenne, born on 11 September 1611.
henri-de-saint-simon: Henri de Saint-Simon was born in Paris on 17 October 1760 into an aristocratic family, a younger relative of the memoirist the Duc de Saint-Simon. Ambitious from youth, he drew up schemes for a canal joining the Atlantic and the Pacific and another from Madrid to the sea. Between 1779 and 1783 he fought alongside the Marquis de Lafayette in the American Revolution and took part in the siege of Yorktown under George Washington. He was captured by British forces near the end of his service, and on his release he studied engineering and hydraulics at the École de Mézières.

In 1789 he endorsed the ideals of the French Revolution and raised funds by land speculation for a large industrial project. With Talleyrand he planned to buy the cathedral of Notre-Dame, strip its roof and sell the metal. He was imprisoned on suspicion of counter-revolutionary activity and released in 1794. Currency depreciation had made him rich, but a business partner then took his fortune, and he lived in poverty for the rest of his life. His first book, Lettres d'un habitant de Genève (1802), called for a religion of science with Isaac Newton as a saint.

In 1817 he published a Declaration of Principles in L'Industrie. The industrial class, which he also called the working class, covered everyone engaged in productive work, from scientists and bankers to manual labourers. He saw its chief enemy in an idling class of able people who lived from the work of others, and he wanted hierarchies of managers and scientists, ranked by merit, to take decisions, with government limited to keeping production unhindered.

On 9 March 1823, in despair at the lack of results from his writing, Saint-Simon shot himself in the head six times and survived, losing the sight of one eye. His last work, Le Nouveau Christianisme (1825), returned to renewing society through Christian brotherly love. He died on 19 May 1825 and was buried in the Père Lachaise Cemetery.

His disciples formed a Saint-Simonian movement that stressed a planned economy, the abolition of inheritance and the emancipation of women. Marx and Engels counted him among the utopian socialists, while criticising his hope of change by persuading elites, and he also influenced John Stuart Mill, Pierre-Joseph Proudhon and Thorstein Veblen.
henri-giraud: Henri Honoré Giraud was born in Paris on 18 January 1879. He graduated from Saint-Cyr in 1900 and at his own request joined the 4th Zouaves Regiment in Tunisia. In the First World War he was gravely wounded leading a bayonet charge at the Battle of St. Quentin on 30 August 1914 and taken prisoner. With the help of a French nurse he escaped from the hospital at Origny-Sainte-Benoite with Captain Charles Schmitt on the night of 30 October, crossed into the neutral Netherlands with the help of Edith Cavell's escape network and reached Paris in February 1915.

Giraud served in the Rif War in 1925 and from 1930 to 1934 pacified the tribes of the High Atlas. In 1936 he became military governor of Metz, where Colonel Charles de Gaulle served under him from 1937. In 1940 he took command of the disintegrating Ninth Army on 15 May and was captured at Wassigny four days later. He was held at Königstein Fortress, and after he escaped to Vichy France in April 1942 he made contact with the Allies, who preferred him as the French leader.

After the Allied landings of November 1942 he took command of French troops in North Africa and, after the assassination of François Darlan on 24 December, became High Commissioner for French North and West Africa. He retained Vichy-era legislation, but in a speech in March 1943 he broke with the Vichy regime. On 3 June 1943 he and de Gaulle agreed to found the French Committee of National Liberation as co-presidents. De Gaulle gained control of the political situation, and on 9 November 1943 signed a decree removing Giraud from the committee.

In June 1946 Giraud was elected to the Constituent Assembly for Moselle and voted against the constitution of the Fourth Republic. He published Mes évasions in 1946 and Un seul but, la victoire in 1949. He died in a Dijon military hospital on 11 March 1949, the day after he received the Médaille militaire for his escape of 1942. A state funeral followed, and he was interred in the vault of the Cathedral of Saint-Louis-des-Invalides in Paris.
henri-gouraud: Gouraud was born on 17 November 1867 in the 7th arrondissement of Paris, the first of six children of the doctor Xavier Gouraud and Marie Portal. Educated at home and at the Collège Stanislas de Paris, he chose the army, like many of his generation, because of the French defeat in the Franco-Prussian War. He entered the Saint Cyr Military Academy in 1888 and joined the Troupes de marine in 1890, but his father objected to an overseas posting, and he served at first with the 21st Foot Chasseur Regiment at Montbéliard.

Posted to French Sudan in 1894, Gouraud led one of the units hunting Samori, and on 29 September 1898 his men came upon Samori's encampment. The capture ended the last large state opposing French rule in West Africa and made him a celebrity in Paris, then stung by the Fashoda Incident. With the patronage of the colonial party of Auguste d'Arenberg and Eugène Étienne he served for fifteen years in Niger, Chad and Mauritania, and from 1911 in Morocco under Hubert Lyautey, commanding the Fez military region.

Commanding the French Expeditionary Corps in the Dardanelles campaign, he was wounded on 30 June 1915 and lost his right arm. He then led the Fourth Army on the Western Front and became known for his elastic defence in the Second Battle of the Marne in July 1918. On 22 November 1918 he entered Strasbourg, overthrowing the Soviet government proclaimed there eleven days before.

In the Levant he also directed the fighting against Turkish National Forces at the Battle of Marash in early 1920, which ended in a French withdrawal to Syria. Drawing on what he had learned under Lyautey in Morocco, he set up separate administrations for the Druze and Alawite communities to divide their interests from those of urban nationalists. The Syrian nationalist Adham Khanjar tried to kill him on 23 June 1921.

Returning to France in 1923, Gouraud was Military Governor of Paris until 1937 and sat on the Supreme Allied War Council from 1927. He died in Paris on 16 September 1946, and in 1948 his remains were placed in the ossuary at Navarin Farm, on the site of the Second Battle of Champagne, which he had inaugurated in 1924. His division of Syria along confessional lines is still criticised for its effect on the region's stability. Paris has a Place du Général-Gouraud, Beirut a Rue Gouraud, and a cedar near Ifrane in Morocco bears his name.
henri-matisse: Henri Émile Benoît Matisse was born on 31 December 1869 in Le Cateau-Cambrésis in northern France, the oldest son of a wealthy grain merchant. In 1887 he went to Paris to study law and afterwards worked as a court administrator. He began to paint in 1889, when his mother brought him art supplies while he was convalescing from appendicitis, and decided to become an artist, which deeply disappointed his father. In 1891 he returned to Paris to study at the Académie Julian under William-Adolphe Bouguereau and at the École Nationale des Beaux-Arts under Gustave Moreau.

The intensity of colour in the works Matisse painted between 1900 and 1905 brought him notoriety as one of the Fauves, French for wild beasts. The movement lasted only from 1904 to 1908, and he and André Derain were its leaders. In 1904 he painted at St. Tropez with the neo-Impressionists Signac and Henri-Edmond Cross, and in 1905 he worked with Derain at Collioure. Around April 1906 he met Pablo Picasso, eleven years younger, and the two became lifelong friends and rivals. Americans in Paris, among them the Stein family and the Cone sisters of Baltimore, collected his work.

In 1917 Matisse moved to Cimiez, a suburb of Nice. His work of the next decade relaxed and softened, though some critics found his odalisque paintings shallow and decorative, and after 1930 a bolder simplification appeared. He was in Paris when the Germans invaded France in June 1940 but returned to Nice and stayed, though his son Pierre begged him to leave.

Diagnosed with abdominal cancer in 1941, Matisse underwent surgery that left him often bedridden. With assistants he began to make cut paper collages from sheets pre-painted with gouache, and the pieces grew into murals and room-sized works. In 1948 he began designs for the Chapelle du Rosaire at Vence, and after 1951 the paper cut-out was his only medium. He called his last years his second life. He died of a heart attack on 3 November 1954, aged 84, and is buried at Cimiez. The Matisse Museum at Le Cateau was established in 1952 and the Musée Matisse in Nice opened in 1963.
henri-van-der-noot: Henri van der Noot, Hendrik in Dutch, was popularly called Heintje van der Noot or Vader Heintje. He was the son of Nicolas van der Noot, Lord of Vrechem, and on 13 June 1757 was admitted to the Sweerts Lineage, one of the Seven Noble Houses of Brussels. With another lawyer, Jan Frans Vonck, he led the revolt against Joseph II, though each represented a different faction. The Vonckists drew on the ideals of the French Revolution and sought a link with the people and the patriot army, while Van der Noot's Statists sought cooperation with the Dutch Republic and the restoration of privileges such as the Joyous Entry.

Unlike Vonck, who held that the people themselves had to fight the despot of Vienna, Van der Noot trusted in foreign support. In 1788 he travelled to England, the Dutch Republic and Prussia; only Prussia, then anti-Austrian, was inclined to help, and he had less success with Laurens Pieter van de Spiegel, the last Grand Pensionary of Holland. In October 1789 he and General Vander Meersch led a small patriot army from Breda into Brabant. At Hoogstraten on 24 October he published the Manifesto of the Brabant People, which argued that the will of a nation is the highest law and that a nation may revolt against a ruler who violates it.

The patriots defeated the imperial troops at the Battle of Turnhout on 27 October and took Ghent on 13 November, and on 17 November the imperial regents Albert of Saxony and Archduchess Maria Christina fled Brussels. Brabant declared its independence, every other province but Luxembourg followed, and on 11 January 1790 they formed a confederation with Van der Noot as President of the National Congress. After Prussia withdrew with the Convention of Reichenbach of 27 July 1790, the forces of Leopold II, who had succeeded Joseph II, attacked the fragile state.

In November 1790 Van der Noot fled to the Dutch Republic and then to England. In 1792 he appealed for cooperation with the French; he returned to Brabant but was arrested in 1796 and imprisoned in 's Hertogenbosch. He died at Strombeek in 1827, and his tomb is set in the wall of the vicar's compound of the Sint-Amandsparochie in Strombeek-Bever.
henric-van-veldeke: Heinrich von Veldeke, also written Hendrik van Veldeke, is the first writer in the Low Countries known by name who wrote in a European language other than Latin. He was born in Veldeke, a hamlet in what is now Spalbeek, part of Hasselt in Belgian Limburg. He must have been born before or around 1150, since he was writing in the early 1170s, and he died after 1184, because he mentions in his Eneas that he was present at the court day Emperor Frederick Barbarossa held at Mainz at Pentecost of that year. He probably belonged to a family of ministeriales, unfree nobles, and used Latin sources.

His Life of Saint Servatius, probably his first work, was written in Middle Dutch for the sexton Hessel of the Maastricht Servatius chapter and for Agnes van Metz, countess of Loon, and is considered the first literary work in Dutch.
