It adapts earlier Latin lives of the patron saint of Maastricht, whose canons were then promoting pilgrimage to his grave.

His largest work is the Eneas Romance, based on the Old French Roman d'Enéas, itself inspired by Virgil's Aeneid. Veldeke wrote most of it around 1175. According to its epilogue, the countess of Cleves read it when four-fifths were finished, and it was then stolen; Landgrave Herman of Thuringia returned it in 1184 and ordered him to finish it. It is the first courtly romance in a Germanic language and gives much attention to courtly love and virtues. Its closing wedding feast is compared with Barbarossa's court day of 1184, one argument that he wrote for the imperial entourage.

About thirty love lyrics survive, making him one of the first generation of minnesingers. They stand out for humour and irony, and usually open with a description of nature that is then paralleled or contrasted with the lover's feelings.

Wolfram von Eschenbach, whose Parzival was finished between 1205 and 1210, says that Veldeke died prematurely. His lyrics and the Eneas Romance survive only in Middle High German manuscripts, and thirteenth-century writers such as Wolfram, Hartmann von Aue and Gottfried von Straßburg named him as a great example. His influence on Middle Dutch literature seems to have been limited. Statues of him stand in Maastricht and Hasselt.
henrician-articles: The Articles, 18 in number, were written and adopted by the nobility of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the szlachta, in 1573 at the town of Kamień near Warsaw, during the interregnum after the extinction of the Jagiellon dynasty. They took the form of a permanent agreement between the Polish nation, as the nobility called itself, and each newly elected king and grand duke. Henry of Valois was obliged to sign them to take the throne; he nominally agreed to them but refused to sign formally.

The king was to be chosen by election by the szlachta, and his children had no right to inherit the throne. His marriages needed the approval of the Senate. He had to convene a general Sejm at least once every two years for six weeks, and he could not create new taxes or tariffs, call the pospolite ruszenie, the levée en masse, or declare war or peace without its approval. The Articles provided for a standing royal army, the wojsko kwarciane, and bound the king to the guarantees of religious freedom of the Warsaw Confederation.

Between sessions a council of 16 senators, elected every two years, was to advise and oversee the king; four of them, rotating every six months, had to stay at his side, and all royal decrees had to be countersigned by the chancellors or deputy chancellors. If the king broke the law or the nobility's privileges, the szlachta could refuse his orders and act against him, a right that became known as the rokosz.

Every later king-elect had to swear fidelity to the Articles. Unlike the pacta conventa, the personal undertakings drawn up anew for each ruler, they were a permanent constitutional law; accepting them was a condition of elevation to the throne and part of the royal oath at the coronation. They remained the primary constitutional law of the Commonwealth and served in effect as its first constitution until the Constitution of 3 May 1791.
henrik-ibsen: Henrik Johan Ibsen was born on 20 March 1828 into an affluent merchant family in the port town of Skien in Telemark. His father, Knud Plesner Ibsen, was a timber and luxury goods merchant, and his mother, Marichen Cornelia Martine Altenburg, belonged like him to the extended Paus family, which had held wealth and power in Telemark since the mid-1500s. Older biographies pictured a descent from privilege into hardship, with a failed and tyrannical father, but a later reading finds this romanticised. At fifteen Ibsen left school and became an apprentice pharmacist in Grimstad, where he began writing plays. His first play, the tragedy Catilina, was published in 1850 under a pseudonym but not performed.

Ibsen established himself as a theatre director in Norway during the 1850s, though the many plays he wrote in those years were unsuccessful. In 1864 he left Christiania for Sorrento and spent the next 27 years in Italy and Germany, mostly in Rome, Dresden and Munich, before returning to Christiania in 1891. Brand and Peer Gynt, the second with incidental music by Edvard Grieg, brought him critical acclaim and some financial success. After Peer Gynt he abandoned verse for realistic prose, and he came to treat what he called the drama of ideas.

His plays from A Doll's House of 1879 onward, among them Ghosts, An Enemy of the People, The Wild Duck, Rosmersholm and Hedda Gabler, examined the morals and family life of the middle class and caused an uproar not only in Norway but across Europe and in America. Many of them are set in Norwegian bourgeois surroundings resembling Skien, and he took names and characters from his own relatives. Critics often rate The Wild Duck and Rosmersholm his best work, while Ibsen himself regarded Emperor and Galilean as his masterpiece.

Ibsen died at his home in Kristiania on 23 May 1906, after a series of strokes that began in March 1900. When his nurse told a visitor on the previous day that he was a little better, his last word was the reply Tvertimod, meaning On the contrary. He was buried in Vår Frelsers gravlund in Oslo. By 2014 he was the most frequently performed dramatist in the world after Shakespeare, and he influenced writers such as George Bernard Shaw, Oscar Wilde and James Joyce. His son Sigurd Ibsen became prime minister of Norway.
henrique-paiva-couceiro: Couceiro was born in Lisbon on 30 December 1861, the only son of José Joaquim de Paiva Cabral Couceiro, an army engineer, and Helena Isabel Teresa Mitchell, an Irish Protestant who had converted to Catholicism. His mother raised him in a strict religious and military regime, with daily mass and riding and the ideals of the medieval knight. In 1879 he joined the 2nd Cavalry's Royal Lancers Regiment, and from 1881 he studied artillery at the Military Academy in Lisbon. On 24 June 1881 he shot and wounded Luís Léon de la Torre in the Chiado after a quarrel and served a term in military prison, which did not halt his career.

Promoted captain on 4 July 1889, he volunteered for Africa and arrived in Luanda on 1 September 1889. In Angola he travelled thousands of kilometres to the Zambezi to seek the recognition of Portuguese sovereignty by Lewanika, chief of the Barotze people. After service with the Spanish Foreign Legion at Melilla, he went to Mozambique in 1895 as aide-de-camp to the Royal Commissioner António Enes, in the campaign against the peoples encircling Lourenço Marques. On 21 November 1896 he married Júlia Maria de Noronha, daughter of the 3rd Count of Parati, with King Carlos I as best man.

Increasingly scornful of party politics, he sat in parliament for eastern Lisbon from 1906 until João Franco suspended it in May 1907. As governor of Angola from June 1907 he led campaigns against the Cuamato and in the Dembos, extended the railways and sought to diversify an economy dependent on rubber and coffee, resigning on 22 July 1909. During the revolution of 5 October 1910 his battery on the Torel was the only garrison to fire on the republican camp at the Rotunda.

His devotion to the monarchist cause brought him several periods of exile, both before and after the founding of António Salazar's Estado Novo. His writings, on Angola and on a nationalism opposed to parliaments, anticipated in many ways the movement known as Integralismo Lusitano. He died in Lisbon on 11 February 1944, leaving a last political statement that it had been hard to govern Angola but harder to be honest during the 34 years of the Republic.
henry-chee-dodge: Henry Chee Dodge was born near Fort Defiance into the Mąʼii Deeshgiizhnii clan. In Navajo he was known by the nicknames Hastiin Adiitsʼaʼii, Mister Interpreter, and Kiiłchííʼ, Red Boy. During the Long Walk of 1864 he was separated from his mother; a family found him wandering and took him in, and he was raised by his aunt. Because his step-uncle was Anglo-American, he quickly learned English, and he eventually replaced Jesus Arviso as the official Navajo interpreter to the United States military.

In 1883 Dodge became head of the Navajo Tribal Police, and a year later the Bureau of Indian Affairs appointed him Head Chief of the Navajo, a title with no basis in traditional Navajo ideas of government. He held it until 1910 and was the last official holder. As the first chairman of the tribal council he secured over one million dollars in royalties for mineral rights on Navajo land, but he also gave way to demands to grant oil-drilling rights to Anglo companies. Most Navajo knew little of the council's work, and critics said it merely approved the decisions of the local Indian commissioner.

Under the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 Dodge, like many members of federally recognised tribes, became a United States citizen. Elected chairman of the Navajo Tribal Council in 1942, he served until 1946, pressed for better schooling for Navajo children and travelled to Washington to seek more federal funding.

In the election of 1946 Dodge was chosen as vice-chairman, but he died before the sixth Tribal Council met, and Zhealy Tso was appointed in his place. He died in his sleep of complications of pneumonia on 7 January 1947 at Ganado, Arizona, and Father Berard Haile said the Requiem Mass at St. Michael's Mission two days later. His son Thomas Dodge was chairman of the Tribal Council from 1932 to 1936, and his daughter Annie Dodge Wauneka became an activist. Chee Dodge Elementary School in Yatahey, New Mexico, and Chee Dodge Boulevard near Gallup bear his name.
henry-colvile: Henry Edward Colvile was born on 10 July 1852 at Kirkby Hall in Leicestershire, the son of Charles Robert Colvile and Katherine Sarah Georgina Russell. Educated at Eton, he entered the Grenadier Guards in 1870 and in 1880 became aide-de-camp to General Sir Leicester Smyth, commanding the forces in South Africa.

He served in the Intelligence Department of the Suakin Expedition of 1884, fighting at El Teb and Tamai, and on the Nile Expedition of 1884–85, and was created C.B. for his part in it. As chief of intelligence of the Frontier Force he was at the Battle of Ginnis, was promoted colonel, and later wrote the official history of the Sudan campaign. In 1892 he drew up a plan for a military expedition to Abeokuta, which was never needed, as the British reached a settlement with the Egba state.

In 1893 he succeeded the late Sir Gerald Portal as acting Commissioner for Uganda and commanded the Unyoro Expedition, which brought Unyoro into the Protectorate and earned him a knighthood (KCMG); he told the story in The land of the Nile springs (1895). Promoted major-general in 1898, he took command of the infantry brigade at Gibraltar early in 1899.

In the Second Boer War he led the Guards Brigade at the Battle of Modder River in November 1899 and at Magersfontein on 10–11 December, a costly British defeat. On 10 February 1900 he was given the 9th Division. In May 1900, as Lord Roberts closed on Johannesburg, a Yeomanry battalion under his command was cut off and forced to surrender; Colvile was made a scapegoat and sent home, and he retired in 1901.

His case was argued in print in 1901, in Henry Charles Shelley's Colvile's Case and in The scapegoat, and he wrote his own account, The work of the 9th Division in South Africa. He married Alice Rosa Daly in 1878 and Zélie Isabelle Richaud de Préville in 1886. He died on 25 November 1907 after his motorcycle collided with the car of Henry Rawlinson at Bisley.
henry-count-of-portugal: Henry was born in about 1066 in Dijon, in the Duchy of Burgundy, the youngest son of Henry, the second son of Robert I, Duke of Burgundy. His two older brothers, Hugh I and Odo I, inherited the duchy. No contemporary record of his mother survives. One of his paternal aunts was Constance of Burgundy, the wife of King Alfonso VI of León, and one of his great-uncles was Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.

After the defeat of the Christian troops at the Battle of Sagrajas in October 1086, Alfonso VI appealed for aid from Christians beyond the Pyrenees, and many French nobles and soldiers answered, among them Raymond of Burgundy, Henry's brother Odo I and Raymond of St. Gilles. His presence in Iberia is confirmed only from 1096, when he appears confirming the forais of Guimarães and Constantim de Panoias.

Three of these French nobles married daughters of Alfonso VI. Raymond of Burgundy married Urraca, later Queen Urraca of León, Raymond of St. Gilles married Elvira, and Henry married Teresa of León, an illegitimate daughter of the king by his mistress Jimena Muñoz. Between 1096 and 1105 Raymond, whose influence at court was diminishing, made a pact with his cousin Henry, the birth of Alfonso's only son Sancho Alfónsez having alarmed them both. They agreed to share power and the royal treasury. Raymond promised Henry the Kingdom of Toledo and one third of the treasury on Alfonso's death, or Galicia if he could not deliver Toledo.

Some historians date the pact near 1096 and think the king, hearing of it, made Henry governor of the lands between the Minho and the Tagus. Others show that it cannot have been made before 1103. After Raymond's death Urraca married King Alfonso I of Aragon, and Henry took advantage of the family conflicts to serve on both sides and enlarge his domains. He held Astorga under siege by the king of Aragon.

Henry died on 22 May 1112 of wounds received during the siege. By his own orders his remains were taken to Braga and buried in a chapel of Braga Cathedral, whose building he had promoted. His widow then ruled alone. He led a group of French gentlemen, monks and clerics who exerted great influence in the Iberian Peninsula, promoted reforms and introduced institutions from beyond the Pyrenees, such as the customs of Cluny and the Roman Rite. Their prominent positions provoked a strong backlash in the last years of Alfonso VI's reign.
henry-de-beaumont-1st-earl-of-warwick: Henry was a younger son of Roger de Beaumont and Adeline of Meulan, daughter of Waleran III, Count of Meulan. His father gave him the modest lordship of Le Neubourg in central Normandy, about 12 km north-east of the family seat of Beaumont-le-Roger on the River Risle. From it he and his descendants took the surname de Newburgh, often written in Latin as de Novo Burgo.

The Norman monk and historian Orderic Vitalis claimed that Henry joined William the Conqueror's campaign in the Midlands in 1068 and was then given charge of Warwick Castle, but no other evidence supports this late source. Little is known of his early career, although he helped to reconcile the Conqueror with his eldest son Robert Curthose in 1081.

In 1088 Henry acted for the crown in the arrest and trial of William de Saint-Calais, Bishop of Durham, and King William II rewarded his help against the Rebellion of 1088 with the earldom of Warwick. Its lands were assembled from several sources: most of the Warwickshire estates of his elder brother Robert, Count of Meulan, recorded in the Domesday Survey of 1086, together with royal estates in Rutland and the royal forest of Sutton, which became Sutton Chase. The unusual arrangement must have been agreed between Henry's father, his brother and the king.

After William II's sudden death in 1100, Henry's advice was said to have been decisive in the barons' choice of Henry, the Conqueror's fourth son, as king. When many barons favoured Robert Curthose's attempt on the crown the next year, Henry and his brother Robert stayed loyal as the king's foremost advisers. In Wales he gained Gower after the murder of Hywel ap Goronwy, its last Welsh lord, and he or his barons built or reoccupied castles at Penrhys, Llanrhidian, Oystermouth and Loughor as well as Swansea.

Before 1100 Henry married Margaret, daughter of Geoffrey II of Perche. Their son Roger succeeded him as 2nd Earl of Warwick, while another son, Rotrou, became Bishop of Évreux and Archbishop of Rouen, and Henry of Gower recovered the family's Welsh lands around 1136. Henry entered the Abbey of Saint-Pierre de Préaux and died there as a monk on 20 June 1119. An eighteenth-century woodcut of his tomb in the chapter house survives, though the abbey itself is long ruined.
henry-douglas-warden: Henry Douglas Warden was born on 2 February 1800. He went to the Cape in 1819 and joined the Cape Riflemen as an ensign on 25 May 1820, becoming a lieutenant on 15 September 1825. In 1826 he was ordered across the Orange River, and in 1835 he built Fort Warden at the Great Kei Way, 7 km south-east of the meeting of the Kei and Komgha rivers.

Warden served in the Sixth Frontier War and was promoted to captain on 1 March 1839. In 1842 he was sent to Natal, where he took part in the siege of Congela. On 16 January 1846 he was appointed British Resident in Transoranje, the land north of the Orange River, within the territory of the Griqua captain Adam Kok, where he was to keep law and order.

The same year he bought the farm Bloemfontein from Dolf Britz for £37 10s and settled there with his family; the town he founded on it later became the city of Bloemfontein, seat of South Africa's Supreme Court of Appeal. In 1848 Andries Pretorius forced him to leave, but after the Battle of Boomplaats in the same year he returned as British Resident of the Orange River Sovereignty.

After the Orange Free State declared its independence in 1854, Warden sold his farm Douglas Valley outside Bloemfontein. In retirement he lived in the George district, and he died of pneumonia at his residence, Black Waters, on 2 December 1856. The Grahamstown Journal reported that he was 56 years and 10 months old and left a widow and nine children.
henry-dunant: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva on 8 May 1828, the first son of the businessman Jean-Jacques Dunant and Antoinette Dunant-Colladon. His family was devoutly Calvinist and influential in the city. During the religious awakening known as the Réveil he joined the Geneva Society for Almsgiving at eighteen and helped found the Thursday Association, whose young members studied the Bible and helped the poor. On 30 November 1852 he founded the Geneva chapter of the YMCA. In 1856 he created a business in French-occupied Algeria, a corn-growing and trading company.

Because land and water rights were unclear, Dunant went in 1859 to appeal to Emperor Napoléon III, who was with his army in Lombardy. He arrived at Solferino on the evening of 24 June 1859, the day of a battle nearby. Forty thousand wounded, dying and dead lay on the field with little care. Dunant organised the local population, especially women and girls, to help the wounded of both sides, and the slogan Tutti fratelli, all are brothers, was coined by the women of Castiglione delle Stiviere.

In 1862 he published Un Souvenir de Solferino at his own expense and proposed a neutral organisation to care for the wounded. On 9 February 1863 the Geneva Society for Public Welfare, led by Gustave Moynier, created a five-person committee that included Dunant, Moynier, General Henri Dufour and the doctors Louis Appia and Théodore Maunoir. Their first meeting on 17 February 1863 is regarded as the founding of the International Committee of the Red Cross. On 22 August 1864 twelve states signed the First Geneva Convention.

In April 1867 the bankruptcy of the financial firm Crédit Genevois led to a scandal involving Dunant, who declared bankruptcy. He was removed from the committee in September 1867, left Geneva and never returned. He lived in poverty in Paris and other cities and kept working for disarmament, an international court and a world library. From 1887 he lived in the Swiss village of Heiden. In 1895 a journalist rediscovered him, and in 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize with the French pacifist Frédéric Passy. He died in Heiden on 30 October 1910.
henry-dundas: Dundas was born in Edinburgh on 28 April 1742, the fourth son of Robert Dundas of Arniston, Lord President of the Court of Session, and Anne Gordon. He studied law at the University of Edinburgh, joined the Faculty of Advocates in 1763, and became Solicitor General for Scotland in 1766 and Lord Advocate in 1775. In 1776–78 he led the legal team of Joseph Knight, an enslaved man brought from Jamaica, in Knight v. Wedderburn, in which the court declared that no person could be a slave on Scottish soil.

Returned to Parliament for Midlothian in 1774, Dundas served under Lord North, Shelburne and Pitt, and his almost absolute power over Scottish politics earned him nicknames such as King Harry the Ninth. He entered the cabinet as Home Secretary in 1791. On 2 April 1792 he backed Wilberforce's motion against the slave trade in principle but added the word gradual, arguing that immediate abolition would drive the trade underground; the amended motion passed by 230 votes to 85, but the House of Lords later dropped the issue.

As President of the Board of Control and, from 1794, Secretary of State for War, he organised expeditions to seize French and Spanish possessions in the Caribbean and a vain attempt to take Saint-Domingue that cost thousands of British lives. Created Viscount Melville in 1802, he became First Lord of the Admiralty in 1804. An inquiry found that the Navy's paymaster, Alexander Trotter, had profited from public money while Dundas was Treasurer of the Navy, and the impeachment of 1806 ended in his acquittal.

Dundas died in Edinburgh in May 1811 and was succeeded by his son Robert. Widely praised at his death, he was denounced by historians around 1900 as the epitome of corruption, and his reputation was restored in the late 20th century. His part in abolition remains disputed: David Brion Davis and others hold that he delayed it, while Angela McCarthy and Tom Devine point to the wider obstacles of the war with France and the House of Lords. In 2023 Toronto renamed Yonge–Dundas Square as Sankofa Square.
henry-fielding: Henry Fielding was born on 22 April 1707 at Sharpham Park in Somerset, the seat of his mother's family. His father was Edmund Fielding, a scion of the Earl of Denbigh, and his mother was Sarah Gould. At Eton College he began a lifelong friendship with William Pitt the Elder. His mother died when he was 11. In 1728 he went to Leiden to study classics and law, but lack of money forced him back to London, where he began writing for the theatre and criticised the government of Sir Robert Walpole.

Fielding's plays of 1730, The Author's Farce and Tom Thumb, mark his turn to satirical burlesque. From 1734 to 1739 he wrote anonymously against Walpole in the periodical The Craftsman. The Theatrical Licensing Act 1737 is said to have been a direct response to his dramatic satire, and after it passed, political satire on the stage became all but impossible. He joined the Middle Temple in 1737 and was called to the bar in 1740.

He then turned to prose. Shamela (1741) parodied Samuel Richardson's Pamela, and Joseph Andrews (1742) began as parody and became a novel in its own right, which Fielding called a comic epic poem in prose. The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling (1749) is a comic novel in which a foundling comes into a fortune, and Amelia followed in 1751. Ralph Allen, a wealthy benefactor, helped the family through poverty, and Squire Allworthy in Tom Jones is based on him.

Fielding married Charlotte Craddock in 1734; she died in 1744, and he modelled the heroines of Tom Jones and Amelia on her. His support for the Church of England and his anti-Jacobitism led to his appointment as chief magistrate of Westminster. With his half-brother John Fielding he helped found the Bow Street Runners in 1749, and G. M. Trevelyan counted the brothers among the best magistrates of 18th-century London.

Gout, asthma and cirrhosis of the liver left Fielding on crutches, and in 1754 he went to Portugal seeking a cure. He died two months later in Lisbon, on 8 October 1754, and is buried in the British Cemetery there.
henry-francis-fynn: Henry Francis Fynn was born on 29 March 1803 in Grosvenor Square, London, the first of five children of Henry and Elizabeth Fynn. His father served aboard a ship of the East India Company sailing between London and Cape Town until he lost his post in 1806, and by 1807 his parents had sold their property and moved to Cape Town. Fynn stayed in London with an aunt, who in 1809 had him admitted to Christ's Hospital. He left the school in 1816 and, against his father's wish that he come to the Cape, worked two years as a surgeon's apprentice.

In 1818 he gave up the apprenticeship and joined his family in the Cape Colony. After several jobs he went to Grahamstown, where he was hired as supercargo on Henry Nourse's trading vessel Jane, and late in 1823 Francis George Farewell took him into a trading venture to the Bay of Natal in the sloop Julia. He was among the first Europeans to make contact with King Shaka, and by July 1824 he belonged to the trading post at Port Natal.

There he gathered followers of his own, known as the iziNikumbi, or locusts, and was noted for wearing a blanket and a crownless straw hat once his European clothes had worn out. He is counted, with Coenraad De Buys, John Dunn and Nathaniel Isaacs, among South Africa's so-called White Chiefs. By 1832 he was back in the Cape Colony, and he returned to Natal only in 1852, as a resident magistrate.

At Port Natal Fynn took four African wives, with whom he had twelve children; his great wife, the Zulu princess Mavundlase, is said to have succeeded to his chieftaincy at his death. In 1841 he married Christina Brown, and their son Henry Francis Fynn Junior was born in 1846. He died in Durban on 20 September 1861. Robert Powell played him in the 1986 television drama Shaka Zulu.
henry-grattan: Grattan was born in Fishamble Street, Dublin, on 3 July 1746, into the Protestant Anglo-Irish elite, the son of James Grattan MP and Mary, daughter of the judge Thomas Marlay. At Trinity College Dublin he began a lifelong study of classical literature and the orators of antiquity. In London in the late 1760s and early 1770s he attended debates in the House of Commons and met Oliver Goldsmith. Called to the Irish Bar in 1772, he never seriously practised law, and in 1775 he entered the Irish Parliament for Charlemont, soon taking over from Henry Flood the leadership of the national party.

On 16 April 1782 he passed through ranks of Volunteers outside the Parliament in Dublin to move a declaration of its independence; the best-known words of his speech, Ireland is now a nation, appear only in a later edition he revised himself. Parliament voted him £100,000, which he accepted only when it was halved. He sought moderate reform, since two thirds of the Commons were returned by small boroughs in the gift of patrons, and in 1793 he carried the Roman Catholic Relief Act, which gave Catholics the vote. In 1797, with no more than 40 followers left, he retired from Parliament in protest.

After the 1798 rebellion he was dismissed from the Privy Council and his portrait was removed from Trinity College. On 15 January 1800, the opening day of the last session, he bought a seat for Wicklow, and too weak to stand, spoke sitting for more than two hours against the union. His last words there, on 26 May, were that he would remain faithful to Ireland's freedom and faithful to her fall.

In 1805 he entered the united Parliament for Malton, where Fox called him the Irish Demosthenes. He refused office in 1806 and supported a royal veto on the appointment of Catholic bishops, which cost him influence as Daniel O'Connell's more radical party rose. He died at Portman Square on 4 June 1820 and was buried in Westminster Abbey near Pitt and Fox. Grattan Bridge over the Liffey in Dublin is named after him.
henry-hudson: Almost nothing is known for certain of Hudson's early life. His year of birth is variously estimated between 1560 and 1570, and he may have been born in London. When he first appears in the record in 1607 he was already an experienced mariner.

In 1607 the Muscovy Company hired Hudson to find a northerly route to the Pacific coast of Asia, in the belief that the summer sun would melt the ice. He sailed in the Hopewell, reached Spitsbergen and turned back when ice blocked the north coast. In 1608 he tried the route east around northern Russia but found the ice impenetrable at Novaya Zemlya.

In 1609 merchants of the Dutch East India Company chose him to find an eastern passage. Ice stopped the Halve Maen east of Norway's North Cape, and Hudson, acting outside his instructions, turned west. After landfall in Nova Scotia and a landing in which a dozen of his men attacked a village, he reached Cape Cod and the coast to the north. On 3 September he came to the estuary of the river now named for him. Verrazzano had known it since 1524. Hudson sailed up the river for ten days, buying oysters and beans from Lenape in canoes and trading for furs.

In 1610, backed by the Virginia Company and the East India Company, Hudson sailed the Discovery. He passed Iceland and Greenland, entered Hudson Strait on 25 June and, on 2 August, Hudson Bay. Ice trapped the ship in James Bay in November and the crew wintered ashore.

When the ice cleared in spring 1611 Hudson meant to press on exploring, but most of the crew wished to go home and mutinied in June. Hudson, his teenage son John and seven others were set adrift in an open shallop and were never seen by Europeans again; later searches, among them Thomas Button's in 1612, found nothing. The main source, the account of Abacuk Pricket, blames Henry Greene and Robert Juet, and historians have doubted it, since the survivors faced trial in England and the men blamed were dead. Some survivors were tried, but none was punished.

Hudson's 1609 voyage established Dutch claims to the region and to its fur trade; a trading post stood at Albany in 1614, and New Amsterdam became the capital of New Netherland in 1625. Hudson Bay later gave the Hudson's Bay Company access to a fur trade along its shores for more than two centuries.
henry-i-count-of-champagne: Henry was born in December 1127, the eldest son of Count Theobald II of Champagne, who was also count of Blois, and Matilda of Carinthia. He took part in the Second Crusade under Louis VII of France, carrying a letter of recommendation from Bernard of Clairvaux to the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos. He is listed among the notables present at the assembly held by Baldwin III of Jerusalem at Acre on 24 June 1148. In 1164 he married Marie of France, daughter of Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine.

On his father's death Henry chose to take Champagne and left the family's older holdings, Blois, Chartres, Sancerre and Châteaudun, to his younger brothers. The choice may have been surprising, since those territories were richer and better developed. Under his rule Champagne became one of the richest and strongest French principalities. He established orderly rule over the nobles and could fairly reliably count on some 2,000 vassals, a force few in France could equal. This order made Champagne a safe place for merchants, and under the count's protection the Champagne Fairs became a central part of long-distance trade and finance in medieval Europe.

His court at Troyes was a literary centre. Walter Map found hospitality there, and the scholar Stephen of Alinerre, one of his courtiers, became chancellor of the county in 1176. Between 1157 and 1171 Henry built the collegiate church of Saint-Étienne in Troyes, planned as a necropolis for the House of Blois.

In 1179 Henry went again to Jerusalem with French knights, among them his relatives Peter of Courtenay and Philip of Dreux, bishop of Beauvais. He may have been present at the wedding of his niece Agnes to Alexios Komnenos in Constantinople. Returning by the land route across Asia Minor, he was captured and held to ransom by Kilij Arslan II, Seljuk sultan of Rüm, and the Byzantine emperor paid the ransom. Henry died on 16 March 1181 and was buried in Saint-Étienne. He had four children with Marie: Scholastique, Henry II, Marie, who married Baldwin I of Constantinople, and Theobald III. His elder son Henry succeeded him.
henry-i-count-of-schwerin: Henry was the fourth son of Gunzelin I, whom Henry the Lion had invested with the County of Schwerin. When his father died in 1185 the county passed to the eldest brother, Helmold I, and after Helmold abdicated in 1194 Henry shared power with his elder brother Gunzelin II.

With the fall of Henry the Lion, Denmark gained supremacy in northern Germany and along the southern Baltic coast. In 1208 King Valdemar II used a dispute between the brothers and one of their vassals to seize their land; they were allowed back in 1214 only as his vassals, and half of Schwerin went as a dowry to Valdemar's illegitimate son Niels, Count of Halland, who married their sister Oda.

While Henry was away on the Fifth Crusade in 1221, Gunzelin II and Niels both died. Valdemar became guardian of his young grandson and made his nephew Albert II of Weimar-Orlamünde governor. Henry returned in 1223 and negotiated in vain for his lands before taking the king and his son Valdemar the Younger, who were resting after a hunt without their bodyguard, in the night of 6 to 7 May.

As Danish troops held Schwerin, Henry hid his prisoners at Lenzen in Brandenburg and then in a tower of Dannenberg castle, later named the Waldemar Tower. Threats from Denmark and Pope Honorius III did not move him. Backed by Henry Borwin II of Mecklenburg, Count Adolf IV of Holstein and Bishop Gebhard II of Bremen, he defeated the Danes at the Battle of Mölln in January 1225 and captured Albert of Orlamünde. By the Treaty of Bardowick that November, Valdemar agreed to pay 45,000 marks of silver, give up Schwerin and Holstein, renounce overlordship of the German lands except Rügen, grant the German cities free trade and leave three sons as hostages.

When Valdemar tried to win back his losses, he was defeated at Bornhöved on 22 July 1227, and his ally Duke Otto I of Brunswick was brought captive to Schwerin. Henry died in February 1228 and was buried in Schwerin Cathedral. His widow Audacia, a daughter of Bolesław of Kuyavia, and their son Gunzelin III freed Otto, but kept Valdemar's three sons despite an appeal from Pope Gregory IX until a further 7,000 silver marks were paid in 1230.
henry-i-duke-of-brabant: Henry, called the Courageous, was born about 1165, possibly in Leuven, the son of Count Godfrey III of Louvain and Margaret, daughter of Duke Henry II of Limburg. His father also held the titles of landgrave of Brabant, duke of Lower Lorraine and margrave of Antwerp. Henry appeared early as co-ruler with his father. In 1180 he married Matilda of Boulogne, daughter of Marie of Boulogne and Matthew of Alsace, and on that occasion received the County of Brussels from his father. He acted as regent while Godfrey went on pilgrimage to Jerusalem from 1182 to 1184.

Henry took the title of duke of Brabant in 1183, and after his father's death in 1190 King Henry VI confirmed the elevation, while abolishing the Duchy of Lower Lorraine in practice by creating the empty title of duke of Lothier. Henry quarrelled with Count Baldwin V of Hainaut and, with Duke Henry III of Limburg and Count Otto I of Guelders, in further conflicts.

In mid-1197 he joined the Crusade of Henry VI, took part in the recapture of Beirut, and on news of the death of Count Henry II of Champagne, ruler of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, returned to Acre and acted as regent until Aimery of Cyprus arrived. In Germany he supported Otto IV against Philip of Swabia, then changed sides in 1204. He fought alongside Otto IV at Bouvines in 1214 and was defeated. In 1213 he suffered a heavy defeat against the Bishopric of Liège at the Battle of Steppes, and he joined the Fifth Crusade in 1217–1218.

Under Henry there was town policy and town planning. He used the creation of new towns as an instrument in the political organisation of regions, and gave city rights and trade privileges to 's-Hertogenbosch and Eindhoven.

In 1235 Emperor Frederick II appointed Henry to bring his fiancée Isabella, daughter of King John of England, to Germany. Henry fell ill on the way back and died at Cologne on 5 September 1235. He was buried in Saint Peter's Church at Leuven. His tomb there is the oldest of its kind to survive, showing him as an idealised smiling young man in a long robe and the duke's cloak, holding a sceptre. It was damaged during the French occupation in the eighteenth century and restored in the mid-19th century. His bones were dug up in 1929 and returned to the tomb in 1998.
henry-i-duke-of-burgundy: Henry was a younger son of Hugh the Great, Duke of the Franks, and Hedwig of Saxony. His birth name was Odo, and he is sometimes called Odo-Henry or Otto-Henry, in French Eudes-Henri. He entered the church young and was still a cleric when his brother Otto, Duke of Burgundy, died on 22 February 965. The Burgundian counts then elected him to succeed Otto and gave him the name Henry.

The duchy he received was weaker than its title suggested. Henry held only three counties of his own, while his vassals held the other six that had made up the core of the lands of Richard the Justiciar, who died in 921. In 972 he married Gerberga, the widow of Adalbert II of Italy, who had taken refuge at Autun, and through this marriage he came to rule the County of Nevers. In 978 he took part in the invasion of Lotharingia and in the defence of Paris against the counter-raid that followed. His second wife was Gersenda, daughter of William II of Gascony.

Henry died on 15 October 1002 without a son by either wife, although he had at least one illegitimate son, Odo of Beaune, later viscount of Beaune. He had adopted Gerberga's son Otto-William, which made his stepson a contender for the duchy, as was Henry's nephew King Robert II of France. A war of succession followed between the two from 1003 to 1005. Otto-William finally gave up the duchy but kept, within the West Frankish kingdom, the counties of Mâcon and Beaune and the advowson of the abbey of St-Benigne in Dijon.
henry-ii-duke-of-austria: Henry, called Jasomirgott, was the second son of Margrave Leopold III of Austria and Agnes of Waiblingen, a sister of the last Salian emperor Henry V. His younger brothers included Bishop Otto of Freising and Archbishop Conrad II of Salzburg. The nickname is first documented in the 13th century as Jochsamergott and its meaning is unclear; popular etymology derives it from an oath, joch sam mir got helfe, "yes, so help me God". When Leopold III died in 1136 he was succeeded by his third-born son Leopold IV, probably because Henry already administered the Rhenish possessions of the extinct Salian dynasty. In April 1140 King Conrad III enfeoffed Henry with the County Palatine of the Rhine.

Henry became Duke of Bavaria and margrave of Austria in 1141, when Leopold IV died unexpectedly in October, and took his residence at Regensburg. In May 1142 he married Gertrude, daughter of Emperor Lothair and widow of Henry the Proud; she died within a year, giving birth to their only child. He remained loyal to the Hohenstaufens and in May 1147 accompanied Conrad III on the Second Crusade. After the defeat at the Battle of Dorylaeum against the Seljuk Turks he narrowly escaped with the young Frederick Barbarossa, and he attended the Council of Acre and the Siege of Damascus. In late 1148, at the court of the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos, he married the emperor's niece Theodora.

After Frederick Barbarossa was elected king in 1152 he sought a compromise with the Welfs and in 1156 endowed Henry the Lion with Bavaria. As a replacement, the Privilegium Minus raised Henry's margraviate of Austria to a duchy with complete independence from Bavaria. In 1145 Henry had moved his Austrian residence from Klosterneuburg, where his father had mostly lived, to Vienna, which could thereby surpass Krems, Melk and Klosterneuburg, and it has remained the capital. The first St. Stephen's Church was completed in 1147, and in 1155 he founded the Schottenstift monastery in Vienna.

In November 1176, while forces of Duke Soběslav II of Bohemia campaigned in his Austrian lands, Henry fell with his horse from a rotten bridge near Melk and suffered a femoral neck fracture. He died of his injuries in Vienna on 13 January 1177 and, as he had willed, was buried in the Schottenstift. His son Leopold V became Duke of Austria, his daughter Agnes married King Stephen III of Hungary and later Duke Herman of Carinthia, and his son Henry I became Duke of Mödling.
henry-ii-duke-of-bavaria: Henry, called the Wrangler or the Quarrelsome, was the son of Duke Henry I of Bavaria, a younger brother of Emperor Otto the Great. He succeeded his father at the age of four under his mother's guardianship. His sister Hadwig married Duke Burchard III of Swabia in 954, and in 972 Henry married Gisela of Burgundy, a niece of Empress Adelaide. After Otto's death in 973 he could rely on ties to Swabia and Bavaria and to the neighbouring Kingdom of Burgundy. He installed his cousin Henry as Bishop of Augsburg, denying the investiture rights of Otto II, who, not wanting civil war, invested the nominee on 22 September 973.

When Burchard III died without heirs, Henry claimed Swabia, but Otto II gave it to his own nephew Otto of Swabia against Hadwig's opposition. In 974 Henry resolved to oust Otto II, allying with Bavarian and Saxon nobles, Duke Boleslaus II of Bohemia and Duke Mieszko I of Poland; Otto took him captive at Ingelheim. Henry escaped in 976 and raised a revolt in Bavaria, but Otto II occupied Regensburg and stripped him of the duchy, making the Duchy of Carinthia and the Margraviate of Austria from Bavarian lands. After the War of the Three Henries the deposed duke was placed in the custody of Bishop Folcmar of Utrecht.

When Otto II died of malaria in Rome in 983, Henry was released. He abducted the infant Otto III and, according to the chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg, had himself proclaimed King of the Romans at the graves of Otto I and Henry the Fowler in Magdeburg and Quedlinburg. He had lost the support of the German dukes, however, and could not oust Duke Henry the Younger from Bavaria. Through the agency of Archbishop Willigis of Mainz, Henry submitted in 985 to Empress Theophanu and Adelaide at an assembly in Rohr. He regained Bavaria and in 989 also received Carinthia.

Henry died on 28 August 995. His children with Gisela included Henry IV of Bavaria, who succeeded him in 995 and fulfilled his father's ambitions when he was elected King of the Romans as Henry II in 1002 and crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 1014; Bruno, Bishop of Augsburg from 1006; and Gisela, who married King Stephen I of Hungary.
henry-ii-duke-of-guise: Henri was born in Paris on 4 April 1614, the second son of Charles, Duke of Guise, and Henriette Catherine de Joyeuse. At the age of fifteen he became Archbishop of Reims, and according to Gédéon Tallemant des Réaux he had a well-known affair with the actress Marguerite Béguin during this time. The death of his eldest brother Francis in 1639 brought him the dukedom the following year.

Guise opposed Richelieu and conspired with the Count of Soissons, fighting at the Battle of La Marfée in 1641. Condemned to death, with his property seized for lèse-majesté, he fled to Brussels; he was reprieved, returned in 1643 and recovered his property.

Hoping to make good his family's ancient claims to the Kingdom of Naples, he joined the revolt of Masaniello in 1647. The Royal Republic of Naples appealed to the protection of France and was nominally headed by Guise, with the title of doge in imitation of Venice. He soon alienated the Neapolitans by his lack of tact and had little influence with Cardinal Mazarin. Captured by the Spaniards when the republic fell in 1648, he was held until 1652. A second attack on Naples in 1654 failed, partly because an English fleet under Robert Blake supported the Spanish.

He then settled in Paris as Grand Chamberlain of France to Louis XIV, went deeply into debt on horses and entertainments, and was the patron of Pierre Corneille, whom he lodged in the Hôtel de Guise. Two women claimed to be his wife: Anna Gonzaga, who in 1639 appears to have been duped by a clandestine ceremony, and Honorée de Berghes, Countess of Bossut, who said she had married him in Brussels on 11 November 1641. The Sacra Rota declared that marriage valid in March 1666, but the king and the House of Guise refused to recognise the decision, so she received nothing of his fortune.

Anna Gonzaga wrote that he had the figure, the air and the manners of a hero in a novel, especially charming in conversation and gifted at making himself loved, but flighty in his attachments, inconstant in his projects and hasty in carrying things out. Henri died in Paris on 2 June 1664 and was succeeded by his nephew Louis Joseph de Lorraine.
henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was born in May 973, son of Duke Henry II of Bavaria and Gisela of Burgundy, and was a great-grandson of King Henry I of Germany. Because his father rebelled against two emperors, he spent long periods in exile, where he turned to Christianity at an early age, first finding refuge with Bishop Abraham of Freising and later studying at the cathedral school in Hildesheim. He succeeded his father as Duke of Bavaria in 995.

When Emperor Otto III died childless in January 1002, Henry's right to succeed him was contested by rivals including Count Ezzo of Lotharingia, Margrave Eckard I of Meissen and Duke Herman II of Swabia. Henry was crowned king on 9 July 1002 and spent the following years consolidating his power. In Italy, Margrave Arduin of Ivrea proclaimed himself king, but Henry was anointed King of Italy on 15 May 1004, and he was crowned emperor by Pope Benedict VIII on 14 February 1014, after Benedict had fled to Germany and appealed to him for protection.

Where Otto III had pursued a renewal of the Roman Empire, Henry's seal spoke of a renewal of the Frankish kingdom, and he spent most of his reign on the territories north of the Alps. He made only three journeys south of the Alps. His long conflict with Duke Bolesław I of Poland, who had once been a loyal ally of Otto III, filled over sixteen years, with peace treaties made and broken in 1012 and 1013. Henry also relied on bishops and abbots, whom he made princes of the empire, as a counterweight to the secular nobles, and in 1004 he ordered the diocese of Merseburg re-established, appointing the chronicler Thietmar as its bishop.

In 1007 Henry announced a new diocese at Bamberg, a place he was fond of, where he had given estates to his wife Cunigunde of Luxembourg. He died on 13 July 1024 at Göttingen and was buried at Bamberg Cathedral. As the marriage was childless, the Ottonian line ended with him, and the nobles elected Conrad II, the first of the Salian emperors. Henry was canonised by Pope Eugene III in the twelfth century and Cunigunde in 1200. He is the only medieval German monarch honoured as a saint, and the patron saint of the city of Basel.
henry-ii-lord-of-mecklenburg: Henry was the son of Henry I of Mecklenburg, who was taken prisoner on a crusade and was away from 1275 to 1302. In his absence Mecklenburg was ruled by Henry's mother Anastasia with his uncles Nicholas III and John II, and in 1287 Henry became co-regent with his mother and uncle. He became Lord of Mecklenburg on his father's death in 1302. His first wife, Beatrix, was the daughter of Margrave Albert III of Brandenburg, who around 1299 gave or sold him the Lordship of Stargard.

In 1304 Henry joined King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia in his war against Emperor Albert I, in which he earned his nickname, the Lion. In 1310 he went to war with the Hanseatic cities of Wismar and Rostock after Wismar refused to host the wedding of his daughter Matilda to Duke Otto III of Brunswick-Lüneburg. Wismar submitted in 1311, and he took Rostock on 15 December 1312 despite fierce resistance, subduing it again on 12 January 1314 after a rising.

When Beatrix died in 1314 without a male heir, Brandenburg demanded Stargard back, and in the North German Margrave War Henry defeated Margrave Waldemar at the Battle of Gransee and was awarded Stargard by the Treaty of Templin of 25 November 1317. In 1319 he and Count Gerhard III of Holstein-Rendsburg failed to subdue Ditmarschen, and Henry escaped with difficulty from the Battle of Wöhrden. On 21 May 1323 he made peace with King Christopher II of Denmark, who enfeoffed him with Rostock, Gnoien and Schwaan.

His later years brought losses. Prignitz and the Uckermark, which he had conquered after Waldemar's death, were retaken, and the first War of the Rügen Succession ended in 1328 with Rügen going to Pomerania and Mecklenburg settling for money. Henry died at Sternberg on 21 January 1329. His son Albert II succeeded him and in 1348 became the first Duke of Mecklenburg, and another son, John I, became Duke of Mecklenburg-Stargard.
henry-ii-of-castile: Henry was the fourth of ten illegitimate children of King Alfonso XI of Castile and Eleanor de Guzmán, and the first of their sons to survive to adulthood. He was born a twin to Fadrique Alfonso, Lord of Haro. His father made him Count of Trastámara and lord of Lemos and Sarria in Galicia, a large inheritance that made him head of the new Trastámara line. When Alfonso XI died of a fever during the siege of Gibraltar in March 1350, the queen, Maria of Portugal, and her son Peter pushed Eleanor and her sons aside. In 1351 Peter had Eleanor executed at Talavera de la Reina, and Henry and his brothers rebelled repeatedly.

After a long, intermittent war Henry fled to France and served King John II of France, then fought in the army of Peter IV of Aragon against Castile. In the Castilian Civil War he led Castilian allies, Aragonese and mercenaries under Bertrand du Guesclin, expelled Peter and was proclaimed king at Burgos in 1366. Peter returned with an Anglo-Gascon army led by Edward, the Black Prince, and John of Gaunt, and defeated Henry at Nájera in 1367. Henry escaped to France, regrouped and defeated Peter at Montiel on 14 March 1369, killing his captive half-brother with his own hand.

As king he fought two of the three Fernandine Wars against Ferdinand I of Portugal and resisted John of Gaunt's claim to the throne through Constance of Castile. He favoured France over England, and Castilian ships under Ambrosio Boccanegra defeated an English fleet at La Rochelle. At home he began rebuilding the royal administration and held numerous courts. His generous rewards to his allies earned him the name el de las mercedes.

Henry was hostile to the Jews, in contrast to Peter's friendliness. He imposed a war contribution of twenty thousand gold doubloons on the community of Toledo, ordered that Jews wear a badge, and shortly before his death barred them from public office, although financial need led him to employ Jewish tax collectors. He died on 29 May 1379 at Santo Domingo de la Calzada and was succeeded by his son John I. He was buried in the Capilla de los Reyes Nuevos in Toledo.
henry-ii-of-england: Henry was born at Le Mans on 5 March 1133, the eldest child of the Empress Matilda, daughter of Henry I of England, and Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou. By the age of 14 he was involved in his mother's effort to claim the English throne, then held by her cousin Stephen of Blois. In 1150 his father made him Duke of Normandy, and in 1151 Henry inherited Anjou, Maine and Touraine. His marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine brought him that duchy. After a military expedition to England in 1153, Stephen agreed by the Treaty of Wallingford to leave the kingdom to Henry, who inherited it a year later.

Henry was crowned with Eleanor at Westminster Abbey on 19 December 1154. He inherited a country damaged by civil war, with unauthorised castles and a depleted royal income, and in the early years he restored royal administration. His invasion of Wales in 1157 met defeat at the Battle of Ewloe, where he was nearly killed. His desire to control the English Church brought conflict with Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, a controversy that lasted much of the 1160s and ended in Becket's murder in 1170. He also fought Louis VII of France for decades, in a struggle the historian Jean Dunbabin likened to a cold war.

His domains, later called the Angevin Empire, were a loose network of family connections and lands, each with its own customs. Henry travelled constantly, producing what the historian John Edward Austin Jolliffe describes as a government of the roads and roadsides. His court was probably the largest in Europe. He expanded royal justice in England, and the Treatise of Glanvill summarised the system at the end of his reign.

Henry and Eleanor had eight children, three of them kings: Henry the Young King, Richard I and John. Tensions over the inheritance, encouraged by Louis VII and his son Philip II, led in 1173 to a rebellion by Young Henry, joined by Richard, Geoffrey and Eleanor. Young Henry died during a second failed revolt in 1183, and Geoffrey died in 1186. By 1189 Philip had won Richard to his side, and Henry, weakened by a bleeding ulcer, was decisively defeated. He died soon afterwards, on 6 July 1189, and was succeeded by Richard. His empire collapsed quickly under John, but his legal reforms are generally considered to have laid the basis for the English Common Law.
henry-ii-of-france: Henry was born on 31 March 1519 at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye, the second son of Francis I and Claude, Duchess of Brittany. After Francis I was captured at the Battle of Pavia in 1525, Henry and his elder brother were sent to Spain as hostages and stayed there for over four years. On 28 October 1533 he married Catherine de' Medici, both being fourteen.

He formed a close attachment to Diane de Poitiers, more than twenty years older than he, whose colours he wore at a tournament in 1531. He became heir in August 1536 when his brother died after falling ill following a game of tennis; an autopsy report gave no sign of poison. Catherine bore their first son in 1544, and Henry's loyalty to Diane caused a breach with his father until 1545.

Francis I died on 31 March 1547, and Henry was crowned at Reims on 25 July 1547. He intensified the repression of Protestants. An edict of 5 April 1547 reaffirmed punishments for blasphemy, and in October a new chamber of the Parlement of Paris, called the chambre ardente, was set up to hear heresy cases. The Edict of Châteaubriant followed in 1551.

In foreign policy he declared war on Charles V in the Italian War of 1551–1559, allied himself with German Protestant princes at the Treaty of Chambord in 1552 and continued his father's Franco-Ottoman alliance. He occupied the Three Bishoprics of Toul, Verdun and Metz, and secured them at Renty in 1554. After Philip II's victory at St Quentin, French forces took Calais.

Henry raised Mary, Queen of Scots at his court, and she married the Dauphin Francis on 24 April 1558. Under the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis of April 1559, France gave up its claims in Italy and restored Piedmont and Savoy but kept Saluzzo, Calais and the Three Bishoprics. During his reign Henry also introduced the idea of publishing a description of an invention in exchange for monopoly rights, the beginning of the patent specification.

On 30 June 1559, at a tournament held to celebrate the peace, Henry was wounded in the eye by a splinter of the lance of Gabriel Montgomery, captain of his Scottish Guard. Surgeons including Ambroise Paré and Andreas Vesalius could not save him, and he died ten days later. Modern analysis points to an infection from a retained wooden fragment.

His death played a part in the decline of jousting in France. He left four young sons and a widow, Catherine de' Medici. Three of the sons became king, but their youth and Catherine's regency led to challenges from powerful nobles and helped to spark the French Wars of Religion, and in time the Valois dynasty ended.
henry-ii-the-pious: Henry was the second son of High Duke Henry the Bearded and Hedwig of Silesia. His elder brother Bolesław died in 1206, and in 1213 his younger brother Konrad the Curly died during a hunt, leaving Henry as sole heir of Lower Silesia. His father arranged his marriage to Anne, daughter of King Ottokar I of Bohemia. From 1222 he countersigned his father's documents, and when Henry the Bearded was captured in 1229 he acted as interim duke. When his father died on 19 March 1238 he became duke of Silesia, Kraków and Greater Poland.

Henry II was regent of the duchies of Opole and Racibórz and of Sandomierz while their rulers were minors, but he resigned the regency in 1239. The death of Władysław Odonic on 5 June 1239 let him take most of his lands, including Gniezno. He abandoned his family's alliance with the Hohenstaufen emperors and supported Pope Gregory IX, which settled his dispute with the Church. He ended the conflict with Konrad of Masovia by marrying two of his daughters to two of Konrad's sons, and in 1239 he won the Battle of Lubusz and recovered the fortress of Santok.

In February 1241 a Mongol army of about 10,000 men under Orda invaded Poland and destroyed much of the Kraków and Sandomierz nobility at Tursko and Chmielnik. Henry gathered troops at Legnica. Many European rulers, busy with the quarrel between the Holy Roman Empire and the papacy, did not answer his appeals; only a contingent sent by King Wenceslaus I of Bohemia and some Knights Templar joined him.

Henry was defeated and killed at the Battle of Legnica on 9 April 1241. His wife identified his decapitated body by the six toes on his left foot, a detail confirmed when his tomb was opened in 1832. The Mongols did not try to occupy Silesia and moved on to Hungary. His death split the Silesian Piast line into many ducal branches, and later traditions portrayed him as an ideal Christian knight and martyr. In October 2015 the Roman Catholic Diocese of Legnica opened his cause for beatification, giving him the title Servant of God.
henry-iii-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was the eldest son of Conrad II and Gisela of Swabia. Conrad, a Franconian aristocrat with lands along the Rhine, was illiterate, but Gisela, who was descended from Charlemagne, saw to her son's education and Henry learnt to read. His father made him Duke of Bavaria in 1026 and had him elected co-ruler in 1028, when Pilgrim, Archbishop of Cologne, crowned him king at Aachen on Easter. In 1038 he received the duchy of Swabia and the Kingdom of Burgundy. His succession on his father's death was unusually smooth, and he also took the duchy of Carinthia and the Kingdom of Italy.

Henry began with a tour of his domains and made Goslar a future imperial residence. His first campaign, into Bohemia in 1040, ended in an ambush at the Battle of Brůdek and a heavy retreat, but a second campaign a year later brought a peace with Duke Bretislav I of Bohemia at Regensburg. In 1044 he entered Hungary and restored Peter Orseolo to the throne after Samuel Aba had overthrown him. In 1043 he married Agnes of Poitou, despite clerical objections to their kinship. He treated the duchies as royal offices to be filled at his discretion, which led to long conflict in Lorraine with Godfrey, the son of Duke Gothelo I.

In 1046 he went to Italy to deal with three men who claimed the papacy: Benedict IX, Sylvester III and Gregory VI. At Sutri, on 20 December 1046, he deposed all three. He had Suidger of Bamberg acclaimed as Pope Clement II, and on Christmas Day 1046 Clement crowned Henry and Agnes emperor and empress. The Roman citizenry gave Henry the Golden Chain of the Patriciate and the rank of patricius.

Henry's last years brought setbacks. In 1051 he suffered a major defeat at the Battle of Vértes in a third Hungarian campaign, and in 1052 he failed to take Pressburg, after which he never tried again. A Swabian army sent to help Pope Leo in southern Italy was cut to pieces by the Normans at the Battle of Civitate on 18 June 1053. Revolt in Bavaria followed the deposition of Duke Cuno.

His son Henry, born in 1050, was elected king of Germany at Tribur on 26 June 1053 and crowned at Aachen on 17 July 1054. In 1055 the heir was engaged to Bertha of Turin. Henry III died on 5 October 1056, aged only 39. Modern historians see the last years of his reign as the beginning of a crisis in the Salian monarchy, and the dispute over investiture overshadowed the reigns of his son and grandson.
henry-iii-margrave-of-meissen: Henry III, called Henry the Illustrious, of the House of Wettin, was born around 1215, probably at the Albrechtsburg residence in Meissen. He was the youngest son of Margrave Theodoric I of Meissen and Jutta, a daughter of Landgrave Hermann I of Thuringia. He succeeded his father in 1221 as Margrave of Meissen and Lusatia, at first under the guardianship of his maternal uncle, Landgrave Louis IV of Thuringia, and after Louis died in 1227 under that of Duke Albert I of Saxony. He was proclaimed an adult in 1230, and around 1234 he went on crusade in Prussia, fighting the Pomesanians, which led to the building of Balga castle for the Teutonic Knights.

In the struggle between Emperor Frederick II and Pope Gregory IX, Henry sided with the emperor, who in 1242 promised him the inheritance of Henry Raspe in Thuringia. In 1245, after long conflict with the Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg, he had to give up the fortresses of Köpenick, Teltow and Mittenwalde. After Henry Raspe died in 1247 Henry enforced his rights by arms in the War of the Thuringian Succession against Sophie of Thuringia, her husband Duke Henry II of Brabant and Prince Siegfried I of Anhalt-Zerbst. He gave Hesse to Sophie's younger son but kept Thuringia, which he granted to his son Albert II together with the Palatinate of Saxony.

From 1273 he supported Rudolph of Habsburg against King Ottokar II of Bohemia. Henry married Constance of Babenberg in 1234; they had two sons, Albert II and Theodoric of Landsberg, for whom he created the Margraviate of Landsberg without imperial consent. His later years were clouded by disorder caused by Albert, which in time led to the loss of Lusatia and Thuringia. He died on 15 February 1288.

Henry was known across the empire as a glittering prince, a patron of the arts and a model knight. He was a notable minnesinger, poet and composer, and took part in the tournaments and singing contests he sponsored. He commissioned the Christherre-Chronik, and with the express permission of the pope he set hymns to music to be sung in the churches.
henry-iii-of-england: Henry was born at Winchester Castle on 1 October 1207, the eldest son of King John and Isabella of Angoulême. When John died, Henry was at Corfe Castle in Dorset. John's deathbed wishes placed him under the guardianship of William Marshal, who knighted him, and Cardinal Guala Bicchieri, the papal legate, oversaw his coronation at Gloucester Cathedral on 28 October 1216, in the middle of the First Barons' War.

Guala declared the war against the rebels a crusade, and Henry's forces under William Marshal defeated them at Lincoln and Sandwich in 1217. The government reissued a version of Magna Carta, and Henry promised to abide by the Great Charter of 1225.

Hubert de Burgh, made Earl of Kent, dominated the government after William Marshal's death in 1219 until his fall in 1232. A failed invasion of France in 1230 and a revolt led by Richard Marshal in 1232 marked the early years. Henry then ruled in person. He left the post of justiciar vacant, made the chancellor a junior figure and took decisions with a small circle of advisers, which made it harder for outsiders to press grievances.

In 1236 he married Eleanor of Provence, then twelve years old. He was known for piety, attended mass at least once a day and took Edward the Confessor as his patron saint. His expeditions to Poitou in 1242 ended in the Battle of Taillebourg, and he spent large sums in a failed attempt to put his son Edmund Crouchback on the throne of Sicily.

By 1258 his foreign policy, his Poitevin half-brothers and his officials' tax collecting had made him unpopular, and a coalition of barons seized power and imposed the Provisions of Oxford. In 1259, under the Treaty of Paris, Henry gave up his claims in France except Gascony, which Louis IX recognised as his. In 1263 Simon de Montfort seized power, beginning the Second Barons' War. Henry was defeated and captured at Lewes in 1264, and his son Edward beat Simon at Evesham the following year. The Dictum of Kenilworth softened the revenge on the rebels.

Henry also took a heavy toll from the Jews of England, whose position as a source of royal loans he used until it crippled their ability to do business, and he later introduced the Statute of Jewry to separate them from the rest of the population. He died on 16 November 1272, leaving Edward as his successor.

He was buried in Westminster Abbey, which he had rebuilt in the second half of his reign, and his body was moved to its present tomb in 1290. His reign of 56 years was the longest in medieval England and was not exceeded by an English or British monarch until George III.
henry-iii-of-glogow: Henry was probably the second son of Konrad I, Duke of Głogów, and his first wife Salome, daughter of Duke Władysław of Greater Poland. In 1267 he attended the canonisation of his great-grandmother Hedwig of Andechs. He and his brothers were minors when their father died in 1274, and their step-mother Sophie of Landsberg and the chancellor Mikołaj became their guardians. In 1278, the year he fought at the Battle on the Marchfeld, where King Ottokar II of Bohemia was killed, he had to divide the duchy with his brothers, keeping Głogów, Bytom Odrzański and Kożuchów.

In 1281 Henry IV Probus of Wrocław seized him and two other dukes at a meeting in Sądowel and freed them only when they recognised his overlordship; Henry III then stood by him, and was twice excommunicated for it. Named main heir in Probus's will in 1290, he was driven out by the knights and burghers of Wrocław, who called in Henry V the Fat of Legnica. In 1293 Henry V was captured and kept by Henry III in an iron cage for almost six months, and won his freedom only by surrendering almost a third of Probus's lands and paying 30,000 pieces of silver.

After King Przemysł II was murdered in 1296, Henry claimed Greater Poland under an earlier pact, but settled with Władysław I the Elbow-high at Krzywin for the lands south of the Obra. In 1301 he took the title Heir of the Polish Kingdom, Duke of Silesia, Głogów and Poznań. After the deaths of Wenceslaus II in 1305 and Wenceslaus III the following year he pushed Władysław back in 1306 and took Kalisz in 1307. At home he reformed the administration and coinage and founded more than a dozen towns, among them Zielona Góra, Lubin and Kościan.

Henry was buried in the Cistercian church of Lubiąż, and his will left Głogów to his wife Matilda, daughter of Duke Albert I of Brunswick-Lüneburg, as her dower. His five sons, Henry IV the Faithful, Konrad I, Jan, Bolesław and Przemko II, divided his inheritance, which led to the decline of the duchy, and the fragmentation alarmed the nobles of Greater Poland. In the end Władysław I the Elbow-high conquered all of Greater Poland in 1314.
henry-iii-the-white: Henry was the third son of the Polish high duke Henry II the Pious and his wife Anna, daughter of King Ottokar I of Bohemia. When his father fell at the Battle of Legnica on 9 April 1241, he was still a minor and was left in his mother's care with his younger brothers Konrad and Władysław. The death of his brother Mieszko in 1242 made him second after the eldest, Bolesław II the Bald, and he became the head of the opposition to Bolesław's government in Lower Silesia.

Henry first appears as an adult in 1247. Bolesław would not share power until his brothers revolted and even captured him; Henry then became co-ruler, and a year later, under his pressure, the lands were divided. Bolesław chose Legnica, where gold had been discovered in the Kaczawa and Wierzbiak rivers, and Henry received Wrocław, where he almost at once imposed his will on the powerful nobility. In the brothers' quarrels he backed Konrad, who refused to become a priest, against Bolesław.

In the 1250s and 1260s Henry became the most powerful Piast duke of Lower Silesia, allied with the dukes of Opole and Głogów and with the Bohemian kings Wenceslaus I and Ottokar II. When he repudiated his treaty with the Greater Poland dukes Przemysł I and Bolesław the Pious, the Duchy of Wrocław was besieged and plundered in 1253–1254. Under his rule many towns were founded and a huge castle was built on Ostrów Tumski in Wrocław.

His defence of the dynasty's prerogatives angered the nobility, and in mid-1266 a revolt tried to force a division of the duchy between Henry and his brother Władysław, Archbishop of Salzburg. The historian Jerzy Mularczyk named Bishop Thomas of Wrocław and Bolesław II as possible leaders, though direct evidence is lacking. The revolt failed, but a few months later Henry died suddenly, and rumours of poisoning were recorded by the monk Engelbert in the Kronika polska and on his tombstone.

The sources date his death to 3 December, 1 December, 5 December or 29 November. He was buried in the Clare Church in Wrocław, then still under construction, and his son Henry IV Probus, a minor, succeeded him under the regency of Władysław.
henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was born on 11 November 1050, most likely at his father's palace at Goslar, the son of Emperor Henry III and Agnes of Poitou. He belonged to the Salian dynasty, which governed Germany from 1024 to 1125. His father named him successor at Christmas 1050, and at the age of six he became sole ruler while his mother acted as regent. In April 1062 Archbishop Anno II of Cologne and other nobles removed her in the Coup of Kaiserswerth, luring Henry onto a ship on the Rhine; he leapt into the river and was rescued by Egbert I of Brunswick. Henry was girded with a sword at Worms on 29 March 1065.

Around 1069 Henry set out to recover royal estates lost during his minority, most of them in Saxony. He used Swabian ministeriales as officials and built royal castles garrisoned by Swabian troops, which angered the Saxons, and he put down revolts there in 1069 and 1071. His insistence on appointing bishops and abbots brought conflict with Pope Alexander II, who excommunicated some of his advisers in 1073.

After crushing a new Saxon rebellion in 1075 he turned to Italy and appointed Tedald archbishop of Milan against the wishes of Pope Gregory VII, who threatened excommunication. At Worms on 24 January 1076 two archbishops and twenty-six bishops declared Gregory's election invalid. Gregory excommunicated Henry, and in 1077 Henry sought absolution in his penitential walk to Canossa. German opponents then elected Rudolf of Rheinfelden king on 14 March 1077. Excommunicated again in 1080, Henry was supported by an antipope, Clement III, who crowned him emperor in Rome in 1084.

From 1089 to 1096 he campaigned in Italy against Matilda of Tuscany and Welf I of Bavaria; his son Conrad turned against him in 1093. In 1103 he proclaimed the first imperial peace covering all Germany. His diplomas protected the Jews of Speyer and Worms from violence and forced baptism.

In December 1104 his younger son Henry deserted him, and in 1105 forced his abdication. Henry fled to Cologne in February 1106, where the townspeople received him, and he sought allies to regain the throne. He fell ill and died in 1106 without absolution. His conflicts with the popes, his sons and his subjects produced a rich polemical literature in his lifetime. The Song of the Saxon War praised him as pious, while Lampert of Hersfeld said he had inherited a peaceful realm and rendered it bloodstained and a prey to internal conflicts.
henry-iv-of-castile: Henry was born on 5 January 1425 in Valladolid, the son of John II of Castile and Maria of Aragon. He displaced his older sister Eleanor as heir apparent and became Prince of Asturias. In his youth Castile was controlled by Álvaro de Luna, who chose his companions and directed his education. One of them, Juan Pacheco, became his closest confidant. In 1440, at fifteen, he married Blanche II of Navarre. In 1445 he won the First Battle of Olmedo against the Infantes of Aragon, after which Luna's power waned.

John II died on 20 July 1454, and Henry was proclaimed king the next day. In 1455 he married Joan of Portugal, sister of Afonso V, to secure an alliance with Portugal. He convened the Cuéllar Courts to launch an offensive against the Emirate of Granada, but the campaigns of 1455 and 1458 became a war of attrition and were unpopular. Pacheco, by then Marquis of Villena, and his brother Pedro Girón handled much of the government, and Henry took other advisers, among them Beltrán de la Cueva, to balance them.

Nobles formed a League of Nobles in March 1460. On 11 August 1462 Catalonia elected Henry Count of Barcelona, but his intervention failed and he agreed to the Judgment of Bayonne, abandoning the Catalans. Queen Joan gave birth to a daughter, Joanna, in 1462, and rebels doubted her paternity and called her la Beltraneja. Under pressure from the league, Henry at Burgos in 1464 disowned Joanna and named his half-brother Alfonso heir. He later went back on this, and at the Farce of Ávila the nobles deposed him in effigy and crowned Alfonso as a rival king.

Alfonso died in 1468, and his sister Isabella took his place as the rebels' champion. At Toros de Guisando Henry agreed to exclude Joanna from the succession and recognise Isabella as heir. He died on 11 December 1474 and was buried at Santa María de Guadalupe. A war between Joanna, supported by Portugal, and Isabella, supported by Aragon, followed, and Isabella won.

Henry was nicknamed the Impotent, and contemporaries thought him impotent or homosexual. Historians note that the royal chronicles were written or revised under Isabella, who had a strong interest in proving Joanna illegitimate, so Joanna's paternity cannot be settled. During his reign the nobles grew more powerful and the nation less centralised.
henry-iv-of-england: Henry was born at Bolingbroke Castle in Lincolnshire in about April 1367, the son of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, and Blanche of Lancaster, and a grandson of King Edward III. He took the name Bolingbroke from his birthplace. As a youth he rode, hunted and jousted, and was besieged with Richard II in the Tower of London during the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

He joined the Lords Appellant's rebellion against his cousin in 1387, though Richard later made him Duke of Hereford. He went on crusading expeditions with the Teutonic Order to Lithuania in 1390 and 1392, and in 1392–93 made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

In 1398 a remark attributed to Thomas de Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, led to a planned duel, which Richard halted by exiling Henry, and Mowbray for life. When Gaunt died in February 1399, Richard cancelled the documents allowing Henry to inherit automatically. Henry returned from exile with Thomas Arundel, the former archbishop of Canterbury, while Richard was campaigning in Ireland, and gathered enough support to have himself declared king, imprison Richard and bypass Richard's heir-presumptive, Edmund de Mortimer, Earl of March. Richard died in prison in February 1400, probably of starvation, whether self-imposed or forced being a matter of historical speculation.

He put down the Epiphany Rising in January 1400, and invaded Scotland in August 1400, a campaign that accomplished little. Owain Glyndŵr declared himself Prince of Wales in 1400. The Percy rebellions followed, and in 1403 the royal army defeated them at the Battle of Shrewsbury, where Henry Percy, known as Hotspur, was killed and the king's eldest son, Henry of Monmouth, was wounded by an arrow in the face. In 1401 the statute De heretico comburendo prescribed burning for heretics, to suppress the Lollards.

From 1405 Henry suffered a disfiguring skin disease and acute attacks of a grave illness, whose nature medical historians still debate. His son Henry of Monmouth took over much of the government in 1410. Henry died on 20 March 1413 in the Jerusalem Chamber at Westminster Abbey, during a meeting of Parliament.

He was buried not at Westminster but at Canterbury Cathedral beside the shrine of Thomas Becket, with his second wife, Joan of Navarre. Historians connect the choice with his wish to legitimise his dynasty. His son succeeded as Henry V, and the usurpation later contributed to the dynastic disputes of the Wars of the Roses.
henry-iv-of-france: Henry was born at the Château de Pau, the capital of Navarre and Béarn, the son of Jeanne III of Navarre and Antoine de Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme. He was baptised a Catholic but raised as a Huguenot by his mother. Under the Huguenot leader Gaspard II de Coligny he witnessed the battles of Jarnac, La Roche-l'Abeille and Moncontour, and he saw combat for the first time in 1570 at Arnay-le-Duc.

On 9 June 1572 his mother died and Henry became King of Navarre. He married Margaret of Valois in Paris on 18 August 1572, and within days the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre killed several thousand Protestants who had come for the wedding. Henry survived by promising to convert, lived at court until early 1576, then escaped and returned to the Protestant side. When Henry III of France died in 1589 he nominally became king, but the Catholic League, backed by Spain, refused to accept him and Pope Sixtus V excommunicated him. He won at Arques and Ivry but failed to take Paris in 1590.

On 25 July 1593 he converted to Catholicism, which secured the allegiance of most of his subjects and earned the resentment of the Huguenots and of Elizabeth I of England. He was crowned at Chartres on 27 February 1594, since the League still held Reims, and Pope Clement VIII lifted the excommunication on 17 September 1595. After his victory at Amiens in September 1597 the Peace of Vervins ended the war with Spain in 1598, the year of the Edict of Nantes. Working through his minister Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, he regularised finance, promoted agriculture and built roads, bridges and canals.

Henry was the target of at least twelve assassination attempts. On 14 May 1610 François Ravaillac, a Catholic zealot, stabbed him in Paris while his coach was halted on the Rue de la Ferronnerie. Ravaillac was seized and executed days later. Henry was buried at the Basilica of Saint Denis, and his widow Marie de' Medici acted as regent for their nine-year-old son Louis XIII until 1617. His statue was set up on the Pont Neuf in 1614, torn down in the Revolution and rebuilt in 1818.
henry-iv-of-plauen: Henry IV belonged to the elder line of the House of Plauen. He was born in 1510, probably on 24 August, at Hartenštejn Castle, the son of Burgrave Henry III of Plauen and his second wife, Barbara of Anhalt-Köthen. After his father's death in 1519 he grew up first in his mother's care and, after her remarriage in 1521, under a guardian she chose, Zdenko Leo Rosenthal, High Burgrave of the Bohemian crown, who brought him to the court in Prague.

On 5 April 1530 King Ferdinand confirmed the Burgraviate of Meissen as his fief, and Emperor Charles V did the same later that year.
