Visits to the Pope or the Emperor brought new privileges and donations, and in 1237 Hermann obtained the incorporation of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword into the Order.

The knights grew dissatisfied at the absence of their Grand Master and recalled him from political life, though he was less successful as a religious leader. He retired to Salerno in 1238 and died there on 20 March 1239. All communication between Frederick II and Pope Gregory IX broke off with his death, which shows how important his mediation had been. A marble bust of him stood in the Siegesallee in Berlin and has been in the Spandau Citadel since May 2009, and a memorial plaque for him is in the Walhalla memorial near Regensburg.
hermanus-van-wyk: Hermanus van Wyk was born in 1835 to a mixed-race Baster family in the Fraserburg district of the Cape Colony. His clan lived at De Tuin in the Northern Cape and was already led by him in 1868, when it decided to leave the colony because of the discrimination and harassment it suffered from white people. The trek went by way of Pella and across the Orange River to Berseba, which it reached in 1870. Scouts found the fertile country around Rehoboth, largely abandoned by the Nama after an attack by the Oorlam Afrikaners in 1864.

Abraham Swartbooi of the Nama let the Basters settle at Rehoboth for eight horses and a yearly rent of one horse, and the first 30 families arrived in October 1870. Under van Wyk's leadership of the Kaptein's council they repaired the existing buildings and drew up a constitution, the Paternal Laws (Vaderlike Wette). By 1876 the community numbered 800 people with 20,000 sheep and between 2,000 and 3,000 cattle, and van Wyk obtained an option to buy the land from Swartbooi for £2,750, though Swartbooi would not yet sell.

In the Herero-Nama War of 1880 the Basters sided with Jan Jonker Afrikaner and Swartbooi's Nama against the Herero, who killed a group of Baster merchants. In 1882 their Nama allies attacked them; the Basters beat off the attack but lost many livestock, an event marked by a small memorial on Church Street in Rehoboth.

The Nama sold the land to an agent of the Dorsland Trekkers, but before the Boers could settle the German Empire claimed South West Africa. On 15 September 1885 van Wyk signed a Treaty of Protection and Friendship, which recognised the territory the Basters occupied as theirs and left them a degree of autonomy under German rule. He died in Rehoboth in 1905. The German authorities approved no successor and set up a Council of Basters instead; his son Cornelius van Wyk was elected Kaptein in 1914, the year the United Kingdom took over the territory.
hermen-rode: Very little is known of Rode's life. He lived and worked in Lübeck, and from 1468 he owned a house on Johannisstrasse in the city, which suggests that he had gained some wealth and standing. Many altarpieces have been attributed to him, but only one bears his signature: the altarpiece of St. Luke, made in 1484 for St. Catherine's church in Lübeck and now in St. Anne's Museum there.

Like his fellow citizen Bernt Notke, Rode was one of the chief exporters of art from Lübeck to the lands around the Baltic Sea. Several works attributed to him are now in Sweden and seem to have been made for a Swedish market, since they show national Swedish saints. Some are in the Swedish Museum of National Antiquities, while others remain in churches, among them an altar of St. Mary in Sorunda church and an altarpiece of St. Gertrude and St. Dorothy in Falsterbo church.

The high altar of St. Nicholas' Church in Tallinn, a work of his maturity, is now shown in the Niguliste Museum, a branch of the Art Museum of Estonia. Its background holds the first known view of the skyline of Lübeck, with the city's eight church towers of the time.

The Grove Encyclopedia of Northern Renaissance Art describes the marks of his style: a distinctive female head with a prominent forehead, a softly rounded receding chin and half-closed, overcast eyes, set on oddly boneless bodies that keep the pointed, forward-stepping stance of the Late Gothic, in dull and thinly painted colours. In later works the influence of the Netherlands grew stronger, especially of Bruges and Gerard David, bringing bright, clear colour combinations like those of the Westphalian Master of Liesborn.
hermenegildo-gutierrez: Hermenegildo Gutiérrez, in Galician Hermenexildo Gotérrez, was the son of Count Gutierre and his wife Elvira. He married Ermesenda Gatónez, daughter of Count Gatón of Astorga and El Bierzo, who was probably a first cousin of King Alfonso III, since Gatón is believed to have been a brother of Ordoño I or of his wife. Hermenegildo first appears in the records in 869, when he and his father-in-law settled a dispute between the king of Asturias and Bishop Mauro. A claim that he descended from Count Ardabastus rests on a controversial and dubious deed that cannot be independently checked.

He was among the most loyal vassals of Alfonso III, who made him his mayordomo mayor, and he was an active member of the curia regia; the king rewarded his services with many properties and tenencias. In 878 he defeated the Muslim troops who had attacked Porto and then Coimbra, and after expelling them he resettled these cities and neighbouring Braga, Viseu and Lamego with people from Galicia.

In 895 he defeated and captured the Galician noble Witiza, who had taken up arms against the king, and brought him in chains before Alfonso, who gave the count many of the rebel's estates. His last appearance in the records is his confirmation of a donation by his son-in-law, King Ordoño II, to the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela.

His holdings passed to his descendants as the County of Coimbra, which Almanzor retook in 987; the city was regained for good only in 1064 by Ferdinand I of León. He was succeeded by his son Gutierre Menéndez, father of Saint Rudesind. His daughter Elvira married Ordoño II and was the mother of Kings Ramiro II and Alfonso IV of León, and another daughter, Ildonza, was the mother of Queen Adosinda Gutiérrez, first wife of Ramiro II. The marriage gave rise to one of the most prominent noble families of medieval Galicia and the County of Portugal, and his great-grandson Count Alvito Nunes later governed the County of Portugal.
hermeric: Nothing is known for certain about Hermeric before 419, when the bishop Hydatius, who wrote his chronicle around 470, first mentions him as king of the Suebi at Braga, Bracara Augusta. Isidore of Seville, writing two centuries after the events, claims he was king from 406, but the authors on whom Isidore drew do not mention him earlier. Hermeric was a pagan and an enemy of the Roman Empire throughout his life.

Historians reconstruct the movements of the Suevi differently. Thompson reads Isidore as having the Suevi cross the Rhine with the Vandals and Alans in December 406 and settle in Hispania, while Kulikowski argued that they probably stayed in northern Gaul from 407 to 409 and moved to Galicia between 409 and 411. In 411 the barbarian peoples divided Iberia by lot: the west of the province of Gallaecia, with Braga, fell to the Suevi and the east to the populous Hasdingi. Between 416 and 418 the Visigoths under Wallia made war on Hermeric on behalf of Rome.

In 419, after a personal dispute between Hermeric and the Vandal king Gunderic, the Vandals attacked the Suevi and trapped Hermeric in the Narbasian Mountains until the Roman general Asterius intervened. Hermeric stayed peaceful until the Vandals left Iberia for Africa in 429, but in 430 he began to raid Gallaecia. In 431 a Gallaecian named Hydatius appealed to Flavius Aëtius for help, and the comes Censorius was sent in 432. According to Hydatius, the Gallaecian plebs in the better-fortified strongpoints defeated Hermeric's men, inflicting heavy casualties and forcing the release of captured families.

In 435, on episcopal intervention, possibly that of Hydatius, Hermeric made peace with the Gallaecians, and in the same year he negotiated with the western Roman emperor through the Catholic bishop Symphosius. Censorius made a second expedition in 437 with Fretimund. After seven years of illness Hermeric retired in 438 and passed the kingship to his son Rechila. Isidore's story that Hermeric afterwards sent Rechila against Andevotus in Baetica is false, since no contemporary evidence shows that he kept any authority. Hermeric died in 441, and his royal line lasted until 456.
hermes: The earliest written record of Hermes comes from Linear B tablets of the Mycenaean Bronze Age found at Pylos, Thebes and Knossos, where his name appears as e-ma-a, always beside those of goddesses. Later worship of Hermes also took place mostly within sanctuaries dedicated chiefly to goddesses such as Hera and Demeter. The name has long been derived from the Greek herma, a heap of stones, but this is disputed. Hermes began as a god with strong underworld associations, a psychopomp who led souls along the road between the upper and lower worlds. This role widened to roads in general and then to boundaries, travellers, sailors and commerce. He is described as the youngest Olympian and may have joined the Olympian pantheon late.

In myth Hermes is the herald and messenger of the gods, often presented as the son of Zeus and Maia. The Homeric Hymn to Hermes gives the best-known account of him as a divine trickster. He killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus, which earned him the epithet Argeïphontes. He wore winged sandals, and in Roman art a winged cap, and carried the caduceus, a winged staff entwined with snakes. He was also the patron of flocks and shepherds.

His name was given to the herma, first a roadside pile of stones to which each traveller added one. In the 6th century BCE Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, replaced the cairns that marked the midway points between Athenian demes with pillars topped by a bust of Hermes. Such herms stood at crossroads and doorways, served as boundary and grave markers, and were thought to protect a household. Only three temples dedicated to him in Classical Greece are known, all in Arcadia, where Mount Cyllene was among the oldest places of his worship.

In Ptolemaic Egypt Greeks identified the god Thoth with Hermes, and their city Khemenu became Hermopolis. Hermes thereby gained the character of a god of learning and secret wisdom. The Romans adopted him as early as the 4th century BCE under the name Mercury, combining his attributes with those of the Etruscan Turms. After the Christian suppression of pagan worship in the 4th century CE, Christian scholars still treated Hermes Trismegistus as a mortal prophet who had foretold Christianity, and Renaissance philosophers used the Hermetic writings to support a belief in a single true theology shared by all religions.
hermes-of-andros: The statue was found in 1832 by Demetrios Loukrezis while digging in a plot of land he owned on the site of the ancient agora of Andros, two years after Greece won independence from the Ottoman Empire. A headless statue of a richly dressed woman lay beside it. Spyridon Trikoupis announced the find the next year in the Bullettino dell'Instituto di Corrispondenza Archeologica. On a visit to Andros in 1841 King Otto of Greece paid Loukrezis and had the statue taken to the new National Museum, then housed in the Temple of Hephaestus in Athens.

Nearby stood a shrine, probably for hero-worship, with an inscription honouring Egnatia Maximilla and Publius Gleitius Gallus, benefactors of the city under Emperor Nero, around 65 CE. The date suited the female statue, a Herculaneum Woman type, but the Hermes proved older, and it was argued that it had been reused beside her. The statue returned to Andros in 1981.

Carved from Parian marble, the figure is two metres and nineteen centimetres tall, over life size. It is one of many copies, made around the 1st century BCE or CE, of an original once thought Lysippean but, by comparison with the Hermes and the Infant Dionysus, the work of a sculptor of the school of Praxiteles, about 360 BCE. It is of the Farnese type and one of its best-preserved examples.

The young god is nude, his chlamys over his left shoulder and down his back. His weight rests on the right leg, the left slightly bent, and his head tilts to the right; beside him a tree-trunk support carries a coiled snake. The arms and the legs below the knees were missing and have been restored. Other copies, among them one in the British Museum, show that the right hand rested on the hip and the cloak wrapped the left arm, and that he held a caduceus and wore winged sandals.

Its craftsmanship and harmony have been widely praised, and it is counted among the finest surviving statues in Greece, with a naturalness and grace that the similar Atalante Hermes, of Pentelic marble and Lysippean character, lacks.
herminafrid: He was one of three sons of King Bisinus and his Lombard queen Menia; his sister Raicunda married the Lombard king Wacho. Between 507 and 511 he married Amalaberga, a granddaughter of Theodemir, and he sent Theodoric the Great a gift of silver-white horses. When he became king is unclear, but a letter of Theodoric dated to 507 already calls him king of the Thuringii.

He first shared the kingdom with his brothers Baderic and Bertachar. In 529 he killed Bertachar in battle, leaving his young niece Radegund an orphan. According to Gregory of Tours, Amalaberga then urged him against Baderic, once laying only half the table and telling him that a king who owned half a kingdom deserved half a table bare. He made a pact with Theuderic I, king of Metz, against Baderic, who was overcome by the Franks and beheaded, but he refused to keep his side of the bargain, and the two kings became enemies.

Theuderic, his son Theudebert I and his brother Clotaire I of Soissons then attacked the Thuringii, won a battle near the Unstrut and took the royal seat at Scithingi, the modern Burgscheidungen. The Thuringian king escaped, but Radegund and his nephews were captured.

Theuderic then gave him safe conduct to Zülpich and many gifts. While the two talked, someone pushed him from the town walls, and Gregory notes that some people suggested Theuderic had a hand in it. Radegund was forced to marry Clotaire. Amalaberga fled to the Ostrogoths with her children Amalafrid and Rodelinda; later captured by the Byzantine general Belisarius, she was sent to Constantinople, where Amalafrid became an imperial general and Rodelinda married the Lombard king Auduin.

The Thuringian kingdom ended with him: Slavic tribes took the land east of the Saale and the Saxons north Thuringia. Its fall became the subject of many epic retellings, above all in the Saxon foundation myth that Widukind of Corvey wrote in 967, in which Saxons under Duke Hadugato win the battle on the Unstrut as allies of the Franks. Gregory, the main source, gives the Frankish view; Widukind wrote much later and drew on myth.
hermopolis: Hermopolis, or Hermopolis Magna, was a major city of antiquity near the boundary between Lower and Upper Egypt, and its remains lie near the modern town of el-Ashmunein in Mallawi, Minya Governorate. Its Egyptian name Khemenu means Eight-Town, after the Ogdoad, a group of eight primordial deities said to reside there. The name survived in Coptic as Shmun, from which the Arabic al-Ashmunayn comes. The Greeks called it City of Hermes because they identified Hermes with Thoth, the god of magic, healing and wisdom and patron of scribes, whose main cult centre it was.

The city was the capital of the Hare nome, the fifteenth of Upper Egypt, from the Old Kingdom. As a border town it was a place of resort and wealth, ranking second only to Thebes. A castle just south of it collected tolls from river craft from the Thebaid. The dead were ferried across the Nile to the grottos of Beni Hasan. Thoth was represented by the ibis.

In Roman Egypt it became a significant city of the province of Thebais Prima, and a surviving Oxyrhynchus Papyrus of the 3rd century CE indicates that houses of seven storeys stood there. It was an early Christian centre from the 3rd century; the first bishop listed, Conon, dates from about 250, and a tradition holds that the Holy Family found refuge there. The city was abandoned after the Muslim conquest of Egypt, though Arabic papyri from the 8th to 11th centuries refer to it as Ushmun.

The temple of Thoth has left only a portico, a double row of six pillars with architraves of five stones, about 40 feet high with capitals, painted in alternating yellow, red and blue bands; the buildings raised there under the Ptolemies were on a great scale, in an essentially Egyptian style.

Outside the temple precinct stand the remains of a basilica of the 5th century, 55 metres long, with a colonnaded transept ending in exedras. It was found in 1942 by Moharam Kamal and documented from 1987 to 1990 by a Polish-Egyptian expedition. A small open-air museum holds two large statues of Thoth as a baboon worshipping the sun.
hernan-cortes: Hernán Cortés was born around 1485 in Medellín, in Extremadura, to Martín Cortés, an hidalgo of distinguished ancestry but slender means, and Catalina Pizarro; through his mother he was a distant relation of Francisco Pizarro. At fourteen he was sent to study Latin with an uncle in Salamanca. He sailed for Hispaniola in 1504, registered as a citizen of Santo Domingo, received an encomienda and became a notary at Azua de Compostela. In 1511 he accompanied Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar in the conquest of Cuba, where he served as clerk to the treasurer and became a magistrate of the second Spanish town.

In 1518 Velázquez put Cortés in command of an expedition to the mainland, then revoked his charter at the last minute. Cortés ignored the order and sailed in February 1519 with about 11 ships, 500 men, 13 horses and a few cannon. On the Yucatán coast he found Geronimo de Aguilar, a Spanish priest who had learned Chontal Maya, and he also used Doña Marina as his interpreter. He allied with some native peoples against others. In mid-August 1519 he marched on Tenochtitlán with 600 soldiers, 15 horsemen, 15 cannons and hundreds of indigenous carriers and warriors, after Moctezuma II had repeatedly refused to meet him.

Cortés's force reached Tlaxcala after the battle of Otumba, having lost 870 men. With their allies and reinforcements from Cuba, they prevailed. Cortés cut off supplies, subdued the cities allied to the Aztecs and built brigantines on the lake. He destroyed the city block by block, and the siege ended in Spanish victory and the destruction of Tenochtitlán. He wrote to Charles V asking to be rewarded rather than punished for mutiny, and received the title of Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca, while the viceroyalty went to Antonio de Mendoza in 1535. From 1524 to 1526 he led an expedition to Honduras, during which Cuauhtémoc was executed.

Cortés returned to Spain in 1541, hoping to answer lawsuits brought by his opponents, and joined the emperor's expedition against Algiers, in which he nearly drowned in a storm. Heavily in debt after financing his own expeditions, he made a claim on the royal treasury in February 1544 and was ignored for three years. He set out for Mexico in 1547 but was taken ill at Seville and died at Castilleja de la Cuesta on 2 December 1547, aged 62. His letters to Charles V, the cartas de relación, are his only surviving writings. Mexico City was built on the ruins of Tenochtitlán, and the Paso de Cortés, the pass between the volcanoes Iztaccíhuatl and Popocatépetl through which he led his soldiers, bears his name.
hernan-siles-zuazo: Hernán Siles Zuazo was the illegitimate son of Hernando Siles Reyes, the last president of the Republican Party, and Isabel Zuazo Cusicanqui, and was raised by his mother. He was wounded and decorated in the Chaco War of 1932 to 1935, then took a law degree at San Andrés University. Elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1940, he founded the Revolutionary Nationalist Movement (MNR) in 1941 with Víctor Paz Estenssoro and others.

Exiled to Argentina after Gualberto Villarroel was overthrown in 1946, he returned in 1949, was jailed on an island in Lake Titicaca, escaped to Peru and slipped back into Bolivia to take his seat in congress and demand his back pay.

The army refused to recognise Paz Estenssoro's win in the 1951 election, and from 9 to 11 April 1952 the MNR led the Bolivian National Revolution. Siles played a major part while Paz was in exile, and he served as provisional president from 11 to 16 April 1952, then as vice-president. The government introduced universal suffrage, nationalised the largest mines and adopted an agrarian reform.

After his first term, Paz sent him as ambassador to Uruguay and then to Spain. He broke with Paz in 1964 and formed the MNRI in 1971. In 1978 he built the leftist alliance known as the UDP, which led the elections of 1978, 1979 and 1980; the coup of 17 July 1980 kept him from office and he went into exile in Peru.

As president from 6 August 1956 he faced collapsing production and rising inflation. He accepted the United States's Eder plan, cut spending and social programmes in return for aid, and disarmed the worker and miner militias.

Congress elected him again on 5 October 1982, and he took office on 10 October. He restored relations with Cuba in 1983 and extradited the Nazi war criminal Klaus Barbie to France that year. He was abducted for ten hours on 30 June 1984 during a failed military coup. Hyperinflation, strikes led by Juan Lechín and the desertion of his vice-president, Jaime Paz, weakened him, and Congress called early elections. Paz Estenssoro won in 1985. Siles died in Montevideo in August 1996.
hernando-de-soto: Hernando de Soto was born in Extremadura, in what is now the province of Badajoz, to parents who were both hidalgos, nobles of modest means. Badajoz, Barcarrota and Jerez de los Caballeros each claim to be his birthplace; Ursula Lamb considers Jerez most likely, and his will asked that his body be buried there. The region was poor, and young men sought fortune overseas. He sailed to the New World with Pedro Arias Dávila, the first governor of Panama, landing as a teenager in 1514.

De Soto took part in an expedition to Veragua in 1520 and in the conquest of Nicaragua from 1524, where he received an encomienda and an office in León. He became known as a horseman and tactician, and for extorting native villages by seizing their chiefs. He then joined Francisco Pizarro and became one of his captains. At Cajamarca he led one of three mounted groups in the attack on the Inca Atahualpa. During the king's captivity in 1533 he grew friendly with him and taught him chess. He returned to Spain in 1536 with plunder from Peru, entered the Order of Santiago and married Isabel de Bobadilla.

The crown granted him the governorship of Cuba and the right to conquer Florida. With about 620 Spanish and Portuguese men, among them Atlantic Creoles who were enslaved, and with horses and pigs, he landed on the Florida coast in May 1539. He found Juan Ortiz, a Spaniard living among the Mocoso, who served as interpreter in Timucuan-speaking areas. The expedition wintered at the Apalachee village of Anhaica, then went north-east through Georgia and was received by the female chief of Cofitachequi in South Carolina, where it found no gold.

The army crossed the Appalachian Mountains into eastern Tennessee, and reached the Mississippi on 8 May 1541, building flatboats and crossing at night. It then travelled west through Arkansas, Oklahoma and Texas. De Soto died of a fever on 21 May 1542 in the native village of Guachoya. He had persuaded local people that he was an immortal Son of the Sun, so his men hid his death, and by one account sank his body in the Mississippi. Luis de Moscoso Alvarado took command, and the survivors built boats and descended the river. The expedition had lost nearly half its men and found neither treasure nor a site for a colony.

The Spanish counted it a failure. Its pigs escaped and became ancestors of feral razorbacks, and clashes it provoked set many peoples against Europeans. Whether it brought epidemics is disputed, since the first documented smallpox epidemic in the south-east dates from 1696. The route is debated beyond Mabila in Alabama, where John R. Swanton and Charles M. Hudson differ.
hernando-pizarro: Hernando was the only one of the Pizarro brothers born in wedlock; Francisco, Juan and Gonzalo Pizarro were his half-brothers, and through his father he was a second cousin of Hernán Cortés. He was educated and gained influence at the Spanish court, and in 1530 he sailed for the New World with Francisco and accompanied him in the conquest of Peru.

In November 1533 Hernando wrote a letter describing the expedition, in which he praised the paved roads of the Inca mountains and their bridges of stone, wood and network. That year he was sent back to Spain with the royal fifth for the emperor, taken from the treasure collected for Atahuallpa's ransom. He reached Seville on 9 January 1534 and met Charles at Calatayud, who confirmed Francisco's grants and extended them seventy leagues further south, while giving Diego de Almagro a grant two hundred leagues beyond.

Back in Peru, Hernando ruled the Inca capital of Cuzco with Juan and Gonzalo, governing with an iron fist and helping to suppress the uprisings led by Manco Inca. Returning from a fruitless expedition to Chile, Almagro claimed Cuzco as his share, seized it in 1537 and captured Hernando and Juan. Released after negotiations between Almagro and Francisco, Hernando came back with Gonzalo and an army in 1538 and won a decisive victory at the Battle of Las Salinas, capturing Almagro and the city.

Almagro's execution later that year and the disorder of the Spanish infighting caused an outcry at court. Hernando returned to Spain in 1539 to lobby for his brothers, but despite his bribes he was held in the Castle of La Mota from June 1541 until May 1561. In 1552 he married his niece Francisca Pizarro Yupanqui, the 17-year-old daughter of Francisco and Inés Yupanqui, and they had five children; the descendants of their son Francisco Pizarro y Pizarro were the Marqueses de La Conquista. Hernando spent his last years in his palace at Trujillo, where he died in 1578.
hero-and-leander: The myth is attested in Ovid's Heroides and in the epic poem of Musaeus, and Virgil's Georgics allude to it. Ovid is credited with the Double Heroides, which treats it in letters 18 and 19, an exchange between the lovers. In the first Leander has been unable to swim to Hero because of bad weather, and her summons to him to make the effort proves fatal to her lover.

Musaeus was a Byzantine poet of the 6th century. Aldus Manutius made his poem one of the first publications of his press at Venice, around 1493. Bernardo Tasso, Boscán and Clément Marot made early translations into Italian, Spanish and French. In the Renaissance the poem was widely believed to be older than Homer, and George Chapman wrote that the dead lovers were the first that ever poet sung.

Hero was a priestess of Aphrodite who lived in a tower at Sestos on the European side of the Hellespont. Leander came from Abydos on the opposite shore. In the usual telling he persuaded Hero with soft words and with the argument that Aphrodite, as goddess of love, would scorn the worship of a virgin. Their secret affair lasted through a warm summer, and as winter and rough weather approached they agreed to part and resume in the spring.

On a stormy winter night Leander saw the lamp on Hero's tower and set out to swim to her, but a strong wind blew out the light, he lost his way and he drowned. Hero threw herself from the tower when she saw his body. Their bodies washed up together on the shore and were buried in a lovers' tomb.

Christopher Marlowe began a long poem on the subject that ends after the two have become lovers, without the swim or the lamp. George Chapman completed it after Marlowe's death, and the result was often reprinted in the first half of the 17th century, in editions from 1598 to 1637. Walter Raleigh alluded to the story, and John Donne summed it up in a two-line epigram. Lord Byron swam the Hellespont in May 1810, inspired by the myth, and wrote of the feat.

Composers and painters returned to it. Peter Paul Rubens painted it in 1604, George Frideric Handel wrote the solo cantata Ero e Leandro in 1707, and William Etty showed Hero dying on Leander's body in 1829. Franz Grillparzer made it a tragedy in 1831, and Keats wrote a sonnet about an engraved gem of Leander in 1817. Lafcadio Hearn noted a Japanese tale of a girl who swims to her lover guided by a lantern, and observed that in the Far East it is Hero who does the swimming.
hero-of-alexandria: Almost nothing is known of the life of Hero of Alexandria, including his birthplace and background. The first surviving mention of him is in the Collection of Pappus in the 4th century, and scholarly estimates of his dates range widely. Alexandria had been founded by Alexander the Great and was by his time a cosmopolitan city of the Roman Empire, its intellectual life centred on the Mouseion, whose members spoke and wrote in Greek. Because some of his writings read like lecture notes or textbooks in mathematics, mechanics, physics and pneumatics, it has been inferred that he taught there.

Many devices are ascribed to Hero, some of them developed from the work of Ctesibius. The best known is the aeolipile, a steam-driven reaction engine; another engine used air heated in a closed chamber by an altar fire to push water from a sealed vessel, and the weight of the water collected pulled a rope that opened temple doors.

He described a coin-operated machine that released a fixed measure of water for ablutions, a force pump used in a fire engine, a fountain driven by its own water pressure, a self-filling wine bowl with a float valve and a wind-wheel that drove an organ. His mechanical theatre ran an entire play of almost ten minutes from ropes, knots and a rotating cogwheel.

In mathematics he wrote a commentary on Euclid's Elements and the Metrica, a work on applied geometry. The Metrica contains an iterative method for square roots, now called Heron's method, and the formula for the area of a triangle from the lengths of its sides, with which his name is chiefly linked.

He also treated a problem of the shortest path between two points by way of a line, from which he drew the principle that light travelling between two points in one medium takes the shortest path. In the Middle Ages Ibn al-Haytham extended the principle, and Pierre de Fermat stated it in a more general form in 1662.

Much of Hero's original writing has been lost. Some works survive in manuscripts from the Byzantine Empire and, to a lesser extent, in Latin or Arabic translations. Historians have sometimes run the aeolipile together with the temple-door engine and claimed that it did useful work, which the sources do not show.
herod-agrippa-i: Herod Agrippa was born around 11 BCE, the son of Aristobulus IV, a child of Herod the Great and Mariamne the Hasmonean. His mother Berenice was a daughter of Salome, sister of Herod the Great, so he descended from both the Hasmonean and Herodian dynasties. His parents named him after Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, a close collaborator of Emperor Augustus. He spent his childhood and youth at the imperial court in Rome, where he became a friend of the princes Claudius and Drusus.

After the death of Drusus he fell into disgrace and returned to Judaea, having squandered much of his fortune on the favour of the freedmen of Tiberius. Around 26 he married his cousin Cypros, and they lived modestly in a fortress at Malatha in Idumea. Their son became Herod Agrippa II. Pursued for debts, he left for Alexandria, borrowed money there, and sailed for Italy in the spring of 36.

In Rome Tiberius made him guardian of his grandson Tiberius Gemellus, but Agrippa courted the other designated heir, Caligula. When Caligula took the throne, Agrippa received the old tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias, with the title of king over Batanea, Trachonitis, Gaulanitis, Auranitis, Paneas and Iturea. He travelled to his territories in the summer of 38, passing through Alexandria during a period of anti-Jewish feeling in which he was mocked in a street masquerade. In 40 he gained Galilee and Perea after the disgrace of his uncle Herod Antipas.

Caligula was assassinated on 24 January 41. Agrippa's support and manoeuvres seem to have been decisive in raising Claudius to power, and he was rewarded with Idumea, Judea and Samaria, so that he ruled a realm as large as that of Herod the Great. He interceded with Claudius for the Jews, and edicts confirmed the privileges of the Alexandrian Jews and extended them across the diaspora. His regional ambitions drew the opposition of Gaius Vibius Marsus, governor of Syria, who halted the fortification of Jerusalem on the emperor's orders.

Agrippa died unexpectedly in 44, after about three years as king of Judaea. The cause is unknown and rumours of poisoning circulated; some researchers think Romans worried by his ambitions may have been responsible. Acts of the Apostles tells that after a delegation from Tyre and Sidon called his answer the voice of a god, an angel struck him down and worms devoured him. Claudius did not give the kingdom to Agrippa II but made it a Roman province under the procurator Cuspius Fadus.

Josephus describes him as gentle and generous, and rabbinical sources present him as pious. The pagan inhabitants of Caesarea and Sebaste rejoiced at his death. For many Jews the end of his rule closed hopes of even a symbolic independence, and messianic, anti-Roman movements appeared afterwards.
herod-antipas: Antipas was a son of Herod the Great and Malthace, a woman from Samaria. His date of birth is unknown, but he, his full brother Archelaus and his half-brother Philip were educated in Rome. He was not Herod's first choice of heir. That place went to Aristobulus and Alexander, sons of the Hasmonean princess Mariamne, until they were executed, and to Antipater, who was convicted of trying to poison his father. In Herod's final will Archelaus was to be king, while Antipas would rule Galilee and Perea as tetrarch. The three heirs travelled to Rome, where Augustus largely confirmed the division of territory.

Galilee and Perea were separated by the Decapolis, and both were unsettled. While Antipas was in Rome, dissidents had attacked the palace of Sepphoris, and Quinctilius Varus, the Roman governor of Syria, burned the town and sold its inhabitants as slaves. Antipas rebuilt and fortified Sepphoris and added a wall to Betharamphtha in Perea, later called Livias and then Julias. His main construction was his capital Tiberias on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, named for the emperor Tiberius. Pious Jews at first refused to live there because it was built over a graveyard, so Antipas settled it with foreigners, forced migrants, poor people and freed slaves. His coins carried no images, out of respect for Jewish prescriptions against idolatry.

He divorced his first wife Phasa'el, daughter of King Aretas IV of Nabatea, in order to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother Herod II. According to the Gospels, John the Baptist condemned the marriage, and Antipas had him imprisoned at Machaerus and beheaded. Josephus says instead that John's influence made Antipas fear rebellion. In Luke's account Pilate, learning that Jesus was a Galilean, sent him to Antipas, who questioned and mocked him and sent him back. Some scholars doubt that this trial took place.

The divorce added to disputes with Aretas over the border, and in a war around 36 Antipas's army was defeated. Tiberius ordered a counter-offensive under Lucius Vitellius, but it was abandoned when Tiberius died in March 37.

Antipas's nephew Agrippa, brother of Herodias, became a friend of Caligula and received Philip's former tetrarchy with the title of king in 37. According to Josephus, Herodias urged Antipas to ask for the title of king too, but Agrippa accused him before Caligula of conspiring with Sejanus and with King Artabanus. In the summer of 39 Antipas was exiled and his territory passed to Agrippa. Josephus names Lugdunum in Gaul and, elsewhere, Hispania as the place. He died in exile at an unknown date.
herod-archelaus: Herod Archelaus was the son of Herod the Great and Malthace the Samaritan, brother of Herod Antipas and half-brother of Herod II. His name means leading the people. Shortly before his death, according to Josephus, Herod the Great had been involved in a religious crisis: he had placed a golden eagle over the Temple entrance, which was seen as blasphemous, and it was chopped down with axes. Two teachers and about 40 youths were arrested for the act and burned. Archelaus came to power at his father's death in 4 BCE, and ruled over one half of his father's territories.

Josephus describes Archelaus before the Passover of 4 BCE, dressed in white and seated on a golden throne. He appeared kind to the people of Jerusalem, who wanted lower taxes and an end to the imprisonment of Herod's enemies. The crowd then demanded punishment for those who had ordered the deaths of the two teachers and 40 youths, and the replacement of Herod's High Priest by one of greater piety and purity. Archelaus agreed to the latter and asked for moderation until Augustus confirmed him as king.

As the crowd in the Temple area grew threatening, he sent a general and a tribune to reason with them; they were stoned, and many were killed. After midnight Archelaus sent the whole army into the city, and Josephus records a death toll of 3000. Passover was cancelled. The army proclaimed him king, but he declined the title until Augustus had heard his claims, and he sailed to Rome. There his brother Antipas accused him over the uproar and disputed the succession, relying on an earlier will. Nicolaus of Damascus argued for Archelaus, and Augustus divided the kingdom, giving him Judea with the title of ethnarch.

Archelaus divorced his first wife, Mariamne, to marry Glaphyra, the widow of his brother Alexander. Her second husband, Juba, king of Mauretania, was still alive, and his subjects complained to Augustus that the marriage broke the Mosaic law. Archelaus fell into disrepute and was deposed in the tenth year of his rule and banished to Vienne in Gaul. His lands became the Roman province of Judaea.

Archelaus appears in the Gospel of Matthew, in which Joseph, returning from Egypt, hears that Archelaus rules Judaea and is afraid to go there, and turns aside to Galilee; this is Matthew's explanation of why Jesus grew up in Nazareth. Some interpreters think the opening of the parable of the minas in the Gospel of Luke refers to his journey to Rome, while others see a later adaptation in oral tradition.
herod-the-great: Herod was born in Idumea, south of Judea, the second son of Antipater the Idumaean, a high-ranking official under the ethnarch Hyrcanus II, and Cypros, a Nabatean princess from Petra. His father was by descent an Edomite, and his ancestors had been forcibly converted to Judaism. Herod was raised as a Jew. Historians dispute his ethnic background: Strabo held that the Idumaeans were of Nabataean origin, while others argue that the Edomites were not Arab. Josephus, whose works record many details of his life, made him a descendant of the Hasmoneans.

Judea had been ruled by Hasmonean kings from 140 until 63 BCE, when Pompey's conquest made them clients of Rome. Herod's war against the Hasmonean Antigonus began in 39 BCE, and after the conquest of Jerusalem Mark Antony executed Antigonus. Herod ruled under Roman overlordship until his death and established the Herodian dynasty. In 30 BCE Octavian confirmed him as King of Judea at Rhodes.

His most ambitious project was the expansion of the Second Temple in Jerusalem, begun in 20-19 BCE, for which he employed 1,000 priests as masons and carpenters to comply with religious law. It was destroyed in 70 CE, and only the retaining walls remain, including the Western Wall. He also built the fortresses of Masada and Herodium and founded Caesarea Maritima. Late in his reign he had his sons Alexander and Aristobulus tried before a Roman court at Beirut, and they were executed. The Gospel of Matthew describes him ordering the killing of all boys of two and under in Bethlehem, the Massacre of the Innocents.

Herod died in Jericho after a painful illness. Josephus says the pain led him to attempt suicide by stabbing, and that his cousin stopped him. Most 20th-century scholarship followed Emil Schürer's chronology of 1896 in dating his death to 4 BCE. Josephus says he was buried at Herodium, and in 2007 a team led by Ehud Netzer announced the discovery of a tomb there, with a broken sarcophagus but no remains.

Augustus respected Herod's will and divided the kingdom among three sons. Herod Archelaus became ethnarch of Judea, Samaria and Idumea, Herod Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea, and Philip tetrarch of the lands north and east of the Jordan.
herodias: Herodias was the daughter of Aristobulus IV and his wife Berenice, and a full sister of Herod V, king of Chalkis, and of Herod Agrippa, king of Judea. Herod the Great executed her father and his brother Alexander in 7 BCE and engaged her to Herod II, her half-uncle. Antipater II, Herod the Great's eldest son, opposed the marriage, but he was executed in 4 BCE for plotting to poison his father. Days before he died, Herod the Great divorced Herod II's mother Mariamne and dropped her son from the line of succession.

Herodias and Herod II had a daughter, Salome. The Gospels of Matthew and Mark name her husband Philip, but many scholars regard this as an error, since Josephus names him Herod and the Gospel of Luke drops the name Philip. Herodias later divorced him while he was alive, which Josephus says confounded the laws of the country, and she married his half-brother Herod Antipas.

Antipas divorced his first wife Phasaelis, daughter of King Aretas IV of Nabatea, in order to marry her. According to Matthew and Luke it was this proposed marriage that John the Baptist publicly criticised. The divorce also added a personal grievance to earlier disputes between Antipas and Aretas over territory on the border of Perea and Nabatea. Aretas sent an army against him with a disastrous result for Antipas, and a Roman counter-offensive ordered by Tiberius was abandoned on the emperor's death in 37 CE. In 39 CE his nephew Agrippa I accused Antipas of conspiracy against the emperor Caligula, who exiled him to Gaul. Herodias accompanied him there.

In Matthew and Mark, Herodias plays a major part in the execution of John the Baptist: her daughter's dance before Antipas and his guests leads to her request for the Baptist's head. In Mark, Antipas does not wish to kill John, whom he liked to hear preach. Some biblical scholars question whether the Gospels give an accurate account, and some see in the struggle a recollection of the conflict between Ahab and Jezebel and the prophet Elijah.

In medieval Europe her name became associated with beliefs about witches and the supernatural leader they joined at night. Medieval and Renaissance artists often paired her with Salome in depictions of the power of women. Later works include Gustave Flaubert's story Hérodias of 1877 and Oscar Wilde's play Salomé.
herodium: Herodium, in Greek Herodeion and in Arabic Jabal al-Fureidis, Mountain of the Little Paradise, is a fortified desert palace built by Herod the Great, king of Judaea, in the first century BCE. It stands atop a hill in the Judaean Desert about 12 kilometres south of Jerusalem and 5 kilometres southeast of Bethlehem, at an elevation of 758 metres. The hill is artificial and cone-shaped, dominates the surrounding landscape and can be seen from Jerusalem. It is the only site named after Herod the Great. The Crusaders knew it as the Mountain of the Franks, and Edward Robinson identified it as Herodium in 1841 from the description of Josephus.

According to Josephus, Herod fled to Masada in 40 BCE after the Parthian conquest of Syria, clashed on the way with Jews loyal to Antigonus at this spot, and built a town there to commemorate his victory. At the summit his engineers built a fortified palace with double walls, towers, a Roman-style bathhouse, banquet halls and living quarters, and at the base a lower palace with gardens, courtyards and a large pool fed by aqueducts.

Josephus says Herod was buried there after his death in 4 BCE. Jewish rebels held the site in the First Jewish–Roman War, turning Herod's dining hall into a synagogue, until the Roman legate Sextus Lucilius Bassus captured it, likely in early 72 CE. Simon bar Kokhba made it a secondary headquarters in the revolt of 132–135 CE, after which it was abandoned.

Virgilio Canio Corbo and Stanislao Loffreda excavated the upper citadel from 1962 to 1967. From 1972 Ehud Netzer, for the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, worked mostly on the lower palace until his death in 2010. In 2007 he identified what he took to be the tomb of Herod on the northern slope, and in 2010 he found a royal theatre with frescoes of landscapes. A copper-alloy ring found in 1968–1969 and cleaned in 2018 bears the Greek words of Pilates, and some have suggested it belonged to Pontius Pilate.

The site lies in Area C of the West Bank. Israel asserts that the Oslo Accords entitle it to work there, while Palestinian authorities say Israel has no right to dig or remove finds; the dispute was prominent in 2013, when finds from the site were shown at the Israel Museum.
herodotus: Herodotus was, by his own statement at the beginning of his work, a native of Halicarnassus in Anatolia, and it is generally accepted that he was born there in the early fifth century BCE. The Suda, a Byzantine encyclopaedia of the 10th century, says that his family was influential, that he was the son of Lyxes and Dryo and that he was related to the epic poet Panyassis. Since Lyxes and Panyassis are Carian names, he was probably at least partly a Hellenised Carian. Halicarnassus was within the Persian Empire, which made him a Persian subject.

The evidence for his life is slight and late. According to the Suda he learned the Ionian dialect on Samos, to which his family fled from the tyrant Lygdamis, and later returned to lead the revolt that overthrew him. Inscriptions show that Ionic Greek was used in official documents at Halicarnassus, and since the Suda is the only source for the liberation, its account is doubtful.

Herodotus's eyewitness accounts indicate that he travelled in Egypt in association with Athenians, probably after 454 BCE. He probably went to Tyre next and then down the Euphrates to Babylon. For some reason he became unpopular in Halicarnassus and around 447 BCE migrated to Athens, whose people and democratic institutions he openly admired. In 443 BCE or shortly afterwards he moved to Thurii, in modern Calabria, as part of an Athenian-sponsored colony.

He made his researches known through oral recitations. According to Lucian he read the whole of the Histories at the Olympic Games in one sitting. The work deals chiefly with the lives of prominent kings and with battles such as Marathon, Thermopylae, Artemisium, Salamis, Plataea and Mycale, and digresses into cultural, ethnographic and geographical background. Nothing in it can be dated with certainty to later than 430 BCE.

The place of his death is unknown. He may have returned to Athens and died there in the plague, or died in Macedonia or at Thurii. His is the earliest Greek prose work to survive intact. Cicero called him the Father of History, but his many strange stories and folk-tales led critics to brand him the Father of Lies. Thucydides dismissed him as a story-teller. Herodotus answered that he reported what he could see and what he was told.
herophilus: Herophilos was born in Chalcedon in Asia Minor around 335 BCE and moved to Alexandria while fairly young to study. As an adult he taught and wrote at least nine works, among them On Pulses, on the flow of blood from the heart through the arteries, and Midwifery, on the duration and phases of childbirth. His contemporary Erasistratus worked with him at a medical school in Alexandria that is said to have drawn people from all over the ancient world.

Human dissection was banned in most places at the time except Alexandria, where he performed dissections, often in public so that he could explain them to those who came to watch. Celsus and Tertullian state that he vivisected at least 600 prisoners, but many historians dispute this, partly because he appears to have believed the arteries held very little blood, a belief unlikely in someone who had cut open living bodies. His writings are lost and are known chiefly through Galen.

Herophilos stressed the experimental method and considered it essential to base knowledge on observation. He is seen as a forerunner of the Empiric school founded by his pupil Philinus of Cos, though the Empirics attacked him for accepting humoral pathology and for seeking causes behind what could not be seen. He worked within the theory of four humours, but through dissection concluded that veins carry only blood, and he distinguished arteries from veins. He measured the pulse by standards of his own, using a water clock, and used it in diagnosis.

He held that the brain, rather than the heart, houses the intellect, and he was the first to distinguish the cerebrum from the cerebellum. He separated nerves from blood vessels and sensory from motor nerves. In the eye he described the optic and oculomotor nerves and its layers: cornea, sclera, iris, retina and choroid. He called the retina retiform, like a casting net, the source of the modern word. He also named the duodenum, and the confluence of sinuses in the skull was called the torcular Herophili after him.

Herophilos died around 280 BCE. His anatomical findings lived on in the works of later physicians, notably Galen. He is often called the father of anatomy and is credited as the first scientist to carry out systematic dissection of human cadavers.
herostratus: Nothing is known of his family, birth date, residence, work or social place. The historian Albert Borowitz writes that his identity is shrouded in mystery except for the name. He is sometimes assumed to have been a citizen of Ephesus, but because the punishment of erasing a name usually applied only to noncitizens, some historians suggest he was born elsewhere or was a slave or former slave. The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, dedicated to the goddess of childbirth and the hunt, was built over 120 years from about 560 BCE to a design by Chersiphron and Metagenes. It was almost wholly marble except for the wooden statue and the roof, and ancient writers counted it among the Seven Wonders of the World.

On the day Alexander the Great was born in 356 BCE a man burned the temple down; some historians say he set the large wooden roof alight. He was arrested, confessed under torture on the rack that he had acted to win everlasting fame, and was executed. Ephesus passed a damnatio memoriae law forbidding anyone to mention his name. Borowitz notes possible gaps in the story, and the historian Dieter Knibbe, sceptical of his role, proposes that the temple's overseers started the fire in secret because its foundation was sinking. The temple was rebuilt from 323 BCE on a larger scale; the Goths looted and burned it about 262 or 267 CE, and it ended in 401 CE at the hands of a Christian mob.

No evidence reveals his motive. The leading theory since antiquity is resentment at a perceived injustice, while Lucian proposed jealousy and a sense of mediocrity, and Aelian and Valerius Maximus thought sacrilege. The law did not stop ancient writers from recording him, and may have secured the fame he sought. The first to mention him was Theopompus, a contemporary. By the Middle Ages his name was familiar in Europe, and Chaucer used it for unscrupulous quests for celebrity. Alessandro Verri published the first book-length fiction on him in 1815, and Jean-Paul Sartre wrote a short story, Erostratus. Herostratic fame now means fame sought at any cost.
herrenchiemsee: Herrenchiemsee stands on Herreninsel, the largest island in the Chiemsee in southern Bavaria, about 60 kilometres south-east of Munich. According to tradition the Benedictine abbey there was founded about 765 by Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria; newer findings suggest a foundation between 620 and 629 by the missionary Saint Eustace of Luxeuil. About 1130 it became a convent of canons regular, and in 1215 the Salzburg archbishop made its church the cathedral of the Bishopric of Chiemsee. The abbey was secularised in 1803 and the diocese dissolved in 1808; later owners demolished the cathedral and even turned the abbey into a brewery.

King Ludwig II of Bavaria bought the island in 1873, warding off plans to clear its forest, and converted the remaining buildings into the Old Palace. In 1867 he had travelled to France but had to return before he could see Versailles. After he finally visited it in the summer of 1874, he resumed plans drawn by his court architect Georg von Dollmann, and construction of the New Palace began on 21 May 1878 as a homage to Louis XIV. Ludwig stayed there for only a few days in September 1885, in a handful of finished rooms.

The palace was planned as a W with wings round a central block, but only the central portion was built, and 50 of the 70 rooms were still incomplete. Its Hall of Mirrors has 17 arches like that at Versailles, and its ceiling is painted with 25 frescoes showing Louis XIV. The palace has toilets, water and central heating, which the original Versailles lacked, and the garden holds a copy of the Latona Fountain. From 1863 to 1886 16,579,674 marks were spent, bringing the royal finances to the verge of bankruptcy.

All construction stopped at Ludwig's death in 1886, and the palace opened to the public only weeks later. The unfinished north wing was demolished in 1907, and in 1923 Crown Prince Rupprecht ceded Herrenchiemsee to the State of Bavaria. From 10 to 23 August 1948 representatives of eleven German states met in the Old Palace as a Constitutional Convention to prepare the drafting of the Basic Law. The island is maintained by the Bavarian Administration of State-Owned Palaces, Gardens and Lakes and is open to the public, and in 2025 the site was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
herrenhausen-gardens: The gardens lie in Herrenhausen, an urban district of Hanover, the capital of Lower Saxony, and comprise four parts: the Great Garden, the Hill Garden, the Georgen Garden and the Guelf Garden. The Great Garden covers 50 hectares of lawns, hedges, walkways and statues set in strict geometrical patterns. The Hill Garden has grown from a vegetable garden into a large botanical garden, while the Georgen and Guelf gardens are laid out in the style of English gardens.

Herrenhausen served as a summer retreat a few kilometres outside the city, while the Leine Palace was the main residence. Sophia of Hanover commissioned the French gardener Martin Charbonnier in 1683 to enlarge the existing garden. Her son George Louis, who became King George I of Great Britain in 1714, gave up his father's plan for a large baroque palace and concentrated on water features. The Great Fountain, based on ideas of Gottfried Leibniz, was inaugurated in 1719, and in 1721 it reached some 35 metres, the highest fountain in European courts.

The Hill Garden, begun in 1666 as a vegetable garden, became under Sophia a garden for exotic plants. Tobacco and mulberry grew there, and from 1706 the silkworms of Hamelin were fed with its mulberry leaves. Georg Ludwig Friedrich Laves designed its Palm House, completed in 1849, and the mausoleum where King Ernest Augustus and Queen Frederica were buried. In the Guelf Garden the Guelf Castle, begun in 1857, has housed the University of Hannover since 1879.

An air raid in 1943 damaged the palace, although the British Royal Family had asked the Royal Air Force not to attack it, and its ruins were almost entirely torn down after the war. In 1957 George I, his parents Ernest Augustus and Sophia, and other members of the House of Hanover were reburied in the Hill Garden's mausoleum after the destruction of the Leine Palace and its chapel.

The rebuilt Herrenhausen Palace reopened on 18 January 2013. The Great Fountain can reach 80 metres, the grotto was remodelled with glass and mirror mosaics by Niki de Saint Phalle between 2001 and 2003, and the Hill Garden's Rainforest House opened in 2000. The Low German Rose Garden grows about 650 varieties of roses.
herrnhut: Herrnhut lies in Upper Lusatia, in the district of Görlitz in eastern Saxony, in the hilly foreland of the Zittau Mountains on the Petersbach, the longest headstream of the Pließnitz, a tributary of the Lusatian Neisse. It is about 10 km south-east of Löbau, 15 km north-west of Zittau and 25 km south-west of Görlitz. The name Herrn Hut means the Lord's watchful care. The hill above the town, the Hutberg or Hill of Watching, suggested it, and the town's coat of arms shows the tower of the lookout on the Hutberg.

The Unity of the Brethren arose after the reformer Jan Hus was burned at the stake at the Council of Constance in 1415. In the 18th century its members in the Lands of the Bohemian Crown faced the harsh Counter-Reformation measures of the Habsburg rulers. From 1722 refugees came to Upper Lusatia, which the Electors of Saxony had held since the Peace of Prague of 1635. After meeting their leader Christian David, a Moravian missionary, Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760) invited them to settle on his Berthelsdorf estates. David built the first house in what became Herrnhut, and Zinzendorf had a new residence built there in 1725–1727.

The community spread from Herrnhut to Rixdorf near Berlin, to Marienborn near Büdingen, to Herrnhaag and Norden. The first organised Protestant missionary movement began from Herrnhut in 1732, when two Bohemian Brethren went to the Danish West Indies; others went to Greenland. The first North American mission began at Savannah, Georgia, in 1735, and the mission station of Genadendal was founded in South Africa in 1738. Zinzendorf's community influenced John Wesley in creating Methodism and contributed to the rise of Evangelicalism.

Herrnhut is a town of around 6,000 inhabitants and the centre of the worldwide Moravian Church, the Unitas Fratrum. It makes the Herrnhuter Stern, a 25-pointed Advent star that has been produced for over 150 years and is hung in windows and on porches at Christmas. In 2016 the town received the title European City of Reformation, and in 2024 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List with Christiansfeld in Denmark, Bethlehem in the US and Gracehill in Northern Ireland as the serial site Moravian Church Settlements.
hersir: Hersirs were also aspiring landowners who, like the middle class in many feudal societies, supported the kings as they centralised power. The Hávamál, the mythical advice of the god Odin to humankind, praises careful thought and well-planned attack, and in its oral form it was one of the main influences on the outlook of the hersir. Their religion seems to have lain somewhere between Christianity and paganism: some hersirs were baptised, most often to improve trade with Christians or in obedience to a new king rather than for religious reasons.

The hersir's main weapon was the Viking sword with a Type H hilt, the most common hilt of the Viking Age, made according to the owner's wealth of polished steel with inlays of silver, copper or tin; its blade, of Geibig Type 3, dates from the second half of the 8th to the second half of the 10th century. A wooden shield went with it. Armour displayed wealth as much as it protected, and a hersir often wore a rounded or conical helmet and a short mail coat, of which the finds at Gjermundbu are an example.

Vikings travelled long distances on horseback and overseas in longboats that carried thirty people, but they always fought on foot. In the shield wall the hersir stood at the front, with archers and slingers behind, the men standing close so that their shields overlapped; the svinfylking varied this with several wedges pointing at the enemy.

In the poem Rígsþula, Hersir is the name of a man whose daughter Erna married Jarl, the first earl. The Sagas of Icelanders mention several hersirs, among them Bjorn Buna Grimsson of Sognefjord, who lived at Aurland and was the father of Ketill Flatnose; Ketill's daughter was Aud the Deep-Minded. Landnáma traces Bjorn's descent through his foremothers to Thorgerdur Eylaugsdottir, a female hersir of Sogn, which is rare in these stories and points to her importance.
herstal: Herstal is a municipality and city in the province of Liège in Wallonia, lying along the Meuse. It forms part of the Greater Liège agglomeration, which has about 600,000 inhabitants, and consists of the districts of Herstal, Liers, Milmort and Vottem. The name is of Franconian origin, made up of hari, meaning army, and stal, meaning resting place or camp. It is first mentioned in Latin documents of about 718 and 723.

Pippin of Herstal, Mayor of the Palace and de facto ruler of Austrasia and Neustria, founded the family that established the Carolingian dynasty. He probably chose Herstal as his main residence for its closeness to the major cities of Tongeren, Maastricht and Liège. He was the father of Charles Martel and the great-grandfather of Charlemagne, who was supposedly born in Herstal, though this is uncertain. Charlemagne lived there for at least fifteen years but later made Aachen his capital, which ended Herstal's period of medieval importance.

The town was incorporated into the Duchy of Lower Lotharingia, which became part of the Duchy of Brabant at the end of the 12th century. Despite its closeness to Liège, it did not become part of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège until 1740, when the prince-bishop Georges-Louis de Berghes bought it from Frederick II of Prussia. By then it was known for its craftsmen: ceramists, blacksmiths and clockmakers. In the 19th century it became a city of coal and steel, and in 1889 the Fabrique Nationale, a major armaments factory, was founded there. On 7 August 1914, at the start of the First World War, the invading German army executed 27 civilians in Herstal and destroyed 10 homes.

Heavy industry declined for a long period after the World War II. The Fabrique Nationale remains a large armaments employer, and Herstal's industrial zone of Haut-Sart is the largest in Wallonia. Techspace Aero, based in the town, manufactures precision parts for the Ariane rocket of the European Space Agency.
hertfordshire: Hertfordshire is a ceremonial county in the East of England. It borders Bedfordshire to the north-west, Cambridgeshire to the north-east, Essex to the east, Greater London to the south and Buckinghamshire to the west, and covers about 1,640 square kilometres. It centres on the headwaters and upper valleys of the rivers Lea and Colne, both of which flow south. The higher ground lies in the north and west, where the chalk of the Chiltern Hills rises to 244 metres near Tring.

Human life is attested in the county from the Mesolithic period. After the Roman conquest of Britain in 43 CE the Catuvellauni accepted peace and adapted to Roman life, and new towns developed, among them Verulamium, beside modern St Albans. There, around 293, the first recorded British martyrdom is traditionally believed to have taken place, when Saint Alban, a Romano-British soldier, took the place of a Christian priest and was beheaded. After the Roman legions left in the early 5th century the area was colonised by Anglo-Saxons, and by the 6th century most of it belonged to the Kingdom of Essex, which later lost its western areas to Mercia.

In 913 Edward the Elder built a fortress at Hertford to check Norse activity, and the area was assigned to it. His father, Alfred the Great, had fixed the River Lea as a boundary with the Norse lord Guthrum, which put the north and east of the county within the Danelaw. The name Hertfordshire is first recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in 1011. St Albans Abbey was an early drafting place of Magna Carta, and the town saw two battles of the Wars of the Roses. The New River, opened in 1613, brought fresh water to London from Ware. In 1903 Letchworth became the first garden city, and Stevenage was the first town redeveloped under the New Towns Act 1946.

Hertfordshire has ten districts, with Hertford as county town and Watford as its largest settlement, and about 1.2 million people in 2021. Much of its undeveloped land is farmland and part of the Metropolitan green belt. Among its surviving landmarks are the Roman remains of Verulamium, St Albans Cathedral, Berkhamsted Castle and the Jacobean Hatfield House.
herzberg-am-harz: Herzberg am Harz lies in the Göttingen district of Lower Saxony, on the south-western rim of the Harz mountain range and the Harz National Park. The town centre stands on the Sieber river, about 32 km north-east of Göttingen and 90 km south-east of the state capital Hanover. The municipal area also takes in the villages of Lonau, Pöhlde, Scharzfeld and Sieber. Natural monuments in the surrounding area include the Unicorn Cave, the Karst Trail and the Rhume Spring.

Herzberg Castle, in the Duchy of Saxony, was first mentioned in a deed of 1143. The Saxon Welf dynasty seized it in 1144, and in 1158 it became the property of Duke Henry the Lion with the consent of the Hohenstaufen emperor Frederick Barbarossa. It formed part of the Grubenhagen estates that the Welf duke Henry I of Brunswick received in 1291, when he and his brothers divided their inheritance.

A settlement below the castle was first documented in 1337. The Brunswick rulers of the principality of Grubenhagen resided at the castle from 1486 until their line became extinct in 1596. In 1617 Duke George of Brunswick-Lüneburg had his inheritance rights confirmed by Emperor Matthias and lived there again with his wife Anne Eleonore of Hesse-Darmstadt, until in 1636 he moved his residence to the Leineschloss in Hanover.

Herzberg first developed as a centre of cloth and linen manufacturing. In the 18th and 19th centuries its important industries included brewing, metal founding and turning, agricultural machinery and boot making, as well as arms production for the Hanover forces. It received town privileges in 1929, when it was part of the Prussian Province of Hanover.

Herzberg is twinned with Góra in Poland, a link dating from 1993. In 2006 the city council decided to present the town as an Esperanto city, Esperanto-urbo, called Hercbergo-ĉe-Harco in Esperanto, and it is the home of the Interkultura Centro Herzberg, a centre promoting the international auxiliary language Esperanto. Local employers include a paper and corrugated cardboard mill, a foundry and a printing and publishing house. The social welfare pioneer Ida Arenhold (1798 to 1863) and the Prussian colonel general Karl von Einem (1853 to 1934) are among its notable people.
herzegovina: Herzegovina is the southern and smaller of the two main geographical regions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and its borders have never been strictly defined. Its area is about 24 per cent of the country, and Mostar, at its centre, is the largest city and unofficial capital. The terrain is mostly hilly karst, with high mountains such as Čvrsnica and Prenj in the north, except for the central valley of the river Neretva, which flows past Konjic and Mostar to the Adriatic. The region has a coastline of about 20 km. Stolac is perhaps its oldest city, with settlement from the Paleolithic and the Illyrian town of Daorson.

Slavs settled in the Balkans in the 7th century, and the area later called Herzegovina was divided in the early Middle Ages between Croatia, Zachlumia and Travunia. Before the name Herzegovina spread, it was called Hum or Humska zemlja. The Bosnian ban Stjepan Kotromanić annexed Hum in 1326, and the Franciscans, arriving in the 1340s, began to spread Catholicism in a population that was overwhelmingly Orthodox. King Tvrtko I gave parts of Hum to Vlatko Vuković of the Kosača family. Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, the last Bosnian nobleman to hold effective control of the province, took the Slavic title herceg, duke, and the Ottomans, who named conquered lands after their earlier rulers, called the region Herzegovina.

Stjepan died in 1466, and his son Vlatko Hercegović resisted until December 1481, when he agreed with the Ottomans to move with his family to Istanbul. The region was organised as the Sanjak of Herzegovina with its seat at Foča. Serbs rose in 1596–97 and were defeated at Gacko. The Herzegovina Uprising of 1875–78 was backed by Serbia and Montenegro. By the Treaty of Berlin of 1878 Austria-Hungary occupied Herzegovina with Bosnia and annexed them in 1908, which brought on the Bosnian Crisis. In 1918 the region joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

Herzegovina is divided between the two entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its cultural monuments include Mogorjelo, the Stari most at Mostar and the stećci, the large medieval stone grave monuments. Natural landmarks include the Kravica waterfalls on the Trebižat river, the Hutovo Blato bird reserve and the Vjetrenica cave system.
herzog-august-library: Duke Julius began collecting books around 1550 while studying in France. From 1558 he bought theological writings, and in 1567 his first large collection, the library of the Nuremberg councillor Michael von Kaden, rich in legal and humanist works. Between 1570 and 1572, as the Reformation was introduced in the duchy, the libraries of the monasteries of Dorstadt, Wöltingerode, Heiningen and Steterburg were moved to Wolfenbüttel.

His library ordinance of 5 April 1572 counts as the founding document, although the church musician Leonhart Schröter, regarded as the first librarian, had been in charge since 1571. In 1578 manuscripts from the estate of the theologian Johannes Aurifaber were added.

Duke Heinrich Julius, who inherited the library in 1589, added the estate of the theologian Matthias Flacius and the collections of further monasteries. In 1618, however, Duke Friedrich Ulrich handed the whole collection, by then about 5,000 manuscripts and prints, to the library of the University of Helmstedt. Large parts came back to Wolfenbüttel only in 1810, after the university closed.

The present library grew from the collection of Augustus the Younger, who acted as his own librarian from 1604 until his death in 1666. Armies passed back and forth over the centuries, but generals placed the library under special protection, and it is one of the oldest libraries never to have lost part of its collection. Later librarians included Paul Raabe, from 1968 to 1992. The Lower Saxony Ministry for Science and Culture oversees it today.

In 2006 the library held about 11,500 manuscripts and 900,000 books, of which 350,000 were printed between the 15th and 18th centuries, among them 3,500 incunabula. Its manuscripts include the Gospels of Henry the Lion, the Liber Floridus of about 1150, nine volumes from the library of Matthias Corvinus, the manuscripts W1 and W2 of the Magnus liber organi, the palimpsest Codex Guelferbytanus 64 Weissenburgensis and Luther's Wolfenbüttel Psalter, the only surviving copy of his glosses on his lectures on the Psalms from 1513. Hundreds of scholars from abroad work there on projects in the history of culture, religion, law, science and gender from the Middle Ages to the early modern period.
hesbaye: The Hesbaye is a loamy plateau forming the watershed between the drainage basins of the Meuse and the Scheldt. It takes in the southern half of the province of Limburg, with Tongeren, Sint-Truiden, Bilzen and Borgloon, Liège province north of the Meuse, eastern Walloon Brabant and the easternmost part of Flemish Brabant, with Tienen and Zoutleeuw. To the north lies the flat, sandy Kempen region, and across the Meuse to the south the Condroz and the rocky hills of the Ardennes. In medieval Latin the territory was called Hasbania, usually in the form pagus hasbaniensis.

In Roman times the region was the fertile agricultural core of the Civitas Tungrorum, whose capital was Tongeren. When the Salian Franks were allowed to settle in Toxandria to the north in the 4th century, the more heavily populated Hesbaye remained more Romanized, and from at least the 8th century it was an important division of the Frankish kingdom of Austrasia. In the 8th century Robert, proposed as an ancestor of the Capetians, was called Duke or Count of Hasbania, and the Treaty of Meerssen of 870, dividing lands between Charles the Bald and Louis the German, says that it then had four counties.

In the 10th century smaller counties lay within the pagus, among them Avernas, with its seat in modern Hannut, and Huste, perhaps at Hocht in Lanaken. The County of Loon, with its seat at Borgloon, appears in records in the early 11th century, formed from Avernas and Hocht. In 1040 the Emperor Henry III recognised a county called Hasbania as held by the prince-bishop Nithard of Liège, and Loon seems to have been held under it; Loon was much later joined to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, while lands to the west came under the growing County of Leuven.

The region is divided into a northern Humid Hesbaye, with a higher water table and many springs, which is by far the main fruit-growing area of Belgium and has some of its most northerly vineyards, and a southern Dry Hesbaye. In the dry part farmers grow sugar beet, chicory, flax, rapeseed and grains, nine tenths of them wheat and barley.
heshen: Heshen was born on 1 July 1750 as Shanbao, and his name was later changed to Heshen. His courtesy name was Zhizhai. He was the son of a Manchu military officer of the Plain Red Banner and studied at the Palace of Universal Peace, a school for the children of Bannermen. He lost his mother young, and it was said that he and his younger brother had a hard life under their stepmother. He was an excellent student who knew Middle Mandarin, Manchu, Mongolian and Tibetan.

Heshen began work as an imperial bodyguard in 1772 and in 1775 was transferred to the Forbidden City, where he met the Qianlong Emperor. Within a year he was junior vice-president of the Board of Revenue, then a Grand Councillor, and then Minister of the Imperial Household Department. He held several top posts at once, which gave him wide influence over the bureaucracy. In 1790 his son married the emperor's tenth and favourite daughter, Princess Hexiao. His power grew as the emperor aged, and after Qianlong's abdication in 1796, and especially after the death of his opponent Agui in 1797, he was practically a regent.

The records describe him as openly corrupt. He influenced practically every appointment in the country, filled key military and civil posts with his own men, demanded gifts from officials who owed him their places, and took public and military funds and tax revenue. Taxes were raised repeatedly, and officials who pocketed money meant for canals and dams are said to have contributed to the Yellow River flooding 17 times between 1797 and 1819.

Qianlong died on 7 February 1799. His successor, the Jiaqing Emperor, had Heshen arrested on 12 February, and an edict of 15 February declared him guilty of 20 crimes, including abuse of power, disrespect to imperial prerogatives and hoarding wealth. He was condemned to slow slicing, but out of respect for the Qianlong Emperor and for Princess Hexiao the emperor ordered him to hang himself, which he did on 22 February. His confiscated movable property was estimated at 60 to 80 million taels of silver, roughly a year of Qing revenue, with higher estimates disputed by historians.

Historians such as Daniel McMahon argue that the image of Heshen as a classic villain was contrived by the Jiaqing Emperor. Before 1799 official records portrayed him favourably, and the true scale of his wealth and the charges of misuse of public funds are hard to verify. On this view Jiaqing, emperor in name while Heshen dominated the government, made him a scapegoat for the dynasty's problems, and Heshen's supporters were pardoned.
hesiod: What is known of Hesiod's life comes from his own poems, where he lets his audience in on a few details. He describes his family's patrimony, a small piece of ground at the foot of Mount Helicon, which led to lawsuits with his brother Perses. Perses at first seems to have cheated him of his share through corrupt authorities, whom Hesiod calls kings, but later became poor and had to rely on the thrifty poet.

Unlike his father, Hesiod disliked sea travel, yet he once crossed the strait to Euboea to take part in the funeral games of Amphidamas of Chalcis, where he won a tripod in a singing contest. He also tells of meeting the Muses on Mount Helicon while pasturing sheep. They gave him a laurel staff, and scholars have inferred from this that he was not a trained rhapsode, who would have received a lyre. He probably wrote his poems down or dictated them.

Two works are generally accepted as his. The Theogony, commonly considered the earlier, treats the origin of the world and of the gods, beginning with Chaos, Gaia, Tartarus and Eros, and is the earliest known source for the myths of Pandora and Prometheus. According to Herodotus, Hesiod's retelling became the accepted version that linked all Hellenes. The Works and Days, of over 800 lines, rests on two truths: labour is the lot of humankind, and he who is willing to work will get by. It sets out the five Ages of Man, from a golden age through silver, bronze and iron, with a heroic age inserted before the last, and it attacks idleness, usury and unjust judges.
The Shield of Heracles, attributed to him in antiquity, is now known to be spurious. His creation myth has long been held to show Eastern influences, such as the Babylonian Enuma Elis.

Two early traditions place Hesiod's grave. In one, the Delphic oracle warned him that he would die at Nemea, so he fled to Locris, where he was killed at the temple of Nemean Zeus and buried. In the other, first mentioned in an epigram by Chersias of Orchomenus, the people of Ascra took his ashes to Orchomenus and placed them in the agora. Ancient authors credited Hesiod and Homer with establishing Greek religious customs. Later writers began to put Homer earlier, and most scholars today agree, though there are good arguments on both sides.
hesse: Hesse is a landlocked state in Germany and the only one that straddles the western and central parts of the country. It borders Lower Saxony, Thuringia, Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg, Rhineland-Palatinate and North Rhine-Westphalia. Its most populous towns lie in the south-west, in the Frankfurt Rhine-Main region, among them Frankfurt am Main, Wiesbaden, Darmstadt, Offenbach and Hanau. The name Hessen derives from the Hessians, who ultimately continue the tribal name of the Chatti; the ancient name appears by the 7th century as Chassi and from the 8th century as Hassi or Hessi.

Central Hesse was inhabited in the Upper Paleolithic, and the Züschen tomb near Fritzlar, a gallery grave of about 3000 BCE belonging to the Late Neolithic Wartberg culture, is one of the most important megalithic monuments in Central Europe. From 962 the land that would become Hesse was part of the Holy Roman Empire.
