The French Republic occupied the left bank of the Rhine in 1794, and the reorganisation of the Empire in 1803 gave Hesse-Kassel and Hesse-Darmstadt further territories and made the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel a Prince-Elector, so that his state became the Electorate of Hesse.

In the 19th century, before German unification, the territory comprised the Grand Duchy of Hesse, or Hesse-Darmstadt, the Duchy of Nassau, the free city of Frankfurt, the Electorate of Hesse, the Principality of Waldeck and the Landgraviate of Hesse-Homburg. The modern territory was delineated only in 1945, as Greater Hesse under American occupation, and corresponds loosely to the medieval Landgraviate of Hesse. Hesse has been a parliamentary republic since 1918, except under Nazi rule from 1933 to 1945.

Hesse has a population of over six million, nearly four million of them in the Rhine-Main region. Wiesbaden is the capital and Frankfurt the largest urban area, and Darmstadt and Kassel are other major historic cities. Rhenish Hesse, the part of the former Grand Duchy west of the Rhine, has belonged to Rhineland-Palatinate since 1946. Hesse has several UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe in Kassel, Lorsch Abbey, the Messel Fossil Pit and the Saalburg, part of the Roman Limes.
hessian-ludwig-railway: The company grew out of a gap in the railway policy of the Grand Duchy of Hesse. Starkenburg had the Main-Neckar Railway and Upper Hesse the Main-Weser Railway, but the province of Rhenish Hesse had no line. The first push came from outside: the Bavarian Palatinate, which licensed railway building in 1844, wanted a link northwards, and the railway pioneer Friedrich List championed a line from Mainz to Worms, while Prussia, for strategic reasons, and Baden opposed it. The government in Darmstadt, which had passed a law for state railways in 1842, at first held back.

Because the state stayed out, the line was left to a joint-stock company, based not in the capital, Darmstadt, but in Mainz, the capital of Rhenish Hesse. From 1845 some in the government favoured a private railway for the province, and on 15 August 1845 a licence was granted to the Mainz-Ludwigshafen Railway Company, later renamed in honour of the grand duke, though he had at first opposed the line.

Shareholders withdrew money, and work begun in spring 1848 nearly stopped when the revolution of 1848 emptied the state treasury; only in August 1852 did the Hessian government agree to support the company, and a treaty with Bavaria covered the whole line. The 46-kilometre route opened in sections from Mainz to Worms between 23 March and 24 August 1853, and through trains ran to Ludwigshafen from 15 November 1853. The Rhine-Main line from Mainz through Darmstadt to Aschaffenburg opened on 1 August 1858, crossing the Rhine by train ferry until a bridge built by MAN-Werk Gustavsburg opened on 1 December 1862.

Further lines followed, among them the West Rhine Railway to Bingen in 1859, the Main Railway from Mainz to Frankfurt in 1863, the Riedbahn from 1869, the Main-Lahn Railway to Limburg in 1877 and the Odenwald Railway in 1882, until the company had a network of 697 kilometres. It began with six locomotives from the Maschinenfabrik Esslingen, named after figures such as Johannes Gutenberg, and by the end of 1895 it had 216 locomotives and 544 coaches.

The company became the main provider of rail services in the two southern provinces of the grand duchy, Rhenish Hesse and Starkenburg, and one of the largest privately owned railways in Germany. On 1 April 1897 it was nationalised and joined the Prussian-Hessian Railway Operating and Financial Association. Local people said that its initials, HLB, stood for Hoch lebe Bismarck, long live Bismarck.
hesychasm: The word derives from hesychia, meaning stillness, rest or silence. The term hesychast appears in Christian ascetical writing from the 4th century, and the laws of Justinian I treat hesychast and anchorite as synonyms. Practice of inner prayer, aimed at inward stillness of the heart, dates back to at least the 4th century, and Evagrius Ponticus, John Climacus, Maximus the Confessor and Symeon the New Theologian are representatives of this spirituality. John Climacus described stages of contemplative practice in his Ladder of Divine Ascent.

Physical techniques were added later. Nicephorus the Hesychast, a 13th-century monk of Mount Athos, advised bending the head toward the chest, joining the prayer to the rhythm of breathing and fixing the eyes on the middle of the body. Kallistos Ware suggests that the origins of such techniques may be far older and may have been influenced by the Sufi practice of dhikr.

The hesychast repeats the Jesus Prayer, Lord Jesus Christ, son of God, have mercy on me, the sinner, aiming to bring the mind into the heart. Tradition describes three stages: katharsis, or purification, through watchfulness against tempting thoughts; theoria, or illumination; and theosis, or union with God. At the stage called the guard of the mind, the prayer continues free of images. Hesychasts usually experience contemplation of God as light, the uncreated light of Palamite theology.

Orthodox tradition warns against seeking ecstasy for its own sake, which can lead to spiritual delusion, called prelest. Hesychasts take part in the liturgical life of the Church, though a hermit may attend the Divine Liturgy rarely.

About 1337 the Calabrian monk Barlaam of Seminara, trained in Western Scholastic theology, visited Mount Athos and attacked hesychasm, holding that the light the hesychasts claimed to see, identified with the light of the Transfiguration, implied two eternal substances. Gregory Palamas defended hesychasm at synods in Constantinople in the 1340s, distinguishing God's uncreated energies, which can be known, from his essence, which cannot. A synod in 1341 condemned Barlaam, who returned to Calabria. The dispute also played a role in the civil war between supporters of John Cantacuzenus and John V Palaiologos, and in 1351 a synod under John VI Cantacuzenus established hesychast doctrine as the doctrine of the Orthodox Church.

Paisius Velichkovsky and his disciples made the practice known in Russia and Romania. Western theologians tended to reject the real distinction between essence and energies, but the Roman Catholic Church has never condemned Palamism, and in the later 20th century Catholic attitudes towards Palamas changed markedly.
hethum-i: Hethum I was the son of Constantine of Baberon and Princess Alix Pahlavouni of Lampron, and he founded the dynasty that bears his name, the Hethumids, also called the House of Lampron. His father had been regent for the young Queen Isabella of Armenia. Isabella first married Philip, son of Bohemond IV of Antioch, but Constantine had Philip disposed of and forced her to marry his own son Hethum on 14 June 1226, making the couple co-rulers. They had six children, among them Leo II, Thoros, who was killed at the Battle of Mari in 1266 fighting the Mamluks, and Sibylla, who married Bohemond VI of Antioch.

Hethum was a major player in the shifting alliances around the Crusader states, as the Armenians had ties with all sides. When the Mongol commander Baiju attacked the Sultanate of Rum, Sultan Kaykhusraw II called on Hethum for help, but Hethum delayed, probably judging the Mongols the greater threat. After the Mongols crushed the Seljuqs at Kösedağ and approached Cappadocia and Cilicia, he submitted to Mongol suzerainty and sent his brother Sempad to Karakorum. There Sempad made a formal agreement with the Great Khan Güyük in 1247 that made Cilician Armenia a vassal state. In 1245 the Sultanate of Rum had attacked Cilicia, angered that Hethum had handed Kaykhusraw's wife and daughter to Baiju.

In 1254 Hethum travelled through Central Asia to Mongolia to renew the agreement and met Möngke Khan at Karakorum. His companion Kirakos Gandzaketsi recorded the journey, and the narrative is important for its observations of Mongol, Buddhist and Chinese culture, geography and wildlife. Hethum urged other Frankish rulers to submit to the Mongols, but only his son-in-law Bohemond VI of Antioch did so, around 1259. Armenian troops were with the Mongol army that captured Baghdad in 1258, and Armenians fought under Hulagu at Aleppo and Damascus in 1260.

The Mamluks rallied and defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in September 1260. Because of Hethum's support for the Mongols, Cilicia came under increasing attack from the Mamluks under Baybars, who invaded in 1266. The outnumbered Armenians were beaten at the Disaster of Mari, where Thoros was killed and Leo was captured. The cities of Adana, Tarsus and Ayas were assaulted, the capital Sis was sacked and burnt, thousands of Armenians were massacred and 40,000 were taken captive. Hethum ransomed his son by conceding territory to the Egyptians. In May 1268 Baybars overran the Principality of Antioch. Hethum abdicated in favour of Leo and lived out his life as a monk in a monastery.
hetman: Hetman is a title from Central and Eastern Europe, historically given to military commanders and comparable to a field marshal. The Polish spelling comes from the Old Czech hajtman, most likely composed of the German roots Haupt, meaning head, and Mann, meaning man. The Czechs of Bohemia used it first, from the Hussite Wars of the fifteenth century onward. In the Principality of Moldavia and through much of the history of Romania, the hetman stood second in the army after the ruling prince, who held the position of voivode.

In the Kingdom of Poland the title Grand Crown Hetman dates from 1505. Until 1581 the post existed only during particular campaigns and wars; after that it became permanent, like the other offices of the Crown and of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The Commonwealth had four hetmans at any time: a great hetman and a field, or deputy, hetman each for Poland and for Lithuania. From 1585 the title could not be taken away without a proven charge of treachery, so most hetmans served for life. Jan Karol Chodkiewicz commanded the army from his deathbed in 1621. Hetmans were not paid from the royal treasury.

Second only to the monarch in the army's chain of command, hetmans could not be removed by the king, which let them pursue independent policies. The arrangement worked well when a hetman was able and the monarch weak, but could produce disastrous results in the opposite case. It contrasted with neighbouring states, where sovereigns could dismiss their commanders at any time. A military reform of 1776 curtailed the hetmans' powers, and the office was abolished after the Third Partition of Poland in 1795.

Among the Zaporozhian Cossacks, commanders at the end of the sixteenth century were titled Koshovyi Otaman or Hetman. In 1648 the Zaporizhian Host elected a hetman of its own, Bohdan Khmelnytsky, whose uprising began the Cossack Hetmanate; its hetmans, though elected, held very broad powers. Catherine II of Russia abolished the office in 1764, ending with Kyrylo Rozumovsky.

The title was revived during the Ukrainian revolution of 1917 to 1921, when Pavlo Skoropadskyi, after a German-supported coup in early 1918, claimed the title Hetman of Ukraine; his regime lasted until late 1918. In the modern Czech Republic hejtman is the term for the elected governor of a region. The word has also come to mean commander or leader in general, and in Polish the chess queen is called hetman.
heuneburg: The Heuneburg lies in Hundersingen, between Ulm and Sigmaringen, at the centre of a fertile river plain surrounded by rolling hill country. The citadel was only a small, if focal, part of a larger complex. To its west and northwest lay the Aussensiedlung, an exterior settlement of up to 100 hectares made up of fenced lots, each probably a farmstead for an extended family, with an estimated 5,000 to 10,000 inhabitants. Banks and ditches up to 7 metres deep, entered by a monumental gate of limestone ashlar masonry, enclosed the lower ground.

The first settlement on the site dates to the Middle Bronze Age, the 15th to 12th centuries BCE, when the plateau was fortified with a ditch, a bank and a wooden wall. It was abandoned at the start of the Urnfield period. Around 700 BCE the citadel was reoccupied and refortified, and by 600 BCE it was one of the key centres of power and trade in southern Germany, while most of the other hilltop sites of the region were abandoned. Its location gave it access to routes across the Alps from Italy and from the Greek colony of Massalia, and down the Danube.

Finds include a bronze workshop, fragments of about a dozen Greek pots, tin and amber. More than 50 burial mounds surround the site; the Hohmichele, 85 metres across and over 13 metres high, is one of the largest Celtic tumuli in Europe, and one of its graves held a four-wheeled chariot. After the mudbrick wall was burned, the citadel was defended by a wood-and-earth wall until a further destruction in the 5th century BCE. Whether these destructions were acts of war, and whether the site was then abandoned, is now in doubt.

Eduard Paulus identified the site as a prehistoric fortification in 1882, and a systematic excavation programme ran from 1950 to 1979; new excavations began in 2004. An open-air museum on the plateau includes reconstructions of several houses and of part of the mudbrick wall. The Heuneburgmuseum, in a barn of the former monastery of Heiligkreuztal at Hundersingen, displays original finds, and some of the Hohmichele finds are in the Württemberg State Museum in Stuttgart.
heungdeoksa: The temple stood during the Unified Silla and Goryeo periods, in what is now Heungdeok-gu. It is believed to have been built before 848 and was destroyed by fire in the late 1370s, soon after the work for which it is remembered. The Buljojikjisimcheyojoel, a book compiled by the monk Baegun in 1374, was printed there with movable metal type in 1377, the third year of the reign of King Uwang, 78 years before the Gutenberg Bible of 1455.

The printed book left Korea in the reign of King Gojong, when Victor Collin de Plancy, chargé d'affaires of the French Embassy in Seoul, acquired it in 1887; it was later given to the Bibliothèque nationale de France, where it remains. In 1972 it was officially recognised as the world's oldest extant book printed with movable metal type, and in 2001 it was entered in UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

The exact location of the temple was unknown until 1985, when relics came to light during a land development project of the Korean Land Development Corporation. Cheongju University led the excavation and confirmed the site after finding a bronze gong and bowl bearing the temple's name. It was designated Historic Site No. 315 on 7 May 1986, and a reproduction of a Buddhist prayer hall and a three-storey stone pagoda have been built there from the excavation survey. The Cheongju Early Printing Museum opened beside the heritage site on 17 March 1992 to promote the history of printing in Korea, the craft for which the vanished temple is remembered.
heungseon-daewongun: The Daewongun was born Yi Ha-eung, the fourth son of Yi Chae-jung, a member of the royal family who was given in 1816 the name Yi Gu and the title Prince Namyeon. He was a ninth-generation descendant of King Injo through Grand Prince Inpyeong. The Andong Kim clan held great authority over the country, and he was barred from high office although he belonged to the royal Jeonju Yi clan. His early posts were minor and mostly ceremonial, he was poor and humiliated by the rich in-laws of the royal house, and he earned money by drawing orchids and selling them to noblemen.

In January 1864 King Cheoljong died without an heir. Dowager Queen Sinjeong, the oldest of the three dowagers, held the right to designate the next king. On 16 January 1864 she appointed Yi Ha-eung's second son, Yi Myeong-bok, Prince of Ikseong. The next day his father was granted the title Daewongun, which was given only to the biological father of a young king, and on 21 January the boy was enthroned as Gojong. Sinjeong invited the Daewongun to assist, and though she remained titular regent he became the de facto ruler.

His main goal was to crush the old ruling faction that had usurped the sovereign power of the kings. He led an anti-corruption campaign, disciplined the royal clans and taxed the yangban aristocracy; Cumings notes that this aimed at a restoration of the days of King Sejong rather than a revolution. He rebuilt Gyeongbok Palace, perhaps the costliest project of the Joseon dynasty, and stripped the Andong Kim clan of almost all its power. His foreign policy was summed up by Cumings as no treaties, no trade, no Catholics, no West and no Japan.

When Gojong came of age, his wife Queen Min influenced him to take full royal responsibility, and the Daewongun was forced into semi-retirement. He briefly returned to power during the Imo Incident of 1882, but a Chinese diplomat, Ma Chien-chung, arrested him and sent him to Tianjin. China returned him to Korea in the fall of 1885.

In 1894 Japanese soldiers freed him from house arrest to lead the Gabo Reform, but they soon distrusted him. On 8 October 1895 Japanese policemen escorted him to the palace on the morning Japanese agents killed Queen Min; his part in the plot is unclear. He died in 1898, and in 1907 Emperor Sunjong gave him the posthumous title Internal King Heungseon Heonui.
hewahewa: In 1819 the French explorer Louis de Freycinet estimated that Hewahewa had been born around 1774. He grew up among the aristocracy of the island of Hawaiʻi before its unification and came of a long priestly line: his great-grandfather Holoʻae was kahuna to Alapaʻinui and Kalaniʻōpuʻu, his father Puʻou a kahuna of Kamehameha I, and his cousin Kekūhaupiʻo was Kamehameha's instructor and military adviser. The order of Kū to which his family belonged had risen during the wars of unification and displaced the priestly order of the fertility god Lono.

By the time Kamehameha II came to the throne, Hewahewa had grown disillusioned with the kapu, and Kaʻahumanu persuaded him that it had to be broken. At a feast held six months after Kamehameha I's death the young king ate alongside his female relatives, and the women ate forbidden foods, opening the era of ʻAi Noa, free eating. Supported by Kaʻahumanu, the king's mother Keōpūolani and reformers among the priests, Hewahewa then moved against the old religion, though family ʻaumākua were left untouched and the kahuna kept much of their standing as scholars and healers. Keaoua Kekuaokalani, who led the revolt, was a nephew of Kamehameha I and a former pupil of Hewahewa.

Some sources say that Hewahewa foretold the coming of a new god from the sea shortly before the first missionaries arrived. He went on to give thanks to Jehovah at a feast, composed a chant to the new god, ate with women, resigned his office and helped persuade the chiefess Kapiʻolani to become a Christian. When Hewahewa was an old man, Kamehameha III asked him to help restore the native faith, but Hewahewa talked the king out of the attempt.

According to the Ke Kumu Hawaii and the Sandwich Island Gazette, Hewahewa died at his home in Waimea on 16 February 1837 after four months of illness, having asked his friends to pray for his salvation. Nathaniel Bright Emerson, born in 1839, later recalled him as a silent, wrinkled old man living in a valley in Waialua about 1848. Thousands of Hawaiians, among them the lifeguard Eddie Aikau, descend from him; in 2019 several acres of his lands in Waimea Valley were given protected status, and in 2000 he was inducted into the Hawaiian Music Hall of Fame among historical chanters.
hexamilion-wall: Attempts to fortify the isthmus go back perhaps to the Mycenaean period. When Xerxes invaded in 480 BCE many Peloponnesian cities wanted to hold the isthmus rather than Thermopylae, though Herodotus noted that such a wall was useless without control of the sea. The Hexamilion was built between 408 and 450, in the age of the great barbarian invasions, and the attack of Alaric on Greece in 396 or the sack of Rome in 410 by the Visigoths may have prompted it. Under Justinian it gained more towers, 153 in all, with forts at either end and the fortress at Isthmia.

Running from the Gulf of Corinth to the Saronic Gulf, the wall was about 7.5 kilometres long, 7 metres high and 3 metres thick, a rubble and mortar core faced with squared stones. It is the largest archaeological structure in Greece, and its builders took stone from older buildings: the temple of Poseidon at Isthmia was built into it, while the sanctuary of Hera at Perachora and much of the ancient statuary of Corinth were burned for lime. The fortress of Isthmia, with nineteen towers over 2.7 hectares, probably housed the garrison, and its north-east gate was the main way into the Peloponnese.

Local farmers first manned the wall until Justinian replaced them with a professional garrison, and the gates allowed trade to be taxed. Locals seem often to have resisted it: graves were dug at the foot of a key staircase, and the gates were later sealed with hasty walls. Military use fell off after the 7th century, and earthquakes, above all that of 551, damaged it. When Manuel II rebuilt it in 1415 an open revolt had to be put down by force. After Constantine Palaiologos and his brother Thomas restored it in 1444, Murad II's army reduced it to ruins on 10 December 1446. It never fulfilled its purpose, though it may have deterred attack.
hexham: Hexham stands on the south bank of the River Tyne, formed by the meeting of the North Tyne and South Tyne at Warden nearby, and close to Hadrian's Wall. Newcastle upon Tyne lies 40 kilometres to the east and Carlisle 60 kilometres to the west. The name probably comes from the Old English Hagustaldes ea, the stream of the hagustald, a word related to Old High German hagustalt for a younger son who takes land outside the settlement.

In 671 or 672 the Northumbrian queen Æthelthryth gave Saint Wilfrid the site for a church at Hexham, and Hexham Abbey originated as the monastery Wilfrid founded in 674. Its crypt survives and incorporates stones taken from nearby Roman ruins, probably Corbridge or Hadrian's Wall. King Ælfwald of the Northumbrians, murdered by Sicga on 23 September 788, was buried in the church.

The town suffered in the border wars between Scotland and England. William Wallace burnt it in 1297, and in 1312 Robert the Bruce demanded and received £2,000 from the town and monastery to spare them the same fate. During the Wars of the Roses the Battle of Hexham was fought in 1464 somewhere south of the town, and the defeated Lancastrian commander Henry Beaufort, 3rd Duke of Somerset, was executed in the market place. In 1715 James Radclyffe, 3rd Earl of Derwentwater, raised the standard for James Francis Edward Stuart there. In 1761 troops of the North York Militia fired on a crowd protesting about militia service, killing some 45 people.

Hexham is a market town and civil parish in Northumberland with a population of 13,097 in 2011. Hexham Abbey, whose present church largely dates from about 1170 to 1250 in the Early English Gothic style, dominates the town. Nearby are the Shambles, built by Sir Walter Blackett in 1766, and the Moot Hall, a medieval courthouse. The Old Gaol, built between 1330 and 1333, was one of the first purpose-built jails in England. Hexham was long known for glove-making and leather dressing.
hey-slavs: Samuel Tomášik, a Slovak Lutheran minister, wrote the words in Prague in 1834, at first in Czech and under the title Hey, Slovaks. He was appalled that German was heard more often than Czech in the streets of Prague, and his diary records the thought: if Prague, the pearl of the Western Slavic world, were lost in a German sea, what awaited Slovakia, which looked to Prague for spiritual nourishment?

The old Polish song Poland Has Not Yet Perished came to his mind, and he wrote three verses by candlelight in pencil. He left instructions that it be sung to that melody, the Mazurek Dąbrowskiego of 1797. The composer of the Yugoslav version is unknown, though modern renditions often use a wartime arrangement by Oskar Danon.

Tomášik soon altered the words to include all Slavs, and it became a rallying song of Slav nationalism. It was sung at political gatherings and adopted as the organisational anthem of the Sokol physical education movement,. In the First World War Slavic soldiers on opposite sides sometimes used it to prevent bloodshed. In Slovakia it remained an unofficial ethnic anthem, and the Slovak Republic of 1939 to 1945 made it the state anthem.

In Yugoslavia it first appeared in the Illyrian movement, in a translation by Dragutin Rakovac titled Hey, Illyrians. In 1941 the Partisan resistance under Josip Broz Tito avoided the old royal anthem and chose it instead. It was sung at the sessions of AVNOJ and became the de facto anthem of the new Yugoslavia, and a constitutional amendment of 25 November 1988 gave it formal sanction. It stayed the anthem of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and then of Serbia and Montenegro. Its last official playing as a state anthem was at the 2006 FIFA World Cup, a few days after that union dissolved.
heydar-aliyev: According to his official biography, Heydar Aliyev was born in Nakhchivan on 10 May 1923, though some sources claim he was born two years earlier in a village now in Armenia. He studied architecture at the Azerbaijan Industrial Institute from 1939 to 1941. During the Second World War he commanded a Smersh battalion, which conducted intelligence operations on Soviet forces and executed soldiers who deserted or fought insufficiently hard. He joined the Azerbaijan SSR's state security organs in 1944, served 28 years in them to 1969, and became head of the Azerbaijani KGB in 1960, eventually with the rank of major general.

The Azerbaijan Communist Party elected him first secretary on 12 July 1969, reportedly on the advocacy of Semyon Tsvigun, Leonid Brezhnev's brother-in-law. He dominated Soviet-era Azerbaijan, building a patronage network and promoting people from his native Nakhchivan, as well as Azerbaijani culture and language. He became a candidate member of the Politburo in 1976, and on 22 November 1982 Yuri Andropov made him a full member and first deputy chairman of the Council of Ministers, the highest position an Azerbaijani had reached in the Soviet Union. Mikhail Gorbachev dismissed him in 1987, officially on health grounds, after the two fell out.

He returned to Nakhchivan in 1990 and was elected chairman of its Supreme Soviet in 1991. In 1993 a military coup led by Surat Huseynov ousted President Abulfaz Elchibey; historians say Aliyev did not appear to have a direct role. Aliyev was installed as president and won an election on 3 October 1993 with 98.8 per cent of the vote against two little-known candidates. He was re-elected in 1998. A new constitution, confirmed by referendum on 12 November 1995, divided power among a parliament, a president and the courts. On 20 September 1994 an agreement to develop the Azeri and Chirag oil fields in the Caspian was signed with a consortium of 11 companies from six countries.

His health failed from 1999, when he had a major heart bypass operation at the Cleveland Clinic. Less than two weeks before the election of 2003 he withdrew and named his son Ilham as his party's candidate. He died at the Cleveland Clinic on 12 December 2003 and was buried in the Alley of Honor cemetery in Baku. Critics describe his rule as authoritarian, and a cult of personality has developed around him.
hezb-e-wahdat: After the pro-Soviet Kabul government collapsed in the Hazarajat in 1979, the region passed to the Shura-ye Inqilab and then to rival radical Islamist groups, none able to control it. By the later 1980s each held its own pocket of territory. The Shura-ye Etelaf, an alliance of eight Shia organisations formed in Tehran in 1985, gave them a common voice towards the Sunni parties in Peshawar, but these parties left the Tehran alliance out of their talks on an interim government after the Soviet withdrawal was announced in January 1988.

Hazara mujahideen took Bamyan in August 1988, and the town hosted the meeting that declared the Misaq-e Wahdat, the unity treaty, in July 1989. Unlike earlier coalitions it was made inside the Hazarajat rather than in Iran, whose officials feared losing their hold on the movement but came to support the new party. Nasr and Pasdaran, the two main groups, won proportional representation, and smaller ones were pressed to join. Shaikh Asif Mohsini's Harakat Islami, dominated by non-Hazara Shiites, stayed out, and in Jaghori the Nahzat commander Wasiq was defeated in 1993.

A Supreme Supervisory Council of religious figures stood above a Central Council, the party's real deciding body. Planned at 36 members, it grew to more than 80 after the first congress of September 1991, and sharing power in it held the once hostile Hazara groups together. Provincial and district councils reported to headquarters in Bamyan. Most of its leaders held political Shia Islamism, but the party drew steadily closer to its Hazara base.

During the Second Afghan Civil War it was one of the main forces in Kabul, backed by Iran. It suffered three great defeats: its fall in Kabul and the killing of its leader Mazari by the Taliban in March 1995; the fall of Mazar-e Sharif in August 1998, when thousands of Hazaras were massacred or imprisoned; and the loss of Bamyan weeks later. Its cadres fled abroad. After 2001 it entered the new administration with little weight; its last major force, the Ninth Corps, was disbanded in June 2005, and rivalry between Karim Khalili and Muhammad Mohaqiq split it into at least four parties claiming its name.
hezbollah: Hezbollah was conceived in 1982 by Lebanese clerics and funded by Iran, primarily to fight the Israeli invasion of Lebanon. The Israeli invasions of 1978 and 1982 had created a humanitarian crisis: many villages in the south were destroyed and large numbers of Shia were displaced. The Shia had also long been underrepresented in Lebanese politics, and both factors bred resentment among them. The movement was set up by local Shia committees under the leadership of Iran's first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and its forces were trained and organised by about 1,500 Iranian Revolutionary Guards, who reached a base in the Beqaa Valley with the permission of the Syrian government.

In the 1980s Hezbollah emerged in South Lebanon during a consolidation of Shia militias, as a rival to the older Amal Movement. It opposed US forces in 1982–83 and fought Amal and Syria in the War of the Camps of 1985–88. Its manifesto of 16 February 1985, issued by Sheikh Ibrahim al-Amin, named the struggle against what it called US and Israeli imperialism as its first aim, called for the destruction of Israel, and looked to Iran's revolution. Several attacks of 1983 in Beirut, among them the US Embassy bombing and the barracks bombing, were attributed to it by some Western intelligence agencies; Hezbollah denied responsibility, and some scholars doubt it existed in that form yet.

Through the 1980s and 1990s Hezbollah waged a guerrilla campaign against Israeli forces and the South Lebanon Army, and Israel withdrew from southern Lebanon in 2000. In the 1990s it turned from a revolutionary group into a political one, a process called its Lebanonisation. It fought in the 2006 Lebanon War and later alongside the government of Bashar al-Assad in the Syrian civil war. A new manifesto of 30 November 2009 opposed political sectarianism and favoured a national unity government. From October 2023 it fought a war with Israel, which brought a ceasefire in November 2024.

Hezbollah follows the doctrine of the guardianship of the Islamic jurists developed by Khomeini, and its formal structure concentrates authority in its religious leaders. Its military branch is the Jihad Council, which includes the Islamic Resistance, and its parliamentary bloc is the Loyalty to the Resistance Bloc. It runs an extensive social programme of schools, hospitals and reconstruction projects, and since 1991 it has run the satellite station Al-Manar. Its support is concentrated among the Shia in the south, in Beirut and its surroundings, and in the northern Beqaa Valley and Hermel region. Whether to call it a resistance movement or a terrorist group is contested, and many states list it as the latter.
hezekiah: Hezekiah was the son of King Ahaz and of Abijah, the daughter of the high priest Zechariah, according to the Bible, and he married Hephzibah. He was the thirteenth king of Judah and ruled after the Assyrians under Sargon II destroyed the northern Kingdom of Israel. The Second Book of Kings and the Second Book of Chronicles describe him as a very righteous king, and the prophets Isaiah and Micah are placed in his time.

The biblical accounts say that he purified and repaired Solomon's Temple, purged its idols and reformed the priesthood. He destroyed the high places and the bronze serpent, called Nehushtan, said to have been made by Moses, which had become an object of worship. Worship was centralised at the Temple in Jerusalem. Some scholars see this as a way of consolidating royal power and resources rather than a purely religious purge.

In 701 BCE the Assyrian king Sennacherib moved to put down a revolt in the west of his empire, invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem. He took Lachish after determined resistance, and a relief from his palace at Nineveh shows the siege. Hezekiah had prepared by fortifying the walls and having the Siloam Tunnel cut through about 533 metres of rock to bring water from the Gihon Spring into the city.

The Bible says an angel brought death to 185,000 Assyrian troops, so that the army withdrew. Sennacherib's prism says he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage and received tribute, and it does not claim that he took the city. Scholars note that Assyrian kings tended to boast and would hardly record a defeat.

In 2015 Eilat Mazar found a bulla reading Belonging to Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, king of Judah, the first impression of a Judahite king's seal found in a scientific excavation. Jerusalem seems to have grown to about 25,000 people, which Israel Finkelstein attributes to refugees from the north, though Amihai Mazar calls this an educated guess. Rabbinic literature calls Hezekiah a model of trust in God. Historians still debate how far the reforms and the biblical account of the siege reflect events.
hiawatha: Hiawatha, also called Ayenwatha or Aiionwatha, was a co-founder of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in the eastern Great Lakes region. He is believed to have lived in either the 12th or the 15th century. He was a leader of the Onondaga, the Mohawk or both; some accounts say he was born Onondaga and later adopted by the Mohawk. He is known chiefly through legend, and the events of the legend have been dated to the middle 1100s by an eclipse that coincided with the founding of the Confederacy. Little else is known of him, and the time and cause of his death are unknown.

In the Mohawk version told by the chief Seth Newhouse, the founder of the Confederacy, Dekanawidah, the Great Peacemaker, met him early and passed to him the Great Law of Peace. The Onondaga principal chief, Tadodaho, obstructed his councils and was blamed for the deaths of Hiawatha's wife and three daughters by magic. Grief-stricken, Hiawatha wandered, stringing wampum, until he reached the Mohawk, where the Peacemaker consoled him with the words of the Requickening Ceremony. Together they composed the laws of the Great Peace and the Peace Hymn, and visited the other four nations. A solar eclipse helped to convince the Senecas, and Tadodaho was won over by the offer that he become principal chief. The Tuscarora joined in 1722 as the Sixth Nation.

Hiawatha was noted for his oratory and his message of peace; the Peacemaker, a Huron prophet who proposed the union, is said to have had a severe speech impediment. The Hiawatha Belt, a wampum belt of 6,574 or 6,916 beads, shows the five nations joined by a white line, with the Onondaga at the centre as keepers of the Central Fire. Its age is unknown and estimated to be early or later 18th century. The New York State Museum held it from 1900 until 1989, when it was returned to the Onondaga Nation, and its image is on the Confederacy's flag. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's poem The Song of Hiawatha of 1855 has no relationship to the historical figure.
hibernia: Hibernia or Ibernia goes back to the 1st century BCE, when Julius Caesar used it in his Commentarii de Bello Gallico, and it then became the main Latin name for Ireland. Its form was influenced by the Latin word hībernus, as though it meant wintry land. In the 1st century CE the geographer Pomponius Mela and the poet Juvenal wrote Iuverna, and in the 4th century the poet Claudian wrote Hiverne. All these names are thought to come from a Q-Celtic name *Īweriū, meaning fertile land, from which the Irish Ériu and Éire also arose.

After the Roman period the name served in official Latin. From 1172 the Lordship of Ireland gave the King of England the title Dominus Hibernie, Lord of Ireland, and the Kingdom of Ireland later used Rex Hiberniae in Latin texts. Gerardus Mercator wrote Hybernia on his world map of 1541. In 1642 the Irish Confederates, a Catholic administration that ruled much of Ireland until 1650, took the motto Pro Deo, Rege et Patria, Hibernia Unanimis, for God, king and fatherland, Ireland united.

In the classicising 18th century the name revived, as Caledonia did for Scotland and Britannia for Britain. It appeared on Irish coins, and the Anglo-Irish Ascendancy, taught Latin at school, used it for Ireland with overtones of classical civility. The Royal Exchange in Dublin, built between 1769 and 1779, bore the inscription SPQH, for Senatus Populusque Hibernicus, and an 18th-century Spanish regiment of Irish exiles was called the Regiment of Hibernia.

Today Hibernia is a poetic name, rarely used for Ireland except in long-established names such as the Royal Hibernian Academy, founded in 1823, the Ancient Order of Hibernians and Hibernian Football Club. Latin forms survive in titles such as Universitas Hiberniae Nationalis, the National University of Ireland. The compound Hiberno- remains more common, as in Hiberno-Norse and Hiberno-English.
hidalgo-state: Hidalgo is bordered by San Luis Potosí and Veracruz on the north, Puebla on the east, Tlaxcala and the State of Mexico on the south and Querétaro on the west. It covers roughly 20,813 square kilometres and is divided into 84 municipalities. Its terrain is very rugged, running from a few metres above sea level to more than 3,300 metres. It has three geographical regions: the Atlantic Coastal Plain, the Sierra Madre Oriental and the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, which holds the highest peaks. The wet Huasteca area lies near the Gulf Coast, and the very northern part of the Valley of Mexico lies within the state.

Prehistoric artifacts have been found at Tepeapulco, Tulancingo, Actopan and Huichapan, dating from about 14,000 to 2,500 BCE, and the oldest evidence of occupation is at Huapalcalco in Tulancingo. Obsidian was worked in the Sierra de las Navajas during the Preclassic period, and the first evidence of social stratification in the region comes from La Loma. The area lay within Mesoamerica, and many peoples passed through it from the north, often settling in the Valley of Mexico. The Toltecs first settled at Xochicoatlán, now Molango, at the beginning of the 7th century, and later had their capital Tollan, today Tula.

Benito Juárez created the State of Hidalgo in 1869 and made Pachuca its capital. The suffix de Soto was added later to honour Manuel Fernando Soto, regarded as the chief driving force behind the state's creation. Its name honours Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, who began the Mexican War of Independence. Mining has shaped its population: when mining activity fell in the mid-20th century the population fell as well, and recovery began in the 1980s. Cornish miners arrived in the 19th century in the Pachuca and Real del Monte areas, and their descendants keep the Protestant faith in many cases and the Cornish pasty, called pastes, as a signature dish.

The state's population is 2.858 million. The Nahua, Otomi and Tepehua each still speak their own language; the Otomi are the largest group, with over 250,000 speakers in the state. The Mezquital Valley preserves much of the Otomi culinary heritage, including edible insects such as escamoles, and the state dish is barbacoa. Its attractions include the ruins of Tula, thermal springs, old mining haciendas and mountain ranges. Pachuca is nicknamed the Beautiful Windy City because of its strong winds.
hieratic: In the 2nd century CE the Greek scholar Clement of Alexandria first used the term hieratic, from the Greek for priestly writing, of the ancient Egyptian script, because for more than 850 years it had been used traditionally only for religious texts and literature. Hieratic is not the same as cursive hieroglyphs. The two were indistinct in the Old Kingdom but became separate writing systems in the First Intermediate Period. Noncursive hieroglyphic script became largely restricted to monumental inscriptions, although handwritten hieroglyphs continued in some formal contexts, such as manuscripts of the Egyptian Book of the Dead.

Hieratic was the script of daily life and was far more important than hieroglyphs throughout Egyptian history. It was the writing system first taught to students, and knowledge of hieroglyphs was limited to a small minority given extra training. Errors in hieroglyphic texts can often be traced to a misunderstanding of a hieratic original. Scribes wrote it mostly in ink with a reed brush on papyrus, wood, stone or pottery ostraca, and in the Roman period also with reed pens. Thousands of limestone ostraca found at Deir al-Madinah give an intimate picture of the lives of common workers. Some hieratic was written on leather rolls and on linen used in mummification.

In the late sixth dynasty about five hundred mud tablets incised with a stylus, like cuneiform, were made at Ayn Asil in the Dakhla Oasis, far from papyrus production; they record inventories, name lists, accounts and about fifty letters. Hieratic reads from right to left. It could be written in columns or lines at first, but after the reign of Amenemhat III in the twelfth dynasty horizontal writing became standard. In any period it often had two forms: a highly ligatured cursive for administration and a broad uncial bookhand for literary, scientific and religious texts. A very cursive form, Abnormal Hieratic, was used in the Theban area from the later twentieth dynasty until the twenty-sixth, when Demotic replaced it.

Demotic is hieratic's direct descendant, and Demotic signs passed into the Meroitic script and into the Coptic alphabet and Old Nubian. Many signs of the Byblos syllabary seem to have been borrowed from Old Kingdom hieratic signs, and early Hebrew used hieratic numerals. The Unicode standard treats hieratic characters as font variants of the Egyptian hieroglyphs, so Egyptologists transcribe hieratic into hieroglyphs before typesetting and translating it.
hiero-i-of-syracuse: Hiero was the son of Deinomenes and brother of Gelon, and he ruled Syracuse in Sicily as tyrant from 478 to 467 BCE. In succeeding Gelon he conspired against a third brother, Polyzalus. During his reign he greatly increased the power of Syracuse. He moved the inhabitants of Naxos and Catania to Leontini and resettled Catania, which he renamed Aetna, with Dorians. He allied with Theron, the tyrant of Acragas, and took the side of the Locrians against Anaxilas, tyrant of Rhegium.

His most important military achievement was the defeat of the Etruscans at the Battle of Cumae in 474 BCE, by which he saved the Greeks of Campania from Etruscan domination. A bronze helmet commemorating the event, now in the British Museum, was dedicated at Olympia. His reign is believed to have seen the creation of the first secret police in Greek history.

Hiero was a liberal patron of literature and culture. The poets Simonides, Pindar, Bacchylides, Aeschylus and Epicharmus were active at his court, as was the philosopher Xenophanes. He competed in the pan-Hellenic athletic contests, winning several victories in the single horse race and the chariot race. He won the chariot race at Delphi in 470 BCE, a victory marked in Pindar's first Pythian ode, and at Olympia in 468 BCE, his most important victory, commemorated in Bacchylides' third victory ode. Pindar wrote further odes for him, among them his first Olympian ode and his second and third Pythian odes.

He died at Catania, by then called Aetna, in 467 BCE and was buried there. His grave was later destroyed when the former inhabitants returned to the city. The tyranny at Syracuse lasted only about a year after his death.
hiero-ii-of-syracuse: Hiero II, also called Hieron, was the illegitimate son of a Syracusan noble, Hierocles, who claimed descent from Gelon. He had served as a general of Pyrrhus of Epirus. When Pyrrhus left Sicily in 275 BCE, the Syracusan army and citizens appointed Hiero commander-in-chief, and he strengthened his position by marrying the daughter of Leptines, one of the leading citizens of Syracuse.

Hiero proved his military worth against the Mamertines, mercenaries from Campania once employed by Agathocles, the late tyrant of Syracuse. They had seized the stronghold of Messina and used it as a base to harass the Greeks around them. Hiero defeated them in a pitched battle near Mylae on the river Longanus, and was prevented from taking Messina only by Carthaginian interference. Between 275 and 271 BCE he seized total power in the city by allying himself with the demos. Unlike earlier tyrants of Syracuse, he ruled within the law and acknowledged the will of the city's assemblies.

When the Mamertines called for Roman aid, Hiero joined the Carthaginian leader Hanno. After an inconclusive battle with the Romans led by the consul Appius Claudius Caudex, he withdrew to Syracuse. Pressed by Roman forces, in 263 BCE he made a treaty with Rome that left him ruling the south-east of Sicily and the eastern coast as far as Tauromenium. He remained loyal to the Romans until his death and often helped them with men and provisions during the Punic war. He kept a powerful fleet for defence and employed his kinsman Archimedes to build engines that later played a large part in the Roman siege of Syracuse.

Hiero died shortly after the Battle of Cannae. A story told by Vitruvius links him to Archimedes: suspecting that a goldsmith had cheated him over the gold for a votive crown, he asked Archimedes to find out. Archimedes is said to have discovered the principle of displacement in a bath and to have run naked through Syracuse shouting eureka. Vitruvius adds that the method exposed the fraud, since the smith had replaced some gold with silver.

The sixteenth idyll of Theocritus gives a picture of Syracuse's prosperity under his rule. Various forms of architectural decoration introduced in Sicily in his time are called Hieronic architecture, though there is no evidence that they came from a programme of his to legitimise his rule. Machiavelli, in The Prince, cites him as a man who rose from private station to princely power, alongside Moses, Cyrus, Theseus and Romulus.
hieronymus-of-cardia: Hieronymus of Cardia was a Greek officer, administrator and historian from Cardia in Thrace. The date of his birth is unknown, though Heckel favours the late 350s BCE. He was probably the nephew of Eumenes of Cardia and likely accompanied him eastward during the campaigns of Alexander the Great. He first appears securely in 320/319 BCE, when Eumenes, besieged by Antigonus Monophthalmus at Nora, sent him as an envoy to Antipater in Macedonia. He stayed with Eumenes in his campaigns against Antigonus and was wounded and taken prisoner at the Battle of Gabiene in 316 BCE.

After the defeat and execution of Eumenes, Antigonus treated Hieronymus kindly and took him into his service. In 312 BCE he put him in charge of collecting bitumen from the Dead Sea. Diodorus Siculus calls him epimeletes of the operation, while Josephus says Antigonus placed him in charge of Syria; Billows argues that he was then governor of Coele-Syria. He campaigned with Antigonus and was present at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, where Antigonus was killed.

He afterwards withdrew with Demetrius Poliorcetes to Greece, and in 293 BCE Demetrius made him governor of Thebes, with the offices of epimeletes and harmostes. He did not join Demetrius on his last Asian campaign in 286 BCE and attached himself instead to Antigonus Gonatas, under whom he spent the rest of his life, probably at the Antigonid court. Later tradition, preserved by Agatharchides and transmitted through Lucian, credits him with a life of 104 years.

Hieronymus wrote a history of the Successors of Alexander, from the death of Alexander in 323 BCE to at least the early 270s BCE. It drew on official documents and on his own long service in military and administrative posts. His style was plain and unadorned, which may explain its limited popularity in antiquity, but modern scholarship regards the work as careful, detailed and reliable. In its later parts he introduced Greek readers to the character and early history of Rome, an unusual interest for a Greek historian of his generation. Ancient authors accused him of partiality toward Antigonus Gonatas and of hostility toward other Successors.

None of the history survives intact, but later writers excerpted it widely. It was a principal source for Diodorus Siculus in Books XVIII to XX and for Plutarch, notably in the Life of Pyrrhus. The surviving fragments were collected by Karl Wilhelm Ludwig Müller and by Felix Jacoby.
hieronymus-von-colloredo: Colloredo was born in Vienna on 31 May 1732, the second son of Count, later Prince, Rudolph Joseph von Colloredo, a high Imperial official, and Countess Maria Gabriele of Starhemberg. Raised in a strict religious household and too frail for a military career, he was educated at the Theresianum Academy in Vienna, studied philosophy at the University of Vienna and theology at the Collegium Germanicum et Hungaricum in Rome. His brother Wenzel Joseph von Colloredo became an Austrian general. From 1761 he was Prince-Bishop of Gurk.

When Salzburg fell vacant in December 1771, Colloredo was elected on 14 March 1772 on the 13th ballot, under considerable pressure from the Imperial court in Vienna. The historian Clive called it an unpopular choice, and judged him extremely autocratic, his manner at times provoking the cathedral chapter and civic officials.

His reforms resembled those of Joseph II in Austria. According to the historian Halliwell he had to place like-minded people in every institution and persuade a reluctant people to change its whole outlook, and he won admiration across Europe. Pilgrimages and superstitious practices were banned, processions restricted, church decoration limited, musical settings of the Mass shortened and German hymns introduced. Critics called him and Johann Michael Bönike, the author of the pastoral letter behind the changes, secret Lutherans. Throughout his life he was close to Jansenism.

Colloredo grew exasperated with Mozart's frequent absences and after several arguments let him go. Mozart's letter of 13 June 1781 tells how the archbishop's steward, Count Arco, threw him out of the room with a kick. Leopold Mozart stayed in Salzburg and complained of the court music's decline; Colloredo himself sometimes played the violin in the court orchestra. As French troops under Napoleon approached, he left Salzburg, never to return. After secularisation Salzburg went to the Grand Duke of Tuscany. Colloredo remained the non-resident archbishop until his death in Vienna on 20 May 1812, aged 79.
hieronymus-wolf: Hieronymus Wolf was born at Oettingen in Germany, one of nine children of an impoverished office clerk. He was formally educated as an attorney but worked for years as a scribe. He studied for a time at Wittenberg, where he was impressed by Philipp Melanchthon and exposed to Lutheran teaching, and he is said to have saved money from his small income to buy a Latin-Greek dictionary and taught himself Greek. His German translation of the speeches of Demosthenes, published in 1549 by the house of Oporinus, made his name known to the Fugger family in Augsburg.

Wolf became secretary and librarian in Augsburg, where he studied and translated many ancient and medieval Greek authors and made them accessible to German academics. The library became known for its contents, among them 100 Greek manuscripts transferred from Venice, and under Wolf and others it became a respected research centre. He was later appointed the first rector of the Gelehrtenschule in the former Carmelite cloister of St Anne, a Protestant college set up to counterbalance the Jesuit college created at about the same time. He was sick throughout his life and never married, and was reputed an outstanding teacher though secluded and egocentric. He died aged 64.

Until his time no distinction had been made between ancient and medieval Greek works, and the latter were overshadowed by interest in the classics. Wolf turned to the history that had led to the Ottoman conquest of much of eastern Europe, which he lived to see reach the Siege of Vienna. In 1557 he published the Corpus Historiae Byzantinae, a collection of Byzantine sources rather than a comprehensive history. He is credited as the first to call the Eastern Roman Empire Byzantine, a term that spread among western European scholars. In the 17th century Louis XIV prompted a larger edition in 34 volumes with Greek text and Latin translation, built on Wolf's Corpus, which established the term in historical studies.
high-court-of-australia: The court was established after the passage of the Judiciary Act 1903, and its authority derives from chapter III of the Australian Constitution, which vests the judicial power of the Commonwealth in it and in other courts that Parliament creates. The idea of a national court is older: after Earl Grey's proposal of 1846 to federate the colonies, an 1849 report from the Privy Council suggested one.

The first bench had three justices, Samuel Griffith, Edmund Barton and Richard O'Connor, each of whom had taken part in drafting the Constitution. All three have been described as relatively conservative for the time and strongly influenced by United States law. In 1906, at the justices' request, two seats were added and H. B. Higgins and Isaac Isaacs were appointed. A third enlargement, to seven, came in 1913 under the Labor prime minister Andrew Fisher, and one of the new appointees, Albert Bathurst Piddington, resigned after a month amid an outcry.

The court has original jurisdiction under sections 75 and 76 of the Constitution, over matters such as those arising under a treaty, those between states and those in which the Commonwealth is a party. Under section 73 it hears appeals from the supreme courts of the states and territories, and appeals need special leave, granted only where a question of law of public importance arises, where courts conflict or where the interests of the administration of justice require it. The seven justices are appointed by the governor-general in council.

Appeals to the Privy Council were a controversy when the Constitution was drafted. They were barred in matters involving federal legislation in 1968, and the Australia Acts closed direct appeals from state supreme courts in 1986. The court sat in the state capitals, especially Melbourne and Sydney, until it moved in 1980 to a purpose-built building on Lake Burley Griffin in Canberra, designed between 1972 and 1974 by Christopher Kringas.

Historical periods are named for the chief justice. The Griffith court of 1903 to 1919 laid the foundations of constitutional law and asserted its authority over state courts. The Knox court decided the Engineers case, which ended the reserved state powers doctrine. The Latham court upheld most wartime legislation under the defence power and allowed a national income tax scheme. Owen Dixon became chief justice in 1952, and his court is described by some as a golden age. The Mason court decided Mabo v Queensland (No 2) and originated the implied freedom of political communication.
high-king-of-ireland: The title Ardrí na hÉireann was held by those who had, or are claimed to have had, lordship over all of Ireland, and it was also given in later writing to figures of myth. Medieval and early modern Irish literature portrays an almost unbroken line of High Kings ruling from the Hill of Tara over lesser kings for thousands of years. Modern historians believe this scheme was crafted in the 8th century from the genealogical traditions of powerful dynasties, to justify their status by projecting it far into the past. John T. Koch writes that it is unlikely that any king had enough authority to dominate the whole island before the 9th century.

The concept of national kingship is first articulated in the 7th century but became a political reality only in the Viking Age, and then not consistently. High Kings never ruled Ireland as a unified state: the High King was an overlord who received tribute from independent kingdoms beneath him.

Early Irish kingship was sacred in character. In some early sources High Kings gain power through marriage to a sovereignty goddess, and a king free from blemish enforces symbolic prerogatives and avoids symbolic taboos. Diarmait mac Cerbaill, king of Tara in the middle of the 6th century, may have been the last king to marry the land.

Succession was complicated. Before the Norman takeover of 1171 Ireland was divided into many kingdoms, kings were often succeeded by sons but other branches took turns by agreement or force, and genealogies were later edited. The High King was essentially a ceremonial overlord, with real power only in his own realm. For the southern Uí Néill this was the Kingdom of Meath.

The Uí Néill, descendants of Niall of the Nine Hostages, had conquered petty kingdoms from the fifth century. Churchmen developed a theory of a high kingship and received royal patronage in return. The Annals of Ulster record the death of Máel Sechnaill mac Máele Ruanaid in 862 as king of all Ireland, a title his successor Áed Finliath apparently never held, and it is unclear what political reality lay behind it.

In 1002 Brian Bóruma of Munster took the high kingship from Máel Sechnaill II of the southern Uí Néill. Some historians call it a usurpation, while others say that no one had a strict legal right. Brian was killed at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014, Máel Sechnaill II was restored, and he died in 1022. From then until 1171 the high kingship was held alongside kings with opposition. The Uí Briain of Munster, the Meic Lochlainn of the North and the Uí Conchubhair of Connacht later competed for it.
highland-clearances: The Highland Clearances, in Scottish Gaelic Fuadaichean nan Gàidheal, the eviction of the Gaels, took place mostly in two phases from 1750 to 1860. The first phase grew out of agricultural improvement and the wish of landlords, many of them in debt, to raise their incomes. Open fields worked on the run rig system and shared grazing were enclosed and usually replaced by large pastoral farms paying much higher rents. Displaced tenants were expected to find work in fishing, quarrying or kelp harvesting, and their fall from farmer to crofter was a cause of resentment.

Clanship had given clansmen protection and farmland in return for service and rent. The principle of dùthchas held that clan members had an inalienable right to rent land in the clan territory, but Scottish law never recognised it, and chiefs came to think of themselves as commercial landlords rather than patriarchs. The tacksmen, who held leases and sublet land, were the first to feel the change as landlords restricted their power from the 1770s.

The first phase occurred mostly between 1760 and 1815, though it began earlier, when the Dukes of Argyll put farms up for auction, starting in Kintyre in the 1710s. The second phase involved overcrowded crofting communities that had lost the means to support themselves through famine or the collapse of the kelp industry after 1815. Assisted passages became common, with landowners paying their tenants' fares, and the Highland Potato Famine gave the process greater urgency. Some landlords tried to delay evictions at financial cost to themselves, while a few showed no concern for the evicted.

Resistance was more common than once thought. In 1792 tenants from Strathrusdale drove more than 6,000 sheep off the land around Ardross in the first large protest. Michael Lynch suggests there were more than 50 major acts of resistance, and women often stood at the front when confronting officials. Troops intervened on at least ten occasions, but Eric Richards notes that no death has been directly attributed to the physical act of clearance.

The Crofters' Holdings (Scotland) Act 1886, won by the Highland Land League, gave crofters security of tenure and ended the Clearances, though it came late, when the land was already depopulated, and did not cover cottars. Emigrants settled in close communities in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario and the Carolinas. Sorley MacLean's poem Hallaig, about a cleared village on Raasay, is among the best-known Gaelic poems of the 20th century. Historians still debate the causes, and their understanding differs from the popular view.
hiiumaa: Hiiumaa covers 989 square kilometres and lies 22 km from the Estonian mainland, in the West Estonian archipelago of the Baltic Sea. Its relief is low, reaching 68 m above sea level, and it is formed mostly of limestone, exposed in cliffs along parts of the coast. The Soela Strait separates it from Saaremaa to the south and the Muhu Strait from the mainland. Its names include Dagö in Swedish, Dagden in German and Hiidenmaa in Finnish. The island rose from the sea about 8,500 years ago through isostatic uplift after the ice cap retreated, and the land is still rising.

Mesolithic settlements on the Kõpu Peninsula date from about 5500 BCE and seem to have been tied to seal hunting. Because the land has risen, they now lie far from the coast. Stone-cist graves on the island span the Late Bronze Age to the Late Iron Age.

The island is first recorded as Dageida in 1228, when it and the rest of Estonia were conquered by Germanic crusaders. In 1254 it was divided between the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek and the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order, acting partly for the Hanseatic League.

The oldest surviving church, at Pühalepa, was built in 1259, although it was rebuilt in the 18th century, and the Hanseatic League built a lighthouse at Kõpu in the 16th century. As Dagö the island belonged to Swedish Estonia and later passed to the Russian Empire, whose rule left the Swedish population most of its privileges. Most of the numerous Swedish speakers later emigrated or were Estonianised, though a minority remained into the 20th century.

German forces occupied Hiiumaa in the First World War, and in 1918 it became part of independent Estonia. The Soviet Union occupied it in 1940, Germany in 1941 and the Soviet Union again in 1944. Until Estonia regained independence in August 1991 the island was closed to foreigners and to most of mainland Estonia.

Hiiumaa is the main island of Hiiu County, and its largest town is Kärdla. Tourism, livestock, farming and fishing support its economy. The natural environment is protected in the Tahkuna Nature Reserve and the West Estonian Archipelago Biosphere Reserve. A ferry links the island to the mainland, and in winter an ice road can cross the frozen sea.
hijikata-toshizo: Hijikata was born on 31 May 1835 in Ishida village in the Tama region of Musashi Province, now part of Hino in Tokyo, the youngest of ten children of a well-to-do farmer who died a few months before his birth. His mother died when he was six, and he was raised by his second brother Kiroku. In his youth he sold the family's Ishida medicine for bruises and broken bones while teaching himself swordsmanship. Through his brother-in-law Satō Hikogorō, who ran a Tennen Rishin-ryū dojo in Hino, he met Kondō Isami, and in 1859 he enrolled at the school's Shieikan.

In 1863 Hijikata and Kondō joined the Rōshigumi and stayed in Kyoto when the rest returned to Edo; the group, renamed the Shinsengumi, served as a police force under Matsudaira Katamori, the daimyō of Aizu. When the joint leaders Serizawa Kamo and Niimi Nishiki brought the group into disrepute, Hijikata ordered Niimi to commit seppuku and led the killing of Serizawa, leaving Kondō sole leader. At the Ikedaya incident on 8 July 1864 he led the second group of 23 men. After Yamanami Keisuke, who had tried to desert, committed seppuku in 1865, Hijikata became vice-commander, enforcing the rules so harshly that he was called the Demon Vice-Commander.

In the Boshin War he fought at Toba-Fushimi in January 1868 and at Kōshū-Katsunuma, and after Kondō's capture tried in vain to secure his pardon through Katsu Kaishū. Kondō was executed on 17 May 1868. Hijikata went on to Aizu and Sendai, joined the fleet of Enomoto Takeaki, and with Ōtori Keisuke occupied the fortress of Goryōkaku. In the Republic of Ezo he was made vice-minister of the army, and on 6 May 1869 he led the failed attempt to seize the imperial warship Kōtetsu at Miyako Bay.

On 14 June 1869 he gave his page Ichimura Tetsunosuke his death poem, sword, letter, photograph and hair to take to Satō Hikogorō in Hino. On 20 June he was shot in the lower back while leading his troops on horseback near the Ippongi Kanmon, and a week later the forces of the Ezo Republic surrendered. His burial place is unknown. Memorials stand in Hakodate, Hino and Tokyo, a museum near the Sekidenji temple opened in 1994, and Ryōtarō Shiba's novel Moeyo Ken dramatised his life.
hikayat-aceh: The chronicle was written in Malay in the Arabic script, at some time after 1607 and before the end of the 17th century, for the sultanate on the northern tip of Sumatra. It eulogises Sultan Iskandar Muda, who reigned from 1607 to 1636 and was declared a national hero of Indonesia in 1993, and tells his story against a wide background of Chinese, Portuguese and Ottoman-Turkish influences and relations, in which Siam, Cambodia and Johor also play a part.

The Russian linguist Vladimir Braginskiĭ has argued that its structure follows Mughal historiography. He found close similarities with the Mahfuzat-i-Timuri, which tells the life and exploits of Timur, and also with the structure of the Akbarnama.

Only three manuscripts survive. The oldest and most complete, MS. Or. 1954 of about 1675–1700, is held by Leiden University Libraries and was edited as manuscript A by Teuku Iskandar in 1958. Leiden also holds MS. Or. 1983, a copy in Batavian Malay dated 9 March 1847, which Iskandar used as manuscript B. The third, MS. ML 421, is an early 20th-century copy in the National Library of Indonesia in Jakarta, probably meant as the basis for an edition by Hoesein Djajadiningrat.

Both Leiden manuscripts have been digitised. On 18 May 2023 all three were inscribed in the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, affirming their world significance. Historians regard the chronicle as an indispensable tool for the history of Aceh and its political, cultural and religious traits.
hikayat-merong-mahawangsa: The work, also spelt Hikayat Marong Mahawangsa and written in the Jawi script, is a romantic account of the history and tales of the Malay kingdom of Kedah. It is thought to have been written in the late 18th century or some time in the 19th century. Its narrative runs from the opening of Kedah by Merong Mahawangsa, whom it describes as a descendant of Dhu al-Qarnayn, down to the kingdom's acceptance of Islam. Alongside historical facts it contains many fantastic claims.

The opening part tells of kings and the founding of their kingdoms through semi-historical legends and folk stories, some of indigenous origin and some shaped by Islamic elements. Merong Mahawangsa is given family ties to the Romans. While his royal fleet was sailing from Rome to China, it was attacked by the giant bird Garuda, and he came ashore in what is now Kedah. There he founded Langkasuka, a name explained from Sanskrit words for a resplendent land and joy, and later returned to Rome after enthroning his son Raja Merong Mahapudisat. Langkasuka was eventually renamed Kedah Zamin Turan.

Following his father's advice, Mahapudisat is said to have divided the realm among his sons into the kingdoms of Siam, Perak and Pattani. Raja Seri Mahawangsa began the custom of sending flowers of gold and silver to the Siamese king whenever a son was born to him.

A later king, Raja Ong Maha Perita Deria, called Raja Bersiong or the Fanged King for drinking human blood, was driven out by his ministers and fled to Mount Jerai; his story has been read as a symbol of a pre-Islamic order. The last of the line, Raja Phra Ong Mahawangsa, became a Muslim and took the name Sultan Mudzafar Shah. The annals also tell of the tribute Kedah sent each year to the Chola Empire and afterwards to Siam.

The royal family of Kedah traces its lineage back to Phra Ong Mahawangsa and so to Merong Mahawangsa. The Royal Malaysian Navy named the vessel KD Mahawangsa in honour of the first monarch. The legend of the Fanged King was the basis of the Malay-language film Raja Bersiong of 1968, and in 2011 KRU Studios produced a film loosely based on the myth, also titled Hikayat Merong Mahawangsa and directed by Yusry Abdul Halim.
hikone: Hikone lies in central Shiga Prefecture, on the eastern shore of Lake Biwa, and extends inland to the Ibuki Mountains. Parts of the city fall within the Biwako Quasi-National Park. The climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and cool winters that bring light snowfall or none. The site was a natural bottleneck on the route of the Tōsandō, later the Nakasendō, the highway connecting Heian-kyō with the eastern provinces. Strategically it was a vital point for protecting the capital against attack from the east.

Hikone was part of the ancient Ōmi Province and began as a market town around Hogon-ji, a Buddhist temple founded in the Heian period. It has two former post stations on the Nakasendō, Toriimoto-juku and Takamiya-juku, and the Chōsenjin Kaidō also passed through the area. In the Sengoku period the Azai clan of northern Ōmi controlled it and built Sawayama Castle. Oda Nobunaga defeated the Azai and gave the castle to his general Niwa Nagahide. Under Toyotomi Hideyoshi it was entrusted to his close adviser Ishida Mitsunari.

After Ishida Mitsunari's defeat at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu appointed his general Ii Naomasa daimyō of a new domain centred on Sawayama Castle. Ii Naomasa began Hikone Castle, and his son Ii Naokatsu completed it in 1622. The area stayed under the Hikone Domain to the end of the Edo period. The town of Hikone was established on 1 April 1889 under the modern system of municipalities and became a city on 11 February 1937 by merging with neighbouring villages. It escaped major damage in World War II.

Hikone had an estimated 111,958 inhabitants in 2021. Its main industries are the manufacture of butsudan, textiles and valves. Hikone Castle is a National Treasure and Special National Historic Site, and the Sawayama Castle ruins and the Kōjinyama Kofun are also listed sites. The city has three universities and is the home of the Japan Center for Michigan Universities, founded in 1989. It is twinned with Ann Arbor, Michigan, since 1969, and with Xiangtan in China.
hilandar: Hilandar is the only Serbian Orthodox monastery on Mount Athos. The name is probably a Serbian form of the Greek chelandion, a type of Byzantine transport ship. In 1198 Emperor Alexios III Angelos issued a chrysobull giving the ancient monastery Helandaris to the Serbs. Stefan Nemanja, a former Grand Prince of Serbia who had taken monastic vows as Simeon, joined his son Sava, who later became the first Archbishop of Serbia. Together they built the main church, dedicated to the Theotokos, between 1198 and 1200, and Sava issued a Typikon in Serbian. Simeon died there on 13 February 1200, and his remains were moved to Studenica in 1208.

After the sack of Constantinople in 1204 Mount Athos came under Latin occupation and was pillaged. Hilandar was among only 35 of some 300 monasteries to survive the Catalan Grand Company's raids of the early 14th century. King Stefan Milutin rebuilt and expanded it, completely reconstructing the main church in 1320. Under Stefan Dušan, when all of Athos was under his power, it enjoyed its highest prosperity; since his reign Hilandar has owned one fifth of Athos. After a fire in 1722 Bulgarian monks dominated until the late 19th century, and a Serbian presence returned in 1902.

Hilandar houses about 45 working monks and treats the Mother of God through her icon of the Three Hands as its abbess. It holds some 1,200 Slavic manuscripts, 172 Greek and 154 Serbian medieval documents, the icon of the Three Hands, said to have come from John of Damascus, and Stefan Dušan's sword. Its scriptorium developed the Serbian variant of Old Church Slavonic. In 1990 it was converted from an idiorrhythmic monastery into a cenobitic one. A fire on 4 March 2004 destroyed much of the walled complex and all its wooden elements, but the library and the historic icons were saved.
hilarion-of-kiev: Little verifiable information about Hilarion's life survives, though some points are generally accepted. According to the Primary Chronicle he served as a presbyter at the princely residence of Berestove and was known as a well-educated scholar. After the death of Metropolitan Theopemptus, a council of local bishops proclaimed him metropolitan of Kiev and all Rus' on the proposal of Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise. The choice broke with the Byzantine custom of placing Greeks in the episcopal sees, and Hilarion was not appointed by the Ecumenical Patriarch Michael I Cerularius. His time in office fell before or during the East–West Schism of the 11th century.

The appointment met stiff opposition from Luka Zhidiata, Bishop of Novgorod, probably because the right to appoint the Kievan metropolitan belonged to the Patriarch of Constantinople and the appointment was therefore uncanonical. Luka was confined in the Kievan Caves Monastery for three years; at his death his remains were taken back to Novgorod and buried in the Cathedral of Holy Wisdom. Hilarion's term seems to have been short, since some chronicles mention Metropolitan Yefrem in 1055.

Besides the Sermon on Law and Grace, three other works are credited to him: a Confession of Faith, a Sermon on Spiritual Benefit to All Christians and a short collection of instructions for priests, A Word to Brother Stylites. Scholars have also tried to link him to the early chronicles of Rus'. Aleksey Shakhmatov and others have conjectured that he was one of the compilers of an early chronicle at the court of Yaroslav the Wise in the 1030s.

Hilarion remains the best known of the early metropolitans of Kiev, both as the first native of Rus' to hold the see and for his writings. What became of him after his term is not recorded. In the 1920s the Russian historian Mikhail Prisyolkov proposed that he became a monk under the name Nikon at the Kiev Caves Monastery and was the same Nikon who compiled the Caves Chronicle of 1073, a theory that has not been confirmed.
hilary-of-poitiers: Hilary was born at Poitiers, either at the end of the 3rd century or the beginning of the 4th. His parents were pagans of distinction, and he received a good education that included a high level of Greek. Through study of the Old and New Testament writings he abandoned Neoplatonism for Nicene Christianity, and he, his wife and his daughter, traditionally known as Abra of Poitiers, were baptised. Arianism was becoming popular among Christians in this period, though the bishops at the Council of Nicaea, sponsored by Constantine the Great, had rejected it.

Around 355 Hilary wrote to Emperor Constantius II a remonstrance against the persecutions by which the Arians had sought to crush their opponents. At the synod of Béziers in 356 an imperial rescript banished him, with Rhodanus of Toulouse, to Phrygia. The traditional explanation is that he refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius and the Nicene faith. More recently several scholars have suggested that political opposition to Constantius and support for the usurper Claudius Silvanus may have led to his exile.

In Phrygia he continued to govern his diocese and attended several synods, including the council at Seleucia in 359, which saw the triumph of the homoion party. In 360 he failed to gain an audience with Constantius, and when the council at Constantinople ratified the decisions of Ariminum and Seleucia he answered with the bitter In Constantium, which attacked the emperor as Antichrist. His repeated requests for public debates with Ursacius and Valens proved so inconvenient that he was sent back to his diocese, which he reached about 361.

At home he spent two or three years persuading local clergy that the homoion confession was a cover for Arian subordinationism, and synods in Gaul condemned the creed of Ariminum. In 364 he accused Auxentius, bishop of Milan, of heterodoxy, and Valentinian I summoned him to Milan, but Auxentius gave satisfactory answers. Hilary described the failure in a work published in 365.

His early Commentarius in Evangelium Matthaei, written before his exile, is the first Latin commentary on Matthew to survive entire. De synodis, written in 358 and early 359, reviews the creeds of the Eastern bishops and argues that the difference from orthodox belief was sometimes in words rather than ideas, which led him to counsel the western bishops to be more reserved in condemnation. De trinitate, in twelve books, composed in 359 and 360, was the first successful expression in Latin of the theology worked out in Greek. Some regard him as the first Latin Christian hymn writer. Pope Pius IX recognised him as a Doctor of the Church in 1851, and his feast day is 13 January.
hild-of-whitby: Almost all that is known of Hild comes from Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People of 731. She was the second daughter of Hereric, a nephew of Edwin, King of Deira, and his wife Breguswīþ. While she was an infant her father was poisoned in exile at the court of the Brittonic king of Elmet. Edwin then created the Kingdom of Northumbria and Hild grew up at his court. In 625 he married the Christian princess Æthelburh of Kent, who came north with her chaplain Paulinus of York, and Hild was baptised with the court at Easter 627 in a wooden church near the site of the present York Minster.

When Edwin fell in battle in 633 against the pagan King of Mercia, Paulinus took Æthelburh and her household to Kent, where the queen founded a convent at Lyminge; Hild probably stayed with her. At the age of 33, about to join her widowed sister Hereswith at Chelles Abbey in Gaul, she answered instead the call of Bishop Aidan of Lindisfarne and became a nun in her homeland, learning the traditions of Celtic monasticism on the north bank of the River Wear.
