Most of what is known of him comes from Plato, who portrays him as vain and arrogant. The Hippias Minor shows him as ridiculously vain, and the Hippias Major, whose authorship by Plato is sometimes doubted, puts his presumption in a ludicrous light.

Hippias was learned in rhetoric, philosophy and politics and also in poetry, music, mathematics, painting and sculpture. He boasted of wearing nothing he had not made himself, including his seal-ring, cloak and shoes. A lost work on the victors of the Olympiads placed the victory of Coroebus in 776 BCE and became the basis of all later lists. Plutarch criticised it, saying that Hippias had no authoritative basis for his chronology. A mathematical discovery ascribed to him is sometimes called the quadratrix of Hippias.

Hippias is credited with originating the idea of natural law, which he held to be universal. He also wrote about self-sufficiency as a binding principle. His ideas passed on through Cynicism and Stoicism.
hippias-tyrant: Hippias was born around 570 BCE as the eldest son of Pisistratus, the first tyrant of Athens. When his father was forced to flee to Eretria after offending Megakles, Pisistratus took counsel with his sons, and Hippias proposed that they retake the tyranny. Athens fell to Pisistratus for the third time in 546 BCE. Hippias was supported in the restoration by the family of the polemarch Charmus, an old ally of his father, and Pisistratus gave him Charmus's daughter in marriage.

Hippias succeeded his father as tyrant of Athens in 528 or 527 BCE, when Pisistratus died of old age. He was a patron of poets and craftsmen, and Athens enjoyed prosperity under his rule. His brother Hipparchus, who may have ruled jointly with him, was murdered at the Panathenaic festival in 514 BCE by Harmodius and Aristogeiton. Aristogeiton resented Hipparchus's advances toward Harmodius, and the plotters meant to kill both brothers.

Only Hipparchus died. Hippias's soldiers captured the group, and Aristogeiton was executed after torture while Harmodius was killed on the spot. It was said that Hippias afterwards became bitter and cruel over four years, unlike his moderate father. He executed many citizens, exiled others and imposed harsh taxes.

The Alcmaeonidae, whom Pisistratus had exiled in 546 BCE, were concerned about his alliances with the Persian ruling class and planned an invasion. Cleisthenes, who had been archon in 525/4 BCE, is said to have bribed the Pythian priestess of Delphi to tell the Spartans to liberate the Athenians. After a failed expedition, Cleomenes I of Sparta invaded in 510 BCE and trapped Hippias on the Acropolis, took the children of the Peisistratids hostage and made him leave to have them returned. Power passed to the Athenian magistrates, which began Athenian democracy.

Hippias went to Sigeion, then to Lampsakos and to King Darius in Persia. The Spartans later tried to restore him, but the Corinthians and other allies refused to see a tyranny imposed on a Greek city. He made his illegitimate son Hegesistratus tyrant of Sigeion and railed against the Athenians to Artaphrenes, the governor of Sardis. In 490 BCE he urged Darius I to attack Athens, accompanied the Persian fleet and proposed Marathon as suited to their cavalry. According to Herodotus he dreamt the night before that he lay with his mother, which he took as an omen of a return, but a loose tooth fell out on the beach.

He is said to have died at Lemnos on the way back from Marathon. His five sons joined Xerxes's army in 480 BCE, and the Peisistratids never again had influence in Athens. Building continued under his rule on the temple of Olympian Zeus, which was not finished until Hadrian's time.
hippo-regius: Hippo takes its name from a Phoenician word, probably related to the word for harbour, and Phoenicians from Tyre first settled the town around the 12th century BCE. The Romans called it Hippo Regius, the Royal Hippo, because it was one of the residences of the Numidian kings, and to tell it from Hippo Diarrhytus, modern Bizerte. It lay near the mouth of the river Ubus, now the Seybouse, on the bay that was known as Hippo Bay.

Hippo became a Roman colony that prospered into a major city of Africa Province, and was later included in the Diocese of Africa under Diocletian's reforms. The diocese was established around 250. Councils met there in 393, 394 and 426, and the synod of 393 and the Synod of Carthage in 397 drew up a list of the books of scripture still regarded as the Catholic canon. Augustine of Hippo, a Church Father, served as bishop in his later years.

In 430 the Vandals advanced along the coast and besieged the walled city. Augustine died on 28 August 430, three months into the siege, perhaps from starvation or stress. The Vandals lifted the siege after 14 months, and the peace treaty of 435 acknowledged their possession of the city. King Geiseric made it the capital of the Vandal Kingdom until the capture of Carthage in 439. The Eastern Roman Empire conquered Hippo in 534 and held it until the Muslim conquest in 698.

The Caliphate rebuilt the town in the eighth century, and in the eleventh the Berber Zirids founded the town of Beled el-Anab about three kilometres away. France took it in 1832 and renamed it Bône. Hippo Regius is the ancient name of the modern city of Annaba, Algeria. Some ancient ruins remain, together with a basilica dedicated to St Augustine.
hippocrates: Historians agree that Hippocrates was born around 460 BCE on the island of Kos; other biographical information is likely to be untrue. Soranus of Ephesus, a 2nd-century Greek physician, was his first biographer and is the source of most personal information. Hippocrates is mentioned in passing by two contemporaries, in Plato's dialogues Protagoras and Phaedrus and in Aristotle's Politics.

According to Soranus his father Heraclides was a physician and his mother was Praxitela. He learned medicine from his father and grandfather, and studied other subjects with Democritus and Gorgias. He was probably trained at the asklepieion of Kos, and took lessons from the Thracian physician Herodicus of Selymbria. He taught and practised medicine throughout his life, travelling at least as far as Thessaly, Thrace and the Sea of Marmara.

Hippocrates is credited as the first person to hold that diseases had natural causes rather than being sent by gods. In On the Sacred Disease, on epilepsy, the writer argues that the disease is no more divine than others and that people regard it as divine from ignorance and wonder. Hippocratic medicine held that disease came from environmental factors, diet and living habits, though it also held convictions based on incorrect anatomy and physiology, such as humorism. Its therapy was gentle and passive, resting on the healing power of nature, and it gave weight to prognosis and to careful case histories.

The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of around seventy early medical works, written in Ionic Greek and gathered in Alexandrian Greece. Whether Hippocrates himself wrote any of them has not been conclusively answered, and given the variety of subjects and styles the corpus could not have been written by one person. It includes the Hippocratic Oath, Aphorisms and On Airs, Waters and Places, and its works sometimes contradict one another. Very little is known concretely about what Hippocrates himself thought, wrote and did.

Several accounts of his death exist. He died probably in Larissa, at the age of 83, 85 or 90, though some say he lived well over 100. Although he neither founded the school of medicine named after him nor wrote most of the treatises attributed to him, he is traditionally regarded as the Father of Medicine. His teachings were so revered that for a long time they were taken as too great to be improved upon. The Islamic world adopted its methods in the Middle Ages, and after the Renaissance they were revived in western Europe. Clubbing of the fingers is still called Hippocratic fingers, and the Hippocratic Oath is the foundation of later oaths taken by medical graduates.
hippocrates-of-chios: Hippocrates of Chios was born on the island of Chios, where he was originally a merchant. After misadventures, in which he was robbed by either pirates or fraudulent customs officials, he went to Athens, possibly for litigation, and there became a leading mathematician. On Chios he may have been a pupil of the mathematician and astronomer Oenopides of Chios. His mathematics probably shows some Pythagorean influence too, perhaps through contacts between Chios and the neighbouring island of Samos, a centre of Pythagorean thinking, and he has been described as a para-Pythagorean, a philosophical fellow traveller.

His major accomplishment was to write the first systematically organised geometry textbook, the Elements (Stoicheia), setting out basic theorems as building blocks of mathematical theory. It gave mathematicians a common framework to build on. Only one fragment survives, embedded in the work of Simplicius, in which the areas of some lunes, now called Hippocratic lunes, are calculated. This belonged to a programme to square the circle. Hippocrates failed in that, but he was the first to prove an equality of area between a curved shape and a polygonal one. Ferdinand von Lindemann showed in 1882 that the approach could not succeed.

In the century after him at least four other mathematicians wrote their own Elements, improving terminology and logical structure, and his work laid the foundation for Euclid's Elements of about 325 BCE. He is believed to have originated the use of letters for the points and figures of a proposition, as in triangle ABC, and the use of power for the square of a line. He found a way to approach the duplication of the cube, the problem of constructing a cube root, and invented the technique of reduction, which turns a specific problem into a more general one that is easier to solve.

In astronomy he tried to explain comets and the Milky Way. His ideas are not clearly handed down, but he probably thought both were optical illusions, caused by the refraction of sunlight by moisture exhaled by a putative planet near the Sun and by the stars. He also held that light rays originate in the eye rather than in the object seen.
hippocratic-corpus: The corpus has gone under the name of Hippocrates since antiquity, though none of its texts is proven to be by him. Franz Zacharias Ermerins identified the hands of at least nineteen authors, and Howard Clark Kee called it a haphazard collection of anonymous authors. It may be the remains of a library of Cos, or a collection compiled in Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE, and it includes works of the Cnidian school as well as the Coan.

Most of the works date from the last decades of the 5th century BCE and the first half of the 4th. The earliest, from the mid-5th century, include On Diseases II–III, linked to the Cnidian school. Epidemics I and III date to about 410 BCE. A group of surgical treatises belongs to the end of the 5th or the start of the 4th century. Some later works are Hellenistic, and Precepts and On Decorum come from the 1st and 2nd centuries CE.

The collection holds textbooks, lectures, research, notes and philosophical essays in no particular order, written for specialists and laymen and sometimes from opposing viewpoints, so that significant contradictions appear between works. Books I and III of Epidemics contain forty-two case histories, of which 25 ended in the patient's death. Other treatises deal with surgery, women's diseases, skin complaints and the effects of wine. The writers stress a natural approach to health and the harmony between the body and its environment, so that seasons, winds, water and soil are weighed in studying disease.

The physician's conduct is a recurring concern. A maxim in Epidemics I advises the physician to help, or at least to do no harm. The best-known work is the Hippocratic Oath, a declaration of medical ethics that deals with principles and with practical matters, and is probably not the work of one man. The whole corpus is written in Ionic Greek.

The entire corpus was first printed as a unit in 1525, in a Latin edition by Marcus Fabius Calvus in Rome, and the first complete Greek edition followed the next year from the Aldine Press in Venice. Émile Littré spent twenty-two years, from 1839 to 1861, on a complete Greek edition with a French translation. The first English translation of part of the corpus was Peter Lowe's Chirurgerie in 1597, and Francis Adams published a translation of a dozen and a half works judged genuine in 1849. Jacques Jouanna began an edition in the Collection Budé in 1967.
hippodamus-of-miletus: Hippodamus was born in Miletus and lived during the 5th century BCE; his father was Euryphon. Ancient and later writers describe him as an architect, urban planner, physician, mathematician, meteorologist and philosopher. He is referred to in the works of Aristotle, Stobaeus, Strabo, Hesychius, Photius and Theano. Aristotle, in his Politics, records that he had a reputation as a lover of attention: some people thought he carried things too far, with his long hair, expensive ornaments and the same cheap warm clothing worn in winter and summer.

According to Aristotle, Hippodamus was the first urban planner to give attention to the proper arrangement of cities. He laid out the Piraeus, the port of Athens, for Pericles, with wide streets radiating from the central agora, which was generally called the Hippodameia in his honour. He is also said to have built the refounded city of Rhodes in the form of a theatre. In 440 BCE he went out among the Athenian colonists and planned the new city of Thurium, later Thurii, in Magna Graecia, with streets crossing at right angles; for this he is sometimes called Hippodamus of Thurium.

His plans were characterised by order and regularity, in contrast to the intricacy and confusion common to cities of that period, even Athens. The grid plans attributed to him consisted of broad, straight streets cutting one another at right angles, and Miletus offers the prototype, with a wide central area kept unsettled that in time evolved into the agora. His principles were later adopted in Halicarnassus, Alexandria and Antioch. Because rectangular plans were in use among the Greeks as early as the 8th century BCE, he cannot be considered the originator of the concept.

Aristotle treats Hippodamus as the first author to write on the theory of government without any experience of practical affairs. His ideal city was to be inhabited by 10,000 free male citizens, within a total population of 50,000 including women, children and slaves. He divided the citizens into three classes, soldiers, artisans and husbandmen, and the land into sacred, public and private. Aristotle objected that confining arms to one class would lead to the oppression of the others. He also criticised the proposal to reward those who discover something useful to the city, arguing that easy change weakens the force of law. Writings attributed to him include On the State and On Happiness.
hippodrome-of-constantinople: The first Hippodrome was built when the city was still called Byzantium, a provincial town of moderate importance. In 203 CE the Emperor Septimius Severus rebuilt the city and gave it a hippodrome. After his victory at the Battle of Chrysopolis, Constantine the Great refounded Byzantium in 324 as Nova Roma, a name that soon gave way to Constantinople, and he renovated the Hippodrome.

It is estimated to have been about 450 m long and 130 m wide, with starting gates, the carceres, at the northern end and the curved tribune, the sphendone, at the southern end of the U-shaped track. The stands held around 100,000 spectators. The emperor's lodge, the Kathisma, could be entered directly from the Great Palace by a passage reserved for the imperial family.

Through the Byzantine period the Hippodrome was the centre of the city's social life, and large sums were wagered on the races. Four teams took part at first, each backed by a political party: the Blues, the Greens, the Reds and the Whites. The Reds and Whites weakened and were absorbed by the other two. The meetings were among the few occasions on which the emperor and ordinary citizens shared one place, and political matters were often discussed there.

The rivalry of the Blues and Greens often merged with political or religious disputes and sometimes produced riots amounting to civil war. The worst were the Nika riots of 532, in which an estimated 30,000 people were killed and many buildings, including the second Hagia Sophia, destroyed. The last recorded race took place in 1200, and the sack of the city in the Fourth Crusade of 1204 ruined the Hippodrome. The Ottomans, who took the city in 1453, had no interest in chariot racing, and the site served as a source of building stone.

The site is now Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul. The original track lies some 2 m below the present surface. Three monuments of the central barrier survive in excavated pits. The Serpent Column is the base of a tripod cast to celebrate the Greek victory over the Persians in the 5th century BCE, which Constantine ordered moved from Delphi; its heads and top third were destroyed in 1700. The Obelisk of Thutmose III, first raised at Karnak about 1490 BCE, was brought by Theodosius the Great in 390, and its top section stands on a marble pedestal. The Walled Obelisk was built in the 10th century.
hippolytus-son-of-theseus: Hippolytus, in Ancient Greek Hippolutos, was in Greek mythology the son of Theseus and an Amazon, either Hippolyta or Antiope. His name means unleasher of horses, and it may be understood ironically, since the element -lytos suggests something that may be undone or destroyed, giving the sense destroyed by horses. He is a hunter and sportsman, more inclined to hunting than to marriage and love. He worships Artemis, the virgin huntress, scrupulously and refuses to honour Aphrodite. Offended, Aphrodite causes his stepmother Phaedra to fall in love with him. When he rejects her advances, events begin that lead to his death in a fall from his chariot.

In the tragedy of Euripides, Phaedra, the second wife of Theseus, is cursed by Aphrodite and falls so ardently in love that she becomes physically ill and decides to end her life. Her nurse reveals the secret to Hippolytus and urges him to return her love, but he responds only with horror and disgust. In despair Phaedra hangs herself and leaves a note accusing him of raping her. Theseus, furious, uses one of three wishes given him by his father Poseidon to call for his son's death. Hippolytus has gone hunting, and Poseidon sends a sea-monster that terrifies his chariot horses. They become uncontrollable and hurl him out, and he is dragged, entangled in the reins, and fatally wounded.

Artemis then reconciles father and son by telling Theseus that Phaedra's accusation was false. She comforts the dying Hippolytus with a promise that he will be the subject of religious practice, so that his memory will live for ever, and she assigns a band of Trozenian maidens to preserve the story of Phaedra and Hippolytus in a ritual song.
Other writers told versions of the story, among them Seneca the Younger in Phaedra, Ovid in the Metamorphoses and Heroides, Jean Racine in Phèdre and Thomas Sturge Moore in Aphrodite against Artemis.

In Italy, in a later phase of Hellenization, Virbius, one of two figures tied to the ancient cult of Diana Nemorensis, was assimilated to Hippolytus. The version told by Ovid and Pausanias differs from that of Euripides: Asclepius brought Hippolytus back from the dead, but he refused to forgive Theseus, went to Italy, became king of the Aricians and named a city after Artemis. He ruled as Virbius from inside the shrine of Diana, which forbade horses to enter. His cult held that Artemis asked Asclepius to resurrect him because he had vowed chastity to her, and his followers cut off a piece of their hair to dedicate their chastity to him before marriage.
hipponax: Ancient authorities record only the barest details of the life of Hipponax, sometimes contradicting each other. He is dated to 541 or 540 BCE, a date supported by Pliny the Elder, who places the sculptors Bupalus and Athenis, his targets, in his lifetime. The Byzantine encyclopaedia Suda records that he was expelled from Ephesus by the tyrants Athenagoras and Comas and settled in Clazomenae. According to Athenaeus he was small, thin and surprisingly strong, and tradition made him ugly. One scholiast reports that he sought to marry the daughter of Bupalus and was rejected, and that when Bupalus portrayed him as ugly Hipponax retaliated in verse so savage that Bupalus hanged himself. The story resembles that of Archilochus, which invites scepticism.

Hipponax composed within the iambic tradition, which in the work of Archilochus a century earlier seems to have been ritualised abuse tied to the cults of Demeter and Dionysus, and in his day served for entertainment. Unlike Archilochus he often names himself, and his world is sordid and unheroic. He was regarded as the inventor of the scazon, or choliamb, the halting iambic, which replaces the last iambus of the senarius with a spondee or trochee. Ancient scholars credited him with inventing parody. Except in parody he wrote as if Homer had never existed, and his Ionic Greek contains an unusually high proportion of Anatolian, particularly Lydian, loanwords.

Alexandrian scholars collected his poems in two or three books, and they influenced poets such as Callimachus and Herodas. Aristophanes borrowed from him, and in Frogs Dionysus exclaims, Wonderful poet, Hipponax! Few fragments survived the Byzantine period: the Christian fathers disapproved of his abusive verse, and the emperor Julian forbade initiates to read Archilochus or Hipponax. His Ionic dialect and foreign words also made him unsuited to an education built on Attic. The longest surviving run of consecutive verses is only six lines, and a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus published in 1941 has parts of over fifty choliambics.
hiraga-gennai: Born Shiraishi Kunitomo in the village of Shidoura, he was the third son of Shiroishi Mozaemon, a low-ranking samurai of the Takamatsu Domain whose family traced its roots to the Hiraga warlords of Shinano. He began studying as a herbalist in 1741, apprenticed to a physician at the age of 12, and at 18 was given a post in the daimyō's herb garden. After his father's death in 1748 he became head of the family, and in 1752 he was sent to Nagasaki to study Western medicine and other subjects of rangaku, later handing his house to his younger sister's husband.

In Edo from 1757 he studied with Tamura Ransui and grew ginseng, helping Japan move from importing the herb to producing it. He found iron deposits in Izu Province in 1761, helped the Kawagoe Domain open an asbestos mine in 1766, wove asbestos cloth and made a thermometer, and his electrostatic generator, the Elekiteru, is recognised as an IEEE Milestone, dated 1776. Exhibitions of his inventions brought him to the notice of the senior official Tanuma Okitsugu. After finding clay near Nagasaki in 1772 he petitioned to make pottery for export, and the brightly coloured pieces made under him are called Gennai ware. In 1773 Satake Yoshiatsu invited him to Kubota Domain to teach mining.

Under his principal pen name, Fūrai Sanjin, he wrote satirical fiction and essays. On Farting sets him in debate with a Confucian samurai over a performer of flatulence, and Rootless Grass tells of Enma, King of Hell, falling in love with an onnagata actor. He also wrote guidebooks to the male prostitutes of Edo.

His end is uncertain. In the most common account he was arrested late in 1779 for killing two carpenters in a drunken rage after they accused him of stealing plans for a daimyō mansion, and he died of tetanus in prison the following 24 January. The shogunate refused his friend Sugita Genpaku a funeral, which gave rise to stories that he had been spirited away and lived on in obscurity. His grave in Tokyo became a National Historic Site in 1943.
hiraizumi: Hiraizumi lies in Nishiiwai District, Iwate Prefecture, in the Tōhoku region of northern Honshu. It is the smallest municipality in the prefecture by area, about 63 square kilometres, and sits in a basin surrounded by the Kitakami Mountains. Its neighbours are Ichinoseki and Ōshū, and it has a humid climate with mild summers and cold winters. Its population peaked around 1950 and has declined since. The modern village was created on 1 April 1889 and raised to town status on 1 October 1953. The local economy rests on agriculture and tourism.

The area was part of ancient Mutsu Province. It was the home of the Northern Fujiwara clan for about 100 years in the late Heian era and served as the de facto capital of Ōshū, an area covering nearly a third of Japan. At its height Hiraizumi had a population of 50,000 or more than 100,000, rivalling Kyoto in size and splendour. The first structure may have been Hakusan Shrine on Mount Kanzan, which a writer in 1334 recorded as already 700 years old.

About 1100 Fujiwara no Kiyohira moved his home from Fort Toyoda to Mount Kanzan. The site lay at the junction of the Kitakami and Koromo rivers, directly on the Ōshū Kaidō, the main road from Kyoto to the north, and was seen as the exact centre of Ōshū. The Koromo River traditionally marked the boundary between Japan to the south and the Emishi peoples to the north; by building south of it, Kiyohira, himself half Emishi, signalled his intention to rule Ōshū without the court's sanction.

He built the temple complex Chūson-ji, beginning with a large pagoda, and set small reliquaries every hundred metres along the road. The Konjiki-dō was built to represent the Buddhist Pure Land and to be the final resting place of the Fujiwara lords. The golden age lasted nearly a century and ended in 1189, when the town was destroyed. Most of its buildings were lost. In 1689 the poet Matsuo Bashō saw its state and wrote a haiku on the impermanence of glory: 'Ah, summer grasses! All that remains of the warriors' dreams. '

The Historic Monuments and Sites of Hiraizumi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011. Chūson-ji with the Konjikidō Golden Hall, Mōtsū-ji with its Pure Land garden, the ruins of Kanjizaiō-in and Muryōkō-in, the Takkoku-no-Iwaya Bishamon chapel, the Takadachi Gikeidō and the Yanagi-no-Gosho palace site are among its listed sites.
hiralal-shastri: Hiralal Shastri was born on 24 November 1899 into a peasant family at Jobner in Jaipur District, where he received his early education. He passed the degree of Sahitya Shastri in 1920 and in 1921 stood first in the B.A. examination at Maharaja's College, Jaipur. The same year he joined the Jaipur State Service, rising to become Secretary in the Home and Foreign Departments, but he resigned in 1927 to work in the countryside, as he had wished to since childhood.

In 1929 he chose the remote village of Banasthali, 72 km from Jaipur, and founded Jeevan Kutir there, where he trained social workers and pursued a programme of rural reconstruction. These workers later helped spread political awakening in many of the Rajputana States. On 6 October 1935 he and Ratan Shastri, with the help of fellow freedom fighters such as Durgadutt Harit, founded Banasthali Vidyapith in memory of Shantabai, his daughter from his first marriage, who had died very young.

He joined the Jaipur Rajya Praja Mandal in 1937, was twice its general secretary and twice its president, and in 1939 led its satyagraha for civil liberties, for which he was imprisoned for six months. In 1947 he became general secretary of the All India States Peoples Conference and was elected to the Constituent Assembly. When representative government was installed in Jaipur State on 27 March 1948 he became its prime minister, and on the formation of Rajasthan on 30 March 1949 its first chief minister, working to bring the former princely states into a single modern administration.

Shastri resigned as chief minister on 5 January 1951 and later sat in the Second Lok Sabha. He was a member of the Indian National Congress. He died on 28 December 1974, and in November 1976 the Indian Posts and Telegraphs Department issued a commemorative postage stamp in his honour.
hiram-bingham-iii: Hiram Bingham III was born in Honolulu on 19 November 1875, the son of Hiram Bingham II, an early Protestant missionary to the Kingdom of Hawaii, and grandson of the missionary Hiram Bingham I. He attended Oʻahu College, now Punahou School, then Phillips Academy in Andover, and took a B.A. at Yale in 1898, a degree at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1900 and a Ph.D. at Harvard in 1905. He taught at Harvard and Princeton, and in 1907 became a lecturer in South American history at Yale, a pioneer of the subject in the United States.

Bingham was not a trained archaeologist. In 1908, returning from a scientific congress in Santiago, he visited the pre-Columbian city of Choquequirao in Peru. He then organised the 1911 Yale Peruvian Expedition, one aim of which was to find the last capital of the Incas. Guided by locals, he identified Vitcos and Vilcabamba, then called Rosaspata and Espíritu Pampa, but did not recognise Vilcabamba as the last capital. On 24 July 1911 Melchor Arteaga led him to Machu Picchu, which he took for the lost city of the Incas. The site was known to people in the neighbouring valley, and Agustín Lizárraga had left his name on a wall of the Temple of the Three Windows in 1902; Bingham noted this in his journal.

In 1916 he became a captain in the Connecticut National Guard, and in 1917 he became an aviator and organised schools of military aeronautics at eight universities and rose to lieutenant colonel. He was lieutenant governor of Connecticut from 1922 to 1924 and was elected governor in 1924, but on 16 December 1924 was also elected to the United States Senate. He served as governor for one day, 7 to 8 January 1925, before taking his Senate seat. He lost his seat in 1932, and the Senate censured him on 4 November 1929 over a lobbyist's arrangement.

Bingham died at his Washington home on 6 June 1956 and is buried at Arlington National Cemetery. His book Lost City of the Incas became a bestseller in 1948, and a road to the site is named for him. Modern research has found Machu Picchu to be a royal estate, not the religious centre he proposed, and Vilcabamba was later shown to have been the last capital. The roughly 40,000 objects he took to Yale were the subject of an agreement of 2007 for their return to Peru, which began in 2012.
hiram-i: Hiram I was a Phoenician king of Tyre, the son of Abibaal, and was succeeded by his son Baal-Eser I. His regnal years have been calculated by some as 980 to 947 BCE, though the dates are debated. The calculation rests on the Tyrian records and the writings of Menander of Ephesus, preserved in Josephus's Against Apion, which say that Solomon's Temple was begun in the twelfth year of Hiram's reign and that 143 years passed from that start to the founding of Carthage. Josephus adds that Hiram lived 53 years and reigned 34.

During Hiram's reign Tyre grew from a satellite of Sidon into the most important Phoenician city and the centre of a large trading empire. He suppressed the rebellion of Utica, the first Tyrian colony. Josephus says that he extended the harbour, enlarged the city by joining the two islands on which it was built, and constructed a royal palace and a temple for Melqart. The "Tomb of Hiram" near Tyre, a colossal limestone sarcophagus on a pedestal, dates from the Persian period, four to six centuries after the presumed time of Hiram.

The Hebrew Bible says that he allied himself with David, king of Judah, and that his artisans built David's palace in Jerusalem of Lebanon cedar. He kept the alliance with David's son Solomon, addressing him as an equal, "my brother". For the Temple and the royal palace he sent architects, workmen, cedar and cypress wood and gold, and Solomon gave wheat, barley, olive oil and wine in return. The two kings also opened a trade route over the Red Sea from the harbour of Ezion-Geber to a land called Ophir. Beyond the Bible and Josephus the evidence is limited, and the biblical account may be embellished.
hird: Although the word appears often in the Norse sagas and law codes, hird is a medieval term: the sagas were mostly written down in the 12th century, in the language of their own day. It is therefore uncertain what word it replaced in earlier times. Danish sources use hlid or lið for the warrior following of Canute the Great. In Old Norse hirð could also mean herd, and the word has been linked to the idea of a hearthguard, the men of a lord's own home and hearth.

A member of a hird was a hirdman, a word still used in Norwegian and Swedish. The title first described the informal companions or retainers of the powerful, above all their companions in arms in the unruly and often still pagan earlier times, and it appears even in Norse mythology. Later it came to mean something closer to a courtier, a development not unlike that of the thegn or the Roman comes.

In the 13th-century Norwegian court the hird had several grades. The squires were the kertilsveinr, literally candle-men, who were required to hold candles at the hird's ceremonies; the men-at-arms were the hirdmenn; and the knights were the skutilsveinr, literally table-men. In addition there were the gestir, who received only half pay and served as a kind of intelligence service. They were not allowed to sit at the king's table for supper except on Christmas Day and Easter Day.

Once the royal hird had become a formal court, hirdman was the title of the highest of its four ranks: the magnates who were allowed to sit in the royal council, the nearest feudal equivalent of a cabinet, and so had a say in government. Most officials serving away from the court were also enrolled in the hird. During the reign of King Magnus VI the older laws of the hird were brought into the Hirdskraa.
hiri-motu: Hiri Motu is also called Police Motu, Pidgin Motu or simply Hiri. It is a simplified version of Motu, a language of the Austronesian family, and is spoken around Port Moresby, the capital of Papua New Guinea. It is strictly neither a pidgin nor a creole, though it has features of both. Differences in sound and grammar make it not mutually intelligible with Motu, although the two languages are very similar in vocabulary and share a simplified Austronesian structure.

The word hiri names the traditional trade voyages that shaped the way of life of the Motu people, who live along the southern coast of their country. The voyages carried prized goods to the peoples of the Gulf of Papua. The language developed among those taking part in the hiri trade, chiefly in sago and clay pots, between the Motu and their neighbours on the south-east coast of New Guinea, and it is older than European contact.

In early colonial times the use of Hiri Motu spread because the Royal Papuan Constabulary adopted it, which is why it was called Police Motu. By the early 1960s it was the lingua franca of a large part of the country, and it was the first language of many children of policemen and other public servants whose parents came from different language groups.

The name Hiri Motu was proposed in the early 1970s at a conference held by the Department of Information and Extension Services. The committee argued that the New Guinea Police Force had taken up Pidgin when the forces were united in 1946, and that the name should reflect the language's legacy and everyday use rather than the police. Since the early 1970s or earlier its use has declined in favour of English and Tok Pisin. Today its speakers tend to be elderly and concentrated in Central and Gulf provinces, and younger speakers of Motu proper often understand it poorly. It has some statutory recognition.

Hiri Motu has two dialects, called Austronesian (or central) and Papuan (non-central), named for the first languages of the people who used it as a lingua franca. The Papuan dialect was more widely spoken and has been the standard of official publications since about 1964, while the Austronesian dialect, closer to Motu in grammar and sound, was the prestige form. It uses postpositions, such as ai for in, on or at. Sentences end with a verb, and either subject–object–verb or object–subject–verb order is used; a subject marker, ese, is used when meaning would otherwise be unclear. Its pronouns distinguish an inclusive we from an exclusive we.
hirohito: Hirohito was born on 29 April 1901 at Tōgū Palace in Aoyama, Tokyo, the first son of Crown Prince Yoshihito, the future Emperor Taishō, during the reign of his grandfather Emperor Meiji. Ten weeks after his birth he was placed in the care of Count Kawamura Sumiyoshi, and he returned to court at the age of three when Kawamura died. He was proclaimed crown prince on 2 November 1916.

From March to September 1921 he visited the United Kingdom, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Vatican City and Malta, the first European visit by a Japanese crown prince, achieved despite strong opposition in Japan. On his return he became regent on 25 November 1921 in place of his ailing father. He married Princess Nagako Kuni on 26 January 1924.

Hirohito became emperor on 25 December 1926, and the Shōwa era began. The early reign unfolded against financial crisis and growing military power in government. The killing of Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi in 1932 marked the end of civilian control of the military. In 1931 Japan staged the Mukden incident as a pretext to invade Manchuria, and Hirohito did not voice objection. On 27 September 1940 Japan joined Germany and Italy in the Tripartite Pact.

Hirohito formally sanctioned the decision to go to war against the United States and its allies on 1 December 1941. After the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria and Korea, he called on the armed forces to surrender in a radio broadcast on 15 August 1945. Historians agree that he was involved to some extent in strategy and war crimes, but the degree remains disputed.

He was not tried by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East. General Douglas MacArthur believed a cooperative emperor would help a peaceful occupation, and evidence that could have incriminated him was excluded. In 1946 he renounced his divinity, and the constitution of 1947 defined him as the symbol of the State and of the unity of the People.

Hirohito died on 7 January 1989 at the age of 87 and was succeeded by his son Akihito, beginning the Heisei era. His reign of more than sixty years was the longest of any historically attested emperor of Japan.
hiroshima: The site was originally a small fishing village on the shores of Hiroshima Bay, which from the 12th century prospered through its ties to a Zen Buddhist temple, Mitaki-dera, and through growing trade with the rest of Japan under the Taira clan. The warlord Mōri Terumoto founded Hiroshima in 1589 on the delta coast of the Seto Inland Sea, and the name means wide island. His castle was quickly built, and he moved in in 1593. After Terumoto sided with the losers at the Battle of Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu took most of his fiefs, including Hiroshima, and gave Aki Province to the daimyō Masanori Fukushima. From 1619 until 1871 the Asano clan ruled the city.

After the han was abolished in 1871 the city became the capital of Hiroshima Prefecture and, with the building of Ujina Harbor in the 1880s, an important port. The San'yō Railway reached it in 1894. During the First Sino-Japanese War the government moved there temporarily, and Emperor Meiji kept his headquarters at Hiroshima Castle from 15 September 1894 to 27 April 1895. In the Second World War the Second General Army and the Chūgoku Regional Army were headquartered there, and the port was a key centre for shipping and supply depots.

At 8:15 a.m. on Monday, 6 August 1945, the American B-29 Enola Gay, flown by Paul Tibbets, dropped the bomb Little Boy on the city. It directly killed at least 70,000 people, among them thousands of Korean forced labourers, and fewer than 10 per cent of the casualties were military. The population before the bombing was about 345,000. About 70 per cent of the buildings were destroyed and another 7 per cent badly damaged.

Hiroshima is the capital of Hiroshima Prefecture and the largest city of the Chūgoku region of western Honshu. In 1949 the national parliament proclaimed it a City of Peace and passed the Hiroshima Peace Memorial City Construction Law to help rebuild it. The Peace Memorial Park was designed that year, and the Peace Memorial Museum opened in 1955. The Genbaku Dome, formerly the Prefectural Industrial Promotion Hall and the building closest to the explosion that survived, is part of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, a World Heritage Site since 1996. The castle was rebuilt in 1958. The population, which had dropped to 137,197 after the bombing, had returned to its prewar level by 1955.
hiroshima-prefecture: The prefecture covers 8,479 square kilometres and borders Okayama Prefecture to the east, Tottori to the north-east, Shimane to the north and Yamaguchi to the south-west. It also touches Ehime Prefecture for 74 metres on the island of Hyōtanjima. Most of it is mountainous, with the Chūgoku Mountains in the north leading towards Shimane, and rivers have made rich plains near the coast. It faces Shikoku across the Seto Inland Sea, where Hiroshima Bay opens, and it includes many small islands. The sheltered Inland Sea makes the climate very mild.

The area was formerly divided into Bingo Province and Aki Province. It has been a centre of trade and culture since the beginning of Japan's recorded history. Hiroshima is a traditional centre of the Chūgoku region and was the seat of the Mōri clan until the Battle of Sekigahara. The prefecture is known worldwide for the atomic bombing of 1945, after which the city was rebuilt as a major regional centre of industry, education and culture. The Atomic Dome, one of the few remnants of prewar Hiroshima, stands as a reminder of that event.

Hiroshima is the capital and the largest city of the Chūgoku region, and other major cities are Fukuyama, Kure and Higashihiroshima. The population is 2,811,410 in 2019. With Nara and Tokyo it is one of three prefectures with more than one UNESCO World Heritage Site: the Atomic Dome and the Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, famed for appearing to float when the tide fills round it. Mazda has its headquarters in the prefecture, and automobile manufacturing and tourism are among its main industries. Fukuyama and Hiroshima are international container ports, and ferries link Hiroshima Port with Miyajima, Matsuyama and Beppu.
hirsau-abbey: A Christian chapel dedicated to Saint Nazarius stood at Hirsau by the late 8th century. The monastery itself was founded in about 830 by Count Erlafried of Calw at the instigation of his son, Bishop Notting of Vercelli, who gave it the relics of Saint Aurelius, an Armenian bishop who had died about 475. Fifteen monks from Fulda Abbey settled it under Abbot Lutpert, its first church was consecrated in 838 by Archbishop Odgar of Mainz, and it became an important seat of learning.

Towards the end of the 10th century it fell into ruin. A plague in 988 killed sixty monks, among them Abbot Hartfried, and the dozen survivors split between two rival abbots, Conrad and the cellarer Eberhard. The Count of Calw backed Eberhard and in the end brought in armed men: the abbey was pillaged, the monks dispersed and the library destroyed. It stood empty for over sixty years, until in 1049 Pope Leo IX required his nephew, Count Adalbert of Calw, to restore it.

William, a monk of Saint Emmeram's Abbey, arrived in May 1069 and was solemnly inaugurated in 1071. He secured the abbey's independence from the Counts of Calw and built a new complex across the Nagold river, whose abbey church of Sts Peter and Paul, modelled on Cluny II, was consecrated in 1091. Under his Constitutiones Hirsaugienses the community grew to 150 monks, who did manual work and copied manuscripts, and seven new monasteries were founded from Hirsau.

After about the end of the 12th century Hirsau never again rose to importance. Abbot Wolfram (1428–1460) introduced the Melk Reform, and the abbey joined the Bursfelde Congregation. Through Duke Ulrich of Württemberg it passed into Lutheran hands and was secularised in 1558; Duke Christoph of Württemberg set up a Protestant boarding school there. It was Catholic again briefly from 1630, but after the Peace of Westphalia returned to the Dukes of Württemberg.

French troops under General Lieutenant Mélac destroyed the abbey in 1692 during the Nine Years' War, and it was not rebuilt; for a time the ruins served as a quarry. The Church of St. Aurelius was renovated in 1954, when the saint's relics were brought back from Zwiefalten, and it is again a place of worship. In 1991 the city of Calw and the Badisches Landesmuseum founded the Monastery Museum Hirsau in a former monastery building.
hisham-i-of-cordoba: Hisham was born in Córdoba on 26 April 757, the son of Abd al-Rahman I and his wife Halul and the younger half-brother of Suleiman. By reputation he was pious, sober and capable, and Abd al-Rahman favoured him. He came to the throne in 788 with considerable experience and the support of the religious elite.

He was at once opposed by his elder brother Sulayman, who ruled in Toledo, was a seasoned fighter and enjoyed the loyalty of the Syrian troops. Sulayman recruited another brother, Abd Allah. After losing Toledo to Hisham and failing to regain the initiative, the two agreed to accept permanent exile in the Maghrib together with a large cash settlement.

His reign was comparatively stable. At home Hisham continued his father's work, completing the mosque of Córdoba and improving the city, including repairs to the great Roman bridge. He relied heavily on Umayyad family clients and entrenched the emerging Maliki school of scholars in the emirate's power structure; Malik ibn Anas himself was said to have praised him as an example of piety and justice.

In 793, facing Carolingian pressure across the Pyrenees, he called a jihad against the Franks and sent troops to Girona and Narbonne, which held out. His general Abd al-Malik ibn Abd al-Wahid ibn Mughith was more fortunate near Carcassonne, where he defeated William of Orange. The expedition brought loot and many slaves, which paid for the expansion of the Great Mosque of Córdoba and for new mosques.

From 794 Abd al-Malik and his brother Abd al-Karim campaigned each year against Álava, Old Castile and Asturias, and in 794 sacked Oviedo. Alfonso II of Asturias fled and opened contact with Charlemagne. These raids seem to have aimed at loot and at reasserting Córdoba's military superiority over restive garrisons, lords and the Basques, not at destroying the northern principalities.

Hisham died in 796 after a reign of eight years. He is described as living simply and avoiding ostentation, and was known for impartial justice and sound administration, earning the name the just. According to one account, he believed from his horoscope that he had only eight years to live and gave much of his wealth to charity. After his death Abd Allah returned from exile and claimed Valencia, and Suleiman claimed Tangiers, against Hisham's son al-Hakam I.
hisham-ii: Hisham II was the son of al-Hakam II and Subh of Córdoba. He succeeded at ten and was too young to rule. His mother Subh acted as regent with the first minister Jafar al-Mushafi, with Abu Amir Muhammad, known as Almanzor, as her steward. In 978 Almanzor became royal chamberlain, and he and General Ghalib al-Siklabi sabotaged the brother of al-Hakam II, who had been set to succeed. In 981 Hisham handed the reins of power to Almanzor, who led the caliphate until his death in 1002.

Almanzor kept Hisham a prisoner for most of his reign, while his campaigns against the Christian powers of the north, among them Barcelona in 985, León in 988 and Santiago de Compostela in 998, brought the caliphate to its height. His son Abd al-Malik succeeded him, and after Abd al-Malik died in October 1008, possibly poisoned by his brother Abd al-Rahman Sanchuelo, a member of another Umayyad branch, Muhammad II al-Mahdi, took the throne in February 1009 and held Hisham hostage in Córdoba.

On 9 November 1009 a Berber and Castilian army led by Sulayman ibn al-Hakam entered Córdoba and Muhammad II fled to Toledo. Sulayman freed Hisham and reinstated him, but after a few days deposed him and was elected caliph by his Berber troops, taking the title al-Musta'in bi-llah. Hisham was kept under close guard and removed from government. In May 1010 Muhammad II defeated Sulayman's army at the Battle of Aqbat al-Bakr and returned to Córdoba, but did not restore Hisham, who remained a pawn in the civil war.

About a month later Muhammad II was removed by his chamberlain Wadih al-Siqlabi, arrested, tried and executed on 23 June 1010. Hisham was restored and appointed Wadih chamberlain, though real power again lay with others. In November 1010 Sulayman and the Berbers began a siege of Córdoba that lasted two and a half years, during which Hisham took a more active part, encouraging the people to defend themselves. In May 1013 the Berbers accepted the surrender of the city, Wadih having been executed for treason, and Sulayman was appointed caliph again.

Hisham's fate is unclear: some historians believe the Berbers killed him, others that he escaped into exile. Because he vanished, the taifa kings revived him as a symbol of legitimacy. In 1035 Abu al-Qasim Muhammad ibn Abbad, ruler of the Taifa of Seville, announced that Hisham had reappeared and declared his allegiance to him, and other taifas under Seville's sway followed. Only in 1060 did Abbad II al-Mu'tadid acknowledge that this supposed Hisham had died in 1044 without a successor. The fiction of his survival lasted until at least 1082–83, when his name still appears on the coins of the Taifa of Zaragoza.
hisham-iii-of-cordoba: Hisham was a brother of the earlier caliph Abd ar-Rahman IV. In 1025 Yahya ibn Ali of the Hammudid family marched on Córdoba, and Caliph Muhammad III fled. The city's aristocracy set up a council to govern in his absence and after about six months invited Yahya to take the title of caliph; he arrived on 9 November 1025, but the treasury was empty and there was no functioning government, army or police. Yahya left the city to his vizier Abu Ja`far Ahmad ben Musa and returned to his stronghold of Málaga.

Regional Slavic rulers, unhappy that the Hammudids ruled again, assembled a small army and drove Yahya's vizier and forces out, but left no leadership of their own. The aristocracy took control again, and after long negotiations between the governors of the border regions and the people of Córdoba, Hisham was chosen as caliph.

Hisham stayed at his home in Alpuente until December 1029, because the Berber armies of the Hammudids still occupied the capital. Once there he tried to consolidate the caliphate but proved a poor administrator. His chief minister, Hakam ibn Sa'id, spent much of his time indulging the caliph's excesses, and measures such as higher taxes, even when partly meant for mosques, met heavy opposition from the Muslim clerics.

In 1031 a rival Umayyad, Umayya ibn Abd al-Rahman, promised to dethrone Hisham and drew discontented militiamen to his side; they ambushed and killed Hakam ibn Sa'id on 30 November 1031. The murder set off an uprising against the caliph, who was imprisoned until the riot was quelled, after which the aristocracy decided that he should leave the city. With his fall the caliphate's lands, already much reduced from their height a century before, broke up into militarily weak but culturally advanced taifas.
hispania: The origin of the word Hispania is unknown. The Phoenicians called the region i-shphan-im, perhaps meaning land of rabbits or hyraxes, and Strabo called it the land of the rabbits. Under the Republic it was divided into Hispania Citerior, the nearer province, and Hispania Ulterior, the farther one. In 27 BCE Augustus made three provinces: Baetica, with its capital at Corduba; Lusitania, with its capital at Emerita Augusta; and Hispania Citerior, also called Tarraconensis, with its capital at Tarraco. After Diocletian's reforms of 293 CE the peninsula formed a diocese governed by a vicarius, with its capital at Emerita Augusta, and Gallaecia and Carthaginiensis were created from Tarraconensis.

Roman armies landed in the peninsula in 218 BCE and used it as a training ground against the Carthaginians, Iberians, Lusitanians, Gallaecians and other Celts. The long wars of conquest lasted two centuries, and Augustus completed the conquest in 19 BCE in the Cantabrian Wars.

Romanisation proceeded quickly in some regions and slowly in others. Rome improved cities such as Lisbon and Tarragona and founded Zaragoza, Mérida and Valencia. Hispania served as a granary and a major source of metals, exporting gold, tin, silver, lead, wool, wheat, olive oil, wine, fish and garum, and the Romans built irrigation works, some still in use. Iberian-born populations had full Roman citizenship by the end of the first century. Trajan, Hadrian and Theodosius were born there. Christianity reached the peninsula in the first century and spread in the cities in the second.

In September or October 409 the Suevi, Vandals and Alans crossed into Iberia and set up kingdoms in the north-west and in Lusitania. The Visigoths destroyed much of the Alans and Silingi Vandals on Rome's behalf, and the Vandals and Alans crossed to North Africa in 429.

After the death of the emperor Majorian in 461 Roman authority collapsed except in Tarraconensis, which the Visigoths took by occupying Tarragona in 472. They made Toledo their capital in 484 and conquered the Suebic Kingdom of Galicia in 585. In 589 the Visigothic ruler Recared renounced Arianism before the Council of Bishops at Toledo and accepted Catholic Christianity, ensuring an alliance with the native Hispano-Romans. The name Hispania continued to be used under the Visigoths, and the modern names Spain and Hispaniola derive from it.
hispania-ulterior: Carthage expanded into the south of the Iberian Peninsula after losing Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica in the First Punic War. Much of the Second Punic War between Carthage and Rome was fought in Hispania, until Scipio Africanus took control from Hannibal and the Carthaginians at the Battle of Ilipa in 206 BCE. Carthage ceded the region to Rome after its defeat in 201 BCE. In 197 BCE the peninsula was divided into Hispania Citerior, Nearer Hispania, and Hispania Ulterior, Further Hispania, because two Roman military forces were present during the conquest. The boundary ran roughly from Carthago Nova to the Cantabrian Sea.

Peace lasted until 155 BCE, when the Lusitanians attacked, twice defeating Roman praetors and encouraging other rebellions. The peninsula became a centre of military activity and a chance for advancement, as the historian Appian noted of consuls who sought glory, gain or a triumph. The consul Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus largely conquered the area in 138 BCE, but fighting went on until 19 BCE, when Agrippa defeated the Cantabrians. Gaius Julius Caesar governed Hispania Ulterior in 61 and 60 BCE. In 19 BCE Augustus reorganised the provinces, dividing Hispania Ulterior into Baetica and Lusitania, while Hispania Citerior was renamed Hispania Tarraconensis.

Each province was ruled by a praetor. According to the historian Cassius Dio, the peoples of the region came from many tribes and shared neither a language nor a government. Members of the tribal elites were brought into the Roman aristocracy and allowed to take part in their own governance, and Roman latifundia were granted to aristocrats. The emperors Trajan, Hadrian and Theodosius I were all born in Hispania. The economy thrived as a granary and through exports of gold, olive oil, wool and wine.

The name Hispania is attested from at least 200 BCE, when the poet Quintus Ennius used it, and may derive from a Punic phrase meaning coast of hyraxes, a Phoenician misidentification of the peninsula's many rabbits. Ulterior is the comparative of a Latin word meaning beyond. In the early fifth century CE the Vandals invaded and took the south of Hispania. The emperor Honorius commissioned the Visigoth king Athaulf to defeat them, and the Visigoths took control and made Toledo their capital.
hispaniola: Hispaniola lies in the Greater Antilles between Cuba and Puerto Rico, about 80 kilometres east of Cuba across the Windward Passage and 130 kilometres west of Puerto Rico across the Mona Passage. It covers 76,192 square kilometres, of which 27,750 belong to Haiti and the rest to the Dominican Republic. The northeast trade winds drop their rain on the northern slopes and leave a dry southern coast. The Hispaniolan hutia and the Hispaniolan solenodon are its two endemic land mammals.

People of the Archaic Age reached the island from Central or South America about 6,000 years ago. The Taíno, descended from Arawakan speakers who migrated into the Caribbean in the 1st millennium BCE, were the dominant group at European contact. Each society was a small kingdom under a cacique, and in 1492 five kingdoms ruled the island. Early chroniclers recorded its native names as Bohío, Haiti and Quisqueya, though doubts have been raised about Quisqueya.

Christopher Columbus landed in December 1492 and named it Española, or little Spain. His flagship Santa Maria ran aground on 24 December, and he left 21 men in the fort of La Navidad. Hispaniola became the site of the first European fort, the first settlement, La Isabela, and the first permanent settlement, Santo Domingo, founded in 1498. Gold mining with forced Indigenous labour began early. In 1606 Philip III ordered the island's inhabitants to move close to Santo Domingo to fight piracy, but French, English and Dutch pirates then set up bases on the north and west coasts.

The French occupied the west and built a plantation colony on the enslavement of Africans that became the most prosperous of the French empire in the Americas. A slave revolt broke out in Saint-Domingue in 1791, and by the Treaty of Basel in 1795 Spain ceded the eastern two thirds to France. After the Haitian Revolution, Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the Empire of Haiti, and in 1809 Spain regained the east. The United States occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934 and the Dominican Republic from 1916 to 1924.

The island is divided between the Spanish-speaking Dominican Republic in the east, with Santo Domingo as its capital, and Haiti in the west, where Haitian Creole is spoken by nearly the whole population. The name Hispaniola became widely used after 1918, when American leaders recommended it to the National Geographic Society.
hispano-moroccan-war-1859-1860: Throughout the 19th century Morocco suffered military defeats at the hands of European powers, notably in the Franco-Moroccan War of 1844. Since 1840 the Spanish cities of Ceuta and Melilla had often been attacked by Riffian tribesmen. Negotiations with Sultan Abd al-Rahman over reparations were fruitless, and he died in the midst of them and was replaced by his son Muhammad IV. Pressure from Queen Isabella on the Congress to attack added to the attacks as a cause, and a declaration of war promoted by Leopoldo O'Donnell was passed unanimously by the Congress of Deputies on 22 October 1859.

The expeditionary army that left Algeciras numbered about 45,000 men with 3,000 mules and horses and 78 pieces of artillery, supported by a naval squadron. Its objectives were the taking of Tetouan and the occupation of the port of Tangier. Hostilities began on 17 December, when Zabala's column occupied the Sierra de Bullones. Echagüe took the Serrallo Palace, and O'Donnell landed at Ceuta on 21 December. On 1 January 1860 General Prim stormed to the mouth of the Uad el-Jelú with support from Zabala and the fleet.

Skirmishing continued until 31 January, when a Moroccan offensive was contained and O'Donnell began the march towards Tetouan, with the support of Catalan volunteers and with Ros de Olano and Prim on the flanks. Spanish artillery destroyed the Moroccan ranks, the remains of the army took refuge in Tetouan, and the city fell on 6 February 1860. Riffian tribesmen poured into it and pillaged it, mainly the Jewish quarters. The Moroccan historian Ahmad ibn Khalid al-Nasiri described how the mob broke down the doors of houses and shops and kept at it the whole night.

After an armistice of 32 days the Treaty of Wad-Ras, or Peace of Tétouan, was signed on 26 April 1860. Its terms were harsh for Morocco. They provided for the Spanish presence in Ceuta and Melilla in perpetuity, an end to tribal raids on them, Moroccan recognition of Spanish sovereignty over the Chafarinas Islands, and the return to Spain of Santa Cruz de la Mar Pequeña, a territory of uncertain location, ultimately Ifni, for a fishing post. Missionaries were allowed to set up a Christian church in Tétouan, and Spain was to administer the city until reparations of 20,000,000 duros were paid. Once Morocco paid the compensation, partly with money lent by the British, O'Donnell withdrew his troops from Tétouan.
histadrut: The Histadrut was founded in December 1920 in Haifa to look after the interests of Jewish workers. Until then the parties Ahdut HaAvoda and Hapoel Hatzair had been unable to set up a single workers' organisation. Membership grew from 4,400 in 1920 to 8,394 in 1922. By 1927 it had around 22,000 members, 68% of the Jewish workforce, and by 1939 about 100,000, some 75%.

In its first year it lacked central leadership and many initiatives were local. David Ben-Gurion was elected Secretary at the end of 1921. He set up a defined hierarchy, reduced the powers of the local workers' councils and centralised the collection of dues, and he wanted to turn the federation into a national instrument for realising Zionism. Its aims covered settlement, defence, trade unions, education, housing, health, banking, cooperative ventures, welfare and culture.

Absorbing immigrants was seen as a central task, sometimes ranked above financial soundness. The Histadrut's Office for Public Works went bankrupt in 1924 and its successor Solel Boneh in 1927, and the Zionist Executive bailed out both, entering the deficits as expenses for immigration absorption. By 1930 the Histadrut was the central organisation of the Yishuv. According to Tzahor it had become the executive arm of the Zionist movement, but an arm acting on its own, a state in the making. Ze'ev Sternhell argues instead that its leaders had already abandoned socialist principles by 1920 and used them only as mobilising myths.

Through its economic arm, Hevrat HaOvdim, it owned the country's largest industrial conglomerates, its largest bank, Bank Hapoalim, and its largest shipping company, ZIM. It also owned Clalit Health Services, which accepted members only if they belonged to the union, and in the mid-1980s an estimated 70% of Israelis were insured by Clalit.

From the 1980s liberalisation of the economy reduced the Histadrut's role. Hyperinflation left its business empire with large debts, and it lost control of Bank Hapoalim after the 1983 bank stock crisis, when the government nationalised the major banks. In 1994 the Labor Party lost its leadership of the Histadrut, and a new party, RAM, took charge and began to sell off its assets that were not tied to the union.

The National Health Insurance Law, in effect from 1995, severed Clalit's tie to the Histadrut. Membership fell from about 1.8 million, almost 80% of the workforce, to about 200,000. The Histadrut sold real estate to survive, then recovered gradually, and in 2005 it had about 650,000 members.
histiaeus: Histiaeus, the son of Lysagoras, was a Greek ruler of Miletus in the late 6th century BCE. He was tyrant of the city under Darius I, king of Persia, who had subjugated Miletus and the other Ionian states in Asia Minor and generally appointed Greeks as tyrants to rule the Greek cities of Ionia.

According to Herodotus, Histiaeus took part in the expedition of Darius against the Scythians, around 513 BCE, and was put in charge of defending the bridge over the Danube. The Scythians urged the tyrants to abandon it, and a faction led by Miltiades of Athens, then tyrant of the Chersonese, wished to follow their advice. Histiaeus argued that they owed their positions to Darius and would be overthrown if he were killed. He suggested that they pretend to accept the plan, and went as an ambassador to the Scythians to say so, while the others acted as if they were demolishing the bridge. When the Scythians went off to look for the Persians, Histiaeus organised the ships that ferried the Persians across.

During the campaign his troops had begun to build a settlement at Myrcinus on the Strymon River, and Darius granted it to him as a reward. The Persian commander Megabazus suspected him of an interest in a place that controlled roads into Europe and held silver and timber, but Darius thought him loyal and took him to Susa as a friend and adviser. His nephew and son-in-law Aristagoras was left in control of Miletus.

Herodotus writes that Histiaeus, unhappy at Susa, planned to return by instigating a revolt in Ionia. In 499 BCE he shaved the head of his most trusted slave, tattooed a message on it, and sent the slave to Aristagoras once his hair had grown back, telling him to revolt. Aristagoras, disliked at home after a failed expedition to Naxos, obeyed and, with Athenian and Eretrian help, attacked and burned Sardis. Darius let Histiaeus go to put the revolt down, but the satrap Artaphernes suspected him and he fled to Chios. When he returned to Miletus to become tyrant again, its people, who did not want tyranny back, exiled him to Lesbos, and he turned to piracy from Byzantium.

The Persians defeated the leaders of the revolt at the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE. Histiaeus then attacked Chios and blockaded Thasos, and after joining a Greek force in battle against the Persians he was captured by the Persian general Harpagus in 493 BCE. Artaphernes, fearing that Darius would pardon him, executed him by impaling and sent his head to Darius, who, according to Herodotus, did not believe that Histiaeus had been a traitor and gave the head an honourable burial.
historia-brittonum: The Historia Brittonum is dated to about 829. It was written no earlier than the fourth year of the reign of King Mermenus, identified as Merfyn Frych ap Gwriad of Gwynedd, which fits a statement in chapter 4 that 796 years had passed since the Passion of Christ. It survives in numerous recensions from after the 11th century, in at least five manuscripts, of which the Harleian is the most complete.

Some recensions carry a preface in the name of Nennius, to whom the work is commonly attributed. David Dumville called the preface a late forgery and held that the work underwent several anonymous revisions, a view largely accepted by current scholarship, although Peter Field has defended the preface. The compiler says he heaped together all he could find, from written works and from ancient traditions.

Theodor Mommsen divided the work into seven parts, among them the six ages of the world, a history of the Britons, a life of Patrick, genealogies, a list of cities and the wonders of Britain. It describes Britain as settled by Trojan settlers and named for Brutus, a descendant of Aeneas. It tells how Vortigern let the Saxons settle in return for the hand of Hengist's daughter, and how the boy Ambrosius revealed two buried dragons that kept undoing Vortigern's fortress at Dinas Emrys.

It is the first source to portray Arthur, as a dux bellorum, a war leader, not a king. Chapter 56 names twelve battles he won, the last at Mount Badon, where 960 men fell in a single charge by Arthur. At Guinnion he carried an image of the Virgin Mary on his shoulders, perhaps from a confusion of the Welsh words for shield and shoulders. Many sites cannot be identified, and the work gives no dates for them. Its wonders include a dog's footprint in a stone said to be Arthur's dog Cabal's, and the grave of Arthur's son Amr, which changes length.

Modern scholars treat its methods as unreliable, since it blends legend with fact and links separate traditions artificially. Some scholars believe the Arthurian list came from a lost Welsh poem; Caitlin Green argues that the only battles explicitly tied to Arthur in Old Welsh sources are mythological. The work was the main source for Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae, and through it the Trojan origin of Britain entered later chronicles such as the Middle English Brut of England.
history-of-the-haudenosaunee: Knowledge of Haudenosaunee history rests on their own oral tradition, on archaeology, on the accounts of Jesuit missionaries and on later European historians. French Jesuits portrayed the Haudenosaunee as savages without government, law, letters or religion, yet studied their languages and cultures closely, and some came to respect them. Writers from a patriarchal society were often confused by the matrilineal kinship system and the power it gave women. Historian Scott Stevens argues that the European preference for written over oral sources fed a prejudiced view of the Haudenosaunee through the 19th century.
Some scholars argue for an earlier founding of the League than the usual date; one theory ties it to a solar eclipse of 31 August 1142, thought to be recalled in the oral tradition of its origins.

The Beaver Wars were long explained as a struggle to control the fur trade and the European goods bought with it; more recent scholarship sees them as an escalation of the mourning wars, fought to avenge and replace the many dead of battle and smallpox. In 1677 the League adopted most of the Iroquoian-speaking Susquehannock. After the peace with the French in 1701 the Six Nations stayed mostly neutral, playing the French and British against each other; English gifts rose from goods worth £100 in 1689 to £800 in 1701.

After the American Revolution the League's central fire was rekindled at Buffalo Creek. Under pressure from the governor of New York, George Clinton, and from land companies, and with alcoholism spreading, much more land was sold. The Oneida and Cayuga sold almost all of theirs and left their homelands.

Mohawk from Kahnawake worked as voyageurs for the North West Company as far west as the Rocky Mountains, and communities in Alberta and British Columbia claim descent from them. In 1884 about 100 Canadian Haudenosaunee served as river pilots on the Nile for the expedition to relieve General Charles Gordon at Khartoum. From 1886, when Kahnawake men helped build a bridge over the St. Lawrence, Haudenosaunee steelworkers built bridges and skyscrapers across Canada and the United States.

About half of the 4,000 or so First Nations men in the Canadian Expeditionary Force of the First World War were Haudenosaunee. In 1990 a dispute over land at Oka, Quebec, led to the Oka Crisis, a stand-off between Mohawk warriors, the Sûreté du Québec and the Canadian Army that lasted from 11 July to 26 September.
history-of-the-patriarchs-of-alexandria: The History of the Patriarchs is the only continuous narrative of the non-Chalcedonian patriarchate of Alexandria. Its earliest parts derive mainly from Eusebius and Coptic tradition, but from the 6th century onwards the biographies grow longer and often seem to rest on documents written by eyewitnesses. The account of the 6th-century patriarchs, the Muslim conquest of Egypt and the lives of Pope Benjamin I of Alexandria and his four successors down to Pope Simeon I of Alexandria was recorded by George the Archdeacon in the early 8th century. The work also preserves a vivid eyewitness account of the overthrow of Marwan II, the last Umayyad caliph.

Tradition holds that Severus Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, Coptic bishop of Hermopolis, began compiling the book in Arabic, and that it told the miracle of the moving of the Mokattam Mountain under the Fatimid caliph al-Muizz around 975. Others continued it, among them Michael, bishop of Tinnis, who covered the years 880 to 1046, Mawhub ibn Mansur ibn Mufarrig, deacon of Alexandria, and Pope Mark III of Alexandria, for 1131 to 1167. Modern scholarship instead credits the composition to Mawhib ibn Mufarrij of Alexandria (c. 1025–1100). Appendices and continuations carry the text to 1894, and one unpublished manuscript continues it to 1923.

Eusèbe Renaudot published a Latin version, Historia patriarcharum alexandrinorum jacobitarum, in 1713. Christian Friedrich Seybold began a scholarly Arabic edition in 1904. Basil Thomas Alfred Evetts edited and translated the first half of the Arabic text into English as the History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria, in the Patrologia Orientalis series, stopping with the 52nd patriarch, Joseph, who died in 849. Later parts were published and translated by scholars in Cairo led by O. H. E. Burmester.
hitler-youth: In 1922 the Munich-based Nazi Party established its official youth wing, the Jugendbund der NSDAP, announced on 8 March and holding its inaugural meeting on 13 May. After the failed Beer Hall Putsch of November 1923 the party's youth wings were ostensibly disbanded, though many continued underground. In April 1924 the Jugendbund was renamed the Grossdeutsche Jugendbewegung. After a short power struggle with a rival organisation, Gerhard Roßbach's Schilljugend, Kurt Gruber prevailed, and in July 1926 the movement was renamed Hitler-Jugend, Bund deutscher Arbeiterjugend. By 1930 it had enlisted over 25,000 boys aged 14 and upward, with a junior branch, the Deutsches Jungvolk, for boys aged 10 to 14, and a parallel League of German Girls.

Membership rose from about 1,200 in 1923 to 107,956 by the end of 1932. Chancellor Heinrich Brüning banned the movement in April 1932, and his successor Franz von Papen lifted the ban in June. After the Nazis came to power in 1933, with Baldur von Schirach as Reichsjugendführer, membership reached 2,300,000 by the end of that year, partly through the forcible takeover of other youth organisations. A law of December 1936 declared it the only legally permitted youth organisation in Germany. In March 1939 the Youth Service Duty conscripted all German youths into it, even over their parents' objections, and by 1940 it had eight million members. Non-members could be refused a diploma.

Its activities included camping, hiking and sport, but over time many resembled military training, and its members were indoctrinated with Nazi racism. In the war, under Artur Axmann, who succeeded Schirach in August 1940, it became an auxiliary force. In 1944 the 12th SS-Panzer-Division Hitlerjugend fought in the Battle of Normandy. By 1945 boys as young as twelve were being drafted into the Volkssturm, and in the Battle of Berlin Hitler Youth formations were part of the last line of defence.

The Hitler Youth was outlawed by the Allied Control Council on 10 October 1945. Schirach was sentenced to 20 years in prison, for crimes against humanity as Gauleiter of Vienna rather than for his youth leadership. Axmann received a 39-month sentence in May 1949. Because membership had been compulsory, many senior leaders of both West and East Germany had belonged to it. In the Federal Republic of Germany, its symbols may not be used publicly except for educational or research purposes.
hittite-laws: The laws date from about 1650 to 1500 BCE and survive on a number of tablets found at Hattusa, catalogued as CTH 291–292. Copies exist in Old Hittite as well as in Middle and Late Hittite, which shows that they remained valid throughout the life of the Hittite Empire, about 1650 to 1100 BCE. Who drew them up is not known; some historians think their source was a person of high standing in Hittite society, perhaps a king.

The penalties were changed at least twice: first in the kara – kinuna changes, which generally reduced the penalties of an earlier edition that has not survived, and again in the Late Period. Otherwise the laws, in use for some 500 years, were copied slavishly. Apart from changes in grammar the scribes kept the original order, leaving even obvious afterthoughts where they had first been written.

The laws are case laws: a condition is followed by a ruling, as in "If anyone tears off the ear of a male or female slave, he shall pay 3 shekels of silver". They fill two tablets of about 200 clauses each, the first called of a man and the second of a vine; a third set may have existed. Following Dewhirst, the clauses are grouped into eight sets: aggression and assault, marriage, obligations and service, offences against property and theft, contracts and prices, sacred matters, contracts and tariffs, and sexual relations.

The code shows an aversion to the death penalty; for serious offences the usual penalty was enslavement to forced labour, though death was a common punishment among the sexual crimes. Slaves, although counted lesser than free men, could choose whom to marry, buy property, open businesses and purchase their freedom. Clauses 190 and 191 rule that where a man and a woman came together willingly there was no punishment, among the oldest examples of sexual consent in law.

Compared with the Code of Hammurabi and the Middle Assyrian Laws, the Hittite laws set less severe punishments. Like Hammurabi's code they resemble many laws of the Hebrew Bible: Scholz in 2021 found the Hittite rape law, clause 197, reminiscent of Deuteronomy 22:29. The standard edition is Harry Angier Hoffner Jr.'s The Laws of the Hittites: a Critical Edition, published in 1997.
hiv-aids: HIV is a retrovirus of the genus Lentivirus, in the family Retroviridae. It infects components of the human immune system, chiefly CD4+ T cells, macrophages and dendritic cells, and destroys CD4+ T cells directly and indirectly. Infection passes through three main stages: an acute stage, often an influenza-like illness two to four weeks after exposure; a long period of clinical latency; and AIDS, when the risk of tuberculosis, other opportunistic infections and rare tumours rises. Without treatment, average survival after infection is estimated at nine to eleven years.

The virus is spread by sexual contact, by significant exposure to infected body fluids or tissues, such as contaminated needles or blood transfusions, and from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding. Saliva, sweat, tears and urine carry no risk unless they are contaminated with blood. Most infected people develop antibodies within three to twelve weeks of infection.

HIV made the jump from other primates to humans in west-central Africa in the early to mid-20th century. The first news story on the disease appeared on 18 May 1981 in the gay newspaper New York Native, and on 5 June 1981 AIDS was first clinically reported, with five cases in the United States. The patients were injecting drug users and gay men who showed symptoms of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, a rare infection of people with badly impaired immunity. Many cases of the skin cancer Kaposi's sarcoma followed, and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention formed a task force to monitor the outbreak. The cause, HIV infection, was identified in the early part of the decade.
