The disease had a large impact on society, both as an illness and as a source of discrimination. Stigma took the forms of ostracism, rejection, compulsory testing without consent, violence and quarantine, and the fear of it kept many people from seeking testing or treatment. The disease was also drawn into controversies involving religion, among them the Catholic Church's position not to support condom use as prevention.

Antiretroviral therapy changed the prognosis. It reduces the death rate by 80% and raises the life expectancy of a newly diagnosed young adult to between 20 and 50 years. A person with an undetectable viral load as a result of long-term treatment has effectively no risk of transmitting HIV sexually, a finding publicised in the Swiss Statement of 2008 and since accepted as medically sound. Annual deaths from the disease peaked at 2 million in 2005.
hizen-province: Hizen lay in the Saikaidō, the western circuit of the old provinces, and bordered the provinces of Chikuzen and Chikugo. Together with Higo Province it was sometimes called Hishū. It did not include the islands of Tsushima and Iki, which were provinces of their own, although both now belong to Nagasaki Prefecture. The province was divided into districts such as Saga, Ogi, Kanzaki, Kishima, Fujitsu, Sonogi, Takaki and Matsuura.

The name Hizen dates from the Ritsuryō reforms of the Nara period, when the province was separated from Higo Province, and it appears in the early chronicle Shoku Nihongi in an entry for 696. The ancient provincial capital stood near Yamato City.

In the late Muromachi period Hizen was a main point of early contact between Japan and Portuguese and Spanish merchants and missionaries. Hirado and later Nagasaki became major centres of foreign trade, and a large part of the population converted to Roman Catholicism. Toyotomi Hideyoshi directed his invasion of Korea from Nagoya in Hizen, and after foreign contacts were restricted and the Kirishitan religion was banned, the Shimabara Rebellion broke out in the province.

During the Edo period the province was shared among several daimyō but dominated by the Nabeshima clan from their castle town of Saga. Nagasaki itself stayed a tenryō, land held directly by the Tokugawa government and run by the Nagasaki bugyō, and it held the Dutch East India Company's trading post on Dejima.

After the Meiji Restoration of 1868 the han were abolished in 1871 and their lands turned into prefectures. Former Hizen became Saga Prefecture and part of Nagasaki Prefecture; the districts of Higashimatsuura and Nishimatsuura moved from Nagasaki to Saga in 1883, and Kii, Mine and Yabu were merged into Miyaki District on 26 March 1896. The old name stayed in use for some purposes and appears in treaties of 1894 between Japan and the United States and between Japan and the United Kingdom.
hjalmar-schacht: Schacht was born in Tingleff, in Schleswig-Holstein, now in Denmark. His parents had spent years in the United States and first meant to name him Horace Greeley Schacht after the American journalist, but his grandmother insisted on a Danish given name. He took a doctorate at Kiel in 1899 with a thesis on mercantilism, joined the Dresdner Bank in 1903 and became its deputy director in 1908. During the First World War he was dismissed from the staff of the banking commissioner for occupied Belgium after he used the Dresdner Bank to channel remittances of Belgian bonds.

After the revolution of 1918 Schacht helped found the German Democratic Party and supported the Weimar Republic out of reason rather than conviction. On 12 November 1923 he became currency commissioner and took part in introducing the Rentenmark, a currency backed by a mortgage on all German property. He became president of the Reichsbank on 22 December 1923 and resigned on 7 March 1930 after the Young Plan on reparations, which he had helped draw up, was modified.

He moved closer to the Nazis between 1930 and 1932, though he never joined the party. With Wilhelm Keppler he organised a petition of industrial and financial leaders asking President Paul von Hindenburg to appoint Hitler chancellor. Reappointed to the Reichsbank on 17 March 1933, he took over the economics ministry in August 1934 and met the government's deficit with Mefo bills. In 1935 he denounced Julius Streicher's writing against Jews. Göring's appointment as plenipotentiary for the Four Year Plan in October 1936 conflicted with Schacht's authority, and Schacht objected that high military spending would cause inflation. He resigned from the ministry on 26 November 1937, was dismissed from the Reichsbank on 20 January 1939 and from his last post in January 1943.

Schacht was in contact with resisters, among them Carl Friedrich Goerdeler and Hans Gisevius, and took part in plans for a coup if Hitler went to war over Czechoslovakia in 1938. After the attempt on Hitler's life on 20 July 1944 he was arrested and held at Ravensbrück, Flossenbürg and Dachau, and he was freed in South Tyrol in 1945. At Nuremberg he was tried for conspiracy and crimes against peace; the British judges favoured acquittal, the Soviet judges conviction, and he was acquitted on 1 October 1946. A German denazification court sentenced him to eight years of hard labour, but he was freed on appeal in 1948. He led his own bank from 1953 to 1963 and died in Munich on 3 June 1970.
hluboka-nad-vltavou: Hluboká nad Vltavou lies about 7 kilometres north of České Budějovice, on both banks of the Vltava, and has about 5,700 inhabitants. Many fishponds lie within the municipal territory, and the town itself stands on the shore of the largest, Munický rybník, which covers 108 hectares. The territory lies mostly in the Tábor Uplands, with the southern part in the České Budějovice Basin and the eastern part reaching into the Třeboň Basin; forests cover the north, and the highest point is the hill Velký Kameník at 575 metres. The Czech name Hluboká means deep and comes from the castle's position above a deep valley, while the German Frauenberg derives from Old German vrôburg.

The town's history is bound up with its castle, which King Ottokar II founded together with the city of České Budějovice on a rocky promontory above the Vltava. A settlement below it was named Podhrad, literally below-castle. The castle later passed to the Vítkovci dynasty, and under Vilém II of Pernštejn, who held it from 1490, castle and town prospered. In 1496 Podhrad became a market town.

The Schwarzenberg family acquired the estate in 1661, bringing greater wealth. French forces briefly captured the castle in 1742 during the War of the Austrian Succession, and a blaze followed; the medieval fortress was slighted and rebuilt as a Renaissance castle, then between 1839 and 1871 as the present Neo-Gothic castle. The present municipality arose in 1850, the market town was renamed after the castle in 1885, and Franz Joseph I made Hluboká a town in 1907.

Hluboká Castle, originally a 13th-century medieval castle, was rebuilt in the Tudor Revival style in 1839–1871. It is owned by the state, offers guided tours and houses the Aleš South Bohemian Gallery, founded in 1953, which manages about 20,000 art objects. Nearby stands Ohrada Castle, a Baroque hunting castle built in 1708–1713, where the Hunting Museum was established in 1842. The two castles are protected together as one national cultural monument. A zoo of almost 5 hectares breeds about 300 species.
hlukhiv: Hlukhiv, in Russian Glukhov, is a small historic city on the Esman River, a tributary of the Seym, in Shostka Raion of Sumy Oblast. Its population was estimated at 31,789 in 2022. It is best known as the capital of the Cossack Hetmanate after the deposition of Ivan Mazepa in 1708.

Chroniclers first noticed Hlukhiv in 1152 as a Severian town. Around 1247, after the Mongol invasion of Rus, it became the seat of a branch of the princely house of Chernihiv. From 1320 to 1503 it belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, until conquered by the Grand Duchy of Moscow. In 1618 it passed to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, and Władysław IV Vasa granted it Magdeburg Rights in 1644. From 1648 it was part of the Cossack Hetmanate, in the Nizhyn Regiment. In 1664 a Russo-Cossack garrison defended it against a superior Polish army. By the Truce of Andrusovo of 1667 it was ceded to Muscovy, and in 1669 Demian Mnohohrishny was elected hetman there and concluded a treaty that significantly limited Ukrainian autonomy.

In 1708, when Ivan Mazepa sided with Carl XII, Peter the Great ordered the destruction of Baturyn and the transfer of the capital to Hlukhiv. Ivan Skoropadsky was elected hetman there in November 1708. Hlukhiv was the Hetmanate's capital until 1764 and until 1773 the administrative centre of the Little Russia Governorate. Under the last hetmans the town was remodelled in the Baroque style, but frequent fires later left few of its architectural treasures. After the Hetmanate was abolished it became the seat of the Second Little Russian Collegium; in 1782 it became a district centre of the Novgorod-Seversky Viceroyalty. The German army occupied it from 9 September 1941 to 30 August 1943.

The oldest building is the church of St. Nicholas of 1693, in Ukrainian Baroque style. The triumphal arch, dated to 1744 or 1766 and the oldest in Ukraine, was damaged in the Second World War and restored. A singing school opened in 1730, the first in the Russian Empire, and the composers Dmytro Bortniansky and Maksym Berezovsky are believed to have studied there. Hlukhiv has long been a centre of hemp cultivation, and an institute of bast crops there bred low-THC hemp varieties in the 1970s.
hmannan-yazawin: The chronicle takes its name from the Hmannan, the Palace of Mirrors in the Inwa Palace complex where it was written, and from yazawin, from the Pali rājavaṃsa, chronicle of kings. King Bagyidaw ordered the work in early 1829, soon after the First Anglo-Burmese War of 1824 to 1826, which had cost Konbaung Burma Arakan, Manipur, Assam and the Tenasserim coast and burdened the treasury with reparations of one million pounds sterling. The standard chronicle until then was the Maha Yazawin, which reached 1711; the Yazawin Thit, commissioned by Bodawpaya, had been refused official status for its harsh criticism of earlier chronicles.

The 13 members of the Royal Historical Commission, learned monks, court historians and court Brahmins, first met on 11 May 1829. They drew on more than 600 inscriptions collected between 1783 and 1793, earlier chronicles, pagoda histories, Pali religious chronicles and Burmese poetry. The monk Monywe Zetawun Sayadaw led the work with Thawkabin Sayadaw, and the former monk and minister Maha Dhamma Thingyan decided which sources to accept.

The work took three years and four months and falls into two parts: from the earliest times to 1752, and the ruling Konbaung dynasty to 1821. For the dates of the Pagan kings it mostly kept those of the Yazawin Thit, though the Zatadawbon Yazawin later proved the most accurate.

The compilers left much of the Maha Yazawin unchanged, and their commentaries are mostly esoteric. Their main change was religious: in place of the old story that the monarchy descended from Pyusawhti, son of a solar spirit and a dragon princess, they traced it to the Sakya clan of the Buddha through Abhiyaza of Tagaung. Monywe Sayadaw disagreed with parts of the result and issued his own Maha Yazawin Kyaw in 1831.

British colonial scholars dismissed much of the chronicle's early history as copies of Indian legends, a view that prevailed at least to the 1960s, though prominent Burmese historians disagreed. Later research finds that, once the legends, now read as allegories, are set aside, its narratives largely fit the evidence, and its chronology after the 11th century is held reliable. Thai historians used it to correct the pre-1767 chronology of Siamese chronicles. Pe Maung Tin and Gordon Luce translated the part to the end of the Pagan dynasty into English as the Glass Palace Chronicle; the whole has been translated into Chinese.
hmong-people: The Hmong are an ethnic group of East and Southeast Asia who speak languages of the Hmong–Mien family. In China they are classified as a sub-group of the Miao, a name that Chinese texts used loosely for southern peoples long before it was tied to the Hmong; only since the Tang dynasty is its association with them clearer. Hmong traditions place their origin near the Yellow River, which scientific evidence does not support. A linguist, Martha Ratliff, finds evidence that they have occupied parts of southern China for over 8,000 years, and one hypothesis places the Hmong–Mien homeland in southwestern China.

Hmong groups began to migrate into northern Vietnam, then called Tonkin, in the 19th century, settling the high mountains and recognizing the Tai-speaking lords of the valleys. During French colonial rule in Tonkin, from 1883 to 1954, some Hmong joined the Vietnamese nationalists and communists, while many Christianized Hmong sided with the French. In Thailand their settlements are documented from the end of the 19th century.

In Laos Hmong leaders were divided well before the Laotian Civil War. Touby Lyfoung became associated with the French and later the Royal Lao Government, while Faydang Lobliayao and his half-brother Nhiavu Lobliayao joined the revolutionary movement that became the Pathet Lao. In 1960 and 1961 the United States approved a covert CIA programme to build local paramilitary forces in Laos, and a 1964 American review named Touby Lyfoung and Vang Pao as its two principal Hmong leaders. Hmong refugees began resettling in the United States in 1975, after the collapse of the Royal Lao Government.

The Hmong have their own names for their divisions. The White Hmong (Hmoob Dawb) and the Blue or Green Hmong (Hmoob Leeg) are among the largest groups, named for the colour of women's dress; other groups include the Black Hmong and the Flower Hmong, known for embroidery called paj ntaub, or flower cloth. In Vietnam the trade in coffin wood and the growing of opium poppy, not prohibited there until 1993, long gave a regular cash income. Today the Hmong live mainly in southwestern China, Vietnam, Laos, Thailand and Myanmar, with diaspora communities in the United States, Australia, France and South America. The United States has the largest Hmong population outside Asia.
hms-beagle: HMS Beagle was a Cherokee-class 10-gun brig-sloop, one of more than 100 ships of a class designed by Sir Henry Peake in 1807. Her keel was laid in June 1818 and she was launched from Woolwich Dockyard on the Thames on 11 May 1820, at a cost of £7,803. Later reports say that she took part in the celebrations of the coronation of George IV, passing under the old London Bridge. With no immediate need for her, she lay in ordinary, moored without masts or rigging. In 1825 she was fitted out for survey work in the Hydrographic Office. Her guns were reduced from ten to six and a mizzen mast was added, which changed her from a brig to a barque.

On her first voyage, which left Plymouth on 22 May 1826 under Pringle Stokes, she accompanied the larger HMS Adventure on a survey of Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego. Stokes fell into a deep depression and shot himself at Port Famine in 1828, dying on 12 August. Robert FitzRoy, then 23, took command and proved an able surveyor. During this survey the Beagle Channel was identified and named after the ship.

FitzRoy was reappointed on 27 June 1831 for a second voyage and had the ship rebuilt at Devonport with a raised upper deck. She carried 22 chronometers and was one of the first ships fitted with William Snow Harris's lightning conductor. FitzRoy wanted a naturalist for company and for the study of the land, and the search led to the young Charles Darwin. The ship left Devonport on 10 December 1831 and, after surveying South America, returned by way of New Zealand, Sydney and Hobart Town to Falmouth on 2 October 1836.

A third voyage, from 1837 to 1843 under John Clements Wickham and then John Lort Stokes, surveyed the coast of Australia. It explored the Gulf of Carpentaria, which revealed the Albert and Flinders rivers, and on 9 October 1839 Wickham named Port Darwin in honour of their former shipmate.

Darwin combined his diary with his scientific notes in Journal and Remarks, published in 1839 as the third volume of the official account of the expedition. It was widely popular and was reprinted many times as The Voyage of the Beagle. His findings played a pivotal role in the formation of his theories of evolution and natural selection. In 1845 the ship was renamed WV-7 and refitted as a static coastguard watch vessel stationed on the Essex coast to control smuggling.
hms-bounty: Bounty was originally the collier Bethia, reportedly built in 1784 at Hull. The Royal Navy bought her on 23 May 1787, refitted her and renamed her. She was small, at 215 tons, but full-rigged on three masts. The purchase was made solely for a botanical mission: to collect breadfruit plants in Tahiti and carry them to the British West Indies as a cheap food for the region's slaves. The naturalist Sir Joseph Banks promoted the idea and recommended Lieutenant William Bligh to the Admiralty. Bligh, aged 33, was appointed on 16 August 1787. He had served as sailing master of the sloop Resolution on James Cook's third voyage. The complement was 46 men, with Bligh the only commissioned officer.

Bounty sailed from Spithead on 23 December 1787. After a month of trying to round Cape Horn in adverse weather, Bligh turned east, around the southern tip of Africa and across the Indian Ocean. The ship reached Tahiti on 26 October 1788, and the crew spent five months collecting 1,015 breadfruit plants, living ashore and taking Tahitian customs. Fletcher Christian married a Tahitian woman, Maimiti.

Bounty left Tahiti on 4 April 1789. On 28 April, near Tonga, Christian led a mutiny that took the ship without bloodshed. Of the 42 men aboard besides Bligh and Christian, 22 joined the mutineers, two were passive and 18 stayed loyal. Bligh and those who joined him were put into the ship's boat, and after an attack on Tofua killed one of them, Bligh sailed to the Dutch settlement of Coupang, reaching it after 47 days. Sixteen mutineers stayed in Tahiti, while Christian sailed on with eight other crewmen, six Tahitian men and eleven women, and reached Pitcairn Island on 15 January 1790. Bounty was burned there on 23 January.

HMS Pandora, sent to capture the mutineers, arrived in March 1791 and took fourteen men within two weeks. She was wrecked on the Great Barrier Reef on 29 August 1791, with 35 lives lost. The Pitcairn settlers stayed unseen until February 1808, when the sealer Topaz found John Adams, the last surviving mutineer, with the Tahitian women and their children. Bligh's log was used as evidence in the trials. Bligh is often portrayed as an abusive captain, but Caroline Alexander argued in 2003 that he was lenient by the standards of the time. Luis Marden found remains of the ship off Pitcairn in January 1957.
hms-dreadnought-1906: Gunnery developments of the late 1890s and early 1900s pushed expected battle ranges out to 6,000 yards. At that distance gunners had to wait for shells to land before correcting the next salvo, and the splashes of numerous smaller guns obscured those of the large ones. In 1903 the Italian naval architect Vittorio Cuniberti first wrote about an all-big-gun battleship. Admiral Sir John Fisher, who became First Sea Lord on 20 October 1904, pushed through the Board of Admiralty a decision to arm the next battleship with 12-inch guns and give it a speed of at least 21 knots. In January 1905 he convened a Committee on Designs, which he appointed and presided over.

Dreadnought was 527 feet long and displaced 18,120 long tons at normal load. She was the first battleship of her era with a uniform main battery, ten 12-inch guns in five twin turrets, and the first capital ship driven by steam turbines, which made her the fastest battleship in the world at completion. On trials on 9 October 1906 she reached 21.6 knots. Her waterline belt was 11 inches thick. Officers were berthed forward, nearer their action stations, which was unpopular with them.

She was laid down at Portsmouth on 2 October 1905 after months of stockpiling and prefabrication, and the yard worked a 69-hour week. She went to sea on 3 October 1906, a year and a day after construction started, and was commissioned on 11 December 1906.

From 1907 to 1911 Dreadnought was flagship of the Home Fleet. In 1910 the hoaxer Horace de Vere Cole persuaded the Royal Navy to give a tour to supposed Abyssinian royals, who were friends of his in disguise, including the young Virginia Woolf. Designed to fight enemy battleships, her only significant action was ramming and sinking the German submarine SM U-29, which made her the only battleship confirmed to have sunk a submarine. She was reduced to reserve in 1919 and sold for scrap two years later.

Her design eclipsed earlier types so thoroughly that later battleships were called dreadnoughts and older ones pre-dreadnoughts. Her launch helped spark a naval arms race as navies, above all the Imperial German Navy, rushed to match her.
hms-royal-charles-1655: The ship was one of four Second rates authorised by the Council of State on 3 July 1654 under the 1654 Construction Programme, each meant to carry 60 guns. She was designed and built by Peter Pett II at Woolwich Dockyard and named after Sir Thomas Fairfax's victory over the Royalist forces at Naseby in 1645. When the programme was changed to include a First rate fit to serve as a fleet flagship, Naseby was altered on the stocks, given a full battery along the upper deck and lengthened by 7 ft.

Completed, she measured 131 ft on the keel and, after girdling, 42 ft 6 in in breadth. Her lower deck carried 20 cannon-of-seven and 6 demi-cannon, the middle deck 26 culverins and the higher decks 28 demi-culverins; a later pair of demi-culverins brought her to 82 guns. She was larger than the Sovereign of the Seas, built by Phineas Pett, the builder's father.

Before the voyage to fetch the king in 1660, her figurehead of Oliver Cromwell, crowned with laurel and bestriding figures of six nations, was removed while she lay in The Downs off Deal. Sir Edward Montagu captained her, and at Scheveningen she took on board Charles II and his entourage, among them Samuel Pepys. The king and his brother James, Duke of York, renamed her on 23 May 1660, and she landed them at Dover on 25 May.

In the Second Anglo-Dutch War she sailed under the command of the Lord High Admiral, the Duke of York, with Sir William Penn as her captain, at the Battle of Lowestoft in 1665, where she probably destroyed the Dutch flagship Eendracht. In 1666 she fought in the Four Days Battle and in the St. James's Day Battle off the North Foreland.

Captured on 12 June 1667 while out of commission, she was taken to Hellevoetsluis. The Dutch judged that she drew too much water for their coast and did not take her into service; she was kept in dry dock as a public attraction, visited by large parties and foreign guests. After Charles II protested that this insulted his honour, the visits ended, and she was sold for scrap in 1673. Her carved royal arms from the transom passed to a Rotterdam shipyard and in 1855 to the Dutch navy's model collection.
hmt-empire-windrush: Monte Rosa was the last of five nearly identical Monte-class motor ships built by Blohm & Voss in Hamburg for Hamburg Süd, which used them to carry German emigrants to South America and for modestly priced cruises. Launched on 13 December 1930, she sailed between Hamburg and Buenos Aires and on cruises to Norway and the UK, making more than 20 round trips to Buenos Aires before the Second World War.

In the war she served the German navy as a barracks ship and troopship. In November 1942 she carried 46 Norwegian Jews from Oslo, among them Moritz Rabinowitz, and all but two were murdered at Auschwitz. In 1943 her captain, Heinrich Bertram, falsely reported engine trouble so that she could not be used to deport Danish Jews. She survived an air attack near Utsira in March 1944, limpet mines laid by the Norwegian saboteurs Max Manus and Gregers Gram, and a mine near the Hel Peninsula, before British forces captured her at Kiel on 10 May 1945.

Taken by the United Kingdom as a prize of war, she was refitted at South Shields and renamed Empire Windrush on 21 January 1947, after the River Windrush in the Cotswolds. As a troopship she made 13 round trips between Southampton and Hong Kong, extended to Kure in Japan during the Korean War, and in 1950 brought home the last British troops from Greece.

In 1948 she sailed to the Caribbean to repatriate around 500 West Indians who had served in the Royal Air Force. Advertisements in The Daily Gleaner and other papers offered cheap passage on the return voyage, though the cheapest fares, in the troop dormitories, were open only to men. She was not the first such ship: the Ormonde and the Almanzora had arrived the year before.

On 28 March 1954, off Algeria, an explosion in the engine room killed four men and started a fire that cut the ship's power. All the other 1,494 people aboard were rescued, though only 12 of her 22 lifeboats could be launched. HMS Saintes took her in tow, but she sank early on 30 March.

In 1998 a square in Brixton, London, was renamed Windrush Square for the 50th anniversary of the 1948 arrival, and in 2008 a plaque was unveiled at Tilbury. A London Overground service in East London was named the Windrush line in 2024.
ho-chi-minh: Ho Chi Minh was born Nguyễn Sinh Cung in 1890 in Kim Liên, in Nghệ An province in northern Central Vietnam. Details of his early life are uncertain: at least four official biographies differ on names, dates and places, and he is known to have used between 50 and 200 pseudonyms. His father, Nguyễn Sinh Sắc, was a scholar and teacher, and the boy studied with him and then with the scholar Vương Thúc Quý, mastering Chinese characters, the basis of Confucian study. At ten he received the name Nguyễn Tất Thành. On 5 June 1911 he left Saigon as a kitchen helper on a French steamer, reaching Marseille on 5 July, and worked on ships until 1917.

In Paris from 1919 he joined the Groupe des Patriotes Annamites, whose members published articles for Vietnamese independence under the name Nguyễn Ái Quốc. Their petition to the powers at the Versailles peace talks was ignored. In 1923 he went to Moscow, where he worked for the Comintern, and in 1924 or 1925 he was sent to Canton to assist the Comintern envoy Mikhail Borodin. There he organised the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League and trained young Vietnamese revolutionaries.

He returned to Vietnam in 1941 to lead the Việt Minh. Jailed by Chiang Kai-shek's local authorities in China, he was released in 1943 and from then regularly used the name Hồ Chí Minh. He read the Declaration of Independence on 2 September 1945. An agreement with France of 6 March 1946 soon broke down, and the First Indochina War followed. His government carried out a land reform campaign between 1953 and 1956 that included the execution of landowners. After the 1954 Geneva Conference he remained president of North Vietnam and, from 1959, urged aid to the Việt Cộng in the south, supplied along the trail that bears his name.

Ho Chi Minh died of heart failure at his home in Hanoi on 2 September 1969, aged 79. The government delayed announcing it until the next day because 2 September was Independence Day. About 250,000 people attended the funeral. His will asked for cremation and the scattering of his ashes across a united Vietnam, but his embalmed body lies in a mausoleum in Ba Đình Square. Saigon was later renamed Ho Chi Minh City in his honour.

He was also a poet and journalist who wrote in Chinese, Vietnamese and French. His Poems from the Prison Diary, written while imprisoned in China, has been recognised as a Vietnamese national treasure since 2012. In 1987 UNESCO recommended that its member states commemorate the centenary of his birth.
ho-chi-minh-city: Ho Chi Minh City lies in south-east Vietnam on the Mekong Delta, and its geography is defined by rivers and canals, the largest being the Saigon River. The centre stands about 5 metres above sea level, and the city is fringed by tidal flats that have been altered for agriculture. It has a coast 89 kilometres long on the South China Sea. In the rainy season, tides, rain, river flow and land subsidence together flood parts of the city.

The first known settlement was a Cham one called Baigaur. The Khmer renamed it Prey Nokôr, a fishing village, and Vietnamese settlers in the early 17th century took over the Khmer name as Sài Gòn. It was officially renamed Gia Định in 1698. The name Ho Chi Minh City was given in 1976, after reunification, to honour Ho Chi Minh. Sài Gòn remains in everyday speech and refers to the city centre.

An early Funan temple, said to be the site of the later Phụng Sơn Buddhist temple, was founded in the 4th century CE, and a Champa settlement dates to the 11th century. The Khmer Empire took Baigaur around 1145. In 1620 Princess Nguyễn Phúc Ngọc Vạn, daughter of Lord Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên, married King Chey Chettha II of Cambodia, which eased relations and let people of the two countries move freely. Chey Chettha II in exchange gave Prei Nokor to the Nguyễn lords.

After the fall of the Citadel of Saigon in the Cochinchina campaign in 1859, the city was the capital of French Cochinchina from 1862 to 1949. It was capital of French Indochina from 1887 to 1902 and again from 1945 to 1954, and of the State of Vietnam from 1949 to 1955. After the 1954 partition it was the capital of South Vietnam until its capture by North Vietnam, which led to a unified state in 1976.

Ho Chi Minh City is the most populous city of Vietnam, with more than 14 million people after the merger of Bình Dương and Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu into it in 2025. French colonial buildings such as the City Hall, the Saigon Central Post Office and the Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica stand in the centre. The Thien Hau Temple, first built around 1760, is in the Chinese quarter of Chợ Lớn, and the Independence Palace dates from the era of the Republic of Vietnam.
ho-chi-minh-trail: The trail was also called the Annamite Range Trail, and the communists named it the Trường Sơn Strategic Supply Route, after the Vietnamese name for the Annamite Range. It ran mostly in Laos, and was divided into West Trường Sơn in Laos and East Trường Sơn in Vietnam. Parts of it had existed for centuries as primitive footpaths for trade. The terrain was among the most challenging in Southeast Asia: sparsely populated mountains 500 to 2,400 metres high, with triple-canopy jungle and dense rainforest.

It was named by the U.S. after the North Vietnamese leader Hồ Chí Minh, perhaps echoing a Viet Minh maritime line of the First Indochina War, the Route of Ho Chi Minh. It was believed to be the main supply route, though the Sihanouk Trail through Cambodia later proved to carry significantly more material.

During the First Indochina War the Việt Minh expanded the old paths into north–south supply lines. After the North Vietnamese and Pathet Lao forces invaded Laos on 28 July 1959, Hanoi established the 559th Transportation Group in September, under Colonel Võ Bẩm, to supply the insurgency against the South Vietnamese government. At first the trail carried only manpower, while supplies moved more efficiently by sea. Porters, bicycles and oxcarts gave way to Soviet, Chinese and Eastern Bloc trucks, the first motor transport unit working the trail as early as December 1961.

Systematic bombing by the U.S. Air Force began with Operation Barrel Roll on 14 December 1964, followed by Steel Tiger and Tiger Hound. After the Tet Offensive the North Vietnamese modernised the system, building a fuel pipeline into Laos in early 1969 that eventually reached 5,000 km, and defending the trail with over 1,500 anti-aircraft guns. Operation Commando Hunt followed from November 1968, with Igloo White using air-dropped sensors. In February 1971 about 16,000 South Vietnamese troops entered Laos in Operation Lam Son 719, aiming at Tchepone. Faced with some 60,000 North Vietnamese troops, they withdrew by 25 March 1971, having lost half the force.
ho-chunk: The Ho-Chunk, also known as Hoocąk, Hoocągra or Winnebago, speak a Siouan language that they believe their creator, Mą’ųna, gave them. Their name, meaning People of the Sacred Voice, comes from an oral history in which they are the originators of the Siouan languages. They say that their ancestors built the thousands of effigy mounds of the Late Woodland period, and they claim descent from both the mound builders and the Oneota culture that followed. In the 16th century they were the dominant people of their territory, living in permanent villages and growing corn, squash, beans and wild rice, and hunting and fishing. Winnebago is the name used by the Potawatomi, adopted by the French and English.

The French explorer Jean Nicolet made contact in 1634 and found the Ho-Chunk around Green Bay. Their population fell sharply in the 17th century, perhaps to about 500, a loss that has been attributed to the drowning of several hundred warriors in a storm on a lake, to epidemics of European diseases and to war with the Illinois Confederacy, and to competition from Algonquian peoples who had moved west. It recovered to more than 2,900 by 1806, but the smallpox epidemic of 1836 killed nearly a quarter of the people. They ceded land in Wisconsin in 1829, 1832 and 1837.

Through the 19th century the United States moved them to reservations in Iowa, Minnesota, South Dakota and finally Nebraska; oral history holds that some of them were forcibly moved as many as thirteen times. After the Dakota War of 1862, about 2,000 Ho-Chunk were interned at Camp Porter in Mankato and expelled in 1863 to Crow Creek, in Dakota Territory. Many left for Nebraska, where the Winnebago Reservation was founded in 1865, and many returned to Wisconsin, often resisting removal without violence by going back home.

The Ho-Chunk traditionally had twelve clans, each with its own role: the Thunderbird Clan supplied chiefs and the Bear Clan kept discipline. People generally married outside their clan. Women grew and processed food and gathered roots, nuts and maple sap, and men hunted and, when needed, fought. Boys fasted at puberty to gain a guardian spirit.

Two separate sovereign nations are federally recognised today: the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin, with its headquarters at Black River Falls, and the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska, whose reservation lies in Thurston County. About 12,000 people belong to the two. In 2015 it took control of a 1,500-acre parcel in Sauk County, Wisconsin, the site of the former Badger Army Ammunition Plant.
ho-quy-ly: Hồ Quý Ly was born in 1336 at Đại Lại village in Ái Châu, of a family descended from Chinese named Hu who had moved from present-day Zhejiang in the tenth century. Adopted by Lê Huan, he took the name Lê Quý Ly, a surname that appealed to the local elite. Two of his paternal aunts entered the court of King Tran Nghe Tong and were honoured in 1371 and 1372, which opened his way to power, and in 1371 he married a princess, a daughter of King Tran Minh Tong.

In 1375 he received a high military rank, and in the war against Che Bong Nga of Champa he handled supplies for the campaign that ended in disaster in January 1377, when King Tran Due Tong was killed. The Chams then sacked Hanoi more than once. Made chief minister in March 1387, he urged the old king Nghe Tong to remove the young King Tran Phe De, who was deposed and executed in 1388; the new king, Tran Thuan Tong, married Quý Ly's eldest daughter. The war with Champa ended in February 1390 with the death of Che Bong Nga.

In the 1390s Quý Ly centralised the state, brought in Confucian learning, held examinations from 1393, had the Book of Documents translated into Nom, regulated official dress, issued the first Vietnamese banknotes and in 1397 began a new capital, Tay Do, in Thanh Hoa, renaming Hanoi Dong Do. In 1398 he made Thuan Tong abdicate in favour of the two-year-old Tran Thieu De.

In 1400 he deposed Thieu De, took the throne and renamed the kingdom Đại Ngu. After a failed Trần coup he had 370 dissidents executed, their goods seized, their female relatives enslaved and their male kin buried alive or drowned. In 1401 he abdicated in favour of his second son, Hồ Hán Thương, but kept power as Emperor Emeritus.

Three expeditions against Champa followed; the second, in 1402, won southern Quảng Nam and northern Quảng Ngãi. Captured by the Ming in Thiên Cầm cave, he was exiled to China and made to serve as a common soldier. Vietnamese historians still debate whether he was a reformer or a usurper, and the remains of his Thanh Hóa citadel are a World Heritage Site.
hoa-hao: Hòa Hảo grew from the Miền Tây region of the Mekong Delta, a frontier society where Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism and spirit cults mixed and the French imposed their rule in 1867. It claims to rest on the teaching of Phật Thầy Tây An (1807–1856), the Bửu Sơn Kỳ Hương tradition, whose prophecies of the fall of Nguyễn Vietnam to Western powers helped inspire rebellions in 1875 and 1913. Its founder, Huỳnh Phú Sổ, came from a Roman Catholic family of smallholders and is regarded as a saint by devotees. Fearing revolt, the Vichy governor Jean Decoux had him imprisoned in Bạc Liêu as a lunatic, and in 1942 the French exiled him to Laos.

The movement flourished under the Japanese occupation and became a militant nationalist force with a private army. After Japan's surrender it joined the front of the August Revolution, then clashed with the Việt Minh and the Cao Đài. The Việt Minh kidnapped and executed Sổ in 1947, and the movement split into factions whose leaders carried out public burnings, beheadings and mass executions of Khmers and Vietnamese, and drowned Việt Minh sympathisers. The French funded its forces, arming some 20,000 men against the Việt Minh. After 1954 it fought Ngô Đình Diệm's government, and from the mid-1960s, left to rule the Miền Tây in return for recognising South Vietnam, it waged war on the Việt Cộng until the Fall of Saigon in 1975.

Hòa Hảo is described either as a syncretistic folk religion or as a Buddhist sect, blending Buddhism with ancestor worship, animistic rites, Confucian ideas and the White Lotus tradition. It avoids elaborate rituals and temples, keeps no monastic order and teaches practice at home, holding that each believer can commune directly with the Buddha and that inner faith matters more than rites. Daily observance is four prayers, and funerals are simple, which kept the cost of religion low for peasants and earned it the name poor man's Buddhism. Disbanded after 1975, the faith was officially recognised by the Vietnamese state in 1999, and most of its followers live in the Mekong Delta.
hoan-kiem-lake: Hoàn Kiếm Lake is a freshwater lake of some 12 hectares in the historical centre of Hanoi, and one of the city's major scenic spots and a focal point of its public life. It is also known as Sword Lake (Hồ Gươm) or Tả Vọng Lake. In the past it was called Lục Thủy Lake, Green Water Lake, after the colour of its water, or Thủy Quân Lake, Mariner's Lake.

In the legend, Emperor Lê Lợi was boating on the lake after his victory over Ming China when the Golden Turtle God, Kim Quy, surfaced and asked for his magic sword, Heaven's Will. Lợi understood that the turtle had come to reclaim the sword its master, the Dragon King (Long Vương), had given him to defeat the Ming, and he handed it back, renaming the lake to mark the event. The Turtle Tower, on a small island near the middle of the lake, is linked to the story.

Large soft-shell turtles, either of the species Rafetus swinhoei or of a separate species named Rafetus leloi in honour of the emperor, were sighted in the lake for many years. The last known individual was found dead on 19 January 2016.

Near the northern shore lies Jade Islet, where the Temple of the Jade Mountain (Ngọc Sơn Temple) was built in the 18th century. It honours Trần Hưng Đạo, the 13th-century military leader who three times helped defeat the Mongol invasions of Vietnam, the classic scholar Văn Xương, and Nguyễn Văn Siêu, a writer and official who repaired the temple in 1864. The islet is joined to the shore by the wooden Thê Húc Bridge, painted vermilion red, whose name is poetically rendered as Perch of the Morning Sunlight.
hoang-hoa-tham: Hoàng Hoa Thám was born Đoàn Văn Nghĩa in Tiên Lữ, Hưng Yên. Hoàng Hoa Thám was the adopted name by which he became known, and Đề Thám his nom de guerre: Đề is short for Đề đốc, the rank of a commander, a title he took for himself, since the Nguyễn court never commissioned him. His parents both died after joining a resistance group in the mountains that had risen against the court of Huế. Seeking anonymity, his paternal uncle fled to the Yên Thế area and changed the family name from Trương to Hoàng.

Thám became the feudal lord of Yên Thế and the leader of the Yên Thế Insurrection against the French protectorate in Tonkin. As the protectorate tightened its hold, French troops under Joseph Gallieni swept through Yên Thế in 1890-91 and routed most of the resistance fighters. Gallieni's campaign was halted when Đề Thám attacked the railway, seizing trains and supplies and even capturing a local official for ransom.

Against Gallieni's wishes, the French authorities made peace and granted Đề Thám a regional fiefdom, which made him a rallying point for other anti-French movements. Later military campaigns reduced the fiefdom piece by piece, but his exploits and fame troubled the protectorate well into the early decades of the 20th century.

Đề Thám was assassinated at Thái Nguyên on 10 February or, by another account, 18 March 1913 by one of his own men, Lương Tam Kỳ, a former commander of the Black Flag Army who had become an agent of the French in Tonkin. He had three wives and left four sons, two of them adopted, and a daughter, Hoàng Thị Thế, also known as Marie Beatrice Destham. He is honoured as a national hero in Vietnam, where many buildings and streets bear his name, and an operation of the Vietnam War was also named after him.
hobart: Hobart lies in the south-east of Tasmania, on the estuary of the River Derwent, and is the southernmost capital city in Australia. Its skyline is dominated by kunanyi / Mount Wellington, which rises to 1,271 metres, and its harbour is the second-deepest natural port in the world, with much of the waterfront built on reclaimed land. The city is built chiefly on Jurassic dolerite around the foothills. It has a cool to mild oceanic climate.

The land was known to the Muwinina people as nipaluna, a name that includes features such as kunanyi / Mount Wellington and the River Derwent. Before British colonisation it had been occupied, possibly for as long as 35,000 years, by Aboriginal Tasmanians, who generally call themselves Palawa or Pakana.

The first European settlement began in 1803 as a military camp at Risdon Cove on the eastern shore of the Derwent, amid British concern over French explorers. The camp was the site of the 1804 Risdon Cove massacre. Later in 1804 Captain David Collins moved the camp, together with soldiers, settlers and convicts from the abandoned Port Phillip settlement, to a better site at Sullivans Cove, the present site of Hobart. He named it Hobart Town, or Hobarton, after Lord Hobart, then British Secretary of State for war and the colonies. The city took the singular name Hobart in 1881.

Whaling soon became a major local industry, and for a time Hobart was the main whaling port of the Southern Ocean. Penal transportation ended in the 1850s, and the city then went through periods of growth and decline. A railway opened in 1876 and Australia's first fully electric tram network in 1893, which allowed the urban area to spread. The early 20th century brought a boom based on mining, agriculture and other primary industries. The first general work of Australian literature to be published appeared in Hobart, and in 1824 Andrew Bent, proprietor of the Hobart Town Gazette, established the first free press in Australia.

Hobart is the capital and most populous city of Tasmania and the seat of the Parliament of Tasmania. Greater Hobart had 247,068 people at the 2021 census, nearly half of the state's population. The city is the home port for Australian and French Antarctic operations.

Hobart is known for its well-preserved Georgian and Victorian buildings. The Theatre Royal, established in 1837 and designed by the colonial architect John Lee Archer, is Australia's oldest continually operating theatre. The Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery was founded by the Royal Society of Tasmania. Salamanca Market and the Museum of Old and New Art, which opened in 2011, are well-known attractions.
hobyo: Hobyo stands on the coast of the north-central Mudug region of Somalia, today within Galmudug state, and has a hot arid climate. Its harbour long linked the interior to the sea: goods harvested along the Shabelle River were brought there for trade, and ships making their way down the Somali coast stopped to trade and take on supplies. The growth of cities further south, such as Mogadishu, increased this traffic and with it the prosperity of the port.

Hobyo developed, together with Mareeg, as a coastal outpost of the Ajuran Empire in the 13th century. In the late 17th century the Hiraab revolted against the Ajuran and founded an independent imamate, which local oral tradition, as recorded by the historian Lee Cassanelli, describes as an alliance of related lineages ruling from the Shabeelle valley and the Benaadir to the arid lands of Mudug. Livestock, hides, aromatic woods and raisins were exported, while rice, foodstuffs and cloth came in, and merchants came to Hobyo for textiles, precious metals and pearls.

As the imamate declined in the late 19th century, Yusuf Ali Kenadid of the Majeerteen, who had failed to seize the neighbouring Majeerteen Sultanate from his cousin Boqor Osman Mahamud and gone into exile in Yemen, returned with Hadhrami musketeers and took Hobyo. His sultanate kept a bureaucracy, a titled nobility, a flag, a professional army and written records. In late 1888 he made it an Italian protectorate by treaty. Relations soured when he refused to let British troops land to fight the Dervish forces, and the Italians exiled him and his son Ali Yusuf to Aden and then Eritrea.

Hobyo has about 11,800 inhabitants, and its wider district 67,249. It has a seaport and is served by Obbia Airport. In August 2019 Qatar began a project to build a new port there under agreements signed with Somalia in December 2018.
hochburg: The Hochburg, whose name means high castle, stands between the town of Emmendingen and the village of Sexau in Baden, in south-western Germany. It was presumably built in the 11th century and was first known as castle Hachberg. Historians are unsure where that name comes from; one theory links it to a man called Hacho in Charlemagne's retinue, and a document of 1161 calls it Castro Hahberc. Before its destruction it was the second largest fortification in Baden.

Dietrich von Emmendingen, who later called himself von Hachberg, most likely founded the castle to exploit the surrounding forests for timber; its first mention dates from 1127. A document of 1161 on the founding of Tennenbach monastery suggests that Hermann IV of Baden then held it. When his sons Hermann V and Henrich I divided the margraviate in 1212, it became the seat of the margraves of Baden-Hachberg, who ruled from it for two centuries until Margrave Bernhard I of Baden bought it in 1415 from the indebted Otto II, the last of their line.

The castle survived the war of the Oberrheinischer Städtebund against Bernhard I in 1424 and a siege during the peasants' rising of 1525. Karl II strengthened it in 1553 as a Renaissance fortress, and Margrave Georg Friedrich added seven bastions, some named after sister castles such as Rötteln, Sausenberg and Badenweiler. Besieged for two years in the Thirty Years' War, it was slighted after surrendering, and rebuilt from 1660 under Margrave Friedrich VI. After the Peace of Nijmegen the French destroyed its defences in 1681, a fire started by peasants burned the living quarters three years later, and French troops then reduced what remained to a ruin.

Work to preserve the ruin began towards the end of the 19th century and has continued since, halted only during the two world wars. A society for the conservation of the Hochburg has cared for it since 1971. The ruin is open free of charge, belongs to Baden-Württemberg's state programme for castles and gardens, and has had a small museum in its cellar since 1991.
hochdorf-chieftains-grave: The grave lies near Hochdorf an der Enz in the municipality of Eberdingen, within sight of the Hohenasperg, a fortified settlement and princely seat of the Hallstatt era surrounded by other elite burials such as the Grafenbühl grave and the Kleinaspergle. Its burial mound was originally 6 metres high and about 60 metres across, but centuries of erosion and farming had worn it down to about 1 metre, so that it could hardly be seen.

An amateur archaeologist found the grave in 1968. The excavation was carried out by the Baden-Württemberg Landesdenkmalamt under the archaeologist Jörg Biel, with the excavation technician Fritz Maurer. The dead man was about 50 years old and 180 cm tall. Besides his torc he wore a bracelet on his right arm and a hat of birch bark, and he was buried with a gold-plated dagger of bronze and iron, rich clothing, amber jewellery, a razor, a nail clipper, a comb, fishing hooks and arrows.

The cauldron at the foot of the couch is decorated with three lions around the brim and was altered after it came from Magna Graecia. Hemp or cannabis was also found, the wagon was of wood plated with iron, and elaborate textiles lined the whole chamber. Krausse argued in 1999 that the burial may mark a man who was both chief and priest, a sacral king, and Gaspani held in 1998 that the diagonals of the chamber were aligned with the major lunar standstill, which recurs every 18.6 years.

After the excavation the burial mound was rebuilt to its original height. The Keltenmuseum Hochdorf was built nearby and opened in 1991. While it was being built, the foundations of an ancient Celtic village were found, possibly the one to which the chieftain belonged, and these were incorporated into the museum.
hod-hill: Hod Hill stands in the Blackmore Vale, 3 miles (5 km) north-west of Blandford Forum, on a chalk hill 143 m high between the Dorset Downs and Cranborne Chase, with the hill fort of Hambledon Hill just to the north. Its name probably comes from the Old English hod, a shelter, though hod could also mean hood, after the shape of the hill. The fort is roughly rectangular, 600 by 400 m, enclosing 22 ha. A steep natural slope falls to the River Stour on the west; the other sides have a rampart, ditch and outer bank, with a second rampart on the north.

Radiocarbon analysis suggests a date of about 500 BCE for the main rampart. Whether the people who fortified the hilltop in the middle Iron Age were the same tribe as the Durotriges who lived there in the late Iron Age is unknown. There is extensive evidence of settlement inside, including platforms for roundhouses. Hod Hill is the second in a chain of Iron Age earthworks that runs from Hambledon Hill through Spetisbury Rings, Buzbury Rings, Badbury Rings and Dudsbury Camp to the port at Hengistbury Head.

The Romans built their camp in the north-west corner of the old fort, possibly for a mixed force of legionaries and auxiliaries. It passed out of use by about 50 CE, when, after a fire, the troops were withdrawn for the campaigns against Caractacus in Wales and the rest moved to a new fort further west at Waddon Hill.

Sir Ian Richmond excavated the site in the 1950s and published his final report in 1969. The hill is a calcareous grassland habitat known for its wild flowers and butterflies, and the hillfort is a Scheduled Monument in the care of the National Trust, open to the public. It was removed from the Heritage at Risk Register in 2022 through the Hillforts and Habitats Project.
hodeidah: Hodeidah lies on a flat plain that slopes gently towards the Red Sea, part of the Tihama coastal plain, which stretches about 300 kilometres from al-Luhayyah in the north to al-Khawkhah in the south and is 60 to 150 kilometres wide. Valleys such as Wadi Mour, Wadi Siham and Wadi Zabid carry flood and rainwater from the highlands to the sea. More than 40 Yemeni islands lie off the coast, among them Kamaran and the Hanish Islands. The climate is hot desert.

Islamic chronicles first mention Hodeidah in 1454/55, and the city grew in importance in the 1520s, when the Ottomans took over the Tihama. In the 1830s Ibrahim Pasha's troops controlled it and handed its administration to Sherif Husayn ibn Ali Haydar, and in 1849 it became part of the Yemen Eyalet. The Malay writer Abdullah bin Abdul Kadir, who visited on his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1854, noted that chewing khat was common. In the 19th century the city had a large slave market, supplied from the Oromia region of modern Ethiopia.

In 1914 German troops under Major Othmar von Stotzingen set up a wireless station at Hodeidah, which relayed messages from Constantinople to German East Africa and broadcast propaganda to Sudan, Somaliland and Abyssinia. Britain occupied the city in January 1919 after the collapse of Ottoman Yemen and left on 29 January 1921, letting the Emirate of Asir take it. The Kingdom of Yemen captured it in April 1925. Saudi forces occupied it briefly during the Saudi-Yemeni war of 1934. A fire in January 1961 destroyed much of the city, which was rebuilt with Soviet aid, and a highway to Sanaa was completed that year.

Hodeidah is the principal port of Yemen on the Red Sea and the capital of Hodeidah Governorate. The Ottomans developed it as a seaport in the mid-19th century. Its harbour was poor: in 1920 the British noted that large ships had to anchor more than two miles out, and a new harbour 10 miles to the north-west was linked to the town by a small railway. The city exported coffee, hides, cotton and dates, and was a centre of dhow building, tanning and sandal making. Hand-woven striped cotton cloth was made by artisans moved there from Zabid and Beit el-Faki. The port of Ras Isa lies just to the north.
hodna-mountains: The Hodna Mountains, Monts du Hodna in French, are a massif of the Saharan Atlas, part of the Atlas Mountain System. They rise on the northern side of the Hodna natural region in M'Sila Province, near the town of Maadid, about 200 km south-east of Algiers. The ridge lies south of Kabylie and runs roughly east to west between the Bibans in the north-west and the Belezma Range in the east, towards the transition to the Aurès Mountains.

The highest peak is the Djebel Tachrirt, at 1,902 metres. The Maadid Range, the Kiyāna Range and the 'Aqqār Range are among its subranges. One of the mountains forms part of a religious pilgrimage of some of the region's native tribes.

In 945, as Abu Yazid besieged Sousse, the Fatimid caliph al-Qa'im Bi-Amrillah died and was succeeded by his son al-Mansur. Under al-Mansur the Fatimid forces broke the siege of Sousse and drove Abu Yazid's forces out of Kairouan into the Aurès Mountains. In 947 they finally defeated them in the Kiyana Mountains of the Hodna massif, near the place that later became the Beni Hammad Fort.

The fortified Hammadid city, settled in 1007 and abandoned in 1090, lies on the southern slopes of the range within a line of walls 7 km long. Inside are four residential complexes, a large mosque with a minaret 20 m tall, likened to the Grand Mosque of Kairouan, and the remains of the emir's palace, Dal al-Bahr, three residences separated by gardens and pavilions. Excavations have brought to light terracotta, jewels, coins and ceramics, among them decorative fountains with the lion as a motif.

The former inhabitants of the mountains built water-retention walls called jessour, laid parallel to the contour lines so that they formed steps in the valley floors. On the northern slopes of the Djebel Tachrirt the walls stood above the ground, so that snow gathered behind them and melted slowly, spreading the water of the thaw. Most of these works are now in ruins.

The Beni Hammad Fort was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980. The range lies mostly in M'Sila Province, with its easternmost part in Batna Province towards the Aurès Mountains, and a natural cedar forest of about 8,000 ha grows in fairly dry conditions near Boutaleb.
hodonin: Hodonín is a town of about 23,000 inhabitants in the South Moravian Region, about 51 kilometres southeast of Brno. It lies on the right bank of the Morava River in the flat Lower Morava Valley, where the river forms the border between the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The Kyjovka River marks the western boundary of the municipality and feeds a system of eight fishponds. The name derives from the personal name Hodona, written Godonín in Old Czech, from which the German name Göding comes.

The castle of Hodonín was founded in the 11th century, though the document of 1046 that is the oldest mention of it is demonstrably a forgery. The first credible written mention is from 1169, and in 1228 Hodonín became a town. It was severely damaged in the Thirty Years' War and lost population. In the 18th century the castle was rebuilt as a tobacco factory, whose production helped to repopulate the town. The railway reached Hodonín in 1841 and was extended to Holíč in 1891. The town began to grow significantly only in the 19th century, with industrialisation, and lignite was mined nearby from the beginning of that century until 2009.

Hodonín was the first town in the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia to be freed from German occupation at the end of the World War II. The battle began on 11 April 1945, after the Red Army captured nearby Holíč, and Soviet troops crossed the Morava River. After about 24 hours of fighting the town was fully liberated by 8 p.m. on 12 April.

The main sights stand on the town square. The Church of Saint Lawrence is a Gothic building of the first half of the 13th century, rebuilt in the Baroque style in 1780–1786. The Art Nouveau town hall, built in 1902–1904 by the architect Ernst von Gotthilf, has a tower open to the public as a lookout. The Museum of Oil Extraction and Geology presents the history of local oil extraction and lignite mining. Hodonín is known as the birthplace of Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk (1850–1937), the first president of Czechoslovakia.
hoelun: Most of what is known of Hö'elün comes from the Secret History of the Mongols, a mid-13th-century epic that is very favourable to her; its anonymous author probably had links to her. According to it she was born into the Olkhonud clan of the Onggirat tribe and was married at around fifteen, in about 1160 or 1161, to Chiledu, brother of the Merkit chief. On the journey to his lands the couple were ambushed by Mongols out hawking, led by Yesügei of the Borjigin clan. The kidnapping, omitted from most official chronicles, left a grudge among the Merkit that later became a blood feud.

Yesügei already had a wife, usually named Sochigel by historians, and a son, Behter, but Hö'elün became his primary wife. She bore him four sons, Temüjin, Qasar, Hachiun and Temüge, and a daughter, Temülen. The year of Temüjin's birth is disputed, with 1155, 1162 and 1167 each favoured by different historians.

Yesügei was poisoned by Tatars when Temüjin was about eight. The Tayichiud faction excluded Hö'elün from the ancestor ceremonies and abandoned her camp. The Secret History says the whole Borjigin clan followed, though other sources, such as the Persian historian Rashid al-Din, imply that Yesügei's brothers stood by her. When Temüjin and Qasar ambushed and killed Behter, the Secret History has her angrily reprimand them.

After Temüjin married Börte, the two women managed the economy of his camp, and he turned to them first for counsel when he split from Jamuqa. After his defeat at Dalan Balzhut in 1187, Hö'elün married Münglig, an old retainer of Yesügei, in her third and final marriage. In the following years she probably arranged marriages for her youngest children and maintained alliances while Temüjin was away. The Secret History says she raised numerous foundlings, but problems of chronology indicate that the best known, Shigi Qutuqu, was in fact raised by Börte.

At the assembly of 1206 Hö'elün was reportedly granted 10,000 followers jointly with Temüge, and felt that this undervalued her work; Münglig, by contrast, received the seat at the khan's right hand. When Münglig's son, the shaman Kokechu, divided Genghis Khan from his brothers, she defended Qasar and Temüge vigorously, and with Börte persuaded Genghis that Kokechu must be eliminated. The Secret History claims that she died soon after, worn out by her efforts, an account that some historians, such as Igor de Rachewiltz, have called poetical melodrama. By the time of the Yuan dynasty she had received the posthumous name Empress Xuanyi.
hoffmann-la-roche: F. Hoffmann-La Roche, commonly known as Roche, was founded in 1896 by Fritz Hoffmann-La Roche and has its headquarters in Basel. It was known early on for various vitamin preparations and their derivatives, and in 1934 it became the first company to mass-produce synthetic vitamin C, under the brand name Redoxon. Descendants of the founding Hoffmann and Oeri families own slightly over half of the voting bearer shares.

During the Second World War Roche is reported to have collaborated with the Nazi regime and to have used forced labour in its German and Polish factories; it also moved all its Jewish employees to the United States. In 1957 it introduced the benzodiazepines, among them Valium and Rohypnol.

In 1973 Stanley Adams, a manager in Basel, gave the European Economic Community evidence of price fixing and market sharing for vitamins; he was imprisoned under Swiss law, and in 1999 the firm pleaded guilty to a worldwide conspiracy to fix vitamin prices and paid 500 million dollars in United States fines. In 1976 an accident at a chemical factory at Seveso in Italy, owned by a Roche subsidiary, caused a large dioxin contamination.

Roche bought the patents for the polymerase chain reaction technique in 1992, acquired Syntex in 1994 and Chugai Pharmaceuticals in 2002, and in 1998 bought Corange, parent of Boehringer Mannheim, which became Roche Diagnostics. In 1995 the United States FDA approved its HIV protease inhibitor saquinavir. In 2009 it acquired Genentech, in which it had held a majority stake since 1990, for 46.8 billion dollars.

Roche operates two divisions, Pharmaceuticals and Diagnostics. Roche Diagnostics makes equipment and reagents for research and medical diagnosis, and was organised into five business areas: Applied Science, Professional Diagnostics, Diabetes Care, Molecular Diagnostics and Tissue Diagnostics. The holding company, Roche Holding, has shares listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange. Roche also owns Genentech as a wholly owned independent subsidiary and the Japanese firm Chugai.
hoffmann-von-fallersleben: Hoffmann was born on 2 April 1798 in Fallersleben, then in the duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg, the son of a merchant who was mayor of the town. He was educated at the classical schools of Helmstedt and Braunschweig and at the universities of Göttingen and Bonn. He first intended to study theology but soon devoted himself entirely to literature.

In 1823 he became custodian of the university library at Breslau, a post he held until 1838. He was made extraordinary professor of German language and literature there in 1830 and ordinary professor in 1835. He lost his chair in 1842 because of his Unpolitische Lieder (1840–1841), which gave great offence to the authorities in Prussia.

During his exile he travelled in Germany, Switzerland and Italy and lived for two or three years in Mecklenburg, of which he became a naturalized citizen. After the revolution of 1848 he could return to Prussia, where his rights were restored. He married in 1849 and lived in Bingerbrück, Neuwied and Weimar, where he edited the Weimarische Jahrbuch with Oskar Schade from 1854 to 1857. In 1860 he became librarian to Victor I, Duke of Ratibor, at Corvey, where he died on 19 January 1874.

Hoffmann was one of the most popular poets of his time and an ardent sympathizer with progressive tendencies, among the earliest political poets who paved the way for the revolution of 1848. His verse is noted for the ease and simplicity with which it expressed the aspirations of daily life. He composed melodies for many of his songs, and his children's songs, among them Alle Vögel sind schon da and Morgen kommt der Weihnachtsmann, are known to nearly every German child.

The Lied der Deutschen, beginning Deutschland, Deutschland über alles, was set to a tune by Joseph Haydn of 1797. Its pan-German sentiments were thought inflammatory in the German principalities, and the phrase über alles then meant loyalty to a united Germany above regional loyalties rather than conquest. As a scholar he edited Reineke Vos and the Monumenta Elnonensia and wrote a history of the German church song up to Luther. His autobiography, Mein Leben, appeared in six volumes in 1868–1870.
hofuf: Al-Hofuf, also spelt Hufuf and known as Al-Hasa or Al-Ahsa, is the seat of the Al-Ahsa Governorate and the second-largest city of the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, after Dammam. It lies inland from the Persian Gulf, southwest of Abqaiq, on the road south to Haradh. It is the closest city to the Ghawar oil field, one of the world's largest conventional land-based fields.

The city proper has about 150,000 inhabitants and forms part of a larger oasis of towns and villages with some 600,000 people. The climate is hot desert, with long, very hot summers and short, mild winters. Legend places the burial of Laila and Majnoon, the star-crossed pair of the most popular love story in the Arab and Muslim world, at Hofuf, and the Queen of Sheba is fabled to have visited from her kingdom in South Arabia.

Hofuf was originally a Twelver Shi'a stronghold with a Shi'ite majority, and it produced much of the Shi'ite scholarship of the Gulf. Two of its theologians, Ibn Abi Jumhur al-Ahsa'i and Shaykh Ahmad al-Ahsa'i, are counted among its notable figures. The city served as a headquarters of the Ottoman administration and remained under Ottoman control until 1913, when it was captured by Wahhabi forces under Ibn Saud. The German explorer Hermann Burchardt photographed it in 1904.

After the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was founded in 1932, the city took the name Hofuf. Its population is now about half Shi'a and half Sunni Maliki, mostly descended from the same migrations as those to Bahrain and Kuwait.

Historically Hofuf made textiles out of wool, silk and cotton. It was known for its dates, and the khalasi variety grown there, with the fardh variety of Oman, was counted among the best. In 1920 it was known for coffee pots of silver and brass. It remains one of the largest date-producing areas in the world and is known for its old markets and palaces. Faculties of King Faisal University are in the city, and a railway station links it with Riyadh and Dammam. The population was 729,606 in 2022.
hogen-rebellion: The Hōgen rebellion, fought from 28 July to 16 August 1156, was a short civil war over the imperial succession and over how much control the Fujiwara clan, should keep. The former Emperor Toba had forced one of his sons to abdicate in favour of the son of another consort, and after 1142 the former Emperor Sutoku expected his own son to follow Emperor Konoe. When Konoe died in 1155, Toba's fourth son became Emperor Go-Shirakawa, frustrating Sutoku's hopes. Toba died on 20 July 1156, and the supporters of Go-Shirakawa and of Sutoku then disputed the accession and the continuation of cloistered government.

The dispute split the great houses. Fujiwara no Tadamichi sided with Go-Shirakawa, and his younger brother Fujiwara no Yorinaga with Sutoku. Minamoto no Tameyoshi, head of the Minamoto, and Taira no Tadamasa sided with Sutoku. Tameyoshi's eldest son Minamoto no Yoshitomo and Taira no Kiyomori, Tadamasa's nephew and head of the Taira, sided with Go-Shirakawa.

On 28 July 1156 the forces faced each other in Kyoto. Minamoto no Tametomo, a younger son of Tameyoshi, proposed a night attack on the enemy palace for Sutoku's side, but Yorinaga rejected it. Yoshitomo proposed the same on the other side and carried it out.

On the night of 29 July Kiyomori and Yoshitomo led 600 cavalry against Sutoku in the siege of Shirakawa-den. Tametomo held the west gate with his archers and repulsed both attacks, until Yoshitomo suggested setting the palace on fire. Sutoku's samurai fled from the flames and the fighting.

Sutoku was banished to Sanuki Province on Shikoku, Yorinaga was killed in the battle, and Tameyoshi and Tadamasa were executed. Tametomo survived and fled. Go-Shirakawa became cloistered emperor in 1158 and exercised power through the reigns of five emperors until his death in 1192. Yoshitomo became head of his clan, and he and Kiyomori established the Minamoto and Taira as major political powers in Kyoto. The rivalry between them led to the Heiji Rebellion in 1159, and the events are regarded as the first in a chain leading to the first of three samurai-led governments in Japan's history.

The Kamakura period epic Tale of the Disturbance in Hōgen tells of the samurai who took part. Together with the Tale of the Disturbance in Heiji and the Tale of Heike, it describes the rise and fall of the Minamoto and Taira clans.
hohenstaufen: The origin of the family remains unclear. Staufer counts are mentioned in a document of Emperor Otto III of 987 as descendants of counts of the Riesgau in the Duchy of Swabia. A count Frederick, who died about 1075, appears as progenitor in a pedigree drawn up in 1153 at the request of Frederick Barbarossa. His son Frederick of Büren married Hildegard of Egisheim, a niece of Pope Leo IX, and their son Frederick I was appointed Duke of Swabia by the Salian king Henry IV in 1079, when he was also engaged to the king's daughter Agnes.

The name Hohenstaufen was first used in the 14th century to tell the high conical hill in the Swabian Jura from the village below, and historians applied it to the dynasty in the 19th century. German historians now often prefer Staufer.

When the last Salian emperor, Henry V, died without heirs in 1125, Duke Frederick II and his brother Conrad, grandsons of Henry IV through their mother Agnes, lost the election to Lothair of Supplinburg. A civil war ended with Frederick's submission in 1134. After Lothair died, Conrad was elected king as Conrad III in 1137 and took part in the failed Second Crusade. His nephew Frederick Barbarossa, king from 1152 and emperor after 1155, struggled to restore royal power against the dukes and spent decades fighting in Italy, where the papacy and the Lombard League under Pope Alexander III denied him complete victory. He died in 1190 on the Third Crusade.

His son Henry VI married Constance of Sicily and gained the Kingdom of Sicily, a source of vast wealth, but died in 1197. A civil war followed between Philip of Swabia and the Welf Otto IV, and Philip was murdered in 1208. Frederick II, raised in Sicily, was elected king in 1215 and crowned emperor in 1220. He spent little time in Germany, founded the University of Naples in 1224 and issued the Constitutions of Melfi in 1231. Popes excommunicated him in 1227 and 1239 and a church council condemned him as a heretic in 1245. After Conrad IV died in 1254 the Great Interregnum followed.

The Staufer line ended when Charles of Anjou, promised the Kingdom of Sicily by the popes, defeated Manfred at the Battle of Benevento on 26 February 1266. Manfred was killed. Conradin's campaign to retake Sicily ended with his defeat at the Battle of Tagliacozzo in 1268, after which Charles had him publicly executed at Naples. The Kyffhäuser Monument, inaugurated in 1896, commemorates Frederick I, and the Hohenstaufen arms were adopted by Baden-Württemberg in 1954. Frederick II's Castel del Monte in Apulia, built in the 1240s, was designated a World Heritage Site in 1996.
hohenzollern-castle: The castle on Mount Hohenzollern is the third of three hilltop castles built on the site. Its name derives from Söller, meaning terrace, from the Latin solarium. The first castle was built in the 11th century by the Counts of Zollern. The House of Hohenzollern is first mentioned in 1061, and the castle itself under the name Castro Zolre in 1267. It remained with the Swabian branch of the family, the dynastic seniors of the Franconian-Brandenburgian branch that later acquired its own imperial throne.

The second castle, larger and sturdier, was begun in 1454 and served as a refuge for the Catholic Swabian Hohenzollerns, including during the Thirty Years' War. Württemberg troops captured it in 1634, and it then came under Habsburg control for about a century. French soldiers occupied it in the winter of 1744/45. After the last Austrian owner left in 1798 it fell into ruin, and by the beginning of the 19th century only the Chapel of St Michael remained usable.

The present castle was the work of Crown Prince Frederick William IV of Prussia, who climbed the mountain in 1819 on his way to Italy to learn about his family's roots. As king he wrote in 1844 of his wish to see the castle made habitable again. He engaged the architect Friedrich August Stüler, whose design of 1846 drew on English Gothic Revival architecture and the châteaux of the Loire Valley. Construction began in 1850 and was completed on 3 October 1867 under Frederick William's brother, King William I, funded by the Brandenburg-Prussian and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen lines of the family.

The castle covers almost the whole summit. The Eagle Gate and its drawbridge form the entrance, and the palatial buildings stand on the outline of the second castle. The Count's Hall has rib vaulting supported by eight free-standing red marble columns, with grisailles by Stüler depicting the history of the House of Hohenzollern. Like Neuschwanstein, it is a monument to German Romanticism and an idealised vision of a medieval knight's castle.

After its completion the castle was not regularly occupied but used mainly as a showpiece, and none of the Hohenzollern emperors lived there. The last Prussian Crown Prince, Wilhelm, stayed there for several months after fleeing Potsdam ahead of Soviet forces in 1945, and he and his wife Cecilie are buried there. From 1952 Prince Louis Ferdinand of Prussia added artworks and memorabilia, among them the Crown of Wilhelm II and a uniform of Frederick the Great. An earthquake on 3 September 1978 caused some turrets to collapse, and repairs lasted until the mid-1990s. The castle is privately owned by the House of Hohenzollern.
hohhot: Hohhot is the capital and largest city of Inner Mongolia, in the south-central part of the region. It is encircled by the Daqing Shan, the Great Blue Mountains, to the north and the Hetao Plateau to the south. The Mongolian name means Blue City, and in Chinese it can be rendered Qīng Chéng. The climate is cold and semi-arid, with long, dry winters and hot, somewhat humid summers.

In antiquity the area belonged to Yunzhong Commandery, created in the reign of King Wuling of Zhao. Under Qin and Han it was the frontier with the Xiongnu, and from the reign of Emperor Wu it became a base for operations against them. In 127 BCE General Wei Qing led a cavalry force of 40,000 from Yunzhong and conquered the Hetao and Ordos regions. In 386 the Tuoba chieftain Tuoba Gui refounded the Dai state and later renamed it Wei.

In 1557 the Tümed Mongol leader Altan Khan began building the Da Zhao Temple to persuade the Ming government of his leadership of the southern Mongol tribes. The town that grew around it was called Kokegota, the Blue Town. In 1570 Altan Khan negotiated an end to the Ming blockade of Mongol access to iron, cotton and seeds by establishing a vassal-tributary relationship, and in 1575 the Ming renamed the town Guihua. In 1631 Ligdan Khan razed the city. Under the Qing, the garrison town of Suiyuan was built 2 kilometres to the north-east, and in 1913 the Republic of China united the two towns as Guisui.

In the 1930s the Japanese, who created the puppet state of Mengjiang, renamed it Hohhot, and after 1945 it became Guisui again. After 1949 it was renamed Hohhot, and in 1952 the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region chose it as its administrative centre, replacing Zhangjiakou.

Hohhot had 3,446,100 inhabitants at the 2020 census, most of them Han Chinese; many of the Mongols in the city speak Chinese. By regulation, street signs and public transport announcements are in both Chinese and Mongolian. It is known for its historical sites and temples, among them the Da Zhao, and is home to Inner Mongolia University.
hojo-clan: The Hōjō are alleged to have been an offshoot of the Taira of the Kanmu branch, originating in Izu Province, though modern theories question whether the clan really descended from the Taira. They gained power by supporting the warlord Minamoto no Yoritomo in the Genpei War, through military assistance and through marriage to his blood relatives. Hōjō Tokimasa helped his son-in-law Yoritomo defeat the Taira and become Japan's first shōgun, and Tokimasa's daughter Hōjō Masako was married to Yoritomo.

When Yoritomo died, eighteen years later, the Hōjō usurped power from his family. Tokimasa appointed himself shikken, regent, to the former shōgun's young son, which effectively transferred control of the shogunate to his clan permanently. The shōguns became puppets and hostages of the Hōjō.

The imperial court at Kyoto resented the decline of its authority, and the Hōjō in turn despised the weak Emperor Go-Toba. In 1221 the Jōkyū War broke out between forces loyal to the recently retired Go-Toba and the second regent, Hōjō Yoshitoki. The Hōjō forces won easily. The court was brought under the direct control of the shogunate, the emperor was exiled to the Oki islands, and the court had to seek the shōgun's approval for all its actions. It kept its estates in Kyoto, since it conveyed needed legitimacy on an otherwise unlawful shogunate.

In 1225 the third regent, Hōjō Yasutoki, established the Hyōjōsho, the Council of State, which let potential rivals share in decision-making and ended the threat of civil war. The regent presided over it. In 1232 came the Goseibai Shikimoku, Japan's first military code of law. It stressed the duties of stewards and constables, provided means for settling land disputes, set rules on inheritance and stipulated punishments, and it remained in effect for the next 635 years. The Hōjō are also known for fostering Zen Buddhism and for leading the successful opposition to the Mongol invasions of Japan.

Resentment of Hōjō rule eventually culminated in the overthrow of the clan and the establishment of the Ashikaga shogunate. The office of shikken passed through the clan from Hōjō Tokimasa, who held it from 1203 to 1205, to Hōjō Sadayuki in 1333.
