The Taiheiki, an epic of the late 14th century, tells of the fall of the Hōjō and the rise of the Ashikaga, and of the period of war between the Northern Court of Ashikaga Takauji in Kyoto and the Southern Court of Emperor Go-Daigo in Yoshino.
hojo-soun: Hōjō Sōun, also known as Ise Sōzui, was a daimyo and the first head of the Later Hōjō clan, one of the major powers of Japan's Sengoku period. He belonged to a cadet branch of the Ise family. Tradition held him to be a rōnin who rose almost overnight in the Kantō, but he came from a prestigious family in the direct employment of the Ashikaga shogunate and had important connections: his sister married Imagawa Yoshitada, a major daimyo from a cadet branch of the Ashikaga family. It has been said that he was born at Takakoshi castle in Okayama. In 1483 Ise Moritoki, as he then was, became one of the mōshitsugishū, the shogunal liaison officials, serving Shogun Ashikaga Yoshihisa.

About 1475, under the name Ise Shinkurō, he worked for the Imagawa, constables of Suruga Province, and eventually became an independent leader with a number of warriors joining him. After Yoshitada died in 1476, he supported his nephew Ryūōmaru, later Imagawa Ujichika, in a succession dispute with Oshika Norimitsu and mediated between the two sides. In 1487, operating from Ishiwaki Castle, he attacked the Imagawa residence and defeated Norimitsu, and Ujichika rewarded him with Kōkokuji Castle.

In 1493 he invaded Izu Province and attacked Ashikaga Chachamaru at the Horigoe residence. The conquest took several years, and he made Nirayama Castle his headquarters. Most historians credit him as the first Sengoku daimyo for this conquest. In 1494 he secured Odawara Castle, which became the centre of the Hōjō domains for nearly a century; he seized it by treachery, after arranging for its lord to be murdered while out hunting. By his siege of the castle of Arai in 1516 he was virtual master of all Sagami.

In 1518 Sōun handed the leadership of the clan to his son Hōjō Ujitsuna, and he died at Nirayama Castle in 1519. The surname Hōjō was adopted by Ujitsuna in 1523, after his death, changing the clan's name from Ise. In 1521 Ujitsuna had built the Sōun-ji temple dedicated to his father. Sōun had a wife, Nan'yoin-dono, who bore Ujitsuna and Hōjō Ujitoki, and two concubines, one of whom bore Hōjō Genan.
hojo-tokimune: Tokimune was born on 5 June 1251, the second son of Hōjō Tokiyori, fifth shikken of the Kamakura shogunate, and was seen from birth as the future tokusō, head of the Hōjō clan. The shikken was officially the regent of the shōgun but the de facto ruler of Japan, and by Tokimune's lifetime the Emperor, the imperial regent (sesshō), the chief advisor (kampaku) and the shōgun had all been pushed aside by the Hōjō. He became shikken himself in 1268, at the age of 18.

A threatening letter and envoys from the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan had reached Japan in January 1268, demanding a tributary relationship. Many in the government, including members of the imperial family, urged a compromise, but Tokimune sent the envoys back without an answer and had later embassies, in 1269, 1271 and 1272, driven away without leave to land. After the first invasion of 1274 he had five envoys who arrived in Kyūshū in September 1275 brought to Kamakura and beheaded; their graves remain at Tatsunokuchi. Five more were beheaded at Hakata in 1279.

Expecting another attack, the Imperial Court on 21 February 1280 ordered all temples and shrines to pray for victory over the Mongol Empire. Kublai Khan's second invasion, in 1281, failed again, in part because of a typhoon later called kamikaze, divine wind, and in part through the resistance of the samurai, whose defence Tokimune planned and led. In 1271 he had also banished the monk Nichiren to Sado Island.

Tokimune had followed the Ritsu school of Buddhism as a young man but turned to Zen, seeking the advice of his master Mugaku Sogen on overcoming fear. After the wars he founded Engaku-ji as a memorial to the samurai who had died against the Mongols, and on the day of his death, 20 April 1284, he took the tonsure as a Zen monk. Through his influence Zen became firmly established in Kamakura, then in Kyoto and across Japan, above all among the warrior class.
hojo-ujimasa: Ujimasa was born in 1538, the second son of Hōjō Ujiyasu, and bore the childhood name Matsuchiyo-maru. His elder brother Shinkuro died young, so he became his father's heir. When Ujiyasu allied with Takeda Shingen and Imagawa Yoshimoto in 1554, Ujimasa married Shingen's daughter Ōbai-in, and he took over formal leadership of the family around 1559, on his father's retirement. Under him the clan reached the largest territory in its history.

In 1560 the clan seized Iwatsuki Castle and took almost all of Musashi Province, and Ujimasa fought at the Battle of Konodai in 1564 and in the Siege of Odawara of 1569. In 1574 he forced the surrender of Sekiyado Castle in Shimosa and won over Yuki Harutomi, a vassal of the Uesugi, and in 1575 he took Gion Castle in Shimotsuke. In 1577 he invaded Kazusa and made peace with his old enemy Satomi Yoshihiro, in the first battle of his heir, Hōjō Ujinao.

In 1580, after Takeda Katsuyori backed Uesugi Kagekatsu, Ujimasa allied with Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu and attacked Takeda lands in Suruga, joining the conquest of Kai in 1582. When Nobunaga died suddenly that year he attacked Oda territory at the Battle of Kanagawa, and a settlement with the Tokugawa gave the Hōjō Kozuke Province while Kai and Shinano went to the Tokugawa.

In 1588 Toyotomi Hideyoshi asked Ujimasa and Ujinao to attend the imperial visit to his residence, the Jurakudai, in Kyoto. Ujimasa refused, and Hideyoshi rejected his offer to come in 1590 instead. That year Hideyoshi's army, the largest in Japan, surrounded Odawara, then the biggest castle in the country, and took the Hōjō's other Kantō castles one by one. After Odawara fell, Ujimasa died by seppuku with his brother Ujiteru on 10 August 1590, leaving two death poems.
hojo-ujinao: Ujinao was born at Odawara Castle in 1562, the son of Hōjō Ujimasa and the grandson of Hōjō Ujiyasu, and was given the childhood name Kuniōmaru. His mother was a daughter of Takeda Shingen. He came of age early in 1577 and took the formal name Ujinao. His marriage to Tokuhime, the second daughter of Tokugawa Ieyasu, was a condition of peace between the two clans. He held junior fifth court rank, lower grade, and the title Sakyō-dayu, and fought his first battle in his father's invasion of Kazusa Province.

After the death of Oda Nobunaga in 1582 the Hōjō invaded Kai and Shinano Provinces, lands held by the remnants of small clans that had served the Takeda. Tokugawa Ieyasu and the Uesugi clan sought the same territory, and the three-way struggle became known as the Tenshō-Jingo war. Ujinao attacked Takigawa Kazumasu, a senior retainer of the Oda, at the Battle of Kanagawa on the border of Kōzuke and Musashi; Kazumasu, with 18,000 troops against 55,000, was defeated and retreated to Nagashima.

Ujinao then led around 50,000 men against about 8,000 Tokugawa soldiers near Wakamiko Castle. In the final phase, at Kurokoma, a Tokugawa raiding force of 2,000 under Mizuno Katsushige and Torii Mototada drove back a Hōjō detachment of 10,000 led by Ujinao, and the Hōjō failed to encircle the Tokugawa army. As the war turned in Ieyasu's favour and Sanada Masayuki went over to the Tokugawa side, the Hōjō negotiated a truce, mediated by Oda Nobukatsu, Oda Nobutaka and Toyotomi Hideyoshi. An invasion of Hōjō territory by Satake Yoshishige also pressed them to accept it.

When Odawara fell to Hideyoshi's siege in 1590, Ujinao's father and uncle were forced to commit suicide. Ujinao was spared as Ieyasu's son-in-law and went into exile on Mount Kōya with his wife, dying there in 1591. With him the Later Hōjō clan lost its entire domain. His adopted son, Hōjō Ujimori, became the first daimyō of Sayama-han in Kawachi Province. Among his children by Tokuhime were a son and a daughter, Hoshuin-dono, who married Ikeda Toshitaka.
hojo-ujitsuna: Ujitsuna was the son of Hōjō Sōun, the founder of the Go-Hōjō clan, and he carried on his father's effort to win control of the Kantō, the region around present-day Tokyo. In 1524 he took Edo Castle from Uesugi Tomooki, which began a long rivalry between the Hōjō and Uesugi families. In 1526 he was defeated by Takeda Nobutora at the Battle of Nashinokidaira.

The Uesugi then attacked and burned the shrine of Tsurugaoka Hachimangū in Kamakura. The loss weighed heavily on the Hōjō as a symbol, because the earlier Hōjō clan, from which they had taken their name, had fallen in the Siege of Kamakura in 1333. Ujitsuna soon began rebuilding the shrine, a work completed in 1540. In 1530 his son Ujiyasu defeated Uesugi Tomooki at the Battle of Ozawahara.

When the Uesugi attacked Edo again in 1535, while Ujitsuna was away fighting the Takeda, he returned, defeated Tomooki and recovered his lands. After Tomooki died in 1537, Ujitsuna occupied Musashi Province and seized Kawagoe Castle to secure his hold on the Kantō. In 1538 he won the Battle of Kōnodai, which secured Shimōsa Province for the Hōjō, and in 1539 he defeated Yoshiaki, the Oyumi Kubo, and gained control of Awa Province.

In the years before his death on 10 August 1541, Ujitsuna oversaw the rebuilding of Kamakura, which he made a symbol of the growing power of the Hōjō, along with Odawara and Edo. He was succeeded as head of the clan and lord of Odawara by Hōjō Ujiyasu, his son by his wife Yōjuin-dono. His other children included Hōjō Tamemasa, Hōjō Ujitaka and the adopted Hōjō Tsunashige, and his daughters married into other houses; one of them, Hōshun’in, became the wife of Ashikaga Haruuji.
hojo-ujiyasu: Ujiyasu, whose childhood name was Chiyomaru, was a son of Hōjō Ujitsuna. He fought his first battle at fifteen, against Uesugi Tomooki of the Ōgigayatsu Uesugi clan at the Battle of Ozawahara in 1530. His only known wife, Zuikei-in, was a sister of Imagawa Yoshimoto. When his father died in 1541, enemies of the Hōjō tried to seize their strongholds, and the almost constant warfare pushed Ujiyasu to reorganise the administration of his lands.

He ordered cadastral surveys in 1542 and 1543 and in 1550 overhauled the Kandaka taxation system. Odawara, the town of his home castle, grew into a trading centre as its roads were redirected and an artisans' guild was set up in the castle town, while post stations and markets spread through Hōjō lands.

At Kawagoe the garrison of Hōjō Tsunashige, about 3,000 men, faced a besieging army of Uesugi Tomosada, Uesugi Norimasa and the Koga Kubo Ashikaga Haruuji said to number 80,000. Ujiyasu came with 8,000, used ninja to learn the enemy's plans, and attacked by night with men who wore light armour and were ordered not to stop to take heads. The victory ended the Ōgigayatsu Uesugi line, and many Kantō warlords became Hōjō vassals. In 1551 he drove Norimasa from Hirai Castle to Echigo, into the care of Nagao Kagetora, the later Uesugi Kenshin.

Ujiyasu retired in 1559, at 45, and his son Hōjō Ujimasa became formal head of the family, but he remained active. Kenshin besieged Odawara Castle in 1561 and burned the town before withdrawing after two months. Allied with Takeda Shingen, Ujiyasu retook Matsuyama Castle in 1563 and won the Battle of Kōnodai against Satomi Yoshihiro in 1564, extending Hōjō rule over Sagami, Izu, Musashi, Shimōsa and Kazusa. Satake Yoshishige checked him at the Battle of Numajiri in 1567.

Shingen turned on the Hōjō in 1568 and in 1569 burned the town of Odawara, before Ujiyasu's sons Ujiteru and Ujikuni attacked his withdrawing army at Mimasetoge. Ujiyasu then made peace with both rivals, letting his son Hōjō Saburō be adopted by the childless Kenshin and accepting Shingen's hold on Suruga. He died on 21 October 1571, leaving his domains to Ujimasa in a relatively favourable position. He was known as the Lion of Sagami.
hoki-province: Hōki, abbreviated Hakushū, lay in the San'in region and was bordered by the provinces of Inaba, Mimasaka, Izumo, Bitchū and Bingo. In the Gokishichidō system it belonged to the San'indo circuit, and the Engishiki classed it as one of the 35 superior countries in importance and one of the middle countries in distance from the capital. The provincial capital stood in what is now the city of Kurayoshi, and its ichinomiya was the Shitori Shrine. Because of close ties with Izumo, the two are sometimes grouped as the Unpaku region, while Mount Daisen divides Hōki itself into an eastern Tōhaku and a western Saihaku.

From before the Kofun period the area belonged to the Izumo cultural sphere, producing iron and forging swords, and it was drawn gradually under Yamato rule from the late Kofun to the Asuka period. The Hōki Fudoki explains the name by the legend of Princess Inada, who fled the serpent Yamata no Orochi into its mountains crying out to her mother, and the Kojiki places the grave of the creator kami Izanami on its border with Izumo. At the end of the Kamakura period the exiled Emperor Go-Daigo, escaping from the Oki Islands, made Hōki his first base against the shogunate.

In the Muromachi period the Yamana clan were nominal shugo but held little real control. In the Sengoku period the Amago and Mōri clans and Oda Nobunaga contested the province until his general Hashiba Hideyoshi took it. Under the Edo shogunate the whole province was ruled by a branch of the Ikeda clan as part of the 320,000 koku Tottori Domain, although the temple and pilgrimage centre of Daisen-ji remained independent. An early Meiji survey counted 778 villages with a kokudaka of 245,034 koku.

Hōki became part of Tottori Prefecture on 29 August 1871 and now forms its western half. Tottori was merged into Shimane Prefecture in 1876 and separated again in 1881, and the old province name remained in legal use for some time, appearing in treaties of 1894 with the United States and the United Kingdom.
hokkaido: Hokkaido is separated from Honshu by the Tsugaru Strait, and the two islands are connected by railway through the Seikan Tunnel. It has coastlines on the Sea of Japan, the Sea of Okhotsk and the Pacific Ocean, and lies about 43 kilometres south of Sakhalin. The centre of the island is mountainous, with volcanic plateaux, and its plains include the Ishikari, Tokachi and Kushiro plains. It has a colder climate than the rest of Japan and heavy winter snowfall, yet it is an agricultural region for many crops.

During the Jōmon period a hunter-gatherer culture flourished in Hokkaido, beginning over 15,000 years ago, and Jōmon beliefs in natural spirits are theorized to have given rise to Ainu spirituality. About 2,000 years ago Yayoi people colonized the island, and much of its population shifted from hunting and gathering to agriculture. In the Muromachi period (1336 to 1573) the Japanese established a settlement at the south of the Oshima Peninsula. Disputes with the Ainu developed into a war, and in 1457 Takeda Nobuhiro killed the Ainu leader Koshamain and defeated the opposition.

His descendants ruled the Matsumae domain, which held exclusive trading rights with the Ainu in the Azuchi-Momoyama and Edo periods and relied on that trade for its economy. The Matsumae held authority over the south of the island, then called Ezochi, until the end of the Edo period.

Shortly after the Boshin War in 1868, Tokugawa loyalists led by Enomoto Takeaki occupied the island temporarily. Their rebellion, commonly but mistakenly called the Republic of Ezo, was defeated in May 1869. Ezochi was then annexed into Japanese territory through colonial practices, and the Meiji government, setting up the Development Commission, renamed it Hokkaido, written 北海道 and translated as "northern sea route". Japanese settlers dispossessed the Ainu of their land and forced them to assimilate. In July 1945 ports, cities and military facilities in Hokkaido were attacked by the United States Navy's Task Force 38, and the Soviet Union prepared an invasion before the Japanese surrender.

Hokkaido is the second-largest of Japan's four main islands, and with its surrounding islands it forms the largest and northernmost prefecture. Its capital and largest city is Sapporo. It became equal with the other prefectures in 1947, when the revised Local Autonomy Act came into effect. The Hokkaido Development Agency was founded in 1949 and absorbed into the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport in 2001. The island has more brown bears than anywhere else in Asia except Russia.
hokuriku-region: The Hokuriku region lies in the north-western part of Honshu, along the Sea of Japan, and forms part of the larger Chūbu region. It is almost equivalent to the former Koshi Province and to the Hokurikudō area of pre-modern Japan. Its four prefectures are Ishikawa, Fukui, Niigata and Toyama, although Niigata is sometimes counted as an addition rather than one of the core prefectures. Other regional definitions overlap it: Hokushin'etsu includes both the Hokuriku and Shin'etsu regions, Kōshin'etsu takes in Niigata, Nagano and Yamanashi, and Shin'etsu covers Niigata and Nagano.

The region has the highest volume of snowfall of any inhabited and arable region in the world. Dry Siberian air masses pick up high humidity over the Sea of Japan and are forced upwards by the mountains of Honshū, so that the moisture condenses as snow. The long winters and deep snow are depicted in Hokuetsu Seppu, an encyclopedic work of the late Edo period describing life in the Uonuma district of Niigata Prefecture, and in Yasunari Kawabata's novel Snow Country.

From the Heian period until the Edo period the Hokuriku was a core recipient of population. It grew to be proportionately much larger than it is today, despite its rural character. In modern times its population has remained consistent, and most urban growth in the 20th century took place instead in Kanto, Chūkyō and Kansai. The region is also known for traditional culture that originated elsewhere and has long since been lost along the Taiheiyō Belt.

The main population centres are Jōetsu and Nagaoka, which are special cities, the core cities of Kanazawa, Toyama and Fukui, and Niigata, a designated city and the largest, with a population of over 800,000. The main industries include chemicals, medicine, tourism, textiles and textile machinery, heavy machinery, farming and fishing, and Koshihikari, a popular variety of rice, is a special product of the region.

The Hokuriku Shinkansen, formerly the Nagano Shinkansen, was extended from Nagano to Kanazawa in March 2015, which gave direct bullet train services from Tokyo and cut the journey from Tokyo to Toyama to about two hours. In March 2024 the line was extended to Tsuruga via Fukui.
holdfast-bay: Colonel William Light, surveyor general of South Australia, named the bay in mid-1836; his journal records his pleasure at the quality of the anchorage after riding out a storm there. The pioneers who were to found the colony landed at Holdfast Bay in 1836 and 1837. On 8 November 1836 Robert Gouger, the Colonial Secretary and Chief Magistrate, arrived aboard the Africaine and set up camp near the Old Gum Tree.

With Governor Hindmarsh's arrival and proclamation of the colony on 28 December, the settlement at Holdfast Bay became the first seat of government of South Australia, and it remained so until mid-March 1837. On 31 December 1836 the settlement was renamed Glenelg. The Corporate Town of Glenelg, later the City of Glenelg, was established in 1855 to govern the township and its surroundings, and the local government area along the shore today is the City of Holdfast Bay.

The small bay lies in Gulf St Vincent next to Adelaide and holds both natural and artificial reefs. The Brighton and Glenelg jetties and The Blocks, a disused maritime structure of concrete and steel columns that now acts as a broken breakwater and reef, can be reached by swimming from the shore. A reef of tyre tetrahedrons was laid about 5 km west of Glenelg in 1983, and two vessels, the Glenelg barge and the South Australian, were scuttled in 15 to 20 metres of water.

The natural reefs lie between 8 and 24 metres deep. Among them are Devil's Elbow, where two shelves meet at a right angle and giant Australian cuttlefish are found; Fred's Rock, at 24 metres, part of a ground that includes the wreck of the Claris; and Seacliff Reef, the remains of a shoreline about 10,000 years old, which supports the largest known population of western blue devils in the waters around metropolitan Adelaide.
holetown: The English first came ashore at the site in 1625, when an expedition led by John Powell, blown off course on its way from South America to England, claimed the island for the Kingdom of England, left some possessions behind and sailed on; a Captain Cataline had landed earlier, in 1620, to collect water. Captain Henry Powell, John's brother, returned in 1627 with the merchant Sir William Courteen, fifty other shareholder settlers and ten captives. A monument to this first landing gives the date wrongly as 1605.

The town takes its name from a stream, The Hole, which gave the settlers a safe landing place. Until 1629 it was the island's only town, and it holds the island's first five plantations, its first major fortification, first place of justice and first Governor's House. St. James Parish Church, the oldest church on the island, was built there in 1628. The settlement traded across the Atlantic with Bristol, London and Boston, though the trade with Boston was deemed illegal.

After Lord Carlisle gained control of Barbados as a protectorate of the Crown, he founded his own settlement in the south of the island along Carlisle Bay. That settlement grew into Bridgetown, and the capital moved there.

Holetown is a small town in the parish of Saint James on the sheltered west coast of Barbados. Since 1977 it has held the Barbados Holetown Festival each year to mark the first landing of the settlers. The town is home to McGill University's Bellairs Research Institute.
holkars: The Holkars were of Dhangar origin. Malhar Rao Holkar, born at Murum in Satara district, led Maratha armies in Malwa in the 1720s under the Peshwa Bajirao I and in 1733 was granted nine parganas near Indore. He set up the camp later called Malharganj in 1734 and in 1747 began his palace, the Rajwada. By his death in 1766 he looked after much of Malwa for the Peshwas and was acknowledged as one of the five houses of the Maratha Empire.

His daughter-in-law Ahilyabai Holkar, who ruled from 1767 to 1795, moved the capital to Maheshwar on the Narmada and built and endowed Hindu temples from Dwarka in Gujarat to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple at Varanasi. Yashwantrao Holkar, who ruled from 1797, tried in the unsuccessful Second Anglo-Maratha War to free the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II from the British, and the Treaty of Rajghat of December 1805 recognised him as a sovereign king.

After his death in 1811 the four-year-old Malhar Rao Holkar III succeeded him, and his mother, Tulsabai Holkar, ran the government until Gaffur Khan Pindari, who had secretly come to terms with the British, killed her on 19 December 1817. Defeated in the Third Anglo-Maratha War, the Holkars accepted a treaty at Mandsaur on 6 January 1818, lost much of their territory and became a princely state of the Central India Agency with its capital at Indore. Bhimabai Holkar rejected the treaty and fought on with guerrilla raids.

Tukojirao Holkar II, installed in 1844, stayed loyal to the East India Company during the rebellion of 1857 and in 1872 appointed T. Madhava Rao as his diwan. Yashwantrao Holkar II, the last ruling maharaja, signed a covenant on 22 April 1948 with the rulers of neighbouring princely states to form Madhya Bharat, of which Indore became a district; Madhya Bharat was merged into Madhya Pradesh in 1956.
holocaust: Jews have lived in Europe for more than two thousand years. Throughout the Middle Ages they were subjected to antisemitism based on Christian theology, which blamed them for killing Jesus. In the 19th century many European countries granted Jews full citizenship, and political antisemitism, positing an international Jewish conspiracy, emerged with the rise of nationalism and industrialization. After the First World War the German military promoted the untrue idea that Germany had been stabbed in the back by socialists and Jews.

Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933. Within months all other parties were banned and tens of thousands of political opponents arrested. The regime passed anti-Jewish laws, encouraged violence and orchestrated the nationwide pogrom known as Kristallnacht in November 1938, meaning to force all German Jews to emigrate.

After Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, the occupation authorities began to establish ghettos to segregate Jews. Following the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, German forces and local collaborators murdered 1.5 to 2 million Jews. Most historians agree that Hitler issued an explicit order to kill all Jews in Europe, but disagree about when. Reinhard Heydrich convened the Wannsee Conference on 20 January 1942, and the Final Solution was implemented to murder all Jews in Europe.

Victims were deported to extermination camps, chiefly Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Belzec, Sobibor, Chełmno and Majdanek in occupied Poland, where those who survived the journey were gassed. Others were sent to forced labour camps, where many died of starvation, abuse and exhaustion. The murder rate was highest during Operation Reinhard, from March 1942 to November 1943. In 1944 about 437,000 Hungarian Jews were deported in eight weeks, mostly to Auschwitz. The killings continued until 1945.

Around six million Jews were killed, about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population. Half of the victims came from Poland. Many survivors emigrated from Europe after the war, and the Kielce pogrom convinced many that they could not stay in eastern Europe. Relatively few perpetrators faced criminal trials, and billions of dollars in reparations have been paid, though they fall short of the losses suffered. The Holocaust is considered the largest genocide in human history and has become central to Western historical consciousness.
holodomor: The Holodomor was part of the wider Soviet famine of 1930 to 1933, which affected the major grain-producing areas of the Soviet Union. Ukraine was one of the largest grain-producing states in the USSR and was subject to unreasonably high grain quotas compared with the rest of the country in 1930. Several repressive policies came before and during the famine, among them the persecution of the Orthodox Church, the Law of Spikelets, the blacklisting of villages, the internal passport system and harsh grain requisitions. Between 1926 and 1939 the Ukrainian population grew by only 6.6 per cent, while Russia's grew by 16.9 per cent.

The famine struck the Ukrainian SSR in spring 1932 and again from February to July 1933, with most victims recorded in spring 1933. The authorities continued the grain requisitions and left the population without means of subsistence. The oblasts of Kyiv and Kharkiv had the highest losses although they produced far less grain than other areas, and their quotas had been doubled in 1931 against a national average increase of 9 per cent. Cannibalism was documented, and at least 2,505 people were sentenced for it in 1932 and 1933, though the real number was certainly much higher.

The exact number of victims is unknown. A joint statement to the United Nations signed by 25 countries in November 2003 declared that 7 to 10 million people died, and more recent scholarship has estimated between 3.5 and 5 million. Soviet authorities tried to hide the scale of the disaster, but it became known abroad through journalists such as Gareth Jones and Malcolm Muggeridge.

The Soviet Union long denied that the famine had occurred, and public discussion of it was banned until the glasnost reforms of Mikhail Gorbachev in the 1980s. Scholars agree that it was primarily man-made, but they dispute whether it was intentional, whether it targeted Ukrainians and whether it was a genocide, because no document explicitly orders the starvation of any area. Some historians conclude that Stalin deliberately engineered it to eliminate a Ukrainian independence movement, while others hold that it was chiefly a result of collectivisation and industrialisation.

Ukraine has recognised the Holodomor as a genocide since 2006, and so have the European Parliament and a number of other states. In 2008 the Russian State Duma condemned the Soviet regime for neglecting the lives of people in pursuit of economic and political goals.
holon: Holon lies in the Tel Aviv District, south of Tel Aviv, and is part of the Gush Dan metropolitan area. Its name comes from the Hebrew word holon, meaning a little sand, and refers to the sand dunes on which the city was built. The name also appears in the Book of Joshua (21:15), in the words Holon with its suburbs and Debir with its suburbs. The city has the second-largest industrial zone in Israel, after Haifa.

Holon was founded in 1935 on sand dunes about six kilometres from Tel Aviv. The Łódzia textile factory was established there by Jewish immigrants from Łódź in Poland, along with many other industrial enterprises. In February 1936 the cornerstone was laid for Kiryat Avoda, a Modernist building complex designed by the architect Joseph Neufeld to ease the shortage of housing for municipal workers.

In the early months of the 1948 Arab-Israeli War Holon was on the front line, with constant shooting along the border with the village of Tel al-Rish, a suburb of Arab Jaffa to its north-west, and clashes towards the town of Yazur to the east. An attack on Tel al-Rish by Haganah militia units based in Holon was repulsed with considerable losses. After the establishment of the state, Holon grew to take in Tel al-Rish, renamed Tel Giborim, and the orange groves of Yazur.

Holon is home to more than half of the world's Samaritan population. In 1954 the president of Israel, Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, helped to establish a Samaritan quarter on the outskirts of the city. It was named Neve Pinchas after Pinhas Ben-Abraham, the high priest of the Samaritan community, and has its own synagogues and street signs in Samaritan Hebrew. Holon is one of only two places with a Samaritan community, the other being the village of Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim above Nablus.

The city once had the image of a working-class dormitory community, and has presented itself as a children's city. It has the Holon Children's Museum, the Israeli Museum of Caricature and Comics, the Design Museum Holon, the first Israeli museum of design, and an annual street carnival for the festival of Purim, the Adloyada. Landmarks slated for preservation include Derech Habitachon, paved during the 1948 war, and several water towers.
holstentor: Lübeck was reached by three gates, the Citadel Gate in the north, the Mill Gate in the south and the Holsten Gate in the west. The western exit led towards Holstein, which gave the Holsten Bridge over the Trave River and its gate their name. The bridge is first mentioned in a deed of the king of Denmark of 1216. The standing gate was in fact the fourth in a series of Holsten gates, first called the Outer and later the Middle Holsten Gate.

In the fifteenth century the older gate was judged inadequate against firearms and cannon. Funds came from a legacy of 4,000 Lübeck marks left by the councilman John Broling. The city architect Hinrich Helmstede began construction in 1464, on a hill raised to seven metres. The ground was marshy, and the south tower began to sag while the building was still going up.

The gate consists of a north tower, a south tower and a central block, built of red brick. On the field side, facing west, the towers form semicircles that project 3.5 metres beyond the central block, and the wall there is 3.5 metres thick, against less than one metre on the city side, which is richly windowed. The towers held gun chambers behind loopholes, and windows above the passage could be used to pour pitch or boiling water on intruders. Two bands of terracotta tiles run around the building.

Other Holsten gates were demolished in 1808, 1828 and 1853, the last for the first Lübeck railway station, and in 1855 a petition with 683 signatures asked the Senate to remove the remaining gate. Opposition to the loss of old buildings grew. In 1863 Lübeck's citizens decided by a majority of one vote to restore it, and work continued into 1871. Further stabilisation followed in 1933 and 1934 and again from 2005 to 2006.

The German Association of Cities took the gate as its symbol in 1925. It appeared on the 50 DM banknote issued from 1960 to 1991 and on the German two-euro coin of 2006. In 1950 it became a museum of city history, which was modernised in 2002.
holy-alliance: The Holy Alliance, also called the Grand Alliance, linked the absolute monarchies of Austria, Prussia and Russia. It was created after the final defeat of Napoleon at the behest of Emperor Alexander I of Russia and signed in Paris on 26 September 1815. Alexander wanted to instil the divine right of kings and Christian values in European political life, under the influence of his spiritual adviser Baroness Barbara von Krüdener. The text was written by Alexander and edited by Ioannis Kapodistrias and Alexandru Sturdza.

Under the treaty European rulers would govern as "branches" of the Christian community and offer one another mutual service. The first draft appealed to mysticism through a proposed unified Christian empire, which the other monarchies found disconcerting, and a more pragmatic version was adopted. About three months after the Final Act of the Congress of Vienna, the monarchs of Catholic Austria, Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia promised to act on the basis of "justice, love, and peace". The French diplomat Dominique-Georges-Frédéric Dufour de Pradt called the document "an apocalypse of diplomacy".

The agreement was at first secret and was mistrusted by liberals. The United Kingdom rejected it, though George IV consented as King of Hanover, as did the Papal States and the Ottoman Empire. Lord Castlereagh, the British Foreign Secretary, called it "a piece of sublime mysticism and nonsense". Britain nevertheless took part in the Concert of Europe.

In practice the Austrian chancellor, Prince Klemens von Metternich, made it a bastion against democracy and nationalism. It also coordinated the suppression of Polish efforts to restore an independent state, by Austria in Galicia and Lodomeria, by Russia in Congress Poland and by Prussia in Posen and West Prussia. At the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1818 the monarchs demanded stern measures against university demagogues, carried out in the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819. At Troppau in 1820 and Laibach in 1821 Metternich sought to align his allies against the Carbonari revolt against Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies, and in 1822 the Congress of Verona advised against the Greek Revolution and resolved on the French invasion of Spain.

The alliance is conventionally taken to have become defunct with Alexander's death in 1825, and France went its own way after the July Revolution of 1830. The three eastern powers agreed the Münchengrätz Convention in September 1833 and met again to suppress the revolutions of 1848. The Austro-Russian alliance broke up in the Crimean War, when Austria declared itself neutral and occupied the Danubian Principalities in 1854. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck reunited the three powers as the League of the Three Emperors after German unification in 1871, but it faltered in the 1880s over the decline of the Ottoman Empire.
holy-cross-abbey: Holy Cross Abbey, in Irish Mainistir na Croise Naofa, stands at Holycross near Thurles and takes its name from its relic of the True Cross, the Holy Rood. This supposed fragment was brought to Ireland around 1233 by the Plantagenet Queen Isabella of Angoulême, the widow of King John, who gave it to the Cistercian monastery and rebuilt it.

Over time the abbey and its relic drew pilgrims, and after the Protestant Reformation it became a rallying point for victims of religious persecution. As a symbol of the Catholic Church in Ireland and of resistance, and allegedly of the struggle for Irish independence, it moved Sir Henry Sidney, Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, to complain of it to Queen Elizabeth I in 1567. In September 1583 Dermot O'Hurley, the fugitive Catholic Archbishop of Cashel, made a pilgrimage there shortly before his arrest; he was hanged outside Dublin in 1584 and is one of the 24 officially recognised Irish Catholic Martyrs.

During the Nine Years War, as the Annals of the Kingdom of Ireland record, the clan chief Hugh Roe O'Donnell, Lord of Tyrconnell, venerated the relic on St Andrew's Day, 30 November 1601, on his way to the Battle of Kinsale. From the abbey he sent an expedition to Ardfert that recovered the lands of his ally Thomas Fitzmaurice, 18th Baron Kerry, his last victory before the defeat at Kinsale.

The Holy Rood was last shown for public veneration in 1632, and after the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland the abbey fell into ruin. From 1740 local people buried their dead in the roofless church. In 1880 it became a scheduled national monument, to be preserved and not used for worship.

Special legislation in the Dáil, passed for an anniversary of the foundation on 21 January 1969, allowed it to be restored as a Catholic church, an exception for a national monument, and the sacristan of St Peter's Basilica supplied an authenticated relic of the Cross. Masked raiders stole two crosses, among them the relic, on 11 October 2011; the Garda recovered them almost undamaged, as was announced in January 2012.
holy-crown-of-hungary: The crown has two main parts. The lower hoop, the corona graeca, carries enamel plaques that are mainly or entirely Byzantine work, presumed to have been made in Constantinople in the 1070s. They show Emperor Michael VII Doukas and King Géza I of Hungary, both named in Greek. The upper cross straps, the corona latina, are of different style and carry Latin inscriptions, and were probably made in another period. The most widely accepted view dates the present form to the late 12th century, perhaps under Béla III, who was brought up at the Byzantine court.

Popular tradition held the crown to be older and of papal origin. In a legend written by Bishop Hartvik around 1100 to 1110, King Stephen I sent Archbishop Astrik of Esztergom to Rome, where the pope gave him a crown. Historians reject it: Vatican records show no such gift, and an earlier life of Stephen, from around 1083, mentions no Roman crown.

The crown is of gold, decorated with nineteen enamel pictures of Christ Pantokrator, saints and rulers, together with pearls and semi-precious stones. It is elliptical and larger than a normal head, so a leather liner was worn inside it. The cross on top is tilted, a result of damage in the 17th century. The coronation regalia also include a sceptre, an orb and a mantle, and uniquely in Europe most of this medieval ensemble has survived. The mantle, made around 1030 for Stephen I and Queen Gizella, is the oldest piece.

The name Holy Crown was first used in 1256, and by the 14th century the crown was the unique symbol of royal power. More than 50 kings were crowned with it, the last being Charles IV in 1916. The doctrine of the Holy Crown, set out by the crown guard Péter Révay in 1613 and 1659, holds that the crown is a legal person identical to the state and superior to the monarch, who rules in its name.

Its history includes theft, hiding and loss. Lajos Kossuth buried it near Orsova after the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, and it was returned to Buda in 1853. In 1945 United States troops recovered it in Austria. It was held at Fort Knox until President Jimmy Carter ordered its return, and it came back to Hungary on 6 January 1978. Since 1 January 2000 it has been displayed in the Hungarian Parliament Building.
holy-grail: The word graal comes from Old French graal or greal, related to Old Occitan grazal and Old Catalan gresal, meaning a cup or bowl of earth, wood or metal. The most widely accepted derivation is from Latin gradalis, via cratalis, from the Greek krater, a large wine-mixing vessel. In the 15th century John Hardyng invented a derivation from sang réal, royal blood, which Thomas Malory used and which later fed the theory of a bloodline of Jesus.

Scholars disagree about where the idea came from. Roger Sherman Loomis, Alfred Nutt and Jessie Weston looked to Celtic myth, such as the magical cauldrons of Welsh tradition and Bran the Blessed in the Mabinogion. Others argue for a Christian origin; Joseph Goering points to 12th-century wall paintings from churches in the Catalan Pyrenees showing the Virgin Mary holding a bowl radiating tongues of fire.

The first grail appears in Chrétien de Troyes's unfinished Perceval, the Story of the Grail, dated between 1180 and 1191. Perceval, a guest in the castle of the Fisher King, sees a procession in which a girl carries a decorated graal, a serving dish, and a bleeding lance is borne before him. He stays silent, and later a hermit tells him that the grail holds a host that keeps the crippled king alive; had he asked the right questions he would have healed the king and restored the Wasteland.

Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival makes the Grail a gemstone, lapis exillis, the sanctuary of the neutral angels in Lucifer's rebellion. In Robert de Boron's Joseph d'Arimathie, composed between 1191 and 1202, the Grail becomes the Last Supper chalice in which Joseph of Arimathea caught Christ's blood; Joseph then carries it to Britain. The Lancelot-Grail cycle introduced Galahad as its hero, who achieves the Grail in the Queste del Saint Graal. In the German Diu Crône it is Gawain who does so.

Relics later came to be identified with the Grail, though traditions of a Last Supper relic stayed rare beside those of the True Cross and Holy Lance. The pilgrim Arculf reported a Last Supper chalice near Jerusalem in the 7th century, before the romances. Glastonbury became tied to the legend, and from the 15th century the Grail was prominent in its stories.

In 1818 Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall linked the Grail with the Knights Templar, though no historical evidence connects the order with a search for it, and in 1906 Joséphin Péladan identified the Cathar castle of Montségur with the Grail castle. Richard Wagner's Parsifal premiered in 1882, and Tennyson's Idylls of the King and T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land of 1922 drew on the legend.
holy-land: The term Holy Land denotes areas of the Southern Levant that hold great significance in the Abrahamic religions, chiefly because of their association with people and events in the Hebrew Bible. It is traditionally synonymous with the Land of Israel or the Promised Land in a religious context and with Canaan or Palestine in a secular or geographic one, a region mostly between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River. Christian books often carry maps of it, taken to include Galilee, Samaria and Judea.

In Judaism the land is called Eretz HaKodesh, and researchers hold that the idea of a land made holy as the earthly dwelling of the God of Israel was present by the time of Zechariah in the 6th century BCE. The Tanakh treats it as given to the Israelites by God, and many commandments can be kept only there. Jerusalem was the site of the Temple, the central place of worship for Israelites and Jews.

For Christians the land is holy through the birth, ministry, crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus. In the Middle Ages Christian pilgrimage contributed to the beginning of the Crusades, launched under the banner of restoring Christian sovereignty after the region was lost to the early Muslim conquests. Muslims hold that Muhammad made a night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa Mosque and ascended to heaven from there, and Jerusalem was the first direction of prayer for Muslims before it was changed to the Kaaba. In the 19th century the land became a matter of international diplomacy as part of the Eastern Question about the Ottoman Empire, which led to the Crimean War of the 1850s.

Pilgrims from across the Abrahamic world visit the Holy Land to see and touch physical expressions of their faith. Jerusalem is regarded as the holiest city in Judaism and Christianity and the third-holiest in Islam, after Mecca and Medina. Some sites are contested between religious groups and subject to the Status Quo in Jerusalem and Bethlehem, which bars even minor change without the agreement of all parties concerned. For the Baháʼí Faith, the shrines of Bahá'u'lláh at Acre and of the Báb at Haifa are the holiest places of pilgrimage.
holy-league-1571: The Holy League was a military coalition arranged by Pope Pius V and formally opened on 15 May 1571, with the aim of breaking Ottoman control of the eastern Mediterranean. Its members were the Papal States, the Spanish Empire under Philip II, including Naples and Sicily, the Republic of Venice, the Republic of Genoa, the Knights of Malta, the Grand Duchy of Tuscany with the Order of Saint Stephen under Cosimo I de' Medici, the Duchy of Savoy under Emmanuel Philibert, the Duchy of Urbino under Guidobaldo II della Rovere and the Duchy of Parma under Ottavio Farnese.

The League kept places open for the Holy Roman Empire, France and Portugal, but none joined. The Empire preferred its truce with Constantinople, France had an anti-Spanish alliance with the Ottomans, and Portugal had no forces to spare.

Each year the members were to have ready by 1 April 200 galleys, 100 other ships, 50,000 infantry and 4,500 cavalry. John of Austria, illegitimate half-brother of Philip II, was supreme commander. The fleet first assembled to help the Venetian defenders of Cyprus, invaded by Ottoman forces under Lala Mustafa in July 1570, but arrived too late to prevent the island's capture.

On 7 October 1571 the League won a decisive victory over the Ottoman fleet at the Battle of Lepanto in the Gulf of Patras. It fielded 212 warships carrying 28,500 infantry, most of them Venetian, followed by Spanish and Genoese galleys. The victory confirmed a de facto division of the Mediterranean, the east under Ottoman control and the west under the Habsburgs and their Italian allies. In 1572 the fleet, facing a renewed Ottoman navy of 200 vessels under Kılıç Ali Pasha, failed to take the chance of a decisive blow at Navarino, owing to friction among its leaders and the reluctance of John of Austria.

Pius V died on 1 May 1572 and the diverging interests of the members began to show. In 1573 the fleet did not sail at all; John of Austria instead took Tunis, which the Ottomans retook in 1574. Venice, fearing for its Dalmatian possessions and eager to resume trade with the Ottoman Empire, negotiated alone with the Porte. The League ended with the peace treaty of 7 March 1573, which concluded the War of Cyprus.
holy-league-1684: Under Sultan Mehmed IV the Ottoman Empire had made large gains in Eastern Europe. After Poland gave up most of right-bank Ukraine in 1681 it bordered Poland, the Habsburg monarchy and Russia, and Wallachia, Transylvania and Moldavia were its vassals. Pope Innocent XI and Friar Marco d'Aviano saw these advances as a threat to Christianity.

King John III Sobieski of Poland sought an alliance with Leopold I, and the Treaty of Warsaw was signed on 31 March 1683 only with the backing of Innocent XI, who gave a subsidy of 200,000 imperial thalers to Poland. It took effect six months later when the Ottomans besieged Vienna. Innocent feared that Vienna could not withstand another attack without the help of Venice, which wanted to recover its Mediterranean territory.

Modelled on the Treaty of Warsaw, the Holy League was signed at Linz on 5 March 1684 by the Holy Roman Empire, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Venice, and sworn in at Rome on 24 May, when the Pope became its patron. Members were to act independently and keep the land they conquered, with an amendment giving Venice all reconquered land in Dalmatia. The Tsardom of Russia accepted the Pope's invitation on 26 April 1686, after making peace with Poland, on condition that it keep Kiev in exchange for 1.5 million florins.

France, allied with the Ottomans, refused to help defend against them. When the Habsburgs made large gains, France attacked them in 1688, and this Nine Years' War prolonged the Ottoman refusal to surrender. Brandenburg-Prussia pledged 7,000 men in 1685, while Persia was invited but did not join. Money strained the League: within a year Innocent XI gave Poland over 1.5 million florins, yet Poland began fighting the Ottomans only late in 1686. Ottoman overtures for peace in 1688 failed, and the League's victory at the Battle of Zenta in September 1697 brought immediate calls for peace.

The League ended with the war. The Treaty of Karlowitz of 26 January 1699 left each power the land it held, so the Habsburgs recovered Hungary, Venice regained the Morea and parts of Dalmatia, Poland regained Podolia and Russia took parts of Novorossiya and Azak, though Russia did not sign. The war has been called a 14th crusade, and the name Holy League a propaganda term. Historians describe it as a turning point that shifted the balance towards the Habsburgs.
holy-roman-emperor: The title was originally and officially Emperor of the Romans. In the West the imperial title lapsed after the death of Julius Nepos in 480. In 800 Pope Leo III, who owed a great debt to Charlemagne, King of the Franks, declared the throne vacant, on the pretext that a woman could not rule, since the Eastern Emperor Constantine VI had been deposed in 797 and replaced by his mother Irene. He crowned Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans on Christmas Day, using the concept of translatio imperii. The Eastern Empire eventually recognised Charlemagne's successors, but only as Frankish or German emperors.

Carolingian descendants and others held the title until the death of Berengar I of Italy in 924. Traditional historiography assumes continuity between the Carolingian Empire and the Holy Roman Empire, while a modern convention takes the coronation of Otto I in 962 as the starting point. The word sacrum, "holy", was first used in connection with the empire in 1157 under Frederick I Barbarossa. The English term "Holy Roman Emperor" is a modern shorthand that gained currency in the 1920s and 1930s.

Since 911 the German princes had elected the King of the Germans from among their peers, and that king was then crowned emperor by the pope. From a Carolingian autocracy the title evolved by the 13th century into an elective monarchy. The seven prince-electors are named in the Golden Bull of 1356: the archbishops of Mainz, Trier and Cologne, the king of Bohemia, the count palatine of the Rhine, the duke of Saxony and the margrave of Brandenburg. Candidates made concessions to the electors, known as electoral capitulations. The Ottonians, the Salians and the Hohenstaufen each held the title for long periods.

The interregnum of the 13th century left Rudolf I, Adolf and Albert I as kings who were never crowned emperor, until Henry VII was crowned on 29 June 1312. From 1452 to 1806 the Habsburgs held the title with only one interruption, Charles VII, a Wittelsbach, and the last emperors were from the House of Habsburg-Lorraine from 1765. The emperor was widely perceived to rule by divine right, though he often rivalled the pope, most notably in the Investiture Controversy.

The emperor-elect had to be crowned by the pope until 1508, when Pope Julius II allowed Maximilian I to use the title of elected Roman emperor without a coronation in Rome. Charles V was the last emperor crowned by a pope, at Bologna in 1530. The Empire never had an empress regnant, though women such as Theophanu and Maria Theresa exerted strong influence. After the Reformation the elected emperor was always a Catholic. Francis II dissolved the Empire after Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz, and the final emperor-elect abdicated in 1806.
holy-roman-empire: The Holy Roman Empire developed in the Early Middle Ages, and its beginning is dated either to 800 or to 962. On 25 December 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks, as Roman Emperor, reviving the title more than three centuries after the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476. The title lapsed again by 924 and was revived in 962 when Pope John XII crowned Otto of Saxony, known as Otto the Great, as emperor. At first the empire consisted of three kingdoms, Germany, Italy and, from 1032, Burgundy, held together by the emperor's overlordship. The term holy was first used under Frederick Barbarossa in 1157, and the form Holy Roman Empire is attested from 1254.

From 962 until the 13th century the empire was one of the most powerful monarchies in Europe. The Investiture Controversy set Pope Gregory VII against Henry IV, who made the Walk to Canossa in 1077 to have his excommunication lifted. The empire reached its apex in the mid-13th century under the House of Hohenstaufen, but this was an overextension and led to a partial collapse. Difficulties in electing the king led to a fixed college of prince-electors, whose procedures the Golden Bull of 1356 set down. By the 15th century governance was concentrated on the Kingdom of Germany.

Martin Luther launched the Reformation in 1517 and it divided the empire along religious lines, the north, the east and cities such as Strasbourg, Frankfurt and Nuremberg becoming Protestant while the south and west largely stayed Catholic. Lutheranism was recognised in the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 and Calvinism in the Peace of Westphalia of 1648. Rivalry between Austria and Prussia dominated the empire's history after 1740. On 6 August 1806 Emperor Francis II abdicated and formally dissolved the empire, after Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine from client states loyal to France.

The empire was neither a centralised state nor a nation-state. It was divided into dozens, and eventually hundreds, of entities governed by kings, dukes, counts, bishops, abbots and other rulers, collectively known as princes. Emperors could gain little control over the lands they formally owned and had to grant more and more autonomy to local rulers, a process that began with the Investiture Controversy and was more or less concluded by the Peace of Westphalia. The Imperial Diet was more a forum for negotiation than a legislature. The imperial office was traditionally elected, mostly by a handful of prince-electors and archbishops, and until 1555 Catholicism was the single official religion.
holy-spirit-movement: The movement rose from the collapse of Tito Okello's Uganda National Liberation Army (UNLA). Some of its soldiers formed the Uganda People's Democratic Army (UPDA) under Odong Latek, while former UNLA officers gave weapons to Alice Auma, then 27, and her followers. She said that Lakwena, one of her spirits, directed her to form the movement in August 1986. Formally the Holy Spirit Movement was the political wing and the Holy Spirit Mobile Force the military one, but the names were used interchangeably.

Alice was a medium and healer in Gulu, a common role for women, but she claimed to be a prophet rather than an ordinary medium. She said that spirits had possessed her in January or May 1985 and that she had then spent 40 days and 40 nights in the bush. Her chief spirit, Lakwena, the messenger in the Acholi language, was said to be an Italian who had drowned in the Nile at the age of 95.

Her Holy Spirit Battalion was one of four rebel groups fighting for control of the Gulu and Kitgum districts. It was allied with the UPDA until the Battle of Corner Kilak, and after a UPDA attack on Gulu on 20 April 1987 many UPDA soldiers went over to her. She also forced young men from the villages to join by killing members of their families. In August 1987 she opened an offensive into southern Uganda. On 26 December 1987 she and 118 followers crossed into Kenya and were arrested as illegal immigrants. Afterwards several groups led by spirit mediums, known together as Lakwena Part Two, took up arms again, and the movement may have inspired Joseph Kony's Lord's Resistance Army.

Her stated aim, at first to purify the Acholi people of their sins, widened over time to the purity of Africa and the world. The rules, called the Holy Spirit Safety Precautions, forbade sex, alcohol, tobacco, certain foods, anger and the killing of snakes. Fighters were told that stones would turn into grenades, that blessed water would turn bullets into water, and that charms of snake-bone and beeswax would become swarms of animals and insects. A Department of Information and Publicity worked to soften the movement's image.
holyhead: Holyhead is the largest town in the county of the Isle of Anglesey. It stands on Holy Island, bounded by the Irish Sea to the north and separated from Anglesey by the narrow Cymyran Strait, which was once crossed by the Four Mile Bridge, so called because it lay four miles from Holyhead on the old turnpike. The English name has existed since at least the 14th century and refers to the holiness of the locality. The Welsh name Caergybi means Cybi's fort, from the Roman fortification and from Cybi, a sixth-century saint believed to have founded a monastery on the site.

Settlements in the area date from prehistoric times, with circular huts, burial chambers and standing stones in the highest concentration in Britain. The Old Town is built around St Cybi's Church, which stands inside one of Europe's few three-walled Roman forts, the fourth side having been the sea. The Romans also built a watchtower on Holyhead Mountain inside Mynydd y Twr, a prehistoric hillfort.

In the early 19th century it was undecided whether Porthdinllaen on the Llŷn Peninsula or Holyhead would be the main sea link on the route from London to Dublin. Thomas Telford's road improvements made Holyhead more accessible, and a bill to make Porthdinllaen a harbour for Irish trade was rejected in 1810. Telford's post road made Holyhead the port from which the Royal Mail went to Dublin. After the Union with Ireland Act 1800 the South Stack Lighthouse was lit in 1809, a harbour was built in 1810 and a substantial breakwater was added between 1848 and 1873. The mail contract passed to Liverpool when the railway to that port opened, and returned only after the Chester and Holyhead Railway was completed in 1850.

Holyhead is a busy ferry port with services to Dublin, and its railway station is the terminus of the North Wales Coast Line. The Stanley Embankment, known as the Cob, designed by Thomas Telford and named after the local benefactor John Stanley, carries the railway and the A5 to Anglesey, and the A55 expressway reaches the town. The town proper had 12,084 inhabitants at the 2021 census, and the 1927 National Eisteddfod was held there. Holyhead Maritime Museum occupies what is claimed to be Wales's oldest lifeboat house, a station established in 1828.
holyrood-abbey: The name Holyrood means Holy Cross, rood being a word for the cross on which Jesus Christ was crucified. Legend relates that in 1127, while King David I was hunting east of Edinburgh on the Feast of the Cross, a hart startled his horse and threw him. In one version a holy cross descended from the sky, in another sunlight shone from a crucifix between the hart's antlers, and the animal was startled and the king saved. In thanksgiving David founded the abbey in 1128.

Its first community was of Augustinian canons from Merton Priory. The church held a reliquary said to contain a fragment of the True Cross, known as the Black Rood of Scotland, which fell into English hands at the Battle of Neville's Cross in 1346.

The church was largely rebuilt between 1195 and 1230. Around the abbey lay a five-mile area of sanctuary, where debtors and people accused of crimes could appeal for protection. The Parliament of Scotland met at the abbey several times between 1256 and 1410, and Robert I signed the Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton in its King's Chamber in March 1328. James II was born there in 1430 and crowned there in 1437. Between 1498 and 1501 James IV built a palace beside the cloister, converting the refectory into a Great Hall.

English armies under the Earl of Hertford damaged the abbey in 1544 and 1547, and a mob destroyed its altars in 1559, during the Scottish Reformation. In 1570 the choir and transepts were demolished, leaving the nave as the parish church of the Canongate. The church was remodelled for the coronation of Charles I in 1633. In 1686 James VII established a Jesuit college in the palace, and the following year the abbey became a Roman Catholic Chapel Royal, which the Edinburgh mob broke into in 1688. A stone roof put on between 1758 and 1760 proved too heavy for the walls; the church was closed in 1766, and on 2 December 1768 the roof collapsed.

The ruined nave stands beside the Palace of Holyroodhouse at the end of the Royal Mile, and the site is a scheduled monument. The abbey saw the coronations of Margaret Tudor in 1503, Mary of Guise in 1540 and Anne of Denmark in 1590, and the wedding of James IV and Margaret Tudor in 1503. David II, James II and James V were among the kings buried in its Royal Vault. In 1829 Felix Mendelssohn visited the ruins, which he said inspired his Scottish Symphony.
home-on-the-range: Higley's poem My Western Home appeared in the Smith County Pioneer newspaper and was reprinted in March 1874 in The Kirwin Chief. Daniel E. Kelley (1843–1905), a friend of Higley and a member of the Harlan Brothers Orchestra, worked out a melody for it on his guitar. The original words resemble the modern song but are not the same; the poem did not contain the words on the range. Higley's cabin is listed on the National Register of Historic Places as the Home on the Range Cabin.

Ranchers, cowboys and other settlers took the song up as a rural anthem, and it spread across the United States in various forms; cowboys on the Chisholm Trail seem to have helped carry it through several states. The folklorist John Lomax printed it in 1910 in Cowboy Songs and Other Frontier Ballads, reporting that he had learned it from a black saloon keeper in Texas who knew it from the trail. In 1925 the Texas composer David W. Guion arranged it as sheet music, published by G. Schirmer.

The song's authorship was long disputed. On 26 February 1876 The Kirwin Chief accused The Stockton News of printing a nearly identical poem credited to Mrs. Emma Race of Raceburgh, Kansas. After Bing Crosby recorded the song with Lennie Hayton and his orchestra for Brunswick Records on 27 September 1933, William and Mary Goodwin sued for copyright infringement in 1934, claiming $500,000; they had published a similar song, An Arizona Home, in 1905. Samuel Moanfeldt, investigating for the Music Publishers Protection Association, found another similar song, Colorado Home, but within a few months concluded that Higley had written the poem and Kelley set it to music.

Home on the Range became the state song of Kansas on 30 June 1947 and is often called the unofficial anthem of the American West. A version is one of the seven fight songs of the University of Kansas, played by the Marching Jayhawks at the end of every home athletic event. In 2010 members of the Western Writers of America named it one of the top 100 western songs. Gene Autry, Burl Ives, Pete Seeger and Frank Sinatra were among those who recorded it, and it served as the theme of the 1950s television series The Range Rider.
homer: The identity of Homer is a mystery, and scholars generally regard the ancient picture of a single author behind the Iliad and the Odyssey as a fictional narrative. Their composition is thought to date to the late eighth or early seventh century BCE. Many accounts of his life circulated in antiquity. The most widespread made him a blind bard from Ionia, a region including the central west coast of Anatolia and the islands of Chios and Samos, but modern scholars regard these accounts as apocryphal. The earliest implicit references to Homer, in the 7th century BCE, are in works by Archilochus, Alcman, Tyrtaeus and Callinus.

Pindar is credited with saying that Homer came from Chios and Smyrna. The historian Ephorus held that he studied poetry with the bard Phemius and was born in Cyme, Philochorus thought Argos was his birthplace, and later writers believed it was Pylos or Athens. The Byzantine Suda described him as descended from a Muse, Apollo, Orpheus or others. No account of his origin became mainstream, but most place his death on the island of Ios, where two epigrams by Alcaeus of Messene commemorate his burial.

The Iliad centres on a quarrel between King Agamemnon and the warrior Achilles in the last year of the Trojan War. The Odyssey chronicles the ten-year journey home of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, after the fall of Troy. Both are in Homeric Greek, a literary language mixing Ionic and Aeolic features, and are composed in unrhymed dactylic hexameters. Most researchers believe they were first transmitted orally, and set phrases such as crafty Odysseus and rosy-fingered Dawn aided the bard. Both begin with an invocation to the Muse.

The poems were put into written form between the eighth and sixth centuries BCE. Ancient tradition held that Pisistratus collected them in Athens in the late sixth century BCE. After the 24 books were fixed, scholars at Alexandria such as Aristarchus of Samothrace helped establish a canonical text.

The Homeric poems were widely used as school texts in Greek and Hellenistic cultures, the first literary works taught to all students. Plato said that Homer had educated Greece. Interpreters, especially the Stoics, read the poems as allegories containing hidden wisdom. The first printed edition was produced in Florence in 1488 by Demetrios Chalkokondyles. In 1873 Heinrich Schliemann announced the discovery of Homer's Troy at Hisarlik in modern Turkey.

Ancient chronology dated the sack of Troy to 1184 BCE, and some scholars think the destruction of Troy VIIa around 1220 BCE gave rise to the myth. The poems depict customs from different periods: their heroes use bronze weapons but are cremated, an Iron Age practice. Virgil's Aeneid was heavily influenced by Homer, and later works from Tennyson's Ulysses to James Joyce's Ulysses retell his stories.
homeridae: In classical Greek the name should mean children of Homer, on the pattern of the Asclepiadae, a guild of physicians called children of Asclepius. Yet the existence of the Homeridae is attested while that of Homer is not, and the common noun homeros means hostage, so it was suggested even in antiquity that they were really descendants of hostages. One story told that the women of Chios once went mad at a festival of Dionysus and fought the men, and that peace came only when brides and bridegrooms were exchanged as pledges, whose descendants were the Homeridae. Some have taken the further step of treating Homer as a back-formation from the guild's name.

The evidence belongs to the late sixth, fifth and fourth centuries BCE, after which nothing more is heard of them. Pindar, in a poem of about 485 BCE, says that the Homeridae, singers of stitched words, usually begin with an address to Zeus. Isocrates, writing around 350 BCE, reports their story that Helen appeared to Homer in a dream and told him to compose a poem about the Trojan expedition. Plato mentions them reciting hymns to Eros, and in his Ion the rhapsode Ion claims he should be crowned by the Homeridae.

Later antiquarian sources, of uncertain value, add details. A commentary on Pindar names Cynaethus of Chios as a member of a group that composed new poems and attached them to Homer's works, and calls him the author of the Homeric Hymn to Apollo and the first to perform Homer at Syracuse. The local historians Acusilaus and Hellanicus of Lesbos derived the name from Homer, while Seleucus denied it.

The Homeridae appear to have been a guild of oral performers who claimed to inherit Homer's tradition, travelled widely like other rhapsodes and were perhaps based on Chios. They recited poems ascribed to Homer, doubtless including the Iliad and the Odyssey, and told stories about how the poems came to be. Their influence on the early transmission of the texts, though impossible to measure, was surely conservative. When Pisistratus, tyrant of Athens, made a fixed text compulsory, they switched to a version they had approved themselves, helping to produce some of the first authoritative texts of Homer.
homs: Homs lies on the Orontes River in western Syria, 162 km north of Damascus, and is the central link between the interior cities and the Mediterranean coast. For about 2,000 years it has been a key agricultural market and trade centre for the villages of northern Syria. Excavations at the Citadel of Homs show settlement from around 2300 BCE. In 1274 BCE Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire fought at Kadesh on the Orontes, near Homs, in what may have been the largest chariot battle ever fought.

The Emesene dynasty, an Arab line, gave the city its Latin name Emesa. After Pompey's submission of the Seleucid state of Syria to the Roman Republic in 64 BCE, the dynasty was confirmed as client kings of Rome, and its kingdom reached from the Bekaa Valley to the border with Palmyra. Emesa was a centre of worship of El-Gabal, a sun god, and gained importance in Christianity under the Byzantines. In 637 CE the Rashidun army under Khalid ibn al-Walid captured the city peacefully, since its inhabitants agreed to pay a large ransom. Caliph Umar made Homs the capital of Jund Hims, a district of Bilad al-Sham.

In 1098 the Crusaders besieged Homs but failed to take it. It came under Duqaq, the Saljuqid ruler of Damascus, who made it a fortified camp from which Muslim forces raided the Crusader coast. In 1149 the Zangids under Nur al-Din captured it. In 1516 Homs became part of the Ottoman Empire. It lost political importance but remained an economic centre, known for silk and wool weaving, and by the end of the 16th century it had about 24,000 people. Its cotton industry boomed in the 19th century. The French moved their military academy there in 1932, and many of its graduates became officers in the Syrian army.

Homs is the capital of the Homs Governorate. Its population includes Sunni and Alawite Muslims and Christians, and the city has a number of historic mosques and churches. It lies close to the Krak des Chevaliers castle, a World Heritage Site. Large parts of the city were devastated in the Syrian civil war.
honaine: Honaïne lies at the extreme north-west of Algeria, in the north of Tlemcen Province, about 60 km north-west of Tlemcen. The town stands on the south-western shore of the Mediterranean Sea, north of the Trara Mountains. Since 1984 the commune has also included the localities of Tafsout, Ouled Youcef, Tadjera and Ouled Amar.

Under the Roman Empire the town, known as Gypsaria or Gissaria and as Artisiga, belonged to the province of Mauretania Caesariensis. In late antiquity it was caught up in the Donatist controversy: at the Conference of Carthage of 411 it was represented both by the Catholic bishop Germano and by the Donatist bishop Fidentino. Gissaria survives as a titular bishopric of the Roman Catholic Church.

The founder of the Almohad dynasty, Abd El Moumen Ben Ali, was born near Honaïne, at Tajra, a hill about two kilometres to the west. In 1162 Oran and Honaïne joined in building a hundred ships for his fleet. The harbour, first a port of the Ifrenides, became the most important port of the Almohads in North Africa and later one of the two ports of the Zianides of Tlemcen. The Spanish, who called the town Hone, occupied it briefly, and in 1534 its port was partly destroyed. Honaïne then received a large number of Moorish refugees.

Honaïne is a small Mediterranean port whose main activity is artisanal fishing, and a seaside resort with beaches at the centre, Tafsout, Agla and Bni Kheled. Berber remains from the Almohad period survive, above all the ramparts. The site, including the walled town, the ramparts, the Casbah, the site of the old port and the watchtower, has been a classified historic site since 1982.
honda-tadakatsu: Honda Tadakatsu, also called Honda Heihachirō, was born on 17 March 1548 at Kuramae in Mikawa Province, the eldest son of Honda Tadataka, of one of the oldest families of hereditary vassals serving Tokugawa Ieyasu. He fought his first battle at Washizu Fort in 1560 beside his father. When the Ikkō-ikki rose in Mikawa, he left the Jōdo Shinshū sect for Jōdo-shū and stayed loyal to Ieyasu, helping to suppress the rising. In 1566, aged 19, he was made a hatamoto with command of 54 horsemen.

Tadakatsu won distinction at the Battle of Anegawa in 1570, where he charged alone against the advancing Asakura army, and in 1572 at Hitokotosaka his antler helmet and his spear Tonbokiri drew the enemy's notice as he held off the units of Baba Nobuharu. At Mikatagahara in 1573 he commanded the left wing and organised the cover of the Tokugawa retreat. At Nagashino in 1575 he led a rank of musketeers and helped stop the breakthrough of Naitō Masatoyo's men towards Ieyasu's camp.

After the Honnō-ji Incident of 1582 he helped escort Ieyasu from Sakai back to Mikawa through bands of samurai hunters. In the Komaki campaign of 1584 he rode out with a handful of men to challenge Toyotomi Hideyoshi's host across the Shōnai River. He commanded Tokugawa forces against the Hōjō in 1590, taking Tamanawa and helping to take Iwatsuki and Hachigata, and at Sekigahara in 1600 he broke into the camps of Shimazu Yoshihiro and Ukita Hideie until his horse Mikuni-Guro was shot under him.

Tadakatsu retired in 1609, handing the headship of the clan to his son Tadamasa, and died in his sleep in December 1610. His daughter Komatsuhime married Sanada Nobuyuki, and his grandson Tadatoki married Ieyasu's granddaughter Senhime. He grew estranged from the shogunate as it turned from a military to a civil government. Tradition holds that he took part in 57 campaigns and was never seriously wounded. Oda Nobunaga called him a samurai among samurai. His spear Tonbokiri, made by Fujiwara Masazane, is counted among the Three Great Spears of Japan.
honen: Hōnen was born in Mimasaka Province, in what is now Okayama, to a prominent family. His father, Uruma no Tokikuni, was a provincial official who headed the local police. In 1141 his father was assassinated by an official sent to govern the province, and is believed to have told his son not to hate the enemy but to become a monk.

Hōnen trained as a Tendai monk and left Mount Hiei in 1150 for the quieter temple of Kurodani. He later studied at Saga and Nara, then returned to the libraries of Mount Hiei. He was struck by the contrast between the suffering of ordinary people and the lives of elite monks in ornate temples. At forty-three he read the Commentary on the Meditation Sutra by the Chinese Pure Land master Shandao.

Hōnen moved to the Ōtani district of Kyoto, where he taught the recitation of the nembutsu to crowds of laymen and laywomen. The Genpei War of 1180–1185 brought many people to the capital seeking refuge, and his message of universal salvation appealed to them. By 1204 he had around 190 disciples, a number taken from the signatures on the Seven Article Pledge.

Monks of other schools kept criticising him. In 1207 a ban on exclusive nembutsu was imposed after two of his followers held a retreat attended by court ladies, and the disciples were accused of using it as a cover for sexual liaisons. Hōnen, then eighty, was exiled to Shikoku together with disciples including Shinran, and four disciples were executed. He was later pardoned and returned to Kyoto, where he died in 1212.

Hōnen wrote his main work, the Senchakushū, in 1198 at the request of his patron Kujō Kanezane. In 1211 his disciples completed woodblocks for it, making it the first printed text of a Japanese Buddhist author. Tendai monks attacked the print shop and destroyed the blocks in 1227, and his followers cut them again in 1239.

He taught that rebirth in the Pure Land comes through reliance on the other-power of Amida, expressed by reciting his name, and not through the self-power of difficult practice. He held that women, the uneducated and even those who had done the worst deeds could be born there, and that sincere faith mattered more than the number of recitations.
hong-kong: Hong Kong is situated on China's southern coast, 60 kilometres east of Macau and on the eastern side of the Pearl River estuary. It is surrounded by the South China Sea on all sides except the north, where it neighbours the city of Shenzhen along the Sham Chun River. The territory consists of Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, the New Territories, Lantau Island and over 200 other islands. Its highest point is Tai Mo Shan, at 957 metres, and about 70 square kilometres of its land has been reclaimed from the sea.

The name was first romanised as He-Ong-Kong in 1780 and originally referred to a small inlet between Aberdeen Island and the southern coast of Hong Kong Island. It is generally believed to be an early phonetic rendering of a Cantonese phrase meaning 'fragrant harbour' or 'incense harbour'. The second colonial governor, Sir John Davis, offered an alternative origin, 'red torrent'. The name was often written as one word, Hongkong, until 1926, when the government officially adopted two words.

The earliest known human traces date to 35,000 to 39,000 years ago, based on knapped stone tools found at Wong Tei Tung in the Sai Kung Peninsula. About 6,000 years ago the region was widely occupied, and rice cultivation had been introduced by the Late Neolithic. The Qin dynasty incorporated the area into China for the first time in 214 BCE, after conquering the indigenous Baiyue. After the Qin collapsed it was consolidated under the Nanyue kingdom, and China recaptured it after the Han conquest. During the Mongol conquest in the 13th century the southern Song court was briefly located at the Sung Wong Toi site in Kowloon City, before its defeat at the Battle of Yamen in 1279.

The Qing dynasty ceded Hong Kong Island to the British Empire in 1841 to 1842 after losing the First Opium War. The colony expanded to the Kowloon Peninsula in 1860, and in 1898 the United Kingdom obtained a 99-year lease of the New Territories. Japan occupied Hong Kong from 1941 to 1945 during the Second World War. The territory was handed over from the United Kingdom to China in 1997.

Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China. Under the principle of one country, two systems and the Sino-British Joint Declaration, its Basic Law serves as the regional constitution, and it keeps separate governing and economic systems from those of mainland China. Its population was estimated at 7,413,070 in 2021, the great majority of them Chinese. Its culture is described as a hybrid of Eastern and Western influences.
hong-kong-island: Hong Kong Island is the second largest island in Hong Kong, after Lantau, with a land area of about 78.59 square kilometres. It was known originally, and on road signs, simply as Hong Kong. Its northern coast forms the southern shore of Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters, favoured by large trading ships, were largely responsible for the development of Hong Kong.
