Jewish tradition holds that his tomb is a structure there, though Emil G. Hirsch and Victor Ryssel, writing in The Jewish Encyclopedia, call the tradition historically worthless. The Talmud claims that he was the foremost prophet of his generation, and he was the only prophet of Israel in his time who left any written prophecy.
hoshang-shah: Hoshang Shah was born Alp Khan around 1375 and was also known as Arslan Khan before he took the title Hoshang Shah. His father, Dilawar Khan Ghori, had belonged to the court of Firuz Shah Tughlaq, Sultan of Delhi, and was appointed governor of Malwa, probably by Firuz. In 1401 Dilawar Khan made himself independent of the Delhi Sultanate for all practical purposes. When he died in 1406, Alp Khan succeeded him peacefully.

A rumour that Hoshang Shah had poisoned his father gave Muzaffar Shah of Gujarat a pretext for war. Muzaffar invaded Malwa late in 1406 and in 1407 reached Dhar, where Hoshang was wounded, defeated and forced back into the fort. When the siege proved difficult, Muzaffar proposed peace with an oath on the Quran. Against his advisers' warnings, Hoshang met him several times and was arrested. Malwa was annexed by the Gujarat Sultanate under Muzaffar's brother Nusrat Khan, and Hoshang was taken captive to Gujarat.

Local soldiers and nobles soon drove Nusrat Khan out and by December 1408 chose Hoshang's cousin Musa Khan as their leader at Mandu. Muzaffar then sent his grandson Ahmad Khan, who restored Hoshang at Dhar. Musa Khan refused to submit until Hoshang seized the surrounding districts to cut off the fort's revenue and key nobles, among them Malik Mughith, deserted him. Hoshang re-entered Mandu, made it his capital and appointed Malik Mughith his naib and wazir.

Hoshang kept friendly relations with Nasir Khan Faruqi of Khandesh, a buffer against the Deccan, founded Hoshangabad on the Narbada to guard his south-eastern frontier and gained suzerainty over Kalpi by marrying his sister to Qadir Shah. No forced conversions or temple demolitions are recorded in his reign, and a Jain temple was built at Lalitpur in 1424. He founded a madrasa at Mandu and drew scholars and Sufi saints to Malwa.

In his last years a rivalry between his sons by two wives troubled the court. When Usman Khan revolted, Hoshang imprisoned the sons of his first wife, a daughter of Malik Ahmad Khan Farooqui of Khandesh, which cleared the way for Ghazni Khan, who later reigned as Muhammad Shah. According to Nizamuddin Ahmad, Hoshang suffered from diabetes. He fell gravely ill and died in July 1435 while being carried back to Mandu, where he was buried the next day.
hoshea: Hoshea was the nineteenth and last king of the northern Kingdom of Israel and the son of Elah, not the earlier Israelite king of that name. Under Ahaz, Judah had rendered allegiance to Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria, when Pekah of Israel, in league with Rezin of Aram-Damascus, tried to coerce the Judean king into joint action against Assyria.

Hoshea, a captain in Pekah's army, placed himself at the head of the Assyrian party in Samaria and removed Pekah by assassination. Tiglath-Pileser rewarded him by making him king over a reduced northern kingdom. An undated Assyrian inscription records that the Assyrian king overthrew Pekah and set Hoshea over the people.

Hoshea remained loyal while Tiglath-Pileser lived, but when Shalmaneser V succeeded he sought independence and negotiated with So, King of Egypt, and stopped paying tribute. Shalmaneser took this for rebellion and marched on Samaria. The Assyrian Eponym Canon shows him campaigning in 727, 726 and 725 BCE, and the Babylonian Chronicle says he ravaged Samaria. It is likely that Hoshea, disappointed by Egypt, tried to resume tribute but was distrusted, forced to fight and taken prisoner. The capital nevertheless mounted an effective defence, and the Assyrians captured Samaria after a siege of three years, according to 2 Kings.

Shalmaneser died soon after the city fell, and Sargon II returned with the army in 720 BCE, after the land had revolted again, and conquered the kingdom. His inscription counts 27,290 people deported beyond the Euphrates, and people from Babylon, Kutha, Avva, Hama and Sepharvaim were settled in their place.

The Books of Kings attribute the destruction to the sins of the Israelites. What became of Hoshea, and when and where he died, is unknown. An unprovenanced seal impression reading Belonging to Abdi, servant of Hoshea, dated by André Lemaire to the second half of the 8th century BCE, would, if authentic, be the only attestation of Hoshea in an Israelite inscription.
hoshiarpur-district: Hoshiarpur district lies in the north-east of Punjab and covers 3365 square kilometres. With neighbouring districts it forms the cultural region called Doaba or Bist Doab, the land between the Beas and the Sutlej. It falls into two nearly equal parts of hill and plain: the westward slope of the Solar Singhi Hills on the east, a line of lower heights of the Siwalik Range, and between them a valley known as the Jaswan Dun. The western plain is alluvial, and the Beas has a fringe of very fertile lowland where rice is grown. The climate is comparatively cool and humid. It is also called the City of Saints, and religious fairs are held at Anandpur Sahib, Dasuya, Mukerian and Chintpurni.

Excavations show that the area near the Shivalik foothills was inhabited from the early Paleolithic, and the district was part of the Indus Valley Civilization. Legend ties Dasuya to the Mahabharata as the seat of Raja Virata, in whose service the Pandavas spent their exile. The country formed part of the old kingdom of Katoch in Jalandhar, which broke up, and the district was divided between the rajas of Datarpur and Jaswan, who kept their territories until 1759, when Sikh chieftains began to encroach on the hill tracts.

In 1815 Maharaja Ranjit Singh forced the ruler of Jaswan to give up his lands for an estate on feudal tenure, and three years later the raja of Datarpur was treated in the same way. By the end of 1818 the whole country from the Sutlej to the Beas was governed from Lahore, and in 1846, after the First Anglo-Sikh War, it passed to the British. The deposed rajas, bitterly disappointed not to be restored, organised a revolt in 1848, at the start of the Second Anglo-Sikh War, but were captured and their estates confiscated. Under the British the district belonged to the Jullundur Division and had four tehsils: Hoshiarpur, Dasuya, Una and Garhshankar.
hoshina-masayuki: Hoshina Masayuki was born in Edo on 17 June 1611, the illegitimate fourth son of the second shōgun, Tokugawa Hidetada, by a servant, Oshizu no Kata. To protect the child, then named Komatsu, from Hidetada's wife Oeyo, his birth was hidden and he was secretly adopted by Hoshina Masamitsu, a former Takeda retainer and daimyō of Takatō Domain. In 1629 he first met his father, his elder brother the third shōgun Tokugawa Iemitsu and his brother Tokugawa Tadanaga, and received mementos of his grandfather Tokugawa Ieyasu in recognition of his place in the Tokugawa lineage.

In 1631 he inherited the headship of the Hoshina clan and the Takatō fief and took the name Masayuki. After Hidetada's death he became one of Iemitsu's closest confidants, with power far beyond his rank as a 30,000 koku daimyō. He built Hidetada's mausoleum at Zōjō-ji and helped write the Buke shohatto regulations of 1635, which governed the conduct of daimyō and samurai. Moved to Yamagata Domain at 200,000 koku in 1636, he was named general of reinforcements in the Shimabara rebellion of 1637, which was crushed before they could set out.

At Aizu, in Mutsu Province, his domain was officially assessed at 230,000 koku, but the administration of the shogunate's own lands in the area more than doubled his true income. During the regency for his nephew Ietsuna he was for several years the virtual ruler of Japan. He refused leave to use the Tokugawa crest and the surname Matsudaira, out of respect for the family that had raised him and to show he had no designs on the main line; they were adopted under his son Masakata.

Masayuki patronised the Neo-Confucian scholar Yamazaki Ansai, and together they wrote the Aizu House Code with its injunction of loyalty to the shōgun. He retired in 1669 in favour of his son Hoshina Masatsune and died at the clan's residence at Mita in Edo in 1673. A disciple of Yoshikawa Shintō, he was buried with Shinto rites at Hanitsu Shrine near Lake Inawashiro and deified as the kami Hanitsu-reishin.

His words that loyalty to the shogunate was absolute later weighed on his house. Matsudaira Katamori held to them, and his service to the shogunate drew the hostility of Satsuma and Chōshū, so that Aizu became one of the most tragic battlefields of the Boshin War.
hosni-mubarak: Hosni Mubarak was born on 4 May 1928 in Kafr El-Meselha, in the Monufia Governorate of Egypt. On 2 February 1949 he left the Military Academy for the Air Force Academy and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 13 March 1950. He served in various units, including two years in a Spitfire fighter squadron, and returned to the Air Force Academy as an instructor until early 1959. From February 1959 to June 1961 he trained in the Soviet Union, at a pilot school in Moscow and at Kant Air Base near Bishkek. He commanded the Egyptian Air Force from 1972 to 1975 and became air chief marshal in 1973.

In April 1975 President Anwar Sadat appointed Mubarak vice president. In September of that year he travelled to Riyadh and Damascus to win Saudi and Syrian acceptance of the Sinai II disengagement agreement with Israel; Syria's president Hafez al-Assad refused to meet him, but in Saudi Arabia he formed a friendship with Crown Prince Fahd. Mubarak was injured when soldiers led by Lieutenant Khalid Islambouli assassinated Sadat in October 1981, and he became the fourth president of Egypt in a single-candidate referendum. He renewed his term by single-candidate referendums in 1987, 1993 and 1999.

Mubarak upheld the Camp David Accords with Israel, though Israeli journalists wrote of a cold peace. Egypt had been suspended from the Arab League because of the treaty; Mubarak met King Fahd of Saudi Arabia in 1982, and in 1989 Egypt's membership was restored and the League's headquarters returned to Cairo. Egypt joined the coalition in the 1991 Gulf War, and afterwards the United States, the Gulf states and Europe forgave about 20 billion dollars of its debt. In 2005, under United States pressure, he held the country's first multi-party election and won it; observers said it was marred by rigging.

The state of emergency in force since the 1967 war was never lifted. Human rights organisations reported arbitrary detention and the systematic use of torture by the security services, and corruption was widespread.

Protests began in Cairo and other cities on 25 January 2011. On 1 February Mubarak announced he would not contest the election due in September, but the demonstrations continued, and on 11 February Vice President Omar Suleiman announced his resignation and the transfer of power to the military. Mubarak was tried on charges of killing protesters, sentenced to life imprisonment in 2012, retried after an appeal, and acquitted by the Court of Cassation on 2 March 2017. He died on 25 February 2020 and was given a military funeral.
hosokawa-shigekata: Shigekata was one of 21 children of Hosokawa Nobunori, the 4th daimyō of the Hosokawa clan. He came to rule as the 6th daimyō of Kumamoto after his elder brother, the 5th, was killed because another man's family crest resembled that of the Hosokawa clan. The domain was in deep difficulty: deficits under his father had reached 400,000 ryō, made worse by the bakufu's sankin-kōtai system and by famine. Shigekata is said to have kept a pawn shop ticket so as not to forget his hard early years.

In 1752 he made Hori Katuna great bugyō. Refused by the Kohnoike family and other Osaka houses, Hori borrowed a large sum from Kajimaya in return for 100,000 koku of rice. The reform of the Hōreki years cut samurai stipends from 40 koku in every 100 to 20 and then 13, promoted washi paper and silk, made wax a domain monopoly and resurveyed the land. By the end of the Hōreki era (1751–1763) the finances had greatly improved, and stored grain later helped the domain through the Tenmei famine.

The reform met resistance, above all from samurai. In 1772 the metsuke Matsuno Hichizou set out three faults of Hori, and in 1774 Masuda Yaichiuemon attacked the reform in 18 secret letters. The travel writer Furukawa Koshoken, visiting late in Shigekata's rule, found that the common people's lives did not match their ruler's popularity. Shigekata also replaced exile and tattooing with caning, penal labour and the shaving of eyebrows, and paid convicts for their work so that they could return to society; the system later served as a model in the Meiji Restoration.

He founded the domain school Jishūkan within the grounds of Kumamoto Castle in 1755. Unusually, it was open to students of any class and from other provinces, with scholarships for the brightest, and it later produced Yokoi Shōnan, Inoue Kowashi and Kitasato Shibasaburō. In 1756 he founded Saishunkan, the first public domain medical school, which opened the following year. In later life he studied plants and animals, and 16 albums of his pictures survive in the Eisei Bunko. He died on 27 November 1785; his son Hosokawa Harutoshi was born to his concubine Yokoshi.
hosokawa-tadaoki: Tadaoki was the eldest son of Hosokawa Fujitaka and Numata Jakō, and his childhood name was Kumachiyo. For most of his life he went by the name Nagaoka Tadaoki, which his father had adopted from a town in the family's domain; he took back the name Hosokawa only shortly after Sekigahara. He fought his first battle at the age of 15 in the service of Oda Nobunaga, married Gracia, the daughter of Akechi Mitsuhide, in 1578, and was granted the Province of Tango in 1580.

When Mitsuhide rebelled against Nobunaga at Honnō-ji in 1582, causing Nobunaga's death, he turned to Fujitaka and Tadaoki for help. Father and son refused, and Mitsuhide was soon defeated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi.

Tadaoki fought on Hideyoshi's side at the Battle of Komaki and Nagakute in 1584 and in the Odawara Campaign of 1590, where he took part in the siege of Nirayama in Izu Province before joining the main army outside Odawara. During the 1590s he became a friend of Tokugawa Ieyasu, who lent him money to pay off debts owed to Toyotomi Hidetsugu.

After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 he was one of seven generals, among them Fukushima Masanori, Katō Kiyomasa and Kuroda Nagamasa, who turned on Ishida Mitsunari, angered by his unfavourable reports of their conduct in the Imjin War. Popular accounts describe a plot to kill him; the historian Daimon Watanabe argues it was rather a legal dispute, which Ieyasu mediated. Historians see the quarrel as part of the rivalry between the Tokugawa faction and Mitsunari's, and the generals later sided with Ieyasu.

In 1600 Mitsunari tried to take hostage the families living in Osaka Castle, and Gracia's death to avoid capture drove Tadaoki firmly to Ieyasu. At the Battle of Sekigahara he commanded 5,000 men in the Tokugawa vanguard against the forces of Shima Sakon. He was rewarded with a fief in Buzen, centred on Kokura and assessed at 370,000 koku, and he served again in the Siege of Osaka of 1614–1615.

Tadaoki was succeeded by his son Hosokawa Tadatoshi, who in 1632 received a larger fief in Higo, centred on Kumamoto and assessed at 540,000 koku, and who took part in the Siege of Shimabara in 1637–1638. The Hosokawa family remained in Higo until 1871.
hospices-de-beaune: The Hôtel-Dieu was founded on 4 August 1443. The Treaty of Arras of 1435 had brought the Hundred Years' War towards its close, but marauding bands known as écorcheurs still roamed the countryside, pillaging and causing misery and famine. Most of the people of Beaune were destitute, and the area had recently suffered an outbreak of plague. Rolin, having gained permission from Pope Eugene IV in 1441, built the hospital as a refuge for the poor and founded a religious order, Les sœurs hospitalières de Beaune, to serve it.

The design was probably overseen by the Flemish architect Jacques Wiscrère, and records name many Flemish and French masons, painters and glass cutters who worked on it. Its two-storied wings stand around a stone courtyard, with half-timbered galleries, and three of the buildings are under roofs of glazed tiles in red, brown, yellow and green; the present tiles are replicas made between 1902 and 1907. The Room of the Poor, 50 metres long, held two rows of curtained beds, each for two patients, and the chapel was placed so that the bedridden could hear Mass from their beds. Guigone de Salins is buried there.

The elderly, the disabled and the sick, orphans, women about to give birth and the destitute were received there from the Middle Ages onwards, and the building served as a hospital until 1971. Over the centuries the institution gained farms, woodland, works of art and vineyards from benefactors and formed links with similar houses in Pommard, Nolay and Meursault.

The Hôtel-Dieu is now a museum, where the polyptych altarpiece by Rogier van der Weyden is kept; patients are cared for in modern hospital buildings. The charity wine auction has been held every year since 1859 on the third Sunday in November, at the heart of the festival Les Trois Glorieuses. The Domaine des Hospices de Beaune owns around 61 hectares of donated vineyards, much of it Grand and Premier cru, and the auction has been run by Christie's from 2005 to 2020 and by Sotheby's since 2021.
hot-air-balloon: A precursor of the hot air balloon was the sky lantern, called a Kongming lantern in Chinese. Zhuge Liang of the Shu Han kingdom is said to have used such airborne lanterns for military signalling during the Three Kingdoms era (220 to 280 CE). The Mongol army later studied them and used them at the Battle of Legnica in the 13th century, the first time ballooning was known in the western world.

The brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier developed a balloon at Annonay in Ardèche and made a public demonstration in 1783, an unmanned flight of 10 minutes. After trials with unmanned balloons and with animals, Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier made a tethered flight on or around 15 October 1783 and rose to 26 m, the length of the tether. On 21 November 1783 he and François d'Arlandes made the first free flight with people aboard, over Paris. King Louis XVI had decreed that condemned criminals should go first, but the two petitioned successfully for the honour.

A hot air balloon has an envelope holding heated air, with a basket or gondola beneath it that carries the passengers and a burner. Heated air is less dense than the air outside, so the envelope is buoyant, as Archimedes' principle describes. The envelope need not be sealed at the bottom, because the air inside is at about the same pressure as that outside. Lift depends mainly on the difference in temperature, and for nylon envelopes the interior is limited to about 120 °C.

Modern envelopes are made of ripstop nylon or Dacron, cut into panels called gores and sewn together with load tapes that carry the weight of the basket. Baskets are usually of woven wicker or rattan. Burners vaporise liquid propane and typically produce 2 to 3 MW of heat. Precise steering is not possible: a pilot can only change altitude to catch winds blowing in different directions.

The first military use came on 26 June 1794, when the French used the balloon l'Entreprenant for observation at the Battle of Fleurus. Modern balloons with an onboard heat source were developed by Ed Yost and Jim Winker from the 1950s, and their first successful flight was on 22 October 1960. The first modern hot air balloon built in the United Kingdom was the Bristol Belle in 1967. Balloons are now used mainly for recreation.

Long flights have set records. Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones left Château-d'Oex in Switzerland on 1 March 1999 in the Breitling Orbiter 3 and made the first nonstop balloon flight around the world, landing in Egypt after 19 days, 21 hours and 55 minutes.
hotu-matua: According to the legend, the royal adviser Hau-Maka dreamed that his spirit travelled to a far country to look for new land for King Hotu Matuꞌa, and came to a place called Mata ki te rangi, Eyes that look to the sky. When he woke he told the king, who sent seven men from Hiva to find the island. They found it and returned, and the king then sailed there himself with his queen, Vakai. The colonising party travelled in two canoes, or in one double-hulled canoe, and the clans that divided the island claimed descent from his sons.

The island has also been called Te pito o te henua, the Center of the Earth. Hiva was the homeland of the islanders' legends; a comparison of the Rapanui language with other Polynesian languages suggests it was the Marquesas Islands. In all the early accounts the islanders insisted that the first inhabitants came from the east.

The details of the legend are unlikely to be verifiable. Linguistic, DNA and pollen evidence points to a first settlement by Polynesians, but its date is uncertain: published estimates range from about 300 to 400 CE to 700 to 800 CE, and a recent study, with radiocarbon dates from what is thought to be very early material, shows the island was settled by 1200 CE.

The likeness of his name to that of Atu Motua, Father Lord, an early founder god of Mangareva, has led some historians to suspect that Hotu Matuꞌa entered the island's mythology only in the 1860s, when the Mangarevan language was also adopted. On that view the real founder was Tuꞌu ko Iho, who became a supporting figure in the legends centred on Hotu Matuꞌa.

The Norwegian ethnographer Thor Heyerdahl pointed to cultural likenesses with South American peoples and suggested that some settlers came from the continent. Mainstream archaeology doubts any non-Polynesian influence: an analysis of human remains from before European contact, made in 2017, found only Polynesian ancestry, while a 2020 study found contact with South America that likely took place in Eastern Polynesia before Rapa Nui was settled.
hou-jing: Hou Jing, courtesy name Wanjing, came from Huaishuo Garrison, one of the Six Garrisons that Northern Wei kept on its northern border against the Rouran. He appears to have been ethnically Chinese, though the point is not settled: his enemies called him a Jie, which led many modern scholars to place him among the Jie people, while some historians note that the word was a common insult of the time. He probably took on Xianbei ways among the garrisons, and as a young man he belonged to a circle of friends around Gao Huan.

Under Gao Huan he became known as a gifted tactician, although he was no great horseman or archer and walked with a limp. In late 534 he defeated Heba Sheng and won the southern provinces for Eastern Wei, and from 536 he commanded the provinces south of the Yellow River. He had little regard for Gao Huan's heir, Gao Cheng, whom he called the Xianbei boy. In spring 547 he rebelled, surrendering his 13 provinces first to Western Wei and then to Liang; when Yuwen Tai demanded that he come to Chang'an to pay homage, he refused.

Emperor Wu of Liang welcomed him, but when Gao Cheng offered peace, Hou forged a letter from Gao proposing to exchange Xiao Yuanming, a nephew of the emperor held by Eastern Wei, for himself. The emperor's reply, that Xiao Yuanming returned in the morning would mean Hou delivered in the evening, decided him on rebellion, and he gained the secret support of the emperor's nephew Xiao Zhengde, the Prince of Linhe. The years from 548 to 552 are known as the Hou Jing Disturbance. As emperor of Han he took the era name Taishi, and he put captured opponents to death with great cruelty.

Defeated near Jiankang by Xiao Yi's generals Wang Sengbian and Chen Baxian, Hou fled, killing his two young sons born at Jiankang. He made for the sea, but while he slept his guard Yang Kun turned the boats towards Jingkou and killed him with a spear. His body was salted and sent to Jiankang, his head to Xiao Yi and his hands to Northern Qi, and the crowd, among them his wife Princess Liyang, cut off his flesh and ate it. Hou Jing is one of the most reviled figures in imperial Chinese history; about five years after his death Chen Baxian overthrew Liang and founded the Chen dynasty.
hou-junji: Hou Junji's date of birth is unknown, and little is known of his family except that he came from Bin Prefecture, near modern Xianyang in Shaanxi. He was said to be pretentious and eager to impress, and became known as a fighter rather than as an archer. Early in the reign of Emperor Gaozu he entered the service of Gaozu's son Li Shimin, the Prince of Qin, who made him Viscount of Quanjiao and often heard his advice. In 626, with Zhangsun Wuji, Gao Shilian and Yuchi Gong, he urged Li Shimin to strike first against his brothers Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, and he led Li Shimin's forces in the fighting that followed their killing.

When Li Shimin took the throne as Emperor Taizong, he placed Hou among the five officials of the highest merit and made him Duke of Lu. In 630 Hou became minister of defence and a de facto chancellor. In 634 and 635 he served under Li Jing against the Tuyuhun; when the enemy burned the grazing, Hou argued for advancing, and the campaign ended in victory. In 637 his title became Duke of Chen. In 638 he commanded the counter-attack against Songtsen Gampo of Tufan.

Around the new year of 640 Taizong sent Hou against Qu Wentai, king of Gaochang, who had allied with the Western Tujue. Qu Wentai died as the army arrived, and Hou besieged the capital until his son Qu Zhisheng surrendered. On his return to Chang'an Hou was accused of taking treasure from Gaochang's treasury and enslaving captives, and was briefly arrested before Cen Wenben persuaded the emperor to release him.

Resentful at this treatment, Hou joined the plot of the crown prince Li Chengqian through his son-in-law Helan Chushi, the commander of the prince's guards. When the guard Gegan Chengji betrayed the plot, the conspirators were sentenced to death. Taizong wished to spare Hou, but his officials objected, and the emperor and Hou wept as they parted. Hou was beheaded on 29 April 643; his wife and children were pardoned but exiled to the region of modern Guangdong. In the same year his portrait had been among the Portraits at Lingyan Pavilion that Taizong commissioned to honour 24 great contributors to Tang rule.
houegbadja: Houegbadja, also called Wegbaja or Aho, followed his father Dakodonou to the throne, and the story of his rise rests largely on oral traditions. The main tradition makes him the son, or in some versions the adopted son, of Dakodonou. A Gedevi woman named Adanon, of the native people of the Abomey Plateau, was betrothed to Dakodonou, but Houegbadja made her pregnant and was disinherited. Father and son were reconciled only after Houegbadja killed a strong rival of Dakodonou; he was then named heir and became king on his father's death.

Because Houegbadja holds a primary place in the kingdom's ceremonies, he is credited with many administrative developments that he is unlikely to have created alone. Various oral traditions hold that he established the Royal Palaces of Abomey, the general structure of the royal administration, poll taxes and death taxes, and that he made the king's sacrifices to the ancestors the foremost in the kingdom. Militarily he is often credited with the first expansions of the kingdom beyond the Abomey Plateau, and sometimes with creating the Dahomey Amazons, although that claim is considered unlikely.

He is often considered the first king of Dahomey because he established the palace and the many rules that defined the kingdom's administration. In the Annual Customs of Dahomey, the ceremony centred on tributes to the royal ancestors, Houegbadja was the first king recognised. He named his eldest son Akaba as his heir, and on his death around 1685 Akaba came to power.
houmuwu-ding: The Houmuwu ding is a rectangular ding, a sacrificial vessel and one of the common types of Chinese ritual bronze, standing on four legs. It is 133 cm high, 110 cm wide and 79 cm deep, and weighs 832.84 kg. Compared with earlier vessels such as the Duling fangdings, it is wider and has thicker walls. Each side has a blank panel in the middle, framed by a band of taotie, animal-faced creatures, and kuilong, one-legged dragons. Its two handles are decorated on the outside with two tigers facing each other, their jaws closing on a human head, an image also found on the battle axes of Fu Hao.

The vessel was unearthed in 1939 at Wuguan Village in Anyang, Henan, near Yinxu, the site of the last Shang capital. It bears three characters in bronzeware script on its inner wall, and like other inscribed bronzes it is named after them. The inscription, Queen Mother Wu, is read as the temple name of Fu Jing, queen and principal wife of Wu Ding. The ding was made after her death, presumably by her son Zu Geng of Shang. Her tomb, tomb 260 at Yinxu, was not found until 1959, and had been looted.

In October 1946, after an interview on the site by the reporter Shao Shenzhi, the vessel was confirmed as a Shang bronze. In November the scholar Zhang Feng read the inscription as Simu Wu, and it became known as the Simuwu ding.

Guo Moruo, president of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, took si to mean sacrifice, so that the vessel was cast by Wu's son to worship his mother. In 1977 Li Xueqin proposed reading the first character as hou, queen, since such a verb-object phrase is rare in inscriptions, and Sun Ji pointed out that hou is the mirror image of si, a common reversal in oracle bone writing. When the National Museum of China reopened after renovation in March 2011, the vessel was renamed the Houmuwu ding.
house-of-aisin-gioro: The Aisin Gioro traced their ancestry to Bukūri Yongšon, a warrior of the thirteenth century. Emperor Hongtaiji claimed that he was conceived by a virgin birth: a magpie dropped a red fruit near the heavenly maiden Fekulen, who ate it and became pregnant. The same story belongs to another Manchu clan, the Hurha, and the real ancestor of the Aisin Gioro was Möngke Temür, a chieftain of the Odoli tribe under the Mongol Yuan Empire.

When Nurhaci reorganised Jurchen society in 1601, the Gioro clan was partitioned. Descendants of his father Taksi became Aisin, while other Gioros took names such as Irgen Gioro or Hūlun Gioro. The people the clan ruled were ethnically mixed, and in 1635 all of them were designated Manchu.

Nurhaci replaced small hunting groups with banners of some 7,500 warriors and their households, identified by coloured flags. In time there were Manchu, Mongol and Chinese banners, eight of each, and by 1648 fewer than one sixth of the bannermen were of Manchu ancestry. The conquest of the Ming was thus won by a multiethnic army led by Manchu nobles and Han Chinese generals.

Marriage served as policy. Aisin Gioro princesses were given to Mongol princes and to Han Chinese officers, including sons of the generals Sun Sike, Geng Jimao, Shang Kexi and Wu Sangui, to bring them into alliance. Dorgon and Jirgalang acted as regents early in the Shunzhi Emperor's reign, and in 1861 the regents Duanhua, Sushun and Zaiyuan were ousted in the Xinyou Coup.

The core branch numbered 378 people in 1660 and 29,292 in 1915, a smaller increase than the Ming house of Zhu, which had 200,000 members by its fall. After the Qing fell most members took Chinese surnames such as Jin, Zhao, Ai or Luo. Later heads of the house were named under a succession law Puyi approved in 1937: Pujie held the position from 1967 to 1994, followed by Jin Youzhi until 2015 and then Jin Yuzhang. Some 300,000 to 400,000 Manchus in China bear the surname Aisin Gioro.
house-of-albret: The family took its name from the lordship of Albret, or Labrit, in the Landes. The genealogy of Anthony M. H. J. Stokvis traces it to Jimeno of Pamplona, a Basque nobleman of the 800s and patriarch of the Jiménez dynasty. The recorded lords begin with Amanieu I, active around 1050, and for generations bore the names Amanieu or Bernard. In the 14th century the house supported the English cause for a time before going over to France.

Arnaud Amanieu I helped to take Guienne from the English, and his son Charles became constable of France and was killed at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Grants from successive kings and the favour of Charles VI and Charles VII made the house a great territorial power; in 1470 it inherited the County of Périgord and the Viscounty of Limoges, and it then laid claim to the Duchy of Brittany. Alain the Great hoped to marry Anne of Brittany and fought Charles VIII to that end, but when she was betrothed to Maximilian of Austria he surrendered Nantes to the French in 1486.

Alain's son Jean became king of Navarre by his marriage, which also brought the house the County of Foix. Their son Henry II of Navarre was created Duke of Albret and a peer of France in 1550; by his wife Marguerite d'Angoulême, sister of Francis I, he was the father of Jeanne d'Albret, who married Anthony de Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme. A cadet, Jean d'Albret-Orval, governor of Champagne, served Francis I in many negotiations, among them his bid to be elected emperor in 1519.

Their lands, among them Béarn, Foix, Bigorre, Tartas, Castres and Dreux, gave the Albrets a real political role in the Renaissance, but they did not stay long at the top. Jeanne was the last of the name on the throne of Navarre: with the accession of her son as Henry IV, the duchy of Albret was united to the French crown. The title of Duke of Albret was later granted to the family of La Tour d'Auvergne in 1651, in exchange for Sedan and Raucourt.
house-of-andechs: The family first held lands in southwestern Bavaria at Dießen am Ammersee and Wolfratshausen, and at the castle of Ambras near Innsbruck, controlling the road over the Brenner Pass to the March of Verona. A Count Rasso is recorded at Dießen; he is said to have fought the invading Magyars in the early 10th century and founded the monastery of Grafrath. Through their ancestor Count Palatine Berthold of Reisensburg, a grandson of Duke Arnulf the Bad of Bavaria, the family may be linked to the Luitpolding dynasty.

Count Berthold II, who lived at Andechs from about 1100 and died in 1151, is credited as the founder of the comital line. He gained lands in Franconia, where about 1135 he had the Plassenburg built near Bayreuth and founded the town of Kulmbach, and by marrying Sophie, daughter of Margrave Poppo II, he came into lands in Istria and Carniola. In 1180 the family acquired Innsbruck. Otto II of Andechs was bishop of Bamberg from 1177 to 1196, and members of the house were implicated in the murder of Philip of Swabia, King of the Germans, at Bamberg in 1208.

Berthold IV, Duke of Merania, had eight children. His sons included Ekbert, bishop of Bamberg from 1203 to 1231, Berthold, Patriarch of Aquileia, Otto, who succeeded him as duke, and Henry, Margrave of Istria. His daughter Gertrude was the first wife of King Andrew II of Hungary and the mother of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, and Mechtilde became abbess of Kitzingen. Agnes became the third wife of Philip II of France in 1196, after he repudiated Ingeborg, but was dismissed in 1200 when Pope Innocent III laid France under an interdict.
house-of-ascania: The House of Ascania is a princely family documented since the 11th century, also known as the House of Anhalt after its longest-held possession. The name Askanier is a Latinization of its seat at Aschersleben. The family appears first as the Counts of Ballenstedt, from an area now in the Harz district of Saxony-Anhalt, with Ballenstedt as the eponymous seat in the 11th and 12th centuries and Aschersleben and finally Anhalt Castle among the most significant seats. Prince Bernhard III of Anhalt was the first, in 1320, to call himself comes Ascanie, and nineteenth-century historiography applied that term to all members of the family since the 11th century.

Albert the Bear became Duke of Saxony in 1138 and was the first margrave in the formerly Slavic settlement area of Brandenburg. When Pribislav died in 1150 his widow Petrissa handed the land of the Hevelli around Brandenburg Castle to Albert, who took definitive possession in 1157. In 1180 the eastern parts of the Duchy of Saxony passed to Bernhard of Saxony, and as Dukes of Saxe-Wittenberg the family received hereditary electoral dignity in 1356.

After Bernhard III, Duke of Saxony, died in February 1212, his son Henry received the Anhalt house estates between the Lower Harz and the lower Mulde, while his brother Albert inherited the Duchy of Saxony. The division marks the beginning of Anhalt's independent development, with Henry I as its first ruler and the first to be called prince in Anhalt. Henry II founded the Anhalt-Aschersleben line in 1252, and in 1603 another division created the younger lines of Anhalt-Dessau, Anhalt-Bernburg, Anhalt-Köthen and Anhalt-Zerbst.

Alexius Friedrich Christian of Anhalt-Bernburg was the first Anhalt prince to gain the title of duke, in April 1806. The Zerbst line ceased in 1793 and the Köthen line in 1847, and when the Bernburg line died out in 1863 the Duchy of Anhalt was formed under Leopold IV Frederick. It sided with Prussia in 1866, joined the North German Confederation in 1867 and the German Empire in 1871. Aribert of Anhalt abdicated in 1918, during the November Revolution. Leopold III of Anhalt-Dessau had created the Wörlitz Park, an English landscape garden. Since the late 17th century only the Anhalt branch has survived.
house-of-assembly-of-barbados: The legislature of Barbados was introduced by Governor Henry Hawley, who gave the colony a structure of government patterned on the Parliament of England. At first the Parliament had a single chamber, charged with establishing a system of laws, and it was wholly dominated by the island's planter class. Its first meeting, on 22 June 1639, makes it the third oldest legislature in the Americas, after the Virginia General Assembly and the Bermuda House of Assembly, and one of the oldest in the Commonwealth of Nations.

The House of Assembly is the lower house of the bicameral Parliament of Barbados. Its 30 members are elected directly in single-member constituencies by the first-past-the-post system for a term of five years. It sits roughly 40 to 45 days a year under a Speaker; a Speaker chosen from outside the house becomes its 31st member, with a vote when motions are tied. Before taking their seats, members swear allegiance to Barbados under section 59 of the constitution. The chamber is in the east wing of the Public Buildings on Broad Street in Bridgetown.

Under the constitution Parliament stands dissolved five years after its first sitting unless dissolved sooner, and writs for a general election must be issued after every dissolution; since 30 November 2021 that has been done by the President rather than the Governor General.

Two parties have dominated modern elections: the Barbados Labour Party, earlier the Barbados Progressive League, and the Democratic Labour Party. Smaller parties such as the National Democratic Party, the Barbados National Party and the West Indian National Congress Party, as well as independents, have also won seats. The Democratic Labour Party, in opposition since 1994, won 20 seats to 10 on 15 January 2008, and David Thompson became the sixth Prime Minister. On 24 May 2018 the Barbados Labour Party under Mia Mottley won all 30 seats, and she became the first woman to hold the office. The party won every seat again on 19 January 2022 and in February 2026.
house-of-auersperg: The first certain member of the family is Engelbertus de Ursberch, a witness to a deed of 1162 issued by Herman, Duke of Carinthia. Its seat was Auersperg Castle south of Ljubljana, built in 1067 according to an engraving on site, beneath the original arms showing an aurochs, Auerochs in German and Tur in Slovene. The family may have come from Ursberg in Swabia and probably settled in Lower Carniola after the Battle of Lechfeld in 955; its estates stretched from Grosuplje to Velike Lašče and Ribnica.

From 1407 the Auerspergs held the office of hereditary chamberlain of Carniola, and in the 15th century the family split into the lines of Auersperg Castle and Schönberg. Its members fought the Ottomans: Trojan of Auersperg at the Siege of Vienna in 1529, Andreas von Auersperg, called the Carniolan Achilles, at the Battle of Sisak in 1593, and Herbard VIII von Auersperg, commanding general of the Croatian and Slavonian Military Frontier, who fell in battle in 1575 and whose severed head was taken to the Sultan in Istanbul.

Johann Weikhard of Auersperg took part in the negotiations at Osnabrück that led to the Peace of Westphalia and was tutor to Ferdinand IV, after whose election as King of the Romans he was raised to imperial prince. In 1664 he acquired Tengen, which gave the house an unconditional seat in the Council of Princes, and he served as prime minister to Emperor Leopold I from 1665 to 1669. In 1791 the family sold Münsterberg and Frankenstein to Prussia, and its county of Gottschee in Carniola was raised to a duchy.

The annexation of Tengen by the Grand Duchy of Baden in 1806 ended the princes' rule as territorial lords, but as a mediatised house they kept equality of birth with the reigning houses of Europe, and the order of precedence of 1837 placed them fifth among the mediatised houses of Austria. In 1861 Emperor Franz Joseph I made Karl, 8th Prince of Auersperg, the first president of the Austrian House of Lords. The poet Anastasius Grün, Count Anton Alexander von Auersperg, also belonged to the family.
house-of-aviz: The founder, King John I, was born in 1357, the illegitimate child of King Pedro I of the Portuguese House of Burgundy and Teresa Lourenço, a Lisbon merchant's daughter. In 1364 he was made Grand Master of the Order of Aviz and became known as John of Aviz.

The dynasty arose from the crisis after the death of Ferdinand I in 1383. His designated heir was his daughter Beatrice, married to John I of Castile, who claimed the throne in her name. In April 1385, amid popular revolt and civil war, the Cortes of Coimbra declared John, Master of Aviz, king. He was backed by the rising bourgeoisie of Lisbon, while the nobility split, most favouring Beatrice. His rule was secured by the victory at Aljubarrota on 14 August 1385; formal peace with Castile was signed only in 1411.

To mark the victory John founded the Monastery of Santa Maria da Vitória, known as Batalha, whose chapel became the burial place of the dynasty's princes. Under the house Portugal became a world power. The conquest of Ceuta in 1415 was its first colonial venture, followed by exploration of Africa, Asia and Brazil. The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 belongs to the period. The Portuguese Empire reached its zenith under Manuel I, and its decline began under John III.

Sebastian I, John III's grandson, who succeeded in 1557, died childless at 24 at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir. His great-uncle, the Cardinal-King Henry, died two years later, also childless. Catherine, Duchess of Braganza, Philip II of Spain and António, Prior of Crato, claimed the throne. António was acclaimed king in 1580, twenty days before Philip invaded Portugal and defeated his supporters at the Battle of Alcântara. Historians dispute whether those twenty days count as a reign. António held out in the Azores until 1583.

Notable members include Prince Henry the Navigator, Peter, Duke of Coimbra, Eleanor of Portugal, Holy Roman Empress, and Isabella of Portugal, wife of Charles V. John I added the green Cross of the Order of Aviz to the arms of Portugal, and the armillary sphere became a royal badge under Manuel I. Portugal and Spain shared a monarch until 1640, when the Duke of Braganza was proclaimed John IV.
house-of-babenberg: Two groups bear the name. The Elder or Franconian House, called Popponids after Count Poppo of Grapfeld, took its name from Babenburg Castle at the site of Bamberg and lost its influence in Franconia after the Babenberg feud with the Conradines, which ended in 906 at the Battle of Fritzlar. The Younger or Austrian House descends from Margrave Leopold I. Its claim to descend from the elder house has not been verified by scholars, and Leopold may have descended from the Bavarian Luitpolding duke Arnulf of Bavaria.

Leopold I, first mentioned in 962 as a follower of Emperor Otto I, appears in 976 as count of the Bavarian Eastern March, which he received as a reward for loyalty to Otto II. He extended it down the Danube into what is now Lower Austria at the expense of the retreating Magyars. His son Henry I followed in 994 and Henry's brother Adalbert in 1018. Leopold III, called the Pious for founding monasteries such as Klosterneuburg, declined the royal crown in 1125 in favour of Lothair of Supplinburg and was canonised in 1485.

Henry Jasomirgott held Bavaria from 1143 but gave it up to Frederick Barbarossa, and in compensation Austria, whose capital had moved to Vienna about 1155, was raised to a duchy by the Privilegium Minus. Leopold V captured Richard I of England on his way home from Palestine and handed him to Emperor Henry VI, and added Styria under the will of Ottokar IV. His son Leopold VI, called the Glorious, was a lawgiver and patron of letters, and under him Vienna became a centre of the Minnesingers.

Frederick II, called the Quarrelsome for his disputes with the kings of Hungary and Bohemia and with the emperor, was placed under the imperial ban in 1236 but later restored. He was killed in battle in 1246, and the male line died out. After a struggle known as the War of the Babenberg Succession, Austria and Styria fell to Ottokar II of Bohemia and then to Rudolph I of Habsburg, whose descendants ruled Austria until 1918. Babenberg descent entered the Habsburg line gradually, and after 1598 all Habsburg members descended from the Babenberg dukes.
house-of-barcelona: The house descended from the Bellonids, the descendants of Wilfred the Hairy, and held the County of Barcelona and the County of Girona continuously from 878. By the thirteenth century its members had inherited most of the Catalan counties and had established a territorial Principality of Catalonia. Ausona and Besalú joined the family's holdings in 1111, Berga, Cerdagne and Conflent in 1118, Roussillon in 1172 and Pallars Jussà in 1192.

The union with Aragon brought the title of prince of Aragon in 1137; the title of king of Aragon followed in 1162. Further crowns came through conquest and inheritance: Valencia in 1238, Majorca in 1276, Sicily in 1282, and Sardinia and Corsica in 1297. The family also held the lordship of Montpellier from 1204 to 1249, and members of the line were dukes of Athens from 1312 to 1388 and of Neopatria from 1319 to 1390.

The family divided into several lines. Cadet branches ruled Urgell from 992 and Gandia, and others had ruled Ausona intermittently from 878 until 1111. A cadet branch held Provence from 1112 to 1245 and another ruled Sicily from 1282 to 1409. Besalú and Cerdagne came to the main line by inheritance from another branch of the family, and the family held the title of count of Urgell again from 1314 to 1413.

The main line ended with the death of its last legitimate male member, Martin, in 1410. By the Compromise of Caspe of 1412 the Crown of Aragon passed to a branch of the House of Trastámara, descended from the infanta Eleanor of the house of Barcelona, so that the inheritance went through a woman of the old line.
house-of-bernadotte: The founder's family was modest. Its first known paternal ancestor, Joandou du Poey, was a shepherd who married Germaine de Bernadotte in Pau in 1615 and began to use her surname. His descendant Henri Bernadotte (1711–1780) was a local prosecutor from a family of artisans, who had once been imprisoned for debt, and the household occupied a single floor of a house in a peripheral district of Pau. Two branches of the French Bernadotte family survive in France alongside the Swedish royal house; the baronial branch descended from Henri's elder son died out in 1966.

Sweden lost Finland, roughly the eastern half of the realm, in the Finnish War of 1809, and resentment of King Gustav IV Adolf brought a coup that deposed him. His uncle Charles XIII, aged 61 and childless, was elected in his place. The Riksdag of the Estates chose Prince Christian August of Augustenborg as heir, but he died in 1810. Wishing for a ruler of whom Napoleon would approve, the Riksdag elected the French marshal Jean-Baptiste Jules Bernadotte as heir presumptive on 21 August 1810.

Bernadotte had joined the French army as a simple soldier and risen to general after the Revolution. In 1798 he married Désirée Clary, whose sister was the wife of Joseph Bonaparte, and in 1804 Napoleon made him a marshal and in 1806 Prince of Pontecorvo. As crown prince he took the name Charles John and acted as regent. In 1813 he broke with Napoleon and brought Sweden into the Sixth Coalition. When the Treaty of Kiel awarded Norway to Sweden, Norway resisted and a brief war followed, ending when he persuaded Norway to accept a personal union under a common monarch. He reigned from 5 February 1818 until his death on 8 March 1844.

Charles XIV John was followed by Oscar I, Charles XV, Oscar II, Gustaf V and Gustaf VI Adolf, with Carl XVI Gustaf reigning from 1973. The house ruled Norway as well until the union was dissolved in 1905, when Prince Carl of Denmark, a grandson of Charles XV, was elected as Haakon VII of Norway.

The house's arms joined those of the House of Vasa with those of the Prince of Pontecorvo, topped by an eagle; the raven that replaced Napoleon's eagle in 1818 was changed several times, and gold was restored to the eagle in 1908. Princes who married without the king's consent lost their succession rights, and since 1892 their male-line descendants have borne the title Count of Wisborg, granted by the Monarch of Luxembourg.
house-of-borgia: The Borgias, in Spanish and Valencian Borja, came from Xàtiva in the Kingdom of Valencia, and took their surname from the town of Borja in the Crown of Aragon. Rumours that the family was of Jewish descent and only pretended to be pious Catholics were spread by opponents, among them Giuliano della Rovere, but were unsubstantiated. The family itself claimed a spurious descent from Pedro de Atarés, Lord of Borja, a 12th-century claimant to the crown of Aragon who died childless.

Alfons de Borja, born in 1378, was a professor of law at the University of Lleida and a diplomat for the kings of Aragon before becoming a cardinal. He was elected Pope Callixtus III in 1455 as a compromise candidate, at an advanced age, and reigned until his death in 1458. His nephew Rodrigo Borgia, born in Xàtiva in 1431, studied law at Bologna and was made a cardinal by his uncle. He had four children by Vannozza dei Cattanei: Giovanni, Cesare, Lucrezia and Gioffre.

Rodrigo was elected pope in 1492 as Alexander VI. He was recognised as a skilled politician and diplomat but was widely criticised for overspending, the sale of Church offices and nepotism. He made Giovanni captain-general of the papal army and Cesare a cardinal, and used his children's marriages to build alliances: Lucrezia married Giovanni Sforza in 1493, and Gioffre married Sancha of Aragon. The family made enemies of the Medici, the Sforza and the friar Girolamo Savonarola, and under Alexander it was suspected of many crimes, including simony, bribery and murder. He died in Rome in 1503, probably of malaria.

Cesare left holy orders after Giovanni's death, which some suspected him of causing, though no clear evidence exists. After his father's death he failed to keep control of the papacy: his candidate, Pius III, died a month after election, and della Rovere, whom Cesare then backed, turned against him. Cesare was killed in 1507 besieging the castle of Viana in Navarre. Lucrezia's marriage to Sforza was annulled in 1497, and her second husband, Alfonso of Aragon, was strangled. She lived at Ferrara as the wife of Alfonso I d'Este and died in 1519.

The Borgias were also patrons of the arts who contributed to the development of Renaissance art. Francis Borgia, 4th Duke of Gandía, a great-grandson of Alexander VI, became an effective organiser of the Society of Jesus and was canonised by Clement X on 20 June 1670. Gaspar de Borja y Velasco was Archbishop of Seville and Viceroy of Naples. The family's reputation for crime has inspired many novels, plays, operas, films and television series.
house-of-bourbon: The Bourbons began as a branch of the Capetian dynasty, the royal House of France. They date from 1272, when Robert, the youngest son of King Saint Louis IX of France, married the heiress of the lordship of Bourbon. The house then served for three centuries as a cadet branch under the Capetian and Valois kings. The senior line died out in the male line in 1527 with Duke Charles III of Bourbon, who died in the Sack of Rome. When Henry III of France died in 1589 the House of Valois became extinct in the male line, and under Salic law the head of the House of Bourbon became King of France as Henry IV.

Henry IV was raised a Calvinist and became nominal leader of the Huguenots in 1569. On 13 April 1598 he granted the Edict of Nantes, which made Catholicism the official religion but gave the Huguenots a measure of tolerance, ending the religious wars. Bourbon monarchs ruled France and Navarre until the monarchy was overthrown in 1792. Louis XIV succeeded his father at four, and Cardinal Mazarin ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648 and defeated the nobility in the Frondes. Louis XVI convened the Estates-General on 5 May 1789 and was executed in 1793.

Napoleon's abdication on 11 April 1814 restored the dynasty in the person of Louis XVIII, who was restored again after Waterloo. His brother Charles X reigned from 1824 until the July Revolution of 1830, and the cadet House of Orléans then ruled from 1830 to 1848.

In 1700 the Spanish Habsburgs died out in the male line, and Charles II of Spain willed the throne to Louis XIV's second grandson, the Duke of Anjou, who became Philip V. The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 ratified his renunciation of the French throne and so separated the two crowns. Charles III, already king in Naples and Sicily, became king of Spain in 1759. Bourbons ruled Naples from 1734 to 1806, Sicily from 1735 to 1816 and the Two Sicilies from 1816 to 1861.

The Spanish branch has been overthrown and restored several times, reigning 1700 to 1808, 1813 to 1868, 1875 to 1931 and again from 1975. Since 1733 the Bourbons have been the only surviving legitimate branch of the House of Capet.
house-of-bourbon-montpensier: The house took its first name from the marriage of John I, Duke of Bourbon, to Marie de Valois, comtesse de Montpensier (1375–1434), and its second from the family's title. The county had passed to Marie from her brothers Charles and John of Valois, sons of John de Valois, duc de Berry and Auvergne. Her son Louis I de Bourbon (1403–1486) was the first Bourbon count of Montpensier, followed by his son Gilbert (1448–1496) and Gilbert's sons Louis II (1483–1501) and Charles III (1490–1527).

The title passed down the line mainly through women. Charles III's sister Louise de Bourbon (1482–1561) became duchesse de Montpensier, and she was followed by her son Louis III (1513–1582), his son François (1542–1592) and François's son Henri (1573–1608). Henri's daughter Marie de Bourbon (1605–1627) married Gaston, Duke of Orléans, and by then the family had gathered a long list of titles, among them Dauphin of Auvergne, Sovereign Prince of the Dombes, Prince de la Roche-sur-Yon, Prince de Joinville, Duc de Guise, Duc de Châtellerault and Comte d'Eu. Most were used in their feminine forms, since most holders were women.

Marie died in 1627, less than a month after the birth of her daughter Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, La Grande Mademoiselle, who became heiress to what was probably one of the largest fortunes in Europe. She died without heirs in 1693. Some of her titles went to Louis-Auguste de Bourbon, founder of the illegitimate line of Bourbon du Maine, through a scheme of his mother, Françoise-Athénaïs, marquise de Montespan, but most of her fortune passed to her cousin Philippe de France, duc d'Orléans.

The Bourbon-Montpensier fortune thus founded the wealth of the House of Orléans and of the Bourbon-Penthièvre family, which inherited much of it from the du Maines and married into the Orléans family in 1769. The title of duc de Montpensier passed down the Orléans line and is now used as a courtesy title by the Orléans pretender to the throne.
house-of-bourbon-parma: The House of Bourbon-Parma is an Italian cadet branch of the House of Bourbon, descended in the male line from the French Capetian dynasty. Its members ruled as King of Etruria and as Duke of Parma and Piacenza, Guastalla and Lucca. Its founder, Philip, Duke of Parma, was a great-grandson of Ranuccio II Farnese, Duke of Parma, and married Louise Élisabeth of France, so that the Bourbon house and the state of Parma came together.

The Duchy of Parma had been created in 1545 as a fief for Pier Luigi Farnese, the illegitimate son of Pope Paul III. In 1556 the second duke, Ottavio Farnese, was given Piacenza. The Farnese ruled until 1731, when the last male-line duke, Antonio, died.

On Antonio's death the duchy passed to Infante Charles of Spain, the heir through his mother, Elisabeth Farnese. Under the Treaty of Vienna of 1738 Charles had to give it up to Austria. The duchy was ceded back to the Bourbons in 1748 by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, in the person of Charles's younger brother Philip. In 1796 French troops under Napoleon Bonaparte occupied it, and in 1814 it was restored under Napoleon's Habsburg wife, Marie Louise, to rule for her lifetime.

When Marie Louise died in 1847, the duchy returned to the Bourbon-Parma line, which had been ruling the tiny Duchy of Lucca. The Bourbons ruled until 1859, when a revolution following the Franco-Sardinian victory over Austria drove them out. In December 1859 Parma, Piacenza, Guastalla and Lucca joined Tuscany and Modena to form the United Provinces of Central Italy, which were annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in March 1860.

The Bourbons continue to claim the title of Duke of Parma. Carlos-Hugo, a Carlist pretender to the Spanish throne in the 1970s, held it from 1977 until his death. The House of Bourbon-Parma is also the sovereign house of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg through the male line, and all members of the grand ducal family are members of the house, styled princes and princesses with the predicate Royal Highness.
house-of-braganza: The house was founded by Afonso I, 1st Duke of Braganza, an illegitimate son of King John I of Portugal, founder of the House of Aviz, and Inês Pires. His father valued him and arranged his marriage to Beatriz Pereira de Alvim, daughter of Nuno Álvares Pereira, Portugal's most important general and a friend of the king. Afonso was also given the title of Count of Barcelos. The house grew into one of the wealthiest and most powerful noble houses of Iberia during the Renaissance.

By 1640 Portugal was overtaxed, its colonies were unprotected, and Philip III of Portugal had lost the trust of most of the nobility and was loathed by the guild of merchants. The Braganzas deposed the Philippine Dynasty in the Restoration War, and the Duke of Braganza became King John IV. In 1807, facing a Napoleonic invasion, the royal court moved to Brazil, which was made a kingdom alongside Portugal, forming the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves. João VI returned to Portugal in 1821.

On 7 September 1822 his son Pedro, regent in Brazil, declared independence and was acclaimed Emperor of Brazil. Pedro I abdicated in 1831 in favour of his young son Pedro II, who was declared of age in 1840 and brought stability to a country on the verge of disintegration. Under him Brazil won the Platine War, the Uruguayan War and the Paraguayan War, and slavery, restricted by successive laws, was abolished in 1888 by Princess Isabel.

In Portugal, Pedro became King Pedro IV in 1826 and abdicated in favour of his seven-year-old daughter Maria, with his brother Miguel as regent. In 1828 Miguel instead proclaimed himself king and repudiated the liberal constitution. Maria II later reigned, and the house continued in Portugal until Manuel II was deposed in 1910.

The house produced 15 Portuguese monarchs and all four Brazilian monarchs, and consorts to several European kingdoms, among them Catherine of Braganza, wife of Charles II of England. Its crest is a green wyvern, taken to represent Saint George, and it appears on the Portuguese Crown Sceptre and the Sceptre of the Emperor of Brazil. A tradition, the Curse of the Braganzas, holds that after John IV mistreated a Franciscan friar no first-born son of the dynasty would live to reign.
house-of-burgh: In the later 12th and early 13th centuries the de Burghs were led by four brothers: William de Burgh; Hubert de Burgh, Chief Justiciar and Regent of England and Earl of Kent; Thomas de Burgh, Castellan of Norwich; and Geoffrey de Burgh, Bishop of Ely. William arrived in Ireland in 1185 with Prince John and received lands from King Henry II. At John's accession in 1199 he was installed in Thomond and became Governor of Limerick. He backed Cathal Carrach and Cathal Crovderg in turn for the kingship of Connacht, and married a daughter of Domnall Mór Ó Briain, King of Thomond.

William's son Richard Mór de Burgh received Connacht in 1227 and was Justiciar of Ireland from 1228. His second son, Walter de Burgh, obtained from Prince Edward a grant of the county of Ulster about 1255 and was later styled Earl of Ulster. Walter's son Richard Óg de Burgh, 2nd Earl of Ulster, spent forty years fighting Irish kings and Anglo-Norman rivals, supported Edward I in Scotland and marched against Edward Bruce's invasion of Ulster in 1315, although his daughter Elizabeth had married Edward's brother, King Robert I of Scotland. Their son became David II, King of Scots.

When William Donn de Burgh, 3rd Earl of Ulster, was murdered in 1333, his only daughter Elizabeth inherited, and through her marriage to Lionel, 1st Duke of Clarence, the Yorkist kings later derived their claim to the English throne. His male kinsmen, who by Irish custom had the better right, took Irish names and ways, became in effect native chieftains and held most of the de Burgh lands. They formed two branches, Mac William Uachtar or Clanricarde in southern Connacht and Galway, and Mac William Íochtar in Mayo, and the name was gaelicised as de Búrca, then Burke or Bourke.

In 1543 Ulick na gCeann Burke surrendered his lands to Henry VIII and received them back as Earl of Clanricarde. In 1603 Tiobóid na Long Bourke did the same in Mayo and was later made Viscount Mayo. The original Ulster line died out in 1363 and the Clanricarde line in 1916, while the Earls of Mayo still represent the family. Richard Bourke, 6th Earl of Mayo, became Viceroy of India in 1869 and was murdered in the Andaman Islands in 1872.
house-of-chatillon: The family traced its origins to the 9th century. It took its name from Châtillon-sur-Marne in Champagne, where its members held a castle as tenants of the Counts of Champagne. Gaucher V of Châtillon was lord of Châtillon from 1290 until 1303, when he became Count of Porcien, and the lordship was sold in 1400 to Louis of Valois, Duke of Orléans. Other branches held Saint-Pol-sur-Ternoise, which died out in 1360, Blois, which died out in 1397, and Penthièvre, which lasted until 1457.

Odo of Châtillon, who became Pope Urban II, came from the family. Raynald of Châtillon was Prince of Antioch and Lord of Oultrejordain, a Crusader leader whose conflicts in the Kingdom of Jerusalem led towards the Battle of Hattin; his daughter Agnes of Antioch married Béla III of Hungary in 1172. Gaucher de Châtillon, seneschal of Burgundy, escorted Philip II of France to the Holy Land and distinguished himself at the siege of Acre and at the Battle of Bouvines.

His great-grandson Gaucher V de Châtillon was constable of France under Philip IV of France and a minister of Louis X of France. Jeanne de Châtillon became Duchess of Athens, and Jacques de Châtillon died at the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302. Marie de St Pol founded Pembroke College, Cambridge. Charles of Blois, later canonised, claimed the duchy of Brittany in right of his wife, and his claim began the Breton War of Succession; the title passed for a time to his descendants.

Through its marriages and offices the family reached from Champagne to Brittany, Hungary, Athens and the crusader states. It is wholly distinct from the house of Châtillon-sur-Loing, which produced the Coligny brothers Gaspard, François and Cardinal Odet.
house-of-cirksena: The Cirksena descended from a line of chieftains of Greetsiel. Their name is of Frisian origin, probably from the old forename Tzirk or Cirk, and is still a common family name in East Frisia; Enno Attena took it on his marriage to the heiress Gela Syardsna of Manslagt. In 1453, after clashes between rival lines of chieftains, the town of Emden, which Hamburg had placed under direct rule in 1439, was given to the family, which ruled it until 1595.

The family rose by succeeding the tom Brok chieftains after their opponent Focko Ukena was defeated and expelled by allied chieftains led by Edzard Cirksena. Emperor Frederick III raised Ulrich Cirksena to imperial count and enfeoffed him with the Imperial County of East Frisia. Under Edzard I (1462–1528), the most important ruler of the house, the county grew to its widest extent and the Reformation spread through it. In 1654 the emperor made the Cirksena princes.

Charles Edzard, the last ruler of the house, died without issue in the night of 25 to 26 May 1744, reportedly from a glass of buttermilk drunk after a hunt, and Frederick the Great took over the state at once. A second line had meanwhile held Rietberg. Count Enno III gained it by marrying its heiress, Walburg von Rietberg, but ceded it to his daughters in the Treaty of Berum of 1600. In 1601 his brother, Count John III, married Enno's daughter Sabina Catherine with papal dispensation; both converted to Catholicism, founding a Catholic branch whose last male, Count Ferdinand Maximilian, died in 1687.

The family's arms, a crowned golden harpy on a black field, outlived it. Count Rudolf Christian placed the harpy in the comital arms of East Frisia in 1625, and these are still the emblem of East Frisia. The harpy also appears in the arms of Emden, of Delfzijl opposite it, of the Aurich district and of Krummhörn, the family's ancestral homeland. Through the marriage of Agnes Cirksena to Gundakar of Liechtenstein, it is part of the arms of the Principality of Liechtenstein.
house-of-clare: The family descended in the male line from Gilbert, Count of Brionne, whose father Geoffrey, Count of Eu, was an illegitimate son of Richard I, Duke of Normandy. Gilbert was a guardian of the young Duke William, who succeeded in 1035, and when Gilbert was assassinated in 1039 or 1040 his sons Baldwin and Richard fitz Gilbert fled to Baldwin V, Count of Flanders. They returned when William married Baldwin's daughter in 1053 and rose high in his favour.

After the Norman conquest Richard fitz Gilbert received great estates, among them Clare in Suffolk and Tonbridge, and the Suffolk return of the Domesday Survey once calls him Richard of Clare. His brother Baldwin de Meules was put in charge of Exeter on its submission in 1068 and made sheriff of Devonshire.

Richard's English lands passed to his son Gilbert fitz Richard, while a younger son, Robert, founded the line of the Barons FitzWalter. In the next generation the family gained two earldoms. Gilbert fitz Gilbert, settled in Wales, became Earl of Pembroke in 1138 and lord of Striguil, and his nephew Gilbert fitz Richard was made Earl of Hertford, perhaps in 1138 and at least by 1141; the Hertford earls sometimes styled themselves Earls of Clare.

Richard de Clare, 2nd Earl of Pembroke, called Strongbow like his father, outlived his only son, so his Irish and Welsh lands went with his daughter Isabel to her husband, William Marshal. Some came back when their daughter Isabel Marshal married her distant cousin Gilbert de Clare, 4th Earl of Hertford, who also inherited from his mother the earldom and honour of Gloucester and the lordship of Glamorgan from his grandfather William Fitz Robert, 2nd Earl of Gloucester.

At its height the house held Caerphilly Castle, Pembroke Castle, Castell Coch and over 190 manors in England. When Gilbert de Clare, 8th Earl of Gloucester, died without children, the earldoms became extinct and his lands were divided among his sisters. A junior line had become lords of Thomond in Ireland, and its Richard de Clare was summoned to Parliament in 1309, but the death of his infant son in 1321 ended the last line called de Clare, though the male line survived in the Barons FitzWalter. The arms of the Clare earls of Hertford, three red chevrons on gold, derive from Strongbow's simplified version of the family's early chevronny shield.
house-of-commons-of-england: The Parliament of England grew out of the Magnum Concilium, a royal council of churchmen, noblemen and knights of the shire that met for short periods to approve the Crown's taxes. It often demanded the redress of grievances before voting money, and so acquired legislative powers. The rebel leader Simon de Montfort first summoned representatives of the major towns in 1265, during the Second Barons' War, and Edward I adopted the practice for his Model Parliament of 1295.

It became settled that each county sent two knights and each borough two burgesses. The burgesses were at first almost powerless, since the monarch could enfranchise or disfranchise boroughs at will. From 1341, under Edward III, the knights and burgesses met apart from the nobility and clergy, who became the House of Lords.

In the Good Parliament of 1376 the Commons chose Peter de la Mare to put their complaints about taxes, royal spending and the conduct of the war to the Lords, and they impeached some of the king's ministers. De la Mare was imprisoned, but the value of a single voice was recognised and the office of Speaker emerged; released after Edward III's death, he became the second Speaker in 1377. Under Richard II the Commons again impeached ministers and claimed control of taxation and spending, though they remained weaker than the Lords and the Crown.

The civil wars of the late fifteenth century weakened the great nobles and restored royal supremacy, which grew under the House of Tudor. The Reformation Parliament of 1529 to 1536, called by Henry VIII and directed by Thomas Cromwell, legislated on matters once left to the church. Conflicts with James I and Charles I over taxation, religion and royal powers led to the English Civil War. In December 1648 the New Model Army purged the Commons in Pride's Purge, the only military coup in English history; Charles I was beheaded and the Lords abolished, and Oliver Cromwell dissolved the remaining Rump Parliament in 1653.

The monarchy and the Lords were restored with the Commons in 1660, and the Crown's influence fell further after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and the Bill of Rights 1689. The house also seated members for two continental towns while they were English: Calais from 1372 to 1558 and Tournai from 1513 to 1519. The House of Commons of Great Britain that replaced it in 1707 was itself succeeded in 1801 by the House of Commons of the United Kingdom.
house-of-commons-of-the-united-kingdom: The House of Commons of England began to evolve in the 13th and 14th centuries; the first English parliament was called in 1236. In 1707, after the political union with Scotland, it became the House of Commons of Great Britain, with 45 Scottish members added. The Acts of Union 1800 added 100 Irish members at Westminster. In 1922, after the independence of the Irish Free State, it became the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

The chamber's shape comes from St Stephen's Chapel, which housed the Commons until a fire destroyed it in 1834. Benches face one another across the floor as the chapel's choir stalls did, an arrangement that favours adversarial debate.

The Commons went through important reform in the 19th century. Constituency boundaries had not changed since 1660, so declining towns still elected two members each. Among these rotten boroughs were Old Sarum, which had only six voters for two MPs, and Dunwich, largely lost to coastal erosion, while large cities such as Manchester had no separate representation.

In 1909 David Lloyd George, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, introduced the People's Budget, which proposed a new tax on wealthy landowners. The Conservative House of Lords rejected it. After a further election in December 1910 the government of H. H. Asquith secured a bill curbing the Lords, after threatening to create 500 new Liberal peers. Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 the Lords' power to reject legislation was reduced to a delaying power.

The government is responsible solely to the Commons. The House does not formally elect the prime minister, but by convention the monarch appoints the person who commands its support, normally the leader of the largest party, and the prime minister holds office only while keeping the confidence of a majority. The House scrutinises ministers through committees and weekly Prime Minister's Questions.

At the start of each term the House elects one of its members as Speaker, whose election needs the Sovereign's approval as a formality. Its symbol is a portcullis topped by St Edward's Crown, a badge of the Tudors and a favourite of Henry VII.
house-of-dadiani: The Dadiani are presumed to descend from a certain Dadi of the House of Vardanisdze, a Svan noble family with estates in Svaneti. Appointed hereditary eristavi, or dukes, of Odishi, as Samegrelo was also called, in reward for military service, they had become the most powerful feudal house in western Georgia by the 1280s, when branches of the family also governed Svaneti, Guria and Bedia.

In 1542 Duke Levan I Dadiani became hereditary prince, or mtavari, of Mingrelia and established himself as an independent ruler. The original line ended in 1691, when its last prince was forced to abdicate and relatives from the House of Chikovani, until then princes of Salipartiano, inherited both the title and the surname of Dadiani. Genealogists call the line that followed the House of Dadiani-Chikovani.

After accepting Russian sovereignty the Dadiani were raised to the rank of princes of the Russian Empire and kept wide independence in their home affairs. Russia annexed Samegrelo in practice in 1857, but the principality kept a nominal existence until 4 January 1867, when the last prince, Niko Dadiani, was deposed. He formally renounced his rights to the throne in 1868.

Later members of the family included Ekaterine Dadiani (1816–1882), Princess Regent of Mingrelia, the poet and Russian general Constantine Dadiani, the chess player and tournament patron Andria Dadiani (1850–1910), Salome Dadiani (1848–1913), who married Prince Achille Murat, and the writer and dramatist Shalva Dadiani (1874–1959).

In the nineteenth century a Hungarian family ennobled in the late 18th century, the Dadányi de Gyülvész, claimed descent from a Mingrelian prince, George Dadiani, said to have fled to Hungary after a conflict with his brother Grigol Dadiani. Asked for proof, they said the documents had been kept in an iron safe lost in a robbery. In fact the family descended from Moschopolitan merchants of Aromanian ancestry.
house-of-dampierre: The family took its name from Dampierre, in Champagne, where its members first became prominent; the earliest known of them is Guy I of Dampierre, a great-grandson of Guy I of Montlhéry. Its rise in Flanders began in a family quarrel. Margaret II of Flanders had married Bouchard d'Avesnes in 1212, but her sister Joan had the marriage condemned by Pope Innocent III, and while Bouchard was in Rome Margaret remarried, to William of Dampierre, a nobleman from Champagne.

The second marriage was possibly bigamous, and the claims of Margaret's children by each husband led to the long War of the Succession of Flanders and Hainault. In 1246 King Louis IX of France gave Flanders to the Dampierre children and Hainaut to the Avesnes children. The Avesnes side defeated and imprisoned the Dampierres at the Battle of West-Capelle on 4 July 1253, and Louis confirmed his division in 1254. Strife between the two houses went on for decades.

Guy I was imprisoned by John I of Avesnes from 1253 to 1256 and became Count of Namur in 1263, when Baldwin II of Courtenay sold him the county. His son Robert III, known as the Lion of Flanders, ruled Flanders from 1305 to 1322. Through a careful marriage policy the main line added the counties of Nevers in 1280 and Rethel in 1328, and through the mother of Louis II, a daughter of King Philip V of France, Artois and the county of Burgundy, the Franche-Comté.

The senior line ended with the death of Margaret III in March 1405. A junior line, descended from a younger son of Guy I by his second wife Isabelle of Luxembourg, ruled Namur until it sold the county to Philip the Good in 1421.

Margaret III was succeeded in Flanders, Artois, Nevers and Franche-Comté by her eldest son, John the Fearless, and in Rethel by her younger son Anthony, which marked the start of the House of Valois-Burgundy. The lands gathered by the Dampierres formed the core of the dominions of the House of Valois-Burgundy, which, with the Duchy of Burgundy, gave that house a power base from which to challenge its cousins, the Valois kings of France, in the 15th century. A branch founded by Guy II of Dampierre through his marriage to Mathilde of Bourbon became the House of Bourbon-Dampierre.
house-of-david: According to the biblical narrative, David of the Tribe of Judah fought a protracted conflict with Ish-bosheth of the Tribe of Benjamin, who had succeeded his father Saul. The prophet Samuel had anointed David as the true king. After Ish-bosheth was assassinated by his own army captains, David is traditionally believed to have taken the throne around 1010 BCE. He ruled first over Judah alone from Hebron, and after seven and a half years the other tribes, leaderless, chose him as well. He was succeeded by his son Solomon, whose mother was Bathsheba.

Little is conclusively known about the house outside the Bible. The Tel Dan Stele, dated to about 840 BCE, mentions the death of a reigning king from what is interpreted as the House of David, and it is the only explicit mention of David outside the Bible. Some scholars, among them Israel Finkelstein and Neil Silberman, think David and Solomon probably existed but were chieftains of a modest society in Judah rather than rulers of a wealthy empire.

After Solomon's death the ten northern tribes rejected his son Rehoboam and chose Jeroboam as king, forming the Kingdom of Israel in the north, while Judah and Benjamin kept Rehoboam and formed the Kingdom of Judah in the south.
