Apart from Athaliah, only the Judahite monarchs belonged to the Davidic line.

The earliest unambiguously attested king of the line is Uzziah, in the 8th century BCE. After him each king of Judah is attested in some form, except Amon. Ahaz's son Hezekiah appears on royal seals and in Sennacherib's Annals. Jeconiah is named in Babylonian documents listing the rations given to him and his sons as prisoners. The Kingdom of Judah fell to the Neo-Babylonian Empire after the siege of Jerusalem, when Solomon's Temple was destroyed. The Hasmonean dynasty later founded an independent Jewish kingdom, but it was not considered connected to the Davidic line.

Later rabbinical authorities granted the office of exilarch, head of Babylonian Jewry, to families tracing male-line descent from David. The office continued after the Arab conquest in the 7th century and exilarchs were appointed until the 11th century.

In Jewish eschatology the Messiah is expected to be a king whose paternal bloodline traces to David, who will rule during the Messianic Age. Christians hold that the line continued to Jesus, hence the title Son of David, according to the genealogies in Matthew and Luke; Jews do not accept this. The Quran mentions the family of David once.
house-of-dreux: The house was founded by Robert I, Count of Dreux, a son of Louis VI of France, who received the County of Dreux as his appanage. The counts of Dreux remained relatively minor nobles in France, and their senior comital line died out in 1345. Through their kinship with the counts of Vermandois, themselves of Capetian descent, they bore a chessboard of gold and azure, which in the 13th century marked their cousinship with the kings of France.

The family's rise came when the French king, needing an obedient vassal to marry Alix, Duchess of Brittany, turned to his cousin Peter, a younger son of the Count of Dreux. Called Mauclerc, the bad cleric, Peter had at first been devoted to the clergy, and on renouncing it he kept the quarter of ermine that marked such princes. His marriage placed the house in one of the most important fiefs of France. Brittany became a lay peerage of France in 1297 and was formally recognised as a duchy by the French court.

When John III, Duke of Brittany died in 1341, his niece Joan of Penthièvre and his younger half-brother John of Montfort both claimed the duchy. Joan's husband, Charles of Blois, was a nephew of King Philip VI, who backed them, while Edward III of England supported the Montforts. John of Montfort died in 1345, and Charles was killed at the Battle of Auray in 1364 fighting John's son. The Treaty of Guérande, which ended the War of the Breton Succession, made the duchy hereditary in the male Montfort line, with the males of Blois-Penthièvre after them.

The Penthièvre family imprisoned the duke in 1420 in a failed attempt to regain Brittany. When Francis II, the last male Montfort duke, died, the duchy passed to his daughter, Anne of Brittany. The house also left Brittany its arms. In 1316 John III gave up the Dreux chessboard with its ermine quarter, which marked a cadet line and made the duchy a heraldic dependency of the small county of Dreux, and adopted plain ermine, partly because his stepmother Yolande de Dreux bore the same arms as he did.
house-of-elders-somaliland: Councils of clan elders, the guurti, existed long before Somaliland was founded, but they were neither institutions nor permanent bodies: the elders of the clans concerned met whenever a matter arose. In 1991 the Somali National Movement, led mainly by the Isaaq clans of north-western Somalia, declared the Republic of Somaliland. Its military factions could not unite the country, and in 1993 the movement asked the clan elders to mediate between them. At the Great Congress of National Reconciliation in Borama that year the elders were made a House of Elders of 82 members drawn from across Somaliland, and the house nominated Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal as president.

The Guurti is the upper house of the Parliament of Somaliland and considers the bills of the elected lower house, the House of Representatives. It may reject a resolution of that house, but the House of Representatives prevails if it passes the resolution again by a two-thirds majority. Under the constitution its 82 members elect a Speaker, two Deputy Speakers and a Permanent Committee of 25. Honorary members without votes are added: five appointed by the President, former Speakers of either house, and anyone who has served as President or Vice-President. By tradition the house avoids contested votes for its chair.

The interim constitution of 1997 set the house's term at six years, but the house was not re-elected when that term expired. When terms ran out the Guurti repeatedly extended its own, that of the House of Representatives and that of the President: in 2003, in May 2006, twice from April 2008 before the presidential election of June 2010, in September 2010, in April 2013 and on 16 May 2015. In October 2022 it extended the President's term by two years and its own by five, a decision some legislators opposed and the British and United States governments criticised. Suleiman Mohamoud Adan, Speaker from August 2004, resigned in July 2026 at the age of 92, and Muse Haji Abdi Duale succeeded him.
house-of-este: The House of Este is a European dynasty of Longobard origin. The first known member was Margrave Adalbert of Mainz, known as the father of Oberto I, Count palatine of Italy. Oberto's grandson Albert Azzo II, Margrave of Milan, built a castle at Este, near Padua, and named himself after it. His son Welf IV became Duke of Bavaria in 1070 and the ancestor of the elder branch, the House of Welf. Another son, Fulco I, was the ancestor of the younger, Italian line.

In 1154 the two branches, with Duke Henry the Lion of Saxony and Bavaria on the German side, agreed to allot the family's Italian possessions to the younger line, which in time acquired Ferrara, Modena and Reggio.

From 1171 the Italian line was titled Margraves of Este. Obizzo II made the lordship of Ferrara hereditary, and was proclaimed Lord of Modena in 1288 and Lord of Reggio in 1289. Ferrara was a papal fief, and the family became hereditary papal vicars in 1332. Borso was made Duke of Modena and Reggio by Emperor Frederick III in 1452 and received Ferrara as a papal fief from Pope Paul II in 1471.

Ercole I was one of the most significant patrons of the arts in his time, and Josquin des Prez worked for him. His son Alfonso I was the third husband of Lucrezia Borgia and a patron of Ariosto. Alfonso II raised Ferrara's glory to its highest point, and patronised Torquato Tasso. The legitimate line ended with him in 1597; the Emperor recognised his cousin Cesare d'Este as heir, but in 1598 Pope Clement VIII annexed Ferrara to the Papal States on grounds of Cesare's illegitimacy.

The elder branch, the House of Welf, produced dukes of Bavaria and Saxony, the Holy Roman Emperor Otto IV, dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg, and the Hanoverian monarchs of Great Britain from 1714, as well as one Emperor of Russia, Ivan VI. The Italian branch continued at Modena. As the last male heir, Ercole III, had only a daughter, Maria Beatrice, a treaty of 1753 with the House of Austria arranged her marriage to Archduke Ferdinand Karl, a son of Empress Maria Theresa, in 1771, founding the House of Austria-Este.

Ercole III succeeded in 1780 but was deposed by the French in 1796, and his states became the Cispadane Republic. He received the principality of Breisgau in compensation, and the male line became extinct with his death in 1803.
house-of-gonzaga: The first members of the family of historical importance collaborated with the Guelph faction alongside the monks of Polirone Abbey. From the 12th century they became a dominant family in Mantua, growing wealthy when their allies, the Bonacolsi, defeated the Casalodi. In 1328 Ludovico I Gonzaga overthrew the Bonacolsi lordship of the city with the help of the Scaliger, and entered the Ghibelline party as capitano del popolo, or people's captain, of Mantua and imperial vicar of Emperor Louis IV.

Feltrino, lord of Reggio until 1371, founded the cadet branch of the Gonzaga of Novellara, whose state lasted until 1728. In 1433 Gianfrancesco I became Marquis of Mantua with the recognition of Emperor Sigismund, and Federico II received the title of Duke of Mantua in 1530. His brother Ercole Gonzaga became a cardinal, presided over the Council of Trent and was almost elected Pope, while Ferrante, an ally of Emperor Charles V, founded the cadet branch of Guastalla. In 1531 the family acquired the Marquisate of Montferrat through marriage.

Luigi (Louis) Gonzaga married the heiress of Nevers and Rethel in France, and his son Charles later inherited Mantua and Montferrat, which triggered the War of the Mantuan Succession. Marie Louise Gonzaga was queen consort of Poland and grand duchess consort of Lithuania from 1645 to 1667, and two daughters of the house, both named Eleonora Gonzaga, became Holy Roman Empresses. Gonzaga rule continued in Mantua until 1708 and in Guastalla until 1746.

The family included a saint, Aloysius Gonzaga, canonised in 1726, twelve cardinals and fourteen bishops. Gianfrancesco Gonzaga funded a school led by Vittorino da Feltre, and Isabella d'Este supported composers who popularised the frottola. Duke Guglielmo Gonzaga, himself a composer, founded the Basilica palatina di Santa Barbara and brought Claudio Monteverdi to the court, which saw some of the first operas staged, among them L'Orfeo in 1607. The house inspired the play within the play in Shakespeare's Hamlet, The Murder of Gonzago. Only a minor Gonzaga-Vescovato branch survives.
house-of-gramont: The family takes its name from the castle of Gramont, Agramont in Spanish, in the Basque province of Lower Navarre. Its line can be followed through a succession of soldiers, courtiers and later dukes of Gramont and princes of Bidache. Antoine III de Gramont (1604–1678), a soldier and diplomat, was made a marshal of France in 1641. His daughter Catherine-Charlotte de Gramont (1639–1678) became princesse de Monaco and a mistress of Louis XIV.

Antoine III's son Guy Armand de Gramont, comte de Guiche (1637–1673), was an adventurer and a lover of Prince Philippe of France, and allegedly of Philippe's wife, Henrietta of England. Antoine V de Gramont (1671–1725), grandson of Antoine III, was duc de Gramont and became a marshal of France in 1724. His son Louis de Gramont (1689–1745) was defeated at the Battle of Dettingen and killed at the Battle of Fontenoy.

In the 19th century Antoine-Geneviève-Héraclius-Agénor de Gramont (1789–1854) was a court figure close to the Bourbons. His son Agénor de Gramont, 10th Duke of Gramont (1819–1880), was a diplomat and statesman, and the 11th Duke (1851–1925) a soldier. Eugénie de Gramont (1788–1846) was a religious figure, and Antoine Alfred Arnaud Xavier Louis de Gramont (1861–1923) a spectroscopist.

Armand de Gramont, 12th Duke (1879–1962), was a scientist and industrialist, and his sister Élisabeth de Gramont (1875–1954), Duchess of Clermont-Tonnerre, a writer. Louis de Gramont (1854–1912) wrote plays and libretti. Gabriel Antoine Armand, comte de Gramont (1908–1943), a grandson of the 10th Duke, was a hero of the French Resistance. Henri de Gramont, 13th Duke (1907–1995), carried the title on, while Sanche de Gramont (1932–2023) gave up his titles and became a naturalised citizen of the United States under the name Ted Morgan.
house-of-griffins: The dynasty is known by two names: Pomerania, after its main fief, a name that comes from the Slavic po more, land along the sea, and Griffin, after its coat of arms. The first verifiable use of the griffin as the family's emblem is a seal of Casimir II, Duke of Pomerania, attached to a document of 1194, and the family called itself the Griffins only after the 15th century.

Where the family came from is not clear. Most theories derive it either from the local West Slavic nobility or from a cadet branch of the Polish house of the Piasts. The Polish chronicler Jan Długosz connected it with the Świebodzice family of Lesser Poland, who also bore a griffin, and the chronicler Gallus Anonymus called the Pomeranian rulers close cousins of Bolesław III of Poland. In the 17th century the Griffins traced their descent to beings of Sorb mythology called Gryphus or Baltus.

The first known members were the brothers Wartislaw I and Ratibor I. Wartislaw founded the main line of dukes, while Ratibor was the ancestor of the Ratiborides, who ruled the lands of Schlawe and Stolp until the line died out and the area passed to the duchy. A related branch, the Swantiborides, served as castellans of Pomeranian towns such as Szczecin and Kołobrzeg, though their link to the main house remains uncertain.

Through marriage the family reached far beyond Pomerania. Eric of Pomerania, son of Wartislaw VII, became the first king of the Kalmar Union, ruling Denmark, Sweden and Norway. Euphemia of Pomerania married Christopher II of Denmark, Elizabeth of Pomerania became the fourth wife of Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor, and her daughter Anne of Bohemia married Richard II of England. Sophie of Pomerania, daughter of Bogislaw X, became queen of Denmark and Norway as the wife of Frederick I of Denmark.

The death of the last duke, Bogislaw XIV, during the Thirty Years' War led to the division of Pomerania between Brandenburg-Prussia, Sweden and Poland. The main burial places of the dukes are the Ducal Castle in Szczecin, the Co-Cathedral of Saint John in Kamień Pomorski and Saint Peter's Church in Wolgast, while Eric of Pomerania lies in Darłowo. A Pomeranian buttercup, Ranunculus gryphum, was named after the dynasty.
house-of-grimaldi: The Grimaldi family, originally from France, moved to Genoa in 1070 with Inigo Grimaldo. Several families united under the name and became one of the most powerful in the city, later leading the Guelph faction, which supported the Pope against the Ghibellines, who supported the Holy Roman Empire. The Grimaldis descend from Grimaldo, a Genoese consul who lived at the time of the early Crusades and may have been a son of the earlier consul Otto Canella.

As was customary in Genoa, the family organised its ties within a corporation called an albergo. In the political reform of 1528 the Grimaldi became one of the 28 alberghi of the Republic of Genoa, alongside the Doria and Pallavicini. The house provided several doges, cardinals, cabinet ministers and military officers.

The Grimaldis allied with the Fieschi family against rivals in Genoa. In 1271 the Guelphs were banned from the city, and the Grimaldi took refuge in their castles in Liguria and Provence, signing a treaty with Charles of Anjou to retake control of Genoa. The castle of Monaco was taken and abandoned by both Guelphs and Ghibellines, since it was well placed for operations against Genoa. In 1395 the Grimaldis took advantage of discord in Genoa to take possession of Monaco, which they ruled as a condominium; this is the origin of today's principality.

From 1532 to 1641 the Grimaldi princes of Monaco ruled the town of Campagna in southern Italy, after Emperor Charles V granted them the Marquisate of Campagna. They married into the French nobility in the 1600s, inherited French estates and often lived in Paris. Monaco and the County of Nice were taken by the revolutionary army in 1792, and Monaco was re-established by the Congress of Vienna in 1815.

Every Prince of Monaco has been a member of the House of Grimaldi, though since the 18th century the princes have descended in the male line from other families that inherited through the female line and adopted the Grimaldi name. In 1715 Jacques Goyon de Matignon married Louise Hippolyte, the last agnatic Grimaldi heir, and he and his descendants ruled from 1731 to 1949.

In 1911 Charlotte Louvet was legitimised as successor, and her husband, Count Pierre de Polignac, adopted the Grimaldi name and arms as a condition of the marriage. A treaty between Monaco and France provided that sovereignty would revert to France if the prince left no dynastic offspring, until a 2002 agreement changed it. The coat of arms is a red and white diamond pattern.
house-of-guise: The House of Guise was founded as a cadet branch of the House of Lorraine by Claude of Lorraine (1496 to 1550), who entered French service and was made the first Duke of Guise by King Francis I. Claude's daughter Mary of Guise (1515 to 1560) married King James V of Scotland and was the mother of Mary, Queen of Scots. His eldest son Francis, the second duke, became a military hero through his defence of Metz in 1552 and the capture of Calais from the English in 1558, while another son, Charles, became Archbishop of Reims and a cardinal.

In 1558 the Dauphin Francis married Mary, Queen of Scots, and when he became king in 1559 her uncles, the Duke of Guise and the Cardinal of Lorraine, controlled French politics. They crushed the conspiracy of La Renaudie in March 1560. In 1562 Duke Francis's retinue massacred a Protestant congregation at Wassy on his way to court to oppose the regent Catherine's Edict of Saint-Germain, and the Prince de Condé's rebellion began the French Wars of Religion. Francis helped defeat the Huguenots at Dreux on 19 December 1562 and was assassinated at the Siege of Orleans on 24 February 1563.

His son Henry accused Admiral Coligny of orchestrating the murder, and helped plan Coligny's assassination, which spiralled into the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572. In 1576 Henry was instrumental in forming the Catholic League. When the death of the Duke of Anjou in 1584 made the Protestant Henry of Navarre heir to the throne, the War of the Three Henries followed. In 1588 Guise, with Spanish support, took control of Paris. King Henry III had him and his brother Louis, Cardinal of Guise, murdered at Blois in December 1588. Their brother Charles, Duke of Mayenne, led the League until a treaty in January 1596 ended it.

After this the House of Guise receded from prominence in French politics. Several junior branches, among them the dukes of Mayenne and of Elbeuf, continued the male line until 1825. The title of Duke of Guise was later given to a branch of the House of Bourbon and afterwards to the House of Orléans. Prince Jean, Duke of Guise (1874 to 1940), took it as the title of a pretender to the former French crown.
house-of-gurieli: Gurieli, meaning of Guria, was a hereditary title of the governors, or eristavis, of the province. It was adopted as a dynastic name by the Vardanisdze family, hereditary rulers of the highland province of Svaneti in western Georgia. The other notable branch of the Vardanisdze were the Dadiani of Samegrelo, and members of both sometimes used double names, Gurieli-Dadiani or Dadiani-Gurieli. The first prince in the list of rulers, Kakhaber I, governed from about 1385 as eristavi of Guria and Svaneti and was a son of George II Dadiani.

The medieval Gurieli were vassals of the Georgian crown but seem also to have paid homage to the neighbouring Empire of Trebizond. Its last emperor, David Komnenos, is recorded as a gambros of Mamia Gurieli, which is taken to mean that Mamia married a woman of his family; if so, the later princes may have descended from the emperors of Trebizond. From the 1460s, as the Bagrationi dynasty of Georgia declined, the Gurieli pursued separation and became in effect independent rulers of the Principality of Guria, though they paid tribute to the Ottoman Empire and nominally recognised the princes of Mingrelia and the kings of Imereti.

For two centuries their politics were dominated by wars with neighbouring Georgian rulers, Ottoman encroachment, civil strife and palace coups, and powerful neighbours sometimes placed rival branches of the family in power. In the 17th and 18th centuries as many as four Gurieli rulers were chosen kings of Imereti in place of the Bagrationi, though they are usually described as usurpers or counter-kings. Some princes were deposed and restored several times: George IV and Mamia IV each returned to power more than once.

After accepting Russian sovereignty in 1810 the dynasty kept some autonomy in internal affairs until 1829, when the Russian authorities deposed Prince David, the last ruling Gurieli, whose mother Sophia had been regent since 1826. After David's death in 1839 his cousin David Gurieli and his descendants were confirmed as princes, knyaz, in the Russian nobility by an imperial decree of 1850.
house-of-habsburg-lorraine: The House of Habsburg-Lorraine originated in the marriage in 1736 of Francis, Duke of Lorraine and Bar, and Maria Theresa of Austria, later Queen of Bohemia, Queen of Hungary and Archduchess of Austria. Its members are the legitimate surviving line of both the House of Habsburg and the House of Lorraine, and inherited their possessions from the female line of the Habsburgs and the male line of Lorraine. The Habsburgs took their name from Habsburg Castle, built in the 1020s by Count Radbot of Klettgau in Aargau. In 1273 Rudolph of Habsburg became Roman-German King and moved the family's power base to the Duchy of Austria, which the Habsburgs ruled until 1918.

The first member of the house to rule the Holy Roman Empire was Joseph II, who carried out many Enlightenment reforms, most of them to the detriment of the clergy. On his death in 1790 he was succeeded by his brother Leopold II, and in 1792 Leopold's son Francis II was crowned emperor in Frankfurt and joined the First Coalition against Revolutionary France. The Treaty of Campo Formio in 1797 handed the Duchy of Milan to France, while Austria gained Veneto, Istria and Dalmatia. Francis was forced to dissolve the Holy Roman Empire, having already proclaimed himself Emperor of Austria.

After the defeats of Napoleon at Leipzig in 1813 and Waterloo in 1815, the Congress of Vienna restored the old regimes, and Austria recovered the territories it had lost. The Revolutions of 1848 led to the expulsion of Metternich from the imperial chancellery and the rise of Franz Joseph, who replaced the abdicating Ferdinand I. Franz Joseph reigned from 1848 to 1916; the Second Italian War of Independence and the Austro-Prussian War both ended in defeat and ended Austrian supremacy in Italy and Germany. In 1867 he granted Hungary effective autonomy under the Ausgleich.

The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914 led to the First World War. Franz Joseph died in 1916 and was succeeded by his grandnephew Charles I, who after the lost war renounced the exercise of power without abdicating and was forced into exile on 3 April 1919. The Habsburg dominions were divided into independent republics. The family refused to swear allegiance to the Republic of Austria, so its members were exiled and their property confiscated. In 1961 Otto von Habsburg relinquished the monarchy and the succession rights of his descendants in exchange for an end to exile, and in 2007 his son Karl von Habsburg succeeded him as head of the house.
house-of-hanover: The House of Hanover began in 1635 as a cadet branch of the House of Welf, also called the House of Brunswick-Lüneburg. When the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg was divided that year, Duke George inherited the Principality of Calenberg and moved his residence to Hanover. His sons shared Calenberg and Lüneburg among them until his grandson George united the two in 1705. The fourth son, Ernest Augustus, was raised to the rank of prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire in 1692. His wife, Sophia of the Palatinate, was named heiress to the English throne by the Act of Settlement of 1701, which barred Roman Catholics; she was then the senior eligible Protestant descendant of James I.

Sophia died in 1714, and her son George Louis became George I of Great Britain that year. The dynasty gave six British monarchs: George I, George II, George III, George IV, William IV and Victoria. George I, George II and George III were also electors, and as rulers of both Britain and Hanover they kept control of the Hanoverian army and foreign policy. Hanover became a kingdom in 1814, after the Napoleonic Wars.

When William IV died in 1837 the personal union ended. Hanover's succession followed a semi-Salic law that gave priority to all male lines, so the throne passed not to Victoria but to her uncle Ernest Augustus, Duke of Cumberland, who reigned until 1851. His son George V was deposed in 1866 when Prussia annexed the kingdom, and he went into exile in Austria. Victoria died in 1901 and the British crown passed to her son Edward VII of the House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha.

The senior Welf line, which ruled Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, died out in 1884. Prussia opposed a Hanoverian succession in Brunswick until Ernest Augustus, the grandson of George V, married Princess Viktoria Luise of Prussia in 1913 and became duke that year; the marriage settled the quarrel between the houses. He was overthrown in 1918, when Germany became a republic.

The Peace of Westphalia gave the Prince-Bishopric of Osnabrück alternately to a Catholic bishop and to a cadet of Brunswick-Lüneburg, so it became a kind of appanage of the house until it was mediatized to Hanover in 1803. Many places in the British Empire were named for the house and its members, among them the American state of Georgia, New Brunswick in Canada, Victoria in Australia and British Columbia, and numerous towns called Hanover or Brunswick. Georgian architecture takes its name from the styles current between 1714 and 1830. The house is now the only surviving branch of the House of Welf.
house-of-hohenzollern: The family came from the area around Hechingen in Swabia in the late 11th century and took its name from Hohenzollern Castle, on an 855-metre mountain in the Swabian Alps. Its first ancestor mentioned is Burkhard I, Count of Zollern, who according to Berthold of Reichenau was born before 1025 and died in 1061. A founder named Tassilo, said to be a grandson of Charlemagne, was invented in 1560 by the historian Johann Basilius Herold, and his existence was disproved in the 19th century.

The Zollerns received the title of count from Emperor Henry V in 1111, and the county was called Hohenzollern from 1218. The family split into a Catholic Swabian branch and a Protestant Franconian branch, the latter founded by Conrad I, Burgrave of Nuremberg.

The Franconian Hohenzollerns supported Hohenstaufen and Habsburg rulers and were rewarded with territory, adding Ansbach in 1331 and Kulmbach in 1340. In 1411 Frederick VI, Burgrave of Nuremberg, was appointed governor of Brandenburg, and at the Council of Constance in 1415 King Sigismund made him Elector and Margrave as Frederick I; in 1417 he bought Brandenburg for 400,000 Hungarian guilders. In 1525 Albert of Prussia, last Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, became the first Duke of Prussia as a fief of the King of Poland.

Brandenburg and Prussia were ruled together from 1618. John Sigismund turned from Lutheranism to Calvinism, taking communion in the Calvinist rite on 25 December 1613, but strong protest forced him in 1615 to give up forcing his subjects to follow, making Brandenburg-Prussia a bi-confessional state. In 1701 Frederick I took the title King in Prussia with the assent of Emperor Leopold I. In 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed, and William I, as German Emperor and King of Prussia, ruled it until the revolution that followed Germany's defeat in 1918 ended the German and Prussian monarchy.

The Swabian branch, founded by Frederick IV, Count of Zollern, ruled Hechingen, Sigmaringen and Haigerloch and became princes in 1623. Troops of the Swabian League destroyed Hohenzollern Castle in 1423. This branch ruled until 1849. In 1866 Prince Charles of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen became prince of Romania, and king as Carol I in 1881; his line reigned until 1947.

From a minor princely family the Franconian line became one of the most important dynasties of Europe by marriage and by purchasing neighbouring lands. In 1870 the candidacy of Leopold, Prince of Hohenzollern, for the Spanish throne, and Bismarck's altered Ems telegram, led to the Franco-Prussian War. Since 1949 Germany's Basic Law recognises no Hohenzollern claim to royal or imperial prerogatives. Hohenzollern Castle still belongs to the family.
house-of-ibelin: Ibelin was the crusaders' name for the Arab city of Yibna, where King Fulk built the castle entrusted to the founder of the family, Barisan of Ibelin, as a reward for his loyalty during the revolt of his master Hugh II of Jaffa in 1134. The family's origins remain uncertain. The Ibelins claimed descent from the Le Puiset viscounts of Chartres; Peter W. Edbury suggests this could have been a fabrication and that the family may have come from Pisa, while Jonathan Riley-Smith thinks Barisan may have been a younger brother of Hugh II of Le Puiset.

Barisan was a knight in the service of the Count of Jaffa and became Constable of Jaffa in 1115. Around 1122 he married Helvis, heiress of the nearby lordship of Ramla. Their children were Hugh, Baldwin, Barisan, known as Balian, Ermengarde and Stephanie.

The family rose in only two generations. In the crusader kingdom such a rise was easier than in Europe, because individuals and whole families tended to die sooner and had to be replaced. Balian received the lordship of Nablus when he married Maria Comnena, the dowager queen, and he was the last to hold the family's mainland territories before they fell to Saladin in 1187. The castle of Ibelin itself was lost at the end of the 12th century, but by then the family had holdings at Beirut and in Cyprus.

Balian's son John, the Old Lord of Beirut, led the opposition to Emperor Frederick II when he tried to impose imperial authority over the crusader states, and the family briefly regained the castle of Ibelin in 1241. John's sons included Balian, lord of Beirut, Baldwin, seneschal of Cyprus, John, lord of Arsuf and constable of Jerusalem, and Guy, constable of Cyprus. Balian's second son Philip was regent of Cyprus for the widowed Queen Alice, and Philip's son John of Ibelin, count of Jaffa and Ascalon, wrote the Assizes of the High Court of Jerusalem, the most important legal document of the crusader kingdom.

Several members went to the new kingdom of Cyprus early in the 13th century, and most of the rest followed as the mainland kingdom was lost piece by piece. From the 13th to the 15th century the Ibelins were among the highest nobility of Cyprus and married into the royal Lusignans and families such as Montfort, Dampierre and Brunswick. Some of the Embriaco lords of Gibelet took the name Ibelin through a common maternal descent. When the Kingdom of Cyprus was destroyed in the 15th century the Ibelins apparently lost their lands and positions, and the family possibly became extinct.
house-of-keys: The oldest known use of the name is in a Latin document of 1417 by an English scholar, which speaks of the Keys of Man and the Keys of Law, Claves Legis. Its origin is disputed. Some take keys for an English corruption of a form of the Norse verb kjósa, to choose. A likelier explanation is that it is a mishearing of the Manx kiare as feed, four and twenty, the number of members the House has always had, and its Manx name remains Yn Kiare as Feed.

Its members are known as Members of the House of Keys. Twelve constituencies, based mainly on the sheadings and on local government units, each send two members, elected by plurality voting for a term normally fixed at five years. Voters must be over 16, and a candidate must be at least 18 and have lived on the island for three years. The members elect a Speaker, who presides and may abstain but must cast the deciding vote in a tie, and who also acts as Deputy President of Tynwald Court.

The Keys elect eight of the eleven members of the Legislative Council, the other branch of Tynwald. As legislation does not usually begin in the council, which acts as a revising chamber, the Keys hold much more power. About once a month the two branches sit together as Tynwald Court under the President of Tynwald, whom both elect; once a year, on Tynwald Day, the island's national day, the Lieutenant Governor or a member of the Royal Family presides.

The House usually meets in its chamber in the Legislative Buildings in Douglas. Members sit in two rows, by constituency in alphabetical order, with the member who received most votes in each constituency in the front row. On 14 March 2017 the Keys met in the Old House of Keys in Castletown, for the first time since 1874, to mark the sesquicentenary of the first elected House of Keys.
house-of-la-marck: The family descended from Count Adolf I, of a cadet branch of the Rhenish Berg dynasty seated at Altena Castle in Westphalia. Adolf inherited the fortress of Mark, in present-day Hamm-Uentrop, from his father Count Frederick I of Berg-Altena, who died in 1198, together with the older county around Altena. He moved there in the early 13th century, began to call himself count de La Mark and is first documented as comes de Marca in 1202. The family had been ministeriales of the Archbishops of Cologne.

At the height of its power the family ruled the County of Mark and the duchies of Jülich, Cleves, Berg and Guelders, as well as the County of Ravensberg. Adolf III inherited Cleves from his maternal uncle in 1368 and Mark from his brother in 1391, and his line later ruled the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg until John William died in 1609, which was followed by the War of the Jülich succession. Members of the house were prince-bishops of Liège, Münster and Osnabrück and archbishops of Cologne. Anne of Cleves, fourth wife of King Henry VIII of England, was a daughter of John III.

A branch descended from Eberhard I, Lord of Arenberg, held Sedan. William I de La Marck assassinated a Prince-Bishop of Liège, setting off a civil war there; his nephew Érard became prince-bishop in 1506. Robert III de la Marck was made Marshal of France in 1526, and William II de la Marck led the sea beggars in the Eighty Years' War.

Charlotte de la Marck married Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Marshal of France, in 1591 and died without issue in 1594, and her claims to Bouillon passed to her husband. The house died out in the male line in 1773 with Louis Engelbert, Count de la Marck. His daughter Louise-Marguerite married Charles Marie Raymond, Duke of Arenberg, and the title passed to their descendants in the House of Arenberg.
house-of-la-tour-dauvergne: La Tours appear in documents of the 11th and 12th centuries, but the family's history is clear only from the 13th century, when it held the Lordship of la Tour in the County of Auvergne. It married into other families of the French south, among them Ventadour, La Rochefoucauld and Levis-Mirepoix, and kept close ties to the Avignon popes; many of its members became bishops and cardinals, above all after Guy de la Tour married Marthe Rogier of Beaufort, a niece of Pope Gregory XI, in 1352.

The senior line ended in 1501 with Jean III de la Tour d'Auvergne, the last medieval Count of Auvergne, Boulogne and Lauraguais. His elder daughter Anne married John Stewart, 2nd Duke of Albany, and died childless, so both counties passed to Catherine de' Medici, later Queen of France. The junior line descended from Bertrand de La Tour d'Auvergne, lord of Olliergues, who died in 1329. Henry de la Tour d'Auvergne (1555–1623), a Marshal of France, was a faithful supporter of Henri IV's Huguenot cause.

His son Frederic Maurice, compromised in the Cinq-Mars conspiracy, was pardoned on condition that he give up the strategically important principalities of Sedan, Jametz and Raucourt in exchange for the French dukedoms of Albret and Château-Thierry, an exchange formalised in 1651. In the same year the family became Foreign Princes in France. His brother, Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, vicomte de Turenne (1611–1675), was buried at Saint-Denis by Louis XIV. Godefroy Maurice became sovereign Duke of Bouillon in 1678, when the duchy was retaken from the Spaniards, and Grand Chamberlain of France.

The 6th Duke, Godefroy Charles Henri, served in the Seven Years' War and nearly ruined the family by spending almost a million livres on a mistress in three months. The duchy was annexed by the French Republic within three years of his death, and the main line ended in 1802 when his only son died without issue. His Hôtel d'Évreux in Paris, bequeathed to the Empress Josephine, became the Élysée Palace. The duke had adopted Philippe d'Auvergne, a British naval officer, as a possible heir, but the Congress of Vienna gave the duchy to the King of the Netherlands.
house-of-lancaster: The first house of Lancaster was created in 1267, when King Henry III of England gave the Earldom of Lancaster to his second son Edmund Crouchback, who already held the lands of Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester, forfeited after the Second Barons' War. Edmund's son Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster, added the Earldom of Lincoln through his wife and became the most powerful nobleman in England, with an income of £11,000 a year, double that of the next wealthiest earl. His conflict with his cousin Edward II ended in his execution.

The second house descended from John of Gaunt, who married Blanche of Lancaster, heiress of the first house. Edward III had married his sons to wealthy English heiresses, and this match gave John the dukedom and the Lancastrian wealth.

John's son Henry usurped the throne in 1399 as Henry IV. Historians debate the accession, some seeing it as a cause of the Wars of the Roses because force had broken the principles the Plantagenets had upheld for two and a half centuries. His advisers, led by William Thirning, dissuaded him from claiming the throne by conquest. They argued instead that he was heir male to Henry III through Edmund Crouchback, said to have been the elder son set aside for a deformity; the committee he set up found no evidence for this.

Henry V renewed the claim to the French crown. He captured Harfleur, won the Battle of Agincourt although outnumbered, recaptured much of Normandy and secured the Treaty of Troyes and a marriage to Catherine of Valois. He died of dysentery at Vincennes in 1422. During the minority of Henry VI the Lancastrians split over policy in France, and the Duke of Gloucester died in prison in 1447. After the French victories at Formigny in 1450 and Castillon in 1453, the house lost all its French holdings except Calais and the Channel Islands.

The male line ended when Edward of Westminster, Prince of Wales, was killed in battle against supporters of the House of York in 1471 and Henry VI died or was murdered in the Tower of London. Descent through John of Gaunt's daughter Philippa continued in the royal houses of Spain and Portugal, while the Lancastrian cause passed to Henry Tudor, a descendant of the Beauforts, who established the House of Tudor.

The Lancastrians founded Eton College and King's College, Cambridge. Historians regret that Shakespeare's partly fictionalised history plays shape modern views of the dynasty more than scholarship does. The term Lancastrian was not used at the time, and doubts remain whether the red rose was really their emblem in the Wars of the Roses.
house-of-lara: The family arose in 11th-century Castile through a marriage that joined the lands of Gonzalo Núñez around Lara de los Infantes with the inheritance of his wife, Goto Núñez, who represented the holdings of the noble Álvarez and Alfonso families. By the 13th century the Lara family was linked to the heroes of the Cantar de los Siete Infantes de Lara, a 10th-century tale of revenge set in their lands, but there is no evidence that the tale reflects real events, and its names cannot be matched with the family's known ancestry.

From the 12th to the 15th century members of the family by turns supported and opposed their kings. In 1113 Pedro González de Lara backed Queen Urraca of Castile against her former husband, Alfonso I of Aragon, and in 1130 he and his brother Rodrigo confronted her son Alfonso VII, though Rodrigo later helped Alfonso against the Almoravids. Manrique Pérez de Lara, Álvar Pérez and Nuño Pérez de Lara disputed the regency of Alfonso VIII, whose alférez was Fernando Núñez de Lara, and Álvaro Núñez de Lara became regent for Henry I of Castile.

Nuño González de Lara served Ferdinand III and Alfonso X but in 1270 led an alliance of nobles against Alfonso. Juan Núñez I de Lara, lord of Albarracín, opposed the accession of Sancho IV and had to flee for a time to France, and Juan Núñez II de Lara led several rebellions against Alfonso XI. Peter the Cruel stripped the family of much of its land, most of which was returned by his half-brother and rival Henry II.

The only branch to survive the Middle Ages was the Manrique de Lara, who supported the Catholic Monarchs against the partisans of Joanna la Beltraneja. In 1520 Emperor Charles V made this line Grandees of Spain as Dukes of Nájera and Marquises of Aguilar de Campoo, and its members served the crown as viceroys, captains general, ambassadors and cardinals. The writers Gómez Manrique and Jorge Manrique belonged to it, and members of the family established branches as far away as the Philippines and Argentina.
house-of-liechtenstein: The family takes its name from Liechtenstein Castle in Lower Austria, near Vienna, which it possessed from at least 1136 to the 13th century and again from 1807. The progenitor Hugo von Liechtenstein, who died in 1156, built the castle around 1122-36 on a fief received from the Babenberg margraves of Austria.

In 1249 Heinrich I of Liechtenstein received the lordship of Nikolsburg in southern Moravia as free property from Ottokar II of Bohemia, whom he supported politically; it remained one of the family's most important seats until it was sold in 1560. Over the centuries the dynasty gathered vast lands, mostly in Moravia, Lower Austria, Silesia and Styria, always within countries ruled by other dynasties, above all the Habsburgs, to whom several Liechtenstein princes served as close advisers.

At the turn of the 16th and 17th centuries the brothers Karl, Maximilian and Gundakar returned to the Catholic faith before the Thirty Years' War and supported Emperor Ferdinand II in crushing the Bohemian Revolt. Maximilian, as Field Marshal, won the Battle of White Mountain, Gundakar prepared the Catholic League, and Karl, as Viceroy of Bohemia, oversaw the arrest and execution of the 27 Protestant leaders. All three were made princes of the Holy Roman Empire, and they cheaply acquired large lands from expelled Protestant nobles. He also received the Duchy of Troppau and the Duchy of Krnov from the emperor.

Their title was only honorary, since none of their lands depended directly on the imperial crown or carried a seat in the Imperial Diet. Prince Hans-Adam I therefore bought the Lordship of Schellenberg from the Hohenems family in 1699 and the County of Vaduz in 1712. On 23 January 1719 Emperor Charles VI united them as the Principality of Liechtenstein, in honour of Anton Florian of Liechtenstein, and the princes gained a hereditary seat in the Diet. With the end of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806 it became sovereign, as the Congress of Vienna recognised in 1814 and 1815.

The family moved its residence from Valtice to Vaduz in 1939, after the prince had opposed the annexation of Czech territory and the Nazis confiscated his properties. After 1945 the Beneš decrees took about 1,200 square kilometres in Czechoslovakia, 7.5 times the area of the principality. A constitution of 26 October 1993 gives all members other than the reigning prince the titles of Prince or Princess of Liechtenstein and Count or Countess of Rietberg.
house-of-ligne: Counted among the oldest noble families of Belgium, the house takes its name from the village of Ligne, between Ath and Tournai in the present-day province of Hainaut. Its rise in the nobility was gradual: barons in the 12th century, counts of Fauquemberg and princes of Épinoy in the 16th century, then princes of Amblise in 1608. Its arms are blazoned Or a bend gules.

The family also gave several abbots and abbesses. Gérard de Ligne, who died in 1270, was abbot of Cambrai, and women of the family were abbesses of Epinlieu, of Mons and of Cambrai; Catherine de Ligne, who died in 1581, was abbess of Thorn.

The family became imperial counts on 18 December 1544. On 20 March 1601 Emperor Rudolf II made Lamoral I a Prince of the Holy Roman Empire as Prince de Ligne, a title extended to all his agnatic descendants, male and female. When the Imperial County of Ligne was lost through the Peace of Lunéville, the family received in 1803 the secularised imperial abbey of Edelstetten, with a vote in the Imperial College of Princes. It sold Edelstetten to Prince Nikolaus Esterházy on 22 May 1804, two years before the Holy Roman Empire was abolished.

Cadet branches of the house included Barbançon, Barbançon-Arenberg, Moÿ, Ham, Arenberg and La Trémoïlle. Charles-Joseph held the title of 7th Prince from 1766 to 1814 and was followed by Eugène, 8th Prince from 1814 to 1880. In 1923 the Belgian Crown confirmed the style of Highness for all members of the surviving branches on 31 May, and on 22 October recognised the titles of Prince d'Amblise and Prince d'Epinoy for the head of the house.

In the 20th century the family married into several reigning houses. Yolande, daughter of the 11th Prince, became Archduchess Yolande of Austria and the daughter-in-law of Emperor Charles I of Austria. Antoine, 13th Prince from 1985 to 2005, married Alix, a daughter of Charlotte, Grand Duchess of Luxembourg, and Felix of Bourbon-Parma.
house-of-lobkowicz: The first Lobkowiczs were gentry of north-eastern Bohemia. Mikuláš Chudý, the Poor, of Újezd studied at the Charles University in Prague and became a scribe in Kutná Hora; King Wenceslaus IV gave him the village of Lobkovice, after which he styled himself, and made him supreme scribe of the kingdom in 1417. For capturing castles of rebellious nobles he was allowed to keep Hasištejn Castle. His sons were made free lords in 1459. Bohuslav Hasištejnský z Lobkovic was a humanist poet who collected more than 650 books, two thirds of which remain in the Lobkowicz Library.

Zdeněk Vojtěch and his wife Polyxena Pernštejn led the Catholic party at the Habsburg court, and after the Defenestration of Prague in 1618 the Emperor's ministers took refuge in the Lobkowicz Palace. The Catholic victory at the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 restored the property the rebels had confiscated. Their son Václav Eusebius presided over the Imperial War Cabinet from 1652 and the Privy Council from 1669, and rebuilt Roudnice Castle as the family seat.

Joseph II created the 7th Prince Duke of Roudnice in 1786, and the family's immediacy over Störnstein was mediatised to Bavaria in 1807, which placed it among the mediatised houses of the high nobility. Maximilian Lobkowicz served democratic Czechoslovakia as a diplomat and was ambassador to Great Britain for the government in exile in the Second World War. The family regained its property from the Nazis in 1945, lost it to the Communist government in 1948 and went into exile.

The princes built up a large collection of art and music. Ferdinand August added Veronese's David with the Head of Goliath and Rubens's Hygieia and was the first to collect musical scores systematically. Ferdinand Philip brought back two paintings of London by Canaletto from England, where Christoph Willibald Gluck had accompanied him. Beethoven dedicated the 3rd, 5th and 6th symphonies to Joseph František Maximilian. The family has four main branches, of Roudnice, Křimice, Dolní Beřkovice and Mělník, and the Lobkowicz Palace at Prague Castle and Nelahozeves Castle are museums.
house-of-lowenstein-wertheim: The County of Löwenstein had belonged to a branch of the counts of Calw before 1281, when the German King Rudolph I of Habsburg bought it and gave it to his natural son Albert. In 1441 Henry, one of Albert's descendants, sold it to the Palatine branch of the House of Wittelsbach. It later served as the portion of Louis, a son of the elector by a morganatic marriage, who became a count of the Empire in 1494 and received the title of Count of Löwenstein from Emperor Maximilian I. His descendants are the most senior, though morganatic, line of the Palatinate branch of the House of Wittelsbach.

The family lost Löwenstein to Ulrich, Duke of Württemberg, but Count Louis III gained Wertheim on the Main through his marriage to Anna, heiress of the Count of Wertheim. His sons divided the house: Christopher Louis, a Lutheran, founded the line later called Löwenstein-Wertheim-Freudenberg, and John Dietrich, who remained a Catholic, the line later called Löwenstein-Wertheim-Rosenberg. A third line, the Counts of Löwenstein-Scharffeneck, died out in 1633; its heiress Maria Christina married Count Gabriel Oxenstierna.

The head of the Catholic line was made a prince of the Empire early in the 18th century. The heads of the two branches into which the Protestant line divided were made princes by the king of Bavaria in 1812 and by the king of Württemberg in 1813. The county, part of the Franconian Circle, was mediatised when the Holy Roman Empire was dissolved in 1806, and its territory was split among Bavaria, Baden, Württemberg and Hesse; under the protocol of Frankfurt of 20 July 1819 all the family's lands were mediatised. The County of Löwenstein covered about 140 square kilometres.

Through the Rosenberg branch, though not in the male line, the monarchs of Belgium, Luxembourg and Liechtenstein descend from the family, as do the pretenders to the thrones of Portugal, the Two Sicilies, Bavaria and Austria-Hungary. Rupert zu Löwenstein, for many years the financial manager of the Rolling Stones, belonged to the Freudenberg branch.
house-of-lusignan: The House of Lusignan was a royal house of French origin that ruled kingdoms in Europe and the Levant, among them Jerusalem, Cyprus and Armenian Cilicia, from the 12th to the 15th century. It originated at Lusignan in Poitou in the early 10th century, and by the end of the 11th century its castle there made it the most prominent family of petty lords in the region. Hugh VI inherited the County of La Marche in 1091 as a descendant of Almodis of La Marche. In 1200 King John of England married Isabella of Angoulême, to whom Hugh le Brun de Lusignan had been betrothed, depriving Hugh of La Marche.

In the 1170s Aimery of Lusignan, a younger son of Hugh VIII, arrived in Jerusalem, expelled from his lands by Richard the Lionheart, then acting Duke of Aquitaine. He married Eschiva, daughter of Baldwin of Ibelin, and through the patronage of Agnes of Courtenay became Constable of Jaffa and later Constable of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. He became the first Lusignan king of Cyprus, and also King of Jerusalem. After he and most of the royal family died, his surviving son Hugh became King of Cyprus in 1205, while Jerusalem passed to Maria of Montferrat.

Hugh of Antioch, whose maternal grandfather had been Hugh I of Cyprus, took the name Lusignan and founded the second House of Lusignan; he became King of Cyprus and in 1268 was crowned King of Jerusalem. In 1291 the last remnants of the Kingdom of Jerusalem were captured by Al-Ashraf Khalil, the Sultan of Egypt. Henry fled to Cyprus and under his rule the kingdom prospered; he had the Haute Cour keep written records and turned it from an advisory council into a court that tried criminals. Hugh IV, content to be King of Cyprus alone, commissioned Giovanni Boccaccio's Genealogia deorum gentilium.

In 1342 Guy de Lusignan was elected King of Armenia and took the name Constantine II. The Lusignans tried to impose Western Catholicism on the people of Armenia, whose state religion was the Armenian Apostolic Church. The leadership largely accepted it, but the peasantry opposed it, and Constantine was killed in an uprising in 1344. Leon V de Lusignan was crowned in 1374, and in 1375 the Mamluk army invaded and he surrendered, ending the last fully independent Armenian entity of the Middle Ages. His cousin James I of Cyprus claimed the title, uniting it with those of Cyprus and Jerusalem. The Republic of Venice annexed Cyprus in the late 15th century.
house-of-luxembourg: The royal House of Luxembourg were not male-line descendants of the original counts of Luxembourg, a branch of the House of Ardenne that had ruled the county since the late tenth century. They descended from the House of Limburg-Arlon, whose members had been dukes of Lower Lorraine in the eleventh century. In 1247 Henry, a younger son of Duke Waleran III of Limburg, inherited the county on the death of his mother Countess Ermesinde and became Count Henry V of Luxembourg.

His grandson Henry VII became count when his father, Henry VI, died at the Battle of Worringen in 1288. In 1308, after the murder of the Habsburg king Albert I of Germany, Henry was elected Rex Romanorum. His brother Archbishop-Elector Baldwin of Trier backed and orchestrated the election, and Henry prevailed against Charles, Count of Valois.

In 1310 Henry VII arranged the marriage of his son John to the Přemyslid heiress Elisabeth of Bohemia, through whom the family acquired the Kingdom of Bohemia and could compete better with the Habsburg and Wittelsbach dynasties. Henry was crowned emperor at Rome and died in 1313 while campaigning in Italy. The prince-electors, disturbed by the family's rise, passed over John, and Louis of Bavaria of the House of Wittelsbach took the Empire. John concentrated on Bohemia and gradually made the Piast dukes of Silesia his vassals from 1327 to 1335.

His son Charles IV came to the imperial throne in 1346, and his Golden Bull of 1356 served for centuries as a constitution of the Empire. Charles acquired the duchies of Brabant and Limburg, the March of Lusatia, and in 1373 the Margraviate of Brandenburg. Decline began under his son Wenceslaus, whom the prince-electors deposed in 1400 in favour of the Wittelsbach Rupert. In 1410 Wenceslaus' brother Sigismund took over, stabilised the family's rule and helped to end the Western Schism in 1417. Sigismund was king of Hungary and Croatia from 1387 through his wife Mary and was crowned emperor in 1433.

Sigismund left no male heirs, and with his death in 1437 the senior branch of the dynasty became extinct. His son-in-law, the Habsburg archduke Albert V of Austria, succeeded him. Sigismund's only surviving child Elizabeth had married Albert in 1422, and she conveyed the major part of the Luxembourg inheritance to the Habsburgs and, through her daughter Elisabeth of Austria, later to the Jagiellons. The line of the margraves of Moravia continued for a time: George of Luxembourg, who died in 1457, is the last known member of the family.
house-of-mecklenburg: The House of Mecklenburg was a North German family of Polabian origin and one of the longest-ruling families of Europe. It was established by Pribislav, an Obotrite prince who converted to Christianity and accepted the suzerainty of the Saxon duke Henry the Lion, his fallen father's enemy, becoming lord of Mecklenburg. The name derives from Mikla Burg, 'big castle', the family's main fortress. The Obotrites were subsequently Germanized.

From the fourteenth century the dukes pursued a claim to Sweden through descent from Scandinavian noblewomen, among them Christina, a daughter of King Sverker II. Albert II, Duke of Mecklenburg, married Euphemia of Sweden and Norway, and their second son, Albert III, deposed his uncle and became king of Sweden. The family held Sweden from 1364 to 1389. They also claimed Norway through Euphemia, a granddaughter of Haakon V, but when Olav IV died in 1387 the regent Margaret chose Eric of Pomerania, whose mother Maria of Mecklenburg was Euphemia's eldest granddaughter.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the duchy was divided several times among agnates, into principalities such as Mecklenburg-Schwerin, Mecklenburg-Güstrow and Mecklenburg-Strelitz. By the late eighteenth century most parts had returned to Schwerin, and the land stayed divided between Schwerin and Strelitz until the end of the monarchy. The Congress of Vienna recognised both states as grand duchies.

The main line of Strelitz died out in 1918, and the Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin stepped in as regent, but questions of succession involving a junior Strelitz branch in Russia were unsettled when both monarchies became republics. Queen Juliana of the Netherlands, who reigned from 1948 to 1980, was an agnatic member of the house. The Schwerin line became extinct in the male line on 31 July 2001, which left Strelitz as the surviving male line.
house-of-medici: The Medici came from the agricultural Mugello region north of Florence and are first mentioned in a document of 1230. The origin of the name is uncertain; medici is the plural of the Italian word for doctors. Members of the family rose in the early 14th century in the wool trade, though they were far less notable than the Albizzi or the Strozzi. Involvement in a plot in 1400 banned all but two branches of the family from Florentine politics for twenty years.

In 1397 Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the Medici Bank in Florence and became one of the city's richest men. He never held political office. The bank, which lasted until 1494, was the largest in Europe in the 15th century, and was among the earliest businesses to use double-entry bookkeeping.

Giovanni's son Cosimo the Elder was exiled by the Albizzi in 1433, but in 1434 a pro-Medici signoria was elected and he returned. Cosimo, his son Piero and his grandson Lorenzo dominated Florentine government through most of the 15th century without abolishing it, rarely holding official posts. When Lorenzo died in 1492 his son Piero proved unable to meet the French invasion, and within two years he and his supporters were exiled. The family returned in 1512, and Florence was in other hands again between 1527 and 1530.

The senior line ended with the assassination of Alessandro de' Medici, first Duke of Florence, in 1537; power passed to the junior branch, beginning with Cosimo I. The family held the title Duke of Florence from 1532 and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany from 1569. Two Medici popes, Leo X and Clement VII, ruled in the 16th century, and Catherine de' Medici and Marie de' Medici became queens of France.

Cosimo II is remembered as patron of Galileo Galilei, who dedicated his Sidereus Nuncius of 1610 to him. By 1705 the grand ducal treasury under Cosimo III was nearly bankrupt. The last Medici grand duke, Gian Gastone, died in 1737.

Their chief accomplishments were in sponsoring art and architecture. Giovanni di Bicci aided Masaccio and commissioned Filippo Brunelleschi to rebuild the Basilica of San Lorenzo in 1419. Cosimo the Elder's circle included Donatello and Fra Angelico, and Lorenzo invited the young Michelangelo to study the family's collection of antique sculpture and was patron to Leonardo da Vinci for seven years. Contemporaries and later writers disagreed about the family, some calling it corrupt, while Machiavelli's The Prince was in the end dedicated to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici.
house-of-montefeltro: The Montefeltro were a branch of the Lords of Carpegna, as were their long-standing rivals the Malatesta, lords of Rimini. Around 1140 Antonio received the castle of Montecopiolo in a division with his brothers and later acquired San Leo, on the rock of mons feretrius that gave the region of Montefeltro its name. His son Montefeltrano I became count of Montefeltro, and in 1226 Emperor Frederick II appointed Montefeltrano's sons Buonconte I and Taddeo counts of Urbino. In the struggles between Guelphs and Ghibellines the family led the Ghibellines of the Marche and Romagna, while the Malatesta led the Guelphs.

Guido I served as captain of Forlì in wars against French and papal armies; Pope Boniface VIII later absolved him and employed him against Palestrina and the Colonna. Federico I took Fano, Osimo, Recanati, Gubbio, Spoleto and Assisi from the Holy See, but was murdered after levying heavy taxes. Urbino passed back and forth between the family and the papacy: Nolfo was proclaimed lord in 1323, Cardinal Albornoz restored papal control in 1355, and Antonio II used the rebellion of the Marche and Umbria of 1375 to recover the city.

Guidantonio was made ruler of the Duchy of Spoleto by Pope Martin V in 1419 and fought Braccio da Montone. After his son Oddo Antonio was assassinated within months, the Urbinese offered the lordship to Guidantonio's illegitimate son Federico, a pupil of the school of Vittorino da Feltre, under whom Urbino became a centre of the Renaissance.

Federico fought Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta, René of Anjou and Florence. His son Guidobaldo I was forced to flee Urbino before the armies of Cesare Borgia and adopted his sister's son Francesco Maria della Rovere, uniting the signoria of Sinigaglia with Urbino. Pope Leo X later took the territory from Francesco Maria and gave it to Lorenzo de' Medici before it returned to him. The della Rovere ruled the duchy until their line ended in 1631, when it went back to the Papal States.
house-of-nassau: The House of Nassau is a European dynasty named after a lordship associated with Nassau Castle, in what is now Rhineland-Palatinate. Count Dudo-Henry of Laurenburg, who lived from about 1060 to about 1123, is considered its founder; he built Laurenburg Castle on the Lahn around 1090. His son Rupert built Nassau Castle around 1125 and declared himself Count of Nassau, a title the Bishop of Worms did not officially acknowledge until 1159, under Rupert's son Walram. By then the county claimed rights of taxation, tolls and justice and can be considered a state. With the fall of the Hohenstaufen, Nassau emerged as an independent state within the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1255 Henry II's sons Walram II and Otto I divided the Nassau possessions, creating the Walramian and Ottonian lines, a permanent division. The Walramian line concentrated on German lands. Adolf, count of Nassau from about 1276, was elected king of Germany in 1292 and deposed by the prince-electors in 1298, the first healthy ruler of the Empire deposed without a papal excommunication; he died at the Battle of Göllheim, fighting his successor Albert of Habsburg. In 1783 the heads of the branches sealed the Nassau Family Pact to regulate succession.

At the end of the Holy Roman Empire and the Napoleonic Wars the Walramian branch had inherited or acquired all the Nassau ancestral lands and, with the permission of the Congress of Vienna, proclaimed itself the Dukes of Nassau, with its capital at Wiesbaden. The Duchy existed from 1806 as part of the Confederation of the Rhine, and Adolph became its last reigning duke in August 1839, after the death of his father William. It was annexed by Prussia in 1866 after Austria's defeat in the Austro-Prussian War, in which it had been Austria's ally.

The Ottonian line established itself in the Netherlands, and its members became leaders of the Dutch Revolt, stadtholders of the Dutch Republic and eventually kings of the Netherlands. All Dutch and Luxembourgish monarchs since 1815 have been senior members of the House of Nassau, although the male lines of heirs became extinct in 1890 in the Netherlands and in 1912 in Luxembourg, and the thrones have since passed through the female line. By German tradition, which passes the name only in the male line, the house has been extinct since 1985, but neither Dutch nor Luxembourgish tradition and law consider it extinct. Today Nassau names a historical and cultural region of Germany with no political meaning.
house-of-oldenburg: Count Elimar I of Oldenburg was first mentioned in 1091, and the family's ancestral home is Oldenburg Castle. In the 12th century Rastede Monastery near Oldenburg became their house monastery. Marriages of the medieval counts paved the way to the Scandinavian thrones: through marriage with a descendant of King Valdemar I of Sweden and King Eric IV of Denmark, the family staked a claim to Sweden and Denmark as early as 1350.

In the time of Margaret I, queen of Denmark, Sweden and Norway, the chief competitor for the northern thrones was the House of Mecklenburg, and the Duke of Saxe-Lauenburg was among other aspirants. In 1423 Theodoric of Oldenburg married Hedwig of Holstein, a descendant of Magnus Ladulås of Sweden, Haakon V of Norway and the Danish kings Eric V and Abel.

Their son Christian became King of Denmark in 1448, of Norway in 1450 and of Sweden in 1457, ruling the whole Kalmar Union. The main line then ruled Denmark until 1863 and Norway until 1814, and held Sweden in 1457–1464, 1497–1501 and 1520–1521. The kings were also dukes of Schleswig from 1460 and counts, later dukes, of Holstein. The old comital line of Oldenburg itself became extinct in 1667.

The family divided into branches. The Holstein-Gottorp line, which held the duchy of Holstein-Gottorp from 1544 to 1739, gave kings to Sweden between 1751 and 1818, and for a time to Norway in 1814–1818. Its branch commonly still called Romanov provided emperors of Russia in 1762 and from 1796 to 1917, and another Holstein-Gottorp line ruled as dukes and grand dukes of Oldenburg from 1774 to 1918. The Glücksburg branch, whose name changed from Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Beck in 1825, succeeded to the Danish throne in 1863.

The Glücksburg kings also ruled elsewhere: they were kings of the Hellenes from 1863 to 1924 and from 1935 to 1973, kings of Norway from 1905, and kings of Iceland from 1918 to 1944. The Augustenburg branch, extinct in 1931, claimed the dukedom of Schleswig-Holstein in 1863. The line of Elimar I is also traced in the male line to the present kings of Norway and the United Kingdom, and the Danish royal house is a member of the family through descent that is not strictly male. Illegitimate offshoots took the name Danneskiold.
house-of-orange-nassau: The House of Nassau began with Nassau Castle, founded around 1100 by Dudo, Count of Laurenburg. In 1255 the Nassau possessions were divided between Walram and Otto, sons of Count Henry II. Walram's line became Dukes of Nassau and, in 1290, Grand Dukes of Luxembourg. Otto's line inherited properties in France and the Netherlands. The marriage of Henry III of Nassau-Breda and Claudia of Chalon-Orange in 1515 led to the family's claim to Orange: their son René of Chalon inherited the Principality of Orange in 1530, and after his death in 1544 his cousin William of Nassau-Dillenburg inherited his lands and became the founder of the house.

William of Orange stood up for the Protestant, mainly Calvinist, inhabitants of the Netherlands against the persecution begun under Philip II. The Eighty Years' War started in 1568, and the capture of Brielle by rebels in 1572 turned its fortunes, though William was assassinated in 1584 by a hired killer sent by Philip. His sons Maurice and Frederick Henry succeeded him, and Frederick Henry's son William II died of smallpox in 1650, leaving a posthumous son, William III. The regents then left the stadtholdership vacant in the First Stadtholderless Period. William III later became King of England.

When William III died childless in 1702 the principality was disputed between John William Friso of Nassau-Dietz and King Frederick I of Prussia. The Treaty of Utrecht ceded Orange to France in 1713. After the French invasion of 1747 William IV was made stadtholder in several provinces, and the office became hereditary in all of them. William V fled the French in 1795. After the French were driven out in 1813, his son William Frederick, as William VI, became King of the Netherlands in 1815.

Queen Wilhelmina reigned for 58 years, from 1890 to 1948, and became a symbol of Dutch resistance in exile in London during the Second World War. The house died out in the male line with her, but it continues in the female line, and the name Orange is still used by the royal family. Since the Royal House Membership Act 2002, the royal house is a smaller group than the wider royal family. William the Silent was buried in the New Church in Delft, where most of the house, including all Dutch monarchs, has been buried since.
house-of-plantagenet: The house originated in the French county of Anjou. The later counts of Anjou descended from Geoffrey II, Count of Gâtinais, and his wife Ermengarde of Anjou, who in 1060 inherited the title through cognatic kinship from an Angevin family descended from a noble named Ingelger, whose recorded history dates from 870. Plantegenest was a twelfth-century nickname of Geoffrey, Count of Anjou and Duke of Normandy. One theory derives it from the blossom of the common broom, called genista in medieval Latin. In the fifteenth century Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York, adopted Plantagenet as his family name.

Henry II was born in 1133, and his grandfather Henry I is reported to have been delighted, calling the boy the heir to the kingdom. The first three Plantagenet kings, Henry II, Richard I and John, ruled extensive territories in France and are sometimes called the Angevins, though some historians use that term for the whole dynasty.

Henry's marriage to Eleanor, who had already had two daughters by her first husband, King Louis, produced eight children in thirteen years. When Richard I left no heir, a succession crisis arose between supporters of his nephew Arthur and of John. John won a significant victory at the Battle of Mirebeau, but he lost Anjou and most of his other French territories, which made England rather than France the centre of the realm. His son Henry III, king for most of the thirteenth century, faced baronial conflict that helped establish Parliament, and the kings were often forced to accept compromises such as Magna Carta.

Edward I enforced his claims in Britain, and the Statute of Rhuddlan established England's authority over Wales. In 1328 Charles IV of France died without a male heir, and Philip of Valois became king over Queen Isabella's claim on behalf of her son Edward III. By the end of Edward III's reign the dynasty had adopted Middle English as the language of governance. Richard II, who came to the throne as a boy, faced the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 after poll taxes were levied to pay for military campaigns.

After the deposition of Richard II in 1399, two cadet branches, Lancaster and York, ruled England. Henry V won a near total victory at Agincourt and secured the Treaty of Troyes, but his son Henry VI, who succeeded at nine months old, lost the Hundred Years' War. The rivalry of Lancaster and York brought about the Wars of the Roses, which ended at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485, when Richard III died. Henry VII, a Lancastrian through his mother, then married Elizabeth of York, and the Tudor dynasty began.
house-of-representatives-netherlands: The House of Representatives, in Dutch the Tweede Kamer der Staten-Generaal, is the lower house of the States General, whose other chamber is the Senate. It is the main legislative body. Both the cabinet and the House itself may propose legislation, and a bill adopted by a majority goes to the Senate. Ministers and the cabinet as a whole must have the House's confidence and must resign if a majority withdraws it.

The House reviews the cabinet through formal interrogations in plenary and committee meetings, which can end in motions urging a course of action. No one may sit in both the House and the cabinet. The House also submits a list of three names for each vacancy on the Supreme Court and elects the Ombudsman.

The normal term is four years. Seats are filled by party-list proportional representation, using the D'Hondt method with a threshold of 0.67 per cent. After an election a series of negotiations follows to form a government. Since 2012 the House appoints a scout to ask party leaders about coalitions, then an informateur to examine them and a formateur to lead negotiations, roles the monarch appointed before 2012.

From 1815 to 1992 the House met in the former ballroom of the stadtholder William V in the Binnenhof in The Hague, a room first used as a meeting chamber in 1796 by the National Assembly of the Batavian Republic. In 1992 it moved to a new extension of the Binnenhof designed by Pi de Bruijn, which replaced classroom-style benches with a semicircular layout. Historically the House had 100 seats, and in 1956 the number was raised to 150. Standing committees were set up in 1953 to relieve the plenary of detailed discussion.

The low threshold and the nationwide list system have left a typical House with ten or more parties, and since proportional representation took its present form in 1917 no party has come near the 76 seats of an absolute majority. The largest share won by one party was 54 of 150 seats, by the CDA in 1986 and 1989. The Liberal Union, between 1891 and 1897, was the last party to hold an absolute majority, and every Dutch cabinet since then has been a coalition of two or more parties.
house-of-romanov: The Romanovs share their origin with about two dozen other Russian noble families. Their earliest common ancestor is Andrei Kobyla, attested about 1347 as a boyar in the service of Simeon, prince of Moscow. Later genealogies gave him a distinguished pedigree, including descent from an Old Prussian prince, a legend contested by another version that derives the family from a boyar line of Novgorod. His descendants took the names Koshkin, Zakharin and Zakharin-Yuriev, and the grandchildren of Roman Yurievich Zakharyin-Yuriev took the name Romanov.

The family rose when Roman's daughter Anastasia Zakharyina married Ivan IV on 3 (13) February 1547 and was crowned the first tsaritsa of Russia. After Boris Godunov's party prevailed in 1598, he accused Feodor Nikitich Romanov of treason in 1600 and had the family deported to remote parts of the north and the Urals, where most died; Feodor was forced to become a monk with the name Filaret.

The Rurik dynasty ended with Feodor I in 1598, and the Time of Troubles followed. On 21 February 1613 the Zemsky Sobor elected Michael Romanov as tsar. His son Alexei succeeded him in 1645, and after Alexei's death in 1676 his children by two marriages struggled for the throne.

Peter I, who ruled from 1682 to 1725, proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721 and, through wars and reforms, made Russia a major European power. The direct male line ended when Elizabeth died childless in 1762. Her nephew Peter III, of the House of Holstein-Gottorp, succeeded and kept his mother's house name, so later monarchs are sometimes called Holstein-Gottorp-Romanov. His wife overthrew him and reigned as Catherine the Great.

Her son Paul I issued the Pauline Laws, which set semi-Salic primogeniture and required the Orthodox faith. He was murdered in 1801. After Alexander I came Nicholas I in 1825, whose accession met the Decembrist revolt, and Alexander II, who freed the serfs in 1861. The February Revolution of 1917 led to Nicholas II's abdication on 15 March [O.S. 2 March] 1917, ending 304 years of Romanov rule.

After the abdication Nicholas II and his family were held at the Alexander Palace, sent to Tobolsk in August 1917 and moved to Yekaterinburg in April 1918. On the night of 16 to 18 July 1918 the Bolsheviks executed the entire family and several retainers. Of the house's 65 members, 47 survivors went into exile. In 1924 Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich claimed the headship of the defunct imperial house. Living descendants of other members of the imperial house remain.
house-of-saud: The earliest recorded ancestor of the Al Saud is Mani' ibn Rabiah Al-Muraydi, who settled at Diriyah in 1446-1447 with his clan, the Mrudah, at the invitation of a relative named Ibn Dir. The Mrudah are believed to descend from the Banu Hanifa branch of the Rabi'ah tribal confederation. Within the clan the Al Muqrin became the ruling family, and the dynastic name comes from Sheikh Saud ibn Muhammad ibn Muqrin, who died in 1725.

The name is Arabic: Al, meaning family of, is added to the name of an ancestor. The surname is carried by descendants of Muhammad bin Saud and his three brothers Farhan, Thunayyan and Mishari. Other branches, such as the Al Jiluwi and the Al Thunayan, are called cadet branches and are not in the line of succession.

The First Saudi State was marked by conquest and religious zeal, and at its height it held most of the territory of present-day Saudi Arabia. In 1802 forces of Abdulaziz bin Muhammad attacked Karbala and killed more than 2,000 people, and the attack convinced the Ottomans and the Egyptians that the Saudis were a threat. Abdulaziz was killed in 1803. An Ottoman-Egyptian force took Diriyah in 1818, razed it and carried many of the family to Egypt and Constantinople. Abdullah bin Saud was beheaded in Constantinople.

The Emirate of Nejd, the Second Saudi State, had its capital at Riyadh. It never reconquered the Hijaz or 'Asir, and with one exception succession came by assassination or civil war. Abdul Rahman bin Faisal was defeated at Mulayda and went into exile, and in 1902 his son Abdulaziz, known in the West as Ibn Saud, took the Masmak fort in Riyadh. He defeated the Al Rashid in 1921, conquered the Hijaz in 1926 and in 1932 united his realm as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Oil was found near Dammam in 1937, and before that many family members were destitute.

Ibn Saud had dozens of children, and he married into noble clans and tribes, among them the Al ash-Sheikh, descendants of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. Kingship passed from one of his sons to another. Saud succeeded in 1953, and in 1964 the family forced him to abdicate in favour of Faisal, who was assassinated in 1975 by a nephew. Khalid, Fahd and Abdullah followed. In 1986 Fahd replaced the title His Majesty with Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques. The family is estimated to number about 15,000, though most power rests with about 2,000. Members of the family hold the key ministries and all thirteen regional governorships.
house-of-savoy: The house was established in 1003 in the historical region of Savoy, which was originally part of the Kingdom of Burgundy and now lies mostly in south-eastern France. It descended from Humbert I, Count of Savoy, called Biancamano or White Hand, who ruled from 1003 to 1047 or 1048. His ancestry is uncertain, since contemporary documents do not mention his father. The family was traditionally believed to have come from Saxony, but more recent research points to the County of Vienne, where Humbert and his relatives held extensive possessions. Through marriages and diplomacy the family expanded its territory and influence, first as counts of a small Alpine county north-west of Italy.

Amadeus VIII was raised by the Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund to Duke of Savoy in 1416. In 1536 Francis I of France invaded Savoy and Piedmont and took Turin, and Duke Charles III fled to Vercelli. In April 1655, on perhaps false reports of resistance by the Protestant Waldensians to a plan to resettle them, Charles Emmanuel II ordered their general massacre, known as the Piedmontese Easter. It aroused indignation across Europe and prompted John Milton's sonnet On the Late Massacre in Piedmont.

The house gained the crown of Sicily, but in 1720 was forced to exchange it for the Kingdom of Sardinia after the War of the Quadruple Alliance. Charles Emmanuel III gained lands at the expense of the Austrian-controlled Duchy of Milan.
