In 1796 Napoleon beat Piedmont-Sardinia, and in 1798 French troops occupied Turin and forced Charles Emmanuel IV to abdicate. The kingdom was restored in 1814 and enlarged with the former Republic of Genoa by the Congress of Vienna.

By 1861 the House of Savoy, through its cadet branch Carignano, led the unification of Italy and ruled the Kingdom of Italy until 1946. Its Italian kings were Victor Emmanuel II, Umberto I, Victor Emmanuel III and Umberto II. Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini prime minister on 28 October 1922, and his failure to move against the regime later led to much criticism. Umberto II reigned for only a few weeks before being deposed after the 1946 Italian institutional referendum, when the Italian Republic was proclaimed. The residences of the royal house in and around Turin are a World Heritage Site.
house-of-schwarzburg: The House of Schwarzburg was one of the oldest noble families of Thuringia. Schwarzburg Castle is first mentioned in a deed of 1071. In 1123 Count Sizzo of Käfernburg, who appears in the chronicle of Lambert of Hersfeld and who, according to the Annalista Saxo, was a grandson of Prince Yaropolk Izyaslavich of Turov through his mother, rebuilt the castle and began to call himself Count of Schwarzburg. Sizzo also founded Georgenthal Abbey, and in 1157 he accompanied Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa on his campaign against Bolesław IV the Curly of Poland.

In 1197 Sizzo's grandson Henry II divided the family inheritance with his brother Günther III, making Schwarzburg Castle his residence, with the nearby castle of Blankenburg also in his share. The County of Schwarzburg was ruled as a state of the Holy Roman Empire by counts of the house. Its best-known member, Günther XXI, was elected German king in 1349 by a majority of the electors, but as his support waned he renounced the crown a few months later and died shortly afterwards.

The Schwarzburg lands were divided again and again among his successors until 1538, when Count Günther XL the Rich united them, Frankenhausen and Rudolstadt included, under his rule. His eldest son Günther XLI succeeded him, but after Günther XLI's death in 1583 the younger brothers split the county once more. John Günther I took the territory around Arnstadt, later called Schwarzburg-Sondershausen, and Albrecht VII the lands of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt. The partition was confirmed by the Treaty of Stadtilm in 1599.

The Sondershausen line died out in 1909. When Prince Friedrich Günther died in 1971, a claim to the headship of the house passed under semi-Salic primogeniture to his elder sister, Princess Marie Antoinette of Schwarzburg, the wife of Friedrich Magnus V, Count of Solms-Wildenfels.
house-of-schwarzenberg: The family descends from the Lords of Seinsheim, established in Franconia in the Middle Ages. Early in the 15th century Erkinger of Seinsheim acquired the territory and castle of Schwarzenberg at Scheinfeld, and in 1429 he was made Freiherr, or Baron, of Schwarzenberg; a silver tower on a black hill was then added to the family arms. The house was raised to Imperial Counts in 1599, when Adolf von Schwarzenberg received a quarter showing a raven pecking at a Turk's head, for his capture of the Turkish-held fortress of Győr, Raab in German, on 19 March 1598.

Marriages brought the house its lands. Count Georg Ludwig gained the Styrian lordship of Murau in 1623, and an alliance with the House of Eggenberg gave it large holdings in Bohemia in 1661; in the 1670s the family made Bohemia its main seat, and until 1918 it lived chiefly at Český Krumlov. Johann Ludwig II, Count of Sulz, having no male heir, arranged for his rights and property to pass to Prince Ferdinand of Schwarzenberg, his daughter's husband, on his death in 1687. The family later became Dukes of Krumlov, in 1719, and in Bohemia also acquired the property of the House of Rosenberg.

Early in the 19th century the house divided into two princely lines, as Prince Ferdinand's will had foreseen: a senior line holding the Palais Schwarzenberg in Vienna, Krumlov and Frauenberg, and a cadet line founded by Field Marshal Karl Philipp at Orlík Castle. For his victory at the Battle of the Nations, where he commanded the Sixth Coalition, the Austrian emperor allowed him to add the Habsburg arms with an upright sword to his own.

After the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia was set up in 1939, the Nazi authorities seized the possessions of Prince Adolph of Schwarzenberg, and his cousin Heinrich, Duke of Krumlov, was arrested and deported. Czechoslovak law No. 143/1947 of 13 August 1947, the Lex Schwarzenberg, gave the assets of the senior line to the Land of Bohemia. That line died out in the male line in 1979, and the two branches were reunited under Karel Schwarzenberg (1937–2023), who served as Czech Minister of Foreign Affairs. Eighteen members of the family were knights of the Order of the Golden Fleece.
house-of-sforza: The Sforza were a ruling family of Renaissance Italy, based in Milan. Their rule began when they acquired the Duchy of Milan after the Visconti family died out in the mid-15th century. Francesco I Sforza, first son of Muzio Attendolo Sforza, married Bianca Maria Visconti in 1441. She was the daughter and only heir of Filippo Maria Visconti, the last Duke of Milan. After overthrowing the Ambrosian Republic, Francesco became Duke of Milan, ruling from 1450 to 1466, and made the Sforzas the heirs of the Visconti.

Francesco I was succeeded by Galeazzo Maria, who ruled until 1476, then Gian Galeazzo until 1494 and Ludovico until 1499. In 1499, in the course of the Italian Wars, the army of Louis XII of France took Milan from Ludovico. After Imperial German troops drove out the French, Ludovico's son Maximilian became Duke of Milan until the French returned under Francis I of France and imprisoned him. In 1521 Charles V drove out the French and restored Ludovico's younger son Francesco II Sforza to the duchy, after Francesco had waged war on the Emperor.

Francesco II ruled Milan until his death in 1535. Being childless, he left the duchy to revert to the Emperor, who passed it to his son Philip II in 1540, beginning Spanish rule in Milan. His death ended the family's main branch.

Other branches held lands elsewhere. Alessandro, the second son of Muzio, founded the line that held the seigniory of Pesaro until 1512, after the death of Costanzo II Sforza. Bosio, the third son, founded the branch of Santa Fiora, which held the title of count of Cotignola and ruled the small county of Santa Fiora in southern Tuscany until 1624.

The Sforza allied with the Borgia family through the arranged marriage, from 1493 to 1497, of Lucrezia Borgia and Giovanni, illegitimate son of Costanzo I of Pesaro. The alliance failed, since the Borgia family annulled the marriage once the Sforza were no longer needed. Members of the Santa Fiora branch held important ecclesiastical and political positions in the Papal States and moved to Rome in 1674, taking the name Sforza Cesarini. The family's marriages also linked it to other courts: Bianca Maria Sforza became the second wife of the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I, and Bona Sforza the second wife of King Sigismund I the Old of Poland.
house-of-shervashidze: The surname has the standard Georgian form, with the suffix -dze meaning son, but in the 12th century the family was said to take its name from the Shirvanshahs, the dynasty of Shirvan. According to The Georgian Chronicles, Shirvanese princes were granted lands in Abkhazia after King David IV of Georgia extended his kingdom to Shirvan in 1124. The historian Anchabadze disputes this genealogy and argues that the Sharvashidze, whose Abkhazian name was Chachba, were a local dynasty that invented a foreign ancestry, as was not unusual in feudal genealogies.

The first of the dynasty took princely power under the authority of the Georgian kings around 1325. Its early princes included Dardin Sharvashidze, remembered as an anti-Mongol warrior. The princes gained full independence only when the unified Georgian state broke up in the late 15th century, and soon became vassals of the Ottoman Empire.

In the late 18th century the princes embraced Islam, but they moved back and forth across the religious divide as Russia and the Ottomans contended for the region. Kelesh Ahmed-Bey, prince from about 1780 to 1808, brought Abkhazia to its widest extent and was in diplomatic contact with Napoleon's ambassador to the Ottomans, Horace François Bastien Sébastiani de La Porta. The pro-Russian side prevailed, and Abkhazia joined the Russian Empire in 1810 under Sefer Ali-Bey, while the family was confirmed in the Russian princely rank under the Treaty of Georgievsk.

After Abkhazia was incorporated into the Russian Empire, the family continued as a princely house. In the Kingdom of Kartli another branch was founded by Prince Elizbar Sharvashidze, Lord High Treasurer to King Heraclius II, with its domain at Kareli; his son Nikoloz held the same office under King George XII, but the branch later died out. Gülistu Kadın, mother of the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed VI Vahidettin, was of the family.
house-of-stuart: The house was originally spelled Stewart, from the office of High Steward of Scotland, first held by the family's progenitor Walter fitz Alan, around 1150. The family's probable ancestry goes back to Alan fitz Flaad, a Breton who went to England soon after the Norman Conquest and was rewarded by Henry I with lands in Shropshire. His son Walter followed David I of Scotland north after the civil war known as the Anarchy, received lands in Renfrewshire, and held the lordship of the High Steward for life; Malcolm IV later made the office hereditary.

The sixth High Steward, Walter Stewart, married Marjorie, daughter of Robert the Bruce. Their son Robert inherited the Scottish throne as Robert II when his uncle David II died childless in 1371. Mary, Queen of Scots, who was brought up in France, adopted the French spelling Stuart.

In 1503 James IV married Margaret Tudor, daughter of Henry VII, which brought the Stewarts into the line of descent to the English throne. When Elizabeth I of England died without issue in 1603, James VI of Scotland, the son of Mary, Queen of Scots, and Lord Darnley, became king of England and Ireland as James I. This was a personal union: the three kingdoms shared a monarch but kept separate governments, churches and institutions. It did not prevent the Bishops' Wars of 1639, part of the cycle of conflict that marked the reign of Charles I and culminated in the War of the Three Kingdoms.

The trial and execution of Charles I by the English Parliament in 1649 began eleven years of republican government, the English Interregnum. Charles II, whose mother was French, left no legitimate children. His brother James II, who had converted to Catholicism, was deposed by Parliament in favour of his Protestant daughters Mary II and Anne, after the birth of a son to be raised as a Catholic.

Neither daughter had a child who survived to adulthood, so after the death of Queen Anne in 1714 the crown passed to the House of Hanover under the Act of Settlement of 1701. Under the Acts of Union, which came into effect on 1 May 1707, Anne had become queen of Great Britain. The descendants of James II, known as Jacobites, long tried to regain the throne. The royal house became extinct with the death of Cardinal Henry Benedict Stuart, brother of Charles Edward Stuart, in 1807.
house-of-thani: The family traces its origins to the Adnanite Banu Tamim tribe, and its genealogy goes back to Mudar ibn Nizar. The tribe came from the Najdi town of Ushaiger, north-west of Riyadh, and settled at the Gebrin oasis before moving to Qatar around the 1720s. Its first settlement there was Sikak, and it then moved north-west to Zubarah, Al Ruwais and Fuwayrit. In the nineteenth century it settled in Doha under Mohammed bin Thani, and the house takes its name from his father, Thani bin Mohammed.

The Al Thanis emerged as one of Qatar's dominant clans in the 1850s and accepted the suzerainty of the Ottoman Empire to strengthen their position against rivals. In 1868 they received British recognition of their rule, and a stronger treaty with the British Empire in 1916 greatly aided their consolidation. Mohammed bin Thani ruled from 1851 to 1878, and Jassim bin Mohammed Al Thani held power in 1878–1898 and again in 1905–1913. Ahmad bin Ali Al Thani, who ruled from 1960 to 1972, was the first to bear the title emir.

Oil made the family's rule more secure, and the Al Thanis became the only family allowed to style themselves sheikhs, but it also sharpened tensions within the house. Every succession, in 1913, 1949, 1960, 1972 and 1995, was contested. In 1995 Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani took power in a bloodless palace coup, with the support of senior family members and the United States. He changed the constitution so that the emirate could pass only to his sons, and he marginalised rivals within the family. On 25 June 2013 Hamad handed power to his son Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in a televised speech.

The family has three main branches: the Bani Ali, Bani Hamad and Bani Khalid, and it was estimated to number about 20,000 members in the early 1990s. Qatar's short history left it with a weak merchant class and hardly any religious establishment, so other tribes lost almost all their power, and decisions were concentrated in the hands of the emir and sometimes the heir apparent.
house-of-trastamara: The Trastámaras were an illegitimate cadet line of the ruling House of Burgundy of Castile. Their name comes from the County of Trastámara, one of the titles held by Henry II of Castile, the founder of the dynasty, before he became king. When Alfonso XI died in 1350, his illegitimate children by Eleanor de Guzmán, known collectively as the Trastámaras, became rivals of his legitimate son Peter I. Henry of Trastámara, with the support of Aragon, France and mercenaries led by Bertram Du Guesclin, defeated Peter in the Castilian Civil War of 1351 to 1369, in which the nobility played a decisive part, and killed him himself in 1369.

Under Henry II a new nobility rose, gaining large estates and royal privileges, and its rise caused discontent and instability. His son John I succeeded in 1379 and died unexpectedly in 1390. Henry III came to the throne at twelve and took control of the Canary Islands. The change of dynasty also brought a radicalisation of anti-Jewish feeling in Castile, which reached its climax in the pogroms of 1391. After the death of Martin of Aragon without a legitimate heir, the Compromise of Caspe of 1412 installed Ferdinand of Antequera as king of Aragon.

In Castile John II, who came to power in 1418, lacked authority, and nobles fought for influence. His son Henry IV was an unpopular ruler. In 1468 the Treaty of the Bulls of Guisando named his half-sister Isabella as heir. Her marriage in 1469 to Ferdinand, king of Sicily and heir to Aragon, broke the pact in Henry's eyes, and a civil war of about a decade followed over the claims of Isabella and of Henry's daughter Joanna.

Isabella's factions won with Aragon's help, and the marriage of Isabella and Ferdinand, both Trastámaras, united Castile and Aragon in a dynastic union. The house ruled Castile from 1369 to 1504, Aragon from 1412 to 1516, and also Navarre and Naples for parts of that time. It was succeeded by the House of Habsburg when Charles V became king of Castile and Aragon in 1516, even though his mother Joanna lived on, imprisoned from 1509, until 1555.
house-of-trencavel: The name began as a nickname, perhaps from the Occitan trenca avelana, nutcracker, and was at first used only by members of the family named Raymond. The first well-known member was Ato I, viscount of Albi in the early 10th century, followed by five generations of viscounts of Albi in direct descent. From Ato II on, each viscount had a younger brother named Frotarius who was a bishop of Albi, Cahors or Nîmes, so that the family dominated the episcopacy of Languedoc.

In 1069 the three daughters of Peter II of Carcassonne sold their counties to Raymond Berengar I of Barcelona. Raymond Bernard, son of Bernard Ato III, married their sister Ermengard and became viscount of Carcassonne, and his son Bernard Ato IV held Albi, Béziers, Carcassonne, Nîmes and Razès, though he never took the title of count. His sons divided the inheritance: Roger I took Albi, Carcassonne and Razès, Raymond I Béziers and Agde, and Bernard Ato V Nîmes. When Roger died childless in 1150, his lands passed to Raymond, and the elder line of Béziers-Albi-Carcassonne-Razès and the younger of Nîmes-Agde remained separate thereafter.

Their lands lay between those of the counts of Barcelona and Toulouse, and the family mostly sided with Barcelona. It faced revolts in its growing towns: Raymond I was killed in one at Béziers, and in 1120-1124 the Trencavel were driven out of Carcassonne.

The Albigensian Crusade ended the family's power. Bernard Ato VI ceded Nîmes and Agde to Simon de Montfort in 1214. Raymond II, son of Raymond Roger, ceded his titles in 1210, retook Carcassonne in 1224 and lost it to Louis VIII of France in 1226. He was the first to use Trencavel as his surname in his charters. In 1247 he ceded his rights to Louis IX and broke his seals, and he and his sons ruled only the castle of Limoux. A granddaughter was living at Cesseras in 1332, after which the family disappears.
house-of-tudor: The Tudors descended from Ednyfed Fychan and the Welsh noble family of Penmynydd, and from Catherine of Valois. Owen Tudor abandoned the Welsh patronymic custom and took a fixed surname, choosing that of his grandfather, Tudur ap Goronwy. His son Edmund Tudor, half-brother of Henry VI, married Margaret Beaufort on 1 November 1455. Her line came from John Beaufort, born to John of Gaunt and his mistress Katherine Swynford before they married in 1396; the Beauforts were declared legitimate, but Henry IV's proclamation barred them from the throne.

The Tudor name itself was hardly used in the sixteenth century. Monarchs stressed continuity with the English and French royal families rather than their descent from a Welsh adventurer, and the surname was not used in official publications. When Richard III called his rival Henry Tudor, it was to stress his Welshness and unfitness to rule.

Henry VII took the throne by right of conquest after defeating Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field on 22 August 1485. On 18 January 1486 he married Elizabeth of York, daughter of Edward IV, which symbolically united Lancaster and York; the Tudor rose joined the red and white roses. He faced Yorkist risings, among them the one in support of Lambert Simnel, defeated at the Battle of Stoke Field in 1487, and Perkin Warbeck's landing in Cornwall in 1497, ending in Warbeck's execution in 1499.

Henry VIII succeeded on 22 April 1509 and married Catherine of Aragon, his brother Arthur's widow. The Tudors achieved the full union of England and Wales in 1542 and asserted English authority over Ireland. When Henry died on 28 January 1547 his nine-year-old son succeeded as Edward VI, and nobles struggled for influence during the regency. Edward named Lady Jane Grey as heir, but public support went to his half-sister Mary, and Jane was beheaded on 12 February 1554.

Mary I's planned marriage to Philip, son of Charles V, was unpopular and provoked Thomas Wyatt the Younger's rebellion; Mary lost Calais in 1558. Elizabeth I reigned for 44 years, the longest of the dynasty, after the short, troubled reigns of her siblings. She chose William Cecil as chief minister. On her death without children, James VI of Scotland succeeded her on 24 March 1603.

Royal succession, including marriage and the succession rights of women, and the English Reformation were the leading political themes of the period. The Tudor rose has been used as a royal badge by every English, and later British, monarch since Henry VII. The Scottish House of Stuart, which followed, descended from Henry VII's daughter Margaret, who married James IV of Scotland in 1503.
house-of-valois: The Valois descended from Charles, Count of Valois (1270-1325), the second surviving son of King Philip III of France. Philip IV left three sons, Louis, Philip and Charles, who each became king in turn and each died young without a surviving male heir. When Charles IV died in 1328 three candidates had a plausible claim: Philip, Count of Valois, the closest heir in the male line; Joan of Navarre, daughter of Louis X; and Edward III of England, son of Isabella of France. The French magnates rejected a claim passing through a woman and chose Philip of Valois as Philip VI. Joan received the Kingdom of Navarre.

Philip VI confiscated the Duchy of Aquitaine in 1337, and Edward III claimed the French throne himself, which helped launch the Hundred Years' War. The French were defeated at Crécy in 1346 and at Poitiers in 1356, where John II was captured.

Under Charles V they recovered most of their territory, leaving the English only Calais, Bordeaux and Bayonne by 1380. Charles VI's madness let rivalry between the dukes of Burgundy and Orléans grow into the Armagnac-Burgundian Civil War, and after Agincourt in 1415 the Treaty of Troyes made Henry V of England heir to the throne. Joan of Arc raised the siege of Orléans in 1429 and had Charles VII crowned at Reims. By 1453, after the English defeat at Castillon, only Calais remained to them.

Charles VII created France's first standing army since Roman times. Louis XI subdued the great nobles, who had formed the League of the Public Weal against him in 1465, by intrigue and diplomacy, and after Charles the Bold of Burgundy died in 1477 he seized the duchy of Burgundy. Charles VIII invaded Italy in 1494 to press an Angevin claim to Naples, beginning the Italian Wars, and died in 1498 without heirs, ending the senior line. His cousin Louis XII, then Francis I, who was captured at Pavia in 1525, and Henry II continued the wars, which ended with the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559.

Henry II died in a jousting accident in 1559, and his sons Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III ruled through the French Wars of Religion, in which the House of Guise led the Catholic League against the Huguenots. The St Bartholomew's Day massacre took place in 1572. Henry III had the Duke of Guise assassinated, and was himself killed by an assassin in 1589. With his death the male line of the Valois was extinct after 261 years on the throne. Henry of Navarre, as head of the House of Bourbon, the senior surviving Capetian branch, became Henry IV. Junior Valois lines held Orléans, Anjou, Burgundy and Alençon.
house-of-vasa: The Vasa dynasty descended from a 14th-century Swedish noble family, whose agnatic kinship is traced to Nils Kettilsson (died 1378), the fogde of Tre Kronor Castle in Stockholm. Several members held high offices in the 15th century. In 1523, after the Stockholm bloodbath and the abolition of the Kalmar Union, Gustav Eriksson, probably born in 1496, became King Gustav I of Sweden, and the royal house was founded. His reign is sometimes seen as the beginning of the modern Swedish state, as it included his break with the Catholic Church during the Reformation and the foundation of the Church of Sweden.

Gustav's eldest son Eric XIV was overthrown by his younger son, John III, who married the Catholic Polish-Lithuanian princess Catherine Jagiellon. Their son Sigismund III Vasa was elected King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania on 19 August 1587, and he succeeded to the Swedish throne after his father's death. His Protestant uncle, Duke Charles, forced him from the Swedish throne in 1599, and the riksdag at Linköping on 24 February 1604 declared Sigismund to have abdicated and recognised Charles as King Charles IX. The dynasty was now split into a Protestant Swedish branch and a Catholic Polish-Lithuanian one, which contended for crowns in later wars.

In Sweden, Charles IX's short reign was one of uninterrupted warfare, and he was followed in 1611 by his son Gustavus Adolphus, who intervened in the Thirty Years' War. Gustavus Adolphus's daughter Queen Christina abdicated in 1654 after converting to Catholicism, and left for Rome. In the Commonwealth, Władysław IV Vasa was elected king in 1632, and John II Casimir Vasa, who had shown talent as a military commander in the Smolensk War, abdicated in 1668. During the Time of Troubles in Russia, Władysław was also elected tsar by the aristocratic council of the Seven Boyars, but his father Sigismund refused to send him to Moscow or to agree to his conversion to Orthodoxy, and hostilities resumed.

The rivalry between the senior, Catholic branch in Poland and Lithuania and the cadet, Protestant branch in Sweden led to numerous wars between the two states. The Swedish branch ruled the Kingdom of Sweden from 1523 to 1654 and the Polish-Lithuanian branch the Commonwealth from 1587 to 1668. The agnatic line became extinct with the death of John II Casimir in 1672. Later Swedish royal houses emphasised descent from the Vasas through female lines, among them the kings of the house of Holstein-Gottorp, who ruled Sweden from 1751 to 1818.
house-of-waldburg: The house, founded some time before the 12th century, traces its lines to Eberhard von Tanne-Waldburg, who died in 1234. He was steward and adviser to the Staufen dukes of Swabia and later to Emperor Friedrich II. In the anti-Staufen uprising he and his brother Friedrich von Tanne took opposite sides; after Friedrich was killed at Montefiascone in 1197, Eberhard was guardian of his nephew Heinrich until 1220, and the two then administered Swabia while the emperors were away. The imperial regalia were kept at Waldburg from 1220 to 1225.

In 1258 the stewards of Waldburg received the fief of Alttrauchburg, which they bought outright in 1306 from its indebted count and enlarged with a large outer bailey and a strong tower. In 1429 it passed to the Jacobian line of the family, some of whose lords appear in the sources as bad stewards, always in financial difficulties. Damaged in various conflicts, the castle was strengthened in the 16th century into a seat of territorial lordship and government.

In 1628 the Waldburgs became imperial counts, and in 1690 they moved to their schloss at Kißlegg, using Trauchburg as a quarry for it. When the Jacobian line died out with Count Francis Charles Eusebius in 1772, its estate passed to the counts of Waldburg-Zeil, who still own the castle. The house divided into many comital lines, among them Waldburg-Wurzach, Waldburg-Scheer, Waldburg-Trauchburg, Waldburg-Wolfegg and Waldburg-Zeil, and as one of a small number of mediatized houses it belongs to the high nobility.

Members of the house held high office. Conrad of Winterstetten, who died in 1243, was imperial butler, procurator of Swabia and guardian of Henry (VII) and Conrad IV. Georg Truchsess von Waldburg, known as Bauernjörg, was field captain of the Swabian League in the German Peasants' War; at Böblingen on 12 May 1525 he attacked a force of 15,000 armed peasants, of whom 3,000 were killed. Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg was Archbishop and Prince-Elector of Cologne from 1577 to 1588.
house-of-welf: The House of Welf, also Guelf, Guelph or Welph, is a dynasty that has included many German and British monarchs from the 11th century to the 20th, and Emperor Ivan VI of Russia in the 18th. The originally Franconian family from the Meuse-Moselle area was closely related to the Carolingians. The younger House of Welf is the older branch of the House of Este. Its first member, Welf I, Duke of Bavaria, inherited the property of the elder House of Welf when his maternal uncle Welf III died in 1055, and in 1070 he became Duke of Bavaria.
Welf II married Countess Matilda of Tuscany, whose possessions played a role in the Investiture Controversy. Because the Welfs sided with the Pope, his partisans in Italy came to be called Guelphs.

Henry the Proud, son-in-law and heir of Emperor Lothair II, lost the imperial election to Conrad III of the Hohenstaufen and was dispossessed of his duchies. His son Henry the Lion recovered Saxony in 1142 and Bavaria in 1156, and in 1168 married Matilda, daughter of Henry II of England. After he refused to help his cousin Emperor Frederick I in an Italian campaign, he was dispossessed after the Battle of Legnano in 1176 and exiled to Normandy in 1180. He kept only lands around Brunswick, where he died in 1195.

His son Otto IV was the only Welf to become Holy Roman Emperor, was excommunicated by Pope Innocent III in 1215 and was forced to abdicate by Frederick II. Henry the Lion's grandson Otto the Child became duke of part of Saxony in 1235, in the new Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg, which was divided several times among lines of the house. By 1705 these had become the Electorate of Hanover and the Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.

The Act of Settlement of 1701 placed Sophia of the Palatinate, wife of Ernest Augustus, in the line of succession to the British crown. Her son George I succeeded Queen Anne and formed a personal union between the British crown and the Electorate of Hanover from 1714. It lasted until the death of William IV in 1837, when Salic law gave Hanover to his brother Ernest Augustus and the British throne went to Queen Victoria.

The Kingdom of Hanover, created in 1814, was annexed by Prussia in 1866 after George V of Hanover sided with Austria. The senior line of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, which had become the Duchy of Brunswick in 1814, died out in 1884. Ernst August, a son of the Duke of Cumberland, inherited it only in 1913, and the monarchy ended in 1918.
house-of-wettin: The oldest member of the family known for certain is Theodoric I of Wettin, who died about 982 and was most probably based in the Liesgau, at the western edge of the Harz. Around 1000 the family acquired Wettin Castle on the Saale River, originally built by local Slavic tribes, and took its name from it. Around 1030 the Wettins received the Eastern March as a fief. Their prominence there led Emperor Henry IV to invest them with the March of Meissen in 1089.

The family advanced steadily within the Holy Roman Empire. In 1263 it inherited the landgraviate of Thuringia, without Hesse, and in 1350 it gained the Palatinate of Saxony. In 1423 it was invested with the Duchy of Saxony, centred at Wittenberg, which brought the dignity of prince-elector. In 1485 the sons of Frederick II, Elector of Saxony, divided the lands that had been ruled jointly. The elder son Ernest took the electorate and Thuringia, and his younger brother Albert took the March of Meissen, which he ruled from Dresden as Duke of Saxony.

The Ernestine branch played an important part in the beginnings of the Protestant Reformation. Frederick III founded the University of Wittenberg in 1502 and appointed Martin Luther there in 1512. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546 and 1547 the Albertine Moritz sided with Emperor Charles V, who had promised him the electoral rights. After the Battle of Mühlberg, Johann Friedrich had to give up Wittenberg and the electorate to his cousin, and the Ernestines were left with Thuringia, which they divided into many small duchies.

The Albertines kept most of Saxony together, ruling as electors from 1547 to 1806 and as kings from 1806 to 1918, and two of them were kings of Poland between 1697 and 1763. After the Napoleonic Wars they lost about 40 per cent of their lands to Prussia in 1815, and Frederick Augustus III lost his throne in 1918.

Ernestine courts left a mark on culture. In the 18th century Karl August, Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, brought Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Weimar, where what became known as Weimar Classicism took shape. In the 19th century the Saxe-Coburg and Gotha line gained thrones through marriage, and it supplied kings of Belgium from 1831 and of Bulgaria from 1908 to 1946, as well as consorts to the rulers of Portugal and the United Kingdom. In 1917, during the First World War, the British royal family legally took the name Windsor, after advisers rejected Wettin as unsuitably comic.
house-of-wisdom: The House of Wisdom, or Bayt al-Hikma, also called the Grand Library of Baghdad, is described as an Abbasid public academy and intellectual centre. It was founded either as a library for the collections of the caliph Harun al-Rashid in the late 8th century or as a private collection of the caliph al-Mansur for rare books in Arabic. Under al-Ma'mun, who reigned from 813 to 833, it became a public academy and library. Its early name was Khizanat al-Hikma, or Storehouse of Wisdom. The caliph Muawiyah I had earlier gathered a collection of books in Damascus that was also referred to as Bayt al-Hikma.

The House of Wisdom was part of the Translation Movement of the Abbasid era, which rendered works from Greek and Syriac into Arabic and drew on Persian and Indian sources. Scholars, translators, scribes and scientists met there to translate, write and converse. Fields associated with it include philosophy, mathematics, medicine, astronomy and optics. Al-Ma'mun greatly increased its support, and he is said to have preferred scientific texts as the spoils of war; he is reported to have claimed Ptolemy's Almagest as a condition for peace after a war with the Eastern Roman Empire. Scholars of the institution also served as engineers, architects and calendar-keepers, and often as physicians and consultants.

It flourished under al-Mu'tasim and al-Wathiq but declined under al-Mutawakkil, who reigned from 847 to 861. The earlier caliphs had followed the Mu'tazili school, which supported scientific inquiry, while al-Mutawakkil endorsed a more literal reading of the Quran and hadith and saw Greek philosophy as anti-Islamic.

On 13 February 1258 the Mongols entered Baghdad and began a week of pillage and destruction. The House of Wisdom was destroyed with the city's other libraries during the siege by Hulagu's army. Accounts say books were thrown into the Tigris until it ran black with ink. The historian Michal Biran regards the claim that they formed a bridge for a man on horseback as a literary trope associated with the siege.

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi is said to have rescued about 400,000 manuscripts and taken them to Maragheh before the siege. Some historians now challenge the image of the House of Wisdom as a university with departments and organised debate, arguing that nineteenth- and early twentieth-century scholars built it through translation errors and retrospective projection.
house-of-wittelsbach: The origins of the family lie with the Counts of Scheyern, themselves of uncertain origins. When Otto I, Count of Scheyern, died in 1072, his third son Otto II acquired Wittelsbach Castle, near Aichach. In 1119 the counts left Scheyern Castle, built around 940, for Wittelsbach, and gave the former to monks to found Scheyern Abbey. Some have speculated that the family descends from Margrave Henry of Schweinfurt and his father Berthold, and perhaps from the Luitpolding dukes of Bavaria in the 10th century, but their background is itself disputed.

The Wittelsbachs ruled Bavaria from 1180 to 1918 and the Palatinate from 1214 to 1805, succeeding the House of Welf in both. The Golden Bull of 1356 gave the counts palatine the electoral dignity, and the Duchy of Bavaria became an electorate in 1623. The Bavarian branch kept the duchy until it died out in 1777. The Palatinate branch then took Bavaria as well. Napoleon later raised Bavaria to a kingdom, which lasted until 1918. By the Treaty of Lunéville of 9 February 1801 Bavaria lost the Palatinate and the duchies of Zweibrücken and Jülich, and it allied with France.

Members of the family also ruled beyond the Empire. Duke Otto III of Lower Bavaria, a maternal grandson of Béla IV of Hungary, was elected anti-king of Hungary and Croatia as Béla V from 1305 and gave up the throne by 1308. Christopher reigned over Denmark, Norway and Sweden from 1440 to 1448, and Charles X Gustav, Charles XI, Charles XII and Ulrika Eleonora ruled Sweden from 1654 to 1720. Frederick V, Elector Palatine, was king of Bohemia, called the Winter King. In 1699 the death of Joseph Ferdinand, a son of Maximilian II Emanuel, ended the chance that the family would inherit the Spanish throne, for Charles II of Spain had chosen him as heir.

Sophia of Hanover, born a Wittelsbach princess of the Palatinate, inherited the Stuart succession rights under the Act of Settlement of 1701. She died two months before Queen Anne, and her eldest son became George I in 1714, so the House of Hanover inherited the British crown. Wittelsbach archbishops, most of them of the Bavarian branch, ruled the Electorate of Cologne from Bonn between 1597 and 1794. Other members included Elisabeth in Bavaria, known as Sisi, Empress of Austria, and Ludwig II of Bavaria.

In the Nazi period Crown Prince Rupprecht earned Hitler's enmity by opposing the Beer Hall Putsch of 1923. He moved to Italy in 1938 and went into hiding in Florence after German forces occupied the country in September 1943.
house-of-wonders: The largest and tallest building of Stone Town, the palace stands on Mizingani Road on the old town's seafront, facing the Forodhani Gardens, between the Old Fort and the former Sultan's Palace. It was one of six palaces built by Barghash bin Said, second Sultan of Zanzibar, and is said to stand on the site of the 17th-century palace of Queen Fatuma. Intended as a ceremonial palace and official reception hall, it stood 39 metres tall, 50 metres long and 50 metres wide.

Its design is attributed to a British marine engineer. Wide external verandas on cast-iron columns allowed very high ceilings, and it was built of coral rag, concrete slabs, mangrove shoots or boriti and steel beams. A large covered courtyard is surrounded by open galleries; some inner doors are carved with inscriptions from the Quran, and the marble floors and most of the silver decoration came from Europe. Covered passages above the street, the wikios, linked it to the palaces of Beit al-Hukum and Beit al-Sahel, so that the royal women could move about unseen.

The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 destroyed the lighthouse in front of the building and the Beit al-Hukum Palace and badly damaged Beit al-Sahel. During repairs in 1897 a clock tower was set into the facade, and the site of Beit al-Hukum became a garden. Only after the bombardment did the sultan and his harem occupy the whole building. In 1911 it became government offices and the main secretariat of the British authorities.

After the Zanzibar Revolution of 1964 it was turned into a school and a museum for the ruling Afro-Shirazi Party, with North Korean aid. Museum work began in 1992–1994, and the House of Wonders Museum, opened in the early 2000s, showed Swahili and Zanzibari culture, with a mtepe, a traditional Swahili boat, filling the courtyard. Two Portuguese bronze cannons of the 16th century stand at the entrance.

Large parts of the veranda collapsed in 2012 and of the roof in 2015, and the museum moved elsewhere. On 25 December 2020, during a rehabilitation for which the government of Oman had provided the money, much of the front, including the clock tower, fell; four trapped workers were rescued and two died. A similar building is to be reconstructed from drawings.
house-of-zahringen: The earliest known ancestor of the family was Berthold, Count in the Breisgau, who died in 982 and was first mentioned in 962. His great-grandson Berthold, later counted as Berthold I of Zähringen, held lordships in the Breisgau, Thurgau, Ortenau and Baar. Emperor Henry III had promised him the Duchy of Swabia, but Henry's widow Agnes of Poitou gave it to Rudolf of Rheinfelden in 1057. In compensation Berthold received the titular dignity of Duke of Carinthia in 1061, and he lost it when he joined Rudolf's rising against Henry IV in 1073, during the Investiture Controversy.

Berthold II was elected Duke of Swabia in 1092 against Frederick I of Hohenstaufen. In 1098 he reconciled with Frederick, renounced Swabia and took the title Duke of Zähringen. In 1127 his son Conrad claimed the County of Burgundy, lost it to Renaud III of Mâcon but received large parts of the eastern Transjuranian lands and was made rector of Burgundy by Emperor Lothair III. The dukes kept that office until 1218, though their real rule was limited to Upper Burgundy east of the Jura.

Support for the Welfs in a failed feud against Conrad III between 1138 and 1152 halted the plan for a contiguous duchy between Swabia and Burgundy. Instead the dukes tightened feudal control and founded fortified towns. Berthold IV founded Fribourg in 1157 and Berthold V founded Bern in 1191. Berthold V died in February 1218 and the ducal line ended.

After 1218 parts of the territory returned to the crown, and the family's own lands went to the counts of Urach, who called themselves counts of Freiburg, and to the counts of Kyburg, descended from sisters of Berthold V. Less than fifty years later the Kyburgs died out and much of their land passed to the House of Habsburg. Bern became a free imperial city. The fragmentation contributed to the communal movements of the region and to the growth of the Old Swiss Confederacy in the early fourteenth century. A branch continued as the margraves of Baden, who ruled until 1918.
housecarl: In Old Norse a húskarl was a manservant as opposed to the húsbóndi, the master of the house. Housecarls were free men, not to be confused with thralls, and Icelandic laws also call them einhleypingar and lausamenn, men not tied, stressing that they served of their own will. With time the word came to mean a retainer in a lord's hirð or bodyguard; the Turinge stone speaks of housecarls raising a memorial to a commander who fell in Garðar, in Russia.

Danish runestones use the related word heimþegi, a man given a home in return for service. At Hedeby King Svein Forkbeard raised a stone in memory of his housecarl Skardi, and Johannes Brøndsted suggested that the garrison of the fort of Trelleborg may have been made up of royal housecarls. Such retainers still served Niels of Denmark early in the 12th century, but by its end they had probably become a new kind of nobility living away from the court.

According to the 12th-century Danish historian Svend Aggesen, the housecarls of Cnut the Great in England were governed by a law, the Witherlogh. They sat at the king's table by skill in war and birth, and could be moved to a lower place for minor offences; killing a fellow housecarl brought outlawry and exile, treason death. Their pay was monthly, according to Saxo Grammaticus, and they could leave the king's service on only one day of the year, New Year's Eve. Domesday Book records just thirty-three landholding housecarls in 1066, most with small estates.

Cnut is said to have kept 3,000 to 4,000 men in England as his bodyguard, and some historians see the housecarls as a disciplined standing army, a view Charles Oman put forward in 1885. Nicholas Hooper argued instead that it was time to debunk the housecarl: they were retainers with land or pay, hard to tell apart from thegns. Sceptics also note that no such army was used against the revolt of 1051. The Bayeux Tapestry shows them as footmen in mail with conical nasal helmets, fighting with great two-handed axes.
houthi-movement: The movement emerged in Yemen in the 1990s as a Zaydi revivalist organisation. Its first organisation, the Believing Youth, was founded in 1992 in Saada Governorate by either Mohammed al-Houthi or his brother Hussein al-Houthi. According to Ahmed Addaghashi, a professor at Sanaa University, the Houthis began as a moderate theological movement that preached tolerance. The Believing Youth ran school clubs and summer camps to promote a Zaydi revival, and by the mid-1990s between 15,000 and 20,000 students had attended. Zaydism is a branch of Islam found almost only in Yemen, where Zaydis make up about 34 per cent of the population. Zaydi-led governments ruled Yemen for a thousand years until 1962.

Under Hussein al-Houthi the movement became an opposition to President Ali Abdullah Saleh, whom it accused of corruption. In 2003, influenced by Hezbollah, it adopted its official slogan against the United States, Israel and the Jewish people. Al-Houthi was killed by the Yemeni military in Saada in 2004, an event that sparked the Houthi insurgency; the movement has since been mostly led by his brother Abdul-Malik al-Houthi. The Houthis took part in the Yemeni Revolution of 2011 and in the National Dialogue Conference, but later rejected the reconciliation deal of that year.

After the government raised fuel prices on 13 July 2014, Houthi leaders organised large rallies in Sanaa demanding the resignation of the government of Abd Rabbuh Mansur Hadi. In late 2014 they repaired their relationship with Saleh and, with his help, took control of the capital. The takeover prompted a Saudi-led military intervention, which led to a civil war.

The Houthis follow a mixed ideology with religious, Yemeni nationalist and populist elements, modelled on Hezbollah. They present themselves as a national resistance force and as representatives of marginalised tribal groups and the Zaydi sect. Estimates of membership range from 1,000 to 3,000 fighters in 2005 to 100,000 to 120,000 followers, armed and unarmed, by 2010. The movement has held mass gatherings for the birth of the prophet, and launched its own television channel, Almasirah, after the youth uprising of 2011, along with up to 25 print and electronic newspapers.
hovhannes-kajaznuni: He was born Hovhannes Ter-Hovhannisian on 14 February 1868 in Akhaltsikh, in the Tiflis Governorate of the Russian Empire. After school in Tiflis he studied at the Citizens' Architectural Institute in Saint Petersburg, graduating with honours in 1893, and there joined the Armenian Revolutionary Federation. He worked as an architect in Baku, Batum and Tiflis; his best-known building is the Saint Thaddeus and Bartholomew Cathedral in Baku, completed in 1911. In 1911 he left the Caucasus to avoid testifying at a trial of party members, living in Constantinople and Van until 1914.

He sat for his party in the Seym, the Transcaucasian parliament, and joined the delegation that met the Ottomans at the Trebizond Peace Conference from 14 March 1918. After Batum fell in April the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic was proclaimed, with Kajaznuni among its ministers. At the Batum Peace Conference of May 1918 Ottoman forces invaded Erivan Governorate, and the federation broke up; Armenia declared independence on 28 May.

The Armenian National Council elected him prime minister on 6 June 1918, and he served until 7 August 1919, then went on missions to Europe and the United States. His son Aram was killed in June 1920, the second son he lost in battle. He became chairman of parliament on 4 November 1920, was arrested by the Bolsheviks and freed in the February 1921 revolt.

In exile in Bucharest he wrote Dashnaktsutyun Has Nothing More to Do, a report to the party's convention of April 1923 calling for support of Soviet Armenia, and left the party that August. In 1925 he returned to work as an architect in Leninakan and taught construction in Yerevan. Arrested in 1937 in Stalin's Great Terror, he died in prison. In 2006 Mehmet Perinçek, who denies the Armenian genocide, published translations of the report as evidence against it; Viken L. Attarian calls such texts falsified, and the report itself refers to the deportation or extermination of the Ottoman Armenians.
howard-florey: Howard Walter Florey was born on 24 September 1898 in Malvern, a southern suburb of Adelaide, the only son of Joseph Florey, a bootmaker from Oxfordshire who had emigrated to South Australia. He graduated from the University of Adelaide and decided to pursue medical research, which required study overseas. Selected as South Australia's Rhodes Scholar, he began at the University of Oxford in January 1922, and later studied in the United States on a fellowship from the Rockefeller Foundation.

He held posts at the London Hospital, at the University of Cambridge and at the University of Sheffield, where he revitalised the pathology department. In 1935 he was appointed Professor of Pathology at the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology at Oxford and became a fellow of Lincoln College.

At the Dunn School Florey assembled a multidisciplinary staff. Ernst Chain, who had read Alexander Fleming's paper on the antibacterial effects of the Penicillium notatum mould while studying the enzyme lysozyme, joined him in a large project on antibacterial substances made by micro-organisms. Fleming first observed the antibiotic properties of the mould, but it was Chain and Florey who developed penicillin into a useful treatment, with crucial technical contributions from Heatley. They developed techniques for growing, purifying and manufacturing the drug and tested it on animals.

In 1941 they used it to treat a police constable from Oxford, who began to recover but died because not enough penicillin could then be made. Commercial production from a pilot plant of Imperial Chemical Industries became available in January 1942, and later trials in Britain, the United States and North Africa were highly successful. Florey went to North Africa in 1943 and to the Soviet Union in 1944, and was knighted in June 1944. He shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945 with Chain and Fleming.

After the war Florey's team studied further antibiotic substances, and he took part in founding the Australian National University and its John Curtin School of Medical Research in Canberra. He was elected a fellow of the Royal Society in 1941 and served as its president from 1960 to 1965. In 1962 he became provost of The Queen's College, Oxford, and from 1965 until his death on 21 February 1968 he was chancellor of the Australian National University. His discoveries are estimated to have saved over 80 million lives.
hoxter: Höxter lies on the left bank of the Weser, 52 kilometres north of Kassel, in the heart of the Weser Uplands, and is the seat of the Höxter district. The district has about 30,000 people, with the town itself making up around half. Its older names include Hoxer and Huxaria. The municipality was formed on 1 January 1970 by merging eleven communities of the former Amt of Höxter-Land with the main town and Bruchhausen. One of them, Lüchtringen, is the easternmost community in North Rhine-Westphalia.

In the time of Charlemagne, Höxter was a villa regia and the scene of a battle between his forces and the Saxons. Under the protection of the Princely Abbey of Corvey it gradually became prosperous and the chief town of the principality of Corvey. It lay on the long-distance trade route known as the Hellweg. Later it asserted its independence and joined the Hanseatic League. Rivalry with Corvey Abbey and the nearby town called Corvey grew, and in 1265 the burghers of Höxter allied themselves with the Bishop of Paderborn, whose troops destroyed the town of Corvey and damaged the abbey.

The Thirty Years' War hit Höxter severely. In 1634 Imperial troops besieged the town in what became known as the Blutbad von Höxter, the massacre of Höxter. After the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 it was united with Brunswick. In 1802 it passed to Nassau, in 1807 to the Kingdom of Westphalia, and in 1814, after that kingdom was dismembered, to Prussia. In 2005 an explosion in a house in the historic centre killed three people and damaged the town hall and many other significant buildings.

Höxter has a medieval town hall and a half-timbered old town in the Weser Renaissance style, with historic houses with high gables and carved façades of the 15th and 16th centuries. The Protestant church of St Kilian has a pulpit of 1595 and a font of 1631, and a stone bridge about 150 metres long, built in 1833, crosses the Weser. Schloss Corvey, formerly Corvey Abbey, stands on the outskirts. Its abbey church has a Carolingian crypt and an imposing westwork, and the poet Hoffmann von Fallersleben, author of Das Lied der Deutschen, worked there as a librarian and is buried next to the church.
hoysaleswara-temple: The temple stands on the banks of a large man-made lake and was sponsored by King Vishnuvardhana, under whom Dorasamudra became the established capital of the Hoysala Empire. It lacks a dedication inscription, but an inscription found about five kilometres away, near the Kallesvara temple ruins in Ghattadahalli, states that Ketamalla, an officer of the king, built it, and that the king granted lands for its upkeep in 1121 CE. Construction was complete in 1160 CE. In the early 14th century Delhi Sultanate armies twice sacked Halebidu, and the capital and its temples fell into ruin. The site came to be called Halebidu, literally the old camp or capital.

The twin temple has two sanctums of equal size, side by side and facing east, each with a Shiva linga: one for Hoysaleswara, the king, and one for Shantaleswara, the queen, Shantala Devi. Two Nandi shrines stand outside, and a smaller shrine holds a 2.1-metre statue of the Sun god Surya. The towers above the sanctums are lost, so the temple now looks flat. Its outer walls carry about 340 large reliefs and bands of friezes narrating the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Bhagavata Purana. It is a Shaiva monument but includes themes from the Vaishnavism and Shaktism traditions and images from Jainism.

Richard Banner Oakley, who photographed the temple in the 1850s, wrote that it far surpassed any temple he had seen in the south of India. James Fergusson, who never visited it, compared it with the Parthenon in 1876; his wrong dating of its building to 1235 was copied for a while, and Kristen Kasdorf finds his praise shaped by the prevailing imperialist narrative. Percy Brown called it the highest achievement of Hoysala architecture. In 2023 UNESCO declared it, with the Chennakeshava Temple at Belur and the Keshava Temple at Somanathapura, a World Heritage Site.
hpakant: Hpakant, also written Hpakan and Phakant, lies in Hpakant Township of Kachin State, on the Uyu River 350 kilometres north of Mandalay. Its name comes from Shan words for rock fall or building up a wall. The village was founded in 1832 but soon destroyed by a landslide, and was founded again in 1836. Maran Brang Seng, chairman of the Kachin Independence Organisation from 1976 until his death in 1994, was born there in 1930.

The Kachin Independence Army (KIA) held the area until it agreed a ceasefire with the military government in the early 1990s, after which it lost control of the mines. Firms from China, Hong Kong and Singapore won concessions, and later contracts went to Tay Za's Htoo Group and to a subsidiary of the Hong Pang Group of Wei Hsueh-kang, a former drug trafficker and leader of the UWSA. In 2011 fighting broke out between the KIA and the Myanmar Army around the mines, displacing an estimated 90,000 people by September 2012 and killing hundreds.

Mining brought deforestation, landslides and floods, soil dumped into the Uru River and residents evicted when uplands were bulldozed. Locals say that one thousand miners drowned in 2000 when the Uru flooded the underground mines, news the authorities suppressed. The landslide of 22 November 2015 killed over 100 people, most of whom scavenged the waste heaps for jade. More than 162 died in a landslide on 2 July 2020, 32 on 13 August 2023 and another 32 on 13 January 2025.

Hpakant remains the centre of Myanmar's mining of gem-quality jadeite. About 100 jade mining companies operate in the area, and the debris of the mines blocks the drainage of heavy rain into the rivers.
hrabanus-maurus: Hrabanus was born to noble parents in Mainz; the date of his birth is uncertain. In 801 he was ordained a deacon at the Benedictine abbey of Fulda in Hesse, where he was schooled and became a monk. At the insistence of his abbot, Ratgar, he went with Haimo, later of Halberstadt, to complete his studies at Tours. There he studied under Alcuin, who in recognition of his diligence gave him the surname Maurus, after the favourite disciple of Benedict, Saint Maurus.

Returning to Fulda, in 803 he was given the main charge of the abbey school. Under his direction it became one of the most outstanding centres of scholarship and book production in Europe, and its pupils included Walafrid Strabo, Servatus Lupus of Ferrières and Otfrid of Weissenburg. In 814 he was ordained a priest. After a disagreement with Ratgar he withdrew for a time from Fulda, and returned in 817 when Eigil became abbot. At Eigil's death in 822 he became abbot himself, and in 842 he resigned to have more time for study and prayer, retiring to the neighbouring monastery of St Petersberg.

In 847 he returned to public life when he was elected to succeed Otgar as archbishop of Mainz. He died at Winkel on the Rhine in 856. His feast is given as 4 February in the latest edition of the Roman Martyrology, which calls him a saint.

Hrabanus wrote commentaries on much of the Bible, treatises on doctrine and practice, and homilies. In De institutione clericorum he brought forward the views of Augustine and Gregory the Great on the training needed for clerical duties. His encyclopedia De rerum naturis was followed by De universo, in 22 books, which depends heavily on Isidore of Seville's Etymologies and was meant as a help to the interpretation of Scripture. He also wrote an annotated abridgement of Vegetius to improve Frankish warfare, and a set of poems on the cross, De laudibus sanctae crucis, that present the cross in word and image.
Among his hymns the best known is Veni Creator Spiritus, sung at Pentecost and ordinations. He was called Praeceptor Germaniae, the teacher of Germany, and knew some Greek and Hebrew.
hromkla: Rumkale, Roman Castle, stands on a cliff above the Euphrates in Gaziantep Province, 50 km west of Şanlıurfa. It has been suggested to be Shitamrat, taken by the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III in 855 BCE, and tradition holds that the apostle John lived there, but no remains older than about 1000 CE have been found.

The foundations go back to Byzantine rule, when the fortress guarded the frontier and the Roman road along the Euphrates and housed a Syriac Orthodox bishopric in the 5th and 6th centuries. Armenians settled there in the 11th century. After the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 it passed to Philaretos Brachamios and then to Kogh Vasil, whose adopted son Vasil Dgha was tortured by Baldwin II of Edessa and forced to give up his lands in 1116. Catholicos Gregory III bought it from Beatrice of Turbessel as a safe home for the Armenian Catholicosate, and his brother Nerses IV was elected Catholicos there in 1166.

Theological conferences on a union of the Armenian and Byzantine churches met there in 1170 and 1172, and a synod of 33 Armenian bishops in 1179 sent a profession of faith to Emperor Manuel I Komnenos, who died before it arrived. Mamluk forces destroyed the town in 1268 but could not take the citadel, and a siege under Sultan Qalawun in 1280 also failed. In 1292 the Mamluks under al-Ashraf took it after a long siege, massacred the garrison and enslaved or imprisoned the clergy and townspeople. Renamed Qal'at al-Muslimin, it became a base for raids into the Ilkhanate.

Timur's forces damaged the castle in 1400–1, and in 1516 it passed to the Ottomans without a siege after the Battle of Marj Dabiq. After the rebellion of its voivode Bekirzade Mehmed Bey in 1831 the Ottoman government ordered the town emptied and its houses destroyed, and in 1832 Ibrahim Pasha bombarded what remained during the Egyptian–Ottoman War. The residents moved to Kasaba, Halfeti and Aintab.

The fortress is a ruin in the Nizip district of Gaziantep. The reservoir of the Birecik Dam has made its site a peninsula, reached by boat from the neighbouring site of Zeugma or from the town of Halfeti.
hrotsvitha-of-gandersheim: Hrotsvitha was born in about 935 to Saxon nobles in Bad Gandersheim and entered Gandersheim Abbey as a canoness. Almost everything known about her comes from the prefaces of her own works and later readings of them. The abbey housed secular canonesses, who took vows of chastity and obedience but not of poverty and could leave the house at will.

She studied first under the nun Rikkardis, who was younger than she, and then under the Abbess Gerberga, a granddaughter of King Henry the Fowler, who became her friend and adviser. Her reading centred on legends of the saints, and she learned to write verse. By her twenties she was herself a teacher. She wrote at first in secret until she was encouraged to read her work aloud and to revise it.

All her writing is in Medieval Latin. The first book is a collection of eight verse legends, written in the 950s or 960s in honour of Gerberga, among them those of Gongolf, Pelagius, Theophilus, Basilius, Dionysius and Agnes. The second book holds six short dramas in prose: Gallicanus, Dulcitius, Calimachus, Abraham, Pafnutius and Sapientia.

She wrote them as a Christian answer to the Roman playwright Terence, whose women she thought were shown as immoral. Her own plays set the chastity and perseverance of Christian women against such figures, and they turn on conversion, repentance or the martyrdom of virgins. Whether the plays were staged or only read aloud is uncertain, though recent scholarship links her with the theatrical activity of the Ottonian court. The third book is dedicated to Emperors Otto I and Otto II and contains the Gesta Ottonis, a history of the Ottonians from 919 to 965, and the Primordia coenobii Gandeshemensis, a history of her abbey.

Her works were largely ignored until the humanist Conrad Celtis found the main manuscript at St Emmeram in Regensburg and edited it, with illustrations by Albrecht Dürer. It was translated into English in the 1600s. Some doubted that the works were authentic, but later study has supported her authorship. From the 1970s feminist scholars returned to her as one of the few women of the early Middle Ages to write about her own life and world. The asteroid 615 Roswitha and the Roswitha Prize of Bad Gandersheim are named for her.
hrvoje-vukcic-hrvatinic: Hrvoje was the eldest son of Duke Vukac Hrvatinić and the most prominent member of the Hrvatinić noble family. His brothers were Vuk, who became Ban of Croatia, Dragiša and Vojislav, and his sister Resa Vukčić married Batalo Šantić. He is first mentioned in 1376 as a prince and knight under King Louis I of Hungary. His lands were the Donji Kraji, the Lower Edges of medieval Bosnia, facing Croatia and Slavonia to the west. He married Jelena Nelipčić, a granddaughter of the Croatian noble Ivan I Nelipac.

King Tvrtko I made him Grand Duke of Bosnia in 1380, with a seat in Lašva, and in 1387 he led Bosnian troops into Croatia to raise the siege of Bishop Ivan Horvat in Zagreb. In the succession struggle that followed the death of Louis I he sided with Ladislaus of Naples against Sigismund of Luxembourg. He fought the Ottoman Turks in Bosnia in 1392 under King Stephen Dabiša, opposed Queen Jelena Gruba, and took part in the choice of Stephen Ostoja as king in May 1398.

When Sigismund invaded Bosnia, Hrvoje defeated his forces before they reached Vrbas, pursued them across the river Una and took the župa of Dubica. By the end of 1402 he had brought every Dalmatian city except Dubrovnik to recognise Ladislaus, who after his coronation in Zadar named him Vicar General for Sclavonia. Coins Hrvoje minted in Split styled him duke of Split, royal viceroy of Dalmatia and Croatia and supreme voivode of Bosnia. In 1406 he strengthened Prozor Fortress above the Vrlika valley.

Hrvoje later fell out with Ostoja and joined the plot that replaced him with Tvrtko II Kotromanić in 1404. After Sigismund's intervention of 1408 and the massacre of the Bosnian army he came to terms with Sigismund, but Ostoja's return weakened him and he lost Split and the islands. He then turned to the Ottomans. The Hungarian army was defeated at Lašva in 1415, which opened the way to Ottoman expansion into Bosnia. Hrvoje died the next year and was buried in the crypt of his underground chapel at Jajce; his widow married Ostoja. His missal, written in Glagolitic, is now in the Topkapı Palace Museum Manuscript Library in Istanbul.
hryhorii-skovoroda: Hryhorii Skovoroda was born on 3 December 1722 into a small-holder Registered Cossack family in the village of Chornukhy. His mother was partly of Crimean Tatar descent. He studied at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy in several periods between 1734 and 1753 but did not graduate. In 1741 he was taken to sing in the imperial choir in Moscow and Saint Petersburg, and from 1745 to 1750 he was in the kingdom of Hungary with a commission buying Tokaj wine for the imperial court, visiting Pressburg, Buda and Vienna and meeting local scholars. He returned to Kyiv in 1750.

He taught poetics at the Pereiaslav collegium in 1750 and 1751, until a dispute over his methods led the bishop to dismiss him. From 1753 to 1759 he tutored the son of the Cossack noble Stepan Tomara and began composing poems for The Garden of Divine Songs. From 1759 to 1769, with interruptions, he taught poetry, syntax, Greek and ethics at the Kharkiv Collegium. He refused pressure to take monastic vows. His closest student there was Mikhail Kovalensky, who became his first biographer. After a bishop objected to an unordained teacher giving catechism, he resigned in April 1769 and never held an institutional post again.

He then lived as a wandering philosopher, first at an apiary near Kharkiv, where he wrote philosophical fables and dialogues such as Narcissus and the Symphony Called the Book of Askhan. He travelled on foot through Sloboda Ukraine, staying with friends rich and poor and forming a circle of admirers. He also composed liturgical music and songs, and several of his philosophical songs entered the repertoire of kobzar folk musicians. In his last year he walked to visit Kovalensky near Oryol and entrusted him with his collected works.

Skovoroda's works were not printed in his lifetime because of church censorship. His first book appeared in Saint Petersburg in 1798, and the first almost complete edition came in 1861. His native speech was vernacular Ukrainian, but he wrote in a mixture of Church Slavonic, Ukrainian and Russian, and most of his surviving letters are in Latin and Greek. His treatises and dialogues join biblical questions to those of Plato and the Stoics.

He taught that the kingdom of God is within a person, that to know God one must know oneself, and that all work is blessed by God. Each person should seek a congenial work, since those who abandon their calling to chase wealth or prestige become unhappy. He died on 9 November 1794 in Pan-Ivanovka.
hsinbyumashin: She was born Shwe Nanshin Me on 22 November 1821, the daughter of King Bagyidaw and his chief queen Nanmadaw Me Nu, and was granted the appanages of Sagaing and Singu. When her mother was executed under King Tharrawaddy, Princess Setkya Dewi saved her life and took her in. She was married to Mindon Min, who made her Queen of the Central Palace. On 25 November 1877 she received the title Hsinbyumashin, "mistress of the white elephants", on being given a white elephant by the king. Of their seven children only Supayagyi, Supayalat and Supayalay survived.

When Setkya Dewi died, Mindon left the post of chief queen vacant, though Hsinbyumashin received its rights. After Crown Prince Kanaung's assassination in 1866 she proposed marrying Supayagyi to the Mekkhaya Prince, then thought likely to be chosen as heir; his sister, the Kenni Princess, mocked the match, and the queen resented her family from then on. In the Bronze Hall massacre that followed Mindon's death, which accounts attribute to Hsinbyumashin, more than 100 members of the royal family were killed, among them the Kenni Princess and Mekkhaya Prince, and Thibaw was placed on the throne.

At the coronation Supayalat pushed in to be anointed queen beside her sister Supayagyi, which had never happened before in Burma. Hsinbyumashin was treated as queen dowager, but Supayalat later removed her mother's influence over Thibaw. Hsinbyumashin then plotted to replace him with Prince Nyaungyan and, after his death, with his younger brother Prince Nyaungok, but her letter to Nyaungok in Calcutta fell into the hands of Colonel Edward Bosc Sladen.

After Thibaw's defeat in the Third Anglo-Burmese War, she and Supayagyi were sent to Tavoy on a first-grade political pension. A rebellion at Tavoy in 1887 led the British to move her to Calcutta and then to Ratnagiri, which she reached on 22 August 1887. About a year later she settled in Rangoon, on Winsa Road, where she led funeral ceremonies for members of the royal family. She died there on 26 February 1900. Her body was taken by sea to Mandalay and interred within the palace enclosure. Her life has since been told in Thai television dramas and a Burmese film.
hsinbyushin: Hsinbyushin, whose royal name means Lord of the white elephant, was born Maung Ywa on 12 September 1736 at Moksobo, a large village in the Mu river valley about 60 miles northwest of Ava. His father Aung Zeya was the village chief and belonged to gentry families that had administered the valley for generations. The boy grew up as the authority of King Mahadhammaraza Dipadi of the Toungoo dynasty dissolved, Manipuri raiders burned villages in his home region, and the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom broke away in the south.

When his father founded the Konbaung dynasty as King Alaungpaya in February 1752, the 15-year-old prince joined the resistance and, styled Thado Minsaw, soon became a leading commander. His assault on 3 January 1754 recaptured Ava, of which he was made governor. After his father's death he tried to seize the throne from his elder brother Naungdawgyi but found too little support in the army; forgiven at the queen mother's intercession, he succeeded on 28 November 1763, when Naungdawgyi died suddenly at 29.

Hsinbyushin rebuilt the ruined city of Ava and moved his capital there from Sagaing in April 1765. In December 1764 he led an expedition that took Imphal after Manipur revolted, and in 1765 an army under Ne Myo Thihapate brought Vientiane and Luang Prabang under Burmese control. His court invited nine Brahmin scholars from Varanasi to help translate Sanskrit works, compiled the Manusara Shwe Min Dhammathat law book in 1771, and raised the Shwedagon Pagoda to its present height.

Fighting China and Siam at the same time nearly cost the kingdom its independence: the third Chinese invasion forced a hasty withdrawal from Siam until an uneasy truce in 1769. In 1773 the abuses of army commanders provoked a mutiny of ethnic Mon troops at Martaban, which was put down harshly.

From 1774 Hsinbyushin suffered a long illness, and in 1775 Lan Na and Manipur revolted. He died in June 1776, aged 39, leaving 20 queens and 41 children; against Alaungpaya's edict that his sons should reign in order of seniority, he had made his eldest son Singu heir. The Burmese armies withdrew from Siam after his death, leaving Lan Na under Siamese control.

His wars laid the basis of Burma's present border with China and secured Tenasserim, but the destruction of Ayutthaya reinvigorated a militaristic Siam, and Thai enmity towards the Burmese dates largely from his reign. In December 1954 U Nu, the first prime minister of the Union of Burma, publicly apologised in Bangkok for past misdeeds.
htilominlo: Htilominlo, whose name means throne-willing, was also known as Nadaungmya, earrings, and by the regnal name Zeya Theinkha Uzana. He was the son of King Sithu II and Queen Saw Mya Kan. The chronicles disagree on the dates of his birth, death and reign; the Zatadawbon Yazawin, held to be the most accurate chronicle for the Pagan period, gives his birth as 4 February 1175.

A devout Buddhist and a scholar, the king gave up command of the army and left the daily business of government to a privy council of ministers, the forerunner of the Hluttaw, the supreme administrative body of government. He gave his energy to religion and building: besides finishing the Gawdawpalin Temple begun by his father, he built the Mahabodhi, a replica of the temple at Buddhagaya. Most of his temples, however, stood in remote lands outside the Pagan region, a sign of the strained royal treasury.

The one rebellion of his reign, north of Tagaung, was put down by his commander-in-chief, and by all accounts he was popular with his people. Yet he never really governed, and he paid no heed to the shrinking tax base caused by the steady growth of tax-free religious estates.

His 24-year reign is seen as the start of the gradual decline of the Pagan dynasty, the first to feel the effect of more than a century of growth in tax-free religious wealth. His successors also ignored the problem, and by the 1280s two-thirds of the cultivable land of Upper Burma had passed to religious owners.

The throne thus lost the means to keep the loyalty of courtiers and soldiers, opening a cycle of internal disorder and challenges from the Mons, Mongols and Shans. The royal chronicles name his son Kyaswa as his successor, but two contemporary inscriptions show that another son, Naratheinga Uzana, was acting at least as regent towards the end of the reign.
hu-shih: Hu Shih was born in Shanghai on 17 December 1891 to Hu Chuan, a tea merchant who became a public servant in northern China, Hainan and Taiwan, and his third wife Feng Shundi. The family moved to Taiwan in 1893, and shortly before Hu Chuan's death in 1895 the mother and her young son left for their ancestral home in Anhui.

Funded by the Boxer Indemnity Scholarship Program, he was sent on 16 August 1910 to study agriculture at Cornell University. In 1912 he changed to philosophy and literature and was elected to Phi Beta Kappa. At Cornell he led a campaign to promote the newer, easier written vernacular Chinese, and helped found the university's East Asian book collections.

Hu was ambassador to the United States from 1938 until his recall in September 1942, when Wei Tao-ming replaced him. He then served as chancellor of Peking University from 1946 to 1948. In 1957 he became the third president of the Academia Sinica in Taipei, holding the post until his death. In 1928 he and others founded the monthly Crescent Moon, in which he published Human Rights and Law, calling for a written constitution that protects citizens' rights, especially against the government.

He rejected Sun Yat-sen's claim that people are incapable of self-rule, and considered democracy itself a form of political education. Unlike many contemporaries who joined the socialist camp, he held to liberalism and democracy all his life, though during the May Fourth Movement he gained a more favourable view of the centralised organisation of the Soviet Union, and returned to individualism after the early 1930s. In the early 1950s the Chinese Communist Party launched a years-long campaign against his thought, and he answered with English essays questioning its legitimacy.

He translated pragmatism as shíyànzhǔyì, experimental-ism, valuing Dewey's method and scientific spirit more than the content of his philosophy. Thomas H. Huxley, he wrote, influenced him most heavily. He brought scientific method and skepticism into traditional Chinese textual study and in 1919 published the first volume of An Outline History of Chinese Philosophy; the rest was never finished. In January 1917 his article A Preliminary Discussion of Literature Reform set out guidelines for writers, among them to write with substance and not to imitate the ancients.

Hu died of a heart attack in Nankang, Taipei, at the age of 70, during a conference for his former student Chien-Shiung Wu. His work fell into disrepute in mainland China until a 1986 article by Ji Xianlin led to a re-evaluation.
hua-guofeng: Hua Guofeng was born Su Zhu on 16 February 1921 in Jiaocheng, Shanxi, the fourth son of a family from Fan County in Henan, and lost his father at the age of seven. He joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, and took the name Hua Guofeng from the title of a patriotic vanguard organisation. In 1948 he went with the People's Liberation Army to Hunan, where he stayed until 1971. In 1952 he became secretary of the Xiangtan Special District, which included Mao Zedong's hometown of Shaoshan, and built a memorial hall dedicated to Mao there.

Hua supported the Cultural Revolution and led it in Hunan, becoming chairman of the provincial Revolutionary Committee and first secretary of the party's Hunan committee in December 1970. In 1973 he joined the Politburo, and Mao named him Minister of Public Security and vice premier. After Zhou Enlai died on 8 January 1976 Mao made him acting premier, passing over Zhang Chunqiao, and after the Tiananmen Incident of 1976 he became first vice chairman of the party and premier.

Mao died on 9 September 1976. With Marshal Ye Jianying and the security chief Wang Dongxing, Hua decided to use force, and the Gang of Four were arrested on 6 October. The next day he was appointed chairman of the party and of the Central Military Commission, the first to hold the offices of party leader, premier and commander-in-chief together. He ended the constant ideological campaigns and rehabilitated more than 4,600 disgraced cadres, and in 1977 the first national college entrance examination since the Cultural Revolution was authorised. He held to a command economy and a ten-year plan of heavy industry and imported technology, soon scrapped for a cheaper five-year plan. His slogan, the Two Whatevers, committed the leadership to follow whatever Mao had decided.

Deng Xiaoping and his allies forced Hua from power between December 1978 and June 1981; Zhao Ziyang replaced him as premier in September 1980, and Hu Yaobang as chairman. The Historical Resolution of 27 June 1981 said that he had removed the Gang of Four but then committed serious errors. He remained a member of the Central Committee until 2002 and died in Beijing on 20 August 2008.

His legacy is often reduced to the Two Whatevers, though Isabella Weber argues that this is overemphasised, and Andrew B. Kennedy calls him essentially a pragmatic problem solver. His break with Cultural Revolution economic policy and the opening of China's first Special Economic Zone are seen as paving the way for the reform and opening up led by Deng. His ousting also set a precedent in which disgraced party members were stripped of posts but not jailed.
huaca-de-la-luna: The temple stands about 5 kilometres from the Pacific Ocean and 4 kilometres from Trujillo, near the mouth of the Moche River, and with the larger Huaca del Sol it forms the Huacas de Moche. It is a complex of three platforms and several plazas. The largest, Platform I, is 30 metres high, and a new platform was built over the existing one about every hundred years. North of it lies the broad Plaza 1, probably used for large gatherings, with the decorated building Recinto 1, whose murals show warriors leading prisoners.

Its adobe bricks are all wider than they are tall, and many bear one of 128 distinct marks identifying the community that made them. The interior walls carry 10,000 square metres of polychrome murals, painted with mineral pigments such as hematite for red and clay for white as well as organic ones. The deity Ai-Apaec, or Ayapec, a Muchik word meaning all knowing, appears often.
