Archaeologists think the Huaca del Sol served administrative, military and residential purposes, while the Huaca de la Luna was chiefly ceremonial, though it also holds burials, several of high status in Platform I. Human sacrifices took place on the eastern platform, at a black rock and in Plazas 3A, 3B and 3C. The skeletons of adult men at the foot of the rock show signs of imprisonment and fractures, and most died from a severe blow to the head; their bodies were thrown down and left unburied in the patios.

Scholars debate whether these victims were taken in war between communities or in staged combat, since the murals show no victories over other groups and the fighters look alike. Other victims, killed by a clean cut to the neck, lie in muddy deposits that coincide with El Niño floods, and children may have been offered on the completion of a temple, though no causal link to El Niño has been shown.

Spanish conquistadors damaged and looted the Huaca del Sol in the seventeenth century, but the Huaca de la Luna was left largely untouched, and wind-blown sand kept its structure well preserved, though looters destroyed its northern platform. Excavation began in the 1990s after aerial surveys of the late 1980s, and the World Monuments Fund has supported its conservation.
huaca-del-sol: The Huaca del Sol is one of several ruins found near the volcanic peak of Cerro Blanco, in the coastal desert of the Moche Valley. The other major ruin of the site is the nearby Huaca de la Luna, a temple that is smaller but better preserved. The Huaca del Sol itself stood at the centre of the Moche capital city.

By 450 CE eight different stages of construction had been completed on the Huaca del Sol. The technique was additive: new layers of brick were laid directly on top of the old ones, so that very large quantities of bricks were needed. The structure was expanded and rebuilt by different rulers over the course of time, and the number of different makers' marks suggests that more than a hundred communities contributed bricks to the construction of the huacas.

The pyramid was built in four main levels. It is believed to have stood about 50 metres high when complete, with a base of 340 by 160 metres. Archaeological evidence shows that it was used for ritual and ceremonial activities, and that it also served as a royal residence and held burial chambers.

During the Spanish occupation of Peru in the early 17th century, colonists redirected the waters of the Moche River to run past its base in order to loot gold artifacts from the temple, and this hydraulic mine did great damage to the structure. In total about two-thirds of the pyramid has been lost to erosion and looting, and what remains stands 41 metres high. Looting and the erosion caused by El Niño remain major threats to the ruin.
huahine: Huahine is an island among the Society Islands of French Polynesia, in the Leeward Islands group. It is about 16 kilometres long and 13 kilometres wide, with a land area of 75 square kilometres, and consists of two main islands, Huahine Nui to the north and Huahine Iti to the south, separated by a few hundred metres of water and joined by a sandspit at low tide and by a small bridge.

A fringing coral reef with several islets surrounds them. Its highest point is Turi, at 669 metres. In the north-west of Huahine Nui a brackish lake, Lac Fauna Nui, is all that remains of an ancient atoll lagoon.

Human presence on Huahine goes back at least a thousand years, as shown by the many marae, and archaeologists estimate that the Maʻohi people colonized it from at least the 9th century CE. It holds one of the largest concentrations of Polynesian remains dated between 850 and 1100.

Until the late 19th century Huahine was an independent kingdom, which tradition says passed through three dynasties: the Hau-moʻo-rere dynasty, founded in the 17th century, whose last representative was Queen Tehaʻapapa I; the Tamatoa dynasty, which reigned until 1854; and the Teururaʻi dynasty, which reigned from 1854 to 1895. Captain James Cook arrived at Fare Harbour on 16 July 1769 and met the chief Ori, and returned on 3 September 1773.

In 1846 the island resisted French rule and in 1847 proclaimed itself the Kingdom of Huahine. On 20 April 1879 the German Empire signed a treaty of friendship and commerce with its government. French warships bombarded the two largest villages in September 1890. On 15 September 1895 the regent, for Queen Tehaʻapapa, and the principal chiefs renounced their powers in favour of France, and the island was incorporated into the French Establishments of Oceania. Protestant missionaries first reached the island in 1809, and in 1815 the mission ordered the destruction of the idols of the old gods.

Huahine is a commune of French Polynesia; its administrative centre is Fare, on Huahine Nui, and it had 6,263 inhabitants at the 2022 census. Most people are Christian. The main activities are vanilla cultivation, copra production, fishing and tourism. The island is one of four where the Hawaiki Nui Vaʻa canoe race is held, with Bora Bora, Tahaa and Raiatea. The Faʻahia archaeological site has revealed remains of extinct birds killed off by the earliest Polynesian settlers.
huai-army: The army took its name from the Huai River and was also called the Anhui Army, after the province where it was based. Before Anqing was recovered in late 1861, Zeng Guofan ordered his student Li Hongzhang, a commander in the Xiang Army, to take part of that army back to Anhui, Li's home province, and form an independent force under his own command. Li created the Huai Army in October 1861 from 25,000 soldiers, among them Taiping troops who had surrendered at Anqing, and after three months of training it fought its first battle at Shanghai.

Unlike the Eight Banners and the Green Standard Army, the Huai Army was largely a militia based on personal rather than institutional loyalty. Its officers were not rotated: they chose their own soldiers and formed paternalistic ties with them. In 1862 its basic unit was the ying, a battalion of 504 men in four companies, each divided into eight platoons of 12 to 14 men grouped by weapon. Above that level a commander might lead a few ying or as many as 70.

Facing the mounted Nian rebels, the army added cavalry battalions and more firearms. By 1865 over 4,000 of its troops used foreign rifles, and by 1868, at the end of the campaign, 17,400 men served in cavalry battalions, which with their auxiliaries would have brought the army to over 100,000. Officers such as Zha Lianbiao studied Western drill in Germany, and General Zhou Shengchuan rewarded good marksmanship with badges of merit and money.

Units of the army fought the French in Tonkin and on Formosa during the Sino-French War and lost most of their battles, although troops under General Liu Mingchuan beat back French attempts on the Keelung forts and near Tamsui on Taiwan. Around 45,000 of its men were stationed in provinces such as Zhili, Shanxi, Hubei, Jiangsu and Shaanxi, and it also fought in the First Sino-Japanese War. It was succeeded by the New Army and the Beiyang Army in the late 19th century, though it continued to exist until the end of the dynasty in 1911.
huai-river: The Huai River, formerly romanized Hwai, is about 1,110 km long and drains an area of 174,000 square kilometres. It rises in Tongbai Mountain in Henan and flows through southern Henan, northern Anhui and northern Jiangsu, where it pools in Lake Hongze. The river and the Qin Mountains form the Qinling–Huaihe Line, which approximates the January isotherm of 0 °C and the isohyet of 800 millimetres and is sometimes regarded as the geographical dividing line between northern and southern China. In Jiangsu the river system is interconnected with other waterways and forms part of the Grand Canal.

Historically the Huai entered the Yellow Sea at Yunti Pass, in modern Xiangshui County, through a broad and level lower course. It irrigated the surrounding farmland and stood at the centre of an extensive network of canals and tributaries.

From 1194 the Yellow River to the north repeatedly changed course southwards into the Huai. The heavy silting that followed created new high ground, lakes and built-up silt along the Yellow River's old southern course.

After the Yellow River returned to its northern course for the last time in 1897, water from the middle Huai could not flow easily into the lower section, and the lower section had no outlet to the sea. The problem worsened in the Second Sino-Japanese War, when the Nationalist government flooded the lower basin by opening the Yellow River's southern levee, in an attempt to check the Japanese advance. The Yellow River's main stem flowed through the breach for the next nine years. In the 450 years to 1950 the Huai suffered on average 94 major floods per century, with droughts in between.

Today most of the river's flow enters the Yangtze through Lake Hongze and the Sanhe River, ending at Sanjiangying near Yangzhou. A separate passage, the Huaihe Sea Entryway and Subei Irrigation Canal, passes Huai'an and reaches the sea at Biandan Port, and the North Jiangsu Main Irrigation Canal carries some water along the old course to the sea. The Huai remains vulnerable to flooding. It has 15 main tributaries with catchments of more than 2,000 square kilometres each. A national pollution-control programme began in the basin in 1994, with World Bank support from 2000.
huaihai-campaign: After Jinan fell to the communists on 24 September 1948, Su Yu, acting commander of the East China Field Army, proposed a thrust south along the Grand Canal before winter, which he named the Huaihai campaign. Mao Zedong approved it, adding the destruction of the Nationalist 7th Field Army at Xin'an, and widened it by sending the Central Plains Field Army under Liu Bocheng and Deng Xiaoping east to isolate Xuzhou. It was the first operation in which the Chinese Communist Party coordinated several army groups, and its aim was to destroy the Kuomintang forces of about 800,000 men before they could withdraw south of the Yangtze. Chiang Kai-shek chose to make his stand around Xuzhou rather than fall back to the Huai River.

The offensive opened on 6 November 1948 as Huang Baitao's 7th Field Army began moving west to Xuzhou. Delayed at a single bridge over the Grand Canal and exposed when most of the 3rd Pacification Zone defected on the night of 8 November, it was surrounded at Nianzhuang. Relief columns from Xuzhou were blocked, and resistance ended on 22 November, when Huang Baitao killed himself; 25,000 of his men were killed and 80,000 wounded or captured. Meanwhile the Central Plains Field Army took Suxian, cutting the link between Xuzhou and Bengbu.

The communists next trapped Huang Wei's 12th Field Army at Shuangduiji by 25 November. On 28 November Chiang ordered Du Yuming to evacuate Xuzhou, and its garrison of 300,000 left on the night of 30 November, only to be encircled at Chenguanzhuang. The 12th Field Army was destroyed by 15 December and Huang Wei captured. At Chenguanzhuang bad winter weather hampered supply by air and soldiers killed their horses for food. The final assault began on 6 January 1949, and resistance ended on 10 January with Du Yuming captured and Qiu Qingquan killed.

The campaign brought the Kuomintang its heaviest losses of the war and gave the communists a vast area north of the Yangtze, directly threatening Nanjing, Shanghai and Wuhan. The losses of Chiang's own Whampoa-trained troops weakened his position, and under pressure from rivals such as Li Zongren and Bai Chongxi he stepped down as President on 21 January 1949, as American military aid dwindled. The campaign was later the subject of the second film of the trilogy Decisive Engagement of 1991.
huaihai-road: Huaihai Road joins three streets that were once separate. Middle Huaihai Road, the main section and the former Avenue Joffre, runs for 5,500 metres, mostly through the former Luwan District, which was merged into Huangpu in 2010, and on into Xuhui and Changning. West Huaihai Road, 1,510 metres long, forms part of the boundary between Changning and Xuhui, and East Huaihai Road, 373 metres long, was the boundary between Huangpu and Nanshi before those districts merged.

The middle section was built in 1901 as Rue Sikiang, named after the Xi River, partly inside the expanded French Concession and partly as an extra-settlement road beyond it. It became Route Paul Brunat five years later, and the rest of the road came into the concession in 1914. Joseph Joffre attended an official renaming ceremony during a visit in 1922. The eastern part held many shikumen houses, the western part large houses and mansion blocks, and in the 1920s Russians fleeing the Communist revolution made the street a commercial centre of European-style shops, cafes and restaurants.

After the Japanese took over the foreign concessions in 1941, the street was renamed Taishan Road in 1943. The Kuomintang government then named it Lingsen Road after Lin Sen, the former President of the Republic of China, who had died in 1943, and the Communist government, which took Shanghai in 1949, gave it its present name a year later.

East Huaihai Road was built between 1874 and 1898 as Rue Ningpo, just north of the moat of the old city wall, on land of the Siming Gongsuo, an association of families from Ningbo that had premises and a graveyard there from 1797. French attempts to take the land and move the graves led to violent confrontations in 1874 and 1898, and the road was named after Ningbo as part of the settlement. The western section was built by the Shanghai Municipal Council as Jordan Road and lined with apartment buildings and houses of Chinese and foreign elites.

Middle Huaihai Road is one of the two major shopping streets of central Shanghai with Nanjing Road, lined with boutiques, department stores, malls, hotels and restaurants. Line 1 of the Shanghai Metro runs beneath it.
huallaga-river: The Huallaga is a tributary of the Marañón, part of the Amazon Basin, and rises on the slopes of the Andes in central Peru. It joins the Marañón before that river reaches the Ucayali to form the Amazon. Its main tributaries are the Monzón, Mayo, Biabo, Abiseo and Tocache rivers, and coca is grown in most of their valleys, which are exposed to periodic floods. Older names include Guallaga and Rio de los Motilones. Over nearly its whole length it is an impetuous torrent in a succession of gorges, with forty-two rapids, called pongos, and it crosses the Andes through the Pongo de Aguirre gorge. From there, 230 km from the Amazon, larger river boats can ascend to Yurimaguas in Loreto.

The river is divided loosely into three sections: the Upper Huallaga from the source to Tocache, the central Huallaga from Tocache or Juanjuí to Chazuta, and the lower Huallaga from Chazuta to Yurimaguas. Between the Huallaga and the Ucayali lies the Pampa del Sacramento, a level region of alluvial land under dense forest about 480 km long and 40 to 100 km wide, first entered by Christian missionaries in 1726. Indigenous communities such as the Cocama-Cocamilla and Kichwa-Lamista still live there, with peasant farmers.

Since the 1980s the Upper Huallaga Valley has been the centre of Peru's coca growing and drug trafficking. The coca was flown to Colombia, where it was made into cocaine. On 27 August 1994 a Drug Enforcement Administration aircraft crashed into a mountain north of Puerto Pizana in bad weather during a counter-narcotics flight, killing its five occupants, and the accident brought the end of the US anti-drug Operation Snowcap. In 1966 the actor Eric Fleming drowned in the river while a film was shot on location.
The river and its banks suffer pollution from rubbish dumped in them. It supports a rich variety of wildlife and plants and is especially rich in amphibians, with eighteen species of frogs recorded.
huan-wen: Huan Wen was the son of Huan Yi, a commandery governor, and a descendant of the Eastern Han official Huan Rong. His father was killed in 328 resisting the rebellion of Su Jun, and in 329 Huan Wen avenged him by killing the sons of Jiang Bo, the subordinate who had helped his father's killer, an act that brought him great fame. He married Sima Xingnan, Princess Nankang, sister of Emperor Cheng, rose to govern Xu Province, and after the death of Yu Yi in 345 was made commander of the western provinces.

Late in 346 he set out against Cheng-Han, and after a counterattack nearly turned him back, a signal officer who beat the drums for attack instead of the gong for retreat carried the Jin troops to the gates of Chengdu; the emperor Li Shi surrendered. Huan forced the ouster of his rival Yin Hao and led northern campaigns: in 354 he reached the vicinity of Chang'an, capital of Former Qin, but withdrew for lack of food, and in 356 he defeated Yao Xiang and secured the Luoyang region.

His 369 campaign against Former Yan halted at Fangtou on the Yellow River. Murong Chui and Murong De trapped his retreating army and nearly annihilated it, and Former Qin forces dealt him another defeat. He blamed Yuan Zhen, who rebelled at Shouchun; Huan took the city in 371 and slaughtered Yuan's clan. To show his power he then spread rumours that Emperor Fei was impotent, had him deposed, and raised Sima Yu as Emperor Jianwen, killing many members of the Yin and Yu clans on false charges of treason.

Huan had long considered seizing the throne, but when the dying Emperor Jianwen summoned him in 372 he declined, apparently fearing a trap, and power at court passed to Xie An and Wang Tanzhi. He returned to his base at Gushu, fell ill, entrusted his affairs to his loyal brother Huan Chong, and died on 18 August 373. The Huan clan remained entrenched in Jin politics for decades, and after his son Huan Xuan briefly usurped the throne in 404 he was posthumously honoured as Emperor Xuanwu of Chu.
huan-xuan: Huan Xuan was the youngest son of Huan Wen, the paramount general of Jin, and Sima Xingnan, Princess of Nankang, a daughter of Emperor Ming of Jin. When Huan Wen died in 373, his brother Huan Chong detained the heir, Huan Xi, for plotting against him and declared that Huan Wen had wished the title to pass to Huan Xuan, who thus became Duke of Nan Commandery at the age of four.

Distrusted by the court, he received no post until 391. He bore a lasting grudge against Sima Daozi, Prince of Kuaiji, who had once remarked at a feast that Huan Wen had planned treason in old age. Resigning as governor of Yixing Commandery, he returned to his dukedom, where the people feared him more than they did Yin Zhongkan, governor of Jing Province.

After Emperor Xiaowu's death in 396, Sima Daozi ruled as regent for the developmentally disabled Emperor An. Huan Xuan encouraged the provincial governors' risings against the regent's favourites and commanded forward armies for Yin Zhongkan in 398. Around the new year 400, when floods had exhausted Yin's supplies, Huan attacked and killed both Yin and his ally Yang Quanqi, gaining control of two thirds of Jin territory.

When Sima Yuanxian declared him a renegade, the general Liu Laozhi changed sides and joined Huan, whose advance on Jiankang made the regent's forces collapse. Huan executed Sima Yuanxian, exiled Sima Daozi and stripped Liu Laozhi of his command; Liu tried to rebel, was deserted by his officers and killed himself. In power, Huan proved harsh with officials, eager to acquire paintings, calligraphy and houses, and unsteady, ordering and then cancelling a campaign against Later Qin. He had himself made Prince of Chu with the nine bestowments, the customary prelude to usurpation, before taking the throne.

As emperor he honoured his parents posthumously, began heavy palace building and was said to be unable to sleep for fear. A conspiracy of Liu Yu, He Wuji and Liu Yi rose at Jingkou and Guangling, and after minor defeats Huan fled west with Emperor An to Jiangling. Misled into heading for Yi Province, his fleet was scattered by the troops of its governor Mao Qu, and the officer Feng Qian beheaded him on 19 June 404. His five-year-old son Huan Sheng was executed, and his kinsmen were killed or fled within little more than a year.
huancavelica: Huancavelica, Wankawillka in Quechua, lies at about 3,676 metres in the western chain of the Andes. The surrounding area varies from 1,950 metres in the valleys to more than 5,000 metres on snow-covered summits, and the Mantaro and Pampas rivers shape its relief. The mountains hold metallic deposits, chiefly cinnabar, the ore of mercury, together with pyrite, arsenopyrite and realgar. At the time of the Spanish conquest the area was known as the Wankawillka region, or sacred stone.

The mercury deposits were disclosed by an Indian, Nahuincopa, to his master Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera. The Spanish Crown appropriated them in 1570 and operated them until Peruvian independence in 1821. The Viceroy of Peru, Francisco de Toledo, founded the city on 5 August 1572 under the name Villa Rica de Oropesa, after the Santa Bárbara mine near its site had become widely known. A miners' guild administered the mines from 1577 until 1782.

Huancavelica was the most prolific source of mercury in Spanish America. Mercury was needed to extract silver from the ores of Peru and Potosí by amalgamation, so essential that the royal fifth, the tax on precious metals, was levied on the basis of mercury consumption. The deposits were called the jewel of the crown, since they removed the need to ship mercury from Almadén. Most of the quicksilver was produced between 1571 and 1790, more than 1,400,000 flasks. A viceroy declared in 1648 that Potosí and Huancavelica were the two pillars supporting Peru and Spain, and that Spain could do without the silver of Potosí but not the mercury of Huancavelica.

Working the tunnels was extremely hard and mortality was high. Toledo revived and improved the pre-Columbian compulsory service of the mita to supply labour, and a mass for the dead was said each day before the miners went down. The collapse of the Marroquín working in 1786 killed over two hundred Indians. Production stopped from 1813 to 1835.

Huancavelica is the capital of the department of Huancavelica and had 49,570 inhabitants at the 2017 census, many of them Indigenous. Its colonial monuments include eight churches, the most important being the cathedral on the main square, and the former Santa Bárbara mine lies about three kilometres from the city. Centuries of mining have left mercury, lead and arsenic contamination in the surroundings. A 1977 recording of a wedding song sung by a young girl from the region was included on the Golden Record carried by the Voyager probes.
huancayo: Huancayo is the capital of the Junín Region and of Huancayo Province, in the Mantaro Valley, and is crossed by the Shullcas, Chilca and Mantaro rivers. Its name in Wanka Quechua is Wankayu, from wanka, stone, and the suffix -yuq, so that it means the place with a stone. An oral tradition of the city holds that an oval stone of considerable size once stood where the Huamanmarca square is now, though no trace of it survives.

The area was first inhabited by the Huanca people, who were drawn into the Wari Empire as it expanded northward from Ayacucho from about the sixth century. After the fall of that empire the Huancas defended their independence, but around 1460 the Inca ruler Pachacuti subdued them and annexed the region. The Huancas resisted, notably from the fortress of Watury, and Inca policy of introducing their own religion and language kept the area unsettled. The valley was valued for its fertility and lay on the Inca road north towards Cajamarca and Quito.

The Huancas later became allies of the Spanish, taking part in the capture of Cusco and in battles against the Incas of Vilcabamba. After the Spanish arrival in 1534 Huancayo was overshadowed by Jauja, a provisional capital of Peru, until Lima took that role. In 1570 the viceroy Francisco de Toledo made the site the centre of his encomienda, and the town was founded on 1 June 1572 as Santísima Trinidad de Huancayo by the conquistador Jerónimo de Silva. Its cathedral was begun in 1799 and finished in 1831.

The city was freed during the war of independence on 20 November 1820. Simón Bolívar came to the valley in August 1824 and rewarded patriot soldiers, and he expelled the Franciscan friars of the convent of Ocopa, whom he considered recalcitrant royalists. The decree ending slavery in Peru was made law at Huancayo in 1854, and a statue in the Plaza Constitución commemorates it.

The city's growth began with the railway from Callao to La Oroya, built in 1908 and extended from Lima to Huancayo in the early 1930s. Further growth came from migration, partly of people who left the highlands during the violence of the 1980s. Huancayo has a population of over 500,000 and is regarded as the economic and social centre of central Peru. It is known for its crafts and for the festivals of the surrounding towns, and as it has expanded rapidly, few colonial buildings remain.
huang-chao: Huang Chao came from Yuanqu, in the present-day Cao County of Heze, Shandong, and his birth date is not known. His family had been salt privateers for generations, since the state had monopolised the salt trade after the An Lushan Rebellion, and the Huang family became wealthy from smuggling. He was said to be capable in swordsmanship, riding and archery and somewhat capable in writing and rhetoric. He took in desperate men with his wealth, and they served under him.

He sat the imperial examinations repeatedly without passing them and then resolved to rebel against Tang rule. The dynasty had passed its golden age. The power of the provincial military governors, the jiedushi, had grown, and impoverished farmers, tax-burdened landowners, merchants and large salt-smuggling operations formed the base of the rebellions of the mid-ninth century.

Huang Chao joined the rebellion of Wang Xianzhi against the Tang in the mid-870s. After he split with Wang, his army turned south and conquered Guangzhou. In 881 his troops captured the capital, Chang'an, and forced Emperor Xizong to flee. Huang moved into the palace and declared himself emperor of a new state of Qi, making his wife, Lady Cao, empress and Shang Rang among others chancellors.

He at first tried to take over the Tang imperial mandate. Officials of the fourth rank or lower were kept in office if they registered their submission, and those of the third rank or above were removed. Tang officials who would not submit were executed en masse. Several Tang generals submitted to him, but each eventually declared loyalty to the Tang again.

In spring 883 Li Keyong, a Shatuo general, and other Tang generals defeated a Qi force of 150,000 men commanded by Shang Rang. In summer 883 Li Keyong entered Chang'an, and Huang abandoned the city and fled east. Defeated again, including by his former subordinates Zhu Wen and Shang Rang, who had gone over to the Tang, he withdrew into the Langhu Valley. On 13 July 884 his nephew Lin Yan was reported to have killed him, though the reports are inconclusive and an alternative account in the New Book of Tang says that he killed himself. Some have suggested that the heads brought to the Tang were a decoy, and legends of the following centuries said he became a Buddhist monk.
Huang Chao also wrote poetry. One of his lines, "The capital's full of golden armored soldiers", later gave its name to the Chinese title of the 2006 film Curse of the Golden Flower.
huang-chao-rebellion: Late in the Xiantong era of Emperor Yizong (860–874), severe droughts and floods brought famine, yet the government raised taxes instead of granting relief, and survivors formed bands to resist Tang rule. In 874 Wang Xianzhi, like Huang Chao a salt privateer, raised an army at Changyuan with Shang Junzhang, and Huang joined him with several thousand men. In 876 the court offered Wang an imperial commission; Huang, left out, struck him on the head, and the rebel army split into two groups.

After Wang was killed in 878, Huang took the title Chongtian Dajiangjun, Generalissimo Who Charges to the Heavens, and twice refused offers of a guard command. He crossed the Yangzi, marched south and in the autumn of 879 took Guangzhou after a one-day siege. Arab sources claim that the foreign Muslim, Zoroastrian, Jewish and Christian victims there numbered tens of thousands, though Chinese sources do not mention the event. Disease then struck his army, and he turned north.

In 880 he defeated and killed the Tang general Zhang Lin, crossed the Yangtze River north at Caishi and, after a mutiny broke up the imperial defence on the Yin River, advanced with 150,000 men. Luoyang and Tong Pass fell, and on 8 January 881 Emperor Xizong fled towards Chengdu. Huang entered Chang'an, ordered the slaughter of the Tang imperial clan and proclaimed himself emperor of a new state of Qi.

Tang forces briefly retook the capital in 881, and on his return Huang massacred residents who had aided them; famine later drove both sides to cannibalism. His general Zhu Wen went over to the Tang in 882, and in 883 the Shatuo general Li Keyong drove Huang from Chang'an. After a siege of nearly 300 days at Chen Prefecture and a defeat at Wangman Crossing his army was destroyed, and on 13 July 884 his nephew Lin Yan killed him, although the New Book of Tang says he took his own life.

The Tang realm broke into territories held by warlords and fell in 907, when Zhu Wen usurped the throne. Older scholarship held that the rebellion destroyed the aristocratic families; recent studies argue that their privileges had been eroding since the late 7th century, and that many clans survived by moving south, while Luoyang saw no massacre.
huang-daopo: Huang was her family name; Daopo was an honorific she received later in life. She came from a poor family and ran away from home at the age of ten, unable to bear the constant ill-treatment she received after being sold into marriage. She followed the Huangpu River from Songjiang and boarded a ship for the port of Yazhou on Hainan, where she learnt spinning and weaving from the Li people.

Back in Songjiang she taught local women and also made clothing, fine fabrics and weaving machinery, including fluffing machines and crushers. She produced mixed cotton fabrics, coloured fabrics and fabrics with mixed warp and weft fibres. For ginning she improved a machine called the Jiaoche, so that seeds could be taken out of the cotton easily; before this, people in her hometown had peeled the cottonseed by hand, slowly and with difficulty.

In stretching, she increased the vibration of the slingshot on the cotton, making it fluffier and easier to spin. She changed the structure of the spinning wheel so that the yarn snapped less often, and reworked old weaving tools, adding pick-weaving and brocading. The method she spread, known as Wunijing Technology and based on the cotton techniques of the Li, had three parts: processing, yarn spinning and weaving. It raised the efficiency and quality of cotton cloth and laid a foundation for the textile culture of the Yangtze River Delta.

With cotton spinning for home weaving, women in the region could earn more, and their standing in marriage and the family rose. In folklore the sixth day of the fourth lunar month is her birthday, also called the birthday of cotton. On 20 November 1980 the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications issued a set of four stamps honouring scientists with Huang Daopo as the fourth, the first ancient woman scientist shown on a stamp. The People's Bank of China placed her on a commemorative coin in 1989.

The Huang Daopo Memorial Hall, at the Shanghai Botanical Garden in the Xuhui district, opened in 2003 with a statue of her 2.2 metres high in its courtyard. A crater on Venus is named after her. Her life has been told in a stage play directed by Gao Du of the Beijing Dance Academy and in the television series A Weaver on the Horizon.
huang-jinrong: Huang Jinrong was born in Suzhou on 10 May 1868 and moved to Shanghai at the age of five, when his father opened a teahouse there. A bad case of smallpox earned him the nickname Pockmarked. He was apprenticed in a picture-framing shop near the City God Temple and later worked in his father's teahouse, where he made connections among its criminal and hustling customers. Through his father's ties to the constabulary he entered the French Concession police in 1892, at the age of 24.

Huang soon became one of the leading detectives of the French Concession, solving many cases with the help of his teahouse contacts. After a quarrel with his French superior he briefly retired to Suzhou, but was brought back for his skill as a sleuth. At the same time he organised drug trafficking and gambling dens and granted favours to criminals; each day he held court to decide whether a felon should be handed to the police. His wife Lin Guisheng, whom he married in 1900, helped manage his opium business, and he put Du Yuesheng in charge of some of his opium dens.

With Du Yuesheng and Zhang Xiaolin he became one of the three great bosses of the Green Gang, and crime in the concession grew under his protection. He was finally dismissed after publicly beating the son of the Shanghai warlord Lu Yongxiang. Arrested by the Shanghai Garrison, he was released only after Du and Zhang negotiated and paid for his freedom. He remained a gang boss and formally joined the Green Gang in 1927, the year he and Du worked with Chiang Kai-shek to suppress the communist movement in Shanghai.

Huang stayed in Shanghai through the Japanese occupation and the communist takeover. During the Chinese Communist Party's Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries he was made an example, and he died of illness on 20 June 1953, aged 85. Film and television have portrayed him, as the model for characters in The Last Tycoon of 2012 and Lord of Shanghai of 2015, and in his own name in the film 1921.
huangchuan-county: Huangchuan lies in the centre of Xinyang City, straddling the Huang River, a tributary of the Huai River. The Huang sounds the same as the Yellow River but is written with different characters, and local people call it the Little Huang River. To the north the county borders the Huai, which is regarded as part of the dividing line between North China and South China. The annual mean temperature is 15.3 °C and precipitation averages 1,039 millimetres.

A place called Huang is mentioned briefly in the Bamboo Annals during the reign of King Xiang. Under the Zhou dynasty a state of Huang appears again in texts and archaeological records, with its capital at Huangchuan, and it is held to be the origin of the Chinese surname Huang. The remains of its capital were found at Longgu, a township six kilometres northwest of the urban area.

From the Qin dynasty onwards the area was usually governed as a zhou, a commandery or a county, under names that included Yiyang, Dingcheng and Guangzhou. According to the Brief Sketch of North Parts of Ming Dynasty by Ji Liuqi, which records the passage from the Ming to the Qing, the town, then called Guangzhou, was devastated and its people massacred by the peasant army. Most later residents descend from migrants from Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong who settled there in the Kangxi era of the Qing dynasty. The present name dates from 1913.

Huangchuan County has 4 subdistricts, 9 towns and 8 townships, the result of a reorganisation in 2005. China National Highway 106, China National Highway 312 and the Shanghai–Xi'an and Daqing–Guangzhou expressways pass through it, and in 2009 a project was launched to integrate it with neighbouring Guangshan County.
huanggang: Huanggang is a prefecture-level city in the east of Hubei province, north of the middle reaches of the Yangtze River and south of the Dabie Mountains. It is named after Mount Huanggang and borders Henan to the north, Anhui to the east and Jiangxi to the south. Its administrative area covers 17,453 square kilometres and held 5,882,719 people at the census of 2020, 456,862 of them in the Huangzhou urban district. It administers twelve county-level divisions.

In 845 BCE Marquis Wen of Huang, Huang Meng, moved the capital of the State of Huang from Yicheng to Huangchuan, in present-day Henan. His descendants ruled until 648 BCE, when the State of Chu destroyed Huang. The Marquis of Huang fled to the state of Qi, and the people of Huang were forced to move to Chu. They settled in what is now Hubei, in the area that became Jiangxia Prefecture under the Han dynasty, and many places in the region, among them Huanggang, Huangpi, Huangmei, Huangshi and Huangzhou, took their names from Huang.

In the Jin period, Later Zhao forces inflicted great damage on Jin cities and bases north of the Yangtze, during the reign of Emperor Cheng of Jin, and captured Zhucheng, in modern Huanggang. The area has a history of at least 2,000 years.

Cultural sites include the Buddhist Ancestral Hall of Sakyamuni at Doufang Mountain, Wuzu Temple with its Changchun Nunnery, and Dongpo Red Cliff. Huanggang Normal University is in the city. The prefecture is the birthplace of many scholars and inventors, among them Bi Sheng, the inventor of movable type printing, Li Shizhen, author of the Compendium of Materia Medica, the philosophers Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi of the Song dynasty, and Dayi Daoxin and Daman Hongren, the fourth and fifth patriarchs of Chan Buddhism. The economy includes herbal medicine, manufacturing, agriculture and tourism. Local products include the Qichun herbal medicine, Huangmei embroidery and Yingshan green tea. The Beijing-Kowloon railway passes through the prefecture.
huascar: Huáscar was a son of the Sapa Inca Huayna Capac. The origin of his name is uncertain. One story says it came from a huge gold chain made for his birth, since huasca is Quechua for chain, and another that it comes from his birthplace, Huascarpata. His father and his brother Ninan Cuyochi both died of smallpox in the same year while campaigning near Quito, and Huáscar became Sapa Inca in 1527.

The events that brought about his succession are unclear. The Spanish chroniclers wrote down accounts that came from the winners of the civil war that followed, and their versions conflict. Huayna Capac had named the infant Ninan Cuyochi as his first heir, but sources differ on whether the boy died first, was ruled out by an unfavourable divination, or was simply forgotten when the dying ruler was asked to confirm his nomination. The second choice is also disputed. Huayna Capac may have named Atahualpa, who then refused, or Huáscar himself, or the nobles may have put Huáscar forward.

The dispute produced a civil war, fought from 1529 to 1532, between Huáscar, made ruler by a faction based in Cuzco, and his half-brother Atahualpa, backed by leaders based in the north with Huayna Capac's army. The chronicler Juan de Betanzos describes Huáscar as a tyrant who took his lords' wives and seized both the lands of the previous Incas and the lands of the Sun, which supported the cults of dead rulers and of the Sun. His account is biased, since the wife on whose testimony it largely rests had earlier been married to Atahualpa. He reports armies of 60,000 men on each side, led for Atahualpa by his commander Quizquiz.

Huáscar was defeated in the Battle of Chimborazo and the Battle of Quipaipán and was taken prisoner, and Atahualpa's generals Quizquiz and Chalcuchímac occupied Cuzco. Atahualpa had the upper hand when the conquistador Francisco Pizarro arrived. The civil war had depleted the Inca armies and exposed their disunity, shown by the celebrations in the province of Cuzco, loyal to Huáscar, at Atahualpa's capture. After Pizarro seized Atahualpa, Atahualpa had Huáscar killed, so that Huáscar could not offer the Spanish a larger ransom in gold than his own.
huastec-people: The Huastec, or Téenek, a name contracted from Te' Inik, meaning people from here, live in the Huasteca, which covers parts of Hidalgo, Veracruz, San Luis Potosí and Tamaulipas along the Pánuco River and the Gulf coast. Their language descends from Proto-Mayan, and proto-Huastecan was the first language to split from Mayan proper. The other language to arise from it was Chicomuceltec, once spoken near Comitán in Chiapas and now extinct. Linguists have estimated that the split took place between 2200 and 1200 BCE, with 2000 BCE a reasonable date, and the word for writing is different in proto-Huastec and in the other Maya languages.

According to this reconstruction, the Huastecs moved north from the Maya homeland in the highlands of Guatemala, probably along the Usumacinta River, and picked up loan words from Mixe-Zoque, the language most scholars link to the Olmec. They are thought to have been pushed up the Gulf coast by the early Olmecs of San Lorenzo, and they reached the Huasteca between 1500 and 900 BCE. Richard Stockton MacNeish found Middle Formative ceramics and figurines at the Pánuco River sites in 1954 that resemble objects from the Maya site of Uaxactun.

Archaeological remains date the Huastec civilization to about the 10th century BCE, and its most productive period is usually placed in the Postclassic, between the fall of Teotihuacan and the rise of the Aztec Empire. The Huastecs built temples on step pyramids, carved free-standing sculpture and made elaborately painted pottery, and other Mesoamerican peoples admired their music. Their art drew on the coast and made much use of shell: gorgets, fan headdresses, heads and figures of hunchbacked humans. Around 1450 Aztec armies under Moctezuma I defeated them. They then paid tribute to the Aztec Empire but kept substantial local self-government.

The Spanish Empire conquered the Huastecs between 1519 and the 1530s, and many were sold as slaves in the Caribbean. The friar Andrés de Olmos wrote the first grammatical and lexical description of the Huastec language available to Europeans. Their population, perhaps as much as half a million when the Spanish arrived in 1529, was probably much higher than it is today.

About 66,000 people speak Huastec today, two thirds of them in San Luis Potosí and one third in Veracruz. The Huasteca also holds speakers of Nahuatl and Pame. In the late 19th century Huastec chicle-tappers and lumbermen were taken to Campeche to work similar forests there, in effect reuniting them with the Yucatán Maya for the first time in millennia.
huasteca: The region is defined by the lands the Huastecs dominated at their height, and both its extent and its subdivisions are disputed. Geographically it runs from the Sierra Madre Oriental to the Gulf of Mexico, bounded by the Sierra de Tamaulipas in the north and the Cazones River in the south, and covers about 32,000 km², including a very small part of Guanajuato. The Veracruz section, the most extensive, runs from the Cazones to the Tamesí river, and its main city is the port of Tuxpan.

The Huasteca is lowland country with a hot and mostly humid climate, annual temperatures generally between 22 and 26 °C and between 800 and 1600 mm of rain a year, brought by moisture from the Gulf. Drought strikes three years in every ten, and hail and hurricanes come every year.

The name comes from the Nahuatl Cuextecah. The Huastecs, a Mayan people whose language probably separated about 3,000 years ago, were the northernmost Mesoamerican group on the Gulf coast, and their contact with the Chichimeca brought Aridoamerican influences into their culture. They became culturally dominant in the region between 750 and 800 CE, after El Tajín waned, and until the 15th century extended their territory from the Tuxpan River to Tamiahua and west into the Sierra Madre Oriental.

Notable settlements included El Tamuín, Yahualica, Huejutla, Tzicóac, Tuxpan, Temapache, Pánuco and Tanhuijo. Farmers grew corn, beans, squash, chili peppers and tubers such as yucca, camotes and jicamas, but the gathering of wild roots and fruit, and fishing, played a larger part than usual, and salt was produced at Chila Lake. The region's sculpture is distinct, with pieces such as the Adolescente de Tamuín and the goddess Tlazolteotl.

The region has six indigenous ethnic groups and over 250,000 speakers of indigenous languages, about 70 percent of them speaking Nahuatl and 20 percent Huastec; the Huastecs themselves now occupy only a strip of it. Its shared culture includes the festival of Xantolo and the Huapango or Son Huasteco, played on a violin, a jarana huasteca and a quinta huapanguera, with coplas sung in falsetto.
huayna-capac: Huayna Capac was the eleventh Sapa Inca of Tawantinsuyu, the son and successor of Túpac Inca Yupanqui, who ruled from 1471 to 1493 and had extended Inca rule north into present-day Ecuador. The exact place and date of his birth are unknown; he was raised in Cuzco, but may have been born in 1468 in Tumebamba, modern Cuenca, and spent part of his childhood there.

Huayna Capac's first wife was his full sister Coya Cusirimay, who bore no male heirs. He sired more than 50 legitimate sons and about 200 illegitimate children with other women, and took another sister, Araua Ocllo, as royal wife; their son Thupaq Kusi Wallpa became known as Huáscar. His other sons included Ninan Cuyuchi, the crown prince, and Atahualpa.

The empire reached its fullest extent under Huayna Capac, stretching over much of what is now Bolivia, Peru, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador and south-western Colombia, with subjects of more than two hundred ethnic groups. He pushed the southern frontier into what is now Chile and Argentina and tried to annex lands in the north. According to the Ecuadorian priest Juan de Velasco he absorbed the kingdom of Quito by marrying its queen, Paccha Duchicela. Fond of Ecuador, he spent most of his time there, founded cities such as Atuntaqui and rebuilt Quito as a second capital beside Cusco.

He developed Cochabamba, in what is now Bolivia, as an agricultural and administrative centre with more than two thousand silos for maize, greatly expanded the road network and had storehouses built along it so that food could be sent quickly to people in danger of starvation. He knew of the Spanish arrival off the coast of his empire as early as 1515.

Huayna Capac died in 1527. He had contracted a fever while campaigning in present-day Colombia, though some historians dispute this, and the fever may have been a European disease such as measles or smallpox. Other historians doubt that smallpox was the cause, since the earliest accounts are vague or disagree and none of the descriptions of his mummy mentions pockmarks. His eldest son Ninan Cuyochi also died, and the war between Huáscar and Atahualpa over the succession followed. Atahualpa won it.

Huayna Capac's mummy was kept in his palace in Cusco, and was discovered by the Spanish in 1559. Taken to Lima with the mummies of ten other Inca rulers, it was displayed in the San Andrés Hospital and eventually buried or destroyed. A search beneath the hospital in 2001 found only an empty crypt.
hubal: Hubal was a god worshipped in pre-Islamic Arabia, notably by the Quraysh at the Kaaba in Mecca. His icon was a human figure believed to control divination. According to Hisham Ibn al-Kalbi's Book of Idols the image was shaped like a human, with the right hand broken off and replaced by a golden hand, and made of red agate; the early Islamic commentator al-Azraqi gave its material as cornelian pearl. Karen Armstrong writes that the sanctuary was dedicated to Hubal, who was worshipped as the chief of the 360 idols in the Kaaba, which probably represented the days of the year.

Seven arrows were placed before the image and cast for divination in cases of death, virginity and marriage, and the direction in which they pointed answered the questions asked. Al-Azraqi adds that the image had a vault for sacrifice, with an offering of a hundred camels. In a tale recorded by Ibn al-Kalbi, Muhammad's grandfather Abdul Mutallib vowed to sacrifice one of his ten children and consulted the arrows, which pointed to his son Abd-Allah, the future father of Muhammad; the son was saved when 100 camels were sacrificed in his place.

After the Quraysh were defeated at the Battle of Badr, their leader Abu Sufyan ibn Harb is said to have called on Hubal for support in the next battle, saying "Show your superiority, Hubal". When Muhammad conquered Mecca in 630, he broke the statue of Hubal along with the other 360 images and dedicated the Kaaba to Allah.

The name may derive from Baal, possibly from an Aramaic form meaning "he is Baal", and both were depicted with a missing or broken right hand. Ibn al-Kalbi says the image was first set up by Khuzayma ibn Mudrika, while Ibn Ishaq holds that Amr ibn Luhayy, a leader of the Khuza'a tribe, put it in the Kaaba; the Quraysh later became protectors of the holy place in place of the Khuza'a. Al-Azraqi says the image was brought from Hit in Mesopotamia.

Outside South Arabia the name appears only once, in a Nabataean inscription beside the gods Dushara and Manawatu. Evidence is so slight that his role is hard to establish: scholars have called him a warrior and rain god, and the older view that he was a lunar deity has been rejected.
hubei: Hubei borders Henan to the north, Anhui and Jiangxi to the east, Hunan to the south, and Chongqing and Shaanxi to the west. Its name means 'north of the lake', referring to Dongting Lake. The Jianghan Plain takes up most of central and southern Hubei, while the west is mountainous. The Yangtze enters from the west through the Three Gorges and the Han River from the northwest, and the two meet at the centre of Wuhan. Thousands of lakes give the province the name Province of Lakes.

The region was home to sophisticated Neolithic cultures. By the Spring and Autumn period it formed part of the powerful State of Chu, which blended northern and southern culture and controlled much of the middle and lower Yangtze. In the Warring States period Chu lost land to Qin, and in 278 BCE it lost its heartland, which corresponds to modern Hubei. The Han dynasty set up the province of Jingzhou in what is now Hubei and Hunan. After the death of the warlord Liu Biao in 208, Liu Bei and Sun Quan drove Cao Cao out of Jingzhou at the Battle of Red Cliffs, and the Wu kingdom then held it for decades.

The Song reunified the region in 982, the Mongols conquered it in 1279 and created the province of Huguang, and the Qing split it into Hubei and Hunan after 1644. Zhang Zhidong, Viceroy of Huguang from 1889 to 1907, made Wuhan a prosperous centre of commerce and industry. The Wuchang Uprising of 1911 in Wuhan began the Xinhai Revolution that overthrew the Qing dynasty. In 1927 Wuhan became the seat of a left-wing Kuomintang government led by Wang Jingwei, and in the Second World War Japan occupied eastern Hubei.

The province suffered severely from the Yangtze floods of 1954, and large dams followed: the Gezhouba Dam near Yichang was built from 1970 to 1988, and work on the Three Gorges Dam began in 1993. Authorities resettled millions of people from western Hubei to make way for it.

Hubei is a province of Central China with its capital at Wuhan, a major political, cultural and economic hub. The Huazhong University of Science and Technology and Wuhan University are among its institutions. The Wudang Mountains building complex has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994, and the Hubei Provincial Museum in Wuhan is regarded as one of the best places to learn about the ancient state of Chu.
hubert-lyautey: Hubert Lyautey was born in Nancy on 17 November 1854, the son of a prosperous engineer and the grandson of a highly decorated Napoleonic general. His mother, a Norman aristocrat, passed on monarchism, patriotism, Catholicism and a belief in the importance of elites. He entered the military academy of Saint-Cyr in 1873. A holiday in Algeria in 1878 left him impressed by the Maghreb and by Islam, and he chose a career in the colonies over a more prestigious posting in France.

Lyautey served under Joseph Gallieni in Indochina from 1894 and in Madagascar from 1897 to 1902, where in 1900 he became Governor of Southern Madagascar. Posted to the Oran district in 1903, he advanced into Morocco, in disobedience of the Minister of War, and later occupied Oujda. From 28 April 1912 to 25 August 1925 he was Resident-General of French Morocco, after the Convention of Fez established the protectorate. He was elected to the Académie Française in 1912.

His method followed Gallieni's tache d'huile, the expansion of pacified areas followed by markets, schools and medical centres, together with a policy of dealing with each tribe separately. In Morocco he was publicly deferential to the sultan, opposed Christian proselytising and the settlement of French migrants, and invited the planner Henri Prost to design plans for the major cities. In 1917 he was Minister of War for three months, until he resigned after being shouted down in the Chamber on 15 March. He became a Marshal of France in 1921 and resigned in 1925, feeling slighted that Philippe Pétain had been appointed to put down Abd-el-Krim's rebellion in the Rif.

Lyautey was commissioner of the Paris Colonial Exposition of 1931. In his last years he admired Benito Mussolini and was associated with the far-right Croix de Feu. He died at Thorey-Lyautey on 27 July 1934. His remains were placed in a mausoleum in Rabat in 1935, a monument that nationalist and Muslim leaders criticised. After Moroccan independence they were taken to France in April 1961 and interred in Les Invalides. His writings influenced later counterinsurgency theory through David Galula.
hubert-maga: Hubert Maga was born in 1916 to a peasant family in Parakou, in northern Dahomey. His Bariba mother and Voltaic father raised him in the Islamic faith, and in his twenties he converted to Roman Catholicism. He studied at Parakou, Bohicon, Abomey and Porto-Novo and at the Ponty Normal School in Dakar, where he became a friend of Hamani Diori, the future president of Niger. He taught at Natitingou, became director of the school in 1945 and led the Teachers' Union of Dahomey.

Maga was elected to the Dahomey General Council in 1947 and left teaching. He founded a northern party, which later merged into the Dahomey Democratic Rally. His rise came amid intense regionalism, which divided Dahomey into three zones led by Maga in the north, Sourou Migan Apithy in the southeast and Justin Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin in the southwest. He was elected to the French National Assembly in 1951 and was premier of Dahomey from 1959 to 1960.

Maga took the presidency when Dahomey became independent on 1 August 1960 and was officially elected on 11 December. A constitution modelled on that of the French Fifth Republic was adopted on 25 November. In 1961 he closed the opposition newspaper Dahomey-Matin and dissolved Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin's party, and a plot against him in May was led by Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin. The economy faltered, and in January 1962 he launched a four-year plan to raise agricultural output by putting young people to work on the land.

In October 1963 demonstrations began in Porto-Novo over the release of a deputy accused of poisoning an official, and spread to Cotonou, where trade unionists joined and criticised what they called his extravagance. The army chief of staff, Christophe Soglo, took control and forced Maga to resign.

Maga was found guilty of corruption and placed under house arrest, was released in March 1965 and went into exile in Togo and then Paris. He won the election of 28 March 1970 with 252,551 votes and led the three-man Presidential Council for its first two years. When Mathieu Kérékou seized power on 26 October 1972, Maga and the other councillors were imprisoned until 1981. He took part in the National Conference of 1990 and died of a heart attack in Cotonou on 8 May 2000. A hospital in the city bears his name.
hubert-murray: Sir John Hubert Plunkett Murray was born in Sydney on 29 December 1861, the son of the Irish-born Terence Aubrey Murray and his second wife, Agnes Ann Edwards, and was named after his father's friend John Hubert Plunkett. His brother Gilbert Murray became Professor of Greek at Oxford. Hubert was school captain of Sydney Grammar School in 1877, then went to England, where Brighton College expelled him for punching a teacher, and studied at Magdalen College, Oxford. A tall, powerful man, he played rugby for Harlequins and won the English amateur heavyweight boxing title.

Called to the bar at the Inner Temple in 1885, he returned to New South Wales to practise law in Sydney and in 1892 became a legal draftsman for the colony's parliament, work he called living death in Macquarie Street. He helped form the New South Wales Irish Rifles, a volunteer reserve unit, and became its commanding officer in 1898. In 1900 he volunteered for the Second Boer War despite misgivings, commanded New South Wales troops in the advance on Pretoria and at the Battle of Diamond Hill, and disliked the burning of Boer farms his unit was ordered to carry out.

In 1904 he was appointed chief judicial officer of British New Guinea, which had come under Australian authority in 1902; the administration was so small that his duties reached across all three branches of government. He became Acting Administrator in 1907 and Lieutenant-Governor in 1908. He wrote widely on the territory and its peoples, from Papua, or British New Guinea in 1912 to papers on native labour, indirect rule and the population problem. He was knighted as a Knight Commander of the Order of Saint Michael and Saint George in 1925.

Murray died at Samarai on 27 February 1940 and was succeeded as administrator by his nephew Hubert Leonard Murray, Official Secretary since 1916. In Port Moresby the army's Murray Barracks, a primary school, the Hubert Murray Stadium and the main highway bear his name. The more than 3,000 objects he collected for the territory between 1907 and 1933 form the Official Papuan Collection of the National Museum of Australia.
huchuquan: Huchuquan was a younger brother of Yufuluo, the Southern Xiongnu chanyu whose family had been ousted from their domain by rebels among their own people. Yufuluo had come into conflict with the warlord Cao Cao but appears to have surrendered to him shortly before his death in 195. Huchuquan then succeeded him as chanyu, a reign that ran from the late Eastern Han dynasty into the Three Kingdoms period of China, but at first he too remained in exile, around Hedong Commandery.

Soon after his accession his uncle Qubei led their forces to help Emperor Xian of Han escape from Chang'an to Luoyang, where Cao Cao received the emperor. Qubei later helped escort the emperor to Cao Cao's base at Xuchang. In 202 Huchuquan rebelled and allied himself with Yuan Shang, but after Cao Cao's officer Zhong Yao defeated him he surrendered.

In 206 Gao Gan, the warlord of Bing Province, close to defeat by Cao Cao, came in person to ask Huchuquan for help. He refused, and Gao Gan was later killed while fleeing towards Jing Province. In 216 Huchuquan went to the imperial court to pay homage to Emperor Xian. He was given an official rank and kept at Ye as an honoured prisoner.

While Huchuquan stayed at Ye, Cao Cao rearranged what remained of the Southern Xiongnu into the Five Divisions and settled them around Taiyuan Commandery under the supervision of Qubei. Huchuquan kept the title of chanyu, now only a nominal one, until his death, and no new chanyu was proclaimed after him. With him the line of Southern Xiongnu chanyus came to an end.
hudson-bay: Hudson Bay is a body of saltwater of about 1,230,000 square kilometres, about 1,370 kilometres long and 1,050 kilometres wide. It is shallow, with an average depth of about 100 metres, and lies north of Ontario, west of Quebec and south-east of Nunavut. Its southern arm is James Bay, and the Hudson Strait links it to the Labrador Sea. Its water is less salty than the ocean's, and it is largely frozen from mid-December to mid-June. The Eastern Cree call it Wînipekw or Wînipâkw, meaning muddy or brackish water.

The bay is named after Henry Hudson, an Englishman sailing for the Dutch East India Company, who explored it from 2 August 1610 on the Discovery. The ship was trapped in ice over the winter, and on 22 June 1611 the crew mutinied and left Hudson and others adrift in a small boat. Their fate is unknown. In 1668 the ship Nonsuch reached the bay and traded for beaver pelts, which led to the Hudson's Bay Company. In 1670 the English Crown granted it a charter and a trading monopoly over the drainage basin, known as Rupert's Land.

France contested the grant with several military expeditions but gave up its claim in the Treaty of Utrecht, signed on 11 April 1713. The company built forts and trading posts at the mouths of the major rivers, among them York Factory, Fort Severn and the Prince of Wales Fort, where Indigenous peoples brought furs. The monopoly ended in 1870, when the Deed of Surrender ceded Rupert's Land to Canada as part of the Northwest Territories. Churchill, Manitoba, became a deep-sea port for wheat exports in 1929.

The bay is politically entirely part of Nunavut, as are its islands. Its coast is very sparsely populated, with only about a dozen communities, many of them now almost wholly Cree and Inuit. Churchill holds the only deep-water port on the bay. The western shore is the Hudson Bay Lowlands, Canada's largest continuous peatland.
hudson-river: The Hudson rises at Henderson Lake in the Adirondack Mountains, though the nearby Lake Tear of the Clouds is more commonly named as its source. It flows south largely through eastern New York to New York Bay and the Atlantic, and marks the border between New York and New Jersey. The lower half is a tidal estuary occupying the Hudson Fjord, an inlet carved by glaciers, and the tide reaches as far north as the Federal Dam at Troy.

Before Europeans arrived the river ran through the homelands of the Munsee Lenape, the Mohican and the Mohawk. The Mohicans called it Mahicannittuk, the river that flows two ways, a name that refers to its tides. Giovanni da Verrazzano, sailing for Francis I of France, entered New York Harbor in 1524 but left without sailing up the river. Henry Hudson, an Englishman employed by the Dutch East India Company, explored it in 1609 and gave it his name. The Dutch called it the North River, and it formed the spine of the colony of New Netherland. As the gateway to the interior of America, it was the subject of years of competition between the English and the Dutch.

In the American Revolutionary War the British saw that the river would let their navy control the water route from Montreal to New York City. General John Burgoyne planned the Saratoga campaign to control it and cut New England off from the other colonies, and many battles were fought along it. The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, linked Albany on the Hudson to Buffalo on Lake Erie, joining New York to the Great Lakes and becoming a route for western settlers. The valley inspired Washington Irving and the Hudson River School of landscape painting.

The river is navigable by large steamers up to Troy and by ocean-going vessels to the Port of Albany. A 30-mile stretch on the east bank is the Hudson River Historic District, a National Historic Landmark, and the river was designated an American Heritage River in 1997. Landmarks along it include the home and presidential library of Franklin D. Roosevelt and the United States Military Academy. Industrial contamination grew sharply in the mid-twentieth century, but water quality has improved since the Clean Water Act of 1972.
hudson-valley: The valley runs from the Capital District around Albany and Troy south to Yonkers in Westchester County, cutting through Triassic sandstones in the south and far older Precambrian gneiss in the north. In the Hudson Highlands the river enters a fjord cut in earlier ice ages, and near the Tappan Zee its west bank rises in diabase cliffs 400 to 800 feet high. Before European settlers arrived, the Lenape lived along the lower river, the Wappingers from Manhattan Island up to Poughkeepsie, and the Mahicans in the north, with their capital near present-day Albany.

In 1609 the Dutch East India Company financed the English navigator Henry Hudson's search for the Northwest Passage, and he sailed up the river as far as present-day Troy before concluding that no strait lay there. Voyages by Adriaen Block between 1611 and 1614 showed that the fur trade would pay, and the Dutch founded three trading posts along the river: New Amsterdam, Wiltwyck and Fort Orange, later New York City, Kingston and Albany. In 1664 the British took New Netherland, which became New York.

Under British rule the valley became an agricultural hub and the breadbasket of colonial America, its grain shipped down to New York City. On the east bank, landlords let land to tenants who were often kept at a subsistence level, while smaller farms lay west of the river. In the Revolutionary War the British plan of General John Burgoyne aimed to control the water route from Montreal to New York City and cut off New England, and many battles were fought along the river.

In 1807 the North River Steamboat, later known as Clermont, became the first commercially successful steamboat, carrying passengers between New York City and Albany. The Erie Canal opened the valley to the trade of the Midwest, hundreds of factories rose in towns such as Poughkeepsie, Newburgh and Kingston, and by the end of the 19th century 130 brickyards employing 8,000 people made the region the world's largest producer of bricks. Many industrial towns declined in the mid-20th century.

The valley is divided into the Lower, Mid- and Upper Hudson, and the Hudson River Valley National Heritage Area promotes its historic, natural and cultural sites in 11 counties. It is one of the oldest wine-growing regions in the United States, with its first vineyards planted in 1677 at present-day New Paltz, and orchards are common in Orange, Ulster, Dutchess and Columbia counties.
hudsons-bay-company: For much of the 17th century the French colonists of New France held a de facto monopoly of the North American fur trade. Two French traders, Pierre-Esprit Radisson and his brother-in-law Médard des Groseilliers, learned from the Cree that the best fur country lay north and west of Lake Superior, with a frozen sea still further north. They sought French backing for a post on what they took to be Hudson Bay, but the French governor refused permission. They went to the upper Great Lakes in 1659 anyway and returned to Montreal with valuable furs, but French authorities arrested them for trading without a licence and confiscated the furs.

The royal charter of 2 May 1670, issued by Charles II, gave the company the right of sole trade and commerce over Rupert's Land, a territory based on the Hudson Bay drainage basin. Prince Rupert of the Rhine was its first governor.

The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 required France to give up all claims to Hudson Bay. The main rival in the fur trade was the North West Company, and the competition led to the Pemmican War and the Battle of Seven Oaks on 19 June 1816. In 1821 the British government forced the two companies to merge. Of 175 posts, 52 were kept, and the territory reached the Arctic Ocean and, through the Columbia Department, the Pacific.

In 1849 Guillaume Sayer, a Métis trader, was tried for illegal trading before a jury of company officials and supporters while an armed crowd led by Louis Riel Sr. gathered outside. Sayer was found guilty but not punished, and the Métis cry of "Le commerce est libre!" marked the loosening of the company's control of the courts.

The company later turned to retail. Its first department store opened in Winnipeg in 1881, and the first of its grand original six was built in Calgary in 1913. In 1970 it moved its head office from London to Canada and was rechartered under Canadian law. It was the oldest commercial corporation in North America. Its stores closed in 2025 and the company was liquidated, and its royal charter and art collection were auctioned. Its archives were donated to the Archives of Manitoba in 1994.
hudud-al-alam: The Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam is a geography written in Persian by an anonymous author from Guzgan, in what is now northern Afghanistan. Vladimir Minorsky surmised that it might have been written by Šaʿyā bin Farīghūn. Its full title is Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam min al-Mashriq ilá l-Maghrib, the boundaries of the world from the East to the West. In his 1937 translation Minorsky explained that ḥudūd refers to the regions within definite boundaries into which the book divides the world, the author marking the frontiers of each with special care. The book was finished in 982 CE and dedicated to Abu'l Haret Muhammad, ruler of the Farighunids.

The author never visited the countries he describes but compiled the book from earlier works and tales, without naming his sources. Minorsky identified several 9th-century ones: Ibn Khordadbeh's Book of Roads and Kingdoms, a lost work by al-Jayhani, Istakhri's Masālik al-Mamālik, with a debt to Abu Zayd al-Balkhi, and a source shared with al-Masudi's Meadows of Gold, as well as perhaps Hamdani on Arabia.

The author reports on countries, peoples, languages, clothing, food, religion, local products, towns and cities, rivers, seas, lakes, islands, the steppe, deserts, politics and dynasties, and trade. The inhabited world is divided into Asia, Europe and Libya, meaning the Maghreb, and the author counts 45 countries north of the equator. The countries themselves begin with Chinistan, Hindustan and Tibet, then the Turkic peoples such as the Toghuzghuz, Karluk, Ghuz and Pechenegs, then Khurasan, Transoxania, Persia and Iraq, the Arab lands, Egypt, the Maghreb and Spain, Byzantium, which includes all of Christian Europe, and the Slavs, Rus, Khazar and the Alān.

The work appears to mention a Rus' Khaganate and calls the Rus' king Khāqān-i Rus. Its sections on the margins of the Islamic world are of great historical importance, with early descriptions of the Turkic peoples of Central Asia, and its archaic language and style make it a valuable Persian linguistic document.

The Orientalist Alexander Tumansky found a manuscript with a copy of the text in 1892 in Bukhara. The copy was made from the original in 1258 by the Persian chronographer Abu l-Mu'ayyad ʿAbd al-Qayyūm ibn al-Ḥusain ibn 'Alī al-Farīsī, and the text survives as part of a larger manuscript that also holds a copy of the Jahān-Nāma and the Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm of Fakhr al-Din al-Razi. Vasily Bartold published a facsimile edition with introduction and index in 1930. Minorsky's thoroughly commented English translation appeared in 1937, and Manouchehr Sotudeh published a printed Persian text in 1962.
hue: The Perfume River passes through the centre of Huế, which lies roughly in the middle of Vietnam on the transition between the north central and south central regions. The area includes the Tam Giang–Cau Hai lagoon, 68 km long, and has about 128 km of coastline. Mountains line its western and south-western borders, and the climate is tropical monsoon, with most rain falling from September to December.

The oldest ruins in the area belong to the kingdom of Lâm Ấp and date to the 4th century CE. The region, called Thuận Hóa, was ceded by Champa to Đại Việt in 1306: the Cham king Chế Mân gave two prefectures in exchange for marriage with a Vietnamese princess, Huyền Trân.

In the 16th century Nguyễn Hoàng asked to govern Thuận Hóa, then the southernmost region of Vietnam. After he pacified it, he and his heir Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên made it loyal to the Nguyễn family and rose against the Trịnh lords, and Vietnam divided between two ruling clans. The Nguyễn lords moved their palace to Kim Long in 1636 and based themselves at Phú Xuân, the future Huế, in 1687. The Trịnh captured it in 1775, and the Tây Sơn, whose rebellion had broken out in 1771, defeated the Trịnh garrison in 1786 and took Phú Xuân.

Nguyễn Ánh, a successor of the Nguyễn lords, recaptured Phú Xuân and unified the country. He rebuilt the citadel entirely and, as Emperor Gia Long, made Huế the national capital. After the French conquest Phú Xuân was officially renamed Huế in 1899, and the city remained capital of Annam within French Indochina. The imperial court stayed there until Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated in 1945.

Huế became a centrally governed city of Vietnam in 2025, when it was merged with the rest of Thừa Thiên Huế province. Its complex of imperial palaces, tombs and temples is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, including the Imperial City and the Forbidden Purple City, once the emperor's home. The tombs of emperors such as Minh Mạng, Khải Định and Tự Đức lie along the Perfume River, and the Thiên Mụ Temple, the largest pagoda in the city, is its official symbol.
huelva: Huelva lies in the south-west of the Iberian Peninsula on the Gulf of Cádiz, facing the Atlantic. It stands on the estuary formed where the Odiel and Tinto rivers meet, between the two rivers. In ancient times the estuary was rather wide, and it has progressively silted up.

Historians long held that Huelva began as a native Tartessian settlement. Finds of Phoenician material at the Méndez Núñez-Las Monjas site led to the Phoenician chronology being reassessed, and the evidence now favours seeing Huelva as a very early Phoenician colony, founded roughly in the 9th century BCE, though a 10th-century date has also been argued. The Phoenicians called it ʿunʿu baʿl, 'Baal's fort', which Greek texts corrupted to Onoba. The outpost exported silver, copper, purple dye and salted fish and was a node on routes linking the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. The Tartessian world entered a crisis in the 6th century BCE, and the town passed slowly to the Turdetani.

Under Rome it was Onoba or Onuba and had a mint. Musa ibn Nusayr's troops seized it by April 712, and its name became Walba. It was a short-lived independent taifa from 1012 to 1051, was then annexed by Seville and was occupied by the Almoravids in 1091. Alfonso X of Castile took it in 1262.

Huelva was a leading fishing town of Andalusia in the 16th century, became a provincial capital in 1833 and a city by royal decree on 17 September 1876. Mining by Rio Tinto, the main company from about 1873, sent copper and pyrite to its port. On 4 February 1888 soldiers fired on demonstrators against ore-smelting pollution at Rio Tinto, and historians estimate 100 to 200 deaths.

Huelva is the capital of its province in Andalusia, with a population of 149,410 at the 2010 census. Its port still handles copper and pyrite from mines inland. Recreativo de Huelva, founded in 1889 by workers of Rio Tinto, is the oldest football club in Spain, and the Fiestas Colombinas honour Christopher Columbus's departure from the port on 3 August 1492.
huesca: Huesca lies on a plateau in northern Aragon at an elevation of 488 metres, close to the Sierra de Guara, which reaches 2,077 metres. It is the capital of the Spanish province of the same name and one of the smallest provincial capitals in Spain, 71 kilometres from Zaragoza. Its coat of arms carries a block with a V-shaped notch, commonly said to represent the Salto de Roldán, or Roland's Leap, a rock formation about 25 kilometres to the north.

The city dates from before the Roman period, when it was called Bolskan in the Iberian language. As Osca it became a Roman colony under Quintus Sertorius, who made it his base. It minted its own coinage and had a school, founded by Sertorius, where young Iberians were taught Latin and Roman customs. Augustus made it a municipium in 30 BCE. The Arabs conquered the city in the late 8th century and called it Washqah. Part of the Upper March of the Emirate of Córdoba, it was repeatedly troubled by rebellion as the Banu Qasi, Banu Amrus and Banu al-Tawil clans and the Arista dynasty of Pamplona struggled for control. In 1018 it became part of the Taifa of Zaragoza.

In 1094 Sancho Ramírez built the Castle of Montearagón nearby in order to besiege the city, but was killed by a stray arrow as he reached its walls. Peter I of Aragon conquered it in 1096 and moved the royal capital there from Jaca. Peter IV of Aragon founded the University of Huesca in 1354; it was abolished in 1845. Huesca had one of the most important Jewish communities in Aragon, which flourished until the expulsion of 1492. During the Spanish Civil War the city was held by the Nationalists and besieged by the Republicans, among them George Orwell, but did not fall.

Huesca had 52,059 inhabitants in 2009, almost a quarter of the province's population. Its Gothic cathedral was begun by James I of Aragon around 1273, on the foundations of a mosque. The Abbey of San Pedro el Viejo, built between 1100 and 1241, is one of the oldest Romanesque structures in the Iberian Peninsula. The city celebrates the Fiestas de San Lorenzo from 9 to 15 August, in honour of Saint Lawrence, a native of Huesca martyred in 268 CE.
huey-tlatoani: Tlahtoāni is a historical title used by the dynastic rulers of the āltepēmeh, the autonomous city-states that many pre-Columbian Nahuatl-speaking peoples formed in the Valley of Mexico during the Postclassic Period. The word is an agent noun from the verb tlahtoa, meaning to speak, so that it literally means one who speaks. English renders it as king, sovereign, ruler or speaker. The title huēyi tlahtoāni, great ruler or emperor, was used by the rulers of the Aztec Empire, the alliance of Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan. Related titles include tlahtohcāpilli, for princes and prominent noblemen, and cihuātlahtoāni, for noblewomen such as consorts or princesses.

Each āltepētl had its own tlahtoāni, who was at once its ruler, high priest and commander-in-chief. He held ultimate authority over all land in the city-state and oversaw tribute collection, market activities, temple affairs and the settling of judicial disputes. He was typically a ruler from the royal lineage and served for life, although in some cases a council of nobles, elders and priests could elect one from a pool of four candidates. The cihuācōātl, a noble who served as supreme judge, appointed the lower court judges and handled financial affairs, was second in command.

In war the tlahtoāni drew up battle plans from the reports of scouts, messengers and spies sent to an enemy city, and was the main decision-maker. He sought the support of allied rulers by sending gifts and emissaries, was told at once of warriors killed or captured, informed the citizens, and presented gifts to the successful.

There were eleven tlahtohqueh of Tenochtitlan: Acamapichtli (1376 to 1395), Huitzilihuitl (1395 to 1417), Chimalpopoca (1417 to 1427), Itzcoatl (1427 to 1440), Moctezuma I (1440 to 1469), Axayacatl (1469 to 1481), Tizoc (1481 to 1486), Ahuitzotl (1486 to 1502), Moctezuma II (1502 to 1520), Cuitláhuac (1520) and Cuauhtémoc (1520 to 1521). From Itzcoatl onward, the tlahtoāni of Tenochtitlan was also the huēyi tlahtoāni of the Aztec Empire.
hug-roger-iii-of-pallars-sobira: He was born around 1430, the only son of Arnau Roger IV de Pallars Sobirà and Joana de Cardona i de Prades, and a nephew of Joan Ramon Folc III, Count of Cardona. He held the county of Pallars Sobirà from 1451 and, through his marriage to Caterina, daughter of the Roussillon noble Philip d'Albert, was Baron de Ponts from 1478. The couple had no legitimate children.
