In 1461 he belonged to the Catalan delegation that demanded from King John II of Aragon the release of Charles, Prince of Viana. As a member of the Council of the Principality he came into conflict with his uncle, who was also Count of Prades.

When the Catalan Civil War broke out in 1462 he became the supreme military leader of the Principality of Catalonia against John II. He fought the royalist Remensa peasants, besieged Queen Juana Enríquez and Infante Ferran in the Força Vella of Girona and defended Barcelona, and he served as a deputy of the Generalitat de Catalunya in 1464–67. Captured by the king in 1466, he was freed in 1470 after paying a large ransom and promising to support John II, yet he went on fighting as Captain General until the capitulation of Pedralbes in 1472, the only person excluded from its terms.

From his refuge at Valencia d'Àneu he kept up hostilities across Pallars and the neighbouring lands with the backing of King Louis XI of France. He accepted a truce in 1475 and submitted in 1480, obtaining pardon for himself and his supporters, but took up arms again in 1484. Pressed by the Counts of Cardona, he fled, while his wife held out at Valencia d'Àneu through a siege of three years. In 1491 the family's domains passed to the Cardona family as the Marquisate of Pallars.

In exile he entered the service of King Charles VIII of France, went with him to Naples in 1494 and became governor of Castel Nuovo there. In 1503 he was taken prisoner by Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, the Grand Captain, held in that fortress and then brought to Barcelona, where he was sentenced to life imprisonment before his transfer to Xàtiva.
hugh-capet: Hugh was the son of Hugh the Great, Duke of the Franks, and Hedwige of Saxony, daughter of the German king Henry the Fowler. Through his mother he was a nephew of Otto I, and through his paternal grandmother he descended from Charlemagne. His family, the Robertians, were powerful landowners in the Île-de-France, and two of them, Odo I and Robert I, had been chosen as kings in place of Carolingians. When his father died in 956 Hugh, the eldest son, was about fifteen, and his neighbours took advantage: Theobald I of Blois took Chartres and Châteaudun.

In 960 King Lothair agreed that Hugh should have his father's margraviate of Neustria and the title Duke of the Franks. In 978, when Otto II invaded France and besieged Lothair in Paris, a relief army under Hugh helped force him to lift the siege on 30 November, and Otto's rearguard was destroyed crossing the flooded Aisne. The victory restored Hugh's position as the first noble of the kingdom.

Lothair's son Louis V died in a riding accident while hunting in the forest of Senlis on 22 May 987, leaving no children. Charles, Duke of Lower Lorraine, a Carolingian claimant, was accused of having made himself a vassal of the emperor. Adalberon, Archbishop of Reims, argued that the throne was not acquired by hereditary right. Hugh was crowned rex Francorum at Noyon on 1 June and again in Paris on 3 July 987, and he had his son Robert crowned on 25 December that year.

Charles of Lorraine took Laon, and Hugh and Robert twice besieged it without success. Adalberon, Bishop of Laon, then seized Charles in his sleep and delivered him to Hugh, who imprisoned him at Orléans until his death. Hugh's power was narrow. He held towns and estates between Paris and Orléans of about 400 square miles, and a plot of 993 to hand him to Otto III went unpunished, which shows how tenuous his hold was. He had to seek military aid from Richard I of Normandy, though his unanimous election gave him moral authority.

Hugh died on 24 October 996 and was buried at the Basilica of Saint-Denis. His son Robert continued to reign, and the direct Capetians ruled France from 987 to 1328, with cadet branches after that until 1848.
hugh-davranches-earl-of-chester: Hugh was born around 1047, the son of Richard le Goz, Viscount of Avranches. His mother was traditionally said to have been Emma de Conteville, a half-sister of William the Conqueror, but the historian Lewis has argued that the identification rests on unsatisfactory evidence and that her identity is unknown, while Keats-Rohan, accepting the weakness of the evidence, has still argued for some relationship between Hugh and William. Besides Lupus, the Wolf, he was nicknamed le Gros, the Fat.

Hugh received the earldom in 1071, after Gerbod the Fleming, 1st Earl of Chester, was taken prisoner at the Battle of Cassel and the king declared the title vacant. With it came the palatine powers of Cheshire, a county on the Welsh Marches, and many manors once held by Edwin, the last Saxon earl of Mercia. Hugh appointed hereditary barons, among them his cousins Robert of Rhuddlan and Nigel of Cotentin. After his father's death he also became Viscount of Avranches, with large estates in western Normandy. He stayed loyal to King William II in the rebellion of 1088 and later served Henry I as a principal councillor.

In 1081 Gruffudd ap Cynan, King of Gwynedd, was captured and imprisoned in Hugh's castle at Chester. When Robert of Rhuddlan was killed by Welsh raiders in 1093, Hugh took over his lands and ruled most of North Wales, but he lost Anglesey and much of Gwynedd in the revolt of 1094 led by the escaped Gruffudd. In 1098 he campaigned in Anglesey with Hugh of Montgomery, 2nd Earl of Shrewsbury, until a Norwegian fleet under King Magnus III attacked them near the Menai Straits; Shrewsbury was killed, the Normans left the island, and Hugh did not try to recover these lands again.

Hugh married Ermentrude of Claremont, daughter of Hugh I, Count of Clermont-en-Beauvaisis, and had illegitimate children as well. He counted the theologian Anselm a friend and founded the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Sever in Normandy. Falling ill, he became a monk at St Werburgh's on 13 July 1101 and died there four days later. His son Richard d'Avranches succeeded him, and after Richard died in the sinking of the White Ship in 1120 the earldom passed to Hugh's nephew Ranulph le Meschin. He was remembered for gluttony, prodigality and profligacy.
hugh-de-lacy-earl-of-ulster: Hugh de Lacy was the younger son of Hugh de Lacy, Lord of Meath, of a family descended from Walter de Lacy, who had gone to England after the Norman conquest. Around 1189 he was appointed Viceroy of Ireland, an office his father had held, but he was replaced in 1190 by Guillaume la Petil. He raised a motte at Carlow in the 1180s, on the site where Carlow Castle was built in the 13th century; excavation in 1996 found post-holes beneath the walls of its keep.

De Lacy served for a time alongside John de Courcy in Leinster and Munster, but de Courcy, made Earl of Ulster by Henry II in 1181 and later Lord of Connaught, became a rival of the de Lacys and seized land without royal permission. Hugh accused him of failing to pay homage to King John, and with a contingent of English soldiers marched on Ulaid and drove him out. De Courcy's lands and title were forfeited and passed to Hugh.

Hugh pressed on with the conquest of Ulaid, his earldom reaching across the modern counties of Antrim and Down and part of Londonderry, but he could not bring the O'Neill of Tyrone to submit, and in 1207 he went to war with Meiler Fitzhenry, the Lord Chief Justice of Ireland. When his brother Walter de Lacy, Lord of Meath, sheltered William de Braose in 1208, King John brought an army to Ireland, landing at Waterford in 1210. Walter submitted, but Hugh resisted, was defeated and went into exile.

After years in the Albigensian Crusade, de Lacy returned to Ireland in 1223, allied himself with the O'Neill against the English, invaded Ulster and besieged Carrickfergus, but surrendered to William Marshal, 2nd Earl of Pembroke. Henry III gave his Ulster lands to his brother Walter in 1226 and restored them the next year, after which Hugh served the king loyally and was more than once summoned to England to advise on Irish affairs.

He married first Lescaline, daughter of Bertram de Verdun, and then Emeline, daughter of Walter de Ridlesford. His sons Walter and Roger died before him, and although he had several daughters, the earldom reverted to the crown when he died at Carrickfergus. In 1263 it was granted to his great-nephew Walter de Burgh, grandson of Walter de Lacy.
hugh-de-lacy-lord-of-meath: Hugh de Lacy was born before 1135, the son of Gilbert de Lacy of Ewyas Lacy, Weobley and Ludlow, and held large estates in Herefordshire and Shropshire. He is said to have disputed lands in Herefordshire with Josce de Dinan in 1154; he held his father's lands before 1163, and in 1165–66 he held fifty-eight and three-quarters knight's fees. His first wife, Rohese of Monmouth, was a granddaughter of Gilbert Fitz Richard, as Strongbow was, and their children included Walter de Lacy and Hugh de Lacy, 1st Earl of Ulster.

De Lacy crossed to Ireland with Henry II in October 1171 and early in 1172 was sent to receive the submission of Rory, High King of Ireland. Before Henry left he received Meath for the service of fifty knights, with almost royal authority, and charge of Dublin Castle, making him in effect the first Viceroy of Ireland. Tighearnán Ó Ruairc, King of Bréifne, who ruled Meath, would not concede it. At a parley on the Hill of Ward an interpreter was killed by a blow aimed at Lacy, and Ó Ruairc was speared and beheaded; the Annals of the Four Masters say he was treacherously slain.

Lacy began securing Meath with castles such as Trim, put in the charge of Hugh Tyrrel, then the following year fought for Henry in France, holding Verneuil against Louis VII for a month before it capitulated. Sent back as procurator-general in 1177, after the death of Richard de Clare, he had his grant confirmed with Offaly, Kildare and Wicklow added. He built many castles while leaving the Irish in possession of their lands, and was accused of intending to seize the sovereignty of the island.

Recalled in 1181 for marrying Róis Ní Chonchobair without the king's permission, he returned the next winter with a royal clerk, Robert of Shrewsbury, as coadjutor. In 1185 Prince John complained that Lacy would not let the Irish pay tribute. He was killed by Gilla-Gan-Mathiar O'Maidhaigh while supervising a motte castle at Durrow, and John was sent to take possession of his lands. Buried first at Durrow Abbey, his remains were disputed between Bective Abbey and St Thomas's Abbey, Dublin, until in 1205 they were laid in his first wife's tomb at St Thomas's.
hugh-ii-of-jaffa: Hugh's parents, Hugh I of Jaffa and Mabel of Roucy, left Chartres in 1106 to join the campaign of Prince Bohemond I of Taranto, the half-brother of Mabel's mother, Sibylla. Hugh was born in Apulia and left there in Bohemond's care while his father went on to the Kingdom of Jerusalem and received Jaffa as a fief. The historian Hans Eberhard Mayer estimates that the elder Hugh had died by mid-1112, so his son never knew him.

Raised in Apulia as a South Italian Norman, Hugh reached the Levant by 31 January 1120 and obtained his inheritance. In 1123 he married Emma, the wealthy widow of Eustace I Grenier, lord of Sidon and Caesarea, within the year of mourning, which suggests to the historian Malcolm Barber that he enjoyed the favour of King Baldwin II.

Charters show Hugh administering Jericho for Emma and her twin sons, Eustace II and Walter I, and Mayer presumes he also governed Sidon and Caesarea in their names, which would have given him much of the kingdom's coast. After the prince of Galilee, no lord in the kingdom held more. He styled himself comes and princeps of Jaffa, sealed documents with his own seal and kept his own seneschal, chancellor, marshal and constable, while the royal government called him only dominus.

In 1126 and 1127 he gave lands in Ascalon, still held by Fatimid Egypt, to the Knights Hospitaller and to the Abbey of Saint Mary of the Valley of Jehosaphat, and the historian Jonathan Riley-Smith concludes that the city had been promised to him. Mayer suspects that Hugh hoped for an autonomy like that of the counts of Tripoli and Edessa, which King Fulk, who was replacing the Norman nobility with men from Anjou, would not tolerate.

When the Egyptians of Ascalon raided as far as Arsuf, Hugh's support collapsed and his constable, Barisan the Old, went over to the king. The settlement agreed after the siege of Jaffa gave the king his revenues for the years of exile, a sentence Riley-Smith considers extraordinarily lenient. Fulk was widely suspected of having ordered the later attack on Hugh, and Queen Melisende turned on all who had sided against him.

King Roger of Sicily granted Hugh the lordship of Gargano, and he died soon after, possibly from the effects of his wound. Fulk and later kings created several smaller lordships for his former vassals, and the county of Jaffa stayed in the royal family for the rest of the 12th century.
hugh-iii-duke-of-burgundy: Hugh was the eldest son of Duke Odo II and Marie of Blois-Champagne, a daughter of Theobald II, Count of Champagne. He became duke at the age of fourteen and was for three years under the guardianship and regency of his mother. In 1165 he married Alice, a daughter of Matthias I, Duke of Lorraine, and he repudiated her in 1183. Their children included Odo III, who succeeded him in the duchy. In 1183 he married Beatrice, Countess of Albon and Dauphine of Viennois, and their son Guigues VI became Dauphin of Viennois.

Hugh was a belligerent man and was soon in conflict with King Louis VII of France over their borders. When Philip Augustus succeeded Louis in 1180, Hugh took the opportunity to force several men to change their allegiance to Burgundy. Philip II, displeased at the loss of his vassals, invaded the duchy and besieged Châtillon in 1186. The town fell, and with it its garrison, commanded by Odo, Hugh's heir. A peace was negotiated in which Hugh had to pay a high ransom for his son. In 1187 he transferred the capital of Burgundy to Dijon and tried to turn the city into a major commercial centre.

Hugh then turned to the Holy Land and joined the Third Crusade in the retinue of Philip II. He played a major part in the victory at the Battle of Arsuf on 7 September 1191 and at the Siege of Acre. When Philip returned to France in July 1191 he left Hugh in charge of the French troops.
In January 1192 Hugh travelled to Ascalon and argued with Richard I of England over the pay of his troops. He died at Acre on 25 August 1192. His son Odo III succeeded him as duke.
hugh-iv-duke-of-burgundy: Hugh was born on 9 March 1213, the son of Odo III, Duke of Burgundy, and Alice de Vergy. His father died in 1218 during the War of the Succession of Champagne, and Hugh succeeded him as a child. As a young duke he opposed the regency of Blanche of Castile and joined the rebel barons in 1229, which brought him into conflict with Theobald IV, Count of Champagne. In 1237, through an exchange with John l'Antique de Chalon, he gave up the barony of Salon for the counties of Chalon and Auxonne, enlarging the duchy as the wine trade grew.

On the Barons' Crusade of 1239, led by King Theobald I of Navarre, Hugh was among the nobles who wanted to fight against the advice of the king and the military orders. He withdrew to Ascalon with Walter IV, Count of Brienne, and so avoided the defeat at Gaza. He then joined Richard of Cornwall, helped rebuild Ascalon and took part in the peace made with Egypt in 1241.

Hugh reached Cyprus by May 1249 to join Louis IX of France on the Seventh Crusade. During the siege of Mansurah he led one of the two divisions of the army that crossed, the other being led by the king, and he was taken prisoner with Louis in the retreat at Fariskur.

In 1266 Baldwin II, the Latin emperor, promised him the principality of Thessalonica in return for help in reconquering lands lost to Epirus, so that Hugh became titular King of Thessalonica. The campaign never took place, as Pope Gregory X held off any attempt while Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos promised a union of the churches. Hugh joined the Eighth Crusade in 1270 but returned home after Louis IX died.

Hugh married first Yolande of Dreux and later Beatrice of Navarre. Among his children were Robert II, who succeeded him in the duchy, and Isabella, who married King Rudolf I of Germany. He died on 27 October 1272 at Villaines-en-Duismois, and his burial place is unknown.
hugh-low: Low was born on 10 May 1824 in Upper Clapton, England, the son of a Scottish horticulturist also named Hugh, and learned botany in the family nursery. At 20 his father sent him to Southeast Asia to collect orchids. Based at first in Singapore, he soon joined James Brooke, the White Rajah, in Sarawak, and came to know its interior well enough to write Sarawak, Its Inhabitants and Productions (1848). Brooke, appointed Governor of the new colony of Labuan in 1847, made Low his colonial secretary.

On 12 August 1848, at St Andrew's Cathedral in Singapore, Low married Catherine Napier, daughter of Labuan's lieutenant governor, William Napier; she died of fever on Labuan in 1851. He was police magistrate there from 1850 to 1877, became fluent in Malay and built a lasting reputation as a naturalist. From Labuan he visited Mount Kinabalu three times, first in March 1851 and twice in 1858 with Spenser St. John.

In April 1877 he became the fourth Resident of Perak, whose advice the Pangkor Treaty made binding in all matters except custom and religion. The first Resident, J. W. W. Birch, had been murdered in 1874. Low moved his headquarters to Kuala Kangsar to be near the chiefs, saw Raja Yusuf almost daily, gave many chiefs and headmen small subsidies and created a state council of the leading Malay, Chinese and British figures, among them his confidant, the mining magnate Kapitan China Chung Keng Quee.

Within eight years slavery was abolished in the state. In 1882 he planted rubber seeds and grew seven trees at Kuala Kangsar, the beginning of rubber cultivation in Malaysia, and in 1885 he established the first railway line in the Malay Peninsula, from Taiping to Port Weld. He paid off the state's debt of 800,000 Straits dollars and, on retiring in 1889, left a credit balance of 1.5 million.

Low died on 18 April 1905 in Alassio, Italy. He had been made a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George in 1889. He is often considered the first successful British administrator in the region, and his methods became models for British colonial rule across Southeast Asia. Low's Peak, the highest peak of Mount Kinabalu, and Low's Gully are named after him, as are plants and animals such as the pitcher plant Nepenthes lowii and Low's squirrel.
hugh-montgomery-1st-viscount-montgomery: Montgomery was born at Broadstone Castle near Beith, the son of Adam Montgomery, 5th Laird of Braidstane, and his wife and cousin Margaret Montgomery of Hessilhead. After studying at the University of Glasgow and spending time at the royal court of France, he served as a captain of foot in a Scottish regiment under William I of Orange in the early years of the Eighty Years' War. He came home on his parents' death in 1587, inherited Braidstane and married Elizabeth Shaw, who died in 1623; he later married Sarah Maxwell, daughter of the 4th Lord Herries of Terregles.

Montgomery gained influence with King James VI through letters from his brother George, Dean of Norwich from 1602, which carried news of English politics. Drawn into the old feud between Clan Montgomery and Clan Cunningham, he pursued a Cunningham to The Hague and attacked him with a sword in the palace's Inner Court; the man's belt buckle turned the blow. Imprisoned in the Gevangenpoort, Montgomery escaped with a Scottish soldier's help, was reprimanded by the king, but was soon back in favour and accompanied James to his English coronation in 1603.

His Ulster venture began with a bargain with Ellis O'Neill, wife of Con O'Neill, then imprisoned at Carrickfergus Castle: half the O'Neill lands if Montgomery freed her husband and won him a royal pardon. A relative of Montgomery's led the jailbreak, but James Hamilton intervened at court, and the land was split into thirds between Hamilton, Montgomery and O'Neill. The first settlers came in May 1606. Montgomery made his seat at Newtownards, opened a trade route between Donaghadee and Portpatrick, sat with Hamilton for the settlement in the Irish House of Commons in 1613 and built a stone quay at Donaghadee for the ferries from 1616.

Created Viscount Montgomery on 3 May 1622, he died on 15 May 1636 and may have been given a Scottish state funeral at Newtownards on 8 September 1636. His son Hugh succeeded as 2nd Viscount, and another son, Sir James Montgomery of Rosemount, became a noted military commander. With Hamilton he is remembered as one of the founding fathers of the Ulster Scots, and his arms, a fleur-de-lis and hand above a crescent, survive in the crest of Ards Borough Council and the badge of Regent House Grammar School in Newtownards.
hugh-of-ibelin: Hugh was the eldest son of Barisan of Ibelin and Helvis of Ramla. He was old enough to witness charters in 1148, as was his younger brother Baldwin of Ibelin, and since the male age of majority was fifteen this suggests that he was born in the early 1130s. The historian H.E. Mayer has suggested that a limited competence may have been accepted from the age of eight, but his examples come from the royal house, whose situation was somewhat different. Hugh was probably about ten years older than his youngest brother, Balian of Ibelin.

After Barisan died in 1150, Helvis married Manasses of Hierges, the constable of Jerusalem and one of the strongest supporters of Queen Melisende in her power struggle against her son, King Baldwin III. When Baldwin won that struggle in 1152, Manasses was exiled, and Hugh inherited the lordship of Ramla from his mother.

Hugh took part in the Siege of Ascalon in 1153. In 1157 he was captured in battle at Banias, and he was probably released the next year. In 1159 he visited the Principality of Antioch and met the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Comnenus, who had come to assert his suzerainty over the principality. In 1163 he married Agnes of Courtenay, whom Amalric had been forced to divorce before becoming king that year. Some accounts hold that Agnes had already been betrothed or married to Hugh before 1157, and that she married Amalric only after Hugh was taken prisoner.

In 1167 Hugh joined Amalric's expedition to Egypt, where he was responsible for building a bridge over the Nile. The crusaders allied with the sultan against Shirkuh, the general of Nur ad-Din Zangi, who was also fighting for control of Egypt, and Hugh was sent with the sultan's son Kamil to protect Cairo. He was the first crusader to see the sultan's palace. At the siege of Bilbeis during the same campaign, according to Ibelin family tradition, Philip of Milly saved Hugh's life after he broke his leg and fell under his horse.

Hugh died around 1169 while on a pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela. His marriage to Agnes of Courtenay had produced no children, and his lordships of Ibelin and Ramla stayed in his family. The name was borne again in the next generations of the family: a later Hugh of Ibelin, the son of John of Ibelin, the Old Lord of Beirut, was his grand-nephew.
hugh-of-montgomery-2nd-earl-of-shrewsbur: Hugh, also known as Hugh the Red, belonged to the House of Bellême. He was the second surviving son of Roger de Montgomerie, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury, and Mabel de Bellême. As was usual in the first generation after the Norman Conquest, Hugh inherited most of his father's English possessions, while his elder brother Robert of Bellême received the great lordship of Bellême. Hugh was at the castle of Bures-sur-Dives in December 1079 when his mother was murdered; he pursued the killers but could not overtake them.

In the summer of 1080 he and his brothers attested a charter that their father granted to the abbey of Troarn, in the Diocese of Bayeux. Roger made the grant for the redemption of his soul and those of his relatives, especially of his wife Mabel, lately deceased, and of his sons.

On his father's death in 1094 Hugh received his English titles and honours and his Welsh lands. In 1095 he joined the conspiracy of those supporting Robert de Mowbray against King William Rufus, and in 1096 the king pardoned him on payment of a fine of £3,000. In his four years as earl he spent most of his time fighting the Welsh in the Welsh Marches. In 1098 he joined Hugh d'Avranches, 1st Earl of Chester, in an attempt to recover Anglesey, which had been lost in the Welsh revolt of 1094.

On or about 31 July 1098 Hugh was killed at the Battle of Anglesey Sound, fighting a raid by King Magnus Barefoot of Norway. Among Magnus's company was Harold Haroldson, a son of Harold Godwinson, King of England. Several sources agree that Magnus himself shot the arrow, which struck Hugh through the eye slit of his armour as he rode carelessly through the shallows, and that he fell into the sea. Hugh died unmarried, and his English lands and titles passed to his elder brother Robert of Bellême, who became the 3rd Earl of Shrewsbury.
hugh-of-tuscany: Hugh was the son and successor of Hubert, an illegitimate son of King Hugh of Italy, and of Willa, a daughter of Boniface I, Duke of Spoleto and Margrave of Camerino. The Tuscany he inherited was larger than it had been under Adalbert II, the last margrave unconnected with the royal family, and royal intervention there was rare. The march was defined less by geography than by the public institutions the margrave controlled: Hugh had his own tribunals, mints and army, and his power rested on the wealthy cities of the Arno valley as well as his own estates.

Hugh restored the machinery of government in Tuscany after decades in which margraves had looked elsewhere, and he backed the Ottonian dynasty. In 996 Emperor Otto III placed eight Adriatic counties disputed with the papacy under the joint control of Hugh and Conrad of Ivrea, writing to Pope Gregory V that he was leaving him "Hugh of Tuscany, faithful to us in everything". Hugh also supported Otto's church reforms and his policy against Venice, whose duke, Pietro IV Candiano, was his kinsman.

As Duke of Spoleto from 989 to 996, Hugh was responsible for the link between the empire and the principalities of the south. When Aloara, regent of Capua, died in 992 and Prince Landenulf II was murdered in the revolt that followed, Hugh put down the rising and placed Laidulf, the youngest son of Pandulf Ironhead, on the throne. He took an interest in the troubled monastery of Bobbio and corresponded with Gerbert of Aurillac, and in January 1001 he attended the synod Gerbert, by then Pope Sylvester II, held in Rome.

In his last years Hugh gave away growing amounts of public land to found monasteries, and he granted lands around Arezzo to the Guidi family, whom he patronised. He died at Pistoia, leaving no children by his wife Judith, and his state collapsed: war broke out between Lucca and Pisa in 1004. He was buried in the Badia Fiorentina, where Mino da Fiesole later added a monument. The monks still commemorate him each year on 21 December, Peter Damian praised his justice, and Dante called him a great baron in the Paradiso.
hugh-oneill-earl-of-tyrone: Hugh was the second son of Feardorcha "Matthew" O'Neill, 1st Baron Dungannon, and Siobhán Maguire, born into the ruling family of Tír Eoghain during a succession conflict. His uncle Shane O'Neill disputed Matthew's legitimacy, and the family split into rival septs, the MacShanes and the MacBarons, a quarrel the English encouraged. Hugh and his brother Brian became wards of the Crown and were raised by the Anglo-Irish Hovenden family at Balgriffin in County Dublin.

After Brian was killed in 1562 by Turlough Luineach O'Neill, Hugh became 3rd Baron Dungannon. Shane was killed in June 1567, and Hugh returned to Ulster early in 1568 with lands in Oneilland. Turlough remained his rival: in March 1583, on a false report of his death, Hugh hurried to Tullyhogue Fort, where O'Neill chiefs were inaugurated.

Recognised as Earl of Tyrone in the Irish House of Lords on 30 June 1585, he defended the Pale's borders in exchange for soldiers and was nicknamed "The Queen's O'Neill". He built alliances by marriage, above all with the O'Donnells, and in 1591 eloped with Mabel Bagenal, sister of the Marshal Henry Bagenal, his chief rival. Lord Deputy Charles Blount, 8th Baron Mountjoy, estimated his revenue at £80,000 a year, and he armed his largely mercenary forces with firearms and continental tactics.

Historians disagree over his motives in the early 1590s: Hiram Morgan sees a master strategist who feigned loyalty, while Nicholas Canny and others argue he was pushed into rebellion. He was in open revolt by February 1595, when his brother Art MacBaron took the Blackwater Fort, and with O'Donnell he offered Philip II of Spain the kingdom of Ireland for military help. At the Battle of the Yellow Ford on 14 August 1598 half of Bagenal's 4,000 men were killed, Bagenal among them.

After the war James I confirmed him in his title and core estates, but Lord Deputy Arthur Chichester worked to accuse him of treason. In Rome Pope Paul V lodged the exiles in the Palazzo Della Rovere on a small pension, and Tyrone's petitions to Philip III for help in retaking Ireland came to nothing. He died in Rome in July 1616 and was buried in San Pietro in Montorio, at the Spanish embassy's expense.

The historian James MacGeoghegan restored his reputation in the 17th century, and 19th-century nationalists such as John Mitchel made him a romantic hero of Gaelic freedom. He was still often sidelined in favour of Hugh Roe O'Donnell, whose upbringing and early death made him a national hero.
hugh-the-great: Hugh the Great was the son of King Robert I of France and Béatrice of Vermandois, a descendant of Charlemagne, and was born in Paris. His family is known as the Robertians. In 922 the barons of Western Francia revolted against the Carolingian King Charles the Simple, who fled, and elected Robert as king. When Robert died in battle at Soissons in 923, Hugh refused the crown, and it went to his brother-in-law Rudolph. Charles the Simple had sought help from Hugh's cousin Count Herbert II of Vermandois, who instead imprisoned him and used the threat of releasing him to press his own ambitions until Charles died in 929.

At Rudolph's death in 936 Hugh held nearly all the land between the Loire and the Seine, the ancient Neustria, except Anjou and the territory ceded to the Normans in 911. He took an active part in bringing King Louis IV back from England that year. Historians have wondered why he called the young Louis to the throne instead of taking it himself. He had rivals, especially Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, and Herbert II, who would probably have challenged his election, and Richer explains that he remembered his father, who had died for his pretensions.

Hugh married three times: Judith of Maine in 922, Eadhild, a daughter of Edward the Elder, in 926, and in 937 Hedwig of Saxony, sister of Otto the Great and of Gerberga, Louis's wife. Soon afterwards he was drawn into a long quarrel with Louis. In 939 he, Herbert, Count Arnulf I of Flanders and Duke William Longsword of Normandy paid homage to Otto against Louis. When the Normans handed Louis over to him in 945, Hugh released him in 946 on condition that he surrender the fortress of Laon. In 948 a church council at Ingelheim excommunicated Hugh in absentia, and he responded by attacking Soissons and Reims. In 953 he made peace with Louis, the church and Otto.

When Louis died, Hugh was among the first to recognise his son Lothair as king and, at the request of Lothair's mother Gerberga, helped to have him crowned. In return Lothair invested Hugh with the duchies of Burgundy and Aquitaine. Duke Gilbert of Burgundy had acknowledged himself Hugh's vassal and betrothed his daughter to Hugh's son Otto-Henry, and when Gilbert died on 8 April 956 Hugh became effective master of the duchy. He died at Dourdan on 16 June 956. His son Hugh Capet became King of France in 987.
hugo-banzer: Hugo Banzer Suárez was born on 10 May 1926 at the hacienda Concepción in Santa Cruz. His grandfather Georg Banzer was a German immigrant from Osnabrück. He entered the Army Military College at fourteen in 1941 and graduated as a second lieutenant in 1947. He trained in Argentina, at Fort Hood in the United States and at the School of the Americas in Panama. Promoted colonel in 1961, he headed the Ministry of Education and Culture from 1964 to 1966 under General René Barrientos, a personal friend, was military attaché in Argentina, and from 1969 to 1971 directed the Military Academy. He sided with the right wing of the army.

In 1970 President Juan José Torres was leading Bolivia in a leftist direction, with a People's Assembly of miners, teachers, students and peasants, which angered conservative circles and the Nixon administration. An attempt to unseat him in early 1971 failed and Banzer fled to Argentina. On 17 August 1971 he led a successful uprising from Santa Cruz de la Sierra and on 22 August was given full power. According to Stephen Zunes, the coup had significant clandestine financial and advisory support within the Nixon administration. Torres was killed in exile in Buenos Aires in 1976.

Banzer banned left-leaning parties, suspended the Central Obrera Boliviana and closed the universities. From 1974, when it was clear he would hold no elections, he banned all political activity. Human rights groups claim that several thousand Bolivians sought asylum abroad, 3,000 were arrested, 200 were killed and many were tortured. Foreign credit sustained the regime, and external debt rose to record levels. In 1978, under pressure from the Carter administration, he opened a regulated move to elections. After the vote of 9 July was found to be rigged, Banzer had it annulled, and Juan Pereda overthrew him on 21 July.

He then founded the party Acción Democrática Nacionalista and ran for president in 1979 and 1980, finishing third both times. In 1997 he won by a small plurality, at 71, and returned as president with a grand coalition. In 2000, during the Cochabamba Water War, protests over the privatization of the city's water works led to clashes, and he declared a state of siege. The government declared the contract void in April 2000.

Diagnosed with lung cancer in June 2001, Banzer resigned on 7 August and was succeeded by his vice president, Jorge Quiroga. He died of heart failure at Santa Cruz de la Sierra on 5 May 2002, aged 75. He was the first former dictator in recent Latin American history to return to power by election.
hugo-chavez: Hugo Rafael Chávez Frías was born on 28 July 1954 in the rural village of Sabaneta, in Barinas State, in his paternal grandmother's three-room house. His family was of Amerindian, Afro-Venezuelan, Spanish and Italian descent, and his parents were schoolteachers. At 17 he entered the Venezuelan Academy of Military Sciences in Caracas, where a curriculum known as the Andrés Bello Plan brought in civilian professors to teach the cadets. He served as a communications officer in a counterinsurgency unit and, after fighting a Marxist–Hoxhaist insurgency in Anzoátegui in 1977, began to doubt the army.

Chávez formed a secret cell within the military, later the Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement-200 (MBR-200), inspired by Simón Bolívar, Simón Rodríguez and Ezequiel Zamora. Dissatisfied with a political system based on the Puntofijo Pact, he led it in an unsuccessful coup against President Carlos Andrés Pérez in 1992 and was imprisoned. President Rafael Caldera freed him in 1994. He then founded the Fifth Republic Movement and won the 1998 presidential election with 56.2 per cent of the vote. He took office on 2 February 1999 and was re-elected in 2000, 2006 and 2012.

With the high oil revenues of the 2000s his government nationalised key industries, created Communal Councils and ran the Bolivarian missions to widen access to food, housing, healthcare and education. Poverty and inequality fell between about 2003 and 2007, though structural inequalities remained. Critics point to his packing of the Supreme Court, pressure on the media and rising murder and kidnapping rates. Deficit spending and price controls later proved unsustainable, and shortages and inflation grew.

In June 2011 Chávez announced from Havana that he had had operations, including the removal of a tumour with cancerous cells. He won a fourth election on 7 October 2012, but his inauguration was cancelled because of his treatment, and he died in Caracas on 5 March 2013, aged 58. His ideas form the basis of Chavismo, close to Bolivarianism. He supported regional bodies such as the Union of South American Nations and the television network TeleSUR, and he is regarded across the political spectrum as one of the most influential and controversial figures in the modern history of Venezuela and Latin America.
hugo-grotius: Hugo Grotius, also called Hugo de Groot, was born in Delft on 10 April 1583, during the Dutch Revolt, into a patrician family. His father, who had studied with Justus Lipsius, translated Archimedes and gave his son a humanist education. Grotius entered Leiden University at eleven, and at sixteen published an edition of Martianus Capella's work on the seven liberal arts, which remained a reference for centuries. In 1603 his cousin Captain Jacob van Heemskerk captured the Portuguese carrack Santa Catarina off present-day Singapore, and the Company he served asked Grotius to defend the seizure. His treatise of 1604 to 1605, later called De Jure Praedae, grounded it in natural justice and was not published in full in his lifetime.

Grotius advanced as an associate of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, becoming Pensionary of Rotterdam in 1613. A theological dispute between the followers of Jacobus Arminius, the Remonstrants, and the strongly Calvinist followers of Franciscus Gomarus divided the Republic. Grotius drafted for the States of Holland an edict of toleration, which held that only the tenets needed for civil order should be enforced. When Maurice of Nassau moved against Oldenbarnevelt, Grotius was imprisoned at Loevestein Castle. He escaped hidden in a chest of books and fled to Paris.

In France, where he lived almost continuously from 1621 to 1644, he published in 1625 De jure belli ac pacis, On the Law of War and Peace, dedicated to Louis XIII. Begun in prison, it was an effort to restrain conflict on the basis of a broad moral consensus. In 1634 Sweden named him ambassador to France, a post he kept for ten years.

In the summer of 1645 he left Sweden, was shipwrecked and washed up near Rostock ill, and died there on 28 August 1645. His body was laid in the Nieuwe Kerk in Delft. His thought on natural law influenced Samuel Pufendorf and John Locke, and along with the earlier works of Francisco de Vitoria and Alberico Gentili his writings laid foundations for international law. His influence declined with the rise of positivism, but revived after the First World War.
hugo-junkers: Hugo Junkers was born in Rheydt in the Prussian Rhine Province, the son of a wealthy industrialist. After his Abitur in 1878 he studied at the Technische Hochschulen in Charlottenburg and Aachen and completed his engineering studies in 1883. He first worked in his father's company, then attended lectures by Adolf Slaby, who placed him with the Continental-Gasgesellschaft in Dessau, where he worked on the first opposed-piston engine.

Junkers patented a calorimeter and founded a manufacturing company in 1892; the calorimeter won a gold medal at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. He patented a gas-fired bath boiler the next year and founded Junkers & Co. in 1895. From 1897 to 1912 he was a professor of mechanical engineering at Aachen, while his firm produced calorimeters, gas stoves, pressure regulators and fan heaters.

His aeronautical work began in earnest at the age of 50, with the engineer Hans Reissner. Junkers had a wind tunnel built and invented a hydraulic brake. During the First World War the government forced him to concentrate on military aircraft. In 1915 he developed the Junkers J 1, the first practical all-metal aircraft, with a cantilever wing with almost no external bracing. In 1917 the military inspectorate compelled him to merge his firm with Anthony Fokker's.

The F 13 of 1919 was the first of several civil designs, followed by the Ju 52/3m of 1932, and Junkers helped found airlines including Deutsche Luft Hansa. A Junkers W 33 made the first heavier-than-air crossing of the Atlantic from east to west. He also supported the Bauhaus and helped it move from Weimar to Dessau in 1925.

When the Nazis came to power in 1933 Junkers opposed their rearmament plans. They demanded ownership of all patents and market shares of his remaining companies, under threat of imprisonment for high treason. He was placed under house arrest in 1934 and died on 3 February 1935, his 76th birthday, after a visit from Nazi officials. The designers Andrei Tupolev and William Bushnell Stout drew on his corrugated, light-metal construction.
hugo-spadafora: Hugo Spadafora Franco was born in Chitré on 6 September 1940 and graduated in medicine from the University of Bologna in Italy. He served as a combat medic with the independence guerrillas in the Guinea-Bissau War of Independence. At first a critic of the military regime headed by Omar Torrijos, he later served it as Vice-Minister of Health.

In 1978 he organised the Victoriano Lorenzo Brigade, a group of up to 1,200 Panamanian fighters, to fight the regime of Anastasio Somoza Debayle in Nicaragua. Concerned about growing Soviet and Cuban influence over the Sandinista government and the delay of free elections, he then joined the Sandino Revolutionary Front alongside Edén Pastora, known as Comandante Cero, who had led the seizure of the National Palace in Nicaragua in August 1978. As Manuel Noriega rose to power in Panama, Spadafora denounced Noriega's protection of drug trafficking.

Noriega's forces detained him as he entered Panama from Costa Rica in September 1985. His decapitated body was later found stuffed in a post office bag. The autopsy showed that he had endured hours of severe torture and that his head had been cut off while he was still alive; the head was never found. When President Nicolás Ardito Barletta tried to set up a commission to investigate, Noriega forced him to resign, which increased suspicion that the military had ordered the killing.

The brutality of the murder shocked many and contributed to the worsening of relations between the US and Noriega, whom the US under President George H. W. Bush overthrew by invading Panama in 1989. Under President Guillermo Endara a court found Noriega, tried in absentia, and others of his followers guilty of conspiracy to murder Spadafora. In 2013 the exiled Cuban writer Amir Valle published a biography, Hugo Spadafora: Bajo la Piel del Hombre.
hugo-von-montfort: Hugo, counted as Hugo VII, came from the comital house of Montfort at Bregenz, an old and influential Swabian noble family. Through his mother, Countess Ursula of Ferrette, he was related to the House of Habsburg. As a second son he was prepared for a career in the church. About 1373 he married the Styrian countess Margaret, granddaughter of Count Ulrich V of Pfannberg and widow of Count Hans of Cilli, and her estates around Pfannberg in the Mur valley greatly enlarged the lands of his house.

He spent most of his adult life in Habsburg service: as commander of the ducal Austrian troops in Italy, as Hofmeister of Duke Leopold IV, as governor of Styria from 1412 to 1415, and as Landvogt in the Thurgau, the Aargau and the Black Forest lands of Further Austria. After Margaret's death about 1395 he married Countess Clementia of Toggenburg, in 1399 he acquired Festenburg Castle in eastern Styria, and in 1402 he married a third time, the Bohemian noblewoman Anna of Neuhaus, widow of the Styrian governor Hans of Stadeck.

Hugo wrote songs and rhymed love letters, the Minnebrief, as well as political and didactic speeches. About 1402 he had a first manuscript of his works drawn up, and about 40 of his texts survive in an elaborate codex of 1414. Long overshadowed by his contemporary Oswald von Wolkenstein, he is now regarded as one of the last important representatives of the German Minnesang. He died at Pfannberg, aged 66, and was buried in the parish church of Bruck an der Mur.
huguenots: The term Huguenot was in common use by around 1550 and was originally a term of derision whose source is unclear. One hypothesis links it to Besançon Hugues, a burgomaster who defended Geneva against Catholic Savoy. The Huguenots called themselves reformés. Their numbers grew rapidly between 1555 and 1561, chiefly among nobles and city dwellers, and they held their first national synod in Paris in 1558. They were concentrated in the south and west of France, whereas the Protestants of Alsace, Moselle and Montbéliard were mainly Lutherans.

Eight civil wars between 1562 and 1598 took on a dynastic character, as a feud between the Houses of Bourbon and Guise. The Huguenots were led by Jeanne d'Albret, her son, the future Henry IV, and the princes of Condé. On the eve of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572 the community made up as much as 10 per cent of the French population. Catholics killed thousands of Huguenots in Paris between 24 August and 3 October 1572, and similar massacres followed in Aix, Bordeaux, Lyon, Rouen, Toulouse and other towns. Henry IV, who had converted to Catholicism to gain the crown, issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, giving Protestants equality under the crown and a degree of religious and political freedom.

Rebellions in the 1620s cost the Huguenots their political and military privileges. Louis XIV first sent missionaries, then closed Huguenot schools, excluded them from favoured professions and billeted troops in their homes in the dragonnades. In 1685 the Edict of Fontainebleau revoked the Edict of Nantes and made Protestantism illegal. Some converted, others emigrated, chiefly to the Dutch Republic, England, Brandenburg-Prussia and Switzerland. Persecution ended officially with the Edict of Versailles in 1787, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 gave Protestants equal rights.

The exodus drained France of people who had held important places in society, and the kingdom did not fully recover for years. In England some 40,000 to 50,000 settled, and they founded the silk industry there. In Brandenburg-Prussia, Frederick William granted them privileges by the Edict of Potsdam of 1685. In South Africa many Afrikaners bear French surnames. In 2013 the Reformed Church of France merged with the Evangelical Lutheran Church to form the United Protestant Church of France. In 1985 President François Mitterrand announced a formal apology to the descendants of the Huguenots.
huhanye: Huhanye was born Jihoushan, a son of Xulüquanqu Chanyu. In 59 BCE he rebelled with the help of Wushanmu, and the ruling chanyu, Woyanqudi, soon took his own life, leaving the Xiongnu divided among warring factions. By 55 BCE only two claimants remained, Huhanye and his brother Zhizhi Chanyu, and the two fought each other for the leadership of the confederacy.

Defeated by Zhizhi, Huhanye fled south, submitted to the Han dynasty and travelled to Chang'an to visit Emperor Xuan, who allowed his people to settle in the Yinshan area. Zhizhi also submitted to the Han the following year, but in 48 BCE, seeing that the court favoured his brother, he declared his independence and moved west to attack Fergana and the Wusun. Huhanye moved back north in 43 BCE, and when Zhizhi was killed by the Han at the Battle of Zhizhi in 36 BCE he became the uncontested leader of the Xiongnu.

In 33 BCE Huhanye came again to Chang'an under the tributary arrangements between the two governments and asked to become an imperial son-in-law. Unwilling to give him a real princess, Emperor Yuan had a palace girl chosen instead, and the lady-in-waiting Wang Zhaojun volunteered. She is counted among the Four Beauties of ancient China, beside Xi Shi, Diaochan and Yang Guifei.

Wang Zhaojun became a favourite of Huhanye and bore him two sons, of whom only Yituzhiyashi is recorded as surviving, and two daughters; one of them, Yun, was created Princess Yimuo and later became a powerful figure in Xiongnu politics. Huhanye died in 31 BCE. His sons by several wives followed him in turn as chanyu, among them Fuzhulei Ruodi, Souxie, Juya and Wuzhuliu.
huibin-jang: Lady Jang, of the Indong Jang clan, was the daughter of Jang Hyeong and his second wife, a lady of the Papyeong Yun clan. The Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty mention her charm, and she is widely thought to have been one of the most beautiful women of Joseon. On the recommendation of Prince Dongpyeong, the king's first cousin once removed, she became a lady-in-waiting to Grand Queen Dowager Jaui, the step-great-grandmother of King Sukjong.

Sukjong became infatuated with her while visiting Jaui, but his mother, Queen Dowager Hyeonyeol, who belonged to the Seoin faction, feared she would draw him towards the Namin and expelled her from the palace. After the queen dowager's death in 1683, Queen Min allowed her to return. When the Namin pressed for her son Yi Yun to be named heir, the Seoin argued that Queen Min was still young and could bear a son. Queen Min refused to adopt the boy, and in the purge called the Gisa Hwanguk many were killed, among them Song Si-yeol.

Lady Jang was then raised to the senior first rank with the title hui, meaning auspicious, and soon after appointed queen. Her position weakened after 1693, when Lady Choe of the Haeju Choe clan, the king's new favourite, became a royal consort and urged him to restore Queen Min. In the Gapsul Hwanguk of 1694 Sukjong banished her elder brother Jang Hui-jae and the leaders of the Namin, a purge from which the faction never recovered.

The court then divided over the succession, the Soron supporting her son, Crown Prince Yun, and the Noron the son of Lady Choe, Prince Yeoning. After Queen Min's death, Sukjong was said to have found Lady Jang conspiring with a shaman priestess to curse the queen. Unmoved by the pleas of the Soron, he sentenced her, her mother, her brother and her companions to death, and she was poisoned at Chwiseondang, her residence in Changgyeonggung, on 9 November 1701.

Her tomb, Daebinmyo, stood first in Gwangju and was moved in 1969 to the Seooreung Cluster in Goyang, which also holds the tombs of Sukjong and Queen Inhyeon. Her memorial tablet is kept in Chilgung, which houses the tablets of seven royal consorts who gave birth to kings.
huiguan: Native place was a central part of personal identity in Chinese culture. Men who moved away generally meant to return to the home of their extended family and ancestors for marriage, mourning, retirement and burial, and shared origin could bind migrants together for several generations. The first huiguan in Beijing were probably a response to the move of the capital from Nanjing. Temples to regional deities, government lodgings called di or huitongguan, and trade associations resembled them, but a direct link is uncertain. The first known huiguan outside Beijing date from the Jiajing era (1522–1567).

Guilds spread and became more structured from the mid-1700s. They were called huiguan or gongsuo, the latter based on common occupation, and sought to control their trade, restrain competition and enforce agreements. After the mid-1800s they had to collect tariffs and provide firefighting, policing and other public works, and in Chongqing and Hankou they became unofficial municipal governments. In Beijing the halls of scholar-officials clustered in the Xuannan area near Xuanwu Gate. Kang Youwei and other activists of the Hundred Days' Reform organised in them, and the Kuomintang was founded in Beijing's Huguang Huiguan.

Overseas huiguan usually took in all migrants from an area and took on more of a governing role. In San Francisco the Cantonese district associations joined in 1862 as the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, known as the Chinese Six Companies. During the anti-Chinese agitation of the 1870s newspapers accused them of importing coolies, yet they won many legal challenges to discriminatory laws. In Vietnam such communities became official administrative units in 1807 under Gia Long.

Huiguan were mainly led and paid for by prominent officials or merchants. A director might inherit the post, hold it in annual rotation or be chosen by vote or lot, while hired watchmen or managers ran daily affairs. A small hall offered lodging, an altar and a meeting room; large compounds had kitchens, banquet halls, gardens and opera stages, and in Sichuan at least 1,400 huiguan held regular performances. The annual meeting on the patron deity's birthday brought a feast and an opera. Many also kept coffin repositories and charitable cemeteries, and the Tung Wah Coffin Home in Hong Kong received an estimated 100,000 remains sent home in the early 1900s.
huining-prefecture: Huining Fu, or Shangjing Huiningfu, was a prefecture in the Shangjing region of Manchuria. Its site lies in present-day Acheng District of Harbin, Heilongjiang Province, about 2 km from the district's central urban area. After serving as the first superior capital of the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty, it remained a secondary capital after 1173.

In the early years of the empire the Jurchen rulers brought people from elsewhere in China to their capital. Aguda, Emperor Taizu, resettled captives there during his war against the Khitan-led Liao dynasty, and his successor Wuqimai, Emperor Taizong, who conquered most of northern China from the Northern Song, kept to the policy. Wealthy people and skilled craftsmen were moved from Yanjing and from the Song capital Bianjing, present-day Kaifeng. After Bianjing fell in 1127, the Jurchen generals brought several thousand people north, among them about 470 imperial clansmen, scholars of the imperial academy, eunuchs, doctors, artisans, actors, astronomers and musicians, together with valuable goods.

In Aguda's time the palaces were little more than tents. In 1123 the Jurchens built their first ancestral temples and tombs, where the captured Song emperors Huizong and Qinzong were made to venerate the Jin emperors' ancestors in 1128. In 1124 Emperor Taizong ordered a Han architect, Lu Yanlun, to build a new city on a uniform plan, modelled on Chinese cities and in particular on Bianjing, though much smaller.

Wanyan Liang, the fourth Jin emperor, moved the capital to Yanjing, present-day Beijing, which lay more centrally in the empire and was easier to supply with food; most of his officials are said to have supported the move. In 1157 he had all the palaces of the old capital destroyed. Shangjing still had a part to play: Emperor Shizong, who tried to revive Jurchen language and culture, spent a year there from 1184, hunting, dancing in the traditional way and speaking Jurchen.

The ruins of the city have been found and excavated. The site is a national historical heritage site with a museum open to the public, renovated in late 2005, and many of the objects found there are shown in Harbin.
huitzilopochtli: The name combines huitzilin, hummingbird, and opochtli, left-hand side, and is often translated Left-Handed Hummingbird or Hummingbird of the South. Scholars disagree about its full significance. In one account he was the smallest of four sons of the creator couple, with Quetzalcoatl, Xipe Totec and Tezcatlipoca as brothers. In another, the goddess Coatlicue was made pregnant by a ball of feathers on Mount Coatepec. Her other children conspired to kill her, and Huitzilopochtli burst from her womb in armour, beheaded his sister Coyolxauhqui and scattered his brothers across the sky.

In the legend of the Aubin Codex, Huitzilopochtli told the Aztecs to leave Aztlan and to call themselves Mexica, and guided them on their journey. He told them to build their city where an eagle perched on a cactus, eating a serpent. They settled on an island in Lake Texcoco, the site of Tenochtitlan.

Huitzilopochtli was the solar and war deity of the Mexica and patron god of Tenochtitlan. In myth he is the sun, his siblings the stars and the moon, and the daily sunrise was read as his battle with them. Originally of little importance to the Nahuas, he was raised by Tlacaelel's reform of religion to the level of Quetzalcoatl, Tlaloc and Tezcatlipoca. He was shown as a hummingbird or as a figure with a hummingbird helmet and a blue-painted body. Warriors who died in battle or as sacrifices were thought to join him as hummingbirds.

The Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan was dedicated to him and to the rain god Tlaloc, his shrine red and on the south side, Tlaloc's blue and on the north. At the base of the stairway lay the Coyolxauhqui stone, showing the dismembered goddess, so that the temple recalled the mountain of Coatepec.

Aztec worship held that the sun needed nourishment in human blood and hearts, and that the Mexica as people of the sun had to provide it. Captives were sacrificed on a stone, their hearts cut out and their bodies sent down the pyramid, and a warrior who took a victim rose in the social hierarchy. The month of Panquetzaliztli was his festival, with processions, dances and sacrifices of victims dressed in his costume, and a statue of amaranth seeds and honey was eaten in pieces. The Aztecs reported that about 20,400 prisoners were sacrificed at the reconsecration of the Great Pyramid in 1487, a figure some scholars accept and others consider Aztec propaganda.
hukbalahap: The movement's roots lay in the tenancy of Central Luzon, where landowners, as the export trade in rice, sugar and tobacco grew, raised rents and lent to farmers on harsh terms. Before the war the peasant leader Juan Feleo of the Partido Komunista ng Pilipinas had begun to mobilise peasants in Nueva Ecija, and Pedro Abad Santos had ordered Luis Taruc to do the same in Pampanga. After a conference at Cabiao in February 1942, leaders met on 29 March 1942 at Sitio Bawit, where Tarlac, Pampanga and Nueva Ecija meet, and named the army, with Taruc as commander and Castro Alejandrino as his deputy.

The Huks harassed Japanese troops, attacked the tax collection and seized supplies; the group claimed by late 1943 to have 15,000 to 20,000 fighters and 50,000 reservists. In areas they held they divided large estates among peasants, often killing the landlords. Rival guerrillas such as the American Ray Hunt accused them of murder and plunder, and the Huks were denied United States recognition after the war. In 1945 American forces and other guerrillas disarmed Huk squadrons, and 109 Huk guerrillas were massacred at Malolos.

In 1946 Taruc and other Democratic Alliance candidates won seats but were barred from Congress. After Feleo was abducted and killed in Gapan on 24 August 1946, Taruc returned to the field, and the government outlawed the movement on 6 March 1948. In 1949 Huks ambushed and killed Aurora Quezon, widow of President Manuel L. Quezon, with her daughter and son-in-law. In 1950 the movement renamed itself Hukbong Mapagpalaya ng Bayan.

Government hunter-killer units such as the Nenita force under Major Napoleon Valeriano used terror against civilians as well as rebels. From 1950 American aid under President Harry Truman and Ramon Magsaysay as defence minister changed the campaign: battalion combat teams grew to twenty-six, and on 18 October 1950 the party secretariat was captured in Manila. The Huks numbered fewer than 2,000 by 1954, and Operation Thunder-Lightning ended with Taruc's surrender. In the 1960s Pedro Taruc, a distant nephew, led what remained. A monument at Cabiao honours their wartime resistance.
hulagu-khan: Hulagu, also written Hulegu or Hülegü, was born around 1217 to Tolui, a son of Genghis Khan, and Sorghaghtani Beki, an influential Keraite princess. He was a brother of Möngke Khan, Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke. Little is known of his childhood. His mother, a Christian of the Church of the East, arranged for all her sons to become Mongol leaders, and Hulagu was friendly to Christianity; his favourite wife, Doquz Khatun, and his closest friend and general, Kitbuqa, were also Christians.

Möngke, installed as Great Khan in 1251, charged Hulagu with conquering or destroying the remaining Muslim states of south-western Asia, including the Abbasid Caliphate. Two-tenths of the empire's fighting men were gathered for his army in 1253. The Lurs were destroyed and the Assassins surrendered their fortress of Alamut in early 1256. He chose Azerbaijan as his base.

The army set out for Baghdad in November 1257, and the Mongols laid siege on 29 January 1258. The city surrendered on 10 February, and the Mongols entered on 13 February and began a week of destruction, including that of the Grand Library. Death counts vary widely, from a low estimate of about 90,000 to a million. In 1260 the Mongols took Aleppo and Damascus, but Hulagu then withdrew most of his force and left for Mongolia over the succession after Möngke's death. At the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260 the Mamluks of Qutuz and Baybars destroyed the Mongol force left behind.

After Kublai became Great Khan, Hulagu returned to his lands by 1262. He was drawn into war with Berke Khan of the Golden Horde, a Muslim convert who had allied with the Mamluks, and suffered a severe defeat north of the Caucasus in 1263. He sent letters to Europe seeking an alliance, among them one of 10 April 1262 to Louis IX of France, but never gained one. He fell ill in January 1265 and died on 8 February 1265; he was buried on Shahi Island in Lake Urmia, and his tomb has never been found.

He founded the Ilkhanate. He employed Shams al-Din Juvayni as sahib-divan, while Ata-Malik Juvayni governed Baghdad and helped repair it, and he patronised Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, for whom the Maragheh observatory was built.
huldrych-zwingli: Zwingli was born on 1 January 1484 at Wildhaus in the Toggenburg valley, the third of eleven children in a farming family. His father Ulrich was the chief local magistrate. At ten he was sent to Basel for secondary schooling. He studied at the University of Vienna and then at Basel, where he received his Master of Arts in 1506. He served as a pastor in Glarus and later in Einsiedeln, and the writings of Erasmus influenced him.

On 1 January 1519 Zwingli gave his first sermon as people's priest of the Grossmünster in Zurich. Instead of preaching on the Sunday's set Gospel, he read through Matthew verse by verse, and went on through the rest of the New Testament and the Old. In Lent 1522 he and about a dozen others ate sausages in breach of the fast, and the Affair of the Sausages is considered the start of the Reformation in Switzerland. After the first Zurich disputation, on 29 January 1523, the city council allowed him to go on preaching. Zurich severed its ties with the bishop of Constance in 1524 and replaced the Mass with a new communion liturgy in 1525.

Zwingli clashed with the Anabaptists, and after a public debate on 17 January 1525 the council ordered those who refused to have their children baptised to leave Zurich. A Christian Civic Union of Reformed cities was formed in 1528. At the Marburg Colloquy in 1529 he and Martin Luther agreed on many points but not on the Real Presence in the Eucharist, which Zwingli took to be symbolic.

In 1531 the Reformed alliance's food blockade of the Catholic cantons failed. The cantons attacked when Zurich was ill-prepared, and Zwingli died on the battlefield on 11 October 1531. The Zurich council chose Heinrich Bullinger as his successor, who defended him as a prophet and martyr and consolidated his reforms. Zwingli's legacy lives on in the confessions, liturgy and church orders of the Reformed churches.
huliaipole: Huliaipole, whose Ukrainian name means walk-about field, lies in the valley of the Haichul river in Polohy Raion of Zaporizhzhia Oblast. The name of the river is derived from Turkic words meaning free and steppe. The town is 98 kilometres from the regional centre of Zaporizhzhia and 8 kilometres from the railway station of the same name. It is a small city; in January 2022 its estimated population was 12,786.

Before the Russian Empire annexed the Crimean Khanate, the area was settled mostly by Zaporozhian Cossacks and the nomadic Lesser Nogai Horde. The settlement arose in the 1770s after the Dnieper defensive line was built on former lands of the Zaporozhian Sich. When Catherine the Great dissolved the Sich, local Cossacks fled or were brought into serfdom under the Shabelskiys. In 1785 the Yekaterinoslav Governorate ordered a state military settlement founded here for protection from the Crimean Khanate. Its name reflected the fairs that had long been held on the spot.

From the middle of the nineteenth century the village became a commercial and industrial town. The first trades fair took place in 1859, with more than fifty trading companies and a turnover of 1 million rubles. Factories making agricultural machinery opened from 1882, and the Chaplyne–Berdyansk railway was laid nearby in 1898. Between 1917 and 1921, in the turbulence of the Russian Civil War and the Ukrainian War of Independence, the town changed hands no fewer than sixteen times, among Austro-Hungarian forces, the Red Army, the Ukrainian People's Republic, the Hetmanate, Anton Denikin's White Army and Nestor Makhno's Insurgent Army. It became widely known as the headquarters of the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine and the capital of the Makhnovshchina.

Huliaipole gained city status in 1938 during rapid industrial development in the 1930s; at least 108 of its residents died in the Holodomor of 1932–1933. German forces occupied it on 5 October 1941, and Soviet troops retook it on 16 September 1943.

Notable natives include Makhno himself, born in 1888, and the anarchists Semen Karetnyk, Oleksiy Marchenko and Voldemar Antoni, who founded the Union of Poor Peasants. After Ukrainian independence the town's economy rested on an agricultural machinery plant, a paint plant, a shoe factory and food enterprises. In 2020 the city became part of Polohy Raion.
hulu-guang: Hulü Guang, courtesy name Mingyue, was an ethnic Tiele, probably the eldest son of Hulü Jin, a Chile chieftain who helped the general Gao Huan take control of the Northern Wei state and was treated by him almost as an equal. Known in youth for his horsemanship and archery, Hulü Guang once shot the secretary of the Western Wei leader Yuwen Tai, Mozhe Hui, during a campaign, leading to his capture, and Gao Huan made him a general. In 547 he was created Viscount of Yongle and served against the rebel general Hou Jing.

Under Emperor Wenxuan of Northern Qi he fought the Kumo Xi in 552 and as a border governor took a number of minor cities from Northern Zhou. In 560 he became governor of Bing Province and Duke of Julu. His first daughter married the crown prince Gao Bainian, who was killed by Emperor Wucheng in 564; she refused food and died a month later. In 564 he held off the southern prong of a Northern Zhou and Tujue attack and, with Duan Shao and Gao Changgong, the Prince of Lanling, relieved Luoyang. His second daughter became empress of Gao Wei.

On his father's death in 567 he inherited the title of Prince of Xianyang. In 570 and 571 he defeated Yuwen Xian at Yiyang and built forts north of the Fen River. When the prince Gao Yan killed the powerful official He Shikai in 571, Hulü stood by the emperor and broke up Gao Yan's troops. The historian Li Yanshou describes him as frugal, disliking music and beautiful women, refusing gifts, sharing his soldiers' hardships and never losing a battle from his youth.

He made enemies of the officials Zu Ting, whom he scorned as a blind man in power, and Mu Tipo, whose request to marry his daughter by a concubine he had refused. The Northern Zhou general Wei Xiaokuan spread songs in couplets near Yecheng playing on Hulü's names, hinting that he would rise. Zu added lines of his own, and a subordinate, Feng Shirang, claimed that Hulü had plotted a coup when he brought his army near the capital in 571.

On 22 August 572 Gao Wei had his guard commander Liu Taozhi strangle him in the palace. Almost all his clan was killed, sparing only a young grandson, Hulü Zhong. Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou declared a general pardon at the news, and on entering Yecheng later said that he could not have reached it had Hulü lived.
hulwan: Hulwan stood at the entrance of the Paytak Pass. Later Arab tradition, recorded by al-Tabari, made it a foundation of the Sasanian king Kavadh I, but the town was far older: in Assyrian times it was known as Khalmanu and lay on the border between Babylonia and Media. The Seleucids called it Chala, capital of the district of Chalonitis. Diodorus Siculus derived the name from Greek captives from Boeotia whom Xerxes settled there, founding the town of Celonae.

Under the Sasanian Empire the district was called Khusraw Shad Peroz, the joy of Khusraw the victorious, and the city probably Peroz Kavad. Though it belonged with the rest of Media to the quarter of the North, Khosrau II placed it in the quarter of the West, with Mesopotamia, as the kings began to use the Zagros as a summer retreat from Ctesiphon. After the Battle of Qadisiyya in 636 the last Sasanian ruler, Yazdegerd III, took refuge in Hulwan, leaving it after his defeat at Jalula in 637. The pursuing Arabs under Jarir ibn Abdallah Bajali took the town, garrisoning it with troops that included Persian defectors, the Khamra.

Until the 10th century Hulwan was a flourishing town on the Khurasan Road, the first town of the Jibal province on the way east from Baghdad, though it remained fiscally tied to the Sawad of Mesopotamia. Under Mu'awiya I it became the capital of western Jibal. Ibn Hawqal found it half the size of Dinavar, with houses of stone and brick and abundant dates, pomegranates and figs; its dried figs were widely exported. Al-Muqaddasi describes a wall with eight gates, a mosque and a synagogue, and between the 8th and 12th centuries it was a metropolitan province of the Church of the East.

Around the turn of the 11th century the semi-independent Annazid dynasty governed Hulwan until the Kakuyids drove them out. The Seljuq Turks took and burned the town in 1046, and an earthquake in 1049 completed its destruction. It was rebuilt, and its site is now the town of Sarpol-e Zahab, on the road between the Mesopotamian lowlands and the Iranian plateau.
humaid-bin-abdullah-al-qasimi: Humaid bin Abdullah was a nephew of Salim bin Sultan Al Qasimi. When Salim became Ruler of Sharjah in 1868, after the death of his brother Khalid bin Sultan, Humaid took the post of Wali, or governor, of Ras Al Khaimah, and in the following year he proclaimed its independence from Sharjah. An earlier scheme by the Saudi agent in Buraimi, Turki Bin Ahmed, to make Humaid Ruler of Sharjah failed and led to violence in Sharjah.

In May 1869 Salim bin Sultan and his brother Ibrahim moved against Humaid to make Ibrahim Ruler of Ras Al Khaimah, landing 1,500 men from 32 boats. Humaid was backed by some 500 men landed from Umm Al Quwain, and fighting took place at Jazirat Al Hamrah and in Ras Al Khaimah town. Because sending troops by sea breached the Maritime Truce, the British Resident, Colonel Lewis Pelly, sailed from Lingeh with the gunboat Hugh Rose, arrived on 12 May and ordered Salim and Ibrahim to withdraw by sunset the next day.

Alliances shifted quickly. In 1871 Humaid and the Ruler of Umm Al Quwain supported Salim when he used Ibrahim's absence in Abu Dhabi to retake full control of Sharjah, and at the same time Humaid recovered the dependencies of Sha'am, Rams and Shimal, which had broken away from his rule. In 1882 a quarrel with Ahmad bin Abdullah Al Mualla of Umm Al Quwain turned into open fighting after seven Umm Al Quwain boats raided Rams. The British censured and fined Umm Al Quwain's ruler, Ajman backed Umm Al Quwain on land while members of the Na'im backed Ras Al Khaimah, and Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi mediated an end to the affair.
When Sha'am tried to secede again in 1885, Humaid made it pay a fine of 1,600 Marie Theresa dollars. On his death in 1900, Saqr bin Khalid Al Qasimi, the Ruler of Sharjah, took over Ras Al Khaimah.
human-rights-act-1998: The European Convention on Human Rights was drafted by the Council of Europe after the Second World War, under the oversight of Sir David Maxwell-Fyfe, who chaired the committee on legal and administrative questions of the council's Consultative Assembly from 1949 to 1952. As a founding member of the council, the United Kingdom acceded to the convention in March 1951, but British citizens could bring claims before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg only from the 1960s.

During the 1980s groups such as Charter 88, which invoked the 300th anniversary of the Glorious Revolution and the Bill of Rights 1689, argued that a new British Bill of Rights was needed. The Labour Party pledged in its manifesto for the 1997 general election to incorporate the convention, and after its landslide victory the government of Tony Blair set out its plan in the White Paper Rights Brought Home. The act received royal assent on 9 November 1998.

Section 3 requires courts to read past and future legislation, so far as possible, in a way compatible with Convention rights, by reading words in, reading them out or choosing a compliant meaning. Where that cannot be done, sections 4 and 10 let higher courts issue a declaration of incompatibility, which does not invalidate the law but allows a minister to amend it by a remedial order approved by resolutions of each House of Parliament.

Section 6 counts courts and tribunals among public authorities, so the act also reaches disputes between private citizens. Section 19 requires a minister introducing a bill to state whether it is compatible. A late amendment, section 21(5), abolished the death penalty for the military offences that still carried it.

The first case invoking the act was brought by The Times in October 2000. In 2008 Paul Dacre, editor of the Daily Mail, criticised it for creating a right to privacy that Parliament had never passed. Constitutional critics argued that it gave unelected judges power over government policy, and the scholar Paul Craig held that it led courts to strained readings of statutes. Other critics said it hindered the deportation of foreign criminals and terrorism suspects.

In 2005 the Conservatives under Michael Howard promised to overhaul or scrap the act. In 2007 his successor David Cameron vowed to replace it with a Bill of Rights for Britain, and in 2014 the Conservative Party planned its repeal. Section 3 does not apply to the Illegal Migration Act 2023.
human-sacrifice: Human sacrifice is the killing of one or more people as part of a ritual. It is typically meant to please or appease gods, a human ruler, a priestly figure or the spirits of dead ancestors. Its forms include retainer sacrifice, in which a monarch's servants are killed so that they may go on serving him in the next life. The reasons given are those that motivate religious sacrifice in general: to bring good fortune, to pacify the gods when a temple or bridge is dedicated, to win favour in war, or to promote fertility, as in sacrifices to the Aztec god of agriculture Xipe Totec. Closely related practices in some tribal societies are cannibalism and headhunting.

The practice is found in many societies from prehistoric times. At Herxheim in southwestern Germany a Linear Pottery enclosure of the fifth millennium BCE held the fragmented remains of more than 1,000 individuals, and whether they were war captives, sacrificial victims or victims of other ritual violence is debated. At Abydos in early dynastic Egypt there may be evidence of servants buried with a king, but any such evidence disappears at about 2800 BCE. In China the Shang practised sacrifice on a large scale: at least 14,197 victims are mentioned in inscriptions. Slaves were buried alive with their owners under the Shang and Zhou, and Ximen Bao of Wei outlawed the drowning of victims to the river god Hebo.

In the Americas it continued, to varying degrees, until European colonisation. For the re-consecration of the Great Pyramid of Tenochtitlan in 1487 the Aztecs reported that they killed about 80,400 prisoners over four days, while Ross Hassig puts the number between 10,000 and 80,400. In Tahiti, during James Cook's visit in 1777, the chief Tina offered a servant to the war god ʻOro before a campaign. In West Africa the Annual Customs of Dahomey were the most notorious example, and sacrifices followed the deaths of kings and queens, with recorded cases of hundreds or thousands of slaves killed; Rudolph Rummel reports as many as 4,000 in 1727.

By the Iron Age, with the religious developments of the Axial Age, the practice was becoming less common across Africa, Europe and Asia, and in classical antiquity it came to be looked down on as barbaric. Greek myth may preserve a memory of its abandonment: Iphigenia, whom her father Agamemnon was to sacrifice to Artemis, is saved by the goddess, who substitutes a deer. In India human and animal sacrifice became less common after the Vedic period as ahimsa, non-violence, entered mainstream religious thought. Judaism explicitly forbids human sacrifice as murder, and Jews see the Akedah as central to its abolition. Modern secular laws treat it as murder.
humayun: Humayun was born Nasir al-Din Muhammad on 6 March 1508, the son of Babur and his favourite wife Māham Begum. On 26 December 1530 he succeeded his father at 22, an inexperienced ruler. His half-brother Kamran Mirza inherited Kabul and Kandahar, and the two became bitter rivals. Babur had divided his lands between sons, a Central Asian practice since Genghis Khan, and not all nobles saw Humayun as the rightful successor.

Humayun's first campaign was against Sher Shah Suri in Bihar, but he broke it off to annex Gujarat, Malwa and the fort of Mandu. While he was there, Sher Shah invaded Bengal and besieged its capital Gaur, and its wealth gave him a war chest. At the battle of Kannauj on 17 May 1540 Humayun was soundly defeated and retreated to Lahore. Kamran offered to join Sher Shah against him, but Humayun refused to kill his brother, citing Babur's last words: do nothing against your brothers, even though they may deserve it.

He withdrew across the Thar Desert, where his wife Hamida Bano, eight months pregnant, was left without a horse; he later called it the lowest point of his life. He crossed the Indus on 11 July 1543 and fled with a small party to the Safavid Shah Tahmasp I, who received him as a royal guest at Herat. With 14,000 Persian soldiers he besieged Kandahar from 21 March 1545 and entered Kabul on 18 November 1545. At the Battle of Sirhind on 22 June 1555 his general Bairam Khan decisively defeated Sikandar Shah Suri, and the Mughal Empire was re-established.

On 24 January 1556 Humayun was descending the staircase of his library, Sher Mandal, with his arms full of books when the muezzin called the prayer. Trying to kneel, he caught his foot in his robe, fell several steps and struck his temple on a stone edge. He died three days later.
