He was buried at last in Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, commissioned by his chief wife Bega Begum, the first very grand garden tomb of Mughal architecture, which set the precedent for the Taj Mahal. His return from Persia brought Persian noblemen to the Mughal court and changed its culture, and he left a substantial legacy to his son Akbar.
humayun-shah-bahmani: Alauddin Humayun Shah Bahmani was the eldest son of Alau'd-din Ahmad Shah. When his father died, a group of nobles that included Saif Khan, Mallu Khan and Shah Habibullah raised his younger brother Hasan Khan to the throne instead. Humayun, with a personal guard of eighty horsemen, seized it for himself. Saif Khan was executed, Mallu Khan fled to the Carnatic, and Hasan Khan and Shah Habibullah were imprisoned.

On his accession Humayun made Mahmud Gawan lieutenant of the kingdom and governor of Bijapur, with the title Malik-ut-Tujjar. His cousin Sikandar Khan, given charge of Telangana, was dissatisfied and rebelled with the support of his father Jalal Khan and local Velama chiefs, marching on Golconda. Sikandar refused the peace Humayun offered and was killed in the battle that followed. While the sultan was in Telangana, Hasan Khan escaped from prison by fraud and proclaimed himself king at Bir, but he was defeated, fled towards Vijayanagara, and was taken by Siraj Khan Junaidi and sent back to the capital.

In 1460 Hasan and his followers were brought to Bidar, and the punishments for which Humayun became known followed: Hasan was thrown to a tiger, some of his companions were cast into boiling cauldrons, and elephants and other wild animals were set upon others.

Humayun died on 1 September 1461, either naturally or killed in his sleep by a maidservant. His wife Nargis Begum, a granddaughter of Taj ud-Din Firuz Shah, became regent for their son; two sons became the twelfth and thirteenth sultans. Firishta calls him Zalim, the Cruel, but modern scholars such as Haroon Khan Sherwani and Ghulam Yazdani hold that his cruelty has been exaggerated, Sherwani calling him a ruler of the "ordinary Bahmani type" and a strict disciplinarian. Legend says his tomb in the Bahmani tombs complex split when his body was laid in it; the damage came from a 19th-century lightning strike.
humayuns-tomb: Humayun died on 27 January 1556. His body was first buried in his palace in the Purana Quila at Delhi, then taken to Sirhind in Punjab by Khanjar Beg. His widow and chief consort, Bega Begum, devoted herself to building a memorial that would be the grandest mausoleum in the Mughal empire. According to the Ain-i-Akbari she supervised the work after returning from the Hajj. Construction began in 1565 and ended in 1572, and the whole cost of 1.5 million rupees was paid by her. The emperor Akbar visited the tomb in 1571, when it was nearly complete.

The site beside the Yamuna was chosen for its nearness to the Nizamuddin Dargah, the shrine of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya, whom the rulers of Delhi revered. Abd al-Qadir Bada'uni, one of the few contemporary historians to mention the building, says the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, whom the empress chose and brought from Herat, designed it. His son Sayyid Muhammad completed it.

The tomb is built of rubble masonry and red sandstone, clad in white marble, which is also used for the floors, lattice screens, door frames, eaves and the main dome. It stands on a vaulted terrace eight metres high and is essentially square, with chamfered corners that make it look octagonal. A high rubble wall encloses the complex, entered through two double-storeyed gateways 16 metres high. The terrace holds fifty-six cells with over 100 graves.

It stands at the centre of a 30-acre charbagh, a Persian-style garden divided into four squares by paved walkways and two crossing water channels that recall the four rivers of paradise. Each square is divided again into smaller gardens, 32 in all. It was the first such garden on this scale in South Asia, and the first structure to use red sandstone on such a scale. The tomb was modelled on Gur-e Amir, the tomb of Timur at Samarkand.

The tomb marked a leap in Mughal architecture and set a precedent for later royal mausolea, which reached their height in the Taj Mahal at Agra. Beside Humayun it holds the graves of Bega Begum, Dara Shikoh and several later Mughals, among them Jahandar Shah, Farrukhsiyar and Alamgir II. When William Finch visited in 1611 he described the central chamber richly furnished with carpets.

The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, took refuge here with three princes during the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and was captured by Captain Hodson and exiled to Rangoon. The tomb became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture and the Archaeological Survey of India restored the gardens and water channels between about 1999 and 2003.
humber: The Humber is formed at Trent Falls by the meeting of the tidal rivers Ouse and Trent. From there to the North Sea it forms part of the boundary between the East Riding of Yorkshire on the north bank and North Lincolnshire on the south bank, and it is tidal throughout. The River Hull joins it at Kingston upon Hull, and it reaches the sea between Cleethorpes and the headland of Spurn Head. During the Ice Age the Humber had a much longer freshwater course across Doggerland, now submerged beneath the North Sea. Ptolemy recorded it in the 2nd century as Ábou (Latin Abus), a name from an early Celtic word meaning "moving water".

The Humber appears regularly in medieval British literature. In the Welsh Triads it is one of the three principal rivers of Britain with the Thames and the Severn, and in Geoffrey of Monmouth's chronicle it is named for Humber the Hun, an invader who drowned there in battle. It remained an important boundary in the Anglo-Saxon period, separating Northumbria from the southern kingdoms; the name Northumbria means the people north of the Humber. Ptolemy gives the Coritani as the Iron Age tribe south of the Humber and the Parisi as the tribe to the north.

A ferry route from Hessle to Barton-upon-Humber is noted in the Domesday Book and in a charter of 1281. Steam ferries from Hull to New Holland began in 1841 and ran until the Humber Bridge opened in 1981. Until 1974 the Humber formed part of the boundary between Yorkshire and Lincolnshire, and from 1974 to 1996 the counties on both banks together formed Humberside. The Humber Forts at the mouth of the estuary were planned in 1914, begun in 1915 and completed in 1919, and abandoned for military use in 1956. On 23 August 1921 the airship R38 crashed into the estuary near Hull, killing 44 of the 49 crew.

The ports on the Humber include Hull, Grimsby and Immingham, and the estuary is navigable for the largest deep-sea vessels. It is used by wintering birds and forms part of the Severn-Trent flyway, a route for migratory birds crossing Great Britain. Salmon, sole, cod, eel and flounder are among the fish caught in it.
humbert-i-count-of-savoy: Humbert was the son of Amadeus, who may or may not have preceded him as count of Maurienne. His brother was Bishop Otto of Belley. The origins of the family are unknown: his ancestors are variously said to have come from Saxony, Burgundy or Provence. Because Humbert had close connections with Rudolf III of Burgundy, it is likely that his family was Burgundian, descended either from the dukes of Vienne or from an aristocratic family such as the Guigonids, ancestors of the counts of Albon. He was probably also related to Ermengarde of Burgundy, the second wife of Rudolf III. He first held lands around Belley and in the county of Sermorens, before gaining lands in Aosta and Valais.

His service to the Holy Roman Emperors Henry II and Conrad II was rewarded with the counties of Maurienne and Aosta and lands in Valais, all at the expense of local bishops and archbishops. After Rudolf III died in 1032, Humbert swore fealty to Conrad II. He supported the emperor in his campaigns against Odo II, Count of Blois, and Aribert, Archbishop of Milan. In return Conrad appointed him count of Savoy and granted him Maurienne, Chablais and perhaps Tarentaise. These grants to a loyal supporter secured key passes through the Alps, which controlled trade between Italy and Western Europe, and they formed the core of Savoy power for centuries.

Humbert married a woman named Ancelie, also written Auxilia or Ancilia. She may have been the daughter of Anselme of Aoste, or of the master of ceremonies of Burgundy, or a member of a northern Italian dynasty known as the Anselmids. They had at least four sons. Amadeus I and Otto both became counts of Savoy in succession, Aymon was Bishop of Sion and Burchard was Archbishop of Lyon. Humbert is often said to have died at Hermillon, in the Maurienne region of present-day Savoie, France. His descendants, the House of Savoy, held the county and expanded from it.
humbert-ii-of-viennois: Humbert was a son of Dauphin John II of Viennois and Beatrice of Hungary, of the local line of Counts of Albon. His domains, the Dauphiné, belonged to the Kingdom of Burgundy (Arles) under the suzerainty of the Holy Roman Empire. He spent his youth at Naples, and contemporaries thought him incompetent and extravagant, without his brother's warlike ardour. In July 1332 he married Marie of Baux, a niece of King Robert of Naples; their only son, Andrew, died aged two in October 1335.

Humbert inherited the Dauphiné in 1333 on the death of his brother Guigues VIII, in the middle of a war with Aymon, Count of Savoy, and within a year King Philip VI of France brokered a truce. He declined the Kingdom of Arles when Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor, offered it, fearing the conflicts it would bring. His court settled at Beauvoir-en-Royans, and rather than impose oppressive taxes he emptied his treasury. He offered his inheritance to Robert of Naples, then tried in 1339 to sell it to Pope Benedict XII; from 1343 he negotiated with Philip VI, and in 1344 John, Duke of Normandy, was named his heir.

In May 1345 Humbert sailed from Marseille at the head of a papal fleet for the Second Smyrniote Crusade against the Aydınids, founding the Order of Saint Catherine during his command. The fighting for Smyrna in 1346 preceded 56 years of Christian rule over the city, until Timur took it in 1402. In 1349 he sold his domains for 400,000 écus and an annual pension, on the condition that the Dauphiné remain a distinct feudal polity outside the French realm, and before the sale he issued the Delphinal Statute exempting it from many taxes.

After giving up his lands Humbert entered the Dominican Order and within two years became Latin Patriarch of Alexandria. He consecrated Rodolphe de Chissé as Bishop of Grenoble in 1351. He died at Clermont-en-Auvergne in 1355, aged 43, and was buried in the church of the Couvent des Jacobins in Paris, which has since been demolished. The Delphinal Statute was long debated in the region, as local leaders used it to defend their autonomy against the state.
humberto-castelo-branco: Humberto de Alencar Castelo Branco was born on 20 September 1897 into a wealthy family of north-eastern Brazil with roots in Portugal. His father, Cândido Borges Castelo Branco, was a general, and his mother, Antonieta de Alencar, belonged to the family of the writer José de Alencar. He joined the army at the Rio Pardo Military School, entered the Military School of Realengo in 1918 and was commissioned a second lieutenant in 1921. He took part in the Revolution of 1930 and later studied at the French War College.

In the Second World War he headed the operations section of the Brazilian Expeditionary Force in Italy, where he planned manoeuvres at the Battle of Monte Castello and gained great prestige, according to Marshal Cordeiro de Farias. As a general he commanded the Command and General Staff College from 1954 to 1956, and he was chief of staff of the army from 13 September 1963 until April 1964.

Castelo Branco was one of the leaders of the 1964 coup that overthrew Goulart. Congress chose him on 11 April to complete Goulart's term, and he took the oath on 15 April 1964. The First Institutional Act gave him emergency powers, including the power to cancel the political rights of subversive elements for ten years, and he intended to hand power to a civilian in 1966, but hard-line officers backed by War Minister Artur da Costa e Silva wished to stay in power. When opposition candidates won the governorships of Minas Gerais and Guanabara in October 1965, he refused to annul the results, and Costa e Silva persuaded the hard-liners to accept them in return for a promise of a tougher policy.

On 27 October 1965 he issued the Second Institutional Act, which abolished all existing political parties, restored his emergency powers and extended his term to 1967. Two parties replaced them: the pro-government National Renewal Alliance, ARENA, and the opposition Brazilian Democratic Movement, MDB. In 1967 a commission of jurists drafted a new constitution, and a press law, which remained valid until 2009, was issued near the end of his term. His government relied on loans from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and on American investment. He was succeeded by Costa e Silva at midnight on 15 March 1967.

Four months after leaving office Castelo Branco died on 18 July 1967 in a mid-air collision of two Piper aircraft near Fortaleza. He belonged to a more liberal legalist faction within the regime, as opposed to his more authoritarian successors, and he was the first leader of the military regime that lasted after the coup of 1964.
humboldt-university-of-berlin: The university arose during the Prussian Reform Movement on the initiative of the philosopher and linguist Wilhelm von Humboldt, with Johann Gottlieb Fichte and Friedrich Schleiermacher, under King Frederick William III. It was housed in the palace built for Prince Henry of Prussia, brother of Frederick the Great, on Unter den Linden. Humboldt met great resistance and submitted his resignation to the King in April 1810, so he was absent when it opened.

The first students were admitted on 6 October 1810 and the first semester began on 10 October, with 256 students and 52 lecturers in faculties of law, medicine, theology and philosophy. The university keeps 15 October 1810 as its opening date. It set up the world's first academic chair in history. From 1828 to 1945 it was named the Royal Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin.

In the 19th century the university grew to take in many new disciplines, and modern research facilities aided the natural sciences. Researchers such as the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz and the physicians Rudolf Virchow and Robert Koch built its fame. It absorbed other Berlin colleges, among them the Charité, which became its medical campus by 1829. Its principle of uniting teaching and research served as a model elsewhere, for institutions such as Johns Hopkins University.

After 1933 the Nazi regime affected the university like all German universities. Under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, 250 Jewish professors and employees were dismissed in 1933-1934, and nearly a third of the staff was fired in all. On 10 May 1933 some 20,000 books were taken from libraries to be burned in the Opernplatz, now Bebelplatz.

After the Second World War the university lay in East Berlin and reopened in 1946 under the Soviet Military Administration, which required lectures to be approved by Socialist Unity Party officials. The Free University of Berlin was founded in West Berlin in 1948. Because the old name had monarchic origins, the university was renamed in 1949 after the brothers Alexander and Wilhelm von Humboldt.

After German reunification it was restructured by commissions led by West German professors. Alumni and faculty include Hegel, Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, Otto von Bismarck, W. E. B. Du Bois, Albert Einstein, Max Planck and the Brothers Grimm.
hummay: Most versions of the girgam, the royal chronicle of Kanem, make Hummay the son of his direct predecessor, Selema I, also called Abd al-Jalil, and several sources call him ibn Abd al-Jalil or give him the epithet Jilmi, son of Jil. His mother, Tigiram, came from the Kay or Koyam people of Dirkou. The chronicle closes its account of Selema with the words that it will now set down the history of the Banū Ḥummay, and the change of dynasty has therefore often been read, as Barth read it in 1857, as a change of religion within one royal lineage.

What the dynastic shift means remains unclear. Hummay may have overthrown Selema and been linked to the old line only later, as his supposed son, in the royal chronicle. The historian Hiribarren suggested in 2016 that he took power with the help of a pro-Islamic faction at court. Because Kanem is generally thought to have been founded by the Zaghawa, who appear in the 12th century as separate nomads in the north-east, his rise has also been linked to a possible expulsion of the Zaghawa, with Selema as their last ruler of Kanem.

Although Hummay was of local origin, possibly Kanembu, he and his dynasty claimed descent from the Yemeni noble Saif ibn Dhi Yazan, a claim to Arab origin of the kind other African Muslim dynasties of his time also made for prestige. The further spread of Islam in his reign may have caused dissension, leading the Toubou to break from imperial rule and move east.

Hummay is recorded to have died in Masr, that is Egypt, and one source names the place as Rukana, of many mosques, which suggests that he meant to make, or had made, the pilgrimage to Mecca. He was succeeded by his son Dunama I Umemi. The Sayfawa dynasty that later tradition traced to him ruled the Kanem–Bornu Empire until 1846, one of the longest-ruling dynasties in world history.
humphrey-gilbert: Humphrey Gilbert was the fifth son of Otho Gilbert of Compton, Greenway and Galmpton in Devon and of Catherine Champernowne. He was a maternal half-brother of Sir Walter Raleigh. Gilbert was educated at Eton College and the University of Oxford, where he learned French and Spanish and studied war and navigation, and his mentor was Sir Henry Sidney. He was wounded at the siege of Newhaven, in Le Havre, in June 1563.

From 1566 Gilbert served in Ireland under Sidney against Shane O'Neill, and after O'Neill's assassination in 1567 he became governor of Ulster. In 1569 he took part in the fighting that followed the first Desmond Rebellion, capturing thirty to forty castles in Kerry and Connello. Thomas Churchyard recorded that he had the heads of the dead laid along the path to his tent to terrify the people. Sidney knighted him in 1570, and he sat in the English Parliament for Plymouth in 1571.

In 1566 he argued before Queen Elizabeth for a Northwest Passage to Cathay, and Martin Frobisher's voyage of 1576 grew from the support he won. In 1573 he proposed an academy in London, which Sir Thomas Gresham eventually realised as Gresham College. After letters patent of 11 June 1578 he sailed with seven vessels that November, but storms scattered the fleet and forced it back some six months later. Failed expeditions exhausted his family fortune.

In June 1583 Gilbert sailed for North America with five vessels. On 5 August 1583 he took possession of Newfoundland for the English Crown at St. John's, by cutting turf in the manner of English common law. He claimed authority over the fish stations and taxed the fishermen. The ship Delight then ran aground on Sable Island after he ordered a controversial change of course, and only sixteen of its crew survived. He decided on 31 August to turn back.

On 9 September his small ship, the Squirrel, was nearly overwhelmed by heavy seas near the Azores. Gilbert refused to move to the larger Golden Hind and was seen reading in the stern. At midnight the Squirrel's lights went out, and the ship was lost with all hands. A. L. Rowse described him as passionate, impulsive and liable to violence and cruelty, but also visionary and original. His claim was realised in 1610, and the royal charter granted to Raleigh in 1584 drew in part on his patent.
humphrey-ii-of-toron: Humphrey II was born in 1117, the son of Humphrey I of Toron. He had become lord of Toron some time before 1140, when he married the daughter of Renier Brus, lord of Banias, the Herodian city of Caesarea Philippi, and so added Banias to his lands. In 1149, when Hebron became a domain of the royal family of Jerusalem, he was made its castellan.

He became constable when King Baldwin III became sole ruler after a struggle with his mother, Queen Melisende, and was with the king at the Siege of Ascalon. In 1157 Nur ad-Din defeated him at Banias and besieged him in its castle until Baldwin III came to lift the siege; that year he sold Banias and Chastel Neuf to the Knights Hospitaller. He also helped negotiate Baldwin's marriage to Theodora, niece of the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Comnenus, and later married Philippa, sister of Bohemund III of Antioch, a marriage that produced no children.

In 1173 he relieved Nur ad-Din's siege of Kerak in Oultrejordain. From 1176 the influence of Agnes of Courtenay lessened his standing at court, and in 1177 the lordship of Hebron was recreated for Raynald of Châtillon rather than for him, though he kept his post as constable. He supported Raymond III of Tripoli, regent for Baldwin IV, and belonged with him to the faction of old families opposed to newcomers such as Raynald and later Guy of Lusignan.

In 1179 Humphrey rebuilt Chateau Neuf, destroyed in earlier sieges, and helped negotiate a truce between the Knights Hospitaller and the Knights Templar. He accompanied Baldwin IV in an attack on a small Muslim force near Banias, where he saved the king's life but suffered mortal wounds, and he died at his castle at Hunin on 22 April. Toron passed to his 13-year-old grandson Humphrey IV, son of Stephanie of Milly and of Humphrey III of Toron, Humphrey's son by an unknown first wife.
humphrey-iv-of-toron: Humphrey was the son of Humphrey, heir to Humphrey II of Toron, and Stephanie of Milly, who inherited the Lordship of Transjordan. His father died around 1173, and his mother married Miles of Plancy and the following year Raynald of Châtillon. He inherited Toron from his grandfather, who died of wounds from the Battle of Banyas in April 1179. On his betrothal to the eight-year-old Isabella in October 1180 he yielded Toron, Banias and Chastel Neuf to King Baldwin IV for a money fief of 7,000 bezants, perhaps so that he would not unite Toron and Transjordan.

In September 1183 he led the forces of Oultrejordain against Saladin's invasion, and his troops were almost annihilated in an ambush at Mount Gilboa. During his wedding at Kerak that autumn Saladin besieged the castle until King Baldwin and Raymond III of Tripoli relieved it on 4 December. When the barons gathered at Nablus resolved to crown him and Isabella against Sybilla and Guy of Lusignan, Humphrey rode secretly to Jerusalem by night and swore fealty to Guy, which ended the plot.

Captured at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187, he was released when his mother offered the surrender of Kerak and Montréal; the garrisons refused, and Saladin later freed him without ransom. After Sybilla's death in 1190 the barons, led by Balian of Ibelin, wanted Isabella married to Conrad of Montferrat. The Itinerarium Regis Ricardi describes Humphrey as gentle and with a bad stammer. Isabella's mother, Maria Comnena, swore that the girl had been forced to marry at eight, and the papal legate Ubaldo Lanfranchi and Philip of Dreux annulled the childless marriage over the couple's protests.

Humphrey did homage to King Richard I of England at Limassol in May 1191, and being fluent in Arabic he opened talks for Richard with Saladin's brother, Al-Adil, at Lydda. Some contemporaries accused him of hiring the men who murdered Conrad at Tyre on 28 April 1192, but modern historians hold him innocent. He died in 1198. Toron returned to the kingdom in 1229 under the treaty between Sultan Al-Kamil and Emperor Frederick II.
humphrey-of-hauteville: Humphrey, also nicknamed Abelard, was a son of Tancred of Hauteville by his first wife Muriella. The chronicler Goffredo Malaterra makes him the third son, after William Iron Arm and Drogo, while Romuald Guarna makes him the fifth; he was probably younger than Serlo, who stayed in Normandy to inherit the family lands. With too little land for so many sons, several of the brothers sought their fortune elsewhere.

Malaterra and Amatus of Montecassino say that Humphrey went to southern Italy with William and Drogo around 1035 or soon after to serve Rainulf Drengot, Count of Aversa, though the historian Chalandon believed he followed them only between 1043 and 1045.

When Drogo succeeded William as Count of Apulia in 1046, he granted Humphrey the lordship of Lavello. In 1048, during fighting between Normans and Byzantines, Humphrey took Troia and Vaccarizza, and he helped his young half-brother Robert Guiscard settle after his arrival in Italy. On becoming count himself, he punished the instigators of Drogo's murder, especially the chief murderer, while many Norman knights were in rebellion and plundering papal lands.

At the Battle of Civitate on 18 June 1053 Humphrey led the Hauteville forces against the army of the Papacy and the Holy Roman Empire. The Normans held Pope Leo IX in Benevento until 12 March 1054. Humphrey went on to take Oria, Nardò and Lecce by the end of 1055, and in 1053 he received his brother Geoffrey and his half-brothers Mauger and the younger William, granting Mauger the Capitanate and William the Principate.

Fearing the growing power of Robert Guiscard, who had conquered Minervino Murge, Otranto and Gallipoli, Humphrey sent him back to Calabria. He married Gaitelgrima, a daughter of Guaimar III, and had four sons, Geoffrey, Joscelin, Abelard and Herman, and a daughter. At his death he left Guiscard the guardianship of his young sons, but Guiscard took their inheritance for himself.
huna-people: Huna was the name ancient Indians gave to several Central Asian tribes who came into the subcontinent by way of the Khyber Pass. It covered the Kidarites, or Red Huns, and the Alchon Huns, and was also used for the Nezak Huns and the Hephthalites, or White Huns, who did not enter the Indian subcontinent. These groups were not one people, though the name refers to them collectively. Chinese sources link them to the Xiongnu of north-east Asia and to the Huns who settled in Europe, and Gerald Larson suggests they were a Turkic-Mongolic grouping; their relation to the European Huns remains disputed. Their original beliefs are unknown and are thought to have combined ancestor worship, totemism and animism.

The Kidarites, who invaded Bactria in the second half of the 4th century, are generally regarded as the first wave of Hunas, and set up principalities in Gandhara and Punjab. The Alchon Huns later defeated them in the Kabul Valley. Skandagupta of the Gupta Empire repulsed an Alchon attack on the north-west in 460 CE, but after his death the Alchons under Khingila I took the Kidarite principalities and from there fanned out into northern, western and central India.

At their farthest the Huna lands reached Malwa in central India, and they occupied places as far south as Eran and Kosambi. A coalition of Indian princes, among them King Yashodharman and the Gupta emperor Narasimhagupta, defeated the Alchon army and its ruler Mihirakula in 528 CE and drove them out of India; the Guptas are thought to have played only a minor part in the campaign.

The victory of 528 was recorded on a stone pillar set up at Mandasaur in central India in praise of Yashodharman. The Hunas also appear in ancient Indian literature, including the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇas and Kalidasa's Raghuvaṃśa.
hunac-ceel: Hunac Ceel, also called Cauich and known in full as Hunac Ceel Cauich, is described as a Maya general from Telchaquillo. The Maya history attributes the war he led to the kidnapping of a powerful ruler's wife by a powerful lord. Other explanations have been offered: the rulers of Chichen Itza may have been partly descended from Toltec outsiders, disliked as foreign oppressors, or the war may have been a simple one of conquest. Both the attackers and the attacked are, however, labelled Itzá in the sources.

According to the account in the Chilam Balam of Chumayel, in the chapter called The Rise of Hunac Ceel, he fought the Itzá unsuccessfully and was taken captive. Ah Mex K'uuk threw him into the sacred cenote as a sacrifice to the gods, but he survived a whole night in the water and spoke a prophecy of the rain god Chaac about the coming harvest. With Ah Mex K'uuk as his sponsor he became lord of Mayapan, which with Chichen Itza and Uxmal ruled the north of Yucatán. With the help of highland forces he then attacked Chichen Itza, overthrew its ruling elite and left Mayapan sole ruler of the region.

In his commentary on the book, the scholar Ralph L. Roys proposed that someone from Chichen Itza had carried off the bride of Ah Ulil, ruler of Izamal, and that Hunac Ceel and his Mexican allies used this as a pretext or reason to sack the city in Izamal's name and to reorder the whole political landscape.

His actions upset the balance of power in northern Yucatán and changed the population of Chichen Itza and of the Lake Petén Itzá area, where the Itzá were still living at the time of European contact. The feature film Kings of the Sun opens with his forces attacking Chichen Itza, with Leo Gordon in the part, and a Mexican folk dance and music group named Hunac-Ceel was founded in San Luis Potosí in 2000.
hunald-i-of-aquitaine: Hunald, also spelled Hunold, Hunoald or Chunoald, inherited an Aquitaine that his father had enlarged with lands along the Loire, once Neustrian, and the Auvergne, once Austrasian. Nominally an officer of the Merovingian kings, he in practice ruled an autonomous duchy at a time when the mayors of the palace held real power. His brother Hatto seems at first to have shared his rule. In 735 Charles Martel marched across Aquitaine and occupied Bordeaux, and the brothers gave a promise of faith to him and his sons and agreed to remit taxes, after which Charles left the duchy to Hunald.

The brothers rebelled in 736. Hatto was captured and later escaped, and Hunald then invited him to Poitiers, blinded him and shut him in a monastery, probably the price Charles demanded for leaving him his duchy. During Charles's campaigns against the Umayyads in Septimania and Provence in 736–39, Hunald may have harassed his forces. After Charles died in 741, Hunald rose again in 742 with the dukes of Bavaria and Alemannia. Carloman and Pippin crossed the Loire at Orléans, burned the outskirts of Bourges and razed Loches; once they had gone, Hunald crossed the Loire himself and sacked Chartres, where he is said to have burned the church of Saint Mary, the earliest mention of the later cathedral.

When the brothers invaded again in 745, Hunald swore to obey them, gave hostages and paid the taxes owed, then took a monk's vow and handed power to Waiofar. About 752 he went to Rome and joined a monastery attached to Saint Peter's Basilica. He died there in 756 when the Lombard king Aistulf attacked the city, probably leading the defence of Saint Peter's, although he may have been stoned to death. Some historians believed he returned to lead Aquitaine in 768, but that leader was probably a different Hunald, his grandson. He probably inspired the hero of the twelfth-century chanson de geste Huon de Bordeaux.
hunan: Hunan lies on the south bank of the Yangtze River, about halfway along its length, and its name means south of the lake, the lake being Dongting. Mountains and hills cover more than 80 per cent of the province. The Wuling, Xuefeng, Nanling and Luoxiao ranges enclose it on the west, south and east, and the Xiang, Zi, Yuan and Li rivers converge on Lake Dongting in the north. The lake and the Xiaoxiang area figure prominently in Chinese poetry and painting, particularly in the Song dynasty, when they were associated with officials who had been unjustly dismissed. The area was under Chinese rule as far back as 350 BCE.

The forests were first occupied by the ancestors of the Miao, Tujia, Dong and Yao peoples. After Qin conquered Chu in 278 BCE the region came under Qin, and under the Han it formed the Changsha Kingdom. For hundreds of years Han Chinese settlers came from the north, displacing and assimilating the original inhabitants, clearing forests and farming rice in the valleys and plains. Migration was especially heavy when the north was ruled by non-Han groups and in disorder. In the Tang dynasty Changsha was a ceramics district, mass-producing tea bowls and ewers for export; the Belitung Shipwreck, an Arab dhow dated to the 830s, carried more than 60,000 pieces of such wares.

During the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period Hunan had its own independent regime, Ma Chu. Under the Yuan it was joined with Hubei in the province of Huguang, and the Red Turban Rebellions first rose up in Hunan in the 14th century. Hunan province was created in 1664 from Huguang and renamed in 1723. The Yuelu Academy at Changsha made it a centre of Confucian learning, and its grain surpluses fed many parts of China. By the 19th century it was overcrowded and prone to uprisings, among them the Miao Rebellion of 1795 to 1806. A Hunanese army under Zeng Guofan marched into Nanjing to put down the Taiping Rebellion in 1864.

A famine in 1920 killed an estimated 2 million people and led to the Autumn Harvest Uprising of 1927, led by the Hunan native Mao Zedong. Communists held a guerrilla army along the Hunan and Jiangxi border until 1934, when the Long March began. Changsha fell to the Japanese in 1944.

Hunan has a population of just over 66 million at the 2020 census, and Changsha is its capital and largest city. Han Chinese are the majority, with Tujia and Miao among the minorities. Wulingyuan, noted for its quartzite sandstone pillars, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. Mount Heng at Hengyang is one of the Five Great Mountains of China.
hunayn-ibn-ishaq: The Ibad were an Arab community of different tribes that had converted to the Church of the East and lived in al-Hira, once the capital of the Lakhmid kingdom. They were known for their literacy and multilingualism, in Syriac and Arabic. Hunayn's father was a pharmacist, and although al-Hira was known for commerce and banking, Hunayn went to Baghdad to study medicine under the physician Yuhanna ibn Masawayh. His endless questions irritated his teacher, who scolded him and forced him to leave. Hunayn promised himself to return as a physician and went abroad to master Greek.

On his return he displayed his new skill by reciting the works of Homer and Galen, and ibn Masawayh, in awe, was reconciled with him; the two began to work together. The caliph al-Mamun noticed his talent and, placed him in charge of the House of Wisdom, though at least one scholar argues there is no evidence of this. He also gave Hunayn the chance to travel to Byzantium in search of manuscripts.

Hunayn worked with his son Ishaq ibn Hunayn and his nephew Hubaysh. He would translate Greek into Syriac, his nephew would then render the Syriac into Arabic, and Hunayn would correct any mistakes. Unlike many translators of the Abbasid period he largely did not follow the exact wording of a text, but summarised its subject and paraphrased it, and he edited technical works by comparing the available manuscripts. He wrote that he first translated Galen from a faulty Greek manuscript and later, at forty, collated several manuscripts into one correct copy.

His translations included Plato's Timaeus and Republic, Aristotle's Categories, Physics, Metaphysics and Magna Moralia, and the Old Testament, which he rendered from the Septuagint, though that version did not survive. He translated 129 works of Galen, and travelled to Damascus to find half of one of them. Some of Galen's works, lost in Greek, survive in his Arabic. When al-Mutawakkil named him his personal physician, the caliph ended the exclusive use of physicians of the Bukhtishu family.

Hunayn wrote 36 books of his own, 21 of them on medicine, as well as works on philosophy, religion and Arabic grammar. His Book of the Ten Treatises of the Eye, the first known systematic treatment of ophthalmology, describes the anatomy of the eye, its diseases, their symptoms and treatments, including surgery for corneal ulcers and cataracts. He insisted that the crystalline lens lies at the centre of the eye, an idea that was widely held from his lifetime until the late 1500s.
hundi: The word hundi, from the Sanskrit huṇḍikā, means a bill of exchange, draft or promissory note. The Reserve Bank of India describes it as an unconditional order in writing made by a person directing another to pay a certain sum of money to a person named in the order. A hundi could thus move money between places, serve as an IOU for a loan, or settle a trade between merchants.

In a sahyog hundi one merchant drew on another, who was known in the bazaar for his credit, asking him to pay a third. The paper passed from hand to hand until the last holder, after reasonable enquiries, presented it for payment. Sahyog means co-operation in Hindi and in the other main language of the traders, and the name reflects the trust of several parties that took the place of any formal system of credit reporting.

Hundis took many forms according to who could be paid and on what terms. A nam-jog hundi was payable only to the person named on it and could not be endorsed to anyone else. A firman-jog hundi could be paid to the person named or to anyone that person ordered, much like a cheque payable to order, while a dhani-jog hundi was payable to whoever held it, like a bearer instrument.

A jokhim hundi was conditional: the drawer promised to pay only once a certain condition was met, and such a hundi could not be negotiated. A jawabi hundi was used to send money from one place to another when the recipient had to give an acknowledgement, or jawab. A hundi already paid was called a khaka hundi, and a forged or defective one a khoti hundi.

Under colonial rule the British were reluctant to interfere with the system, since it formed so important a part of the Indian economy. Official hundi forms were printed with revenue stamps bearing the image of British monarchs, Queen Victoria among them, and disputes between merchants often came before the courts. Although it worked outside the normal banking channels, the hundi system was therefore never an underground one.
hundred-days-reform: The Hundred Days' Reform, also called the Wuxu Reform, ran from 11 June to 21 September 1898. It followed the defeat of Qing China by Japan in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894 and 1895, after which the Treaty of Shimonoseki forced China to recognise Korean independence, cede Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula and pay a large indemnity. Elites saw the defeat as proof that the Self-Strengthening Movement, which concentrated on weapons and arsenals, had failed, and that institutional change was needed.

Thinkers including Tan Sitong, Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, influenced by the Meiji reforms in Japan, argued that China needed more than technical improvements. Parts of the Qing government were alarmed enough to let Kang and Liang put their proposals to the Guangxu Emperor, who agreed to an ambitious programme.

Over about a hundred days the emperor issued a rapid series of edicts on education, administration, the economy and the military. They called for a modern school system teaching mathematics and science, gradual replacement of the traditional civil service examinations, a bureau for railways and mines, a modern army and naval academy, and a move towards constitutional monarchy on the Meiji model. The Imperial University of Peking, now Peking University, was established.

Conservative opposition was intense among senior Manchu princes, Grand Councilors and provincial governors, who saw the changes to the examinations and the abolition of sinecures as threats to the social and political order. Empress Dowager Cixi supported the principles but feared that sudden change would be disruptive and that Japan and other powers would exploit any weakness. Later accounts say that Tan Sitong asked Yuan Shikai to kill Ronglu and march on Beijing to arrest Cixi, but Yuan told Ronglu instead.

With the support of conservatives and the forces of Yuan and Ronglu, Cixi staged a coup in September 1898 and took over the government. Guangxu was put under house arrest until his death in 1908. The reforms were reversed, and six leading reformers, the Six Gentlemen of Wuxu, including Tan Sitong, were ordered executed. Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao fled to Japan, where they founded the Baohuang Hui and worked unsuccessfully for a constitutional monarchy.

Historians differ. The mainstream view sees heroic but disorganised reformers blocked by Cixi's conservative faction, while some late 20th-century historians hold that Kang and his allies were dreamers unaware of political realities. The failure of the later reforms helped revolutionary forces, and the Xinhai Revolution succeeded in 1911.
hundred-years-war: The tension between the two crowns went back to the Norman Conquest of 1066, which put the Duke of Normandy, a vassal of the king of France, on the English throne. English kings thereafter held lands in France, and the status of those fiefs was a lasting source of conflict.

The immediate cause was dynastic. After Louis X died in 1316, the French crown passed through his brothers, and when Charles IV died, Edward III claimed the succession through his mother Isabella, Charles's sister. In May 1337 Philip VI took Aquitaine back into his hands, since Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. Edward answered by challenging Philip's right to the throne, and in 1340 he formally took the title of king of France.

Historians usually divide the war into three phases, separated by truces. In the Edwardian phase, to 1360, Edward III and his son Edward the Black Prince won at Crécy in 1346 and at Poitiers in 1356, where King John II of France was taken prisoner. The Black Death, which spread through Europe between 1347 and 1351, killed 6 to 12 million people in France, over a third of the population, and 2 to 3 million in England.

In the Caroline phase, under Charles V and the commander Bertrand du Guesclin, the French reconquered most of the lands ceded to Edward at the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360; Charles created a professional standing army, the first in post-Roman western Europe. After the Truce of Leulinghem of 1389, Henry V of England used the madness of Charles VI and the civil war between Armagnacs and Burgundians to renew the war. He won at Agincourt in 1415, where about 40 per cent of the French nobility was killed, and at Verneuil in 1424. In April 1429 Joan of Arc entered the besieged city of Orléans, and the English lifted the siege.

When the war ended, England had lost its continental possessions apart from Calais, which it held until 1558. The French and English monarchies stayed separate, although English sovereigns styled themselves kings of France until 1802. Historians point to the war's lasting effects on European warfare: professional armies replaced feudal levies, artillery became important, and stronger national identities took root in both kingdoms.
huneric: Huneric was the oldest son of Gaiseric and was sent to Italy as a hostage in 435, when his father made a treaty with the Western emperor Valentinian III. He married Eudocia, daughter of Valentinian III and Licinia Eudoxia, in 455 or 456, after she was taken following the Sack of Rome; their one child was the future king Hilderic. Huneric had earlier been married to a daughter of the Visigothic king Theodoric I. He divorced her on the claim that she had tried to poison someone, and she returned to the Visigothic Kingdom after her nose and ears were cut off, which soured relations between the Vandals and the Visigoths.

Huneric became king on his father's death on 25 January 477 and was the first Vandal king to use the title King of the Vandals and Alans. He abandoned his father's imperial politics and concentrated on internal affairs, and he lacked the prestige Gaiseric had enjoyed with other states. In 479 he conducted a purge, exiling his older brother Theoderic with his daughters and younger son. Theoderic's wife and eldest son were executed, as were the official Heldica and his family, and Jucundus, the Arian patriarch of Carthage, was publicly burned to death.

A fervent Arian, Huneric opened his reign with overtures to the Roman population. After an Eastern Roman mission led by Alexander, he restored properties his father had seized from the merchants of Carthage, and he allowed the Nicene Christians to hold a synod, which elected Eugenius as bishop of Carthage. He then reversed himself. On 24 February 484, three weeks after a meeting of Nicene and Arian bishops, he removed the Nicene bishops from office and banished some to Corsica. A few were executed, among them the former proconsul Victorian and Frumentius, killed at Hadrumetum after refusing to become Arians.

Yves Modéran estimated that around 20% of the bishops in Africa converted to Arianism in response. Huneric also murdered many members of the Hasdingi dynasty and persecuted Manichaeans, and near the end of his reign the Moors of the Aurès Mountains successfully rebelled against Vandal rule. He renamed Hadrumetum Hunericopolis. He died on 23 December 484 and was succeeded by his nephew Gunthamund, who allowed the exiles to return; among them was Vigilius, bishop of Thapsus, who published a treatise against Arianism. Only three pieces of Vandal legislation survive, all from Huneric's reign.
hungarian-declaration-of-independence: On 7 December 1848 the Diet of Hungary refused to acknowledge the new Habsburg monarch, Franz Joseph, on the ground that no one could sit on the Hungarian throne without its knowledge and consent, and called the nation to arms. In Hungarian law a king had to be crowned to exercise royal power, and a crowned king could not give up the throne during his lifetime. Franz Joseph's uncle Ferdinand V was still alive, so in Hungarian eyes Franz Joseph was a usurper and a rebel against the ancient constitution.

Four causes led to the dethronement: the Imperial Constitution of Olmütz of 4 March 1849, which threatened to reduce Hungary to a province of a centralised Austrian Empire; Franz Joseph's usurpation; the court's repudiation of the April Laws, sanctioned by Ferdinand V on 11 April 1848; and the attempt of the Habsburg army to overthrow Hungary's constitutional government, which the Hungarian government and parliament called an attempted coup by military force.

The successes of the Spring Campaign made the step possible. Lajos Kossuth presented the declaration to the National Assembly in closed session on 13 April 1849, against the opposition of the Peace Party, and it was proclaimed in the Great Calvinist Church of Debrecen. It severed Hungary's allegiance to the House of Habsburg-Lorraine and dissolved the personal union with the other Habsburg realms; it did not speak of secession from the Austrian Empire, since the Kingdom of Hungary had never been constitutionally a part of it. It accused the dynasty of treachery, treason, perjury and war against the nation, and declared that the house of Habsburg had forfeited the throne.

The act gave the revolt a basis in law, and from then until the revolution's collapse Kossuth, as elected regent-president, was head of state. Later, in a banquet speech before the Corporation of New York, he urged the United States to recognise Hungarian independence, saying that the declaration had been voted unanimously and that every county and municipality had declared its adherence to it.
hungarian-democratic-forum: The Forum first met at Lakitelek in southern Hungary on 27 September 1987, during the one-party rule of the Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party, and was at first a loose movement rather than a party. Its founders, among them Sándor Csoóri, Zoltán Bíró, István Csurka and Sándor Lezsák, stood in the populist or rural-national tradition, sought a third way between capitalism and communism, and were troubled by the plight of the Hungarian minority in Romania under Nicolae Ceaușescu. More moderate than the liberal Alliance of Free Democrats and Fidesz, it sought links with the reform communist Imre Pozsgay.

At a second meeting in Lakitelek in 1988 the Forum announced its foundation, made possible by the Association and Assembly Act of September 1988, and in 1989 it took part in the Opposition Round Table and the National Round Table talks. In October 1989 József Antall succeeded Zoltán Bíró as its president and opened the party to the national-minded and Christian middle class, turning it into a right-of-centre catch-all party.

In the elections of March and April 1990 the Forum won 24.7% of the vote and 164 of 386 seats and formed a coalition with the Independent Smallholders Party and the Christian Democratic People's Party. Antall's government passed laws on local administration, the civil service and the redress of the old regime's wrongs. A radical national faction called for former communists to be purged from public posts and attacked the liberal Free Democrats as cosmopolitan, liberal-bolshevik and Jewish, and in 1993 most of it left with István Csurka to found the Hungarian Justice and Life Party. After Antall's death in December 1993, Péter Boross led the government until May 1994.

The party fell to 12.0% in 1994 and split again in 1996, when centrists around Iván Szabó left. Joint candidates with Fidesz gave it 17 seats in 1998, and it joined Viktor Orbán's coalition government until 2002. Led from 1999 to 2010 by Ibolya Dávid, it quarrelled with Fidesz, and in 2009 its MEP Lajos Bokros joined the European Conservatives and Reformists, which led to its suspension from the European People's Party. With Bokros as its candidate for prime minister it won only 2.67% in 2010 and left parliament for the first time; it was renamed Welfare and Freedom (JESZ) on 8 April 2011.
hungarian-diet: Some researchers trace national assemblies in Hungary to the reigns of King Ladislaus I and King Coloman in the 11th century, when church and lay dignitaries met on important occasions. The word parlamentum first appears in the Golden Bull of 1222 under King Andrew II, which confirmed the rights of the lesser nobles, the royal servants, against the crown and the magnates; their practice of presenting grievances to the king grew into the Diet. In medieval Latin documents it was usually the Congregatio Generalis, while Diéta, taken from the German imperial Reichstag, spread from the Jagiellonian period, alongside the Hungarian országgyűlés.

An institutional parliament emerged in the 14th and 15th centuries, though under Louis the Great and Matthias Corvinus it often did little more than approve royal decisions. It regained much of its power under the Jagiellonian dynasty. In 1492 the Diet limited the serfs' freedom of movement, and after the peasant rising under György Dózsa in 1514 it condemned them to eternal bondage. From the 13th century law-making was a joint right of the king and the Diet, and after the House of Árpád died out the Diet often elected the king. In 1608 it divided into a House of Magnates and a House of Representatives.

The Diet of the Estates ended in 1848. During the revolution an assembly meeting at the Great Church of Debrecen declared Franz Joseph deposed and elected Lajos Kossuth regent-president, before Austrian troops under General Julius Jacob von Haynau suppressed the revolution. Talks after the Battle of Solferino in 1859 failed, and under the Compromise of 1867 the emperor appointed Gyula Andrássy minister-president and the national assembly met again on 27 February. From 1902 it sat in the Parliament Building on the Danube in Budapest.

The House of Magnates had no fixed size: it held princes of the royal house, hereditary peers paying at least 3000 florins a year in land tax, church dignitaries, life peers and three delegates of Croatia-Slavonia. The House of Representatives had 453 members, 413 elected in Hungary and 40 sent by the parliament of Croatia-Slavonia, for five-year terms. Under the Electoral Law of 1874 the franchise rested on property, taxation, profession and ancestral privilege; the Encyclopædia Britannica Eleventh Edition called it probably the most illiberal in Europe. In 1910, in a kingdom about 54.5% Magyar, 405 of the 413 representatives were of Hungarian descent.
hungarian-invasions-of-europe: The raids came at a time when the lands of the former Carolingian Empire were threatened from three sides: by the Magyars from the east, the Viking expansion from the north and the Arabs from the south. Before they settled in the Carpathian Basin the Hungarians already fought as allies and hired troops of their neighbours. They took part in the wars of the First Bulgarian Empire, raided the East Slavic tribes and sold captives to the Byzantines at Kerch, and joined Arnulf of Carinthia against Great Moravia in 892. Driven west by the Bulgarians and the Pechenegs in 895, they occupied the basin around 896, probably under the leadership of Árpád.

In 899 the Hungarians defeated Berengar I of Italy at the Brenta and plundered the north of Italy. Between 907 and 910 they destroyed three large East Frankish armies: the Bavarians at Pressburg in 907, Burchard, Duke of Thuringia, at Eisenach in 908, and the army of Louis the Child at the first Battle of Lechfeld in 910. In the following decades their horsemen burned Bremen, sacked Basel, crossed France to the Atlantic, raided Catalonia in 942 and reached Apulia and Otranto in the south of Italy.

Their armies were mostly light cavalry. They struck without warning, plundered and left before a defence could gather; when forced to fight they shot arrows and pretended to flee, drawing their enemies into broken pursuit. Rulers often bought peace with tribute, as Henry the Fowler did in 924 and the Byzantine Empire did after 934. Historians count 45 or 47 raids between 899 and 970, of which only eight failed. A hymn from Modena around 900 asks to be saved from the arrows of the Hungarians.

The defeat by Otto I at Lechfeld on 10 August 955, where the Magyars lost about 5,000 warriors, ended the raids on the west; the captured leaders Bulcsú, Lehel and Sur were hanged at Regensburg. The defeat helped bring about the revival of the Holy Roman Empire in 962. Raids on the Byzantine Empire went on until 970, when Hungarian auxiliaries fought with Sviatoslav I of Kiev at Arcadiopolis. The Hungarians were the last invading people to settle for good in Central Europe, and in the following centuries they adopted western forms of feudal warfare, above all heavily armoured cavalry.
hungarian-revolution-of-1848: Unlike other Habsburg lands, the Kingdom of Hungary had an old constitution that limited the Crown, going back to the Golden Bull of 1222, and a separate parliament, the Diet. Under Metternich's policy of stability the Diet was not summoned after 1811, but writers such as Mihály Vörösmarty and Ferenc Kölcsey kept alive the ideal of political liberty. The crisis came from abroad: on 3 March 1848, after news of the revolution in Paris, Lajos Kossuth demanded parliamentary government for Hungary, and his speech was read aloud in Vienna before Metternich was overthrown on 13 March.

On 17 March 1848 the emperor assented, and Lajos Batthyány formed the first Hungarian responsible government. The Twelve Points, called the March Laws, received royal assent on 10 April. The April laws created a democratic political system: Act V of 1848 turned the feudal Diet into an elected parliament with the widest right to vote in Europe at the time and erased the privileges of the nobility. The government also demanded that taxes raised in Hungary be spent there and that parliament control the Hungarian regiments.

Conflict followed. Serbs and Romanians, whom the Austrian court manipulated with conflicting promises, took up arms against the Hungarian government, and brutal incidents occurred. When Batthyány resigned, Kossuth became President of the Committee of National Defence at the end of September. In December Austrian forces under Field Marshal Windisch-Grätz entered Hungary, and the government left Pest for Debrecen. Hungarian armies led by Artúr Görgei won victories in the spring of 1849, and General Bem drove the Austrian and Russian troops out of Transylvania.

Austria then sought help from Russia. Franz Joseph I kissed the hand of Nicholas I in Warsaw on 21 May 1849, and Nicholas sent about 200,000 men under Field Marshal Ivan Paskevich, while Julius Jacob von Haynau commanded the Austrian army. The Hungarian army of about 160,000 faced some 380,000 troops, and it was defeated.

Haynau was made plenipotentiary and ordered the execution of the 13 Martyrs of Arad, and Batthyány was executed on the same day in Pest. Hungary was placed under martial law, followed by passive resistance and, from 1851, the regency of Archduke Albrecht, who pursued a policy of Germanisation. Many Hungarians later served in the Union Army in the American Civil War. The revolution is a cornerstone of modern Hungarian national identity, and 15 March, the anniversary of its outbreak, is a national holiday.
hungarian-round-table-talks: The talks grew out of a meeting of opposition groups in March 1989. János Kádár had been removed from power almost a year before, and that month the Central Committee of the Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party admitted the need for a multiparty system. Mass demonstrations on the national day, 15 March, persuaded the regime to negotiate. A week later the new movements, at the initiative of the Independent Lawyers' Forum, formed the Opposition Round Table, so that the party could not keep power by dividing them.

The party first met the opposition on 22 April. Unlike in Poland, the National Round Table, formally set up in June, was trilateral, also including unions and organisations under the party's authority. Instead of one strong movement like Solidarity, several relatively frail groups took part, and their weakness made their demands more radical.

The talks were kept almost entirely from the public under an agreement of 10 June, which led some smaller parties to suspect a hidden bargain between the old and new elites. After Imre Nagy was reburied on 16 June the opposition demanded guaranteed free elections, free media access, the removal of political crimes from the criminal code, a ban on violence and armed forces free of politics. The most contested issues were the electoral system and the presidency: the party wanted a presidential system, expecting the reformer Imre Pozsgay to win, and offered to dissolve the Workers' Militia if his candidacy were accepted.

The agreement signed on 18 September covered six draft laws: an overhaul of the constitution, a Constitutional Court, political parties, multiparty elections, the penal code and penal procedure. About half the deputies were to be elected proportionally and half by majority vote, and the presidency was to be weak. Moderate groups such as the Hungarian Democratic Forum signed, while Fidesz and the Alliance of Free Democrats refused.

When the party turned itself into the Hungarian Socialist Party in October, most members did not join and Pozsgay was not elected its leader. The radicals forced a referendum on 26 November, which decided by 50.07% that parliament should be elected before the president, and the presidency went to Árpád Göncz, elected by the new parliament. László Sólyom and József Antall were among the future leaders who emerged at the talks.
hungary: Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe that spans much of the Carpathian Basin. It is bordered by Slovakia to the north, Ukraine to the northeast, Romania to the east and southeast, Serbia to the south, Croatia and Slovenia to the southwest, and Austria to the west. The whole country lies within the drainage basin of the Danube, which flows north to south through its centre. Its traditional divisions are Transdanubia, the land between the Danube and the Tisza, and the land beyond the Tisza.

Transdanubia is mostly hilly, with the eastern edge of the Alps in the west and Lake Balaton, the largest lake in Central Europe. The Great Hungarian Plain covers most of the east and southeast. Kékes, at 1,014 metres, is the tallest mountain, in the foothills of the Carpathians near the Slovak border.

The Roman Empire took the land west of the Danube in 16 to 15 BCE, and Pannonia was recognised as Roman in 14 BCE. The province of Dacia, which included the east of present-day Hungary, was formed in 106 CE and remained under Roman rule until 271. Later arrivals included the Hunnic Empire (c. 370 to 469), the Gepids, and the Avars, who founded the Avar Khaganate in the 560s. The Franks under Charlemagne defeated the Avars in a series of campaigns during the 790s.

Statehood began in the late ninth century with the Principality of Hungary, which became a Christian kingdom under King Stephen I in 1000. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the kingdom was divided into three regions for over 150 years, until it was reunited under Habsburg rule before the turn of the 18th century. The Treaty of Trianon in 1920 set Hungary's modern borders and cost it 71% of its historical territory; a third of ethnic Hungarians were left outside the new borders.

The Hungarian People's Republic was established in 1949 as a satellite state inside the Warsaw Pact. The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was unsuccessful, and during the Revolutions of 1989 the country moved peacefully to a democratic parliamentary republic. Parliament has 199 members.

The population was 9,689,000 in 2021, down from a peak of 10.8 million in 1980, and around 70% of the population lives in cities and towns, and a quarter of Hungarians live in the Budapest metropolitan area. About 5 million Hungarians live outside the country.
hunminjeongeum: Before Hangul, Korea had used Hanja, Chinese characters, since antiquity. The difficulty of the script limited its use largely to the upper classes, and commoners were mostly illiterate. Hanja also suits Korean poorly, since the two languages belong to different families and differ in structure: Classical Chinese puts the verb before its object, Middle Korean after it.

Because of a lack of records it is unknown when work on Hangul began or how it proceeded. King Sejong the Great, who reigned from 1418 to 1450, was responsible for it and deeply involved. Hangul was introduced to his court, probably in a mostly complete form, in the twelfth month of 1443 by the Korean calendar, between about 30 December 1443 and 28 January 1444. Work then began on applying the script and preparing official documentation. The base text claims publication in the ninth month of 1446. The postface of the commentary is dated to the first ten days of that month, which on the tenth day is 9 October, the date observed as Hangul Day in South Korea.

The base text, written by Sejong in Classical Chinese, has two parts: a short preface and a description of the alphabet, occupying four leaves in the Haerye edition. The preface says that the sounds of the country's language differ from those of the Middle Kingdom, so that ignorant people with something to say were often unable to express it. Sejong writes that he has newly designed twenty-eight letters for everyone to practise at their ease and use daily.

It then introduces the 17 consonants and 11 vowels, each with its shape and a Hanja character showing its sound, and sets out orthographic rules. Initial consonants can serve as final ones, consonants and vowels combine into syllables, and tone is marked by dots at the left of a character: none for the level tone, one for the departing tone and two for the rising tone.

The Hunminjeongeum Haerye, a commentary written separately by a group of scholars led by Chŏng Inji, is believed to be closest to the text as published in 1446. It was lost and forgotten, possibly by the early 16th century, and was rediscovered in 1940 in what is called the Kansong copy. That copy became a National Treasure of South Korea on 20 December 1962 and entered UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 1997. A second, Sangju copy was discovered in 2008.
Other versions include the text in the Veritable Records of Sejong, and Eonhae editions translated into Korean mixed script, the oldest known variant of which appears in the Wŏrin sŏkpo of 1459.
huns: The Huns left no sources of their own, and their origins and links to other steppe peoples remain uncertain. They probably came from Central Asia. Roman writers equated them with earlier steppe peoples, calling them Massagetae, Scythians or Cimmerians. In the 18th century Joseph de Guignes proposed that they were descended from the Xiongnu. Scholars still dispute the connection, though recent archaeogenetic studies show some Hun-era individuals with DNA similar to ancient Mongolian populations.

The Romans became aware of the Huns in 376, when their invasion of the Pontic steppes drove thousands of Goths to seek refuge on the Lower Danube. In 395 they began their first large-scale attack on the Eastern Roman Empire, striking Thrace, Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria. From 434 the brothers Attila and Bleda ruled together, and in 435 they forced the Eastern Roman Empire to sign the Treaty of Margus, which gave the Huns trade rights and annual tribute. Theodosius II gave in to their demands in the Peace of Anatolius in 443. Bleda died in 445 and Attila ruled alone.

In 451 the Huns invaded Gaul and fought a combined army of Romans and Visigoths at the Battle of the Catalaunian Fields, and in 452 they invaded Italy. After Attila's death in 453 his empire faced a struggle between its Germanic vassals and the Hunnic rulers. At the Battle of Nedao, around 454, the Gepid king Ardaric led a Germanic coalition against Attila's son Ellak, and the Huns lost many of their vassals.

The Huns practised pastoral nomadism, and their main method of warfare was mounted archery. Under Attila their economy depended heavily on plunder and tribute from the Roman provinces. Their government is debated: Peter Heather sees a loose confederation, and Hyun Jin Kim argues for a far more centralised system. They ruled many peoples, among them Gepids, Sarmatians, Heruli, Rugii, Suebi and Sciri, whose own kings often remained in place.

Very few archaeological remains are firmly Hunnic. Large copper cauldrons are attributed to them, and between 50 and 80 per cent of burials in the Carpathian basin in the Hun period show artificial cranial deformation. Almost nothing is known of their religion, though divination is attested. Medieval Hungarian chronicles claimed descent from them, a claim mainstream scholarship has dismissed.
hunsruck: The Hunsrück is a long, triangular upland in Rhineland-Palatinate, bounded by the valleys of the Moselle and Saar, the Nahe and the Rhine, and a school rhyme teaches children its limits: Moselle, Nahe, Saar and Rhine enclose our Hunsrück. It continues as the Taunus beyond the Rhine and as the Eifel beyond the Moselle, and Koblenz lies at its north-eastern corner. The range is around 100 km long and 25 to 30 km wide. Its interior is rarely higher than 450 metres, and its highest peak is the Erbeskopf, at 816 metres. The Idar Forest, the Soonwald and the Bingen Forest form an almost unbroken belt of forest, and the climate brings frequent morning mists and more rain than the German average.

Stone axes show that the Hunsrück has been settled since the New Stone Age, and Gravettian sites mark the first settlements in the area. In the La Tène period the Hunsrück-Eifel culture, linked with the Celts, left the Waldalgesheim prince's grave, the circular rampart of Otzenhausen and the Pfalzfeld obelisk. The region was then the tribal area of the Treveri. Between about 50 BCE and 400 CE the Romans opened it up with a dense network of roads, the best known being the Via Ausonia, which linked Trier with Bingen.

The name Hundesrucha is first mentioned in a deed of 1074 from Ravengiersburg Abbey. In the Middle Ages the land was fragmented among the counts Palatine of the Rhine, the archbishops of Trier, the counts of Sponheim and the successors of the Emichones, the Wildgraves, the Raugraves and the counts of Veldenz. Many castles and customs stations were built between the 11th and mid 14th century. The Principality of Simmern emerged in 1410 under a side line of the counts Palatine. In 1689 French troops set fire to Kirchberg, Kastellaun, Simmern and Stromberg in the Nine Years' War.

After the French period, the Congress of Vienna gave most of the Hunsrück to Prussia's Rhine Province in 1815. Poor harvests and the famine of 1817 followed, and in 1823 the agent Georg Anton Schäffer, sent by Emperor Dom Pedro I of Brazil, recruited many emigrants there. The first settled near São Leopoldo in Rio Grande do Sul in 1824, and further waves left in the 1840s and 1861, for Brazil and North America.

The notable towns are Simmern, Kirchberg, Idar-Oberstein, Kastellaun and Morbach, and Frankfurt-Hahn Airport lies at the centre of the upland. Slate is still mined there. The region is best known culturally for the Hunsrückisch dialect and for its depiction in the Heimat film series.
hunza-nagar-campaign: After the Gilgit Agency was set up in 1889, its British political agent, Colonel Algernon George Arnold Durand, worked to extend British influence with roads, telegraph lines and better mail services, including the road from Kashmir towards the Russian frontier that ran through Hunza and Nagar. Their rulers saw this as a threat to the isolation they had enjoyed. In 1890 the British reinforced Chalt Fort near the border, and in May 1891 envoys of the two states demanded that the roadwork stop and the fort be given up as lying on their land.

Durand instead strengthened the fort and hurried the road on. Hunza and Nagar then stopped mail from the British Resident in Chinese Turkestan crossing their territory, which British India treated as a breach of the 1889 agreement with Hunza guaranteeing its free passage. Safdar Ali, the Khan of Hunza, claimed Chalt and warned that an invasion would meet resistance from China and Russia as well; reports from Kashgar said he had sought help from the Russian consul and the Chinese governor. On 29 November 1891 Durand sent ultimatums to him and to Raja Azur, Khan of Nagar.

Durand's force of about 1,000 Gurkhas, Dogras and Kashmiri soldiers, with several hundred Pathan road builders, a mountain battery, 16 British officers and 7 engineers, took a week to reach its base at Chalt, 32 kilometres north of Gilgit. On 1 December it crossed the Hunza River by a temporary bridge, advancing through steep canyons under fire from sharpshooters in stone sangars. At the fort of Nilt the seven-pounder guns did little against its thick walls. Durand was wounded and gave up command, and Captain Fenton Aylmer, himself wounded, blew in the main gate, after which the fort fell with six British casualties.

The force was then held for days before the defences of the Nilt Nala and the fort of Thol. Finally 50 Gurkhas and 50 Dogras climbed a 1,200-foot cliff by night and outflanked the sangars, and 92 defenders surrendered with their rifles.

Hunza and Nagar were occupied without further fighting. The Mir of Nagar was arrested, while Safdar Ali fled into China, many of his followers having deserted him. Nazim Khan and Zafar Khan were installed as rulers of Hunza and Nagar, which kept a degree of autonomy under British rule and later served the British in the Chitral expedition. Durand's column returned to Gilgit on 11 January 1892.
huo-qubing: Huo Qubing was the illegitimate son of Wei Shao'er, daughter of a maid in the household of Princess Pingyang, and Huo Zhongru, a minor official who left to marry in his home town. When he was about two, his aunt Wei Zifu caught the eye of Emperor Wu of Han and was taken to the palace at Chang'an with her half-brother Wei Qing. After Wei Zifu bore the emperor's first child she was made a consort and Wei Qing rose to high office, so that Huo grew up in prosperity. He was also the half-brother of the later statesman Huo Guang.

In 123 BCE, aged 18, he served as Agile Colonel under Wei Qing and led 800 light cavalry on a deep raid that killed the Chanyu's grandfather and over 2,000 enemy troops, winning him the title Marquess of Guanjun. In 121 BCE he campaigned twice in the Hexi Corridor, capturing the Golden Man used in Xiongnu rituals in spring and reaching the Qilian Mountains in summer. That autumn the Prince of Hunxie surrendered, and Huo put down 8,000 of his men who refused to disarm. Han control of the corridor opened the route to Central Asia and its horses, and five commanderies were set up there.

In the great expedition of 119 BCE he led one of two columns, each of 50,000 cavalry. Marching from Dai Commandery, he defeated the Left Worthy Prince at the Battle of Mobei, killing over 70,000 men, held rituals at the Khentii Mountains and pursued the enemy as far as Lake Baikal.

Sima Qian records that he cared little for his men, and he shot Li Gan, who had assaulted Wei Qing, on a hunt, the emperor saying Li Gan had been killed by a deer. His reply to an offer of a household, that the Xiongnu were not yet destroyed, became a patriotic motto. He died in 117 BCE at 23. His tomb near Maoling was shaped like the Qilian Mountains, and its statue of a horse trampling a Xiongnu warrior is the earliest known monumental stone sculpture in China. His son Huo Shàn died young in 110 BCE, ending his title.
huron-carol: The Wendat text tells the Nativity in the people's own terms. It opens by calling on its hearers to have courage, for Jesus is born and the spirit that held them prisoner has fled. Spirits of the sky people come with the message that Mary has given birth, three men of great standing set out led by a new star, and when they find the child they greet him with respect and oil his scalp many times in his honour. Each verse closes with the refrain Iesous ahatonnia.

The English words best known today, beginning 'Twas in the Moon of Wintertime, were written in 1926 by Jesse Edgar Middleton. They were held in copyright by The Frederick Harris Music Co., Limited until they entered the public domain in 2011. Middleton drew on Brébeuf's song and on Huron religious ideas but used imagery familiar in the early 20th century: the child is born in a lodge of broken bark and wrapped in a robe of rabbit skin, hunters take the place of shepherds, and chiefs from afar bring fox and beaver pelts. His version names God with the Algonquian name Gitchi Manitou, which is not in the Wendat original.

The carol is sung in Canadian churches of many denominations and appears in several American hymnals, among them The Hymnal 1982 of the Episcopal Church, The United Methodist Hymnal and Evangelical Lutheran Worship. Its words are sometimes changed again to use imagery that Christians unfamiliar with the cultures of Canada's First Peoples can follow. Because its melody spans a modest range, it suits instruments such as the Native American flute.

Burl Ives recorded it as Jesous Ahatonia on his 1952 album Christmas Day in the Morning and later issued it as a single, Indian Christmas Carol. Bruce Cockburn has recorded it in Huron, Tom Jackson sang it on his annual Huron Carole tour, and versions followed from the Elora Festival Singers in 1997, Crash Test Dummies in 2002, The Canadian Tenors in 2011 and Sarah McLachlan in 2016. In 2002 Heather Dale released a version in Wendat, French and English, using a different English translation attributed to Father H. Kierans.
hurrem-sultan: No document records Hürrem's life before she entered the harem, and her birth name is unknown. Legends of her origins arose in literature, and she has been claimed as Ukrainian, Russian or Polish. Many sources place her in Ruthenia, then part of the Polish Crown. The ambassador Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, in his Turkish Letters, published in 1581, called her Roxelana after Roxolania, the name often given to that territory. According to accounts, Crimean Tatars kidnapped her in a slave raid between 1512 and 1520, and she may have been taken first to Kaffa, a major centre of the Ottoman slave trade, before reaching Constantinople.

Her rise from slave to legal wife attracted jealousy in the harem and among the general population. No law forbade the marriage, but custom was strong and astonished the court. The wedding probably took place around 1533. She bore at least six children, five of them sons, which broke the old custom that a concubine gave the sultan only one son. Her daughter Mihrimah married Rüstem Pasha, later grand vizier, on 26 November 1539.

Suleiman spent nearly ten years of his reign on campaign, and from the 1530s Hürrem wrote to him about the capital and the statesmen. She is known as the first woman in Ottoman history to concern herself with state affairs. Two of her letters to King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland survive, one congratulating him on his accession in 1548, and during her lifetime the empire's relations with Poland were generally peaceful. Her patronage of public buildings extended to Jerusalem, though the full list of works is unknown.

Hürrem died on 15 April 1558 of an unknown illness. The French ambassador Jean de la Vigne reported that Suleiman's grief was so great that he seemed to have aged. Her funeral prayers were led by the chief mufti Ebu Suud, and she was buried in a domed mausoleum decorated with Iznik tiles beside the Süleymaniye Mosque, where Suleiman was laid eight years later. Her son Selim II ascended the throne on 30 September 1566. European artists, barred from the harem, created a largely imagined image of her. The French author Gabriel Bounin wrote the tragedy La Soltane in 1561, and she has since inspired paintings, Haydn's Symphony No. 63, plays and novels.
hurrians: Some historians believe the Hurrians originated in the Armenian highlands or the Caucasus and migrated south into the Fertile Crescent. Several scholars have proposed the Kura-Araxes culture as their ancestor. Excavations at Tell Mozan, ancient Urkesh, show Hurrian artefacts with affinities to Kura-Araxes, though Antonio Sagona finds a connection hard to demonstrate. Others suggest the Hurrians were native to Mesopotamia, linked to the prehistoric Tell Halaf or Samarra cultures, while Igor Diakonoff thought them newcomers who arrived in the third millennium BCE. Their language is agglutinative and related to Urartian, together forming the Hurro-Urartian family; wider connections are disputed.

The Khabur River valley became the heart of Hurrian lands for a millennium. The first known Hurrian kingdom arose around Urkesh in the third millennium BCE. The king Tupkish had a queen named Uqnitum, Akkadian for "girl of lapis lazuli", and there is evidence that the Hurrians were allied with the Akkadian Empire by the reign of Naram-Sin. By 1725 BCE they were found in northern Syria, at places such as Alalakh. The mixed Amorite-Hurrian kingdom of Yamhad struggled with the early Hittite king Hattusilis I around 1600 BCE, and Hurrians settled in Kizzuwatna in southern Anatolia.
