The Hurrians who entered northern Syria at the end of the 17th century BCE brought political and cultural change, establishing feudal states led by a chariot-warrior aristocracy. The Mitanni Empire, which first rose to power before 1550 BCE, was bounded by the Hittites to the north, the Egyptians to the south-west, the Kassites to the south-east and later the Assyrians to the east. Egyptian records of Thutmose I and Thutmose III mention it, usually as Naharin. After an internal succession crisis Mitanni fell to the Hittites and later came under Assyrian control. The kingdom of Shupria, north of the upper Tigris, survived until Assyria conquered it in 673-672 BCE, and by the Early Iron Age the Hurrians had been assimilated into other peoples.

Knowledge of Hurrian culture comes from excavations at Nuzi and Alalakh and from cuneiform tablets, mainly from Hattusa, the Hittite capital. The Hurrians adopted the Akkadian language and cuneiform script about 2000 BCE. They were skilled potters, and their Khabur ware and Nuzi ware were valued as far away as Egypt. They may have been the first in Mesopotamia to recognise the full potential of the horse, and with the Hittites the first in the Near East to use the horse-drawn chariot in war. Hurrian texts from Ugarit hold the oldest known written music, from about 1400 BCE.

Their religion influenced the Hittites, spreading from the cult centre at Kummanni in Kizzuwatna. Teshub was the weather god and Hebat his wife; Kumarbi was the father of Teshub. The Hurrian myth The Songs of Ullikummi, preserved among the Hittites, parallels Hesiod's Theogony.
hurricane-beryl: Beryl grew from a tropical wave off West Africa and formed in the Main Development Region of the Atlantic on 28 June 2024, with near record-warm sea surface temperatures of about 28 °C and light wind shear. It was the second named storm, first hurricane and first major hurricane of the very active 2024 Atlantic season. It strengthened rapidly as it moved west, and on 30 June it became the earliest Category 4 hurricane on record in the basin, beating the mark set by Hurricane Dennis on 8 July 2005.

After striking Carriacou on 1 July, Beryl peaked in the Caribbean Sea early the next morning with maximum sustained winds of 270 km/h and a central pressure of 932 mbar, surpassing Hurricane Emily of 2005 as the earliest Category 5 hurricane. Wind shear then weakened it as it passed south of Jamaica and the Cayman Islands. It came ashore at Tulum, Quintana Roo, on 5 July, crossed the Yucatán Peninsula as a tropical storm, regained hurricane strength over the Gulf of Mexico and made its last landfall near Matagorda, Texas, on 8 July.

On Carriacou 99% of buildings were damaged or destroyed, and 70% on Petite Martinique. In the Venezuelan state of Sucre the Manzanares River overflowed and six people died. In Texas about 2.7 million people lost electricity, and on 8 July the storm set off a tornado outbreak in eastern Texas, western Louisiana and Arkansas, with 113 tornado warnings issued that day, the most for a single day in July. The remnants brought heavy rain to Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia before dissipating over Ontario on 11 July.

Beryl caused 73 deaths, 48 of them in the United States and 8 in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and at least $9.05 billion in damage, $7.2 billion of it in the United States. The United Nations authorised $4 million in aid for Grenada, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Jamaica, and the leaders of Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada asked for debt cancellation. In Houston more than 200 restaurants sued CenterPoint Energy over the slow return of power. In April 2025 the World Meteorological Organization retired the name Beryl, replacing it with Brianna from the 2030 season.
hurricane-david: David developed as a tropical depression on 25 August 1979, about 1,400 km south-east of the Cape Verde Islands, and became the fourth named storm, second hurricane and first major hurricane of the 1979 Atlantic season. It reached hurricane strength on 27 August and then intensified rapidly. Forecasts had it striking Barbados, but a turn in the hours before it reached the area took it straight over the southern part of Dominica. Local radio warnings there were minimal, disaster planning was almost non-existent, and the island had seen no major hurricane since 1930.

On Dominica the winds damaged or destroyed 80 percent of the homes, mostly built of wood, and left 75 percent of the people homeless; the capital, Roseau, suffered worst. Fifty-six people died and 180 were injured. David reached its peak, with sustained winds of 282 km/h, on 30 August, and on 31 August crossed Hispaniola with its eye almost directly over Santo Domingo. In the Dominican Republic river floods swept away whole villages; at Padre las Casas a river carried off a church and a school, killing several hundred people who had sheltered there.

Weakened, the storm struck eastern Cuba on 1 September, crossed the Bahamas, came ashore near West Palm Beach, Florida, on 3 September and made its final landfall just south of Savannah, Georgia, on 5 September. Some 400,000 people evacuated in the United States, where 15 died and damage came to about $320 million; tornadoes in Virginia caused one of the deaths. David became extratropical over New York on 6 September.

With no power on Dominica, a citizen named Fred White first told the outside world of the damage by battery-operated ham radio. The destroyer HMS Fife, on its way back to the United Kingdom, turned back to Roseau and was the only outside help for several days. Within two months aid pledges to the island exceeded $37 million, though its distribution drew accusations, and looting followed the storm.

In the Dominican Republic, which Tropical Storm Frederic struck about a week later, the Civil Defense Secretariat helped about 1.8 million people, and over 12,000 homes were repaired within two months. David is believed to have caused 2,078 deaths in all. Its name was retired and replaced by Danny for the 1985 season.
hurricane-dorian: On 19 August 2019 the National Hurricane Center identified a tropical wave over Guinea and Senegal in western Africa. Crossing the tropical Atlantic, it became Tropical Depression Five on 24 August, 805 miles east-southeast of Barbados, and was named Dorian soon afterwards. It passed through the northern Lesser Antilles from 26 to 28 August. Gusts reached 111 mph in the Virgin Islands, island-wide blackouts occurred on Saint Thomas and Saint John, and one person died in Puerto Rico during precautions. It became a hurricane north of the Greater Antilles on 28 August and then intensified rapidly.

At 16:40 UTC on 1 September 2019 Dorian made landfall at Elbow Cay, east of Abaco, as a Category 5 hurricane with winds of 185 mph and a central pressure of 910 millibars. It struck Grand Bahama several hours later and stayed nearly stationary north of it for about a day.

Gusts exceeded 200 mph, and a storm surge of up to 23 feet swept away buildings; Grand Bahama International Airport was under water. Prime Minister Hubert Minnis called it a deadly monster storm. Dorian then moved up the Florida coast, landed at Cape Hatteras on 6 September at Category 2 strength, and became extratropical on 7 September. Hurricane-force winds reached Nova Scotia that day, and about 412,000 customers lost power there. It dissipated near Greenland on 10 September.

At least 70,000 people in the Bahamas were left homeless, most structures in the hardest-hit parts of Abaco and Grand Bahama were flattened or swept to sea, and 74 direct deaths were recorded there, with 245 people still missing in August 2020. Damage in the Bahamas was estimated at 3.4 billion dollars (2020), and 5.08 billion overall. Cruise lines carried water, meals and evacuees to Florida, and the Jehovah's Witnesses sent more than 100 tons of supplies. The World Meteorological Organization retired the name Dorian in April 2021, and Dexter replaced it.
hurricane-fifi: Fifi grew from a tropical wave that left the west coast of Africa on 8 September 1974 and entered the Caribbean by 13 September. It became a tropical depression on 14 September and Tropical Storm Fifi late on 16 September, just south of Jamaica, where its rains flooded parts of Kingston. It reached hurricane strength about a day later and on 18 September its peak, with sustained winds of 110 mph and a pressure of 971 mbar, a high-end Category 2 storm. Passing within 20 miles of the Honduran coast, it made landfall near Placencia in Belize, weakened over Mexico and dissipated on 21 September; its remnants helped form Hurricane Orlene in the eastern Pacific.

Honduran officials urged hundreds of thousands of people to leave the coast and flood-prone areas, but relatively few did. Rainfall peaking around 24 inches fell for three days. Within 24 hours 182 towns and villages were destroyed, and on 19 September mudslides killed more than 2,000 people. A slide dammed the Choloma River; when a bridge upstream broke on 20 September, the released water swept through Choloma at night, killing thousands of its 7,000 people. Omoa and Armenta were also buried or destroyed. The banana crop was wiped out, and estimates of the homeless ran from 150,000 to the government's 350,000 to 500,000. In Guatemala floods killed at least 200 people, and Nicaragua, Belize and El Salvador also suffered.

Bad roads kept relief minimal for three days. By 24 September planes from the United States, Cuba, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Mexico, Guatemala and Venezuela were bringing supplies, helicopters supplied by the United States from the Panama Canal were lifting survivors from the water, Britain sent 57 soldiers with motorboats from Belize, and Cuban doctors treated nearly 900 people in two days. To prevent disease, between 5,000 and 6,000 bodies had been burned by that date. Some supplies were seized by the Honduran military, and reports of deaths from starvation proved true. The economy suffered for two years, a large rebuilding programme of six housing projects began in 1977, and the name Fifi was retired at the end of the 1974 season.
hurricane-hattie: Hattie formed from an area of low pressure over the south-western Caribbean Sea and was named a tropical storm on 27 October 1961. Moving north, it passed near or over San Andres Island, where it caused one death, and became a hurricane and then a major hurricane the next day. A strengthening ridge to its north turned it west, sparing Cuba, where people had been told to leave low-lying areas, but raising the threat to Central America. Late on 30 October it reached its peak as a Category 5 hurricane with winds of 165 mph.

Warnings from the Miami Weather Bureau allowed wide evacuations: most people in Belize City left or went to shelters, and over 75% of the people of Stann Creek fled. Hattie came ashore just south of Belize City on 31 October with winds of about 150 mph, and a storm tide of up to 14 feet struck a city of 31,000 that lay at sea level. Most of its wooden buildings were destroyed, and the Government House was flooded and all its records washed away.

Governor Colin Thornley estimated that more than 70% of the buildings in the territory were damaged and more than 10,000 people left homeless. Losses came to $60 million and 307 deaths, more than 100 of them in Belize City, including 36 people who had sheltered in a British administration building later destroyed in the storm. Citrus, timber, cocoa, bananas and sugar cane suffered heavily, and 80% of the Belize Barrier Reef was badly damaged, though it recovered. Hattie also killed 11 people in Guatemala and one in Honduras.

Martial law was declared in Belize City, about 200 British soldiers came from Jamaica to keep order, and doctors vaccinated 12,000 residents against typhoid in two days. Homeless people set up a tent city about 16 miles inland that became the town of Hattieville. The British, Mexican, American and Canadian governments sent aid, and Prime Minister George Cadle Price secured £20 million in British loans. Days after the storm the government announced that the capital would move inland to higher ground, and Belmopan was completed in 1970. The name Hattie was retired after the season.
hurricane-iota: Iota began as a tropical wave that left the coast of West Africa on 30 October 2020 and crossed northern South America before reaching the Caribbean Sea. It became a tropical depression north of Colombia on 13 November, the 31st of a record season, and a tropical storm six hours later. In an exceptional burst of strengthening from 14 to 16 November its central pressure fell by 80 mbar in 42 hours, and it peaked with winds of 155 mph. It was first classed as a Category 5 hurricane, but post-season analysis lowered it to Category 4.

On 16 November its eyewall struck the Colombian islands of Providencia and Santa Catalina directly, and an estimated 98–99% of the structures on Providencia were damaged or destroyed. Iota then made landfall near the village of Haulover, south of Puerto Cabezas in Nicaragua, only a few miles from where Hurricane Eta had come ashore two weeks before, with a storm surge of at least 26 feet. It weakened quickly over the mountains of Nicaragua and Honduras and dissipated over El Salvador on 18 November.

At least 67 people were killed, at least 28 of them in Nicaragua and 16 in Honduras, many by landslides on ground already soaked by Eta; on 17 November a landslide at Macizo de Penas Blancas in Nicaragua buried at least 30 people. Floods covered an estimated 70 percent of Cartagena. Damage was estimated at US$1.4 billion, and about 5.2 million people were affected.

Colds, skin rashes, dengue fever and COVID-19 spread after the storm, and some people refused COVID tests for fear of being turned away from shelters. In Honduras about 185,000 people were displaced, and ten health facilities lost the cold-chain equipment needed for COVID-19 vaccines. Colombia declared a year-long state of emergency on Providencia, and President Iván Duque pledged to rebuild all its destroyed housing by 2022. In March 2021 the World Meteorological Organization retired the name Iota and stopped using the Greek alphabet for storm names.
hurricane-irma: A tropical wave left the west coast of Africa on 27 August 2017 and developed into a tropical depression on 30 August, about 120 nautical miles southwest of the Cape Verde Islands. Six hours later it became Tropical Storm Irma, the ninth named storm of the 2017 Atlantic hurricane season. Over warm water and in low wind shear it intensified rapidly, becoming a hurricane on 31 August and a major hurricane by 1 September. After fluctuating between Categories 2 and 3, it became a Category 5 hurricane early on 5 September, and early on 6 September it peaked with sustained winds of 180 mph (290 km/h) and a minimum pressure of 914 hPa.

Hurricane warnings were issued on 5 September for the northern Leeward Islands, Puerto Rico and parts of Hispaniola. More than half of the residents of Barbuda took shelter in expectation of a direct hit. The eyewall passed over Barbuda early on 6 September, and a weather station recorded a gust of 160 mph. Irma damaged or destroyed 95 per cent of the island's structures, including its hospital, schools and both hotels, and three people died there.

The hurricane also caused catastrophic damage in Saint Barthélemy, Saint Martin, Anguilla and the Virgin Islands, and damage to the harbour and airport of Sint Maarten left the Dutch part of Saint Martin unreachable. On Ragged Island in the Bahamas officials declared the island uninhabitable.

Irma weakened briefly to Category 2 as it made landfall in Cuba, then regained Category 4 strength over the Straits of Florida and struck Cudjoe Key on 10 September. It made a second landfall on Marco Island the same day, became a remnant low over Alabama and dissipated on 13 September over Missouri. The Florida Keys suffered the worst of the damage in the United States.

The hurricane caused at least 134 deaths, 92 of them in the contiguous United States. Damage to roads, harbours and airports in the Caribbean hampered the delivery of relief, and the British, Dutch, French and United States governments sent warships and aircraft with supplies. Cuba, itself heavily damaged, sent 750 health workers to other affected countries. Irma was the first Category 5 hurricane on record to strike the Leeward Islands, and Hurricane Maria followed at the same intensity two weeks later. Because of the damage and loss of life, the World Meteorological Organization retired the name Irma in April 2018, and Idalia replaced it for the 2023 season.
hurricane-ivan: Ivan grew from a tropical wave that left western Africa and became a tropical depression on 2 September 2004 south-west of Cape Verde. A day later the National Hurricane Center named it Tropical Storm Ivan, the ninth named storm of the 2004 Atlantic hurricane season, and on 3 September it became the southernmost Atlantic hurricane on record, at 9.5° N. It reached hurricane strength on 5 September and intensified rapidly into a major hurricane.

On 7 September Ivan crossed the Windward Islands with winds of 125 mph. In Grenada, its worst hurricane since Janet in 1955, about 90% of houses were damaged, some 18,000 people were left homeless, and the damage, $1.1 billion, came to about 200% of the country's GDP; 80% of the nutmeg crop, its main agricultural export, was lost. In the Caribbean Sea Ivan reached Category 5 three times, with peak winds of 165 mph, and passed just south of Jamaica, where 17 people died, and of the Cayman Islands.

On 16 September Ivan came ashore at Gulf Shores, Alabama, as a Category 3 hurricane with sustained winds of 120 mph. Its storm surge, which peaked at 12.92 ft at the Escambia Bay Bridge, destroyed parts of the bridge carrying Interstate 10, and 27 people were killed in Florida. Moving inland it set off about 120 tornadoes from Alabama to Maryland, the largest outbreak linked to a tropical cyclone. Its remnant drifted back over Florida, regenerated in the Gulf of Mexico and came ashore in Louisiana as a tropical depression before dissipating on 24 September.

Damage in the United States came to $20.5 billion, making Ivan the country's second-costliest hurricane at the time after Andrew in 1992. Waves destroyed Taylor Energy's Mississippi Canyon 20-A oil platform off Louisiana, and oil was still leaking there fourteen years later. Guyana, Trinidad and Tobago and the United States Agency for International Development sent aid to Grenada, and the Caribbean Development Bank lent it $10 million in 2005. The World Meteorological Organization retired the name Ivan in 2005, replacing it with Igor.
hurricane-maria: Maria grew from a tropical wave that left the west coast of Africa on 12 September 2017. It became Tropical Depression Fifteen at 12:00 UTC on 16 September, about 665 miles (1,070 km) east of Barbados, and a tropical storm six hours later. Warm seas of 29 °C, low wind shear and abundant moisture let it intensify explosively on 18 September. It reached Category 5 strength just before making landfall on Dominica at 21:15 AST that night, with sustained winds of 165 mph (266 km/h).

After crossing Dominica the storm re-intensified and peaked with winds of 175 mph (280 km/h) and a central pressure of 908 millibars. An eyewall replacement cycle weakened it to a high-end Category 4 hurricane, and it struck Puerto Rico near Yabucoa on 20 September with winds of 155 mph (249 km/h). It then passed north of the Bahamas, paralleled the United States East Coast, and became extratropical on 30 September before dissipating by 2 October.

On Dominica the winds damaged the roof of practically every home, including the prime minister's official residence, and cut off cellular, radio and internet services, so that the scale of the damage was unclear for days. Guadeloupe and Martinique suffered flooding, damaged roofs and uprooted trees, and Saint Croix in the United States Virgin Islands was crossed by the hurricane's outer eyewall two weeks after Hurricane Irma had struck St Thomas and St John.

In Puerto Rico the eye had tripled in size before landfall, exposing a far greater area to high winds. Rainfall peaked at 37.9 inches (960 mm) at Caguas, San Juan flooded and the La Perla neighbourhood was largely destroyed. The power grid was effectively destroyed. On 26 September 95 percent of the island had no electricity and less than half the population had tap water. The total death toll was 3,059, of which an estimated 2,975 were in Puerto Rico and 65 in Dominica.

The United States government response was criticised as slow and inadequate. The Department of Homeland Security did not at once waive the Jones Act, which limited aid shipments from United States ports to ships carrying the United States flag, and waived it for ten days from 28 September after Governor Ricardo Rosselló asked. The state power company awarded a 300 million dollar repair contract to Whitefish Energy, a small Montana firm, which prompted accusations of cronyism that Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke denied.

Governor Rosselló estimated the damage at no less than 90 billion dollars. Maria was the deadliest hurricane in Dominica since 1834 and in Puerto Rico since 1899. The World Meteorological Organization retired the name in April 2018 and replaced it with Margot.
hurricane-mitch: Mitch began as Tropical Depression Thirteen on 22 October 1998 over the south-western Caribbean Sea, from a tropical wave that had left Africa on 10 October. It became a hurricane on 24 October and rapidly intensified under warm waters and good outflow, reaching Category 5 on 26 October. At its peak it had sustained winds of 180 mph (290 km/h) and a minimum pressure of 905 millibars while off the northern coast of Honduras.

Forecasters had expected a turn north towards the Yucatán Peninsula. Instead the storm turned south because of a ridge that was not observed while it was active. It weakened over land and struck Honduras on 29 October with winds of 80 mph (130 km/h), then moved slowly westward through Central America. Its remnants reached the Bay of Campeche, redeveloped into a tropical storm on 3 November, crossed the Yucatán and made a final landfall near Naples, Florida, on 5 November. It became extratropical and was tracked until 9 November, when it passed north of Scotland.

Moving slowly between 29 October and 3 November, Mitch dropped historic amounts of rain on Honduras, Guatemala and Nicaragua, with unofficial reports of up to 75 inches (1,900 mm). At least 11,374 people were confirmed killed and over 11,000 were left missing by the end of 1998, so the true toll is unknown. Most deaths came from floods and mudslides, and Honduras suffered over half of them. Roughly 2.7 million people were left homeless across the region, and total damage was estimated at about 6 billion dollars.

In Honduras the storm wrecked about 35,000 houses and damaged another 50,000. More than 70 percent of the transport infrastructure was damaged, mostly highways and bridges, and about 70 percent of the country lost its water sources. In Tegucigalpa a large landslide affected three neighbourhoods and formed a temporary dam. The schooner Fantome of Windjammer Barefoot Cruises was lost with all hands off Honduras.

President Carlos Roberto Flores estimated that Mitch reversed 50 years of progress in Honduras. The economy contracted by 1.9 percent in 1999, and officials thought full reconstruction would take at least 15 years. The government imposed a curfew after reports of looting and restricted constitutional rights for 15 days. Some areas received no help until 12 November, and about 285,000 people were still in shelters three weeks after landfall. Outbreaks of cholera, leptospirosis and dengue followed.

Countries around the world gave aid totalling 6.3 billion dollars. The World Meteorological Organization retired the name Mitch, replacing it with Matthew for the 2004 season. It had been the deadliest Atlantic hurricane since the Great Hurricane of 1780, and the deadliest in Central American history, surpassing Hurricane Fifi of 1974.
husainid-dynasty: The family was of Greek origin, from the island of Crete, and its line is traced to Sidi Ali al-Turki, who died in 1676. Al-Husayn I ibn Ali came to power in 1705, succeeding the Muradid dynasty, and in that year Sultan Ahmed III granted him the title of beylerbeyi. The Ottoman sultans regarded the beys as provincial governors and recognised their right to hereditary succession.

In theory the throne passed by male primogeniture, but this was not always followed, and in later periods it was often granted to an older male member of a collateral branch of the family. The heir apparent held the title Bey al-Mahalla and led the mahalla, a biannual tax collection expedition around the country.

The beys made their own diplomatic agreements with European powers such as France, Great Britain and the Italian states. Their independence grew in the 19th century, above all after Hammuda Pasha suppressed the local Janissary Corps in 1811 following a revolt. They still kept useful ties with the Ottomans, at times asking for their protection and at others sending troops to fight in Ottoman wars.

Major reforms were attempted under Ahmad I Bey (r. 1837–1855), Muhammad II Bey (r. 1855–1859) and Muhammad III as-Sadiq. In 1845, with French support, Ahmad I ended the regular payment of tribute to Istanbul while keeping the Ottoman titles of wali and mushir. He abolished slavery and removed the statutes that kept Tunisian Jews legally inferior. On 10 September 1857 Muhammad II enacted the Fundamental Pact, modelled on the Ottoman Tanzimat reforms, and in 1861 Muhammad III as-Sadiq promulgated a constitution that made Tunisia a constitutional monarchy with a legislative assembly.

Public works and the end of the slave trade left large debts, held mainly by European and especially French interests. Higher taxes, rebellions and further borrowing followed, and in 1869 Muhammad III as-Sadiq had to accept an international financial commission of Tunisia, France, the United Kingdom and Italy to manage the debt. After a French invasion in 1881 the Treaty of Bardo placed Tunisia under French control.

When Tunisia became independent on 20 March 1956, Bey Muhammad VIII al-Amin took the title of King. The Prime Minister Habib Bourguiba deposed the dynasty and declared a republic on 25 July 1957. Princes of the family have since been recognised as its heads, beginning with Muhammad VIII al-Amin himself until 1962.
husam-al-din-timurtash: Born around 1105, Timurtash was still very young when in 1111/12 he was sent as an envoy to the Seljuk sultan Muhammad I Tapar to plead for Dubays ibn Sadaqa. In 1118 he went with his father Ilghazi to Aleppo and governed the city for a time while Ilghazi sought reinforcements at Mardin. When Ilghazi died in 1122, Timurtash took Mardin and his brother Shams al-Dawla Suleiman took Mayyafariqin. The chief sources for his life are the chronicles of Ibn al-Azraq al-Fariqi and Ibn al-Athir, with Michael the Syrian, Ibn al-Furat, Al-Azimi and Ibn al-Adim.

His cousin Belek Ghazi was killed at the siege of Manbij on 6 May 1124, and Timurtash carried his body back to Aleppo and took over the city. Through Sultan, the emir of Shaizar, he agreed terms for the release of Baldwin II of Jerusalem: 80,000 dinars and the cession of Atarib, Zardana, Azaz and other fortresses. Baldwin was freed on 29 August 1124, leaving hostages who included his daughter Ioveta and Joscelin II. Defeated outside Aleppo by Sultan-Shah and Dubays, allies of the Crusaders, Timurtash withdrew to Mardin, and in 1125 Aleppo passed to Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi of Mosul.

The rise of Imad al-Din Zengi dominated the rest of his reign. Zengi took Nusaybin from him by replacing a message carried by pigeon, defeated an Artuqid and Turkmen alliance at Saruj in 1130, and later took Dara and a daughter of Timurtash in marriage when Timurtash refused to hand over a fugitive governor. He also forced Timurtash to return peasants who had left Mosul for Mardin, where, Timurtash said, he took only a tenth of the harvest.

When Zengi was assassinated in 1146, Timurtash at once seized Hani, Siwan and Siirt. In 1148/49 he suffered a heavy defeat by Saif al-Din Ghazi of Mosul, who died in 1149 before achieving anything decisive. Kara Arslan of Amida then recognised Timurtash's overlordship, and around 1150 Timurtash took Samsat. In 1152 the caliph Al-Muqtafi sent him robes and diplomas recognising his possessions. He died in 1154 and was succeeded by his son Najm al-Din Alpi.
husayn-bayqara: Husayn Bayqara was born in Herat in June or July 1438. His father, Ghiyas ud-din Mansur Mirza, was a great-grandson of Timur and died when Husayn was seven or eight, and the boy took the name Bayqara from his grandfather Bayqara Mirza I. After the death of the Timurid ruler of Herat, Abul-Qasim Babur Mirza, in 1457, Khurasan fell into anarchy, divided among many rivals. Husayn lived for some ten years as a mercenary around Merv and Khwarazm, raiding Khurasan and often in dire straits. He took Jurjan from the Kara Koyunlu in 1458 but could not hold it against Abu Sa'id Mirza.

When Abu Sa'id Mirza was defeated and executed after the Battle of Qarabagh, Husayn besieged Herat and captured it on 24 March 1469. He defeated Yadgar Muhammad Mirza, a protege of the Aq Qoyunlu leader Uzun Hasan, at Chenaran on 15 September 1469. Yadgar occupied Herat on 7 July 1470, but Husayn retook it six weeks later, and his realm was then secure, with the Oxus as the border with the other Timurids. He faced revolts, among them one by his eldest son Badi' al-Zaman, who besieged Herat in 1499. He suffered from palsy for twenty years of his reign and banned the drinking of wine and the shaving of beards.

Husayn's court was a centre of literature, with the poets Jami and Ali-Shir Nava'i, the last great classical Persian poet and the founder of Chagatai Turkic literature respectively. About half of all known Timurid building works were carried out in his reign, mostly around Herat, where he built a madrasa and a mausoleum in the Musalla complex, in which he was buried, and the palace Bāḡ-e Jahān-ārā. The Uzbeks conquered Transoxiana in 1501. Husayn began to march against them but died in 1506, just after setting out. His sons Badi' al-Zaman and Muzaffar Husain disputed the succession. The next year Muhammad Shaybani took Herat, ending Timurid rule in Khurasan. His cousin Babur admired his court.
husayn-ibn-ali: Most narrations report that Husayn was born in Medina on 11 January 626, the younger son of Ali and Fatima, both of the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh. He was still a child when his grandfather Muhammad died. During the caliphate of Ali he accompanied his father in the campaigns of the First Fitna. After Ali's assassination he obeyed his elder brother Hasan in accepting the Hasan–Mu'awiya treaty, and the two withdrew to Medina and kept aloof from politics under Mu'awiya I.

Mu'awiya named his son Yazid as successor, which Husayn held to violate that treaty, and Husayn withheld allegiance. After Mu'awiya died on 22 April 680, Yazid ordered the governor of Medina to secure Husayn's allegiance, by force if necessary. Husayn refused and went to Mecca. There letters came from Kufa, where many resented Umayyad rule, asking him to lead them. He sent his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil to assess the situation, but the new governor Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad crushed the revolt and Ibn Aqil was killed. Husayn was advised against going, but held to his decision.

With a retinue of about 72 men, he was intercepted by a force of 1,000 and driven north to the plain of Karbala, where he camped on 2 October. A larger Umayyad army, put at some 4,000 or 30,000 in different accounts, arrived soon after. Ibn Ziyad refused him safe passage unless he submitted, and Husayn declined. Battle was joined on 10 October 680. Husayn was killed with most of his relatives and companions, and his surviving family were taken prisoner.

Karbala gave the pro-Alid party a distinct religious identity with its own rituals and collective memory. Kufans mounted two campaigns of vengeance during the Second Fitna, one by the Penitents and one by Mukhtar al-Thaqafi. For Shia Muslims Husayn is the third Imam, and his martyrdom is a symbol of sacrifice for justice and truth. Sunni Muslims regard the event as a tragedy and Husayn and his companions as martyrs. The battle is commemorated over ten days of Muharram, ending on Ashura. His tomb at Karbala, about 90 kilometres south-west of Baghdad, was at first marked by a simple sign and later given a monument.
husni-al-zaim: Husni al-Za'im was born in 1897 in Aleppo, then part of the Ottoman Empire. His father served as a religious authority in the Ottoman army, and his mother was of Kurdish origin. He was educated in Aleppo and then at a military school in Istanbul. In the First World War he served in the Ottoman army and was captured by British forces; after his release he joined the army of Emir Faisal in Syria. When France instituted its mandate over Syria he became an officer in the French Army, and later he served in the army of the newly independent Syrian Republic. After the early defeats of Abdullah Atfeh in the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, he was made Chief of Staff.

The defeat of the Arab League forces in that war shook Syria and undermined confidence in its unstable parliamentary democracy. On 30 March 1949 al-Za'im seized power in a bloodless coup, the first military coup in the history of Syria. Allegations that the Central Intelligence Agency engineered it are described as highly controversial; most of the available evidence suggests the decision was al-Za'im's alone, though he benefited from some American help in planning. Four days after the coup the Syrian government ratified the controversial Trans-Arabian Pipeline deal. President Shukri al-Quwatli was briefly imprisoned and then released into exile in Egypt, and al-Za'im imprisoned many political leaders, among them Munir al-Ajlani.

His secular policies included support for votes for women, and he suggested they give up the veil, which stirred religious leaders. He also worked to abolish the fez. Higher taxes aggrieved businessmen, and Arab nationalists resented his cease-fire with Israel and his deals with American oil companies. He made a peace overture to Israel, offering to settle 300,000 Palestinian refugees in Syria in exchange for border changes and half of Lake Tiberias, conditional on outside aid for the Syrian economy; it was answered slowly and not taken seriously.

Lacking popular support, al-Za'im was overthrown after about four and a half months by his colleagues Adib al-Shishakli and Sami al-Hinnawi. Hinnawi staged the coup on 13 August 1949, and al-Za'im was tried and executed by firing squad on 14 August, together with Prime Minister Muhsin al-Barazi. His takeover shattered the country's fragile democratic rule and set off a series of increasingly violent military revolts, and two more coups followed in August and December 1949. He had married Nouran in 1947, and she was first lady of Syria from April to August 1949.
hussain-muhammad-ershad: Ershad was born on 1 February 1930 at Dinhata in the princely state of Cooch Behar, the eldest of nine siblings. His father Mokbul Hossain was a lawyer and a minister of the Maharaja of Cooch Behar. The family migrated to East Bengal in 1948, and he graduated from Dhaka University in 1950. Commissioned into the Pakistan Army in 1952, he was interned in West Pakistan as a prisoner of war during the Bangladesh War of Independence and repatriated in 1973. Ziaur Rahman made him Deputy Chief of Army Staff in 1975 and later Chief of Army Staff as a lieutenant general.

On 24 March 1982 Ershad took power in a bloodless coup as Chief Martial Law Administrator, replacing President Abdus Sattar with a civilian president, A. F. M. Ahsanuddin Chowdhury. He became president himself on 11 December 1983. His government promoted the Land Reforms Ordinance of 1984, divested government industries and introduced the Upazila and Zila Parishad system. The Jatiya Party was formed on 1 January 1986, and he was elected president on 15 October 1986 in a contest the opposition criticised. In 1988 parliament made Islam the state religion.

Mass protests led by the Awami League under Sheikh Hasina and the BNP under Khaleda Zia, joined by students, labour unions and government workers, had by late November 1990 shut down government services and paralysed the major cities. Ershad tried to declare martial law, but the Chief of the Army Staff, Lieutenant General Nuruddin Khan, refused to support him, and he stepped down on 6 December 1990.

Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed formed a caretaker government and arrested Ershad, an arrest the Supreme Court ruled illegal in 1998. He was sentenced on 20 November 2000 in the Janata Tower corruption case and was released on bail on 9 April 2001 after four months in jail. He led the Jatiya Party in alliances with both major parties at different times and died at the Combined Military Hospital in Dhaka on 14 July 2019.

The Bangladesh Armed Forces attempted no coups from his takeover in 1982 until 1996, and in 1988 he approved the army's first participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations. His government accelerated privatisation and encouraged private and foreign investment through a New Industrial Policy.
hussein-badreddin-al-houthi: Hussein al-Houthi was born on 20 August 1959 in the Marran area of northern Yemen, the ancestral home of the Houthi tribe; some sources give 1956 as the year. His father, Badreddin al-Houthi, was a prominent Zaydi cleric. According to a disciple, he lived for part of his life in Qom, in Iran, with his family, including his father and his younger brother Abdul-Malik; the same disciple claimed that he was close to Ali Khamenei, Supreme Leader of Iran, and to Hassan Nasrallah of Hezbollah.

He sat in the Yemeni parliament from 1993 to 1997 for Al-Haqq, the Party of Truth, a party of Zaydi and Shafi'i membership. When the party supported South Yemeni separatism it became a target of the government, and he fled, allegedly to Syria and then to Iran. After his return he broke with Al-Haqq. In 1990 or 1992 he founded the Believing Youth movement to teach young people about Zaydi Islam and its history and so to revive Zaydism in Saada Governorate.

The government of Ali Abdullah Saleh accused him of trying to set himself up as an imam, of opening unlicensed religious centres, of creating an armed group called Ansarallah and of staging violent protests against the United States and Israel. His followers held that the government was too closely allied with the United States.

On 18 June 2004 police arrested 640 of his followers who were demonstrating in front of the Great Mosque of Sanaa, and two days later the government offered a bounty of 55,000 US dollars for his capture and began an operation against him. In July the army killed 25 of his supporters and raised the bounty to 75,500 dollars. On 10 September the interior and defence ministries announced that he had been killed with 20 of his aides in Marran.

His father briefly took control of the movement after his death. The government buried him at the central prison of Sanaa so that his grave would not become a shrine. After Saleh stepped down, the new government handed his remains to his family on 28 December 2012, and on 5 June 2013 tens of thousands attended his reburial in Saada. His brothers Abdul-Malik, Yahia and Abdul-Karim are leaders of the movement.
hussein-bin-ali-king-of-hejaz: Hussein bin Ali was born in Istanbul, the eldest son of Sharif Ali bin Muhammad. His grandfather Muhammad bin Abd al-Mu'in had been Sharif of Mecca but was dismissed in 1851 and exiled to Istanbul by the Ottoman authorities. As a Hashemite, Hussein was a descendant of Muhammad in the 37th generation through Hasan bin Ali. His family belonged to the Banu Qatadah, who had ruled the Sharifate of Mecca since 1201.

His main teacher was Ahmad Zayni Dahlan, with whom he became a hafiz. In November 1908 the Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II appointed him grand sharif. On arriving in Mecca, in the midst of the Young Turk Revolution, he was greeted by representatives of the Committee of Union and Progress as the Constitutional Sharif and replied that the constitution of the lands of God was the Shariah.

Relations with the Ottoman government worsened as the Committee of Union and Progress tried to centralise administration in the Hijaz and reduce the Sharif's traditional autonomy. Hussein revolted in 1916 only after attempts to secure hereditary control of the Hijaz by negotiation failed, with a promise of British support for Arab independence, though historians debate how far the British influenced him. He framed the revolt as a defence of the historic rights of the Hejaz. Britain, France and Russia agreed to address him as King of the Hejaz.

After the First World War he refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, in protest against the Balfour Declaration and the mandates in Syria, Iraq and Palestine. His sons Faisal and Abdullah were made rulers of Iraq and Transjordan in 1921. He refused to sign the Anglo-Hashemite Treaty, Britain withdrew its support, and in October 1924, facing defeat by Ibn Saud, he abdicated in favour of his eldest son Ali. On 23 December 1925 Hussein surrendered to the Saudis, ending the Kingdom of Hejaz. He is reported to have saved up to 4,000 Armenians during the Armenian genocide.

The British deported Hussein to Cyprus in June 1925, where he lived under supervised residence, because they feared his presence at Aqaba might provoke conflict with Ibn Saud. After a decline in his health he was moved to Amman in late 1930 and died there on 4 June 1931. He was buried at the Haram al-Sharif in Jerusalem. Later Arab nationalist writers sometimes portrayed him as the father of modern pan-Arabism, though some historians argue that the Hashemites were still new converts to Arabism in 1916.
hussein-dey: Hussein, whose own name was Hüseyin bin Hüseyin, was born in İzmir or Urla in the Ottoman Empire; the sources do not make clear whether he was ethnically Turkish, from a local Greek Muslim family or of another Anatolian or Balkan Muslim group. He joined the cannoneers in Istanbul and rose to the rank of Odabaşı, but was forced to flee to the Regency of Algiers, which was known for taking in fugitives. There he joined the Odjak of Algiers as a Janissary. In 1815 he became Khodjet al-khil, the minister who raised and commanded the dey's cavalry and collected taxes, and he led the cavalry during the bombardment of Algiers in 1816.

In March 1818, after the death of Ali V ben Ahmed, the Divan of Algiers elected Hussein dey. He guaranteed freedom of religion for the Jews and, under threat of British military action, freed European Christian slaves. In 1824 he expelled the British consul, who was pressing him to renew the treaty of 1816 against enslaving European Christians; a British fleet withdrew after a short engagement but returned two weeks later and threatened a bombardment until the treaty was renewed.

The quarrel with France went back to the 1790s, when France had contracted to buy wheat for its army from two Jewish merchants of Algiers, Bakri and Busnach, and fell behind in paying them. The merchants in turn owed money to the dey, who suspected the consul Pierre Deval of working with them. Deval's nephew Alexandre, consul in Annaba, also fortified French storehouses at Annaba and El Kala against earlier agreements. The blow with the fly whisk came after a stormy meeting on 29 April 1827, and Charles X of France, seeking popularity at home, used it to justify the blockade.

When the dey fired cannon toward a blockading ship, France chose force. On 14 June 1830 34,000 French soldiers landed at Sidi Fredj, 27 km west of Algiers, and entered the city on 5 July after a three-week campaign. Hussein surrendered in exchange for his freedom and his personal wealth, ending the Deylik. On 15 July he sailed with his family, harem and fortune on the French ship Jeanne d'Arc. Refused leave to live in France, he settled in Naples, stayed in Italy for three years and died in Alexandria in 1838. A suburb of Algiers and its district bear his name, as does the football club NA Hussein Dey.
hussein-kamel-of-egypt: Hussein Kamel was born on 21 November 1853, the second son of Khedive Isma'il Pasha, who ruled Egypt from 1863 to 1879. He was the uncle of Khedive Abbas Hilmi II, whom the occupying British forces deposed on 5 November 1914.

Hussein Kamel was declared Sultan of Egypt on 19 December 1914. He was the first person to hold the title since the Ottomans killed Sultan Tuman Bay II in 1517, after their conquest of Egypt. The new Sultanate of Egypt was presented as the re-establishment of the sultanate that had existed before Ottoman rule, but it was a British protectorate, with effective political and military power held by British officials. It ended the de jure Ottoman sovereignty over Egypt, which had been largely nominal since Muhammad Ali's seizure of power in 1805.

In 1915 the sultan was the target of two assassination attempts. The first was on 8 April 1915, when an assassin targeted his carriage in Cairo. The second came three months later, on 9 July 1915, when a bomb was thrown at his carriage as he travelled to a mosque for Friday prayers.

He founded and was sovereign of several orders: the Order of Muhammad Ali, the Order of Ismail, the Order of the Nile and the Order of the Virtues. He received foreign honours, among them the Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour of the French Third Republic in 1916 and an honorary Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath from the United Kingdom on 19 December 1914.

Hussein Kamel died on 9 October 1917. His only son, Prince Kamal el Dine Hussein, declined the succession, and his brother Ahmed Fuad ascended the throne as Fuad I. In Naguib Mahfouz's novel Palace Walk a character praises the prince for refusing to ascend his father's throne so long as the British were in charge. Stereoscope photographs of the coronation and burial processions of the sultan are held in the digital library of the American University in Cairo.
hussein-of-jordan: Hussein was born in Amman on 14 November 1935, the eldest child of Crown Prince Talal and Princess Zein al-Sharaf, in the Hashemite dynasty. His baby sister Asma died of pneumonia in a cold winter, which shows how poor the family then was: they could not afford heating. After Talal became king in 1951, he named Hussein crown prince on 9 September 1951. Less than thirteen months into his reign Parliament forced Talal to abdicate because of his mental state, which doctors had diagnosed as schizophrenia. Hussein was proclaimed king on 11 August 1952, three months before his 17th birthday; a regency council acted until he was enthroned in 1953.

The young king inherited a poor country that also held the West Bank, annexed in 1950, whose annexation had made Palestinians two-thirds of the population. Hussein allowed an elected government in 1956 but forced it to resign within months, declared martial law and banned political parties. In 1958, when Egypt and Syria formed the United Arab Republic, he and his cousin King Faisal II of Iraq set up the Arab Federation. He survived dozens of assassination attempts; a bomb killed his prime minister Hazza' Majali, and a second explosion twenty minutes later was meant for the king.

In the Six-Day War, begun on 5 June 1967, misleading information from Cairo led the Jordanian army to attack around Jerusalem, and Jordan lost the West Bank. In 1970 Hussein expelled Palestinian militants from Jordan in what became known as Black September. In 1988 he renounced Jordan's ties to the West Bank, and in 1989 he lifted martial law and reintroduced elections after riots over price rises. In 1994 he became the second Arab head of state to sign a peace treaty with Israel.

In 1998 Hussein, a heavy smoker, was diagnosed at the Mayo Clinic with Non-Hodgkin lymphoma and received six courses of chemotherapy over five months while his brother Hassan, crown prince since 1965, acted as regent. He died on 7 February 1999, aged 63, and was succeeded by his eldest son, Abdullah II. He married four times. Admirers saw him as a regional peacemaker who pardoned political opponents and gave them senior posts, while critics noted that he left a Jordan dependent on foreign aid from British, American, Gulf and Iraqi sources. He was a keen amateur radio operator with the call sign JY1.
hussein-shah-of-johor: Hussein was the elder son of Sultan Mahmud Shah III, who died in 1811 after a reign of more than forty years without formally naming an heir. Both his sons were born of women of Bugis origin. Hussein, who had the better claim by primogeniture, was away in Pahang for his marriage to Tun Encik Puan Bulang. The Bugis faction under the underking Raja Ja'afar quickly crowned his younger half-brother, Abdul Rahman, and Raja Ja'afar became regent. Abdul Rahman offered to abdicate when Hussein reached Lingga but withdrew under Raja Ja'afar's threats, and Hussein lived in exile on Penyengat Island.

Abdul Rahman's legitimacy was in doubt: the royal regalia were held by Engku Putri Hamidah, Mahmud Shah III's primary consort, who supported Hussein, as did the Temenggongs and Malay nobles. Stamford Raffles, who landed at Singapura on 29 January 1819, had Temenggong Abdul Rahman smuggle Hussein from Penyengat. On 6 February 1819 Hussein signed a treaty under which the British recognised him as Sultan of Johor and paid stipends to him and the Temenggong in return for a trading post at Singapore. The Dutch were greatly displeased.

On 2 August 1824 Hussein and the Temenggong signed a Treaty of Friendship and Alliance with John Crawfurd, the second resident of Singapore, and agreed not to correspond with foreigners without the East India Company's permission. A treaty concluded in London between the British and the Dutch broke Johor-Riau into two spheres, Johor under the British and a new Sultanate of Riau under the Dutch.

Malay rulers did not recognise his title, which remained nominal, and the contemporary writer Abdullah Abdul Kadir called him a "tiger without teeth", though in his later years some nobles, notably Bendahara Ali, came to accept him. He made no active claim to rule Johor, even after Temenggong Abdul Rahman died in 1825. He lived at Istana Kampong Glam in Singapore until 1834, when he moved to Malacca, where he died and was buried near the Tranquerah Mosque.
hussite-wars: From about 1402 the priest and scholar Jan Hus denounced what he judged the corruption of the church and promoted some reformist ideas of the English theologian John Wycliffe. His preaching was widely heeded in Bohemia. In 1414 Sigismund of Hungary convened the Council of Constance, and Hus went there under a safe-conduct from Sigismund but was imprisoned, tried and executed on 6 July 1415.

The knights and nobles of Bohemia and Moravia sent the protestatio Bohemorum to the Council on 2 September 1415, condemning the execution in the strongest language. Sigismund, persuaded that Hus was a heretic, threatened to drown all Wycliffites and Hussites, which greatly incensed the people. The death of his brother King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia then brought renewed unrest, and many Catholics, mostly Germans, were expelled from the Bohemian cities.

Fighting in Prague was severe, and Jan Žižka left the city and defeated the Catholics at the Battle of Sudoměř on 25 March 1420, the first pitched battle of the wars. He then founded the Hussite settlement of Tábor. Pope Martin V proclaimed a crusade on 17 March 1420, and Sigismund and many German princes arrived before Prague on 30 June with a large army, but the siege was soon abandoned. The united Hussites set out their demands in the Four Articles of Prague.

Later crusades also failed. A second, in 1421, retreated from Žatec, and Žižka decisively defeated Sigismund at Německý Brod on 6 January 1422. After Žižka's death in October 1424 Prokop the Great took command of the Taborites. A crusade in 1427 under Cardinal Henry Beaufort was defeated at Tachov, and on 14 August 1431 a fifth crusade was routed at Domažlice.

Hussite militias, mostly commoners including women, relied on converted farm equipment and early firearms, and Žižka used transport carriages as wagon forts against cavalry charges. Under Prokop the Great the Hussites also made raids called Spanilé jízdy, or glorious rides, into Silesia, Saxony, Hungary, Lusatia and Meissen.

The Council of Basel invited the Hussites to negotiate in October 1431. In 1434 the Utraquists and Taborites went to war, and on 30 May the Taborite army was almost annihilated at the Battle of Lipany, where Prokop the Great and Prokop the Lesser both fell. The moderates then agreed the compacts, based on the Four Articles, which allowed communion in both kinds. Sigismund, the Hussite delegates and the Church's representatives signed them at Jihlava on 5 July 1436.

The wars left Bohemia ravaged. According to some estimates, the population of the Czech lands, put at 2.80 to 3.37 million around 1400, fell to 1.50 to 1.85 million by 1526. The adjacent Bishopric of Würzburg was left so impoverished that its effects were still evident in 1476.
hussites: The Hussites, also called the Chalice People, were a Czech movement within the Bohemian Reformation. In the 9th century the missionaries Cyril and Methodius had brought the Byzantine rite in Old Church Slavonic to the Czech lands, including communion under both kinds for the laity. German-speaking bishops later imposed the Latin rite, in which only the clergy receive both kinds, and a papal bull banned the Slavonic liturgy. This is why there was no Czech liturgy and no communion in both kinds when Jan Hus proposed these reforms.

Hus was lured to the Council of Constance with a letter of indemnity, tried for heresy and burned on 6 July 1415. His death was felt as a disgrace to the whole country, and disturbances broke out against the clergy. A league of lords pledged to protect free preaching, and from 1417 some nobles replaced Catholic priests with priests willing to give both bread and wine. The chalice became the central symbol of the movement.

King Wenceslaus IV died in 1419, and his heir was his brother Sigismund. A revolution swept Prague, with churches and monasteries destroyed and church property seized by the Hussite nobility. It was disputed whether Bohemia's monarchy was hereditary or elective, and Sigismund could take his kingdom only by force. Pope Martin V proclaimed a crusade, and twelve years of warfare followed. Jan Žižka led resistance to five crusades. The Hussites fought defensively at first, and after 1427 they took the offensive and crossed the borders into neighbouring lands. On 23 March 1430 Joan of Arc dictated a letter threatening to lead a crusade against them unless they returned to the Catholic faith.

The Hussites were invited to the Council of Basel, where talks began on 10 January 1432 and centred on the four articles of Prague. On 30 November 1433 a Bohemian and Moravian assembly accepted the Compactata, granting communion in both kinds to all who wished it, though preaching remained under the Church hierarchy. The Taborites, who followed the more radical teachings of John Wycliffe, refused, and the Calixtines allied with the Catholics and destroyed them at the Battle of Lipany on 30 May 1434. The assembly of Jihlava confirmed the Compactata in 1436, and Sigismund took the crown.

Catholics and Utraquists were given legal equality in Bohemia after the religious peace of Kutná Hora in 1485. Bohemia and Moravia stayed majority Hussite for two centuries, until Ferdinand II reimposed Catholicism after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620. Historians count the Hussites among the forerunners of the Protestant Reformation, and the movement strengthened Czech national awareness. The tradition continues in the Moravian Church, the Unity of the Brethren and, since the end of Austria-Hungary, the re-founded Czechoslovak Hussite Church.
hutelutush-inshushinak: Hutelutush-Inshushinak was a son of Shilhak-Inshushinak I. His predecessors Shutruk-Nahhunte, Kutir-Nahhunte II and Shilhak-Inshushinak had ruled at a high point of Elamite power towards the end of the Middle Elamite period. While the Bronze Age Collapse brought decline to many societies of the Near East from around 1200 BCE, Elam prospered from the weakness of its neighbours. Shutruk-Nahhunte invaded Babylonia, drove out the Kassite kings and carried off ancient statues as plunder, among them the victory stele of Naram-Sin and the Statue of Marduk, and Shilhak-Inshushinak held lands as far north as the Lower Zab river on the Assyrian border.

By the time Hutelutush-Inshushinak came to the throne, around 1120 BCE, the balance was shifting. In Babylon a native dynasty had replaced Elamite rule, and its king Nabu-kudurri-usur I, better known as Nebuchadnezzar I, had taken the throne in 1121 BCE. Assyria, under Ashur-resh-ishi I from 1132 BCE, was recovering from a long decline.

Administrative documents suggest that Elam traded its natural resources with Mesopotamia in his reign. Nebuchadnezzar soon turned against him. A first Babylonian invasion, around 1115 BCE, failed according to later tradition because the army was struck by plague. On a second campaign the two kings met at the Ulai river. A kudurru, a Babylonian boundary stone, tells that a dust storm blinded the Babylonian soldiers in the thick of battle and that when it cleared the Elamite king was nowhere to be found. Nebuchadnezzar went on to plunder Susa and took the Statue of Marduk back to Babylon.

Scholars once thought that Hutelutush-Inshushinak vanished after this attack, but it is now believed that he moved his residence to Anshan. The kingdom declined from then on. After his death only two more Middle Elamite kings are recorded, Shilhina-hamru-Lagamar and Humban-numena II, before a long gap that ends with Humban-tahrah of the First Neo-Elamite Dynasty.
hutsuls: The Hutsuls are an East Slavic people. Their territory, Hutsulshchyna, takes in parts of the historical regions of Halychyna, Bukovyna and Zakarpattia and the basins of the Prut, Cheremosh and Seret rivers. The origin of the name is uncertain. It is first attested in 1816 and is thought to be an exonym used by neighbouring groups.

Like all the Rusyns, the Hutsuls most probably have a diverse ethnogenetic origin. They are generally considered descendants of the White Croats, the Tivertsi and possibly the Ulichs, who had to leave their earlier home near the Southern Bug under pressure from the Pechenegs. A relation to Vlach shepherds who later came from Transylvania is also suggested. In Ukraine they have often been officially treated as a subgroup of Ukrainians, while some scholars and some Hutsuls regard them as their own nation or as part of the Rusyn nation.

The first historical information on the Hutsuls comes from Polish chronicles of the 14th and 15th centuries, and the settlement of Zhabye is first mentioned in 1424. Their lands saw rebellions against Polish rule, such as the Mukha uprising of 1490, and in 1648 an uprising led by Semen Vysochan, a supporter of Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, spread through the area. From the late 17th century bands of opryshky were active there, the best known led by Oleksa Dovbush of Pechenizhyn. Until the 1770s Hutsulshchyna was divided between Poland, Turkish Moldavia and Hungary. Under Austrian rule the most important uprising against serfdom, in the 1840s, was led by Lukian Kobylytsia.

A Hutsul-Bukovyna Legion of the Austrian army was created in 1915-1916, and in 1918-1920 Hutsuls took an active part in the Ukrainian War of Independence; in 1919 a Hutsul kurin fought in the XI (Sambir) brigade of the Ukrainian Galician Army. In the Romanian census of 1930 there were 12,456 Hutsuls in Romania within its borders of that time.

Hutsul society was traditionally based on forestry and logging and on cattle and sheep breeding, and the Hutsuls are credited with creating the Hucul pony. Their emblematic tool is the shepherd's axe, the bartka, a small axe with a long handle, often carved and handed down at marriage. Permanent homes, the grazhda, were built at up to 1,700 metres above sea level as fortified places, and several generations of a family could live in one. The Hutsuls are also known for wooden churches, as at Kryvorivnia, Vorokhta and Yasinia.

Their crafts include clothing, woodworking, brass metalwork, rug weaving, Kosiv pottery and the decoration of eggs, and their instruments include the trembita, a kind of alpenhorn, and the sopilka fife. Most Hutsuls belong to the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church or the Ukrainian Orthodox Church. Their culture inspired writers such as Ivan Franko and Lesya Ukrainka.
hutterites: The Hutterites are a communal ethnoreligious branch of Anabaptists who, like the Amish and Mennonites, trace their roots to the Radical Reformation of the early 16th century. Anabaptism began in Switzerland, where Conrad Grebel and Jörg Blaurock practised adult baptism in Zürich on 21 January 1525. Blaurock appears to have brought it to Tyrol. Jakob Hutter formed the first communes in 1528 in Tyrol, on the basis of the Schleitheim Confession of 1527. Moravia was tolerant, and persecuted Anabaptists fled to it from southern Germany, Austria and South Tyrol. Under Hutter's leadership, from 1530 to 1535, they developed communal living based on Acts 2, 4 and 5 and on 2 Corinthians.

After Hutter's death in 1536 their beliefs, above all the community of goods and nonresistance, led to hundreds of years of diaspora. In 1622 Gabriel Bethlen, the Calvinist prince of Transylvania, forced a group of 186 Hutterites to Alvinc, needing craftsmen and farm workers. The community declined in the later 17th century, the Bruderhof at Alvinc was burned in 1661 during Ottoman incursions, and community of goods was abandoned, probably in 1693 or 1694.

In 1767 the Hutterites, by then 67 people, fled to Wallachia, and in 1770 reached the lands of Count Pyotr Rumyantsev at Vishenka in Ukraine. A new Russian military service law drove almost all of them, 1,265 people, to the United States between 1874 and 1879. About 400 started three communities with community of goods, and most Hutterites descend from them. Mistreatment of conscientious objectors sent them on to Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. In 1942 Alberta passed the Communal Properties Act, restricting expansion; the federal government disallowed it in 1943 and it was repealed in 1973.

Hutterite communes, called colonies, are all rural, with about 10 to 20 families and 60 to 250 people each. When a colony grows near its upper limit, it buys land and builds a daughter colony. All property belongs to the colony, with allowances rather than pay, and meals are taken together in a dining room. Each colony has three leaders: the Minister, the Secretary, who manages business, and the Assistant Minister. Many colonies farm or ranch, and a growing number turn to manufacturing. Their statement of belief is Peter Riedemann's Account of Our Religion, Doctrine and Faith, written in 1540-1541.
huvadhu-atoll: Huvadhu, also called Suvadive, Suvaidu or Suvadiva, lies in the Indian Ocean south of the broad channel known locally as Huvadu Kandu and on old French maps as Courant de Souadou, the widest channel between the atolls of the Maldives. Its 255 islands hold the Guinness World Record for the most islands in any atoll, though only 38.5 km2 of its area is dry land. In the Maldives only Boduthiladhunmathi is larger, with fewer and smaller islands spread over a wider area. Since the 1970s it has formed two districts, Gaafu Alifu in the north and Gaafu Dhaalu in the south.

Suvadive was the atoll's ancient Sanskritised name. Many Buddhist remains survive there, none yet properly investigated, which suggests it was an important atoll in Maldivian history, and its place on the main sea route around southern India brought long contact with mariners of the Indian Ocean. In the 14th century the traveller Ibn Batuta noted that the province of Souweid was the only part of the Maldives that grew grain, a kind of millet sent to Mahal.

The atoll chief, based at Thinadhoo, enjoyed wide self-government and, alone among the atoll chiefs, could fly his own flag on his vessels and at his residence. Sultan Mohamed IV, called Devvadhoo Rasgefaanu, first sultan of the Devvadhoo dynasty, came from the island of Devvadhoo at the atoll's centre, and the master carpenters of the Hukuru Miskiy in Male', Ali Maavadi Kaleyfaanu and Mahmud Maavadi Kaleyfaanu, came from Kondey.

The United Suvadive Republic of 1959 took its name from the atoll. On some islands, such as Gaddhoo, opponents of the secession were forced by threats and coercion to accept it. After Thinadhoo was depopulated and burnt in 1962 it stayed empty for four years, and for the next ten the seat of power was at Gaddhoo, until the repopulated island became the capital again.

Thinadhoo is the capital of Gaafu Dhaalu and Villingili of Gaafu Alifu. The islanders speak a distinct form of Dhivehi, the Huvadu dialect, which differs markedly from other varieties. The finest mats of the Maldives are woven on Gaddū from local grass dyed black and yellow.
huvishka: Huvishka was the son of Kanishka and succeeded him, on the best evidence available in 150 CE, ruling until the succession of Vasudeva I about thirty years later. He was born in Peshawar, but his reign encompassed many surrounding regions. His territory reached from Balkh in Bactria to Mathura in India, places where he is known to have minted coins. Gold coins and amulets bearing his image have been found as far as Pataliputra and Bodh Gaya, one of them as an offering under the Enlightenment Throne of the Buddha, which suggests with other finds that Kushan rule may have reached that far east.

His reign seems to have been essentially peaceful, a period of consolidation that moved the centre of the empire to the southern capital city of Mathura. It is also known as the golden age of Kushan rule.

Huvishka supported Buddhism, although the Buddha does not appear on his coinage, possibly out of respect. A statue found at Govindo-Nagar and now in the Mathura Museum, dated to the twenty-eighth year of his reign, carries the first known epigraphic evidence of the Buddha Amitabha. A Sanskrit manuscript fragment in the Schøyen Collection describes him as one who had set forth in the Mahayana.

His coins show a wide range of deities. Iranian gods include Mitra, Ahura Mazda and Atar, and an inscription at Ayrtam near Termez records a temple to the deities Pharro and Ardoxsho that he founded between 164 and 174. Indian gods include Skanda and Shiva, and he restored a temple at Mathura, where provision was made for hospitality towards Brahmans. One coin shows the Hellenistic-Egyptian Serapis, which suggests an orientation towards Roman Egypt.

Huvishka minted more gold coins than all other Kushan rulers combined, in a great variety of designs, mainly at Balkh and Peshawar, with smaller mints in Kashmir and Mathura. Early in his reign the copper coinage fell in weight from a standard of 16 grams to about 10 or 11 grams and kept declining, until a standard coin weighed only 9 grams at the start of the reign of Vasudeva. The devaluation led to a large production of imitations, and its motives remain unknown.
huy: The first village grew around a Roman castrum on the right bank of the Meuse. It was evangelised by Saint Domitian, bishop of Tongeren, in the 6th century, and is first mentioned in a 7th-century testament as Hoius vicus, taking its name from the river Hoyoux. In the early Middle Ages Huy was one of the most prosperous cities on the Meuse, with an economy based mostly on metallurgy but also on tanning, sculpting, woodworking and wine-making.

In the 10th century it was promoted to county status, but soon became part of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, whose history it shared for more than eight centuries. Its charter of 1066 is the first historically known charter north of the Alps, confirming it as a city. Around that time Peter the Hermit is said to have harangued the locals and persuaded them to join the First Crusade.

In the 13th and 14th centuries the cloth industry brought a boom, and the castle on the hill in the middle of town, strengthened in wartime, had become the city's symbol by the 15th century. The following two centuries saw a gradual decline. In the later 17th century the wars of Louis XIV caused the city to be repeatedly attacked, and in 1715 its frustrated inhabitants dismantled their own castle. The Dutch built a new fortress above the town in 1818, and the 19th century brought relative prosperity from paper and other industries.

Huy lies on the Meuse at the mouth of the small river Hoyoux, in the former industrial backbone of Wallonia. The four wonders of Huy are the bridge over the Meuse, the rose window of the Gothic collegiate church of Notre-Dame, the 15th-century fountain in the middle of the Grand Place and the citadel of 1818 that dominates the city. A religious procession is held every seven years in commemoration of the end of a drought in 1656.
huynh-tan-phat: Huỳnh Tấn Phát was born in 1913 in Châu Hưng village, in Mỹ Tho province, and studied architecture at the University of Hanoi. In 1940 he became the first Vietnamese architect to open a private architectural office in Saigon, and in 1941 he won first prize in the design contest for the Indochina Exhibition and Convention Center held by the Governor General, Jean Decoux. He designed the Hòa Bình Theater and many villas in what is now District 1 of Ho Chi Minh City. He also edited the anti-French magazine Jeunesse and co-founded the Vanguard Youth movement.

He joined the Indochinese Communist Party in March 1945, became Deputy Director of the Information and Press Committee for Southern Vietnam and sat in the First National Assembly of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Arrested when the French reoccupied Saigon after World War II, he was sentenced to two years in prison. On his release he resumed his revolutionary work and in 1949 became a Commissioner of the Administrative Resistance Committee for Southern Vietnam, directing the Free Voice of Saigon-Cho Lon Radio.

He emerged as a leading theoretician of the National Liberation Front and designed its flag. After the Republic of Vietnam surrendered on 30 April 1975, the Provisional Revolutionary Government he headed became the nominal government of South Vietnam until the country was reunified with the North on 2 July 1976. He then served as a vice premier until 1982, when he became Vice President of the Council of State, and from 1983 to 1988 he also chaired the Vietnamese Fatherland Front.

Huỳnh Tấn Phát remained Vice President of the Council of State until his death in Ho Chi Minh City in 1989, at the age of 76. He was awarded the Order of Ho Chi Minh. Many streets in Vietnamese cities and provinces bear his name, among them the former Provincial Road 15 in Ho Chi Minh City, which runs from Tân Thuận Bridge to the Bình Khánh ferry and was renamed after him shortly after his death.
hvalsey-church: According to the sagas, the land around Hvalsey was claimed by Thorkell Farserk, a relative of Erik the Red, and the farm's dwelling stands on an earlier building of Erik's time that may have been Thorkell's home. Christianity reached Greenland around the year 1000, and churches followed. The stone church is thought to date from the early 14th century, though archaeological finds hint that an older church stood on the site. Late medieval documents list it among the 10 to 14 parish churches of the Eastern Settlement, and Ívar Bárðarson, the Norwegian bishop's emissary to Garðar in the late 14th century, describes the homestead as a royal manor called Þjóðhildarstaðir.

The church stands on a narrow strip of land at the head of a fjord, about 70 metres from the water, within a typical Norse farmstead. The main farm building covered about 1,300 square metres, with eleven rooms combining living quarters, a banqueting hall and livestock pens; there were further pens, a horse enclosure for visitors, a storehouse up the hill and a warehouse at the shore.

The church measures about 16 by 8 metres and follows the Anglo-Norwegian style of the early 13th century. It held some 30 to 35 people, and a dyke marked the edge of the churchyard. Its walls, about 1.5 metres thick, are of carefully fitted granite fieldstones, some weighing 4 to 5 tonnes, and mortar made from crushed shells would have made it white; the name of nearby Qaqortoq, the white place, may come from it. The roof was probably of turf on timber. Window openings widen inwards, a feature unknown in Icelandic churches but known in early churches in Britain.

On 14 or 16 September 1408 the church hosted the wedding of Thorstein Olafsson and Sigrid Björnsdóttir, who later settled in Thorstein's native Iceland. An Inuit legend tells of a war in which the Inuk leader K'aissape attacked Hvalsey and burned the Norse in their houses, but archaeologists have found no sign of a fire. Because it was built over graves that were never removed, the church's foundations sank and it has partly collapsed, yet it has withstood the weather better than other Norse buildings. The site is now part of a sheep farm.
hvar: Hvar lies in the Adriatic off the Dalmatian coast, between the islands of Brač, Vis and Korčula. It is about 68 kilometres long and at most 10.5 kilometres wide, a high east-west ridge of limestone and dolomite that was part of the mainland until about 11,000 years ago. The landscape is karst, with little surface water, so farming depends on cisterns, dry-stone walls and terracing. Unusually for the area the island has a large fertile coastal plain and freshwater springs. Its position on the Adriatic sailing routes made it a base for commanding trade.

The first inhabitants were Neolithic people whose pottery gave its name to the Hvar culture, dated from 3500 to 2500 BCE, and later the Illyrians. Greeks from Paros colonised the island from the 4th century BCE, and in 384 BCE the colonists of Pharos defeated Iadasinoi warriors whom the natives had invited against them. Rome took the island in 219 BCE and renamed it Pharia. Later it came under the Byzantine Empire, and the Narentines took it in the first half of the 7th century. In the 11th century it joined the Kingdom of Croatia.

Venice became its long-term owner, and under Venetian rule the town of Hvar became a major naval base, with one of the first public theatres in Europe. The island was a centre of Croatian Renaissance literature, with writers such as Petar Hektorović, who designed Tvrdalj Castle at Stari Grad, and Hanibal Lucić. In the 16th century the Hvar Rebellion and raids by pirates and the Ottoman army led to fortified buildings on the northern shore. The fall of the Venetian Republic in 1797 gave the island to the Habsburg monarchy by the Treaty of Campo Formio, and after French and British occupation it returned to Austria in 1815.

Hvar is part of Split-Dalmatia County in Croatia, with two towns, Hvar and Stari Grad, and two municipalities, Jelsa and Sućuraj. Stari Grad stands on the site of Pharos, and its Plain preserves the field divisions laid out by the Greeks, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Tourism, begun with the Hygienic Association of Hvar in 1868, supports much of the economy, along with lavender, fishing and wine, including red wines from the Plavac Mali grape.
hwacha: Goryeo military leaders came to see firearms as necessary against the Japanese raiders who plundered coastal towns in growing numbers from 1350. Gunpowder was imported from China in 1374, but the Chinese kept the knowledge of making it under strict embargo. Ch'oe Musŏn learned to purify potassium nitrate from visiting Chinese merchants, and a government office for gunpowder and firearms was set up in 1377 with him at its head, producing hand cannons and rockets such as the juhwa.

The first hwacha was made by several scientists, among them Yi To and Ch'oe Haesan. In 1451 King Munjong ordered more powerful types, and by the end of that year fifty stood in Hanseong, present-day Seoul, and another 80 on the northern border.

The name means fire cart. The machine resembled a handcart whose top held a wooden launchpad of 100 to 200 holes for igniters; two arms at the back let the operator push and pull it, and tar oil eased its wheels on their iron axles. Its standard arrow was 1.1 m long, with a gunpowder-filled paper tube below the head, and reached up to 2,000 m. Because it fired light arrows or small iron balls, it was far lighter and easier to move than the cannon of contemporary Western warfare.

The Munjong hwacha, said to have been designed by the king and his younger brother Pe, had interchangeable modules: one fired 100 rocket-powered arrows, another 200 darts from 50 Chongtong gun barrels. The box-shaped Mangam hwacha carried forty barrels of 15 projectiles each, up to 600 bullets a salvo, and was worked by two soldiers.

Operators primed each hole with gunpowder from a bag tied to its igniter, loaded the ammunition, stepped back, covered their ears and pulled the igniter ropes. Against the Japanese invasions of the 1590s the weapons were mostly placed in fortresses and used defensively, and the dense formations of samurai infantry made good targets. At sea, on Panokseon warships, crews fired from the rowers' deck or aimed from the main deck at enemy sails. Some East Asian historians believe the hwacha and the turtle ship had a decisive effect on the war.
hwang-jini: Hwang Jini was born around 1506 to Hwang Chinsa, the son of a politician from a noble family of Kaesong, and a woman named Chin Hyŏn'gŭm, who was either a kisaeng or of cheonmin status. According to the story, her parents met while her mother was doing laundry but could not marry, so she became the youngest illegitimate daughter of Hwang. Another legend makes her the daughter of a blind commoner.

Women in the Joseon period were restricted to the house and treated as property, and a daughter born out of wedlock was regarded as an untouchable. According to legend she became a kisaeng at fifteen, after a coffin carrying a lover of higher class, who had died of a broken heart because her status barred their marriage, stopped at her house until she covered it with her skirt. The life of a kisaeng gave her the freedom to learn dance, music, art, literature and poetry, which were not normally taught to young women.

Only a handful of her sijo, a Korean verse form, and geomungo pieces survive. They show skilled handling of words and of musical arrangement. Her sijo often describe the sights of Kaesong, such as the palace of Manwŏltae and the Pakyon Falls in the Ahobiryong Mountains, the sorrow of lost loves, and responses to well known classical Chinese poems and literature.

One verse plays on a word that means both a sweetheart and a person frozen by winter cold, as the English phrase frozen love may suggest. Another, addressed to a man famed for his virtue, Byok Kye Su, puns on his name, which means green water, and on her own kisaeng name Myŏngwŏl, which means full moon. Like other kisaeng she asked visitors a riddle, and by legend only the yangban Sŏ Kyŏngdŏk solved it.
