Hwang Jini became an almost mythic figure in modern Korea. In the late twentieth century her story drew attention on both sides of the Korean divide. A 2002 novel by the North Korean writer Hong Sok-jung became the first North Korean novel to win a literary award in the South, the Manhae Prize, and a 2004 novel by the South Korean writer Jeon Gyeong-rin was a bestseller. She has also been portrayed in television series from 1982 and 2006 and in films of 1986 and 2007, and a crater on Venus, Hwangcini, is named after her.
hwanjile: Hwanjile came from the village of Home, in an Aja area west of Abomey in the south of present-day Benin. She was reportedly already an adult with two children when she was brought to the palace, and she was married to King Agaja before Tegbesu, the fourth king of Dahomey, appointed her to office. Her kin included the powerful Adanle, Hodonour and Kossou-Naeton merchant families of the trading town of Ouidah. The oral histories that are the chief source for eighteenth-century Dahomey do not explain why she allied herself with Tegbesu.

The title kpojito, also rendered Mother of the Leopard, is often translated as queen mother, though not quite accurately. A kpojito was the female reign mate of a king through a literal or symbolic mother-son bond; the office stood for a balancing of royal power and carried the authority to settle religious disputes.

Hwanjile used religion to make her own rule and Tegbesu's secure, working through the Dahomean vodun, or gods. The creator pair Mawu and Lisa, whom she brought from Aja, were given a home directly outside the royal palace, where she served as their high priest, and she also encouraged the use of fa divination.

Because of the key part she played in creating a strong, centralised kingdom in less than a generation, Hwanjile is counted among the most important figures in the history of Dahomey and of present-day Benin. After her death a direct descendant took her name and duties, and the successive holders of the name have continued to be politically powerful. A number of the gods she introduced are still worshipped in Benin.
hwaseong-fortress: King Jeongjo of Joseon built the fortress to house and honour the remains of his father, Crown Prince Sado, who had been executed by being locked in a rice chest by his own father, King Yeongjo. Jeongjo moved the tomb to the foot of Mount Hwasan in Suwon in 1789. The fortress also appears to have been meant as preparation for moving the capital from Seoul to Suwon. The king wished to leave the factional strife of the court to carry out reforms, and to encourage growth he exempted the people he ordered to move to Suwon from taxes for ten years.

The wall is 5.74 kilometres long and between 4 and 6 metres high, and it originally enclosed 1.3 square kilometres. The fortress has four main gates: Janganmun in the north, Hwaseomun in the west, Paldalmun in the south and Changnyongmun in the east. Janganmun is the largest gate in Korea. The stream Suwoncheon flows through the centre of the fortress and passes under two floodgates, Hwahongmun and Namsumun. Along the wall stood 48 structures, among them gun towers, sentry posts, turrets, secret gates and a beacon tower placed in direct line with the king's temporary palace, Haenggung.

Haenggung stands within the walls. Jeongjo stayed there when he came from Seoul to worship at his father's tomb, and it also served for a banquet on the 60th birthday of his mother and for state examinations. In 1795 the king led a royal procession to the tomb of 5,661 people and 1,417 horses.

The fortress was built over two and a half years, from 1794 to 1796, to designs attributed to Chŏng Yagyong, later a leading figure of the Silhak movement, whose name means practical learning. He drew on fortress designs from Korea and China and on the science of his day. Silhak thought also lay behind the use of brick and of efficient pulleys and cranes. A white paper in ten volumes, the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe, was published in 1801, shortly after Jeongjo's death. It sets out the plans, the royal orders, the wages of the workers, who were assigned by trade, and the quantities of materials used.

The fortress was severely damaged in the Korean War, when its main gates were among the structures destroyed. The records proved invaluable when it was reconstructed in the 1970s. UNESCO designated the fortress and its palace a World Heritage Site in 1997.
hydatius: Hydatius was born around 400 near Civitas Lemica, a Roman town close to modern Xinzo de Limia in Ourense. As a boy he travelled to the Holy Land with his mother and met Jerome at his hermitage in Bethlehem. He joined the clergy about 417 and in 427 was consecrated bishop, probably of Chaves, the Roman Aquae Flaviae. The Suevi had settled in Gallaecia in 411 and imperial control weakened during his lifetime. In 431 he took part in a deputation to the general Flavius Aëtius asking for help against the Suevi. He also worked against heresy, calling the Hispanian heretics Manichees, though they were probably Priscillianists, and petitioned Pope Leo I with Thoribius of Astorga.

His chronicle continues Jerome's from the year 379, and he used four parallel chronological systems, which makes the dating hard to translate into a modern calendar. The entries are brief at first, but from 427 he writes as a contemporary witness, and the text grows fuller until it resembles a literary work more than a chronicle. He aimed to show the dissolution of civil society in the western Roman empire and in Hispania, and painted a dark picture of fifth-century life.

Perhaps he believed the world would end in May 482, as an apocryphal letter of Christ to Thomas was read to show, and on occasion he distorted his account to make events gloomier. This holds especially for the sack of the Suevi capital at Braga in 456 by the Visigothic king Theodoric II.

In 460 local enemies kidnapped and imprisoned him for a time. He probably died in 468 or soon after, since his chronicle breaks off abruptly then. It is the only source for the history of Hispania in the period up to 468. It is doubtful whether he also wrote the Fasti consulares for 245 to 468 that is appended to the chronicle in the only almost complete manuscript. Theodor Mommsen's edition of 1894 was long the standard, and R. W. Burgess published the text with an English translation in 1993.
hyder-ali: The date of Hyder Ali's birth is not known with certainty; sources give years between 1717 and 1722. His father, Fath Muhammad, served in the army of the Nawab of Carnatic and then entered the service of the Wodeyar rajas of Mysore, rising to be a powerful military commander and receiving Budikote as a jagir. Hyder Ali was born there, the fifth child of his father and the second by his third wife, Razia Bibi.

In 1749 the Mysorean army marched in support of Nasir Jung in the struggle that followed the death of the Nizam of Hyderabad, and Hyder Ali and his brother distinguished themselves in the eight-month siege of Devanahalli Fort. In 1757 he restored order in the Mysorean army, which was near mutiny over pay, and he later forced the Marathas to lift a siege of Bangalore in 1758 and defeated a much larger Maratha army at Channapatna in 1759. By 1759 he commanded the entire army.

In 1760 the queen mother and his former financial assistant Khande Rao drove him from Seringapatam. The Maratha defeat at the Third Battle of Panipat in January 1761 led the Marathas to withdraw from Mysore, and Hyder Ali returned. He became ruler in 1761 after overthrowing the prime minister and keeping King Krishnaraja Wodeyar II a prisoner in his own palace. He styled himself Sultan Hyder Ali Khan in his letters to the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II.

He took Sira from the Marathas and, in 1763, the capital of Bednore, Ikkeri, which he renamed Haidernagar. In 1766 he defeated the Zamorin of Kozhikode and absorbed the Malabar region into Mysore. A Maratha invasion in November 1770 led to a peace in 1772 under which he paid tribute and ceded territory as far as Bangalore. He improved the use of rockets, with iron casings better than those then available in Europe, and the rockets of Mysore later stirred British interest, leading William Congreve to develop his own rockets.

In July 1780 Hyder Ali swept down onto the coastal plain of the Carnatic with an army estimated at 83,000. At the Battle of Pollilur on 10 September, he and his son Tipu surrounded a force under Colonel William Baillie and compelled about 3,000 men to surrender. Arcot fell in November. Hyder Ali, who suffered from a cancerous growth on his back, died in his camp in December 1782, leaving his son Tipu Sultan an extensive kingdom. During the American Revolution Patriots praised him, and in 1781 the Pennsylvania State Navy commissioned a warship named Hyder-Ally.
hyderabad: Hyderabad occupies about 650 square kilometres on the Deccan Plateau along the Musi River, in the northern part of South India. The ground is mostly sloping granite dotted with small hills, and the city has numerous artificial lakes, among them Hussain Sagar, built in 1562 near the centre. The climate is tropical wet and dry, with hot, dry summers from March to June. Megalithic burial sites found in 1851 by Philip Meadows Taylor show that the region has been inhabited since the Stone Age.

The region was ruled by the Chalukya dynasty from 624 to 1075 and then by the Kakatiya dynasty from 1158, whose ruler Ganapatideva (1199–1262) built the hilltop outpost later known as Golconda Fort. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah of the Qutb Shahi dynasty established Hyderabad in 1591 to extend the capital beyond the fortified Golconda. The name means Haydar's City, after Caliph Ali Ibn Abi Talib, and the city was first called Baghnagar, city of gardens. The Mughals annexed it in 1687.

In 1724 Asaf Jah I, the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan, defeated Mubariz Khan at the Battle of Shakar Kheda and established his autonomy, founding the Asaf Jahi dynasty, whose rulers are known as the Nizams of Hyderabad. Hyderabad remained their capital until 1948, and as capital of the princely state it housed the British Residency and cantonment until Indian independence in 1947. After a flood of the Musi in 1908 the city was expanded and civic monuments were built, particularly under Mir Osman Ali Khan, the seventh Nizam. The Indian Union annexed Hyderabad in 1948.

Hyderabad is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of Telangana, with 6.9 million inhabitants within the city limits at the 2011 census. Until the 19th century it was known as the City of Pearls and was the only trading centre for Golconda diamonds in the world. The Charminar has come to symbolise the city, and UNESCO lists Hyderabad as a creative city of gastronomy.
hyderabad-state-congress: Hyderabad lay outside British India, but its Nizam was styled the Most Faithful Ally of the British Government. Until 1920 the state had no political organisation of any kind. The Andhra Jana Sangham, later the Andhra Mahasabha, was formed in November 1921 to raise political awareness in Telangana, and despite a gagging order of 1929 that required permission for every public meeting it took up the rights of ryots, women's rights and the uplift of Dalits. Similar bodies, the Maharashtra Parishad and the Karnataka Parishad, followed in Marathwada and Karnataka in 1937.

A Hyderabad People's Convention submitted a report on reform to the Nizam's Constitutional Reforms Committee in January 1938. In February the Indian National Congress passed the Haripura resolution, calling the princely states an integral part of India, and the convention's standing committee then proposed a Hyderabad State Congress. By July 1938 it claimed 1,200 primary members. On 6 September, three days before its first elections, the Nizam passed a Public Safety Act and declared it unlawful.

After talks to lift the ban failed, the party's Committee of Action began a satyagraha on 24 October 1938, its members openly declaring their membership and courting arrest; the Arya Samaj and Hindu Mahasabha launched their own campaign the same day. The Indian National Congress refused its support, and Padmaja Naidu reported to Gandhi that the State Congress lacked unity and was communal. The agitation was suspended on 24 December after 300 activists had been arrested. The Hindu organisations later reached a compromise with the government, but the State Congress stayed banned and its jailed members remained in prison.

In 1942 its leaders launched a new satyagraha for civil rights and representative democracy alongside the Quit India movement, and the ban was lifted only in April 1946. The party then campaigned for Hyderabad to join the Indian Union and called for 7 August 1947 to be kept as Join Indian Union Day. Protests, strikes and flag-hoisting followed across the state; the government banned the party again and made mass arrests, while the Razakars, the militant wing of the Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen, threatened pogroms against Hindu civilians. The crisis lasted until September 1948, when the Indian Army annexed Hyderabad in an operation that led to the massacre of many civilians.
hydra-greece: Hydra is one of the Saronic Islands, lying between the Myrtoan Sea and the Argolic Gulf and separated from the Peloponnese by a narrow strip of water. Its ancient name, Hydrea, comes from the Greek word for water and refers to natural springs, though the island is now almost dry and imports its water by boat.

Evidence of farmers and herders dates from the second half of the third millennium BCE, and in the Helladic period the island probably served as a maritime base for kingdoms on the mainland. The Dorian invasion around the 12th century BCE appears to have depopulated it, and it was resettled in the 8th century BCE. Arvanites, Albanian speakers who came from the Peloponnese, settled in the early 16th century and built the modern harbour town, and Arvanitika was spoken by all Hydriots into the 19th century.

Because the soil is infertile, the inhabitants turned to the sea. Hydra opened its first school for mariners in 1645, and after the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 its shipping grew. In 1757 they launched a vessel of 250 tons. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca gave Russia the right to protect Ottoman Orthodox Christians and allowed free passage between the Aegean and the Black Sea, and Hydriot ships carried goods between southern Russia and the Italian ports of Ancona and Livorno.

In April 1821 Antonis Oikonomou expelled the Ottoman governor and proclaimed Hydra's adherence, but he was hounded off the island and killed by assassins in December 1821. Hydra then contributed some 150 ships and supplies, and the admiral Andreas Miaoulis used Hydriot fire ships to inflict heavy losses on the Ottoman fleet. With Psara and Spetses, Hydra helped to win control of the eastern Aegean. After independence the fleet lost the privileges of the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca and was slow to adopt steamships, and the island declined. About eight per cent of the population died of famine during the Axis occupation of 1941-1943.

The main settlement is Hydra port, built around a crescent-shaped harbour. Wheeled vehicles are not allowed, and rubbish trucks are the only motor vehicles, so horses, mules, donkeys and water taxis provide transport. The island depends on tourism, and Athenians are a sizable share of its visitors. The sea captains' mansions around the harbour survive, among them those of the Tsamados, Tombazis and Kountouriotis families,.
hydroelectricity: The use of water to generate mechanical energy can be traced back to 203 BCE in Han dynasty China. In the late 18th century hydraulic power supplied the energy for the start of the Industrial Revolution. In the mid-1700s the French engineer Bernard Forest de Bélidor published Architecture Hydraulique, describing vertical- and horizontal-axis hydraulic machines, and in 1771 Richard Arkwright's combination of water power, the water frame and continuous production played a significant part in the growth of the factory system. In the 1840s hydraulic power networks were developed to generate and transmit hydro power to users.

On 30 September 1882 the first Edison hydroelectric power station, the Vulcan Street Plant, began operating in Appleton, Wisconsin, with an output of about 12.5 kilowatts. By 1886 there were 45 hydroelectric power stations in the United States and Canada. By 1920, 40 per cent of the power produced in the United States was hydroelectric, and the Federal Power Act created the Federal Power Commission to regulate stations on federal land and water.

As stations grew, their dams took on further purposes, including flood control, irrigation and navigation, and large projects needed federal funding, such as the Tennessee Valley Authority (1933) and the Bonneville Power Administration (1937). Hoover Dam's 1,345 MW power station was the world's largest in 1936 and was surpassed by the 6,809 MW Grand Coulee Dam in 1942. Itaipu, opened in 1984, was surpassed in 2008 by the Three Gorges Dam. Hydropower was called white coal.

Most hydroelectric power comes from the potential energy of dammed water driving a turbine and generator. The power extracted depends on the volume of water and on the height difference between source and outflow, called the head; a large pipe, the penstock, delivers water from the reservoir to the turbine. Pumped-storage schemes move water between reservoirs at different elevations, pumping it up when demand is low and releasing it through a turbine when demand is high. Run-of-the-river stations have little or no reservoir, so that only the water arriving from upstream is available. Tidal power stations use the daily rise and fall of ocean water.
hyecho: Little is known of Hyech'o's life in Silla, and his name does not appear among the monks of the Haedong Goseungjeon; most of what is known comes from his own travelogue. In an age when Korean monks often went to Tang China to study, he came there to learn esoteric Buddhism, first under Śubhakarasiṃha and then under the Indian monk Vajrabodhi, who praised him as one of six living persons well trained in the five sections of the Buddhist canon. His Sanskrit name was Prajñāvikrama.

Probably around 724 he left China by sea, stopping at Sumatra and landing at the port of Tāmralipti in Bengal. He visited Bodh Gaya, Lumbini, Kushinagar, Sarnath, Vaishali and Vulture Peak, finding one sacred site almost deserted, with a single monk, and described a Pillar of Ashoka with its lion capital. From Kannauj he turned south, off the usual pilgrims' route, and noted a great rock-cut monastery, possibly the Ajanta or Nasik Caves. He then walked north to a land he called West India, probably Sindh, which he said had been destroyed by Arabs.

In Kashmir he found many monks and a devout Buddhist king. He passed through lands under Tibetan control in what scholars identify as Baltistan and Ladakh, reached Gilgit and the Afghan lands of a Turkic king, likely of the Turk Shahis, visiting Kapisa in 726, Zabulistan and Bamiyan. Beyond Tokharistan he found no Buddhists; at Samarkand the people followed a fire religion. In Wakhan he met a Chinese envoy, and he returned to Tang territory, where his account ends in 729.

His Memoir of a Pilgrimage to the Five Kingdoms of India, written in Chinese, records diet, languages, climate, customs and politics, the decline of Buddhism in India and the cattle that roamed freely through towns and villages. Paul Pelliot found a fragment in the Mogao Caves in 1908; the original fragment is now in France. In 2017 the scholar Donald S. Lopez Jr. used his journey in Hyecho's Journey: The World of Buddhism to introduce the Buddhist traditions of the period.
hyegong-of-silla: Hyegong, whose personal name was Kim Kŏn-un, was born in 758, the only child of King Gyeongdeok and Lady Manwol, later Queen Gyeongsu, and a grandson of Seongdeok of Silla, who reigned from 702 to 737, and of Queen Sodeok of the Kim clan. He was the 36th ruler of the kingdom. Because he was the last descendant of King Muyeol to sit on the throne, his reign is often regarded as the end of the middle period of the Silla state.

Hyegong became king at the age of eight and did not adapt well to the role. According to the Samguk sagi, his dissolute life as a young monarch kept the palace in disarray. High officials, Kim Daegong among them, led rebellions against him in 768, 770 and 775. He had two queens, Queen Wi of the Wi clan and Queen Changchang of the Kim clan, a daughter of Kim Chang.

In 780 the ichan Kim Chi-jŏng led another rebellion. The king sent the sangdaedeung Kim Yang-sang to put it down, but the rebels stormed the palace and killed Hyegong together with other members of the royal family. Kim Yang-sang, an eleventh-generation descendant of King Naemul, then took the throne himself as King Seondeok.

The records describe Hyegong's behaviour as effeminate, and tradition called him a man by appearance but a woman by nature. The historian Ahn Jeong-bok, in the Dongsa Gangmok, described the reign as peculiar, writing that the king had become a man as a woman and had played with girls' toys as a child. Present-day historians often speculate that Hyegong was a trans woman.
hyeonjong-of-goryeo: Hyeonjong, whose personal name was Wang Sun, was born on 1 August 992, a grandson of the dynastic founder King Taejo of Goryeo. He was the child of an affair between Prince Wang Uk, later given the temple name Anjong, and his widowed niece, Queen Heonjeong. Because of the affair his father was exiled, and his mother died in childbirth.

Wang Sun was heir to the childless King Mokjong, but Queen Dowager Cheonchu wanted the throne for her son by her lover, Kim Ch'i-yang. Wang Sun was forced to become a monk, and when she sent assassins against him the abbot of his temple foiled the attempts. In 1009 Kang Cho, the military inspector of Seobukmyeon, whom Mokjong had called on to destroy a plot by Kim Ch'i-yang, overthrew Mokjong and installed Wang Sun as king.

In 1010 the Khitan Liao dynasty attacked Goryeo, using the deposition of Mokjong as its cause for war. Kang Cho tried to stop the invaders but was defeated in battle and captured. Hyeonjong fled the capital and, with the help of General Kang Kam-ch'an, moved the court far south to the port city of Naju. During the flight he met Kim Un-bu at Gongju and married his daughter, Queen Wonseong. In the end Goryeo repulsed the Khitan and forced them to withdraw.

Because Goryeo still refused to submit or to return the northern territories, the Khitan attacked again in 1019. Goryeo generals, among them Kang Kam-ch'an, inflicted heavy losses on the Khitan army at the Battle of Kwiju, and the Khitan withdrew without achieving their demands. They never invaded Goryeo again, and both the Liao dynasty and Goryeo entered a time of peace in which their cultures reached their height.

Hyeonjong also ordered the compilation of the Tripitaka Koreana, a work of 6,000 volumes. Carving its woodblocks was held to be a way of changing the kingdom's fortune by invoking the help of the Buddha.

Hyeonjong died on 17 June 1031. He had many consorts, among them several queens of the Ansan Kim clan, and a large family of sons and daughters. He is counted among the leading rulers of Korean history, and he has been portrayed on Korean television in the series Empress Cheonchu of 2009 and Korea–Khitan War of 2023.
hyfaidd-ap-bleddri: Hyfaidd was born around 830. Triad 68 in the Red Book of Hergest, a manuscript of the fourteenth century, names him among the "Three Kings who Sprang from Villeins", meaning that his father, Bleddri or Bledrig, was held to have been a serf rather than a member of Dyfed's old royal house, which claimed descent from Aed Brosc. His mother is said to have been Tangwystl, a daughter of the earlier King Owain ap Maredudd.

The historian T. Charles-Edwards argues that Hyfaidd brought together the lands that later formed Deheubarth, annexing Ystrad Tywi and possibly Ceredigion to Dyfed. He is said to have oppressed the clergy of Meneva, the modern St David's, and to have driven Bishop Nobis into exile, which earned him the enmity of Nobis's kinsman, the historian Asser, Bishop of Sherborne. In his Life of King Alfred, Asser reports that Dyfed and Brycheiniog came under sustained attack from Anarawd and Cadell, sons of Rhodri Mawr. Hyfaidd and Elise ap Tewdur of Brycheiniog therefore accepted the overlordship of King Alfred of Wessex in return for his protection.

Hyfaidd's sons Llywarch and Rhodri reigned after him, but both were dead by 905, probably in war; Rhodri ap Hyfaidd was beheaded in Arwystli. Dyfed soon passed to Cadell's son Hywel Dda, who joined his realms together as Deheubarth. Later Welsh histories presented Hywel's inheritance of Dyfed as peaceful, the result of his marriage to Hyfaidd's granddaughter Elen, who died in 929, and the extinction of Hyfaidd's male line. Asser's more contemporary account instead records the sustained attacks on Dyfed by Hywel's father and uncle.
hygelac: Beowulf gives Hygelac's genealogy. According to the poem he was the son of Hrethel and had two brothers, Herebeald and Hæþcyn, as well as an unnamed sister who married Ecgtheow and was the mother of the hero Beowulf. Hygelac married Hygd, and they had a son, Heardred, and an unnamed daughter who married Eofor. His name appears in Old Norse as Hugleikr and in Latin sources as Chlochilaicus or Hugilaicus.

The poem tells of a war with the Swedes in which Hæþcyn was killed. Hygelac arrived at Hrefnesholt one day too late to save his brother, but he rescued the surviving Geatish warriors, who were besieged by the Swedish king Ongentheow and his three sons. The Swedes took refuge in a hill fort, which the Geats stormed, and Eofor killed the Swedish king in the fighting. Hygelac ruled the Geats until he was killed during a raid on Frisia, after which, according to Beowulf, Heardred succeeded him.

The raid allowed N. F. S. Grundtvig to date Hygelac's death, because Gregory of Tours records a raid on the Frankish kingdoms by a king Chlochilaicus in the reign of Theodericus I, son of Clovis. The raiders were caught by a force under Theodericus's son Theodebertus, and the survivors fled to sea so hastily that they left their dead, their king among them. Gregory reports that the corpse, awe-inspiring for its height, was long exhibited at a Merovingian court. Gregory calls him a king of the Danes, while the later Liber historiae Francorum calls him a king of the Goths, as Beowulf does.

The early eighth-century Liber Monstrorum also names him, as Higlacus, a king of the Geats killed by the Franks whom no horse could carry from the age of twelve, and whose bones were shown to travellers on an island at the mouth of the Rhine. Leonard Neidorf argues that Beowulf and the Liber Monstrorum drew on a shared oral tradition from Scandinavia. Other scholars hold that the poem depends on the Liber historiae Francorum, and Walter Goffart estimated that it could not have been written with these details before 923.
hyksos: In modern Egyptology the name Hyksos, from the Egyptian ḥqꜣ-ḫꜣswt, 'rulers of foreign lands', refers to the kings of the Fifteenth Dynasty (c. 1650 – c. 1550 BCE), rather than to a people, although the later Greek writers used it ethnically. Manetho, a Greco-Egyptian priest of the 3rd century BCE, whose work survives only in quotation, portrayed them as invaders who burnt cities and razed temples; modern Egyptology questions this account.

Excavations at Tell el-Dab'a, the site of their capital Avaris, since 1966 indicate a Levantine origin. Their personal names are West Semitic, and they may be called Canaanites for convenience. Canaanite groups may have settled gradually in the Nile Delta from the end of the Twelfth Dynasty and seceded from weakening Egyptian control during the Thirteenth.

From Avaris the Hyksos ruled Lower Egypt and Middle Egypt as far as Cusae, while the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Dynasties coexisted at Thebes. The Turin King List names six Hyksos kings who ruled 108 years, though other scholars read the figure as higher; only the last king, Khamudi, is preserved by name. Khyan left objects at Knossos and Hattusha, and a cuneiform letter found at Avaris shows long-distance diplomacy.

The war between Thebes and the Hyksos is known only from Theban sources, which present it as a war of national liberation, a view scholars no longer hold. Kamose, last king of the Seventeenth Dynasty, called Apepi a chieftain of Retjenu. Ahmose I finally defeated the Hyksos and founded the Eighteenth Dynasty.

Later Egyptians condemned the Hyksos, and the Nineteenth-Dynasty tale of Apophis and Seqenenre claimed they worshipped no god but Set. About eighty years after their defeat, Hatshepsut claimed to rebuild temples they had neglected. Josephus connected them with the Jews, but modern scholars do not accept that the biblical story can be shown by historical methods.

Their rulers took the full Egyptian royal titulary and employed Egyptian scribes, but they also used Near Eastern forms of administration, including a chancellor at the head of the government. Apepi had the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus copied. Avaris had temples in both Egyptian and Levantine style, and the Hyksos worshipped the Canaanite storm god Baal, identified with the Egyptian Set. They buried their dead within settlements and also buried horses and other equids.

The Hyksos have been credited with the horse, the chariot, the sickle sword and the composite bow, but this is disputed. No evidence shows that they possessed chariots, which first appear in Egyptian hands in the account of Ahmose, son of Ebana, at the end of their rule. Avaris was the commercial capital of the Delta, trading mainly with Canaan and Cyprus.
hymn-of-the-pearl: Some scholars believe the hymn is older than the Acts of Thomas, since it appears in only one Syriac manuscript and one Greek manuscript of that work. Its author is unknown. Some attribute it to Bardaisan of Edessa, the Syriac gnostic, because of parallels between his life and the story it tells. The hymn shows influences from the heroic folk epics of the region, and its vocabulary is full of Parthian loanwords.

The hymn tells of a boy, the son of the king of kings, whose parents send him from Parthia to Egypt to bring back a pearl guarded by a hissing serpent in the middle of the sea. In Egypt the people perceive that he is not of their country and make him eat their food. He forgets that he is a son of kings, serves their king, forgets the pearl and falls into a deep sleep. His parents send him a letter signed by every noble, telling him: "Awake and arise from your sleep".

Remembering his mission, he charms the serpent to sleep by naming his father's name over it, snatches the pearl and strips off their filthy and unclean clothing. His parents send his glorious garment to meet him, and clothed in it he ascends to the palace of peace and worship. The boy is implicitly Thomas rather than Jesus, since he is said to be next in line to an elder brother not otherwise mentioned in the text.

The hymn is commonly read as a Gnostic view of the human condition: spirits lost in a world of matter and forgetful of their true origin, who may be awakened by a revelatory message delivered by a messenger, a role generally ascribed to Jesus. The letter thus stands for gnosis. The hymn was preserved and especially treasured in Manichaeism, and a version appears in a Coptic Manichaean psalm book as the Psalms of Thomas. Orthodox Christian thinkers and members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints have also admired it.
hymn-to-liberty: The Hymn to Liberty is a Greek poem written by Dionysios Solomos in 1823 and set to music by Nikolaos Mantzaros in 1828. It was printed in Messolonghi a year after it was written, and in October 1824 the Philhellenic Committee published it in London. An Italian translation appeared at about the same time in the Messolonghi newspaper Ellinika Chronika.

Mantzaros, a Corfiot operatic composer, wrote a choral version in 24 parts and dedicated it to Otto, the first king of Greece, who rewarded him with the Silver Cross of the Order of the Redeemer. During Otto's reign, from 1832 to 1862, however, an anthem based on God Save the King with a text praising Otto was used instead.

Solomos wrote the hymn, inspired by the Greek War of Independence, to honour the struggle of the Greeks against centuries of Ottoman rule. It tells of their misery under the Ottomans and their hope of freedom. It describes events of the war, among them the execution of Patriarch Gregory V of Constantinople, the reaction of the Great Powers and, at length, the Siege of Tripolitsa, and it stresses the Christian character of the struggle.

After Otto was ousted in 1862, the hymn was adopted in 1864 as the national and royal anthem of Greece, using its first two stanzas. It remained the royal anthem from 1864 to 1924 and again from 1935 to 1973, each time until the monarchy was abolished. An adapted version served the short-lived Cretan State as its anthem.

Cyprus adopted the hymn as its national anthem in 1966 by order of its Council of Ministers, after an anthem by the Cypriot composer Solon Michaelides, shared with Turkish Cypriots, was abandoned in 1963 during intercommunal conflicts. The hymn is performed at every closing ceremony of the Olympic Games to honour Greece as their birthplace, usually in an instrumental version. The arrangement played by military bands is by Lieutenant Colonel Margaritis Kastellis.
hyogo-prefecture: Hyōgo covers about 8,400 square kilometres and borders Kyoto Prefecture to the east, Osaka Prefecture to the south-east and Okayama and Tottori prefectures to the west. It has coasts on the Sea of Japan to the north and the Seto Inland Sea to the south, and on Awaji Island it also meets the Pacific. The north is sparsely populated, apart from Toyooka, and the central highlands hold only tiny villages. Most people live on the southern coast, part of the Osaka–Kobe–Kyoto metropolitan area. The north gets abundant snow in winter.

The prefecture includes the former provinces of Harima, Tajima and Awaji and parts of Tanba and Settsu. In 1180, near the end of the Heian period, Emperor Antoku, Taira no Kiyomori and the imperial court moved briefly to Fukuhara, in what is now Kobe, and the capital stayed there for five months. In 1995 the Great Hanshin earthquake, of magnitude 6.9, devastated southern Hyōgo, destroying large parts of Kobe and Awaji as well as Nishinomiya and Ashiya and killing nearly 6,500 people.

Kobe is the capital and largest city, and other major cities are Himeji, Nishinomiya and Amagasaki. Kobe Port is one of the largest in Japan, and since 1975 prefectural law has kept it free of nuclear weapons. Hyōgo belongs to the Hanshin Industrial Region and holds two Riken research institutes, at Kobe and Harima, as well as the SPring-8 synchrotron at Harima. Its cultural sites include several National Treasures, the preservation districts of Izushi and Sasayama, the hot springs of Arima and the Takarazuka Revue. In 1963 Hyōgo became the first Japanese prefecture to enter a sister state relationship with an American state, Washington.
hypaspists: The Greek word hypaspistes means shield bearer. In Homer's Iliad Deiphobos advances under cover of his shield, and by the time of Herodotus the word had come to mean a soldier of high status. A hypaspist differed from a skeuophoros, a baggage carrier, because the shield bearer was a free warrior and the baggage carrier a servant. The word may have had Homeric and heroic connotations that led Philip II of Macedon to use it for an elite military unit.

The Macedonian hypaspists were probably armed in the hoplite manner, with a large concave shield and a spear, a body armour of spolas or linothorax, a helmet, greaves and a sword, though their equipment was likely more ornate than that of ordinary soldiers. The main Macedonian phalanx instead consisted of pikemen called phalangites, armed with the sarissa, a pike of between 4 and 6.7 metres, and a small flat shield.

In set-piece battles the hypaspists stood on the flanks of the phalanx, and light infantry and cavalry protected their own flanks. Their task was to guard the flanks of the large and unwieldy pike phalanx, since the phalangites were not agile or quick to turn. The phalanx served as the anvil, and the Companion cavalry as the hammer, in the tactic of Philip II. The hypaspists could carry out manoeuvres that phalangites could not. Arrian's phrase describing them has often been rendered 'lightest armed', although it is more properly translated as 'nimblest' or 'most agile'. They may have been raised from the whole kingdom rather than by canton, in which case they were the king's army rather than the army of the kingdom.

All references to a unit called Hypaspists are much later than the time of Philip, and modern historians must assume that later writers such as Diodorus Siculus and Arrian had access to earlier records. In the Hellenistic period hypaspists apparently continued under different names, such as the agema, in the Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Antigonid kingdoms, as royal bodyguards, elite infantry and military administrators. Polybius mentions a hypaspist sent by Philip V of Macedon to Larissa to burn state papers after the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE. In Macedon the fighting unit seems to have lived on as the Antigonid peltasts, originally 3,000 men and 5,000 by the Third Macedonian War.
hypatia: Hypatia was the daughter of Theon of Alexandria, whose main achievement was a new edition of Euclid's Elements correcting scribal errors made over nearly 700 years of copying; it became the most widely used edition for centuries. Like her father, Hypatia rejected the teachings of Iamblichus and embraced the original Neoplatonism of Plotinus. Alexandria was regarded as second only to Athens as the philosophical capital of the Greco-Roman world, and she taught students from all over the Mediterranean. According to Damascius, she lectured on Plato and Aristotle, and walked through the city in a tribon, a cloak associated with philosophers, giving impromptu public lectures.

Hypatia was probably more a teacher and commentator than an innovator. No evidence shows that she published independent philosophical works, but scholars of her time preserved and commented on classical mathematical texts rather than publishing new ones. She is now known to have edited Book III of Ptolemy's Almagest; its title in Theon's commentary describes an edition revised by his daughter Hypatia, the philosopher. Her contribution is thought to be an improved tabular method for the long divisions needed in astronomical computation. She also wrote a commentary on Diophantus's Arithmetica, which may survive in part, and one on the conic sections of Apollonius of Perga, which has not survived.

A letter of her pupil Synesius, the future bishop of Ptolemais, says she taught him to construct a silver plane astrolabe as a gift for an official. Ancient sources record that she was widely loved by pagans and Christians alike.

According to Socrates Scholasticus, in March 415, during Lent, a mob of Christians led by a lector named Peter seized Hypatia's carriage as she travelled home, dragged her into the Kaisarion, a former pagan temple turned church, and killed her. Her body was torn apart and burned. Although no firm evidence linked the bishop Cyril to the murder, it was widely believed that he had ordered it, and the Alexandrian council sent an embassy to Constantinople; the advisers of Theodosius II began an investigation. Her death shocked the empire, and Neoplatonists such as Damascius grew more fervent in their opposition to Christianity.

Neoplatonism survived in Alexandria for centuries afterwards. In the Middle Ages she was part of the basis for the legend of Saint Catherine of Alexandria. Charles Kingsley's novel Hypatia of 1853 called her the last of the Hellenes. Some modern portrayals link her death to the destruction of the Library of Alexandria, although the library no longer existed in her lifetime.
hypocaust: The word hypocaust comes from the Ancient Greek hupó, under, and kaustós, burnt. A system that produces and circulates hot air below the floor of a room, and may also warm the walls through a series of pipes, it could warm upper floors as well. The earliest reference to such a system suggests that the Temple of Ephesus was heated in this way in 350 BCE. Vitruvius attributes the invention to Sergius Orata, around 80 BCE. It improved the hygiene and living conditions of citizens and was a forerunner of modern central heating.

The floor of a hypocaust was raised above the ground on pillars called pilae stacks. These carried a layer of tiles, then a layer of concrete, then the floor tiles of the rooms above. Hot air and smoke from the furnace circulated through the enclosed space and rose through clay or tile flues in the walls, called caliducts, to outlets in the roof. This warmed the floors and walls above. The rooms meant to be warmest lay nearest the furnace, and the heat was regulated by the amount of wood fed to the fire.

Vitruvius describes its construction and operation in De architectura, around 15 BCE. He explains how fuel could be saved by placing the men's hot room, the caldarium, next to the women's, both beside the tepidarium, so that public baths ran efficiently. He also describes a bronze ventilator in the domed ceiling for adjusting the heat.

Hypocausts heated hot baths and other public buildings in ancient Rome, and also private homes. Wealthier merchants considered them proper and necessary for their villas across the empire. They were expensive and labour-intensive, since they needed constant attention to the fire and much fuel, and so were found mostly in large villas and public baths. Remains survive in Italy, England, Spain, France, Switzerland and Germany, and in western Asia and northern Africa. In the Georgian settlement of Dzalisi, excavations in 1984-1985 uncovered a castle complex with a well-preserved hypocaust built between 200 and 400 CE. Korean ondol floor heating and the kang bed-stove of northern China work on similar principles.

With the decline of the Roman Empire the hypocaust fell into disuse in the western provinces, but not in the Eastern Roman Empire. Some monasteries used an evolution of it in warming rooms, or calefactories. In the Iberian Peninsula the Roman system was adopted for the Hispano-Islamic baths of Al Andalus, and a derivative, the gloria, was used in Castile until modern heating arrived. In the 1720s the house of the Maryland governor Charles Calvert was built with a hypocaust to heat a greenhouse for tropical plants.
hyrcania: Hyrcania was the land of the Hyrcani people south-east of the Caspian Sea, in what is now Iran and Turkmenistan. It was bounded on the south by the Alborz mountains and on the east by the Kopet Dag, and bordered Parthia to the east, Dihistan to the north, Media to the south and Mardia to the west. The Greek name borrows the Old Persian Verkana, from a word meaning wolf. Its capital and largest city in antiquity was Zadracarta. Immediately to the north lived the Dahae.

Hyrcania was part of the Median Empire by 600 BCE, and it submitted willingly to Cyrus the Great, who occupied it in 549 to 548 BCE. A revolt in support of the Median leader Phraortes broke out there in December 522 BCE and was put down in May 521 BCE. Hyrcanian soldiers served in the Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. Alexander the Great reached Hyrcania in 330 BCE, accepted the surrender of the satrap Phrataphernes and took Zadracarta.

After Alexander's death Hyrcania passed to several satraps and then to the Seleucid Empire. Arsaces conquered it in 235 BCE, and it became part of the Arsacid Empire. Under Arsacid rule a long wall of forts, the Great Wall of Gorgan, was built against raids by the Dahae. Hyrcanians rebelled during the Roman-Parthian War of 58 to 63. Ardashir I annexed the region to the Sasanian Empire in 225, and its centre moved to Gurgan, where Yazdegerd I was assassinated by nobles in 420.

The region lies in modern Iran and Turkmenistan. In antiquity Zoroastrianism dominated it, but Christianity and Judaism were also practised, and a diocese of the Church of the East existed at Gurgan from 424. In Latin literature Hyrcania is known above all for its tigers, which Virgil names in the Aeneid, and Shakespeare later used the image of the Hyrcanian tiger.
hyrcanus-ii: Hyrcanus was the elder of two sons of Alexander Jannaeus, king and high priest, and Salome Alexandra. After Alexander died in 76 BCE his widow ruled as queen of Judea and installed Hyrcanus as high priest in 73 BCE. When she died in 67 BCE she named him her successor as ruler as well, but he and his younger brother Aristobulus II soon began fighting over the throne. Hyrcanus was supported by the Pharisees, especially later in his tenure, although his father had had numerous conflicts with them.

Hyrcanus had scarcely reigned three months when Aristobulus rebelled. Near Jericho many of Hyrcanus's soldiers defected, and he agreed to give up the throne and the high priesthood while keeping the revenues of the office. Antipater the Idumaean then convinced him that Aristobulus planned his death, and he took refuge with Aretas III, king of the Nabataeans, whom Antipater had bribed with the promise of returning Arabian towns taken by the Hasmoneans. A Nabataean army of 50,000 besieged Aristobulus in the Temple for several months.

Both brothers appealed to Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, the deputy of Pompey, who ruled for Aristobulus after a gift of 400 talents. When Pompey reached Syria in 63 BCE he favoured Hyrcanus, judging the elder, weaker brother a more reliable ally of the Roman Republic. The Romans captured Jerusalem by force, badly damaging the city and the Temple, and took Aristobulus to Rome as a prisoner. Hyrcanus was restored as high priest but not as king. In 47 BCE Julius Caesar appointed him ethnarch, but Hyrcanus yielded to Antipater in everything.

In 40 BCE Aristobulus's son Antigonus II Mattathias allied himself with the Parthians and was proclaimed king and high priest. Hyrcanus was seized and his ears mutilated, which according to Josephus Antigonus did by biting them off, to make him permanently ineligible for the priesthood. The Parthians took him to Babylonia, where he lived for four years among the Babylonian Jews, who paid him every mark of respect. In 36 BCE Herod the Great invited him back to Jerusalem. In 30 BCE Herod charged him with plotting with the Nabataeans and put him to death; Josephus states that he was 80 years old.
hyspaosines: Hyspaosines was of Iranian descent, and his name is a Hellenized form of a Persian or Bactrian name, possibly from the Old Iranian vispa-čanah, one who appreciates all things. His father, Sagdodonacus, seems to have been of Bactrian origin and served the frataraka, the local dynasts of Persis, who ruled independently of the Seleucids for three decades and briefly held Characene. The Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes restored Greek rule over Persis and Characene and made his general Noumenios governor of Characene.

Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great as a port for Babylon, had never prospered and was destroyed by floods in the mid 3rd century BCE. Rebuilt under Antiochus IV and named Antiochia, it was fully restored by 166/5 BCE, and Hyspaosines was appointed its governor, or eparch. The city flourished until Antiochus IV died of disease in 163 BCE. As Seleucid power weakened and neighbours such as Elymais broke away, Hyspaosines stayed loyal, perhaps to protect the profitable trade between Antiochia and Seleucia.

The Parthian king Mithridates I conquered Media and Atropatene in 148/7 BCE and held Babylonia by 141 BCE, events recorded in the Babylonian astronomical Diaries, and the threat drove Hyspaosines to declare independence. When his son and successor Phraates II died suddenly in 127 BCE fighting nomads in the east, Hyspaosines seized Babylon, where records call him king (šarru), until the Parthian general Timarchus retook it at the start of November.

His troops went on plundering the Babylonian region as late as 126 BCE, but in 124 BCE he accepted Parthian suzerainty and ruled Characene as a vassal. He wrote to the Parthian general of Babylonia about Mithridates II's defeat of Elymais and returned the wooden throne of Arsaces as a gift to the god Bel. The Diaries record that he fell ill on 3 June 124 BCE and died on 11 June; the Roman writer Lucian gives his age as 85. His young son Apodakos, by Queen Thalassia, succeeded him, and the Parthian commander Sindates was made governor of Characene.
hyuga-province: Hyūga Province lay in south-eastern Kyushu and corresponded to modern Miyazaki Prefecture. It bordered Ōsumi to the south, Higo to the west and Bungo to the north. Its short names were Kōshū and Nisshū. It belonged to the Saikaidō circuit and was ranked as a middle country in importance and a far country in distance from the capital. Its provincial capital stood in Koyu District, probably at the Terasaki ruins in the present city of Saito, though that identification is uncertain. The kokubun-ji was also at Saito, and the ichinomiya, the Tsuno Shrine, is at Tsuno.

Paleolithic ruins and Jōmon red pottery made from cinnabar have been found in the area. The Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki place many stories of the age of the gods in Hyūga, including the descent of kami on the peak of Takachiho, and have Emperor Jimmu set out from Hyūga on the expedition that led to Yamato.

Burial mounds like those of the Kinai region appear from the 4th century, among them the Saitobaru Kofun Cluster. The Kumaso people were subjugated either by Yamato Takeru or by his father Emperor Keikō. The province was set up under the Ritsuryō system, first including what became Satsuma and Ōsumi, which were separated in 702 and 713. The Hayato rebelled four times between the end of the 7th century and the early 8th, culminating in the Hayato rebellion of 720-721, a sign that Yamato rule was still tenuous.

In 1185 Tadahisa Koremune was made jitō of the Shimazu estate and took the name Shimazu, and his clan ruled southern Kyushu for 800 years. In the Nanboku-chō period the province broke into semi-independent estates and became a battleground between the Ōtomo clan of Bungo, the Shimazu in the south and the Itō clan, who ruled from Obi. In 1587, after Hideyoshi's conquest of Kyūshū, the Shimazu surrendered and Hyūga was divided among lords who had distinguished themselves under Hideyoshi. In the Edo period no single daimyō dominated it: it was split between lands governed directly by the Tokugawa shogunate and a few small domains, and the Satsuma and Hitoyoshi domains held scattered lands.

After the Meiji restoration the area became Mimisu Prefecture, north of the Ōyodo River, and Miyakonojō Prefecture in December 1871. They merged as Miyazaki Prefecture on 15 January 1873. It was merged with Kagoshima Prefecture on 21 August 1876 and re-established on 9 May 1883, minus some border areas that stayed with Kagoshima.
hywel-dda: Hywel was born in the late 9th century, son of King Cadell ap Rhodri of Seisyllwg and a member of the Dinefwr branch of the dynasty of Rhodri Mawr. Rhodri had become steward of Seisyllwg after the last king in the traditional line, Gwgon, drowned in 872, and he installed his son Cadell there as a subject king. When Cadell died, around 909, his lands seem to have been divided between Hywel and his brother Clydog. Hywel was reputed to have married Elen ferch Llywarch, supposed heiress of Dyfed, a link later used to justify his family's rule there.

Hywel and Clydog seem to have ruled together and jointly submitted to Edward the Elder of England in 918. Clydog died in 920 and Hywel became sole king of Seisyllwg. He soon joined it with Dyfed into a single realm, Deheubarth. In 928 he made a pilgrimage to Rome, the first Welsh prince known to have made the journey and returned. He then forged close relations with Æthelstan of England, whose aim was to secure the submission of all the kings of Britain. Hywel embraced submission and used it to his advantage, and in 934 supported Æthelstan's invasion of Scotland. A single coin in his name, struck at Chester around 946, is known.

In 942 his cousin Idwal Foel of Gwynedd took up arms against the English king Edmund and was killed in battle with his brother Elisedd. Hywel sent Idwal's sons Iago and Ieuaf into exile and made himself ruler of Gwynedd, and probably of Powys, which was under its authority. He then ruled nearly all of Wales except Morgannwg and Gwent, and the Annales Cambriæ and Annals of Ulster call him King of the Britons.

Hywel died around 950, and his kingdom soon split. Iago and Ieuaf took back Gwynedd, and Deheubarth and Powys passed to his sons. His name is linked above all with the codification of Welsh law. The prologues to the Laws of Hywel Dda say that he gathered lawyers and priests from every commote at Whitland, but none of the law manuscripts dates from his time, and the meeting seems highly unlikely to have taken place. The prologues aimed to stress the royal and Christian origins of the laws.

Those laws remained in force until the English conquest of 1283 replaced them in criminal cases, and survived in civil law until the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 to 1542. The Senedd building Tŷ Hywel is named after him.
